t.till@51.8,6.2:
The Lower Rhine around Kalkar and Kleve is wide, flat country: green polders, willows along drainage ditches, brick farmhouses and church spires visible for miles. Till is a small village here, part of Bedburg-Hau, just off the Rhine embankments between Kalkar and Kleve, with Emmerich across the river. It lies close to the line of the Roman frontier, the Lower German Limes, which followed the Rhine to the North Sea.

The Romans built a chain of forts and watchposts along the Rhine, and traces of them have been found all along this stretch. The frontier is now part of the UNESCO Frontiers of the Roman Empire site, but there is little to see above ground here; the story is mostly told in museums, such as the Archaeological Park at Xanten, about twenty-five kilometres upstream, where a Roman town has been partly reconstructed.

Nearby, the Schloss Moyland, a moated castle rebuilt in neo-Gothic style, houses a museum of modern art with a large collection of works by Joseph Beuys, who grew up in Kleve. Kalkar has a lovely medieval market square and a church famous for its carved wooden altars. It is also known for the Wunderland Kalkar, an amusement park built in the shell of a nuclear power plant that never went into operation, which is about as odd as tourism gets.

The riding here is flat and relaxed. The roads along the dykes and through the villages are narrow, with lots of farm traffic and cyclists, and they suit a gentle pace. Wind is the main hazard, as there is nothing to stop it. For more interesting riding, cross the Rhine over the long suspension bridge at Emmerich and head into the hills of the Reichswald forest or across the border into the Netherlands. The light here, with big skies and long horizons, has drawn painters for centuries.

Kalkar, about six kilometres away, and Kleve have fuel and everything else. Local food leans toward hearty fare, with asparagus in spring a particular treat; the sandy soils of the Lower Rhine grow excellent white asparagus. Autumn brings huge flocks of wild geese that spend the winter in the meadows along the river.
t.iversheim@50.6,6.8:
Iversheim is a village in the valley of the Erft, at the northern edge of the Eifel, just downstream from the old spa town of Bad Münstereifel. It is known for one thing: a Roman lime-burning works, one of the best preserved in Europe. The Romans built a series of kilns here to burn limestone from the surrounding hills into quicklime, which was used to make mortar for the forts, towns and roads of the province of Lower Germany. The kilns were worked by detachments of soldiers from the Rhine legions, as inscriptions found on the site show.

The kilns, about six of them in a row, have been excavated and are protected by a building where you can see the stone ovens and learn how they worked. The site is part of the UNESCO Frontiers of the Roman Empire, Lower German Limes, because it served the frontier army. It is a small, specialist site, open in the warmer months, but it gives a real sense of the industrial scale of the Roman military.

Bad Münstereifel, about four kilometres away, is a lovely medieval town enclosed by walls, with half-timbered houses along the river, a Romanesque church and a castle. It has become known for its outlet shopping, which fills some of the old buildings. Nearby, the Effelsberg radio telescope, one of the largest fully steerable radio telescopes in the world, sits in a valley in the hills.

The riding in the Eifel is excellent. The roads through the hills and valleys around Bad Münstereifel, toward Blankenheim, the Ahr valley and the Nürburgring, are twisty and scenic, through forest and farmland. The Nürburgring, about forty kilometres to the south, is a mecca for motorcyclists and car enthusiasts, and the roads around it are popular, so expect a lot of bikes at weekends and police checks. Weather in the Eifel can change quickly, with rain and fog common, even in summer.

Bad Münstereifel and Euskirchen have fuel and food. Local food is hearty: Eifel ham, potato pancakes and game. Spring and autumn are the best seasons for riding.
t.tiel inundation canal@51.9,5.4:
Tiel is a river town on the Waal, the main branch of the Rhine in the Netherlands, in the middle of the Betuwe, a region of orchards, dykes and meadows between the Waal and the Lower Rhine. Just outside the town, a wide, straight channel runs through the fields, crossed by bridges and lined by dykes. This is the Tiel inundation canal, built in the late nineteenth century as part of the New Dutch Waterline, the defensive system of controlled flooding that protected the heart of Holland, and it is now part of the UNESCO-listed Dutch Water Defence Lines.

The New Dutch Waterline relied on flooding a strip of land to a depth of about half a metre, too deep to march through, too shallow for boats. The Tiel canal was designed to let water from the Waal flow into the Betuwe, flooding the polders east of the main line and slowing an enemy advance. It was used only once in earnest, during the mobilisation of 1939 and 1940, and the German invasion in May 1940, with its paratroopers and aircraft, showed how obsolete the system had become.

Tiel itself is known as a fruit town. The Betuwe is the Netherlands' main fruit-growing region, with orchards of apples, pears and cherries, and in spring the blossom transforms the landscape. Tiel is the home of Flipje, a cartoon raspberry that served as the mascot of a local jam factory and is now the town's symbol. In September, the town hosts a fruit parade with floats decorated with fruit.

The riding in the Betuwe is flat and gentle. The roads along the dykes, on top of the embankments, offer views over the river and the orchards, with gentle curves following the river. They are narrow, and you will share them with cyclists and farm vehicles. The routes along the Waal and the Linge, a smaller river that winds through the region, are particularly pleasant. Wind is the main challenge.

Tiel, about two kilometres away, has fuel and all services. Local food includes fruit pastries and jams, and the river fish of the Waal. Spring, when the orchards blossom, usually in April, is the best time to visit.
t.fort werk iv@52.3,5.2:
The Gooi, the area east of Amsterdam around Bussum, Naarden and Hilversum, is one of the few places in the western Netherlands with hills, if you can call low sandy ridges hills. It is a region of heathland, woods and wealthy villages. On the edge of Bussum, close to the fortified town of Naarden, stands Fort Werk IV, a small fortification that was part of the New Dutch Waterline and the Defence Line of Amsterdam, and is now part of the UNESCO-listed Dutch Water Defence Lines.

The fort was built in the nineteenth century to guard the routes into Naarden and the waterline, and it is a typical example of the forts of the period, with earthworks, a moat and brick buildings. It has been restored and is now used as an event space. The surrounding area, with its waterways, is part of the defensive landscape that once could be flooded.

Naarden, next door, is one of the best-preserved fortified towns in Europe: a star-shaped town with double walls and moats, built in the seventeenth century. Its fortifications are intact and can be walked around, and the Fortress Museum inside the walls explains how they worked. The town is pretty, with old houses and a big church. The Czech philosopher and educator Comenius is buried in Naarden, in a mausoleum that is a place of pilgrimage for Czechs.

The riding in the Gooi is pleasant but gentle. The roads through the woods and heathland around Hilversum and Bussum are quiet and scenic, with gentle curves. The roads along the Vecht river, to the south-west, pass through a landscape of country houses and villages. Traffic around Amsterdam can be heavy, and the area is busy with cyclists. The Gooi is also the home of Dutch television, with the studios at Hilversum.

Bussum, about one kilometre away, and Naarden have fuel and all services. Local food includes the poffertjes, small pancakes, and the cakes and pastries of the Dutch bakeries. Spring, when the heath and woods turn green, and late summer, when the heather blooms purple, are the best times to visit.
t.watchtower wp 3 38@50.2,8.4:
The Taunus is a range of wooded hills north-west of Frankfurt, rising to 878 metres at the Großer Feldberg, and it has long been the city's playground, with forests, spa towns and winding roads. Through these hills ran the Upper Germanic Limes, the Roman frontier that stretched for over five hundred kilometres across Germany, and one of its watchtowers, numbered WP 3/38, stood near the village of Glashütten, close to Waldems and Königstein im Taunus.

The Limes in the Taunus was a line of palisades, ditches and banks, with watchtowers every few hundred metres and forts behind. The towers were made of wood at first, later of stone, and soldiers in them kept watch over the frontier and signalled to each other. Today, the line of the Limes can be followed through the forest as a low bank and ditch, with the foundations of towers marked or reconstructed in places. The Saalburg, a Roman fort near Bad Homburg, has been fully reconstructed and is one of the best places in Germany to understand the Limes. The whole frontier is part of the UNESCO Frontiers of the Roman Empire site.

Glashütten takes its name from the glassworks that operated here in the Middle Ages, using wood from the forest as fuel. Königstein, nearby, has an impressive castle ruin and is one of the most exclusive towns in the Frankfurt area, with grand villas.

The riding in the Taunus is excellent and popular. The roads that climb to the Großer Feldberg and wind through the forest around Glashütten, Königstein and Oberreifenberg are twisting, with good surfaces and great views over the Rhine-Main plain. On weekends, they are packed with motorcyclists, and the police are often present, with speed checks and sometimes noise restrictions; certain stretches have been closed to motorcycles on weekends in the past, so check the current rules. Weekdays are quieter.

Glashütten, about one kilometre away, has basic services, and Königstein and Idstein have fuel and food. The local apple wine, Ebbelwoi, is a Frankfurt speciality. Spring and autumn are the best seasons.
t.watchtowers wp 3 24 to 3 40watchtowers w:
On the western side of the Taunus, the hills are lower and the forest gives way more often to farmland, with villages in the folds of the valleys. Idstein, a small town with a remarkable old centre, sits on this side, with Waldems and Glashütten nearby. Through the woods above them ran the Roman frontier, and the stretch of watchtowers numbered WP 3/24 to 3/40 followed the ridges here, part of the Upper Germanic Limes and of the UNESCO Frontiers of the Roman Empire site.

The Limes in this area is best experienced on foot or by following the signposted Limes routes, which trace the line of the frontier through the forest. The bank and ditch are often clearly visible, running straight over hills and through valleys with the indifference to terrain that characterises Roman engineering. Here and there, the stone foundations of watchtowers survive, and a few have been rebuilt. Standing at one of these sites, in the quiet of the forest, it is easy to imagine a lonely Roman soldier keeping watch over the wild lands beyond.

Idstein, about five kilometres away, is a gem. Its old town is full of half-timbered houses, some of them richly carved, grouped around a market square, and the town's landmark is the Hexenturm, the witches' tower, a tall medieval keep with a pointed roof, part of the castle of the Counts of Nassau. The Unionskirche has a remarkable interior covered with Baroque paintings. The town is less well known than other half-timbered towns in Germany, which makes it all the more pleasant to visit.

The riding here is good. The roads through the western Taunus, toward the Weil valley, Bad Camberg and the Aar valley, wind through forest and farmland, with good bends and moderate traffic. They are quieter than the roads around the Feldberg, which are packed with bikes at weekends. The surfaces are excellent. The weather in the Taunus can be cooler and wetter than in the Rhine valley.

Waldems has basic services, and Idstein has fuel and all services. Local food includes the Handkäse mit Musik, a sour milk cheese marinated with onions, and apple wine. Spring and autumn, when the forest colours change, are the best times to ride here.
t.kottenforst sud heiderhof@50.7,7.1:
There is very little to see at first glance here, which is exactly what makes the place oddly moving. South of Bonn, in the edge of the Kottenforst near the Heiderhof quarter of Bad Godesberg and the town of Wachtberg, the forest floor hides the faint outlines of Roman practice camps. Legionaries stationed at the fortress of Bonna on the Rhine marched out here to train at the hard, boring work that won the empire its wars: digging ditches, throwing up earth ramparts and laying out a camp to the standard plan in a few hours. A handful of these training camps in the Kottenforst are part of the Lower German Limes, the Roman frontier along the Rhine recognised by UNESCO in 2021.

What survives are low banks and shallow ditches under the beech and oak, often only readable thanks to laser scanning from the air or an information board pointing them out. Walk slowly, look for straight lines where nature does not usually draw them, and you may catch the rounded corner of a rampart. It is quiet in the woods, with woodpeckers, jays and the smell of wet leaves, and only the distant hum of the city reminds you how close you are to a capital that once ran West Germany.

The riding is not epic, but it is useful and green. Heiderhof and Wachtberg sit on a gentle plateau between the Rhine valley and the Ahr, with small roads curling through fields, orchards and villages, and the Drachenfels and Siebengebirge rising across the river at Königswinter. Head south and you are quickly into the Ahr valley and the volcanic Eifel, where the real curves begin. Traffic around Bonn can be thick at rush hour, and the forest tracks themselves are for walkers and cyclists, so park at the edge and go in on foot. Spring and autumn are lovely, with mist in the trees on cool mornings.

Wachtberg and Bad Godesberg have fuel, bakeries and cafés in abundance, so practical worries are minimal. If you have time, combine the visit with the Roman collections in Bonn, where the LVR museum explains what the frontier looked like in its prime, or cross the Rhine by ferry at Bad Godesberg for a coffee in Königswinter and a look at the dragon rock the Nibelung saga made famous.
t.fort site and civil settlement of selige:
Seligenstadt is one of those Main valley towns where every era has left something on the table. The Romans came first: here the frontier of the Upper German-Raetian Limes ran along the river itself, and a fort with a civilian settlement around it guarded the Main crossing. The fort site lies under the old town, so you are walking over it rather than looking at it, but the logic of the place is obvious when you stand by the water. The river was the border, the road and the supply line all at once.

The town's real fame comes from a few centuries later. Einhard, the scholar and courtier who wrote the famous biography of Charlemagne, founded an abbey here in the ninth century and brought relics of the martyrs Marcellinus and Peter, and the great basilica still dominates the town. Einhard and his wife Imma are buried in it, and there is a romantic legend about Imma being Charlemagne's daughter who eloped with Einhard; nice story, poor evidence. The abbey buildings and their baroque gardens behind the church are worth an hour, and the half-timbered houses around the market square are as handsome as anything in Hesse.

Riders come for a stop more than for the roads, which are flat around here. The Main plain between Hanau and Aschaffenburg is busy, built-up and crossed by railway lines and motorways, so this is a place to pause on the way to better things. Those better things are close: south into the Odenwald, with its tight valleys and forest climbs, or east into the Spessart, whose quiet roads through deep beech woods are a favourite with bikers from the Rhine-Main area. A small car ferry crosses the Main here to the Bavarian bank, a pleasant two-minute ride when it runs.

Practically, Seligenstadt has everything: fuel at the edge of town, plenty of ice cream, cafés and beer gardens in summer, and benches by the river where you can watch barges push slowly upstream. The old town streets are cobbled and narrow, some pedestrianised, so park outside the centre and walk in. Summer weekends are busy with day-trippers from Frankfurt, so a weekday or an early evening visit is calmer, with the low sun turning the basilica's sandstone a warm red.
t.fagus factory in alfeld@52.0,9.8:
Stand across the railway tracks and look at the Fagus works, and you are looking at one of the buildings where modern architecture started. In 1911 the shoe-last maker Carl Benscheidt hired a young Walter Gropius and his partner Adolf Meyer to design a new factory in Alfeld, in the Leine valley of Lower Saxony. They gave it walls of glass that seem to wrap around the corners with no column to hold them, a radical trick at the time, and the result was so influential that it became a UNESCO site in 2011. The best part: it is still a working factory making shoe lasts, not a museum frozen in place.

Benscheidt placed his showpiece facing the railway on purpose, so every passenger on the line between Hanover and Göttingen would see it as an advertisement. There is a visitor centre and exhibition in one of the old buildings, covering Gropius, the Bauhaus that he went on to found, and the craft of carving lasts from beech wood, which is where the name Fagus, Latin for beech, comes from. Allow an hour and you will see the glass curtain wall with new eyes.

Alfeld itself is a modest market town of around nineteen thousand people with a half-timbered centre, a tall church and a historic Latin school, and it has fuel, supermarkets and the usual cafés. The surrounding Leinebergland is the real draw for riding: forested ridges such as the Sieben Berge, the Hils and the Sackwald rise around the valley, and the roads between villages like Delligsen and Freden twist through beech woods and over little saddles with views over fields of rapeseed and wheat. Surfaces are generally good, traffic light outside rush hour, and the weather typically mild but changeable, so pack a rain layer even in summer.

From here it is a short hop to the Weser Uplands and the Solling to the west, or east to the Harz, with Goslar and the Rammelsberg mine that one of the rides links in. Hildesheim, with its Romanesque churches, is about thirty kilometres north. If you only have a few minutes, stop where the road crosses the railway, look at those corners of glass with the afternoon sun behind them, and remember that a shoe-last factory in a small country town changed the way the whole world builds.
t.krefeld gellep@51.3,6.7:
Most people pass Krefeld-Gellep without a second thought, because the view is dominated by the harbour of Uerdingen, chemical works and Rhine barges. Yet this is one of the most important Roman and early medieval sites on the Lower Rhine. The Roman fort here was called Gelduba, and it belongs to the Lower German Limes, the frontier along the river that UNESCO recognised in 2021. Tacitus mentions Gelduba in his account of the Batavian revolt of 69 and 70 AD, when legions and rebels fought around the camp, and archaeologists have found traces of that violence in the ground.

The bigger story is the cemetery. Around the fort grew one of the largest burial grounds north of the Alps, used from Roman times into the Frankish period, with thousands of graves excavated over the last century. The most famous is the rich burial of a Frankish noble with a gilded helmet, part of a treasure trove now displayed in the museum at Burg Linn in Krefeld. That museum, set in a moated castle a few kilometres away, is the best place to see what came out of the earth here, and the castle itself makes a fine stop.

As for riding, be honest with yourself: this is the flat, built-up Lower Rhine, where the road is about getting from one place to the next. Dikes, poplar rows, harbour cranes and industrial chimneys line the river, and the light can be beautiful in a melancholy, Dutch-painting way, especially when evening haze settles over the water. Wind sweeps across the plain unhindered, so a gusty day can feel more tiring than the distance suggests. The Rhine ferries in this area, where they run, give the trip some charm and are worth seeking out instead of the bridges.

Krefeld, the old silk town, is less than ten kilometres away and has everything you need: fuel, bike shops, restaurants and a Saturday market. Uerdingen has bakeries and snack bars close to the harbour. If you combine Gellep with other Limes points along the river, such as the fort at Moers-Asberg on the opposite bank or Xanten further downstream, the Roman frontier starts to come together as a line rather than a scatter of names. Allow time; the region rewards curiosity more than speed.
t.gyo dong and songhyeon dong tumuli@35.5,:
The rounded grassy mounds rising behind Changnyeong look almost like natural hills until you notice how regular they are. These are the Gyo-dong and Songhyeon-dong tumuli, burial mounds of the rulers of Bihwa, one of the small kingdoms of the Gaya confederacy that flourished in the south of the Korean peninsula between roughly the first and sixth centuries before being absorbed by Silla. In 2023 they became part of a UNESCO listing that brings together seven Gaya tomb clusters, and they are among the most atmospheric of the group.

Gaya is the forgotten middle child of early Korean history, squeezed between the better-known kingdoms of Silla, Baekje and Goguryeo. Its people were famous for ironworking and traded iron across the sea to Japan, and the tombs have yielded gilt-bronze crowns, pottery, weapons and, in one case, evidence of human sacrifice. A small museum near the mounds explains the finds, and paths wind between the tumuli on the hillside with views over the town and the plain. Early evening is lovely here, when the light turns the grass golden and local families come up for a walk.

Changnyeong is a county town of tens of thousands, with fuel, convenience stores and many simple restaurants, so it is an easy stop. The riding nearby is better than you might expect: Hwawangsan, the mountain just east of town, has a winding road partway up and is famous in autumn for vast fields of silver grass on its summit plateau, while the roads along the Nakdong River to the west are flat, quiet and green. Korean country roads are generally well surfaced but busy with trucks near towns, and speed cameras are everywhere, announced with signs; take them seriously. Note too that motorcycles are not permitted on Korean expressways, so plan on national roads.

Do not leave the area without visiting Upo Wetland, about fifteen minutes northwest, the largest inland wetland in South Korea, where herons, egrets and migrating geese gather among reeds and willows and mist lies over the water at dawn. Spring brings cherry blossoms to the town, summer is hot and humid with monsoon rain in July, and autumn is the most comfortable season, with clear skies, red maples and those silver grass slopes waving in the wind.
t.remagen@50.6,7.2:
On 7 March 1945, soldiers of the US 9th Armored Division reached Remagen and found the Ludendorff railway bridge across the Rhine still standing, despite German attempts to blow it. They rushed across, and for the first time the Allies had a foothold on the far bank of the great river. Ten days later the damaged bridge collapsed, but by then pontoons had been built and the war in the west had entered its last chapter. What remains today are the black stone towers on both banks, and those on the Remagen side house a small peace museum telling the story with honesty and without glorification.

Remagen had a long past before that. The Romans built a fort called Rigomagus here, and it is part of the Lower German Limes UNESCO site; traces turn up under the town centre, and a Roman museum shows what was found. On the hill above the town stands the neo-Gothic Apollinaris church, with its spires visible from far up and down the river, and the Arp Museum at the old Rolandseck railway station combines the art of Hans Arp with a striking modern building by Richard Meier.

For riders, Remagen is a crossroads. The B9 along the left bank of the Rhine and the B42 on the right bank are scenic but often busy, especially with trucks and weekend traffic, and the Rhine valley has a long running debate about motorcycle noise; behave, keep the revs reasonable through villages, and you will be welcome. The real pleasure lies a few kilometres away: the Ahr valley with its vineyards and tight bends, the volcanic Eifel to the west and the Westerwald heights across the river. A small ferry runs from Remagen across to Linz am Rhein and Erpel, a pleasant way to cross with a view.

Remagen has around sixteen thousand people, fuel, cafés and an ice cream shop on the riverside promenade, where you can sit and watch the barges and passenger boats glide past the bridge towers. Erpel, directly opposite, sits under the Erpeler Ley, a basalt cliff you can climb for a fine view of the river and the bridge site. Spring and autumn are especially good, with the light softer and the valley less crowded.
t.watchtowers wp 1 11 to 1 20 including th:
Here is where the Upper German-Raetian Limes, the longest stretch of Roman frontier in Europe, begins. The Romans started the line at the Rhine near Rheinbrohl and ran it up over the hills of the Westerwald, then on through the Taunus and beyond for more than five hundred kilometres to the Danube. The section with watchtowers numbered WP 1/11 to 1/20 follows the first climb away from the river through the forests above Rheinbrohl, Hammerstein and Niederbreitbach. Most of the towers survive only as low mounds of stone in the woods, but the course of the frontier ditch and rampart can often be traced on foot, and there are information boards and a few reconstructions along the way.

In Rheinbrohl, the RömerWelt museum makes an excellent introduction: it explains how the frontier worked, how soldiers lived and what the watchtowers looked like, with hands-on displays and a reconstructed tower. It is a good place to start if the forest bumps are going to mean anything.

Now the riding, because this area is a small paradise for it. The Wied valley, which cuts through the hills just behind the Limes line, has a road along the river that is a long-time favourite with bikers, winding through forest, past mills and old villages, with plenty of corners and changing gradients. The roads climbing from the Rhine at Bad Hönningen and Rheinbrohl up onto the plateau are steep and twisty, with views back over the river. Weekend traffic includes many other riders, and the area has had noise and speed complaints, so expect speed checks and ride with respect. In autumn, the forests turn gold and red, but the roads can be wet and leafy.

Bad Hönningen, about six kilometres away, is the nearest town of over five thousand people and has fuel, shops and cafés, as well as thermal baths if your body needs some care after a long day. Niederbreitbach and other villages in the Wied valley have inns serving hearty local food, and the Rhine promenades offer a pleasant place for an ice cream and a view of the passing ships.
t.watchtower wp 2 31@50.2,7.9:
Holzhausen an der Haide is a small village on the high ground of the western Taunus, between the Rhine and the Lahn, and it has one of the better-preserved Roman fort sites along the Limes. The stone walls of Kastell Holzhausen still stand to a modest height in the fields just outside the village, outlining the fort's rectangle with its rounded corners and gates. Watchtower WP 2/31 belongs to the chain of towers that linked forts like this one along the frontier, and in this open landscape you can easily imagine the signals passing from hill to hill.

The area around Holzhausen and Nastätten is known as the Blaues Ländchen, the little blue country, supposedly because of the blue flax flowers that once covered the fields. It is a rolling upland of farmland and forest, crossed by quiet roads, with distant views to the Hunsrück and Westerwald, and on a clear day the sky feels enormous.

The main road through here, the B260, is known as the Bäderstraße, the spa road, linking Bad Ems with Bad Schwalbach and Wiesbaden. It is a favourite with bikers for its long, flowing curves through forest and over hills, with a few tighter sections dropping into valleys. The surface is generally good, but there are speed limits and occasional controls, and weekend traffic can be heavy with motorcycles. The smaller roads leading down to the Rhine at St. Goarshausen and the Loreley rock, or to the Lahn valley at Nassau, are steep and twisty, with spectacular views. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with less traffic and fresh air.

Nastätten, about four kilometres away, has fuel, a supermarket, bakeries and a few restaurants. For a more substantial break, ride down to the Rhine, where the towns of St. Goar, St. Goarshausen and Kaub have riverside terraces with views of castles and passing ships. Bad Schwalbach, about fourteen kilometres away, is an old spa town with elegant buildings and parks, and its mineral springs are known for their iron content. Local specialities include Riesling wine from the Rhine slopes and hearty dishes like Handkäs mit Musik, a tangy cheese served with onions and vinegar.
t.donam seown@36.2,127.2:
Donam Seowon is a Confucian academy in the countryside near Nonsan, in South Chungcheong province, and it is one of nine seowon that UNESCO listed together in 2019. Seowon were private academies founded by scholars of the Joseon dynasty, where young men studied the Confucian classics and honoured the memory of great teachers through rituals. Donam was founded in the early seventeenth century to commemorate Kim Jang-saeng, a renowned scholar of rites, and his students, and it played an important role in the intellectual life of the period.

The academy consists of a group of wooden buildings with tiled roofs set on terraces in a quiet valley, with a lecture hall, dormitories and a shrine at the top of the site. The architecture is simple and elegant, designed to create an atmosphere of contemplation and study, and the surrounding trees and hills add to the sense of peace. Ceremonies to honour the scholars are still held here twice a year, and the academy hosts cultural programmes and events.

The area around Nonsan is mostly agricultural, with rice paddies, greenhouses and orchards, and the roads are flat and straight, with little to excite a rider. But Gyeryongsan National Park, about twenty kilometres to the northeast, offers mountain roads, forests and temples, including Gapsa and Donghaksa, and the old Baekje capitals of Gongju and Buyeo, with their fortresses and royal tombs, are within an hour's ride. Korean roads are generally in good condition, but traffic can be heavy near cities, and speed cameras are common. Motorcycles cannot use expressways, so plan on using national and provincial roads.

Nonsan is a city of about forty thousand people, with fuel, convenience stores and restaurants. It is known for its strawberries, celebrated with a festival in spring, and for the Gwanchoksa temple, home to the Eunjin Mireuk, a huge stone Buddha statue from the Goryeo period that is one of the largest in Korea. The Korea Army Training Center is also in Nonsan, which is why you might see many young men with shaved heads and their families in the city. Local food includes hearty stews, grilled meats and fresh vegetables.
t.watchtower wp 3 23@50.2,8.3:
On the wooded ridges near Idstein, the Taunus Limes crossed some of its highest and most remote ground, and Watchtower WP 3/23 is one of the many sites along this stretch. The asterisk in the official label suggests a site whose exact location is uncertain or reconstructed from survey work, which is common along the frontier, where many towers survive only as faint mounds in the forest. Still, walking the Limes trail here, with the bank and ditch running through the beech woods, gives a real sense of the Roman border.

Idstein, three kilometres away, is one of the prettiest towns in the Taunus, with a perfectly preserved old town of half-timbered houses, including the elaborately carved Killingerhaus, which now houses the tourist office. The Hexenturm, the witches' tower, is a reminder of the darker times of witch trials in the seventeenth century, and the castle and the Unionskirche, with its baroque paintings, are also worth a look. The town has a lively square with cafés and restaurants, and it is a pleasant place to break a ride.

The Taunus is the playground of the Frankfurt area, and its roads are popular with motorcyclists, especially on weekends. From Idstein, routes lead through forests and valleys toward the Großer Feldberg, the highest peak in the Taunus at 879 metres, with its observation tower and views over the Rhine-Main area, and down to the Rhine at Eltville or Rüdesheim. Roads around the Feldberg have a long history of accidents and noise complaints, with speed limits and controls to match, so check for current restrictions and ride responsibly. The roads are well surfaced but can be crowded, and the forest shade keeps them damp after rain.

Idstein has fuel, shops and restaurants, and the nearby towns of Niedernhausen and Bad Camberg also offer services. The local food is typical of Hesse: Grüne Soße, a herb sauce served with potatoes and eggs, Handkäse and apple wine. If you are following the Limes, the Saalburg, a reconstructed Roman fort near Bad Homburg, is worth the detour, offering a vivid picture of life on the frontier.
t.works along the ij before diemerdam@52.3:
Just east of Amsterdam, where the city's suburbs give way to water and polders, a narrow strip of land runs out along the old shore of the IJ and the IJmeer toward Muiden. The Diemerdam is an old dike, and the works along the IJ before it are part of the Dutch Water Defence Lines, the system of forts, dikes, sluices and inundation fields that the Dutch built over centuries to defend their cities by flooding the land around them. The Defence Line of Amsterdam, a ring of forts around the capital, was listed by UNESCO in 1996 and later joined with the New Dutch Waterline into a single site.

The idea was ingenious: in case of attack, the defenders would open sluices and flood the polders to a depth of about forty centimetres, too deep for soldiers to wade through and too shallow for boats. Forts guarded the dikes, roads and railways that crossed the flooded areas. The Diemerdam had a fort and batteries, and you can still see earthworks and bunkers among the greenery. Out in the IJmeer, the island fortress of Pampus, reachable by boat from Muiden, is the most spectacular of the forts.

The area is a popular recreational zone, with paths for walking and cycling, beaches and wetlands full of birds. The views over the water, with sailboats and the distant skyline of Amsterdam, are beautiful, especially at sunset.

As a rider, you will find the roads flat, straight and busy, with motorways, bridges and urban traffic all around. The dike roads are narrow and often reserved for bicycles and local traffic, so park and walk if you want to explore the defences. Wind is the main challenge, blowing hard across the open water and polders. Muiden, about four kilometres away, is a charming small town with a medieval castle, the Muiderslot, where the poet P.C. Hooft entertained artists and scholars in the seventeenth century, and a harbour full of yachts.

Diemen has fuel, shops and services, and Muiden has cafés and restaurants by the harbour where you can enjoy fresh fish or apple pie with a view of the castle. For a longer ride, follow the dikes along the IJmeer and the Gooimeer toward Naarden, a star-shaped fortress town that is another highlight of the waterline.
t.moers asberg@51.4,6.7:
Asberg is a quiet district on the southern edge of Moers, on the left bank of the Lower Rhine, and beneath its houses and fields lies the Roman fort of Asciburgium, one of the earliest military bases on the Rhine frontier. It was founded around the time of the emperor Augustus or soon after, garrisoned by cavalry and auxiliary troops, and abandoned toward the end of the first century, when the Rhine shifted its course and moved away from the fort. The site is now part of the Lower German Limes UNESCO site, and although there is little to see above ground, information boards and outlines help you imagine the scene.

The Grafschafter Museum in Moers castle, a moated castle in the town park, has finds from Asciburgium and tells the story of the region from the Romans to the present. The castle itself is lovely, surrounded by water and gardens, and Moers has a pleasant old town with half-timbered houses and a lively square. The town is known for its jazz festival, held every year at Pentecost since the early 1970s, which attracts adventurous musicians from around the world.

The riding around Moers is typical of the Lower Rhine: flat, with straight roads through farmland, villages and industrial areas, and the occasional dike or windmill. The Ruhr area begins just across the Rhine in Duisburg, with its huge harbour, steelworks and motorways, and traffic can be heavy. Head northwest, however, and the landscape opens up, with quieter roads leading toward Kamp-Lintfort, home to the Cistercian monastery of Kamp with its terraced gardens, and on to Xanten, with its Roman archaeological park. The wind from the west can be strong, and the weather changes quickly.

Moers, about three and a half kilometres away, has fuel, shops, restaurants and cafés. Local food includes hearty dishes like Himmel und Erde, mashed potatoes with apple sauce and black pudding, and the local beer, Altbier, is a dark top-fermented brew popular along the Lower Rhine. For a break with a view, cross the river to Duisburg and visit the Landschaftspark, a former steelworks transformed into a park, with climbing walls, gardens and a lookout at the top of a blast furnace.
t.kleve keeken@51.8,6.1:
Here the Rhine stops being a German river. Just downstream of the village of Keeken, the great river crosses the border into the Netherlands, and a few kilometres further on it divides, with the Waal carrying most of the water west and the Pannerdens Canal leading to the Nederrijn and the IJssel. The coordinates of this point fall on the Dutch side near Tolkamer and Lobith, the place where the Dutch measure the Rhine's water level as it enters their country. In Roman times, this was the northern frontier of the empire, the Lower German Limes, and Keeken is one of the sites listed as part of the UNESCO frontier, with traces of Roman military installations along the old river course.

The landscape is the Lower Rhine at its most typical: wide flood meadows, dikes, poplars and willows, cows grazing on the floodplains, and the river busy with barges heading to and from Rotterdam. The sky is huge, and the light is soft and changing, beloved of Dutch painters. Birdwatchers come for the geese that winter here in huge numbers, and in the evening their calls fill the air.

Riding here is flat and peaceful, with narrow dike roads offering views over the river and the meadows, though some are closed to motor traffic or have weight restrictions. The wind can be strong, blowing across the open land. To the south, the hills of the Reichswald, a large forest near Kleve, offer a change of scenery, and the roads through it are pleasant. Traffic is light, apart from local farmers and cyclists, and the border is open, so you can wander back and forth between Germany and the Netherlands without noticing.

Kleve, about seven kilometres away, is the nearest larger town, with fuel, shops and restaurants. The Schwanenburg, the swan castle on a hill in the centre, is linked to the legend of Lohengrin, the swan knight, and the town has beautiful baroque gardens. Emmerich, across the river, has a long Rhine promenade, and Tolkamer and Lobith have riverside cafés where you can watch the ships go by. Local specialities include asparagus in spring and hearty Lower Rhine dishes.
t.fortlet lochmuhle@50.3,8.6:
The Lochmühle is a small fortlet on the Limes in the Taunus, near Wehrheim and the famous Saalburg, and it guarded a spot where the frontier crossed the valley of the Erlenbach stream. Fortlets like this were small outposts, housing a handful of soldiers who watched the border and controlled traffic, and they formed a link between the watchtowers and the larger forts. Its remains are modest, but the location, in a quiet valley surrounded by forest, has a peaceful charm. The name comes from a nearby mill, now a popular leisure park for families with play areas and farm animals.

The real star of this stretch of the Limes is the Saalburg, a few kilometres away, a Roman fort reconstructed in the early twentieth century at the wish of Kaiser Wilhelm II. It is the only Roman fort in Germany rebuilt on its original foundations, with walls, gates, barracks and a headquarters building, and it houses a museum with an impressive collection of finds. Whatever you think of the reconstruction, it gives a vivid idea of what a frontier fort looked like.

The Taunus is close to Frankfurt, and its roads are popular with motorcyclists, especially on weekends. The roads around Wehrheim, Usingen and the Hochtaunus offer winding routes through forests and valleys, with climbs toward the Großer Feldberg and views over the Rhine-Main plain. Some of the most popular roads have speed limits and frequent checks because of accidents and noise complaints, and on sunny weekends they can be crowded. Weekdays are better. The forest keeps the roads shaded and cool in summer, but also damp after rain.

Wehrheim, about two and a half kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants, and Bad Homburg, a few kilometres further, is an elegant spa town with a castle, a beautiful park and a casino. Friedrichsdorf, nearby, was founded by Huguenot refugees and is known for its rusks. Local food includes Grüne Soße, a herb sauce made from seven herbs, served with eggs and potatoes, and apple wine, the regional drink, best enjoyed in a garden tavern, though not before riding.
t.castles of augustusburg and falkenlust a:
Clemens August of Bavaria, prince-elector and archbishop of Cologne in the eighteenth century, loved two things above all: hunting with falcons and building in the latest style. At Brühl, just south of Cologne, he created two of the finest rococo buildings in Germany. Augustusburg Palace, his summer residence, has a staircase designed by Balthasar Neumann that is one of the masterpieces of the period, a whirl of marble, stucco and frescoes, and a formal French garden that stretches toward the forest. Falkenlust, a smaller hunting lodge at the end of a long avenue, was built for falconry, with a delightful interior decorated with tiles and lacquerwork. The two castles were listed by UNESCO in 1984.

Augustusburg was used by the West German government for state receptions for decades, when Bonn was the capital, and many world leaders have walked up Neumann's staircase. Guided tours of the interiors run regularly, and the gardens are free to explore.

Brühl is a town of about forty-five thousand people, and it is also home to Phantasialand, one of the biggest theme parks in Germany, which brings heavy traffic on summer weekends. The riding around Brühl is mostly flat and suburban, with busy roads between Cologne and Bonn, but the Ville, a low ridge to the west with forests and lakes created from old lignite mines, offers quieter roads and a pleasant landscape. Further south, the Eifel and the Ahr valley, less than an hour away, are a riders' paradise, with endless curves and the Nürburgring, the legendary race track, where on certain days anyone can ride a lap of the Nordschleife for a fee.

Brühl has fuel, shops, cafés and restaurants, and the old town, close to the palace, has a pleasant pedestrian zone. Cologne, about fifteen kilometres north, has everything, including its cathedral and the beer halls serving Kölsch, the light local beer, in small glasses that are refilled until you put a beer mat on top. Local dishes include Himmel un Ääd, potatoes and apples with black pudding, and Halve Hahn, which despite its name is a rye roll with cheese. The palace gardens are lovely in spring and early summer.
t.kanghwa dolmen sites@37.8,126.4:
Ganghwa Island lies in the mouth of the Han River, just north-west of Seoul and Incheon, and on a clear day you can look across a narrow channel of tidal water straight into North Korea. The town of Kaesong is barely twenty-five kilometres away. That closeness gives the island an edge, with watch posts and fences along parts of the shore, but its fame is much older. The Ganghwa dolmens, together with those at Gochang and Hwasun in the south, were listed by UNESCO in 2000, and Korea holds a remarkable share of all the dolmens known in the world.

The most famous is at Bugeun-ri, a huge table-shaped tomb of two upright slabs carrying a massive capstone, standing alone on a lawn like a piece of stage scenery. Built in the Bronze Age, these monuments were probably graves for important people, and how the stones were moved remains a satisfying puzzle to stand and think about. Dozens more lie scattered across the hillsides of the island, many of them half hidden in woods.

Ganghwa has played a starring role in Korean history more than once. During the Mongol invasions of the thirteenth century the Goryeo court moved its capital here, trusting the tidal currents to keep the horsemen out, and in the nineteenth century French and American warships fought small battles at the island's forts. On Manisan, the highest peak, there is an altar tied to the legendary founder of the Korean nation.

The riding is relaxed and rural. Bridges link the island to the mainland at Gimpo, and inside you will find quiet roads through rice paddies, low wooded hills and fishing harbours with mudflats stretching out at low tide. There are some pleasant climbs and bends along the coast, but this is not a racetrack, and farm vehicles and tourist traffic on weekends set the pace. One crucial point for visitors: motorcycles are not allowed on South Korean expressways, so plan your route from Seoul along ordinary national roads.

Ganghwa town, with around twenty-five thousand people, has fuel, markets and plenty of places to eat. Look for the island's famous ginseng, its purple turnips in autumn and its woven rush mats, and finish with a bowl of something hot at the market while the tide runs out.
t.bongjeongsa temple@36.7,128.7:
Tucked into the wooded slopes of Cheondeungsan, a modest mountain north-west of Andong in North Gyeongsang province, Bongjeongsa is a temple that wears its age quietly. Its main claim to fame is a small, plain hall called Geungnakjeon, believed to be the oldest surviving wooden building in Korea, dating back to the Goryeo dynasty. Repairs in the twentieth century turned up records suggesting the hall had been rebuilt in the thirteenth century, which makes it older than almost anything else made of timber in the country. Bongjeongsa is one of seven mountain monasteries inscribed by UNESCO in 2018 as Sansa, Buddhist Mountain Monasteries in Korea.

The temple feels lived in rather than preserved. Monks still practise here, and the courtyard is calm, with stone lanterns, old pine trees and the sound of wind chimes. A short walk up the slope leads to Yeongsanam, a small hermitage with a lovely garden and terraced buildings that has appeared in Korean films. When Queen Elizabeth II visited Korea in 1999, she came to Andong and this temple, and locals still mention it.

Andong is a city that takes its traditions seriously. It is known as a centre of Confucian learning, home to Hahoe Folk Village and the Dosan Seowon academy, both listed by UNESCO. Its food is famous too: salted mackerel, once carried inland from the coast, jjimdak, a braised chicken dish with glass noodles and chilli, and Andong soju, a strong distilled spirit.

The riding around Andong is varied and pleasant. Country roads wind through hills, orchards and rice paddies, and the big reservoir of Andong Lake has scenic roads along its shores. The final stretch to the temple is a short climb on a narrow road through forest, with a car park at the end. Remember that motorbikes are barred from Korean expressways, so national roads are your routes in. Spring blossom and autumn foliage are the most beautiful times, and autumn especially, when the maples blaze red around the temple roofs.

Andong, about eleven kilometres away, has fuel, shops, markets and countless restaurants. If you stop in town, try the mackerel at a market stall, or a bowl of heotjesabap, a mild rice dish once served to scholars, before riding up to the temple in the quieter hours of the afternoon.
t.elst grote kerk@51.9,5.8:
Elst is a commuter town in the Betuwe, the flat river island between the Rhine and the Waal, halfway between Arnhem and Nijmegen. At first glance there is nothing remarkable about its big brick church on the market square. The surprise lies underneath it. Excavations in the twentieth century found the remains of two Roman temples beneath the floor, built one after another on the same spot, dedicated to a local god adopted into the Roman world. The site belongs to the Frontiers of the Roman Empire, Lower German Limes, inscribed by UNESCO in 2021, and the foundations can be seen in the church cellar when it is open.

The Romans held the Rhine as their frontier for centuries, and the Betuwe was the land of the Batavians, a tribe famous as soldiers and horsemen who served in the Roman army, and who rose in revolt against Rome in the first century. Nijmegen, a few kilometres south, grew from a Roman settlement and claims to be the oldest city in the Netherlands.

The twentieth century left its mark too. In the autumn of 1944, after Operation Market Garden failed to take the bridge at Arnhem, the area between the rivers, nicknamed the Island by Allied soldiers, became a front line for months, and Elst was badly damaged in the fighting. The church tower was hit and rebuilt after the war.

The Betuwe is fruit country, with orchards of apples, pears and cherries stretching across the polders, and in April the blossom turns the landscape white and pink. That is the best time to ride here. The roads are flat and mostly straight, but the dikes along the Waal and the Nederrijn carry narrow lanes with gentle bends, views over the floodplains and the slow procession of barges on the river. Watch for cyclists, farm vehicles, and strong winds that sweep across the open polders. Dutch roads are generally excellent, but speed limits are low and enforced with cameras.

Elst has over twenty thousand inhabitants, so fuel, supermarkets and cafés are all close by. For a snack in true Dutch style, buy fresh fruit or apple juice from a farm stall in the orchards, or sit on the square with a coffee and a slice of apple pie.
t.alpen drupt@51.6,6.5:
On the flat farmland of the Lower Rhine, between Alpen and Rheinberg, there is little to catch the eye: fields of maize and potatoes, poplars along ditches, brick farmhouses and the occasional windmill. Yet this was once the edge of the Roman world. The Rhine formed the frontier of the empire, and along its banks the Romans built legionary fortresses, forts, watchtowers and temporary camps. Alpen-Drüpt is one of the sites included in the Frontiers of the Roman Empire, Lower German Limes, inscribed by UNESCO in 2021; like many on the list, it survives mainly below ground, known from aerial photographs and excavations rather than standing ruins.

For something you can actually walk around, ride a short distance north to Xanten. The Romans founded a major town there, Colonia Ulpia Traiana, and today its site is an archaeological park with reconstructed walls, a temple, an amphitheatre used for summer concerts, and a museum full of finds. Xanten is also linked to the legend of Siegfried, the dragon-slaying hero of the Nibelungenlied, who was said to come from here.

Rheinberg, a few kilometres away, is known for Underberg, a herbal digestif sold in tiny bottles wrapped in paper, still made in the town. Kamp-Lintfort has Kamp Abbey, the first Cistercian monastery in the German-speaking lands, founded in the twelfth century, with terraced gardens on a hill above the plain.

The riding is flat and relaxed. Country roads run between villages and farms, and the dykes along the Rhine offer lanes with views over the broad river, where long barges carry coal, containers and gravel between the Netherlands and the industrial Ruhr. The landscape is open, so wind can be strong, and fog is common in autumn and winter. Traffic is moderate, but tractors and cyclists are everywhere, and speed limits are strictly enforced in villages. Small ferries cross the Rhine at several points and make a nice change from bridges.

Alpen, about two kilometres away, has fuel, shops and cafés. For lunch, look for local asparagus in spring, served with ham, potatoes and hollandaise sauce, or a hearty plate of potato pancakes with apple sauce, and finish with a coffee overlooking the river.
t.tokhwa ri tombs no 1@39.2,125.5:
This is a place almost no one reading these words will be able to reach on two wheels, and it is better to say so plainly. Tokhwa-ri Tomb No. 1 lies in the countryside north of Pyongyang, in the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, among a group of burial mounds from the kingdom of Goguryeo. Independent travel in North Korea is not possible. Foreign visitors, when the country admits them at all, travel only on organised tours with official guides, follow fixed itineraries and are not allowed to drive or ride. Citizens of some countries, including the United States, are barred from travelling there by their own governments, and many others are strongly advised against it.

The tombs themselves are remarkable. Goguryeo was one of the Three Kingdoms of ancient Korea, a powerful state that at its height ruled much of the Korean peninsula and Manchuria. In the fifth century it moved its capital to Pyongyang, and its kings and nobles were buried in earth mounds covering stone chambers. Many of these chambers were painted with vivid murals: scenes of hunting, processions, daily life, dancers and musicians, along with guardian animals of the four directions and star maps on the ceilings. The Complex of Koguryo Tombs was listed by UNESCO in 2004, and a related group lies across the border in China, around the old capitals near the Yalu river.

The landscape around Pyongyang is a mix of low hills, rice paddies and villages, with the Taedong river running through the capital. Seasons are sharply marked: winters are long and bitterly cold, summers hot and humid with heavy monsoon rains, and spring and autumn are short but beautiful.

If you are interested in Goguryeo, there are alternatives. In South Korea, museums in Seoul display replicas of the murals and artefacts from the period, and in China, the Goguryeo sites around Ji'an in Jilin province can be visited more freely, with tombs, mountain fortresses and a famous stele. Those trips are possible with a vehicle, at least in principle, though riding a motorbike in China has its own hurdles.

There is no question of fuel stops or roadside cafés here. Think of this point as a window into a remarkable ancient culture, seen from a distance.
t.bunnik vechten marsdijk@52.1,5.2:
Two layers of Dutch defence history sit on top of each other just south-east of Utrecht. Around two thousand years ago, the Romans built a fort here called Fectio, at the point where a branch of the Rhine met the Vecht, with a harbour for the fleet that patrolled the river frontier. Its remains lie buried in the fields near Vechten and are part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire, Lower German Limes, a World Heritage site since 2021. Close by stands Fort bij Vechten, a nineteenth-century fortress of the New Dutch Waterline, a defensive system that could flood large areas of land to stop an invading army. That system is itself part of the UNESCO site of the Dutch Water Defence Lines. The fort now houses a museum explaining how the waterline worked, and how a country below sea level turned water into a weapon.

The idea was simple and clever: open sluices and flood the polders to a depth of around half a metre, too deep for soldiers to wade and too shallow for boats. Forts like this one guarded the dikes, roads and railways that crossed the flooded zone.

Utrecht, a few kilometres away, is a lively university city with a medieval centre, canals with wharves at water level and cellars turned into cafés, and the Dom tower, the tallest church tower in the Netherlands, which you can climb for a view over the whole province. The Kromme Rijn, a winding remnant of the old Rhine, flows east through meadows and villages, lined with willows.

The riding around Bunnik is flat and gentle, with country lanes along dikes and rivers, past farms, orchards and country houses. To the east, the Utrechtse Heuvelrug, a ridge of wooded hills left by the ice age, offers a little elevation, sandy heaths and roads through forests. Traffic around Utrecht is heavy, with motorways, cyclists and complex junctions, so give yourself time and patience.

Fuel and services are easy to find in Bunnik, Lunetten and Utrecht. Try a local speciality, the Utrecht sprits, a buttery biscuit, or stop for a coffee and a slice of apple pie in a village café, and enjoy the flat, wide horizon that defines the Dutch landscape.
t.fortsite and civil settlement of ober fl:
The Wetterau is a broad, fertile basin north of Frankfurt, a land of rich loess soils, wheat fields, orchards and old villages, and the Romans wanted it badly. Their frontier, the Upper Germanic-Raetian Limes, bulged out here to take in the whole basin, looping around it in a wide arc. At Ober-Florstadt stood a fort with a civilian settlement beside it, where soldiers' families, traders and craftsmen lived. Today little is visible, but the site is part of the World Heritage frontier, and information boards help to picture the scene.

The Wetterau has always been a crossroads. Friedberg, a few kilometres west, has a large castle and a medieval Jewish ritual bath, a deep shaft descending to the groundwater. Bad Nauheim, next door, is a spa town with Art Nouveau bathhouses, and it was here that Elvis Presley lived while serving with the American army in the late 1950s, stationed in Friedberg. Fans still come to see the house where he stayed.

To the east, the land rises towards the Vogelsberg, one of the largest volcanic massifs in Central Europe, a wide, rounded dome of basalt covered with forests and pastures. Its roads are popular with riders from the Rhine-Main area, with long climbs, plenty of bends and quiet villages, and the summit area of the Hoherodskopf has views across the region.

The riding in the Wetterau itself is gentle, with country roads through fields and villages, mostly flat or slightly rolling. Traffic can be heavy closer to Frankfurt, but quieter further north. The Vogelsberg offers more challenging roads, but some are restricted for motorbikes at weekends because of noise and accidents, so check local rules. Weather is moderate, with warm summers and cool, damp winters.

Florstadt, about a kilometre away, has fuel, shops and inns. The Wetterau is apple country, and the local drink is Apfelwein, cider served in a ribbed glass or poured from a stoneware jug called a Bembel. Try it with Handkäs mit Musik, a sour milk cheese marinated with onions, vinegar and oil, or a plate of Frankfurt green sauce with boiled eggs and potatoes, though with a ride ahead, a single glass of cider is wise.
t.haeinsa temple janggyeong panjeon@35.8,1:
High in the forested folds of Gayasan, in South Gyeongsang province, a temple keeps one of the great treasures of the Buddhist world. Haeinsa holds the Tripitaka Koreana, more than eighty thousand wooden printing blocks carved in the thirteenth century with the complete Buddhist scriptures, an act of devotion undertaken while the Mongols were invading Korea, in the hope that the Buddha's protection would save the country. The blocks are kept in the Janggyeong Panjeon, a pair of long, plain wooden halls built in the fifteenth century, and the halls are the real marvel. Their design uses natural ventilation, windows of different sizes on opposite walls, and a floor packed with charcoal, lime, clay and salt to regulate humidity and temperature, and they have protected the blocks for centuries without modern technology. The halls were listed by UNESCO in 1995.

Visitors can look through the slatted windows at the shelves of blocks but cannot enter the halls. The rest of the temple is lively, with monks, pilgrims and visitors, and the setting is beautiful, with wooded ridges and streams all around. Haeinsa offers temple stay programmes, where you can spend a night following the rhythm of monastic life, including the dawn ceremony with drums and bells.

The valley leading up to the temple, Hongnyu-dong, is famous for its autumn colours, when the maples along the stream turn fiery red, and the stream tumbles over rocks and pools. Gayasan National Park offers hiking trails to the rocky summit, with views across the mountains of southern Korea.

The riding to the temple is a pleasure, with winding roads through valleys and over hills, past villages, rice fields and orchards. The final approach climbs gently along the stream through the forest. Traffic is moderate, heavier on weekends and in autumn, when visitors flock to see the colours. Remember that South Korea bars motorcycles from its expressways, so plan your route along national and provincial roads. Spring and autumn are the best seasons; summer is hot and humid, with heavy rain during the monsoon.

Fuel is available in the small towns of Hapcheon county, and the nearest larger town listed is Waegwan, about thirty-four kilometres away. Restaurants near the temple serve sanchae bibimbap, rice with mountain vegetables, a fitting meal after a visit.
t.watchtowers wp 2 5 to 2 6@50.3,7.7:
WP 2/5 and 2/6 sound like spare parts, but they are the numbers archaeologists gave to two watchtower positions on the Upper Germanic-Raetian Limes, the fortified frontier Rome drew across southern Germany. Here, in the hills above the Lahn near Bad Ems, the line ran up from the Rhine and over the high ground, and every few hundred metres a tower stood with a view to the next. Today most of what survives are low mounds, traces of the bank and ditch, and in some places a reconstructed tower to give you scale. The whole frontier became part of the UNESCO Frontiers of the Roman Empire in 2005.

It helps to imagine the tower crews: a handful of auxiliary soldiers, signals by fire or horn, patrols along the palisade, and the big forts behind them for when real trouble came. The fort at Niederbieber, near Neuwied, was one of those bases. On the ground today, it is mostly forest, meadow and the sound of buzzards, which makes the scale of the old frontier all the more remarkable.

The riding is where this place earns its place on a route. The Lahn valley below is a deep, wooded cut through the slate of the Rhenish Massif, and the road along it follows every meander, with the railway and the river for company. Climb out toward Dachsenhausen or Fachbach and you get tighter, steeper bends through beech woods and onto open plateau farmland with long views. Watch for wet leaves in autumn, forestry mud on the smaller lanes and plenty of other bikers on sunny weekends, because this corner between the Rhine, Lahn and Taunus is a regional favourite. Spring and early autumn, with mist burning off the valley, are the best.

Bad Ems, five kilometres away, is the natural stop. It is an old spa town with grand nineteenth-century bathhouses along the river, and it was here in 1870 that King Wilhelm of Prussia sent the telegram Bismarck edited into the Ems Dispatch, the spark for the Franco-Prussian War. The town has fuel, cafés and bakeries, and a riverside promenade where you can sit with a coffee and watch the Lahn slide past. Koblenz and the Rhine are only a short ride further if you need a bigger town.
t.watchtower wp 1 73@50.4,7.7:
The Roman frontier in Germany starts at the Rhine near Rheinbrohl and climbs into the hills of the Westerwald, and Watchtower WP 1/73, near Hillscheid, belongs to that first stretch. The numbers tell you where you are: section one, tower seventy-three. All that survives is a low mound in the woods, but in the second and third centuries it was a stone tower with a view over the frontier line and, behind it, the palisade and ditch that ran across the landscape. The Upper Germanic-Raetian Limes has been part of the UNESCO Frontiers of the Roman Empire since 2005, and this is where it all begins.

The area around Höhr-Grenzhausen and Hillscheid is known as the Kannenbäckerland, the land of the jug bakers, because of its rich deposits of clay and its long tradition of making salt-glazed stoneware. The typical grey jugs with cobalt-blue decoration have been produced here for centuries, and you can visit workshops and a ceramics museum. Further east, Montabaur has a striking yellow castle on a hill, and the Westerwald plateau stretches away in a patchwork of forests, meadows and small villages.

The riding is enjoyable, especially if you like rolling hills and forests. The roads between Koblenz and the Westerwald climb steeply out of the Rhine valley, with tight bends and great views back over the river. Up on the plateau, the roads become more open, with long curves through farmland and woods. Weather in the Westerwald can be harsh, with rain, fog and even snow in winter, so check the forecast. Traffic is moderate, but busier near Koblenz and the motorway junctions.

Höhr-Grenzhausen, five kilometres away, has fuel, shops and cafés, and Koblenz, a city of over a hundred thousand at the confluence of the Rhine and Moselle, has everything else. Look for a local inn serving Westerwald dishes such as Döppekuchen, a hearty potato cake with bacon, or a simple schnitzel with fries. If you are interested in pottery, pick up a small stoneware jug as a souvenir; it travels well in a tank bag if you wrap it carefully.
t.zollverein coal mine industrial complex:
The headframe of Shaft XII at Zollverein, with its red steel lattice and double wheels, is the Eiffel Tower of the Ruhr, and it is easy to see why. Designed by the architects Fritz Schupp and Martin Kremmer and opened in 1932, the shaft and its surrounding buildings were built in a clean, functional style influenced by the Bauhaus, and it was hailed as the most beautiful coal mine in the world. At its peak, Zollverein was one of the largest and most productive mines in Europe, and the adjacent coking plant processed coal into coke for the steel industry. The mine closed in 1986, the coking plant in 1993, and UNESCO listed the complex in 2001.

Today, Zollverein is a cultural hub. The former coal-washing plant houses the Ruhr Museum, which tells the story of the region from prehistory to the present day, and the old boiler house is home to the Red Dot Design Museum. The vast site has walking trails, an ice rink in winter, a swimming pool made from shipping containers in summer and events throughout the year. At night, the buildings are lit up in red and blue, a spectacular sight.

The Ruhr was once the industrial heartland of Germany, and it has reinvented itself as a region of culture, parks and lakes. Riding here is mostly urban: busy roads, traffic lights, roundabouts and motorways. The Autobahns are crowded, especially at rush hour, and the cities blend into one another without clear boundaries. For more enjoyable riding, head south to the Ruhr valley, where the river winds through green hills, with the Baldeneysee lake and villages, or north into the Münsterland, with its flat farmland and moated castles.

Essen and Gelsenkirchen, both a few kilometres away, are big cities with all services. The local food is hearty and unpretentious: currywurst with fries, the Ruhr's favourite snack, or Pfefferpotthast, a peppery beef stew. A cold Pils from a local brewery is the classic drink. If you are a football fan, Gelsenkirchen's Schalke stadium is close by, and the derby with Borussia Dortmund is one of the fiercest in Germany.
t.jangneung cluster@37.6,126.7:
The Joseon dynasty ruled Korea for over five hundred years, and its kings and queens were buried in carefully chosen spots around the capital, in tombs designed according to Confucian ritual and the principles of geomancy, with a hill behind, water in front and mountains framing the view. In 2009, forty of these tombs were listed by UNESCO as the Royal Tombs of the Joseon Dynasty. Jangneung, in Gimpo, just west of Seoul, is the tomb of Wonjong, the father of King Injo, who was elevated to royal rank after his death. It is a quiet, wooded place, with a grassy burial mound, stone statues of officials and animals, and a T-shaped shrine where ancestral rites were held.

The tombs are popular with locals for walks, and the forests around them, protected for centuries, are rich in old trees and birdlife. The approach to each tomb follows a stone path that splits into two: the slightly raised one on the left was for the spirits, the lower one on the right for the king. Visitors are asked to walk on the lower path, out of respect.

Gimpo lies at the mouth of the Han River, where it meets the Yellow Sea, and the area is a mix of new apartment blocks, farmland and wetlands. To the north, just across the estuary, lies North Korea, and the riverbanks are lined with fences and guard posts. The island of Ganghwa, a short ride west, has a rich history, with fortresses, dolmens and temples, and is a popular day trip from Seoul.

Riding in Korea comes with one big rule: motorcycles are banned from the expressways, so you will use the national and local roads, which can be busy and full of traffic lights. Around Gimpo and Seoul, traffic is heavy, but the roads to Ganghwa and along the coast are quieter, with views of mudflats and fishing villages. Gimpo has fuel, convenience stores and restaurants everywhere. Try a bowl of naengmyeon, cold buckwheat noodles, or grilled eel, a local favourite along the Han estuary.
t.blegny mine@50.7,5.7:
Blegny-Mine is one of the few places in Europe where you can still go down a real coal mine in the lift cage, with former miners as your guides. The mine, in the Pays de Herve northeast of Liège, closed in 1980, and it was soon turned into a museum, with guided tours that take you down to galleries tens of metres underground, where you can see the machinery, the narrow seams and the conditions in which miners worked. In 2012, it was listed by UNESCO as one of the four Major Mining Sites of Wallonia, along with Grand-Hornu, Bois-du-Luc and Bois du Cazier. It is a powerful reminder of how coal built the industrial wealth of Belgium, and at what cost.

The Pays de Herve is a surprisingly green and pastoral area, with rolling hills, hedges, orchards and pastures dotted with farms. It is famous for its cheese, Herve, a soft, pungent cheese with a reddish rind, and for sirop de Liège, a thick, sticky spread made from apples and pears, eaten on bread or with cheese. The landscape is a patchwork of small fields bordered by hedges, a rare example of bocage in Belgium.

The riding is pleasant, with narrow, winding roads through the hills, past farms and villages, with views over the countryside. Traffic is moderate, but watch for tractors, cows and mud on the roads. To the north, the Meuse valley at Visé has some nice curves along the river, and to the east, the Voer region, a Flemish enclave between Wallonia and the Netherlands, has quiet roads and great views. The weather is changeable, with rain possible at any time.

Blegny, with nearly thirteen thousand inhabitants, has fuel, shops and restaurants, and the mine has a café where you can get a drink and a snack. Liège, about fifteen kilometres away, is a lively city with plenty of food and accommodation. Try boulets à la liégeoise, meatballs in a sweet and sour sauce made with sirop de Liège, with fries, or a Liège waffle, with crunchy pearl sugar. A local beer, such as Jupiler, brewed in Liège, is the classic drink, once the riding is done.
t.petroglyphs along the bangucheon stream@:
On a cliff face above a quiet stream in the hills west of Ulsan, prehistoric people carved hundreds of images into the rock: whales, turtles, deer, tigers, boats full of men, hunters with spears and nets. The whales are the most striking, with species that can still be identified, such as right whales and humpbacks, and scenes that seem to show whaling from boats, making the Bangudae petroglyphs one of the oldest records of whaling anywhere. A little upstream, the Cheonjeon-ri petroglyphs, with geometric patterns, animals and later inscriptions from the Silla period, add another layer. In 2025, the Petroglyphs along the Bangucheon Stream were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List.

There is a complication. A dam built downstream in the 1960s raises the water level for part of the year, submerging the Bangudae carvings and causing erosion, and the debate over how to protect them has gone on for decades. You view the main panel from an observation point across the stream, so bring binoculars. A museum nearby displays replicas and explains the carvings.

Ulsan is now a huge industrial city, home to shipyards, car factories and petrochemical plants, but it also has a whaling past of its own. At Jangsaengpo, a former whaling village on the coast, a whale museum tells the story. The countryside west of the city is green and hilly, with rice paddies, orchards and forests, and Gyeongju, the ancient capital of the Silla kingdom, with its royal tombs, temples and museums, is a short ride north.

Riding in Korea means staying off the expressways, which are closed to motorcycles, and using the national and local roads, which are busy around Ulsan but quieter in the hills. The roads west toward the Yeongnam Alps, a range of mountains over a thousand metres high, are winding and scenic, with climbs, hairpins and views. Ulsan has fuel, food and accommodation everywhere. Try bulgogi, grilled marinated beef, or a bowl of eonyang bulgogi, a local variation, thin patties of grilled beef, famous in the nearby town of Eonyang.
t.hwaseong fortress@37.3,127.0:
Hwaseong is a love letter from a son to his father, written in stone. In 1762, Crown Prince Sado was locked in a rice chest by his own father, King Yeongjo, and left to die, one of the darkest episodes in Korean royal history. His son, who became King Jeongjo, never forgot, and he moved his father's tomb to a site near Suwon and built a grand fortress there, completed in 1796, intended perhaps as a new capital. The engineer and scholar Jeong Yak-yong used cranes and pulleys to speed up construction, and the walls, gates, towers and bastions combine Korean, Chinese and Western ideas of fortification. UNESCO listed it in 1997.

The fortress walls run for nearly six kilometres around the old centre of Suwon, climbing over a hill and crossing a stream on a stone floodgate with arches. Walking the walls takes a couple of hours, with views over the city and the surrounding mountains. Parts of the fortress were damaged during the Korean War, but they were rebuilt with the help of a detailed royal record of the original construction, published in 1801, which described every stage of the work, with drawings and accounts.

Suwon is a big city, part of the urban sprawl south of Seoul, and riding here means dealing with heavy traffic, traffic lights and congestion. As elsewhere in South Korea, motorcycles cannot use the expressways, so you will be on the busy national roads and city streets. For better riding, head east or south into the hills and countryside of Gyeonggi province, where the roads are quieter and more scenic. The weather is hot and humid in summer, with heavy rain during the monsoon season, and cold and dry in winter.

Suwon has fuel, food and accommodation everywhere. The city is famous for galbi, beef ribs marinated and grilled at the table, and there is an entire street of galbi restaurants near the fortress. Try also fried chicken, a Korean obsession, with a cold beer, and in the old town, cafés and traditional tea houses offer a break from the bustle.
t.duisburg werthausen@51.4,6.7:
Werthausen sits on the left bank of the Rhine in Duisburg, across the river from the steelworks, harbour cranes and bridges of one of Europe's great industrial cities. It is an unexpected place to look for Rome, but the Lower Rhine was the frontier of the Roman Empire for centuries, and the line of forts, fortlets and watch posts along it is now inscribed on the UNESCO list as the Frontiers of the Roman Empire, the Lower German Limes. The site at Werthausen is one of these components, part of the chain of military posts that watched the river between the legionary bases at Neuss and Xanten.

The Rhine has shifted its course many times since Roman days, so the site lies in a landscape of old river arms, meadows and dykes. On the ground there is very little to see, and the interest lies in imagining the river as a defended border, with patrol boats on the water and Germanic tribes on the far bank. Nearby, at Moers-Asberg, the Roman fort of Asciburgium was one of the earliest on the Lower Rhine.

Duisburg itself is worth a look on its own merits. The Landschaftspark Duisburg-Nord, a former ironworks turned into a park, is one of the best examples of industrial heritage in Germany, and you can climb the blast furnace for a view over the Ruhr. The inland harbour is said to be the largest in Europe, and a boat trip there shows the scale of it. For food, the Ruhr's culture of currywurst and simple pubs is alive and well.

For riders, the area is flat and built-up, with heavy traffic, frequent lights and many speed cameras. The rewards come along the Rhine dykes and the small roads heading north toward Xanten, where the countryside opens into meadows, willows and big skies. Fuel and services are everywhere. Ride early on a Sunday morning to see the river at its quietest, with mist over the meadows and barges sliding past.
t.kalkar kalkarberg@51.7,6.3:
Near the Dutch border, where the Rhine flows through wide meadows and dyked farmland, the small town of Kalkar holds a surprising amount of history. The Kalkarberg is a low rise near Altkalkar, and on it stood the Roman fort of Burginatium, one of the posts along the Lower German Limes, now part of the UNESCO-listed Frontiers of the Roman Empire. The rise would have given a valuable view over the river plain, and the fort controlled the road between Xanten and Nijmegen. Today it is fields and trees, but the shape of the land still hints at the old fortification.
