Kalkar itself is a medieval market town of fourteen thousand people with a fine market square and a brick town hall. The church of St. Nicolai houses an exceptional collection of late Gothic carved altars, made by local workshops when Kalkar was prosperous from cloth and trade. It is one of the treasures of the Lower Rhine, and even if you are not a church person, the detail in the carvings is extraordinary.

There is also a more recent curiosity. On the edge of town stands a fast-breeder nuclear reactor that was completed but never operated. After years of controversy, it was sold and turned into an amusement park, Wunderland Kalkar, with a climbing wall on the cooling tower. It is a strange and very German monument to the politics of the 1980s and 1990s.

For riders, the area is flat and open, with straight roads, wind and wide skies. The dyke roads along the Rhine are narrow and quiet, and give views over the river with barges moving slowly. Watch out for cyclists and sheep. Fuel and food are easy in Kalkar, and nearby Xanten, with its Roman archaeological park and cathedral, makes a good next stop. Spring, with geese on the meadows, and autumn, when tens of thousands of Arctic geese winter on the Lower Rhine, are especially atmospheric times to visit.
t.cologne cathedral@50.9,7.0:
Six hundred and thirty-two years. That is how long it took to finish Cologne Cathedral, from the laying of the foundation stone in 1248 to the completion of the spires in 1880, and when you stand at its foot by the main station it feels as though the building is still growing. The twin towers climb to around 157 metres, black with soot and weather, and for a few years after completion they made it the tallest building in the world.

The reason for all this ambition lies inside: a golden shrine said to hold the relics of the Three Kings, brought from Milan in 1164 after Frederick Barbarossa's men sacked the city. The relics turned Cologne into one of the great pilgrimage destinations of medieval Europe, and the cathedral was built as a stone reliquary on a gigantic scale. Work stalled for centuries, a crane stood on the unfinished south tower for so long it became part of the skyline, and only the romantic nationalism of the nineteenth century and Prussian money got it done. In the Second World War it took many bomb hits yet stayed standing while the old town around it burned.

Let's be honest about the riding: this is a city centre stop, not a ride destination in itself. Getting here means Cologne traffic, tram tracks that bite in the wet, one-way systems and a lot of pedestrians who do not look before crossing. Motorcycles do not need an emissions sticker for German low-emission zones, which helps. Come early on a Sunday morning and the streets are surprisingly calm, the square almost empty, and you can climb the south tower's five hundred or so steps for a view over the Rhine before the crowds wake up.

Afterwards, walk across the Hohenzollern Bridge with its thousands of padlocks left by couples, then look back for the best view of the cathedral rising above the river. For food, the old town brewhouses serve Kölsch in small straight glasses that the waiter keeps replacing until you put a beer mat on top; on a riding day, the halve Hahn, a rye roll with cheese, is the safer choice. Fuel is everywhere in the city. When you leave, the Bergisches Land to the east and the Eifel to the south both offer far better roads within an hour.
t.watchtowers wp 1 41 to 1 50 including th:
The Upper Germanic Limes begins a few kilometres from here, at Rheinbrohl on the Rhine, and in its first miles it climbs straight up into the Westerwald. Watchtowers numbered WP 1/41 to 1/50 mark a short run of that frontier in the wooded hills behind Neuwied and Bendorf, near the villages of Stromberg, Anhausen and Heimbach-Weis. Do not expect towers. What remains is a low bank, a ditch you can trace through the beech trunks, and here and there the outline of a tower base marked by archaeologists.

It is the idea that gets under your skin. From this ridge the frontier ran some 550 kilometres across Germany to the Danube, a line of palisade, bank, ditch and timber or stone towers placed so that each could signal to the next. Soldiers stood here in Westerwald drizzle looking north into country they never conquered. The Limes is a UNESCO site, and in this corner of Rhineland-Palatinate it is signposted on walking trails rather than presented with big visitor centres, which suits its quiet atmosphere.

The riding in the Westerwald is honest, rolling stuff. The plateau is cut by deep little valleys running down to the Rhine, so roads alternate between fast straights across open farmland and tight descents through forest, often damp and leaf-covered in autumn. The Sayn valley below Bendorf is a lovely piece of road, passing Sayn Castle and the cast-iron hall of the Sayner Hütte, an early nineteenth-century ironworks that looks more like a cathedral of iron. Expect wind and rain more often than the weather forecast admits; the Westerwald has a reputation for it, and fog sits in the hollows on autumn mornings.

Fuel and food are easy in Bendorf and Neuwied, both proper towns down in the Rhine basin, and Neuwied has the Roman Museum and riverside promenade if you want more context. The hill villages offer the odd bakery and inn. A good plan is to ride up from the Rhine early, park at a forest car park, walk ten minutes along the trail to stand on the actual bank of the frontier, then drop down to the river for lunch. In spring the beech woods turn an astonishing bright green, and in October they burn copper, which is the season I would choose.
t.watchtowers wp 4 82 to 5 8 including for:
Out here on the eastern rim of the Wetterau, between Altenstadt, Hammersbach and the Büdingen forest, the Roman frontier did something unusual. Having come over the Taunus and swung north around the fertile plain, the Limes turned and ran almost due south towards the Main, enclosing the Wetterau like a hand cupped around something precious. The towers numbered WP 4/82 to 5/8, along with small fortlets, guarded this eastern flank, and their remains lie in fields and woodland edges where only a shallow bank or a marker stone gives them away.

Why bother with such a bulge in the frontier? Because the Wetterau was worth it. Its deep loess soils are among the best farmland in Germany, and Rome wanted the grain to feed the garrisons along the Rhine. Altenstadt itself had a fort, and the village of Marköbel in Hammersbach sat right on the line. Long before the legions came, the Celts had already made this landscape their own: seven kilometres away at the Glauberg, archaeologists found a princely burial and a life-size sandstone warrior statue from around 500 BC, now displayed in a striking museum on the hillside. If you only make one detour around here, make it that one.

The riding is open and easy. Roads run across a wide, slightly rolling plain of wheat, rapeseed and orchards, with villages every few kilometres and long sightlines that let you see traffic coming. It is not a place for knee-down cornering. It is a place for steady, contemplative miles with the Vogelsberg rising as a blue dome to the north-east, and the forested hills of the Büdinger Wald offering a few twisting kilometres if you want them. Wind sweeps the plain freely, and in high summer the heat shimmers off the fields, so mornings are kinder.

Altenstadt, three kilometres away, is a town of twelve thousand with fuel, bakeries and supermarkets, so there is no need to plan supplies carefully. Büdingen, a little further north-east, is worth the ride for its astonishingly intact half-timbered old town and walls. Late in the day the low light rakes across the plain and picks out every ripple in the land, which is exactly when old banks and ditches become visible. Walk a few hundred metres along the marked Limes path at that hour and the frontier almost reappears.
t.fortlets and site of the fort and civil:
The western Taunus is wonderfully empty. Away from the commuter belt around Frankfurt and Wiesbaden, the hills north of Bad Schwalbach turn into a quiet patchwork of forest, small meadows and villages in the Heidenrod municipality, and right through the middle runs the Limes. At Kemel, close to these coordinates, there was a Roman fort with its civil settlement, and the frontier line nearby carried a string of small fortlets and towers. Today you find grassy outlines, a few markers and the bank and ditch disappearing into the beech woods.

It helps to know what you are looking at. The fort stood on the high ground where an old ridge route crossed the frontier, and the Roman road network here would have linked it back towards Wiesbaden, the spa the Romans called Aquae Mattiacorum. Hot springs were a big part of Roman life on this frontier, and the whole Taunus is still dotted with spa towns. Bad Schwalbach, five kilometres away, built its fortune on iron-rich mineral springs and became a fashionable resort in the nineteenth century; its elegant spa park and old pump rooms make a pleasant place to sit with a coffee.

This is a fine corner for riding. The B260, known as the Bäderstraße, runs from Wiesbaden through Bad Schwalbach towards Nassau and Bad Ems, linking spa towns through wooded valleys with an excellent rhythm of curves. The Aar valley road towards Diez is another favourite. Around Kemel itself the roads cross open upland with long views, then dive into forest where the tarmac stays damp in the shade well into the morning. Deer cross at dusk, and you will see plenty of other bikes on sunny weekends, so ride as if somebody is always coming the other way.

Practical matters are simple. Bad Schwalbach and Taunusstein have fuel, supermarkets and places to eat; the hill villages offer an inn or a bakery at best. Spring brings a haze of bluebells and wood anemones under the beeches, and October paints the slopes rust and gold. Stand on the line of the Limes in that light and look north into the folded hills, and you will see roughly what a bored soldier saw: trees, mist and an awful lot of Germany.
t.carolingian westwork and civitas corvey@:
Corvey sits in a loop of the Weser just outside Höxter, a baroque abbey palace set among meadows with the wooded hills of the Solling and the Weser Uplands closing in around it. The baroque part is handsome but not why people come. Hidden behind it, forming the entrance to the church, is a westwork built between 873 and 885, and it is one of the very few Carolingian buildings in the world still standing more or less as it was built.

The abbey was founded in the ninth century under Louis the Pious, the son of Charlemagne, as a missionary base among the recently conquered Saxons, and it grew into one of the great intellectual centres of the early medieval empire. The westwork, a tall, solid block of stone with an upper chamber, was where the emperor could attend services when he visited. Inside, fragments of wall paintings from that time survive, including scenes from the Odyssey, which is a wonderful surprise in a monastery. Since 2014 Corvey has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Later the abbey library employed August Heinrich Hoffmann von Fallersleben, the poet who wrote the words of the German national anthem; he worked here as librarian in his later years and is buried in the little cemetery by the church.

The Weser Uplands are underrated motorcycle country. The river winds between steep wooded slopes, and the road along it from Höxter towards Holzminden and Bodenwerder is easygoing and scenic, while the roads climbing up into the Solling or out to the west into the Eggegebirge offer proper bends and real elevation changes. Surfaces are generally good. Watch for the little river ferries that still cross the Weser here and there, a charming way to change banks, and for the many cyclists on the Weser cycle route in summer.

Höxter, two kilometres away, is a town of thirty thousand with fuel, supermarkets and a lovely half-timbered centre, so supplies are no problem. Across the river at Fürstenberg, a white castle on a hill houses the porcelain manufactory founded in the eighteenth century, with a museum and café and a fine view down the valley. On a misty autumn morning, with the Weser steaming and rooks in the meadows, Corvey feels very far from the twenty-first century, and very close to the ninth.
t.fort site and civil settlement of arnsbu:
Arnsburg confuses people, and for good reason. The name belongs first to a Cistercian monastery in the Wetter valley near Lich, whose roofless Gothic church stands in a meadow as one of the most romantic ruins in Hesse. But on the wooded hill nearby lies an older layer: a Roman fort on the Limes, sometimes called the Alteburg, with its civil settlement, and the frontier itself running past on its way around the northern edge of the Wetterau.

The fort was part of the line that guarded the fertile Wetterau basin, and like many forts here it had a settlement of traders, craftspeople and families clustered outside its gates. Nothing stands above ground; you look at banks, hollows and information boards among the trees. The monks came a thousand years later and chose the valley bottom for its water. They built the abbey in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries and ran it until secularisation in the early nineteenth century. Part of the old monastery is still in use, and there is a café and inn in the grounds, which makes this one of the few Limes stops with a proper place to sit and eat.

The area offers two moods of riding. To the south and west lies the open Wetterau, wide fields and long views with straight roads that tempt more speed than the villages allow. To the north-east the land climbs towards the Vogelsberg, an old volcano with some lovely winding routes through forest and pasture, and plenty of local riders on summer evenings. Münzenberg, just to the south, is crowned by a twin-towered castle ruin that locals call the inkpot of the Wetterau, visible for miles and a great landmark to navigate by.

Lich, four kilometres away, is a town of thirteen thousand with fuel and shops, and its name will be familiar to beer drinkers because the Licher brewery has been here a long time. The old town has fine half-timbered houses and a collegiate church. Münzenberg is smaller but has the basics. Come in late spring when the meadows around the abbey ruin are full of flowers, or in autumn when the Gothic arches frame yellow trees against a grey sky. Either way, give the ruin twenty minutes; it repays them.
t.fort site and civil settlement of saalbu:
If you want to know what a Roman frontier fort actually looked like, this is the place. The Saalburg, on the ridge of the Taunus above Bad Homburg, is the only Limes fort in Germany rebuilt in full: walls, gates, towers, granary and the headquarters building, all standing again on their original foundations. The reconstruction was ordered by Kaiser Wilhelm II around 1900, who liked his Romans grand and imperial, and while archaeologists today debate some details, walking through the main gate is still a jolt.

The fort guarded a pass where an old road crossed the Taunus ridge, and it grew from a small earthwork into a stone fort for a cohort of about five hundred men, with a large civil settlement down the slope. The museum inside displays finds from the site and from the whole Limes, including shoes, tools and weapons, and the reconstructed buildings hold exhibitions and a café. Wilhelm's enthusiasm made the Saalburg the founding place of Limes research in Germany, and it remains the headquarters of that work today.

The road over the Saalburg pass, the B456 from Bad Homburg towards Usingen, is part of the attraction: a fast climb through forest with long, well-sighted bends. Riders love the whole Hochtaunus, and the Großer Feldberg, at 879 metres the highest summit of the range, is a classic meeting point a few kilometres west. That popularity has a downside: police checks and speed limits are frequent here, and weekend traffic on the ridge roads can be heavy. Come on a weekday, ride with restraint near the villages, and you will enjoy it far more.

For fuel, Wehrheim and Schmitten are close, and Bad Homburg and Oberursel at the foot of the hills have everything a rider needs. Bad Homburg's spa park and casino quarter are pleasantly grand for a coffee stop. Just north of the Saalburg, the Hessenpark open-air museum near Neu-Anspach has rebuilt villages of old Hessian farmhouses, a good companion stop if you are in a history mood. The beech forests on the ridge smell of earth and wet leaves even in summer, and from the fort's walls the view runs south over Frankfurt's towers, a reminder that the Romans' frontier is now commuter country.
t.xanten cut@51.7,6.4:
Xanten is an old Roman town that still behaves like a small, cosy market town on the Lower Rhine, and right next to it lies one of the largest archaeological parks in Germany. Colonia Ulpia Traiana, CUT for short, was founded around AD 100 under the emperor Trajan, who gave it the rank of a colonia and his family name. At its height it was a walled city of several thousand people, the second most important Roman city in the province of Lower Germany after Cologne.

After Rome's power faded, the city was abandoned and its stones carted away for building, which ironically preserved its ground plan beneath open fields. The LVR Archaeological Park has rebuilt parts of it at full scale: a section of the city wall with a gate, a temple partly raised on its original podium, a large amphitheatre that hosts summer events, and a reconstructed inn and bath house. A modern museum built over the original baths shows the finds. Xanten itself grew up around the burial place of a Christian martyr, Victor, and its Gothic cathedral of St. Victor dominates the town. Legend also makes Xanten the home of Siegfried, the dragon-slaying hero of the Nibelungenlied.

The Lower Rhine is flat. Very flat. Roads run along dykes and between farms and willow-lined meadows, with church towers and windmills marking the horizon. It is relaxing riding, but the wind can be strong and constant off the open country, and long straights tempt you to forget the frequent speed cameras in towns. The real charm lies in the small river roads, the ferry crossings of the Rhine, and the light, which in the late afternoon turns the water silver and the brick villages warm.

Xanten has fuel, supermarkets and plenty of cafés around its market square, so it is an easy stop. The two lakes created by gravel extraction just outside town are popular for swimming and sailing in summer. Give the archaeological park a couple of hours if you can; it is spread over a big area and best explored on foot. In winter fog lies on the fields, and the reconstructed walls appear out of the white as if the city had just been built again.
t.gaya tumuli@35.2,128.9:
Right in the middle of Gimhae, a busy city just west of Busan, a low ridge of grassy mounds rises between apartment blocks and roads. These are the Daeseong-dong tumuli, the burial ground of the rulers of Geumgwan Gaya, one of the small kingdoms of the Gaya confederacy that flourished in the south of the Korean peninsula from the first centuries AD until it was absorbed by Silla in the sixth century. In 2023 a group of Gaya burial sites, including these, was added to the UNESCO World Heritage list.

Gaya was rich in iron. Its smiths produced armour, weapons and iron ingots that were traded across the peninsula and to Japan, and the tombs have yielded helmets, horse armour and pottery that show a sophisticated culture. A museum beside the mounds displays the finds, and a short walk takes you along the ridge between the tombs, some of which have been opened to show their structure. Gimhae also holds the tomb of King Suro, legendary founder of Geumgwan Gaya, who according to legend hatched from a golden egg, and the tomb of his queen, Heo Hwang-ok, said to have come from a distant land across the sea.

Riding in this part of Korea means dealing with dense urban traffic, wide multi-lane roads and a lot of trucks, especially around the industrial areas between Gimhae, Busan and Changwon. Beyond the city, the Nakdong River delta offers flat roads along the water, and the mountains to the north and west have winding routes with good surfaces. Korean drivers can be assertive, so stay alert. Note that motorcycles are generally not allowed on Korean expressways, so plan routes on national and local roads. Summers are hot and humid with a rainy season; spring and autumn are ideal.

Gimhae has fuel and all services, and the area around the tumuli has cafés and restaurants. Korean food is a pleasure for hungry riders: try dwaeji gukbap, a pork and rice soup popular in the Busan area, or bibimbap. Convenience stores are everywhere. In spring, cherry blossoms around the tombs make the park particularly lovely, and on a quiet evening the mounds are a peaceful refuge from the bustle of the modern city around them.
t.donggureung cluster@37.6,127.1:
Nine kings and ten queens of the Joseon dynasty lie at Donggureung, in the city of Guri, just north-east of Seoul. The name means the Eastern Nine Tombs, and it is the largest royal burial ground of the dynasty, which ruled Korea for over five centuries from 1392 to 1910. The tombs are spread across a wooded hillside, each a grassy mound surrounded by stone figures of officials and animals, set according to the rules of geomancy with a mountain behind and water in front.

The most famous tomb is Geonwonneung, the tomb of King Taejo, the founder of the dynasty. According to tradition, his mound is covered not with grass but with reeds brought from his hometown in the north, at his own request, and these reeds are trimmed only once a year in a special ceremony. The Joseon royal tombs, forty of them in all, were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2009, recognized for their remarkable preservation and the continuity of ancestral rites still performed there.

The tombs are in a park with walking paths through pine and oak forest, and a visit takes an hour or two on foot. Getting there by motorcycle means riding through the Seoul metropolitan area, with heavy traffic, complex intersections and a lot of buses and delivery scooters. Remember that motorcycles are not allowed on expressways in Korea, so use local roads. Beyond Guri, the Han River valley and the mountains of Gyeonggi province to the east offer pleasant riding, with roads along the river and winding climbs into the hills. Weekends bring heavy traffic out of the city.

Guri has fuel and all services, and the area around the tombs has restaurants serving Korean food. Try naengmyeon, cold buckwheat noodles, in summer, or galbi, grilled marinated ribs, any time. The park is quiet on weekday mornings, and in autumn the leaves turn red and gold around the tombs, making the visit particularly beautiful. Standing in front of the stone guardians, with the city's noise muted by the trees, you get a sense of the continuity of Korean history.
t.fort site and civil settlement of friedb:
Friedberg's castle stands on a basalt ridge above the Wetterau, a walled enclosure so large it is almost a town of its own, with a tall round tower, the Adolfsturm, rising above the trees. What most visitors walking through the castle gate do not know is that they are standing on a Roman fort. The legions chose this same ridge in the first century AD, and a fort with a civil settlement grew up here, linked by road to the Limes a few kilometres to the north and west.

The Romans valued the Wetterau for its fertile soil, and Friedberg's fort was one of the bases that held the region. In the Middle Ages the Hohenstaufen emperors built the castle on the old Roman site, and the town grew up beside it, an imperial city with a broad main street and a fine Gothic church, the Stadtkirche. Friedberg also has a rare Jewish ritual bath, a mikveh, built in the thirteenth century and descending some twenty-five metres into the ground, one of the most impressive in Germany.

A more recent chapter brings American visitors. In 1958 Elvis Presley was stationed in Friedberg with the US Army, at the Ray Barracks, and he lived in nearby Bad Nauheim during his service. Both towns remember him with plaques, a statue and an annual festival, and fans still come to see the places where he lived. The riding around Friedberg mixes the open, gently rolling Wetterau with the Taunus hills to the west, where roads climb into forest with plenty of bends, and the Vogelsberg to the north-east. Traffic near Frankfurt is heavy, so escape early.

Friedberg, a town of twenty-seven thousand, has fuel, shops and restaurants, and its main street, the Kaiserstraße, is lined with cafés. Bad Nauheim, three kilometres away, is a spa town with an art nouveau bathhouse complex, the Sprudelhof, one of the largest of its kind in Europe, and a pleasant park for a walk. Hessian food includes Handkäse mit Musik, a sour cheese with onions, and green sauce, Grüne Soße, made with seven herbs. From the top of the Adolfsturm, the view stretches across the Wetterau to the Vogelsberg and the Taunus.
t.ir d f woudagemaal@52.8,5.7:
The Netherlands has always had to fight water, and Friesland's battle was won in part by a single building on the shore of the IJsselmeer near Lemmer. The Ir. D.F. Woudagemaal, a steam pumping station opened in 1920, is the largest steam-driven pumping station ever built that is still in working order, and it was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1998. When the water in Friesland's canals and lakes rises too high, the old steam engines can still be fired up to pump it out.

The station was named after the engineer Dirk Frederik Wouda, who designed it, and its brick building, in the style of the Amsterdam School, houses four steam engines driving eight huge pumps. In full operation it can pump an enormous volume of water per minute, and it is still used in emergencies, usually a few times a year after heavy rain. A visitor centre explains how it works, and on certain days you can see the engines in action, with steam and the smell of hot oil.

The riding in Friesland is flat, with wide skies and long straight roads along canals and dykes, and the wind is the main challenge: it blows steadily from the west, often strongly, and can make riding tiring. The dyke along the IJsselmeer offers views across the water, and the roads through the Frisian lake district pass villages, windmills and farms. Watch for cyclists, who are everywhere, and for narrow bridges and roads. Lemmer itself is a busy water sports town, with locks and harbours full of boats in summer.

Lemmer, two kilometres away, is a town of ten thousand with fuel, shops and restaurants along the canals. Balk and Sint Nicolaasga are smaller villages. Frisian food includes suikerbrood, sugar bread with cinnamon, and smoked eel from the IJsselmeer. Friesland has its own language, Frisian, and you will see bilingual signs. The Elfstedentocht, the legendary skating race through eleven Frisian towns, is held only when the canals freeze hard enough, which is now rare. In the evening, the light over the IJsselmeer is vast and golden.
t.beguinage de tongeren@50.8,5.5:
Tongeren calls itself the oldest town in Belgium, and it has a Roman name, a Gallic hero and a weekly antiques market to back up the claim. Under the Romans it was Atuatuca Tungrorum, and in the main square stands a romantic nineteenth-century statue of Ambiorix, the chieftain who gave Julius Caesar a very bad winter. A few minutes' walk from all that pomp lies the béguinage, a quiet quarter of low brick houses, cobbled lanes and small gardens that once housed communities of beguines, religious women who lived a semi-independent life without taking the full vows of nuns.

The Flemish béguinages were listed together by UNESCO in 1998, and Tongeren's is one of the more lived-in examples: people still occupy the houses, and the atmosphere is calm rather than museum-like. Look for the church, the little pump, the way the houses huddle round the courtyards. It is easy to imagine the women who lived here working, praying and running their own affairs in an age when that was far from common.

Riding in, you cross the Haspengouw, the gently rolling fruit country of Belgian Limburg, where orchards of apples, pears and cherries line the lanes and spring blossom turns everything white and pink. The roads are mostly smooth, with long views and few real corners; the Jeker valley to the south and the Voeren enclave to the east offer more relief and some proper small-road fun. Watch for cobbled stretches in the old town, tractors at harvest time and the usual Belgian habit of cyclists appearing from nowhere.

Tongeren is a town of thirty thousand people, so food, coffee and petrol are all easy. Sunday mornings bring the antiques and flea market, which fills the streets and makes parking a bike a creative exercise. The Gallo-Roman Museum is excellent if you want context, and the Basilica of Our Lady towers over the centre.

For something local, try a Limburg fruit tart, a vlaai, or a glass of syrup made from the region's apples and pears on a slice of bread. Then walk back through the béguinage at the end of the day, when the light falls low over the red brick and the only sound is a bicycle bell somewhere beyond the wall.
t.kottenforst nord am wei en stein 1@50.7,:
The Kottenforst looks like an ordinary Rhineland woodland of oak, beech and hornbeam, with walkers, joggers and the odd horse rider, but in the second half of the first century and beyond it was a training ground for the Roman army. In clearings of the forest, the legion stationed at Bonna, today's Bonn, built a series of temporary camps as exercises, digging ditches and raising ramparts to practise the rapid construction they would need in the field. The remains of these camps, faint earthworks under the trees, are included in the Lower Germanic Limes, which UNESCO listed in 2021. Am Weissen Stein is one of the northern groups.

You need a sharp eye to read them: low banks and shallow ditches under the leaves, best seen in late autumn and winter when the undergrowth dies back. Information boards on the forest paths help, and the effort of finding them makes them more memorable than a museum case.

The Kottenforst covers part of the Ville, a low ridge between the Rhine plain and the Swist valley, south-west of Bonn. The roads through and around it are pleasant, fairly straight forest roads with good surfaces, popular with cyclists and local traffic, and the edges of the forest open onto the Vorgebirge, the gentle slope toward Bornheim and Alfter that is famous for vegetable growing and, in spring, asparagus. Head south into the Eifel and the roads become far more interesting, with valleys, curves and the Ahr wine region not far off.

Alfter and Bornheim are sizeable towns with fuel, shops and cafés, and Bonn, eight kilometres away, has everything a city can offer. Bonn's Rheinisches Landesmuseum is a good place to see Roman finds from the legionary fortress, and the city's old centre, Beethoven's birthplace and the Rhine promenade are easy additions to a day.

The forest smells of damp leaves and moss after rain, and it is surprisingly quiet once you are a few hundred metres from the road. On a warm summer day it offers welcome shade, and in spring the forest floor is carpeted with wood anemones. Stand at the edge of one of those faint ditches and picture a group of legionaries, sweating and cursing, digging a camp they would leave the next day.
t.koln alteburg@50.9,7.0:
The Roman navy is not the first thing most people associate with Cologne, but for almost two centuries the Rhine fleet, the Classis Germanica, had its main base here at Alteburg, just south of the Roman city. The fort sat on a terrace above the river in what is now the leafy district of Marienburg, near Bayenthal, and from here warships patrolled the Rhine, carried supplies and soldiers, and kept watch on the frontier. The site belongs to the Lower Germanic Limes, listed by UNESCO in 2021, though today it lies mostly under villas, streets and gardens, with only traces and information boards to show where it stood.

Marienburg is one of Cologne's grandest residential areas, with big houses set in green gardens along the river, and walking or riding slowly through its streets is a pleasant contrast to the dense city centre. Down at the river, the Rheinufer offers paths, views across to Poll and the bridges, and a sense of the big working waterway that the Romans controlled.

Riding in Cologne is typical German city riding: busy ring roads, tram tracks, many cyclists and frequent traffic lights. The old town has cobbled streets, and the low-emission rules and parking restrictions can make life complicated. Approach Alteburg along the Rhine from the south, and once your visit is over, head out to the Bergisches Land east of the river or the Eifel to the south-west for proper riding country.

You are in a city of a million people, so fuel, food and coffee are everywhere. In the centre, the cathedral is unmissable, and the Romano-Germanic Museum beside it holds the Dionysus mosaic and a wealth of finds from Roman Cologne, which was a major provincial capital called Colonia Claudia Ara Agrippinensium. Afterwards, sit in a traditional brewery tavern and drink Kölsch, the local beer, served in slim glasses by waiters who keep bringing new ones until you put a beer mat on top.

The Rhine at Alteburg is broad and brown, with barges sliding past and gulls crying over the water. It takes no great leap to swap the barges for oared galleys heading upstream on patrol, the city walls of Roman Cologne glinting on the rise behind them, and to realise that this stretch of river has been a busy workplace for two thousand years.
t.watchtower wp 3 1 to 3 14 including the:
The Taunus is the green upland that keeps Frankfurt's weekend riders sane, and running right across it is the line of the Roman frontier. The stretch of watchtowers numbered 3/1 to 3/14 lies near Taunusstein, north of Wiesbaden, where the Upper Germanic Limes crossed the ridge, and it includes the remains of forts and their civilian settlements. One of the best known nearby is the fort of Zugmantel, near the hamlet of Orlen, where the outline of the fort, the palisade line and reconstructed watchtowers give a real sense of the frontier. The whole line is part of the UNESCO Frontiers of the Roman Empire.

The Limes here is often visible as a low bank and ditch in the forest, followed by a long-distance walking trail. Walking a short stretch under the beech trees, past reconstructed towers, is the best way to feel how this border worked, a narrow line of control across endless forest.

For a rider, the Taunus is a fine playground. Roads climb from the Rhine and Main valleys through forested hills, with smooth tarmac, flowing curves and some steeper, tighter sections. The routes around the Grosser Feldberg, the highest summit of the Taunus, are legendary among local motorcyclists, and on sunny weekends the car park at the top is a gathering point. Because of that popularity, expect police checks, noise controls and speed limits on some routes, and be careful of cyclists, walkers and the occasional deer. The B260, the Bäderstrasse, links the spa towns and is a pleasant route through the hills.

Taunusstein is a town of nearly thirty thousand, with all the fuel and food you could need. Bad Schwalbach, a spa town with a long history of mineral springs, and Idstein, with its beautiful half-timbered old town and castle, are both close by and worth a coffee stop.

Visit in spring or autumn, when the beech forests are fresh green or copper-coloured and the air smells of damp leaves. In summer the forest gives shade, in winter the higher roads may be icy. The reconstructed towers are small, draughty and lonely, and that is the honest lesson they teach: frontier duty in the Taunus was mostly long hours, wet wool and a view of more trees.
t.okjeon tumuli@35.6,128.3:
On a ridge above the Hwang river in Hapcheon County, a row of grassy mounds rises against the sky, each one the burial of a ruler or noble of Dara, one of the small kingdoms of the Gaya confederacy that flourished in the south of the Korean peninsula between the first and sixth centuries. Gaya was famous for its iron, traded across the region and to Japan, and its tombs held armour, weapons, horse gear, pottery and gold ornaments. The Okjeon tumuli are one of seven groups listed together by UNESCO in 2023 as the Gaya Tumuli.

The mounds are simple and serene, set among trees and grass with paths running between them, and a small museum nearby displays finds from the excavations, including crowns, helmets and pottery. Walking among the tombs, especially in the early morning or late afternoon, has a quiet, contemplative feel, with views over the river valley and the hills of Gyeongsangnam-do.

Hapcheon County is also home to Haeinsa, one of the most important Buddhist temples in Korea, on the slopes of Gayasan mountain. The temple houses the Tripitaka Koreana, more than eighty thousand wooden printing blocks carved in the thirteenth century, stored in buildings designed with remarkable ventilation; temple and halls are both UNESCO-listed. Hwangmaesan, another mountain in the county, is famous for its pink azalea blossom in spring.

The riding in this area is excellent. Roads wind through river valleys and over wooded hills, with good surfaces, light traffic and plenty of curves. The roads around Hapcheon Lake and up toward Haeinsa are particularly scenic. Korean traffic drives on the right, and drivers can be assertive, so stay alert, especially in towns and on main roads. Speed cameras are common.

Fuel is available in Hapcheon town and larger villages, and Changnyeong, about twenty kilometres away, is a bigger town with full services. Korean food is a highlight: bibimbap, grilled meats, spicy stews and endless small side dishes. Temple food at Haeinsa is simple and vegetarian. Come in spring for blossoms, or autumn for brilliant foliage and clear skies. Summers are hot and humid, with a monsoon season in July. The ridge is a lovely place to sit for a while with a can of cold coffee from the last convenience store, the mounds rising like soft green waves beside you.
t.seosamreung cluster@37.7,126.9:
The kings and queens of the Joseon dynasty, who ruled Korea for more than five hundred years until 1910, chose their graves with enormous care. Geomancers studied hills, water and wind to find sites with the right energy, and the royal tombs were laid out with burial mounds, stone guardians, ceremonial halls and long processional paths. Forty of these tombs are listed together by UNESCO as the Royal Tombs of the Joseon Dynasty, and Seosamreung, the three western tombs in Goyang just north-west of Seoul, is one of the clusters.

The setting is a calm, wooded hillside where pine trees shelter the mounds, and the stone figures of civil and military officials, horses and sheep stand in silent watch. A visit is a lesson in Confucian ritual and order: the T-shaped shrine where offerings were made, the path of the spirit and the path of the king, the careful placement of each element in the landscape. Some parts of the cluster have been closed for conservation in the past, so check access before you go.

Goyang is a big city of more than a million people, part of the sprawl of greater Seoul, and the area around the tombs is a patchwork of farmland, greenhouses, apartment towers and new suburbs. Riding here means heavy traffic, multi-lane roads, frequent traffic lights and assertive driving, especially at rush hour. Motorcycles are not allowed on Korean expressways, so you will be on ordinary roads, which can be slow. Head north toward Paju and the Imjin river, or east into the mountains of Bukhansan National Park, for more interesting riding.

Fuel, food and coffee are everywhere. Korean food is a reason to stop in itself: a bowl of naengmyeon, cold buckwheat noodles, in summer, or galbi grilled at the table, with endless side dishes of kimchi and vegetables. Convenience stores offer quick snacks and cold drinks at any hour.

Come in spring, when cherry and forsythia blossom brighten the hills, or in autumn, when the maples turn brilliant red and the skies are clear. Summers are hot and humid, with a monsoon season in July, and winters are cold and dry. Walk slowly along the processional path at Seosamreung, past the stone guardians, and feel how carefully the Joseon court arranged the meeting of landscape, power and the afterlife.
t.gochang getbol@35.5,126.5:
At low tide on the coast of Gochang, the sea pulls back so far that it seems to disappear, leaving a vast plain of mud, sand and shell banks glistening in the light. These tidal flats, called getbol in Korean, are among the richest on earth, teeming with crabs, shellfish, worms and the birds that feed on them, including rare migrating shorebirds that stop here on their journeys between Siberia and Australia. Gochang's flats are part of the Getbol, Korean Tidal Flats, listed by UNESCO in 2021.

Gochang is a county of surprises. Its dolmens, ancient stone tombs from the first millennium BC, are among the densest concentrations in the world and are also UNESCO-listed, with hundreds of massive stones scattered across the hillsides. The walled fortress of Gochang Eupseong, also called Moyangseong, has a local tradition of women walking the walls with stones on their heads to bring good health. Seonunsa, a Buddhist temple in the hills, is famous for its camellias in spring and red spider lilies in autumn.

The riding along the coast is relaxed and scenic, with flat roads running past rice fields, salt farms and fishing villages, and the tidal flats stretching out to the horizon. Inland, the hills offer more curves and wooded roads. Traffic is light outside the towns, but watch for farm vehicles, scooters and the occasional slow-moving truck. Winds off the Yellow Sea can be strong, and the weather changes quickly.

Gochang town has fuel, shops and restaurants, and larger towns like Buan and Yeonggwang are within reach. The county is famous for two delicacies: grilled freshwater eel from the Pungcheon river area, rich and smoky, and bokbunja, a sweet wine made from Korean black raspberries. Fresh seafood from the flats, clams, crabs and octopus, is another highlight.

Spring and autumn are the best seasons, when migratory birds pass through in large numbers and the weather is mild. Summer can be hot and humid, with typhoons possible, and winter brings cold winds off the sea. Walk out onto a boardwalk at low tide, listen to the popping and clicking of countless crabs in the mud, and watch the tide creep back in across the flats.
t.watchtowers wp 1 1 to 1 2@50.5,7.3:
This is where it all begins, or ends, depending on which way you are walking. At Rheinbrohl, on the east bank of the Rhine between Bonn and Koblenz, the Upper Germanic-Raetian Limes left the river and struck out across country, running more than five hundred kilometres to the Danube near Regensburg. The first watchtowers, numbered 1/1 and 1/2, stood here near the river, and the line can be followed into the hills from the edge of the village. The whole frontier is part of the UNESCO Frontiers of the Roman Empire, and Rheinbrohl has a modern museum, the RömerWelt, which brings the frontier to life with reconstructions, exhibits and hands-on activities.

The Rhine valley here is broad and gentle, with vineyards on the slopes, small towns along both banks and barges sliding past on the river. Bad Hönningen and Rheinbrohl face Bad Breisig across the water, linked by a ferry, and further south, at Andernach, a cold-water geyser erupts high into the air on a peninsula in the river, said to be the highest of its kind in the world.

The riding along the Rhine is scenic but busy, with heavy traffic on the main roads on both banks, frequent towns and speed limits. The real fun lies in the hills: east of the river, the Westerwald offers rolling roads through forests and small villages, and to the west, across the ferry, the Eifel and the Ahr valley have twisting roads, volcanic lakes and the Nürburgring, the legendary race track, within reach. Weekends bring many motorcyclists, and the police are attentive.

Bad Hönningen, about a kilometre away, has fuel, shops and cafés, and its thermal baths are a pleasant place to relax. Rheinbrohl has smaller shops, and Bad Breisig across the river has more. Local food includes Rhineland dishes like Reibekuchen, potato pancakes with apple sauce, and Sauerbraten, marinated pot roast, and the local wines from the Rhine and the Ahr.

Come in spring, when the vineyards turn green, or in autumn, when the grape harvest brings wine festivals to many towns. Walk up from the river to the line of the first towers, and look out over the Rhine, the natural frontier that the Romans relied on for so long, before following the line into the hills.
t.watchtowers wp wp 2 23 to 2 26 including:
North of the Taunus ridge, the Limes crossed a high, open plateau between the Rhine and the Lahn, and the stretch with watchtowers 2/23 to 2/26 runs through the farmland and woods near Miehlen and Singhofen in the Rhein-Lahn district. The remains here are subtle, mostly low banks and the traces of towers in fields and forest edges, but the line of the frontier is marked by the long-distance Limes trail and information boards. This is part of the UNESCO Frontiers of the Roman Empire, a stretch of the line that few visitors ever see.

The plateau is quiet, rural and peaceful, with fields of grain, meadows and small villages of half-timbered and slate-roofed houses. To the north, the land drops steeply into the Lahn valley, one of the loveliest river valleys in Germany, winding between wooded slopes, castles and small towns. Nassau, about nine kilometres away, gave its name to the House of Nassau, whose branches include the royal family of the Netherlands, and the ruins of the family's ancestral castle stand on a hill above the town. Bad Ems, upstream, is a spa town where the Prussian king's famous telegram of 1870, the Ems Dispatch, helped trigger the Franco-Prussian War, and it is another of the Great Spa Towns of Europe listed by UNESCO.

The riding here is a delight. The plateau roads are smooth, gently curving and quiet, and the roads that drop into the Lahn valley twist and turn through forest. Along the Lahn itself, the road follows the river past castles and villages, with good surfaces and moderate traffic. Watch for cyclists, farm vehicles and deer in the forests at dawn and dusk.

Miehlen and Singhofen are small villages with basic shops, so for fuel and wider choice head for Nassau or Bad Ems. Local food includes hearty German dishes, from schnitzel to sausages, and the wines of the Lahn and the nearby Rhine. Cafés in the Lahn towns serve cakes and coffee in the afternoon.

Come in late spring or early autumn, when the plateau is green or golden and the Lahn valley glows. Ride along the plateau, stop by a stretch of the Limes trail and enjoy the quiet, then drop down into the Lahn for a coffee by the river.
t.fort site and civil settlement of grossk:
Großkrotzenburg sits at a turning point of the Roman frontier. Here, on the Main east of Frankfurt, the river border that ran north from Miltenberg came to an end, and the Limes turned away from the water to head north across the Wetterau toward the Taunus. A fort guarded the spot, with a civilian settlement, and parts of its walls and gate can still be traced in the old town, where the fort's outline is marked in the streets. The site belongs to the UNESCO Frontiers of the Roman Empire, and the local museum displays finds from the fort and the vicus.

The area today is a mix of small towns, gravel pits turned into lakes, riverside meadows and, rather incongruously, a large power station on the river at Großkrotzenburg, whose chimney is a landmark for miles around. Seligenstadt, a few kilometres upstream, is a charming town with half-timbered houses and a Carolingian basilica founded by Einhard, the biographer of Charlemagne, who is buried there. Hanau, a short way downstream, is the birthplace of the Brothers Grimm, and the German Fairy Tale Route starts there.

The riding here is flat to gently rolling, with roads along the Main and across the plain, moderate to heavy traffic near Frankfurt and Hanau, and plenty of cyclists along the river. For more interesting riding, head east into the Spessart, a forested upland with winding roads, or north into the Vogelsberg, an extinct volcano with a network of quiet, curving roads through farmland and forests.

Großkrotzenburg has fuel, shops and cafés, and Kahl am Main and Seligenstadt, nearby, have more choice. Local food includes Hessian specialties such as Handkäse mit Musik, a tangy sour-milk cheese marinated with onions, Grüne Soße, a green herb sauce from Frankfurt served with potatoes and eggs, and Apfelwein, the local cider, drunk in traditional taverns from ribbed glasses.

Spring, with the river meadows green and full of birdsong, is the nicest season here. Summer evenings by the lakes are pleasant, with swimmers and picnickers. Walk the outline of the fort in the old town, then ride upstream to Seligenstadt for a coffee in the shadow of Einhard's basilica.
t.watchtowers wp 2 20 to 2 22@50.3,7.9:
A few kilometres west of Miehlen, the Limes crosses the Einrich, a high, open plateau of fields and meadows between the Rhine and the Lahn, and the stretch with watchtowers 2/20 to 2/22, near Singhofen and Holzhausen an der Haide, is one of the quietest parts of the whole frontier. Nearby, the fort of Holzhausen is one of the best-preserved Roman forts on the Limes, with its stone walls, gates and corner towers clearly visible in the forest, a rare sight on a frontier where most remains have vanished into the fields. The whole line is part of the UNESCO Frontiers of the Roman Empire.

The Einrich is rolling, rural country, with big skies, scattered villages and wind turbines turning on the ridges. To the west lies the Blaues Ländchen, the little blue land, a gentle hilly area around Nastätten named, so one story goes, for the blue flax flowers that once covered its fields. Further west the land drops abruptly into the gorge of the Upper Middle Rhine, a UNESCO-listed landscape of castles, vineyards and the famous Loreley rock, around which the river makes a tight bend that sailors once feared.

The riding on the plateau is relaxed and pleasant, with smooth roads, gentle curves and light traffic. The roads that drop down to the Rhine, toward St. Goarshausen or Kaub, are far more dramatic, twisting steeply through forest and vineyards to the river. The Rhine has no bridges between Koblenz and Mainz, so ferries carry traffic across, adding a little adventure to any loop. Weekends bring many motorcyclists to the Rhine valley roads, and police checks are frequent.

Singhofen and Holzhausen are small villages with basic shops. For fuel and wider choice, Nassau, about eight kilometres away, and Nastätten are the nearest towns. Local food includes the hearty dishes of the region, wild game from the forests and the Riesling of the Middle Rhine, grown on steep slate slopes above the river.

The plateau is softest in its colours in May and in late September. Visit the fort at Holzhausen in the morning, walk the walls among the trees, then ride down to the Rhine and take a ferry across the river in the afternoon sun.
t.royal tombs in neungsan ri@36.3,126.9:
Seven grassy mounds rise on a hillside outside Buyeo, smooth and green, looking almost like a landscape garden. They are the royal tombs of Neungsan-ri, burial places of kings of Baekje, one of the three kingdoms of ancient Korea, during the period when Buyeo, then called Sabi, was its capital, from 538 to 660. The tombs were robbed long ago, but their stone chambers survive, and one has painted walls showing the guardian animals of the four directions and lotus flowers. They are part of the UNESCO listing of the Baekje historic areas, together with sites in Gongju, Buyeo and Iksan.

Next to the tombs, archaeologists excavated the site of a Buddhist temple, and in 1993 they found one of the masterpieces of Korean art: a gilt-bronze incense burner, decorated with mountains, animals, musicians and a phoenix on top. It is now displayed in the Buyeo National Museum. The city also has the Busosan fortress on a hill above the Geum river, and the Nakhwaam cliff, where, according to legend, the court ladies of Baekje threw themselves into the river rather than be captured when the kingdom fell to the allied armies of Silla and Tang China.

The riding in this part of South Chungcheong is pleasant and easy. The roads follow the Geum river and wind through low hills covered with pine woods and rice fields, with little traffic away from the main routes. Note that motorcycles are not allowed on expressways in South Korea, so you will be using national and local roads, which are generally well-maintained. Summer is hot and humid with monsoon rains; autumn is the best season, with clear skies and colourful leaves. Winter is cold and dry.

Buyeo has a filling station and somewhere to eat. Korean food here includes dishes based on lotus, a local speciality, from lotus leaf rice to lotus root side dishes, and the usual banquet of banchan. Convenience stores are everywhere, with coffee and snacks. Walk among the tombs slowly, especially in the early morning when mist lies in the valley, and then visit the museum to see the incense burner; it is one of those objects that seems to contain a whole world.
t.jongmyo shrine@37.6,127.0:
In the middle of busy central Seoul, behind a gate on Jongno street, lies a forest of trees and a long, low hall that seems to come from another world. Jongmyo is the royal ancestral shrine of the Joseon dynasty, which ruled Korea from 1392 to 1910, and its main hall, the Jeongjeon, houses the spirit tablets of kings and queens in a row of identical rooms behind a single facade of red pillars, stretching for more than a hundred metres. It is one of the longest wooden buildings of its kind in Asia, and its austerity is deeply impressive.

The Jongmyo Jerye, the royal ancestral rite, is still performed here every year on the first Sunday of May, with music, dance and offerings, by descendants of the royal family. The music and ritual are recognised by UNESCO as part of the intangible heritage of humanity, and the shrine itself is a World Heritage site. Visits are usually guided, except on certain days, so check the schedule. Next to the shrine, Changdeokgung palace and its secret garden are within walking distance.

Riding in central Seoul is a challenge. Traffic is dense, the streets are wide and full of buses and taxis, and delivery motorcycles weave between the cars. Motorcycles are banned from expressways and some major roads, so plan your route carefully. Parking is limited, but you can often find space near markets and side streets. Outside the city, the mountains around Seoul offer twisty roads and great views, especially in autumn. Summer is hot and humid with monsoon rains; winter is cold and dry.

Fuel, food and every service are easy to find. Opposite the shrine, Sewoon Sangga, a long electronics arcade from the 1960s, has been revived with workshops and cafés, and Gwangjang Market, a short walk away, is famous for its street food: bindaetteok, mung bean pancakes, mayak gimbap, small rice rolls, and raw beef. The area around Jongmyo is also a favourite of older men who gather in the park to play chess and talk. Walk through the shrine slowly, sit under the trees, and listen to the city noise fading away; it is one of the most peaceful places in Seoul.
t.fort pannerden@51.9,6.0:
Right where the Rhine enters the Netherlands and splits in two, the Dutch put a fort. Fort Pannerden was built around 1870 at the point where the river divides into the Waal, flowing west toward Nijmegen and Rotterdam, and the Pannerdens Kanaal, which feeds the Nederrijn and the IJssel. Control the split, and you control how much water goes where, which in a country defended by deliberate flooding mattered enormously. The fort, a low, heavy brick and earth structure surrounded by a moat, guarded the dykes and sluices that could send water into the defensive lines further west. It is counted among the Dutch Water Defence Lines listed by UNESCO.

The fort had an eventful recent history: in the first decade of this century it was occupied by squatters, who were evicted and came back more than once before a deal was struck, and it has since been restored and opened to visitors by a foundation. Inside are casemates, gun positions and a lot of damp brick corridors that are cool even in summer. From the ramparts you look over the water meadows of the Gelderse Poort, the gateway where the river comes in from Germany.

The landscape is the Netherlands at its most watery and green. The Millingerwaard and other floodplains around here have been returned to nature, with Konik horses and Galloway cattle grazing semi-wild, beavers in the side channels and big flocks of geese in winter. For riding, the dyke roads are the attraction: narrow, raised ribbons of tarmac following the rivers, with views over the water on one side and farms on the other. They are flat, of course, but full of corners as they follow the river bends, and you share them with cyclists, farmers and the occasional flock of sheep. Wind is a constant companion.

Pannerden and Doornenburg are small villages; Doornenburg has a fine moated castle. For fuel and shops, head to Gendt, a few kilometres away, or the town of Zevenaar. The local cafés serve coffee with apple pie and, in season, asparagus. The fort is reached by a short walk or a small ferry depending on the access route, so check opening days before setting out. Sit on the rampart for a while and watch the barges negotiating the split: the river traffic here is heavy, and the Rhine never stops.
t.beguinage de diest@51.0,5.1:
Diest has one of the largest béguinages in Flanders, a walled town within the town, with its own streets, gates, church and some ninety houses. The béguines were laywomen who lived a religious life without taking permanent vows, earning their own living and sharing a community, and their béguinages flourished in the Low Countries from the thirteenth century onward. The Flemish béguinages are listed together by UNESCO. In Diest, the béguinage has been restored with care, and its cobbled streets, whitewashed houses and quiet gardens feel worlds away from the traffic outside.

The town itself is a pleasant place on the river Demer, at the edge of the Hageland, a region of gentle hills, orchards and vineyards, where Belgian wine is made in increasing quantities. Diest was a barony of the House of Orange-Nassau, and William of Orange, the leader of the Dutch revolt against Spain, was its lord; the Dutch royal family still carries the title Baron of Diest. The large Gothic church of St Sulpitius dominates the main square, and the town's fortifications from the nineteenth century, with a citadel and ramparts, have become a green belt.

The riding around Diest is gentle and enjoyable. The Hageland roads climb over low hills with curves, through orchards and vineyards, with views over the countryside, and traffic is generally light. Cobbles appear in villages and old town centres. Scherpenheuvel, a few kilometres west, has a large baroque basilica that is the most important Marian pilgrimage site in Belgium, and the roads around it are busy on pilgrimage days. The weather is changeable, with frequent rain and wind, but the light on a clear day is soft and lovely.

Diest has fuel, shops, restaurants and cafés. Flemish food here includes stews, fries, waffles and local beer; Diest has its own brewing tradition, and the Hageland produces fruit, especially cherries and apples. Visit the béguinage in the late afternoon, when the light falls on the white walls and the streets are quiet; the only sounds are footsteps on the cobbles, birds in the gardens and perhaps a bell from the little church.
t.sosu seowon@36.9,128.6:
Pine trees older than anyone can remember shade the entrance to Sosu-seowon, the first Confucian academy in Korea to receive a royal charter. It was founded in 1543 by Ju Se-bung, a local magistrate, to honour An Hyang, a scholar of the Goryeo period who brought Neo-Confucianism to Korea from China. A few years later, the famous philosopher Yi Hwang, who also served in the area, petitioned the king to grant it official recognition, and the academy received a royal plaque in 1550 with the name Sosu. Since 2019 it has been part of the UNESCO World Heritage site of Seowon, Korean Neo-Confucian Academies.

The seowon was a place where young men of the yangban, the scholar-aristocracy, studied the Confucian classics, prepared for civil service exams and performed rituals in honour of great scholars. The buildings are simple and elegant, wooden halls with tiled roofs set among the trees beside a stream. There is a lecture hall, a shrine, dormitories and a library, and the whole complex has a calm, contemplative atmosphere. Next door is the Seonbichon, a reconstructed village of traditional houses where visitors can experience the life of the Joseon scholars.

The area around Yeongju is mountainous and green, at the foot of the Sobaek range. Not far away is Buseoksa, one of the oldest and most beautiful temples in Korea, with a wooden hall, the Muryangsujeon, that dates from the Goryeo period and is one of the oldest wooden buildings in the country. The view from the temple over the ridges of the mountains, especially at sunset, is famous.

The riding is excellent, with winding roads through the mountains and valleys, little traffic and good surfaces. The road over the Jukryeong pass, an old route between the southeast and Seoul, climbs through forest with tight bends. Note that motorcycles are not allowed on Korean expressways, so you will be riding on the national and provincial roads, which is no hardship here.

Yeongju has fuel, shops and restaurants. The region is known for ginseng, especially from Punggi, and for its apples. Try a bowl of bibimbap or a hearty stew. Autumn, with red maples and clear skies, is the best season; winters are cold and snowy, summers hot and humid with a monsoon season.
t.koch ang dolmen site@35.4,126.6:
Korea has a remarkable concentration of the world's dolmens, and Gochang, on the southwest coast, has the largest cluster of all. Hundreds of these megalithic tombs are scattered along the foot of a range of low hills, some standing like tables on stone legs, others with a massive capstone resting almost directly on the ground. They were built during the Bronze Age by the people who farmed these lands, as tombs for the elite or as markers of territory and ritual. Together with the dolmen sites at Hwasun and on Ganghwa Island, they were listed by UNESCO in 2000.

A path winds through the dolmen park, and you can walk among the stones, some of them weighing many tonnes. There is a museum explaining how they were built: the stones were quarried from the hillside, moved on rollers and raised with earth ramps. The setting is peaceful, with fields, hills and the occasional heron. In autumn the area fills with flowering silver grass and bright fields of colour.

Gochang has other treasures. Its old town is surrounded by a walled fortress, Moyang, built in the fifteenth century, and there is a tradition of women walking around the walls carrying stones on their heads to ensure health and good fortune. The nearby temple of Seonunsa, in the hills, is famous for its camellias in spring and its autumn colours. The coastal tidal flats near Gochang are part of the UNESCO site of the Getbol, Korean Tidal Flats, listed in 2021, a vital habitat for migratory birds.

The riding is pleasant, on quiet rural roads through rice paddies, hills and small villages, with gentle bends and little traffic. The coast road offers views of the tidal flats and the Yellow Sea. Korean roads are generally in good condition, but watch for farm vehicles, scooters and sudden stops. Remember that motorcycles are banned from expressways.

Gochang has fuel, shops and restaurants. The area is famous for its freshwater eel, grilled and served with a sweet sauce, and for bokbunja, a wine made from black raspberries. Spring and autumn are the best seasons; summer is hot and humid, with the monsoon in July. Take your time walking among the stones, and imagine the effort it took to raise them.
t.onze lieve lievevrouwebasiliek met stads:
Tongeren likes to remind you that it is the oldest town in Belgium, and it has a strong claim. The Romans founded a settlement here, Atuatuca Tungrorum, on the road between Cologne and Bavay, and the remains of its walls can still be seen around the town. Before that, the area was home to the Eburones, a Celtic tribe whose chieftain Ambiorix famously ambushed and destroyed a Roman legion in 54 BC. His statue, a heroic nineteenth-century figure with a winged helmet and a magnificent moustache, stands in the main square, the Grote Markt.

The Basilica of Our Lady dominates the town, a Gothic church built over many centuries on the site of earlier churches, perhaps the first north of the Alps dedicated to the Virgin. Its tower is listed by UNESCO as one of the belfries of Belgium and France, a symbol of civic pride. Inside, the treasury holds some of the finest medieval religious objects in the country, and the cloister is a peaceful place. Below the church, excavations have revealed Roman and early Christian remains.

Tongeren also has a béguinage, listed by UNESCO with the other Flemish béguinages, a quiet enclave of houses and lanes. The Gallo-Roman Museum, near the basilica, is one of the best archaeological museums in Belgium. And on Sunday mornings the town hosts a huge antiques and flea market, drawing dealers and collectors from across the region.

The riding around Tongeren is gentle and pleasant. The town lies in Haspengouw, a fertile region of rolling hills, orchards and fields, famous for its apples, pears and cherries; in spring, when the trees are in blossom, the landscape is beautiful. To the east lies the Voeren, a pocket of Flemish territory with hills, valleys and narrow lanes. The roads are generally good but can be narrow, with farm traffic and cyclists.

Tongeren has fuel, shops and plenty of restaurants and cafés. Try the local syrup, made from apples and pears, spread on bread, or a glass of Belgian beer in a café on the Grote Markt. Limburg weather swings between bright and damp within an hour, so a waterproof layer earns its place. Climb the basilica tower if it is open, and look out over the town and the orchards of Haspengouw.
t.signaltower wolferheimer wald@50.4,8.8:
The Roman frontier in Germany, the Limes, ran for over five hundred kilometres from the Rhine to the Danube, a line of palisades, ditches, walls, watchtowers and forts that marked the edge of the empire. In the Wetterau, north of Frankfurt, the Limes swung east in a great bulge to enclose this fertile plain, which the Romans valued for its farmland. In the woods near Wölfersheim stood a signal tower, one of the many small posts along the line, and today its remains are part of the Upper German-Raetian Limes, listed by UNESCO in 2005 as part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire.

There is not much to see on the ground: a low mound or the outline of foundations in the forest, perhaps with an information board. But it is a peaceful spot, and the woods are pleasant for a short walk. Elsewhere along the Limes, reconstructions of towers and forts help you imagine what the frontier looked like.

The Wetterau is a gentle landscape of fields, orchards and villages, with the hills of the Taunus to the west and the Vogelsberg to the east. Above the small town of Münzenberg rises a castle with two tall round towers, known locally as the Wetterau inkwell for its shape. It was built in the twelfth century by imperial officials and is one of the finest Romanesque castles in Germany. The views from the top over the plain are excellent.

The riding in the Wetterau itself is flat and easy, with straight roads through fields and villages. Traffic can be heavy near Frankfurt and on the main roads. The best riding lies to the east, in the Vogelsberg, an extinct volcano with a network of winding roads through forests and meadows, very popular with motorcyclists. The roads around Schotten and the Hoherodskopf are particularly good, with many bends, climbs and views. Be aware that some roads in the region have weekend restrictions or speed limits for motorcycles because of noise and accidents.

Wölfersheim and Münzenberg have fuel, shops and restaurants. The region is known for its apple wine, Ebbelwoi, served in a grey and blue stoneware jug, and for hearty Hessian food, such as Handkäs mit Musik, a sour cheese with onions. The weather is mild, with warm summers and cool winters.
t.key planning decision@53.4,6.9:
The name on the map is bureaucratic, but the place is anything but. Key Planning Decision is a translation of the Dutch legal designation used to protect the Wadden Sea, and the spot here sits on the coast near Delfzijl, at the eastern edge of the province of Groningen, where the Dutch Wadden meets the estuary of the Ems. The Wadden Sea is the largest unbroken system of tidal flats in the world, stretching along the coasts of the Netherlands, Germany and Denmark, and it was listed by UNESCO in 2009.

Twice a day, the tide goes out and exposes vast expanses of mud and sand, crossed by channels and gullies, teeming with worms, shellfish and crabs. Millions of migratory birds stop here to feed on their way between the Arctic and Africa, and seals rest on the sandbanks. At low tide, guided groups go mudflat walking, wadlopen, across the flats to the islands, an adventure that requires an expert guide, as the tides and channels can be dangerous. The tradition is particularly strong along the Groningen coast.

Delfzijl is a port town, with a harbour, industry and a seawall along the waterfront. The area around it is flat and green, with farmland, canals and villages built on terps, artificial mounds raised over centuries to protect people from floods before the dikes were built. Groningen province has also been in the news because of earthquakes caused by decades of natural gas extraction, which have damaged many houses and led to a decision to end production.

The riding here is flat and windswept. The roads run along the dikes and across the polders, straight and open, with views over the sea and the fields. The wind is a constant companion, often strong and gusty, blowing in from the sea with nothing to stop it. Cyclists are everywhere, and Dutch drivers expect you to respect them. Traffic is light outside the towns. It is not exciting riding, but there is a beauty in the vast skies, the light and the space.

Delfzijl has fuel, shops and restaurants. Try fresh fish, or a portion of kibbeling, battered fish pieces, from a stall. The weather is changeable, with rain, wind and grey skies common. Bring warm, waterproof clothing, even in summer.
t.upper middle rhine valley@50.2,7.7:
Between Bingen and Koblenz, the Rhine cuts a deep, winding gorge through the slate hills of the Rhenish Massif, and for centuries this has been one of the great landscapes of Europe: steep slopes covered with vineyards, castles on every crag, villages of half-timbered houses along the river, and barges gliding past. The Upper Middle Rhine Valley was listed by UNESCO in 2002, and Sankt Goarshausen sits at its heart, at the foot of the most famous rock on the river.

The Loreley is a slate cliff that rises steeply from the water at a narrow bend, where the current is strong and rocks once made navigation dangerous. Legend tells of a beautiful maiden who sat on the rock combing her golden hair and singing, distracting boatmen so that they crashed on the rocks. Heinrich Heine's poem, set to music, made the story famous across Germany. From the top of the rock, the view down the gorge is superb. Across the river, Sankt Goar is dominated by the huge ruins of Rheinfels Castle, once one of the mightiest fortresses on the Rhine, and above Sankt Goarshausen stands Burg Katz, the Cat castle, facing Burg Maus, the Mouse, a little downstream.

There are no bridges across the Rhine between Mainz and Koblenz, so ferries link the two banks, including one between Sankt Goarshausen and Sankt Goar. They run frequently, and crossing by ferry is part of the charm.

The riding is superb. The roads along the river, the B42 on the east bank and the B9 on the west, are scenic, with views of the river, castles and vineyards, though they can be busy, and the railway lines on both banks bring noisy freight trains. The best riding is up in the hills, on the roads that climb from the river into the Taunus on the east and the Hunsrück on the west, with hairpins, steep gradients and views over the gorge. Traffic is light on these roads, and the surfaces are generally good.

Sankt Goar has fuel, shops and restaurants, and many villages along the river have inns and wine taverns. Try a glass of Riesling from the steep slopes, and Rhine specialties such as Sauerbraten. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with blossom or harvest; summer brings crowds, and winter fog.
t.watchtower wp 3 49@50.2,8.5:
High in the Taunus, the wooded hills northwest of Frankfurt, the Roman Limes followed the ridge line, and its watchtowers looked out over the forests to the north. Watchtower WP 3/49, near Schmitten and Glashütten, is one of hundreds of such posts recorded along the frontier, and today its remains lie in the woods, a low mound or a scatter of stones. The Limes path, a long-distance walking trail, follows the line through the forest, and walkers can trace the ditch and bank of the old frontier for kilometres. The whole line is part of the Upper German-Raetian Limes World Heritage site.

A short ride east, near Bad Homburg, the Saalburg is the best place to understand the Limes. It is a Roman fort that was reconstructed in the early twentieth century under the patronage of Kaiser Wilhelm II, with walls, gates, barracks and a museum. It gives a vivid picture of life on the frontier, and the reconstructed watchtowers nearby show what posts like WP 3/49 looked like.

The Taunus is Frankfurt's playground, a region of forests, hills and spa towns. The highest point, the Großer Feldberg, rises to 878 metres, with a tower and views over the Rhine-Main plain and the city's skyscrapers. Königstein, below, has a ruined castle and an elegant old town. The forests are full of walkers, cyclists and riders at weekends.

The riding in the Taunus is excellent and popular. The roads that wind up to the Feldberg and through the hills have many bends, steep gradients and good surfaces, and on sunny weekends the car park at the summit fills with motorcycles. But the popularity has a downside: accidents and noise have led to speed limits, controls and sometimes weekend closures for motorcycles on certain roads. Check current restrictions, ride sensibly and respect the locals.

Schmitten, Glashütten and Königstein all have fuel, shops and restaurants. Try a glass of apple wine and a plate of Grüne Soße, Frankfurt's green herb sauce served with eggs and potatoes. The weather in the hills is cooler and wetter than in the plain, with fog, rain and snow in winter. Spring and autumn are lovely, with fresh green or golden forests. Go on a weekday for quieter roads.
t.watchtowers wp 1 58 to 1 59@50.4,7.6:
The Upper German-Raetian Limes began its long march across Germany on the banks of the Rhine at Rheinbrohl, and climbed from there into the hills of the Westerwald. The stretch between Watchtowers 1/58 and 1/59, near Höhr-Grenzhausen, is part of this first section, where the frontier ran through forests and over hills above the Rhine valley. Remains are scarce here, perhaps a mound or a line in the forest floor, but the Limes path follows the route, and information boards explain the history.

Höhr-Grenzhausen is the centre of the Kannenbäckerland, the land of the jug bakers, where potters have made salt-glazed stoneware for centuries. The grey and blue Westerwald stoneware, decorated with cobalt patterns, was exported across Europe and beyond, and you can still see potters at work in workshops and visit the Keramikmuseum Westerwald in the town. The tradition is alive, with modern ceramic artists alongside the old crafts.

The Westerwald is a region of rolling hills, forests and small towns between the Rhine, the Lahn and the Sieg. It is quieter than the Rhine valley, with fewer tourists, and the landscape is green and peaceful. Koblenz, a short ride south, sits at the confluence of the Rhine and the Moselle, at the Deutsches Eck, where a huge equestrian statue of Kaiser Wilhelm I stands. Across the Rhine, the fortress of Ehrenbreitstein looms above the city.

The riding is good. The roads through the Westerwald are winding, with gentle hills, forests and villages, and traffic is light. The descent to the Rhine valley offers views over the river, and from there you can follow the Rhine south through the gorge or the Moselle west, both superb riding routes. Surfaces are generally good, though minor roads can be patched. Watch for deer, farm traffic and cyclists.

Höhr-Grenzhausen has fuel, shops and restaurants. Try a hearty Westerwald dish such as Döppekuchen, a potato cake baked with bacon, or a glass of local beer. The weather in the hills is cooler and wetter than in the Rhine valley, with fog and snow in winter. Spring and autumn are lovely, with blossom or golden leaves. Pick up a stoneware jug as a souvenir, if you have room in the panniers.
t.historic villages of korea hahoe and yan:
The Nakdong river makes a wide loop around Hahoe, almost turning it into an island, and inside that loop a village of tiled-roof mansions and thatched cottages has stood for some six centuries. Hahoe is the ancestral home of the Pungsan Ryu clan, a lineage of scholar-officials during the Joseon dynasty, and its layout follows Korean principles of geomancy, with houses arranged to face the river and the cliffs of Buyongdae across the water. It was added to the World Heritage list in 2010, together with Yangdong village near Gyeongju, as the finest surviving examples of clan villages of the Joseon period.

The village is still lived in, which gives it a different feel from a museum. Families maintain the old houses, some of which offer simple homestay rooms, and the narrow lanes between earthen walls are shaded by old trees. Hahoe is also known for its mask dance drama, a satirical folk play performed with carved wooden masks that mock the aristocracy and clergy. Performances take place regularly in season, and the masks themselves are considered national treasures. The Andong Mask Dance Festival every autumn draws large crowds.

The roads around Andong are a pleasure to ride. The countryside is a patchwork of rice paddies, orchards and wooded hills, with the Nakdong winding through it, and the routes between villages offer gentle curves, light traffic and good surfaces.
