A short ride from Hahoe, the Confucian academy of Byeongsan Seowon sits on the river under steep cliffs, reached by a narrow road, partly unpaved. North toward Dosan Seowon and the mountains of Bonghwa, the roads become more winding and hilly. Autumn, with its red maples and harvest colours, is the best time to come.

Andong, about twenty kilometres away, is a city of well over a hundred thousand people with all services. Andong is famous for its food: jjimdak, a braised chicken dish with noodles and vegetables, and salted mackerel, a reminder of the days when fish had to travel inland from the coast. Try both in town, then walk the riverbank at Hahoe in the late afternoon, when the light on the cliffs is golden.
t.complex of koguryo tombs@38.9,125.4:
Near the town of Kangso, southwest of Pyongyang, three earthen mounds rise from the farmland of the Taedong river plain, and inside them lie some of the most beautiful paintings of ancient East Asia. These are the Kangso tombs of the Koguryo kingdom, which ruled much of northern Korea and Manchuria from the first centuries AD until 668. The inner chamber walls are painted with the four guardian animals: the Blue Dragon of the east, the White Tiger of the west, the Red Phoenix of the south and the Black Tortoise of the north, intertwined with a snake. The colours, though faded, are still vivid, and the line work has an energy that photographs barely capture. The Complex of Koguryo Tombs was inscribed by UNESCO in 2004.

Koguryo was one of the Three Kingdoms of Korea, alongside Paekche and Silla, and it was a powerful military state that resisted invasions by Chinese dynasties several times. The tombs in this complex, scattered around Pyongyang and Nampo, show scenes of daily life, hunting, dance, warriors and celestial beings, as well as the guardian animals. They are a crucial source for understanding the culture of early Korea and its connections with China and Central Asia.

The reality for riders, however, is stark. North Korea does not permit independent travel. Foreign visitors can only enter on organised tours, accompanied by official guides at all times, and riding your own motorcycle on North Korean roads is not possible for ordinary travellers. Travel restrictions have been very tight in recent years, and many governments advise against all travel to the country. Even if you visit on a tour, access to the tomb interiors is limited to protect the paintings, and you may see replicas rather than the originals.

So this is a place to know about rather than to ride to. If you are curious, look for published reproductions of the paintings or the replicas displayed in museums in South Korea and elsewhere. The guardian animals of the Kangso tombs, especially the Black Tortoise and Snake, have become iconic images in Korean art history. Perhaps one day the roads across the Taedong plain will be open to riders, and the mounds of Kangso will be a stop on a long ride through a united peninsula.
t.stadhuis met toren@50.8,5.2:
Sint-Truiden's Grote Markt is one of the largest market squares in Belgium, and at its centre stands the town hall with its belfry, a tower that has watched over the town since the Middle Ages and been rebuilt and remodelled several times. The belfry, with its carillon, is part of the UNESCO listing of the Belfries of Belgium and France, inscribed in 1999 to honour these civic towers that symbolised the freedom and wealth of the medieval towns. Climb it if you can, and you will see the whole of the Haspengouw region spread out around you, a gently rolling landscape of orchards and fields.

Sint-Truiden grew up around a Benedictine abbey founded in the seventh century by Saint Trudo, and the abbey's towers still dominate the skyline near the market. The town has a beautiful beguinage, a quiet enclave of small houses around a green, with a church whose walls are covered in medieval murals. Haspengouw is Belgium's fruit basket, famous for its apples, pears and cherries, and in April, when the orchards are in bloom, the countryside turns white and pink.

The riding around Sint-Truiden is gentle and relaxing. The roads wind through the orchards and fields of Haspengouw, with small villages, châteaux and farms, and gentle hills that are enough to make the routes interesting without being challenging. Surfaces are generally good, but cobbles appear in some villages and town centres, and farm traffic is common, especially during the fruit harvest in late summer. The light is lovely in the evenings, and spring blossom season is magical. Wind can be strong on the open plateaus, and rain is never far away in Belgium.

Sint-Truiden is a town of nearly forty thousand people with petrol, coffee and proper meals around the market square. Try a local fruit tart or a glass of cider, or a Belgian beer if you have stopped riding for the day; there are also excellent waffles and chips. Sit on a terrace on the square, listen to the carillon, and watch the town go about its business. It is a pleasant, unpretentious place, and the fruit country around it is a joy to ride through.
t.st mary s catholic cathedral@52.1,9.9:
In the courtyard of Hildesheim Cathedral, a rose bush climbs the wall of the apse, and the legend says it has been growing there for a thousand years. The "thousand-year rose" is linked to the founding of the bishopric in 815, when, so the story goes, Emperor Louis the Pious hung a reliquary on the branches of a wild rose and found it impossible to remove, taking it as a sign to build a chapel. Whatever the truth, the rose survived the bombing of March 1945, which destroyed the cathedral and much of the old town, and sprouted again from its roots in the rubble. The cathedral and the nearby Church of St Michael were inscribed by UNESCO in 1985 for their outstanding Romanesque architecture and art.

The treasures of the cathedral are remarkable. The bronze doors commissioned by Bishop Bernward and cast in 1015 show scenes from the Old and New Testaments in lively relief, and the Bernward Column, also in bronze, spirals with scenes from the life of Christ. Inside, the great wheel chandeliers symbolise the heavenly Jerusalem. The cathedral was carefully restored and reopened in 2014, and its museum holds a rich collection of medieval art. St Michael's, on a hill a short walk away, has a wonderful painted wooden ceiling.

Riding into Hildesheim means navigating city traffic, but the surroundings offer good riding. To the south, the hills of the Leine uplands and the Hildesheim forest have winding roads through woods and villages, with moderate gradients. Further south, the Harz mountains, about an hour away, are a classic motorcycle destination, with steep climbs, tight bends and wonderful forest scenery, though they are crowded on weekends and police controls are frequent. The countryside around Hildesheim is a fertile plain of beet and wheat fields, with long straight roads.

Hildesheim is a city of around a hundred thousand people with petrol, places to eat and accommodation. The market square, rebuilt after the war with replicas of its timber-framed houses, including the huge Knochenhaueramtshaus, the Butchers' Guild Hall, is a great place for coffee and cake. Visit the cathedral, look at the bronze doors and the rose, and then walk up to St Michael's. It is a town that has rebuilt itself from ashes, and its treasures are worth the stop.
t.watchtowers wp 2 35 to 2 48 including th:
West of the Taunus ridge, where the high country rolls down toward the Rhine gorge and the Lahn, the line of the Upper German Limes runs through farmland and forest near the villages of Holzhausen an der Haide, Katzenelnbogen and Nastätten. Archaeologists have catalogued the sites of the watchtowers along this stretch, numbered WP 2/35 to 2/48, and near Holzhausen are the remains of a stone fort, well preserved and easily visited, with its walls and gate outlines clear in the grass. The Limes here consisted of a palisade of wooden stakes, later backed by a ditch and bank, with watchtowers at regular intervals and forts a few kilometres behind. It formed the frontier of the Roman Empire for more than a century and a half.

The countryside is the Hintertaunus, a quiet, thinly populated upland of fields, meadows and beech forests, with small villages and little traffic. Katzenelnbogen, with its castle, gave its name to the medieval counts of Katzenelnbogen, a powerful family who controlled lucrative Rhine tolls and built castles along the river, including Burg Katz above St. Goarshausen. The Rhine gorge, part of the UNESCO Upper Middle Rhine Valley, with its castles, vineyards and the Loreley rock, is a short ride to the west.

The riding here is excellent. The roads across the Hintertaunus are quiet and winding, rolling over the hills through forests and fields with good surfaces and moderate gradients. The descent to the Rhine at St. Goarshausen or toward the Lahn valley at Nassau and Bad Ems offers steep, twisting roads with tight hairpins and great views. The B260, the Bäderstraße, running from Lahnstein toward Wiesbaden, is a well-known motorcycle route with many curves, though it is busy on weekends and has speed controls. Weather can be cool and damp on the high ground, and fog is common in autumn.

Holzhausen and Katzenelnbogen are small, with a few shops and inns, and Nastätten, a little larger, has fuel and more services. Bad Schwalbach, about twelve kilometres away, is the nearest town of more than ten thousand people. Local food includes hearty country dishes, and Rhine wines are close at hand. Stop at the fort near Holzhausen, walk around its walls, and imagine the soldiers who watched over the forests from here. Then ride down to the Rhine for a view of the castles.
t.watchtowers wp 2 50 to 2 55 including ju:
Bad Schwalbach is a spa town that never quite lost its nineteenth-century manners: a long, leafy valley, a Kurpark with pavilions, and iron-rich springs that once drew the fashionable from across Europe to take the waters. Just above it, on the high ground of the Taunus, the Roman frontier ran through the forests, and the stretch catalogued as watchtowers WP 2/50 to 2/55 passes within a few kilometres of the town. Here the Upper German Limes followed the ridge, with wooden and later stone towers set at intervals within sight of one another, a palisade in front, and a ditch and bank added later. In the beech woods you can still trace the low line of the bank in places, a quiet scar running through the trees for kilometre after kilometre.

The Taunus is an old mountain range of slate and quartzite, worn down into rounded ridges and deep valleys, and its forests are among the most extensive in Hesse. The Aar and other small rivers cut their way north toward the Lahn, while to the south the land drops steeply to the Rhine and the vineyards of the Rheingau, one of Germany's most famous wine regions, known especially for Riesling. Wiesbaden, the state capital, lies just beyond the ridge, with its own hot springs and grand spa architecture.

The roads around Bad Schwalbach are a favourite with riders from the Rhine-Main area. The B260, known as the Bäderstraße, winds through the valleys toward Schlangenbad and Wiesbaden on one side and toward the Lahn on the other, with plenty of curves, climbs and descents through the forest. The roads down to the Rheingau, through Schlangenbad or over the ridge toward Eltville and Kiedrich, are steep and twisting, with great views over the Rhine. Weekend traffic, including many bikes, can be heavy, and speed controls are common. Mist and wet leaves make autumn riding slippery under the trees.

Bad Schwalbach, about three kilometres away, has fuel, cafés, bakeries and restaurants, and Taunusstein is close by too. If you have time, ride down to the Rheingau for a glass of Riesling at a wine tavern, but only at the end of the day. A coffee in the Kurpark is an elegant alternative. Stop in the woods near the Limes line, walk a few hundred metres along the bank, and listen to the wind in the beeches. It is a peaceful place, and its history runs deep.
t.veenhuizen@53.0,6.4:
Veenhuizen does not look like a prison town at first. It looks like an orderly village in the flat green countryside of Drenthe, with long avenues of trees, neat brick buildings, canals and fields. But read the inscriptions on the gables, with mottos like "Werken is zalig", work is blessed, and the history starts to show. In 1818, a philanthropic organisation called the Society of Benevolence, founded by General Johannes van den Bosch, began establishing colonies in the poor, empty peatlands of the northern Netherlands, where poor families from the cities could be resettled and taught to farm. Veenhuizen became a colony for orphans, beggars and vagrants, and over time it turned into a state institution, and then into a prison village.

The Colonies of Benevolence, including Veenhuizen, Frederiksoord, Wilhelminaoord and Wortel in Belgium, were inscribed on the UNESCO list in 2021 as an experiment in social reform. Veenhuizen still has working prisons, but much of the village is now open, and the National Prison Museum in one of the old institutional buildings tells the story of the colony and of imprisonment in the Netherlands. Walking the avenues, you see the strict geometry of the planned landscape, with straight roads, canals and rows of houses built for the guards and staff.

The countryside around Veenhuizen is quiet and flat, with farmland, forests and heathland. The roads are straight and narrow, often lined with trees, and surfaces are good. Traffic is light, but cyclists are everywhere, and they have priority on many roads. The forests and heaths around Norg and the Drents-Friese Wold national park, to the west, offer more interesting riding, with winding roads through pine and beech woods and open heath. The landscape is gentle, and the best time to ride is in late summer, when the heather blooms purple.

Veenhuizen has a few places to eat and drink around the old institutional core. For fuel and more services, head for Norg, Haulerwijk or Oosterwolde, which is around nine kilometres away. Drenthe is known for hearty food, such as pea soup, and local cakes. Walk the avenues, read the gable mottos, and visit the museum. It is a strange and fascinating place, where good intentions and harsh discipline went hand in hand.
t.namhansanseong@37.5,127.2:
Just beyond the south-eastern edge of Seoul, the city stops abruptly against wooded mountains, and on top of them runs a stone wall with gates, watchtowers and command posts. Namhansanseong was built as an emergency capital, a mountain fortress where the king and court could retreat in time of invasion, and in the winter of 1636 to 1637 it was put to the test. King Injo fled here from the invading Qing army and held out for forty-seven days before hunger and the fall of other strongholds forced him to surrender. The fortress became a World Heritage Site in 2014.

Today the wall is a popular hiking circuit, and the little settlement inside, with its temples, restored royal residence and command posts, is full of restaurants specialising in slow-cooked chicken and duck. On weekends thousands of Seoulites come up, so weekdays are calmer. In autumn the maples and oaks turn the ridges red and gold, and on clear winter days you can see across the whole city to the mountains north of the Han river.

Before you plan anything else, know this: motorcycles are not allowed on South Korea's expressways. Everything has to be done on national and local roads, which in a crowded urban area means traffic lights, delivery scooters and buses. The reward is the climb to the fortress itself, a twisty road through forest that local riders love, with tight hairpins and good surfaces. Weekend crowds of cars and hikers mean you should keep your speed sensible, especially near the gates and car parks.

Seongnam and Hanam, the big cities at the foot of the mountain, have plenty of fuel, motorcycle shops and food. Gwangju to the south-east, not to be confused with the southern city of the same name, gives access to quieter roads along the Han river and towards Paldang Lake.

Korean summers are hot and very humid, with the monsoon rains of late June and July, and typhoons can bring heavy storms in late summer. Spring, with cherry and azalea blossom, and autumn are the best riding seasons. A bowl of chicken soup inside the fortress, with the noise of the city replaced by birdsong and temple bells, is a good reward for the ride.
t.works along the ij before durgerdam@52.4:
East of Amsterdam, where the IJ widens into the IJmeer and the city gives way to water and sky, the old dike village of Durgerdam sits on a strip of land between the sea wall and the polders. Its wooden houses, painted in strong colours and leaning on each other along the dike, look out over a lake that was once the Zuiderzee, open to the North Sea until the Afsluitdijk closed it in 1932. The works along the IJ here belong to the Defence Line of Amsterdam, now part of the Dutch Water Defence Lines World Heritage Site.

The Defence Line was a ring of forts, dikes, sluices and inundation fields built around the city in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. In time of war, the Dutch planned to flood the land around Amsterdam to a depth that would stop soldiers but was too shallow for boats, while forts covered the dikes and roads that crossed the water. It was obsolete almost as soon as it was finished, thanks to aircraft, but it remains a remarkable example of using water as a weapon. The fortified island of Pampus, out in the IJmeer, is part of it and can be visited by boat.

Riding here is a very Dutch experience. The dike roads are narrow, sometimes single track, and cyclists are everywhere, often in large groups and with priority on many stretches. Speed limits are low and enforced. The wind is the main character: it blows hard across the IJmeer, and on an open dike you feel every gust. In return you get wide views, big skies and the special light of the Dutch waterlands that painters loved.

Nearby Muiden has the Muiderslot, a medieval moated castle where the poet P. C. Hooft gathered a circle of writers and artists in the seventeenth century. Further north, the Waterland area of meadows, ditches and wooden villages such as Ransdorp and Holysloot offers more quiet dike riding.

Diemen and the eastern districts of Amsterdam have fuel and shops. Watch out for Amsterdam's environmental rules, scooter and moped lanes and the constant flow of bikes. Durgerdam itself has a few places to eat with a view of the water, and on a sunny day it is hard to believe the city centre is only a few kilometres away.
t.aachen cathedral@50.8,6.1:
Charlemagne chose Aachen for its hot springs, and the springs still bubble up under the old town, smelling faintly of sulphur at the fountains where they surface. Around the end of the eighth century he built a palace here and, at its heart, a chapel: an octagon under a dome, ringed by a sixteen-sided ambulatory, designed by Odo of Metz with columns and marble shipped from Ravenna and Rome. That chapel is the core of Aachen Cathedral, and in 1978 it became the first site in Germany on the World Heritage list.

Charlemagne was buried here in 814, and for some six centuries afterwards German kings came to Aachen to be crowned, climbing to the plain stone throne in the gallery that tradition links to the emperor himself. Later centuries added a soaring Gothic choir with walls that are almost all glass, so that the building now reads as two eras glued together: the dark, heavy Carolingian octagon and the bright cage of windows behind it. The treasury next door holds some of the most precious medieval objects in Europe, among them a bust reliquary of Charlemagne.

As a place to ride to, Aachen is a city stop, compact and walkable once you have parked. The centre has narrow lanes, pedestrian zones and plenty of traffic, and the cathedral sits right in the middle beside the town hall, itself built on the foundations of Charlemagne's palace hall. German low emission zones do not apply to motorcycles, which helps, but parking close to the cathedral is tight, so leave the bike at the edge of the old town.

The rides out are the reward. Vaals, across the Dutch border five kilometres away, sits at the foot of the Vaalserberg, where Germany, Belgium and the Netherlands meet and where the Netherlands reaches its highest point. South, the Eifel begins within half an hour, with the twisting roads around Monschau, the Rur reservoir and the high Venn moorland straddling the Belgian border. Weather in this corner shifts quickly between rain and bright sun, and the Venn can be foggy and cold when the city is mild.

Fuel, food and workshops are everywhere in a city this size. Do not leave without a packet of Aachener Printen, the spiced, hard gingerbread the city has baked for centuries, which keeps for weeks in a tank bag and improves every coffee stop.
t.limessection between watchtowers wp 1 34:
North of Neuwied, the hills of the Westerwald rise steeply from the Rhine, and through their forests ran the Roman frontier known as the Upper German-Raetian Limes. The section between the watchtowers numbered WP 1/34 and its neighbours lies near Melsbach and Rengsdorf, and it is part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire World Heritage Site, inscribed in 2005 for this stretch. The Limes began on the Rhine at Rheinbrohl, a little downstream, and ran for over 500 kilometres to the Danube, a line of wooden palisades, ditches, ramparts and watchtowers.

In the forest here you can sometimes trace the line of the rampart and ditch as a low bank and hollow among the trees, and the sites of watchtowers are marked. It takes imagination to picture the frontier as it was: cleared land, a palisade of oak stakes, towers every few hundred metres with soldiers watching for signals. Neuwied had a large Roman fort at Niederbieber, one of the biggest on the Limes, and a museum in the town displays finds from it.

The Westerwald is a land of low mountains, forests, meadows and small villages, with a slightly rough, upland character. The valleys are cut by rivers, including the Wied, which flows through a narrow, wooded valley to the Rhine. The Wied valley road is a favourite with local riders, with curves, river views and little traffic.

Riding around here offers a mix of fast country roads, winding valley routes and steep climbs. The Rhine valley itself is busy, with traffic on both banks, but the roads into the hills are quieter. Watch for speed cameras and police checks, especially on weekends. Weather can be changeable, with rain and fog in the hills even when the Rhine valley is sunny.

Neuwied, five kilometres away, is the obvious fuel stop. Rengsdorf, a small spa village, has cafés and accommodation. The Westerwald is known for its stoneware pottery and its hearty food, including potato dishes and sausages. On a hot summer day the climb from the sticky Rhine valley into these cool woods feels like opening a fridge.
t.civil settlement of saalburg east of b 4:
The Saalburg is the Roman fort that Germany rebuilt. On the crest of the Taunus north of Bad Homburg, where the Limes crossed a pass, archaeologists excavated the remains of a fort in the nineteenth century, and between 1897 and 1907, with the enthusiastic support of Kaiser Wilhelm II, it was reconstructed with walls, gates, barracks and a headquarters building. Today it is a museum and archaeological park, and the civil settlement, or vicus, that grew up outside the fort lies east of the B 456 road. It is part of the Upper German-Raetian Limes World Heritage Site.

The vicus was where soldiers' families, traders, craftsmen and innkeepers lived, and excavations have revealed houses, wells, baths and a mansio, a guesthouse for travellers. The foundations are marked out in the forest, and walking among them gives a sense of a small Roman town on the edge of the empire. The reconstructed fort itself is a striking sight, whatever the purists say about its accuracy.

The Taunus is a range of low mountains north-west of Frankfurt, covered with forests and crossed by winding roads. The Großer Feldberg, the highest point at 879 metres, is a magnet for riders from the Rhine-Main area, and its roads are full of bikes at weekends. That popularity has brought problems, and the police are very active, with speed checks and, on some roads, noise or weekend restrictions. Ride respectfully and check local rules.

Bad Homburg, six kilometres away, is an elegant spa town with a palace, park and casino, while Friedrichsdorf, founded by French Huguenot refugees, has long been known for its zwieback, a twice-baked rusk. The roads through the Taunus to the Rhine and the Lahn valley offer great riding, with curves, forests and villages.

Wehrheim, three kilometres away, can refuel you, and the Saalburg itself has a café. Frankfurt is close by, with all services. The local drink is apple wine, Apfelwein or Ebbelwoi, served in ribbed glasses with hearty food like green sauce, a cold herb sauce, and potatoes.
t.monheim haus burgel@51.1,6.9:
Haus Bürgel is a manor farm that sits on top of a Roman fort, quite literally. The walls of a late Roman fortification, built in the fourth century to guard the Rhine frontier, form part of the foundations and outer walls of the medieval and later farm buildings, and the site is part of the Lower German Limes World Heritage Site, inscribed in 2021. Between Monheim and Düsseldorf-Urdenbach, it lies in a broad meadow landscape on the right bank of the Rhine.

The curious thing is that the fort was originally on the left bank. The Rhine has shifted its course many times, and according to local accounts a great flood in the Middle Ages moved the river to the other side of Bürgel, leaving the site on the opposite bank from where the Romans had built it. The meadows around, the Urdenbacher Kämpe, are now a nature reserve with old river channels, pollarded willows, orchards and wildlife, including storks, herons and many birds.

Across the river, the medieval customs town of Zons has walls, towers and a castle, one of the best preserved small fortified towns on the Rhine. The ferry between the two banks is a pleasant way to cross, and Zons is worth a stroll. Düsseldorf, with its old town, Rhine promenade and art collections, is just to the north, and Cologne is not far to the south.

Riding in this area is mostly flat and urban, with dense traffic around Düsseldorf and Cologne and busy roads along the Rhine. But the dyke roads and lanes through the meadows are quiet and pleasant, and the small villages and farms give a feel of the old Rhineland. Watch for cyclists, who are many, and for speed cameras.

Monheim, four kilometres away, and Dormagen across the river are both big enough for fuel and a meal without any searching. The Rhineland is beer country: Altbier in Düsseldorf, Kölsch in Cologne, and the rivalry between them is serious. A plate of Rhineland food, such as Sauerbraten or Himmel und Ääd, black pudding with potato and apple, is a good way to round off a ride.
t.watchtower wp 1 60@50.4,7.6:
Above Koblenz, on the edge of the Westerwald, the potters of Höhr-Grenzhausen have been making grey, salt-glazed stoneware with cobalt-blue decoration for centuries, giving this corner of Germany its nickname, the Kannenbäckerland, the land of jug bakers. In the forest nearby, the site of Roman watchtower WP 1/60 on the Upper German-Raetian Limes is part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire World Heritage Site. The tower was one of hundreds along the frontier, a wooden or stone structure from which soldiers watched the land beyond and signalled to their neighbours.

Not much remains of the tower, but the line of the Limes can sometimes be traced in the forest as a bank and ditch, and signposted trails follow it. Imagine the frontier as it was: a cleared strip, a palisade, towers at intervals, and beyond it the territory of the Germanic tribes.

The stoneware tradition is alive and well. The Keramikmuseum Westerwald in Höhr-Grenzhausen shows the history of the craft, and many workshops sell their wares. The clay deposits of the region are among the richest in Europe, and the industry has evolved into modern ceramics and technical materials.

The riding in this area is enjoyable. The Westerwald is a land of rolling hills, forests and villages, with winding roads and little traffic. The roads down to the Rhine and the Lahn valleys are steep and twisty, with views over the rivers. Koblenz, where the Moselle meets the Rhine at the Deutsches Eck, is a short ride away, and the Rhine gorge to the south, with its castles and vineyards, is one of the most famous landscapes in Germany. Traffic can be heavy along the rivers, especially in summer.

Höhr-Grenzhausen, two kilometres away, has fuel and cafés, and the A48 motorway passes close by if you need to cover distance towards Koblenz. Several pottery workshops welcome visitors, and a salt-glazed beer mug makes a surprisingly robust souvenir if wrapped in a fleece in the top box.
t.national park wadden sea niedersachsen@5:
At low tide, the sea simply leaves. Twice a day the North Sea withdraws from the Wadden Sea, exposing vast flats of mud and sand, channels and banks, where birds feed by the hundreds of thousands and seals haul out to rest. The Lower Saxony Wadden Sea National Park protects this coast, and together with the Dutch and Danish parts it forms the Wadden Sea World Heritage Site, inscribed in 2009. The coordinates put you near the Butjadingen peninsula, between the Jade Bay and the mouth of the Weser.

The Wadden Sea is one of the most important areas in the world for migratory birds, a refuelling stop for millions on their journeys between the Arctic and Africa. Spring and autumn bring huge flocks of waders, geese and ducks, a spectacle of sound and movement. The mudflats are full of life: worms, shellfish and crabs feed the birds, and the channels are nurseries for fish.

Walking on the mudflats, Wattwandern, is a unique experience, but it should only be done with a guide, as the tides come in quickly and the channels can be dangerous. Fedderwardersiel, on the Butjadingen coast, is a small harbour where shrimp boats unload their catch, and you can buy fresh North Sea shrimps on the quay.

The riding is flat and windy. The roads run along the dykes and through the marshland, with sheep grazing on the dykes and wide views over the sea and land. The wind can be very strong, especially in autumn and winter, and rain is common. Cattle grids and gates on dyke roads are common, so take care. The landscape is open, with farms, villages and church towers on the horizon.

Wilhelmshaven, across the Jade Bay, is a naval port with museums and a deep-water container terminal, and Nordenham on the Weser has more services. Butjadingen's villages have fuel and shops. Order a shrimp roll on the quay, then tea the Frisian way: rock sugar in the cup, strong tea poured over it so it crackles, and a spoon of cream laid on top and never stirred.
t.uedem hochwald hochwald 7 2@51.7,6.4:
The Hochwald, a low wooded ridge between Uedem, Xanten and Kalkar in the Lower Rhine region, hides the traces of Roman military camps, temporary enclosures where troops trained, camped or prepared for campaigns. Uedem-Hochwald 7.2 is one of these, and the camps are part of the Lower German Limes World Heritage Site, inscribed in 2021. The camps were discovered through aerial photography and laser scanning, and they show how intensively the Romans used this area near their great base at Xanten.

Xanten, seven kilometres away, was one of the most important Roman sites in Germany. The legionary fortress of Vetera stood nearby, and the city of Colonia Ulpia Traiana grew into a major town. Today the LVR Archaeological Park in Xanten has reconstructed parts of the Roman city, including walls, a temple and an amphitheatre. The medieval town has a magnificent Gothic cathedral, St Victor's, and according to the Nibelungenlied, the hero Siegfried was born in Xanten.

The Lower Rhine landscape is flat, with fields, meadows, woods and old towns. The Rhine flows broad and slow, with dykes and floodplains. Kalkar, nearby, is a well-preserved medieval town, and its outskirts hold a curiosity: a nuclear power plant that was built but never switched on, now converted into an amusement park. The Reichswald forest to the north was the scene of fierce fighting in early 1945, and war cemeteries mark the battles.

Riding here is relaxed, with straight roads, gentle curves and little traffic. The roads along the Rhine and through the villages are pleasant, and cyclists are common. The weather is mild but changeable, with rain and wind coming off the North Sea.

Xanten, Uedem and Kalkar are all large enough for fuel and food. In May and June the Lower Rhine goes asparagus-mad, with white spears and hollandaise on every menu, and Xanten's market square is a pleasant place to sit with a coffee after a walk through the Roman park.
Bulguksa sits on the lower slopes of Tohamsan, a forested mountain above Gyeongju, and it is the most famous Buddhist temple in Korea. It was largely built in the eighth century under the Silla kingdom, at a time when Gyeongju was its capital and one of the largest cities in Asia, and tradition credits the work to the minister Kim Dae-seong. Stone staircases and terraces from that time still carry the wooden halls, which have been rebuilt after fires and wars, most destructively during the Japanese invasions of the 1590s.

In the main courtyard stand two stone pagodas that every Korean schoolchild knows. Dabotap is intricate and almost playful, with balustrades and stairs carved in granite; Seokgatap beside it is simple and severe. Seen together they feel like a conversation between two ideas of beauty. Arrive early on a weekday to have the courtyards nearly to yourself; by mid-morning the school groups pour in.

From the temple a road climbs up Tohamsan to Seokguram, and this is the part for a rider. It is a winding mountain road with tight bends through thick forest, steep in places and busy with tour buses at peak times, so ride it with care and look out for cyclists. At the top, a short walk leads to the grotto, an artificial cave built of granite blocks in the eighth century, housing a seated Buddha facing east toward the sea. The statue is now behind glass, but its calm and the precision of the dome above it are remarkable. Locals have long climbed here before dawn to watch the sun rise over the East Sea, and on a clear morning it is worth the early start.

Gyeongju is often called a museum without walls. Grassy royal tombs rise like small hills in the middle of town, the Cheomseongdae observatory stands in a field, and the reconstructed pavilions of Donggung Palace and Wolji Pond are reflected in the water at night. Lake Bomun, between the town and the temple, is lined with cherry trees that make April the busiest and prettiest month.

Fuel and food are easy in Gyeongju and the surrounding towns. Bear in mind that motorcycles are not allowed on Korean expressways, so plan routes on national roads, which are often more interesting anyway. Try Gyeongju bread, a small round pastry filled with sweet red bean, and a bowl of ssambap, rice with a spread of leaves and side dishes, in one of the restaurants near the tombs.
t.mausoleum of king kongmin@38.0,126.5:
Of all the places on the list of world heritage, the Mausoleum of King Kongmin must be one of the hardest to reach on two wheels, because it lies in North Korea, in the hills west of the old city of Kaesong. The coordinates put it a few kilometres from the town, close to the line that has divided the peninsula since 1953, and independent travel there, let alone riding a motorcycle, is not something a visitor can simply decide to do.

The tomb itself is a beautiful thing, by the accounts of the people who have seen it. King Gongmin ruled the Goryeo kingdom in the fourteenth century, a reformer who tried to loosen the grip of the Mongol Yuan dynasty on his country. He married a Mongol princess, Queen Noguk, and when she died in childbirth he was devastated, spending years building her tomb and then his own beside it. The two mounds stand side by side on a hillside, guarded by stone figures of officials and animals, with a view across a valley that was chosen with great care according to the principles of geomancy. Gongmin was assassinated in 1374, and Goryeo did not long outlast him.

Kaesong was the capital of Goryeo for nearly five centuries, and the monuments in and around it were inscribed together by UNESCO in 2013. The kingdom gave Korea its name in Western languages and is remembered for its celadon ceramics, with their soft blue-green glaze, and for early metal movable type.

In practical terms, this is not a ride anyone can plan at present. Access to North Korea for foreigners has been tightly restricted and only possible on organised tours at the best of times, and the border region near Kaesong is heavily militarised. From the southern side, the observatories along the demilitarised zone, near Paju and on Ganghwa island, let you look across the Han estuary toward the north, and the riding along the coastal roads of Ganghwa is easy and quiet. Ganghwa town, about twenty-five kilometres from the tomb as the crow flies, has fuel, food and a market famous for ginseng and pickled fish.

It is worth knowing the place exists, a love story carved in stone just out of reach, and thinking about the line that keeps it there.
t.gwangneung cluster t@37.8,127.2:
Gwangneung is the tomb of King Sejo of Joseon and his queen, Jeonghui, and it sits inside one of the best-preserved forests in Korea, north-east of Seoul between Namyangju and Pocheon. Sejo seized the throne in 1455 from his young nephew Danjong, who was later exiled and killed, and he spent much of his reign strengthening royal power. In death, though, he asked for modesty: he ordered that his tomb be built without the usual stone burial chamber and without some of the stone ornaments, to save the people labour and expense. The two mounds lie on separate ridges, with a shrine between them.

The royal tombs of the Joseon dynasty were listed together by UNESCO in 2009, and each follows a careful layout based on geomancy, with mountains behind, water in front and an approach that moves from the everyday world to the sacred. Walking up the path at Gwangneung, under tall trees, you feel that transition quite physically: the noise of the road fades, the air cools, and the grassy mounds appear above you on their slope.

The forest is the other reason to come. Because the land around the tomb was protected as royal property for centuries, cutting trees was forbidden, and the result is a mature woodland of oaks, firs and pines that is now home to the Korea National Arboretum. It is a sanctuary for birds, insects and plants that have vanished from much of the rest of the country, including a famous woodpecker that is a national natural monument. Visits to the arboretum usually need booking in advance, and it is closed on certain days.

The roads through this area are a welcome escape from the city. Small routes run through the wooded valleys between Uijeongbu, Pocheon and Namyangju, with gentle curves and short climbs over low passes, and on weekday mornings they are pleasant and calm. Weekends are a different story, when half of Seoul seems to be heading out to the hills. Remember that motorcycles are banned from Korean expressways, so plan your route on national and local roads.

Uijeongbu and Namyangju are large cities with fuel and food everywhere. Uijeongbu is known across Korea for budae-jjigae, the army stew of sausages, ham, noodles and kimchi that grew out of the post-war years around the American bases, and it makes a hearty lunch after a morning among the kings.
t.seocheon getbol@36.0,126.6:
The tide here goes out so far that the sea simply disappears. The Seocheon getbol, a vast sweep of tidal flats on the west coast of Korea where the Geum river meets the Yellow Sea, is one of four areas listed by UNESCO in 2021 as the Korean Tidal Flats. Twice a day the water withdraws over kilometres of glistening mud and sand, leaving channels, pools and a hum of life: crabs, worms, shellfish and mudskippers, and above all birds.

This coast is a critical stopover on the East Asian–Australasian Flyway, the migration route that carries shorebirds between Siberia and Alaska in the north and Southeast Asia and Australia in the south. In spring and autumn the flats fill with flocks of waders feeding to rebuild their strength, and some of the world's rarest species pass through, including the spoon-billed sandpiper and the black-faced spoonbill. Bring binoculars and time the visit for a rising tide, when the birds are pushed closer to the shore. The National Institute of Ecology, a large research centre with excellent exhibitions and glass domes recreating climates of the world, is in Seocheon and makes an informative stop.

The area has its own traditions. Hansan, in the north of the county, is famous for mosi, a fine ramie fabric woven by hand from plant fibre that was once worn by the court in summer, and for sogokju, a strong rice wine. In spring the fishing harbours celebrate jjukkumi, small webfoot octopus, and the camellia forest at Maryang-ri blooms red above the sea.

The riding is coastal and gentle, along small roads that follow the dykes and bays, through fish farms, reed beds and salt fields, with the light changing all the time over the mud. Wind is a constant companion on this exposed shore, and in winter it comes straight off the sea with a bite. Across the estuary, the city of Gunsan is linked by a road along the river barrage and has a lovely old quarter of colonial-era buildings from the early twentieth century, when the port shipped rice out to Japan.

Motorcycles are not allowed on Korean expressways, but the national roads along this coast are perfectly adequate. Fuel and food are easy in Seocheon town and in Gunsan. Try a bowl of seafood kalguksu or grilled shellfish at one of the harbours, and watch the tide come back as you eat.
t.jeongneung cluster@37.6,127.0:
Jeongneung is a royal tomb in the middle of Seoul, in the wooded hills of Seongbuk district just north of the old city, and it carries one of the more spiteful stories of the early Joseon court. It belongs to Queen Sindeok, the second wife of the dynasty's founder, King Taejo. Her son was named crown prince ahead of Taejo's older sons by his first wife, and one of those older sons, Yi Bang-won, struck back violently, killing his half-brothers and eventually taking the throne as King Taejong.

Sindeok had died before all this, and Taejo had buried her in a fine tomb inside the city. Once Taejong was in power, he had it moved out to what was then the countryside, beyond the walls, and reduced its status. Stone pieces from the original tomb were reused in Gwangtonggyo, a bridge over the Cheonggyecheon stream, where people would walk over them every day. Some of those carved stones can still be seen there. The tomb was only restored to proper honours centuries later.

Today Jeongneung is a quiet, forested place, much smaller and more intimate than most of the Joseon royal tombs, with a path leading up through tall trees to the mound on its hillside. It sits on the lower slopes of Bugaksan and the ridges leading toward Bukhansan National Park, and walking trails head up into the hills from nearby. In spring the azaleas and cherry blossoms light up the slopes; in autumn the maples turn red and the city below seems a long way away.

The riding is city riding, through a dense, hilly district of apartment blocks and narrow streets. Seoul traffic is fast and impatient, buses have priority lanes, and motorcycles are not allowed on Korean expressways or on the urban expressways that ring the city, so plan routes along ordinary roads. The roads that wind over the ridges north of the centre can be enjoyable in the early morning, with views back over the old city and the palaces.

Fuel, food and coffee are everywhere. The neighbourhoods around Seongbuk have traditional houses, small museums and good restaurants, and a bowl of naengmyeon, cold buckwheat noodles in icy broth, is welcome after a hot climb in summer. Afterwards, ride down into the city and look for Gwangtonggyo, to see a queen's grave stones under your feet.
t.changdeokgung palace complex@37.6,127.0:
Changdeokgung was built in 1405 as a secondary palace for the Joseon kings, and it ended up being the one they actually liked living in. Where the main palace, Gyeongbokgung, was laid out on a strict axis, Changdeokgung was fitted into the foot of the hills, following the folds of the ground, and its halls, gates and courtyards feel more relaxed and more human as a result. After the Japanese invasions of the 1590s burned all of Seoul's palaces, this was the first to be rebuilt, and it served as the main royal residence for some two and a half centuries.

The highlight is the garden behind the palace, known as Huwon or the Secret Garden. It covers a wooded valley with ponds, pavilions, a library where young scholars studied, and paths that wind under old trees. The most famous view is the square pond of Buyongji with a pavilion standing with its feet in the water, an image of the old Korean idea of a square earth and a round heaven. Access to the garden is by timed guided tour, with limited numbers, so book ahead or arrive early, especially in autumn when the maples blaze and every Seoul resident with a camera wants a ticket.

The palace sits right in the old heart of Seoul. Next door is Changgyeonggung, another palace linked by gates and paths, and just to the west lies Bukchon, a hillside district of traditional hanok houses with tiled roofs and narrow lanes. Ikseon-dong, a little to the south, has turned its old alleys into cafés and small restaurants. On a weekday morning you can walk through four or five centuries of the city in a couple of hours.

For a rider, Seoul is an exercise in patience and alertness. Traffic is dense, delivery scooters dart everywhere, and motorcycles are banned from the national expressways and the city's urban expressways, so you will be on surface roads with plenty of traffic lights. Park outside the palace and walk; the old quarter is a place for feet, not wheels. The best riding out of the city starts once you cross the northern ridges toward the hills.

Fuel, food and coffee are everywhere. The markets of nearby Jongno serve everything from mung-bean pancakes to bowls of rice with raw beef, and Gwangjang Market in particular is a lively, steamy place to eat standing at a counter among the locals before heading back to the bike.
t.berg en dal de holdeurn north@51.8,5.9:
Just east of Nijmegen, where the Netherlands suddenly remembers how to make hills, a wooded slope near the village of Berg en Dal hides the remains of a Roman industrial site. De Holdeurn was where the Tenth Legion, Legio X Gemina, stationed at Nijmegen in the late first and early second centuries, made roof tiles, bricks and pottery, stamped with the legion's name and shipped all over the region. The kilns and workshops have been excavated, and the site is one of the many places that make up the Frontiers of the Roman Empire – the Lower German Limes, listed by UNESCO in 2021.

The landscape explains why the Romans liked it. The hills here are an ice-pushed moraine, piled up by glaciers during an ice age, with clay deposits and wood for fuel close at hand, and the river Waal nearby for transport. Nijmegen grew from a Roman base into a town and claims to be the oldest city in the Netherlands. The Museum Het Valkhof in the city has a superb collection of Roman finds from the area, including objects from De Holdeurn.

For riders, this corner is a rare treat in a flat country. The roads around Berg en Dal, Groesbeek and the Duivelsberg climb and dip through beech woods, with short, steep gradients and proper bends, and they are popular with cyclists too, so ride with consideration. To the north, the Ooijpolder spreads out between the hills and the Waal, a landscape of dykes, meadows, side channels and grazing cattle, where narrow dyke roads give long views across the floodplain. Over the border to the east, the German roads around Kranenburg and the Reichswald forest add more variety.

There is twentieth-century history here as well. Groesbeek, a few kilometres to the south, was one of the landing zones for American paratroopers during Operation Market Garden in September 1944, and the National Liberation Museum and the war cemeteries in the area tell the story of the bitter fighting that followed through the winter of 1944–45.

Practical needs are easily met. Hengstdal, a district of Nijmegen just four kilometres away, and the city itself have fuel, cafés and shops. On a fine day, the terraces in Berg en Dal and along the Ooijpolder are lovely places for a coffee and a slice of apple pie, the Dutch answer to every question, before heading back into the hills.
t.fortlet of pfarrhofen@50.2,7.9:
In the second century, the Roman frontier in Germany ran across the hills of the Taunus north of the Rhine as a line of wooden palisades, ditches, earth banks, watchtowers and forts, stretching over five hundred kilometres from the Rhine to the Danube. The Upper Germanic-Raetian Limes, as it is called, is part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire, listed by UNESCO in 2005, and the fortlet of Pfarrhofen, near Holzhausen an der Haide in the western Taunus, is one of the many small installations along its course. A fortlet was a small fort with a garrison of a few dozen men, guarding a road crossing or a section of the frontier between larger forts.

At Pfarrhofen, the remains are modest: low earthworks and stones in a forest clearing, with information panels explaining the site. Walking along the line of the frontier, which is marked by a trail, you can see the remains of the bank and ditch in the forest, and imagine the soldiers who patrolled it.

The western Taunus is a quiet, rural area of forested hills, fields and small villages, between the Lahn and the Rhine. The roads through it are narrow, winding and generally well surfaced, with little traffic, and they offer pleasant riding through the forest and over the hills. To the west, the Rhine gorge, the Upper Middle Rhine Valley, is a UNESCO site, with castles on the cliffs, vineyards on the slopes and the famous Loreley rock, and the roads along the river, on both banks, are scenic though busy. Ferries cross the Rhine at several points, as there are no bridges between Koblenz and Mainz.

To the north, the Lahn valley offers another lovely ride, with the spa town of Bad Ems and the town of Nassau, home of the counts of Nassau, ancestors of the Dutch royal family. The road along the river winds through a narrow valley with forests and castles.

Nastätten, about four kilometres away, has fuel and basic services; Nassau, about twelve kilometres away, is larger. In the villages, try a plate of Handkäs mit Musik, a sour milk cheese marinated in vinegar, oil and onions, a speciality of Hesse and the Rhineland, or a glass of Riesling from the Rhine vineyards. And walk for a while along the frontier line in the forest, where the silence of the trees is broken only by birdsong.
t.watchtoers wp 2 26 to 2 30@50.2,7.9:
Kastell Holzhausen is one of the best-preserved Roman forts along the German Limes, and it lies in a forest clearing near the village of Holzhausen an der Haide in the western Taunus, where the remains of its stone walls, gates and corner towers still stand to a height of a metre or more. The fort housed an auxiliary cohort of several hundred soldiers in the second and third centuries, and it guarded a section of the frontier, the Upper Germanic-Raetian Limes, along with a chain of watchtowers spaced at regular intervals along the line. The watchtowers numbered WP 2/26 to 2/30, part of the UNESCO listing, stood on this section between the fort and its neighbours.

The watchtowers were the eyes of the frontier. Built first of wood and later of stone, they stood a few hundred metres apart, within sight of each other, so that signals could be passed along the line. Soldiers stationed in them watched the palisade and the land beyond, and could call for help from the forts if trouble appeared. Most of the towers survive only as low mounds in the forest, but walking the Limes trail, you can still trace the line of the frontier, with the bank and ditch visible among the trees.

The western Taunus is a quiet, rolling landscape of forests and fields, with small villages and farms, between the Rhine, the Lahn and the Aar. The roads are narrow and winding, with generally good surfaces and light traffic, and they offer relaxed riding through the forest and over the hills. The B260, the Bäderstraße, runs from Wiesbaden north-west through the Taunus to Bad Ems and the Lahn valley, a scenic route through forests and villages, popular with riders.

Nearby, the Aar valley, with the towns of Hohenstein and Michelbach, has winding roads and castle ruins, and to the west, the Rhine gorge, with its castles and vineyards, is a short ride away.

Nastätten, about five kilometres away, has fuel and basic services; Nassau, about eleven kilometres away, is larger. In the villages, look for a country inn, a Landgasthof, serving local dishes like Sauerbraten, marinated pot roast with red cabbage and potato dumplings, or schnitzel with mushroom sauce. And take the time to walk around the walls of the fort, imagining the soldiers who once lived here, on the edge of the empire, far from home.
t.watchtower wp 1 52@50.4,7.6:
The Roman frontier in Germany began on the Rhine at Rheinbrohl, a few kilometres downstream from Koblenz, where the first watchtower of the Upper Germanic Limes, WP 1/1, stood on the riverbank. From there, the frontier ran south-east through the Westerwald and the Taunus, and the watchtower WP 1/52, near Bendorf, stood on this early section, close to the Rhine and the confluence of the Moselle at Koblenz. The tower is long gone, but its site is part of the UNESCO listing of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire, and the Roemerwelt museum at Rheinbrohl brings the life of the frontier soldiers vividly to life with reconstructions and hands-on exhibits.

Bendorf is a small town on the right bank of the Rhine, just north of Koblenz, and its district of Sayn has two attractions worth visiting. The Sayn ironworks, the Sayner Hütte, is a remarkable cast-iron foundry hall built in the early nineteenth century, an early masterpiece of industrial architecture. Above it, the ruins of Sayn castle overlook the valley, and the Sayn palace, in the valley below, has a garden of butterflies, where tropical butterflies fly freely in a glasshouse.

Koblenz, across the river, sits at the meeting of the Rhine and the Moselle, at a point called the Deutsches Eck, the German Corner, marked by a huge equestrian statue of Emperor Wilhelm I. Above the city, the fortress of Ehrenbreitstein, one of the largest fortresses in Europe, offers wonderful views over the rivers and is reached by a cable car across the Rhine.

For riders, the area around Koblenz offers some of the best riding in Germany. The Moselle valley, to the south-west, winds through steep vineyards and wine villages, with a road along the river and side roads climbing up to the hills. The Rhine gorge, to the south, has castles on every hill. To the north and east, the Westerwald, a rolling upland of forests and fields, offers quiet, winding roads. The Eifel, to the west, with its volcanic lakes and the Nürburgring, is another riders' paradise. Traffic around Koblenz can be heavy, but the side roads are much quieter.

Bendorf, a town of over seventeen thousand people about two kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants. Try a plate of Döppekuchen, a hearty potato cake with bacon, a speciality of the Westerwald, or a glass of Moselle Riesling, and take a ride along the Rhine in the evening light, with the castles glowing on the hills.
t.watchtowers wp 4 1 to 4 19a including fo:
Kaiser Wilhelm II took a personal interest in the Roman frontier, and at the beginning of the twentieth century, he ordered the complete reconstruction of the Saalburg, a Roman fort on the crest of the Taunus near Bad Homburg. The result, with its walls, gates and buildings rebuilt on the original foundations, is the most complete reconstruction of a Roman fort in Germany and houses a museum of Roman life on the frontier. A few kilometres north-east, near Rosbach vor der Höhe, the ruins of the Kapersburg fort lie in the forest, and the watchtowers numbered WP 4/1 to 4/19a, on the section of the Limes running from the Taunus ridge toward the Wetterau, are part of the UNESCO listing of the Upper Germanic-Raetian Limes.

The Taunus ridge rises north of Frankfurt, a range of forested hills with the Großer Feldberg, at 879 metres, the highest point. On a clear day, the view from the top stretches over Frankfurt's skyline and the Rhine-Main plain. The ridge is crossed by roads that climb through the forest, and on fine weekends, the Feldberg is a magnet for riders from all over the region, with a car park at the top where bikes gather in rows.

For riders, the roads of the Taunus are a favourite, with tight bends, steep climbs and descents through the forest, and good surfaces. But be aware that their popularity has led to problems: accidents and noise have brought lower speed limits and regular controls on the favourite stretches, and police are frequently present on sunny weekends. Ride responsibly and check for any current restrictions before you go. To the north, the Wetterau is a flat, fertile plain of fields and villages, with straight roads and little excitement, but with interesting small towns.

Bad Homburg, below the Saalburg, is an elegant spa town with a palace, a casino and a park, and Friedrichsdorf, nearby, was founded by Huguenot refugees and is known for its rusks. Frankfurt, half an hour away, has everything you could want.

Rosbach vor der Höhe, a town of over eleven thousand people about four kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants; Friedrichsdorf and Wehrheim are also close. Try a plate of Grüne Soße, a cold green sauce made with seven herbs, served with boiled eggs and potatoes, a speciality of Frankfurt, or a glass of Apfelwein, the local cider, in a traditional tavern. And at the Saalburg, take a moment to walk through the reconstructed gate, and imagine the frontier as it was nearly two thousand years ago.
t.watchtowers wp 4 53 to 4 57@50.5,8.8:
The Wetterau is the broad, fertile plain north of Frankfurt, between the Taunus and the Vogelsberg, and the Romans considered it so valuable that they bent their frontier around it to include it in the empire. The Limes ran along the northern edge of the plain, and the watchtowers numbered WP 4/53 to 4/57, near the town of Lich, stood on this section, part of the Upper Germanic-Raetian Limes listed by UNESCO in 2005. Like most watchtowers, they survive only as mounds or traces in the fields and forest, but the line of the frontier can be followed on foot or by bicycle.

The countryside around Lich has much to offer. A few kilometres south of the town, the ruins of Arnsburg Abbey, a Cistercian monastery founded in the twelfth century, stand in a peaceful setting by the river Wetter, with a Gothic church open to the sky and a monastic garden. To the south-west, the castle of Münzenberg, with its two tall towers, rises on a hill above the plain; locals call it the Wetterauer Tintenfass, the inkwell of the Wetterau, for its shape. Lich itself is a small, charming town with half-timbered houses and a brewery whose beer is known across Hesse.

For riders, the real attraction lies to the east, in the Vogelsberg, a vast extinct volcano, the largest volcanic massif in Central Europe, now a rolling upland of forests, pastures and small villages. The roads up into the Vogelsberg are winding and scenic, with good surfaces and light traffic. Near Schotten, the Schottenring, a public road circuit, hosted motorcycle races in the 1920s and 1950s, including world championship events, and riders still come to ride its curves, though it is an ordinary road today with traffic and speed limits.

The Hoherodskopf, near the summit of the Vogelsberg, has a car park, a restaurant and views over the surrounding countryside, and it is a popular meeting point for riders on weekends. In winter, snow can cover the higher roads, and fog is common in autumn.

Lich, a town of over thirteen thousand people about three kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants; Münzenberg and Hungen are smaller. Try a plate of Ahle Wurst, a dried sausage typical of northern Hesse, or a Schmandkuchen, a sour cream cake, with a glass of local beer. And take a walk through the ruins of Arnsburg in the evening, when the light falls through the empty windows of the church.
t.fortsite of holzhausen and civil settlem:
Up on the high, rolling plateau between the Rhine and the Lahn, where the Taunus fades into fields and beech woods, the Romans built one of the better preserved stone forts on the Upper German Limes. Holzhausen an der Haide is a quiet village of a little over a thousand people, and the fort sits just outside it in the trees, the outline of its walls still traceable on the ground, with the gates and corner towers marked out where the stone survives. It is part of the UNESCO-listed frontier that once ran from the Rhine near Koblenz all the way to the Danube, a line of palisade, ditch, watchtowers and garrisons meant less to stop armies than to control who came and went, and what they paid for the privilege.

Around the fort there was a civil settlement, the vicus, where soldiers' families, traders, tavern keepers and craftsmen lived off the garrison's pay. Nothing much of that stands today, but walking the perimeter you get a sense of how exposed this place was: a ridge of open country, wind coming over from the west, and the dark forest of the Germanic side not far beyond.

The riding up here is unhurried and genuinely pleasant. Small roads link Nastätten, Katzenelnbogen and the villages of the Einrich, as this corner is called, with long open bends across farmland and short wooded sections where the tarmac can stay damp well into the day. Traffic is light outside harvest time, when tractors own the lanes. Katzenelnbogen is worth the short detour for its castle above the village; the counts who took their name from it grew rich on Rhine tolls before the line died out in the fifteenth century. Further south the road down towards Bad Schwalbach drops through proper Taunus forest, all beech and spruce, with tighter turns and a few steep pitches.

For fuel, Nastätten is the nearest place you can rely on, and it also has bakeries and somewhere for a coffee. Bad Schwalbach, the old spa town with its mineral springs, is the bigger option if you want lunch with a terrace. Come in late spring or early autumn, when the fields are green or gold and the light lies low across the plateau; on a grey November day the place feels exactly like the edge of an empire, which, to be fair, is what it was.
t.watchtowers wp 5 15 to 5 16@50.1,9.0:
Great forts are rare on the Limes; most of the frontier was watchtowers, small timber and later stone posts within sight of each other, each with a handful of men and a fire for signalling. The towers numbered 5/15 and 5/16 stood near Großkrotzenburg, at the point where the land frontier coming down from the Wetterau met the Main, and from here southward the river itself became the border as far as Miltenberg. Little of them remains to see, but the location tells the story: the Romans used water where they could and built palisades only where they had to.

Großkrotzenburg sits on top of a Roman fort, and traces of it have been found beneath the old village. Today the skyline is dominated by the chimneys and cooling tower of the big power station on the river, a slightly jarring neighbour for a heritage site, but a good landmark when you are trying to find your way across the flat country between Hanau and Aschaffenburg.

This is not mountain riding. The roads along the Main are straight, built-up and often slow, linking commuter towns where Hesse and Bavaria meet. The pleasure lies in the stops. Seligenstadt, a few kilometres upstream, is the one not to miss: a handsome old town of half-timbered houses around a market square, and a great basilica founded by Einhard, Charlemagne's biographer and adviser, who is buried there. A small car and passenger ferry crosses the Main from Seligenstadt to the Bavarian bank, and taking it on a bike is a quietly happy few minutes.

If you want curves, they are close. North of the river the hills of the Spessart rise behind Alzenau and Kahl, with forest roads that climb and twist through oak and beech, and to the south the Odenwald begins within half an hour. The Main valley itself is better treated as the link between them.

Fuel is easy: Großkrotzenburg, Kahl and Seligenstadt all have stations, and Seligenstadt has plenty of cafés around the square and along the riverbank, where in summer half the region seems to sit with an ice cream. Expect heavy traffic around Hanau at rush hour and come instead on a weekend morning, when the river is misty and the only sound is a barge working upstream.
t.oksan seowon@36.0,129.2:
Oksan-seowon sits in a quiet valley northwest of Gyeongju, beside a clear stream that tumbles over smooth granite slabs. It was founded in 1572 to honour Yi Eon-jeok, one of the great Neo-Confucian scholars of the Joseon dynasty, who lived in retreat nearby, and it served as a private academy where young men studied the Confucian classics, prepared for the state examinations, and performed rites in honour of the master. The buildings are arranged according to the strict logic of Confucian architecture: a lecture hall, dormitories for students, a library and, at the back, a shrine for the rites. The architecture is restrained, with wooden halls, tiled roofs and open courtyards, designed to harmonise with the landscape. Oksan is part of the UNESCO listing of the Seowon, Korean Neo-Confucian Academies, inscribed in 2019.

A short walk upstream stands the Dongnakdang, Yi Eon-jeok's own house, built in the sixteenth century, a beautiful example of the residence of a scholar, with a pavilion over the stream. A little further, the temple of Jeonghyesa has an unusual thirteen-storey stone pagoda from the Unified Silla period. Not far away, the Yangdong Folk Village, a UNESCO site in its own right since 2010, is a living village of traditional houses belonging to two aristocratic clans, the Son and the Yi, spread over a hillside. Many of the houses are still inhabited, and walking among them feels like stepping into another century.

Gyeongju, about twenty kilometres south, was the capital of the Silla kingdom for nearly a thousand years, and it is often called a museum without walls. Royal tombs like grassy hills rise in the middle of the city, and the temple of Bulguksa and the Seokguram grotto, with its serene stone Buddha, are on the slopes of Mount Toham.

The riding in the area is pleasant. The roads along the Hyeongsan river and through the valleys north of Gyeongju are quiet, winding gently through rice fields, orchards and villages, with forested hills on both sides. The surface is good, the traffic light outside the towns, and the speed limits enforced by cameras. Korea drives on the right.

Angang, Gyeongju and Pohang have fuel and every service. Try Gyeongju bread, a small round pastry filled with red bean paste, sold all over the city.
t.namgye seowon@35.5,127.8:
Hamyang is a quiet county in the mountains of South Gyeongsang, on the eastern edge of Jirisan, the great massif in the south of the Korean peninsula, and Namgye-seowon stands on a gentle slope a few kilometres from the county town. Founded in 1552 to honour the Neo-Confucian scholar Jeong Yeo-chang, it was one of the earliest private academies in Korea and served as a model for many others. Its layout set a pattern: the lecture hall at the front, dormitories on either side, and the shrine for the rites at the top of the slope, so that the buildings climb the hill in a hierarchy of importance. Unusually, the dormitories have small raised pavilions overlooking ponds, where students could rest and contemplate the landscape. Namgye is part of the UNESCO listing of the Seowon, Korean Neo-Confucian Academies.

Hamyang has another historic treasure. The Sangnim forest, along the river in the county town, was planted more than a thousand years ago by Choe Chi-won, a great scholar of the Silla kingdom, to protect the town from floods. It is one of the oldest man-made forests in Korea, and its old oaks and hornbeams form a cool, shady walk, especially beautiful in autumn.

Jirisan, the second-highest mountain in South Korea, dominates the region. Its national park, the first in the country, covers a vast area of forested ridges, deep valleys and Buddhist temples, and its peaks are often in the clouds. The roads around it are among the best in Korea for motorcycles. The road from Hamyang over the Odo pass towards Jirisan climbs in a beautiful series of hairpins, with views over the ridges, and the roads through the valleys on the eastern side of the massif are winding and scenic, with temples and hot springs. The surface is excellent, the traffic light on weekdays, and the speed limits enforced by cameras. Watch for wild boar and deer.

Hamyang has fuel, shops and restaurants, though it is not listed among the larger towns nearby. The region is famous for mountain herbs and wild ginseng, and Hamyang hosts a festival dedicated to wild ginseng. Try sanchae bibimbap, rice with mountain vegetables, in a restaurant near the park.

The best seasons are spring and autumn; summer is hot and humid, with monsoon rains, and winter brings snow to the mountains.
t.muan hamhaeman getbol@35.1,126.4:
The southwest coast of Korea is a maze of bays, peninsulas and islands, and when the tide goes out, it reveals immense mudflats, the getbol, stretching to the horizon. Hamhae Bay, in Muan county, is one of the finest examples, a sheltered bay where the tides deposit fine mud rich in nutrients, supporting an extraordinary variety of life: crabs, shellfish, worms, mudskippers and octopus, and the birds that feed on them. The Korean tidal flats were listed by UNESCO in 2021, recognising their importance for migratory birds on the East Asian-Australasian Flyway, including endangered species like the spoon-billed sandpiper and the black-faced spoonbill.

Walking on the boardwalks over the mud at low tide, you can watch the mudskippers, small fish that live out of water, skipping across the surface, and the crabs waving their claws. The smell is salty and earthy, the light reflects off the wet mud, and the horizon dissolves into the sky. The local fishermen, often women, go out on the flats with wooden sleds to collect shellfish and octopus, as they have for generations.

Muan is famous for its small octopus, nakji, which is caught in the mudflats and eaten in every way: stir-fried with chilli, in soups, or raw and still wriggling, a dish that tests the courage of visitors. The county is also known for its white lotus pond, the Hoesan Baengnyeonji, one of the largest in Asia, which blooms in July and August.

The riding is gentle and coastal. The roads around Hamhae Bay follow the shoreline, flat and winding, with views over the mudflats and the islands, and long bridges connect the peninsulas and islands of the southwest. Traffic is light outside the towns, the surface good, and the scenery changes constantly with the tide. Mokpo, a port city at the tip of the peninsula, is the gateway to the islands of the southwest, with ferries to hundreds of islands and the Mokpo bridges spanning the harbour.

Muan, about fifteen kilometres away, has fuel and every service, and Mokpo has more. The best seasons are spring and autumn, when migratory birds pass through. Check the tide tables: the mudflats are only visible at low tide, and the sea comes in quickly.
t.schokland and surroundings@52.6,5.8:
Schokland was once an island in the Zuiderzee, a long, narrow strip of peat and clay surrounded by an inland sea that constantly threatened to swallow it. For centuries, its inhabitants lived on raised mounds and fought a losing battle against the water, as storms ate away at the island's edges. By the mid-nineteenth century, life had become so precarious that in 1859 the Dutch government ordered the island to be evacuated. Then, in the twentieth century, the Dutch did something extraordinary: they enclosed the Zuiderzee with a dam, the Afsluitdijk, completed in 1932, and drained large parts of it to create new land. The Noordoostpolder, drained in 1942, swallowed Schokland, and the former island now rises slightly above the surrounding fields, a long green ridge in a flat landscape of farmland. In 1995, Schokland became the first Dutch site to be listed by UNESCO, as a symbol of the Netherlands' heroic struggle against the water.

Today you can walk along the old island, with its church, a museum, the remains of the harbour and the wooden posts that once protected the shore from the waves. The contrast is striking: on one side, the remains of an island life shaped by the sea; on the other, the perfectly straight lines of the polder, with its fields, ditches and farmhouses.

Urk, a few kilometres west, was another island in the Zuiderzee, now joined to the polder, and it remains a fishing town with a strong identity, a tight old village of narrow streets and a lighthouse looking out over the IJsselmeer. Emmeloord, the main town of the polder, was built from scratch after the war, with a water tower in the centre.

The riding is flat, straight and windy. The roads of the polder run in long straight lines between fields, with right-angle turns, and the wind blows across the open landscape with nothing to stop it. It is not a destination for curves, but the sense of space, the enormous sky and the history of the place make it interesting. Watch for cyclists, who have priority on many roads, and for tractors.

Emmeloord has fuel, shops and restaurants, and Urk has fish restaurants serving fresh catch. Try kibbeling, battered fish pieces, at a stand in Urk harbour.
t.wesel fluren flurener feld 1@51.7,6.6:
The Rhine at Wesel is broad and powerful, the main artery of northwestern Europe, and in Roman times it was the frontier of the empire. The Lower German Limes, listed by UNESCO in 2021, ran along the river from the Alps to the North Sea, with forts, camps and watchtowers guarding the crossings. At Flüren, on the edge of Wesel, archaeologists have found traces of Roman activity on the Flürener Feld, probably a temporary camp or military installation linked to campaigns across the river into Germania. Nothing is visible on the surface, but the site sits on the edge of the Rhine plain, with the river and its floodplain stretching away to the horizon.

The great Roman centre of the region was Xanten, a short ride downstream, where the Roman city of Colonia Ulpia Traiana has been partly reconstructed in an archaeological park, with an amphitheatre, a temple and city walls. Before that, the legionary fortress of Vetera stood on a hill nearby, and it was from here that Roman legions set out in AD 9 on the campaign that ended in disaster in the Teutoburg Forest.

Wesel itself was a prosperous Hanseatic town in the Middle Ages, but its history in the twentieth century was brutal. In 1945, as the Allies prepared to cross the Rhine, the town was almost completely destroyed by bombing; very few buildings survived. In March of that year, the Allied armies crossed the Rhine at Wesel in a massive operation, with paratroopers landing on the eastern bank. The town was rebuilt after the war, and today it is a modern, pleasant place, with a reconstructed town hall façade, a citadel, and a museum of the Prussian era.

The riding is flat and easy. The roads along the Rhine and through the countryside of the Lower Rhine are straight or gently curving, with fields, farms, windmills and dykes. The Rhine bridge at Wesel, a modern cable-stayed bridge, offers views over the river. Watch for cyclists and tractors, and for wind on the open plain.

Wesel has fuel, shops and restaurants, and Hamminkeln is nearby. Try Rhenish dishes like Himmel und Erde, mashed potatoes and apples with black pudding, in a traditional pub.
t.neuss reckberg kleinkastell@51.2,6.8:
The Rhine was the northern frontier of the Roman Empire for centuries, and the string of forts, towers and camps along its western bank is now recognised as the Lower Germanic Limes, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2021. Reckberg was one of the small forts, a Kleinkastell, built to watch the river and the road, and I have no confident knowledge of exactly what visitors will see at the pin today; it is likely to be subtle, with a marker or information board rather than standing walls.

The better story is Neuss next door, which began as Novaesium, one of the oldest Roman military sites in Germany. A large legionary camp stood here in the first century, with troops guarding the crossing and supply route, and a civilian town grew beside it. The name survives in the modern city, and the Quirinus minster, a large Romanesque and Gothic church, shows how the place continued as a religious centre. Across the river, Düsseldorf was a small fishing village for most of the Roman era and only became a big city much later.

The riding here is flat Rhineland, a landscape of fields, power lines, industry and suburbs, where the pleasure is in the history rather than the road. Surfaces are good, traffic can be dense around Düsseldorf and Neuss, and the roads are full of commuters and lorries, so choose your time with care. The quieter back roads through farmland near the river offer a more relaxed ride, and the Rhine promenade in Düsseldorf is pleasant for a stroll. Autumn mist along the river and the smell of cut sugar beet are characteristic of the region.

Fuel is available on all main roads in Neuss and Düsseldorf, with many stations and supermarkets. The Altstadt of Düsseldorf is famous for its pubs, which serve Altbier, a dark, copper-coloured beer brewed locally, with a plate of roast pork and mustard, and Neuss has its own brewers and restaurants. Plan a short stop at the fort, read the board, and imagine a squad of soldiers on a cold morning, watching the river for movements on the far bank.
t.koln deutz@50.9,7.0:
Opposite the great cathedral of Cologne, on the right bank of the Rhine, stands Deutz, which began as a Roman fort named Divitia. Around the year 310 the emperor Constantine had a fortress built here, connected to Colonia Agrippinensis on the opposite bank by a stone bridge, one of the first permanent bridges across the Rhine. The fort was about a hundred and fifty metres square, with massive walls and towers, and it gave the Romans a bridgehead on the edge of the Germanic lands. Sections of the walls have been excavated and can be seen in the area, and the fort belongs to the Lower Germanic Limes.

Cologne itself is older than Deutz and was among the great Roman cities on the Rhine, with a harbour, temples, and a governor's palace.
