Visitors can see the Praetorium cellars, Roman roads and the Dionysus mosaic in the Roman-Germanic Museum beside the cathedral. The view from the Deutz bank across the river to the cathedral's twin spires is one of the best in Germany, especially at dusk, when the lights come on and the river turns from grey to gold.

The riding in Cologne is urban, with bridges, tram tracks, cobbles and busy junctions. The Rhine is crossed by a series of bridges, among them the Hohenzollern Bridge, famous for its railway arches and for the thousands of padlocks left on its fence by couples. Traffic is heavy at rush hour, and events at the exhibition grounds and football stadium can add to congestion. Outside the city, the Bergisches Land to the east offers curving roads through forests and valleys, a good reward after the city traffic. Spring and early autumn are the most comfortable seasons.

Fuel stations are easy to find in Deutz and the surrounding districts, and the riverfront has cafés and bars, with Kölsch, the local pale beer, served in tall thin glasses called Stangen. Try a Himmel un Ääd, black pudding with apples and mashed potato, or a simple rye roll with cheese. Parking for motorcycles is generally easier than for cars, but be aware of street rules and avoid the pedestrian zones. An hour on the Deutz promenade, looking at the cathedral across the water, is time well spent.
t.watchtowers wp 1 67 to 1 66@50.4,7.7:
The Westerwald is a low, rain-washed plateau of beech, meadow and clay pits, and the Roman Limes cut straight across it. This stretch, marked by the surveyors' numbers for two watchtowers, lies close to Höhr-Grenzhausen, where the Limes was a palisade and ditch with timber towers every few hundred metres, replaced later by stone. You will not find tall walls. What you find is a gentle bank in the woods, a mound where a tower stood, and a signpost telling you that soldiers once watched the horizon from this exact spot.

The Upper Germanic Limes starts at the Rhine near Rheinbrohl and runs east and south for hundreds of kilometres, and in 2005 it was added to the UNESCO list as part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire. It was a border of observation and control more than of defence, a way to see who crossed and to tax what they carried, and the straightness of the line is its most striking feature, since it ignores hills and valleys in favour of an engineer's ruler.

Höhr-Grenzhausen is a name worth remembering for another reason. This is the Kannenbäckerland, the jug-bakers' land, where the local clay has been used for stoneware since the Middle Ages, and the town has a ceramics museum and several working studios. The grey salt-glazed stoneware with blue patterns that you see in German pubs came from here. Clay and woodland make the area feel earthy and quiet, and the smell of wood smoke from a kiln on a cold morning is hard to forget.

Riding is calm and pleasant on the minor roads of the Westerwald, with moderate bends, forest sections and quick changes of light. The surface is mostly good, though shaded corners stay damp and leaf-covered in autumn, and there are logging lorries on weekdays. May and October are the best months. The area is crossed by marked hiking trails, so you may meet walkers on forest tracks, and a slow ride will serve you better than a fast one.

Höhr-Grenzhausen, two kilometres away, has fuel, supermarkets and bakeries, and Hillscheid and Simmern are smaller villages with a shop or two. Bring a rain jacket, because this plateau collects clouds.
t.crooked wall area 4@54.5,9.3:
Here the ground is flat, wet and green, and a long, low bank runs across it for no obvious reason. The bank is the Krummwall, the Crooked Wall, one of the oldest sections of the Danevirke, the great system of ramparts that the Danes built across the neck of the Jutland peninsula against their southern neighbours. The first banks go back to the early Middle Ages, and the line was added to and rebuilt for centuries, in timber, earth and brick, until the nineteenth century. UNESCO recognised the Danevirke, together with the Viking town of Hedeby, in 2018.

The nearby village of Hollingstedt matters for a reason that sounds odd to a rider: it was a port. The river Treene, now a gentle stream among meadows, once carried ships, and in the Viking age goods were unloaded here and hauled overland a short distance to Hedeby, the trading town on the Schlei inlet of the Baltic. It was a shortcut across the peninsula that spared sailors the long and dangerous trip around the north of Denmark, and the place made its money from tolls and trade. Today it is nearly silent, with a small museum and information boards.

For a motorcyclist, Schleswig-Holstein is wide, level and windy, a country of dykes, hedgerows, brick farms and long views. Roads here are straight and well surfaced, with small villages, level crossings and agricultural traffic, and the wind off the North Sea can push a bike sideways on open stretches. Summer evenings are long and light, and spring brings rape fields in brilliant yellow, though showers are quick and cold. It is easy riding with little of the drama of the Alps, but it has a beauty of space and weather.

Fuel is available at Kropp, about twelve kilometres off, and at larger towns such as Schleswig and Husum, but the villages in between have little. Expect simple north German food, with fish rolls, labskaus, and tea or coffee with a slice of cake in a village café. Stop at the bank for a few minutes, walk up onto it, and notice how the land falls away on both sides, then imagine it topped with a palisade and a watchman.
t.watchtowers wp 2 17 to 2 19 including fo:
In the Taunus and Westerwald country of Rhineland-Palatinate, the Limes crosses hills so wooded that it is easy to miss. The numbering here records three watchtower positions and a fort, and from the start of the sequence you can follow the frontier as a line of mounds through forest and field. I cannot say exactly what stands at the pin today; typically you will find a marker, a low bank and the outline of a tower base, rather than a reconstructed building.

The fort in this stretch belongs to the series of small garrison posts that held the frontier. Troops of auxiliary soldiers, recruited from provinces across the empire, lived in such forts, and a civilian settlement of traders, craftsmen and families usually grew up outside the walls. The garrisons were not large, perhaps a few hundred men, but they controlled the roads and watched the border, and when pressure from the Germanic tribes grew in the third century the system collapsed and the Romans withdrew to the Rhine.

The nearby town of Nassau has a different claim to fame: it is the seat of the old counts of Nassau, whose family later produced the royal houses of the Netherlands and Luxembourg. The castle ruins stand on a hill above the Lahn river, and the town below is a quiet spa with half-timbered houses. The Lahn valley is a charming ride, with a river threaded between wooded slopes, vineyards on the sheltered sides and small villages with church towers.

The riding in this part of the Westerwald and Taunus is varied, with gentle climbs, long curves and open meadows, and the roads between Miehlen, Singhofen and Nastätten wind through forest and fields at a pleasant pace. Surfaces are generally good but can be patched, and wet leaves and tractor mud are the usual hazards. Traffic is light, apart from commuter times and summer weekends, and the best seasons are late spring and early autumn.

Nastätten and Nassau both have fuel, shops and cafés, and Miehlen and Singhofen offer a bakery or a village inn. A glass of Riesling from the Rhine or Lahn valley, or a plate of roast pork with dumplings and red cabbage, is a good reward after a day among the towers. Bring a map or a phone with offline maps, since forest tracks branch in confusing ways.
t.watchtowers wp 1 69 to 1 72 including th:
Roman soldiers on this part of the frontier spent most of their time watching, and the towers that you can trace in the woods near Hillscheid are the evidence. Four tower positions follow one another here, each within sight of the next so that a fire or a flag could pass a message along the line in minutes, and a fortlet and the remains of a fort and civil settlement lie nearby, forming a small military zone around the Limes. This was the first stretch of the Upper Germanic frontier after it left the Rhine, so every day brought traders, patrols and tax collectors through the gap.

The towers began as simple timber structures, with a platform on four or six posts, a ladder, and a small hut for the garrison, and were later rebuilt in stone. Imagine the conditions: a handful of men in a damp forest, living on bread, bacon and local beer, with wind howling through the trees in winter. They were far from the Mediterranean sun that most had been born under, and some came from North Africa or Syria. Their lives left small traces, such as coins, pottery and iron nails, which archaeologists have found in the ground.

The landscape is the western Westerwald, on the edge of the Rhine valley, with hills of beech and oak and meadows between. To the south the Rhine at Koblenz is only a short ride away, where the Moselle joins it at the Deutsches Eck, a corner of land crowned with a monument that attracts crowds. In the other direction the hills become more rural, with orchards and small farms.

Riding here is relaxed and mildly twisty. Country roads link Hillscheid, Neuhäusel and Kadenbach through forest and farmland, with gentle gradients and good views, and the surface is generally fine, with occasional rough patches. Traffic is light on small roads and heavier near Koblenz and the motorway. Mist hangs in the valleys on autumn mornings, and the light after rain can be extraordinary.

Höhr-Grenzhausen, about four kilometres away, has fuel and shops, while the villages have a bakery or a pub. Bring a rain jacket, and allow time to walk a short section of the Limes trail.
t.watchtower wp 4 17@50.3,8.6:
The Limes crosses the Wetterau, the fertile plain north of Frankfurt, in a long arc, and Watchtower 4/17 is one small point in it. The Wetterau is loess farmland, rich and flat, with wide fields of wheat and sugar beet, and the Romans valued it as an agricultural region, planting farms and estates beside the frontier. The tower itself, as at most of these sites, is represented today by a low mound or a marker, and a short walk will let you see the line of the frontier running across the fields.

Close by is Bad Nauheim, a spa town with salt springs that have been used since the Celtic period, when salt was boiled here for trade. In the early twentieth century the town became a fashionable spa with elegant Jugendstil buildings, a park and a long series of bathing halls, and it remains a handsome place with a relaxed, slightly old-fashioned air. Elvis Presley lived in a house nearby during his military service in the late 1950s, which draws a steady trickle of fans. The Taunus hills to the south rise to wooded ridges, and the Saalburg, a reconstructed Roman fort, lies a short ride away.

The riding here is easy. Country roads cross the Wetterau through villages with timber-framed houses, church towers and orchards, and the surfaces are usually smooth, with long open bends and modest hills. Traffic is heavier near Frankfurt and on motorways, so avoid the commuter hours if possible. In the Taunus the roads climb through forest and are more demanding, and a trip up to the Feldberg is a good addition. Spring blossom and autumn colour are the best times, and in summer the plain can be hot.

Ober-Mörlen, about five kilometres away, is large enough for a bakery and shops, but for dependable fuel and a meal, head to Bad Nauheim or Rosbach vor der Höhe, where there are stations and several cafés. Apple wine, called Ebbelwoi, and green sauce with eggs and potatoes are regional specialities. Take a few minutes to read the marker and look along the line of the frontier, and notice how the road follows the same ground that soldiers once patrolled.
t.watchtowers wp 1 53 to 1 57@50.4,7.6:
This stretch of the Limes sits close to Bendorf and Stromberg, on the plateau above the Rhine near Koblenz, and the watchtowers numbered here, five in all, follow the line as it climbs from the river. The frontier was a controlled boundary: a palisade or bank, a ditch, and a series of towers within sight of each other, with a patrol path behind. Traces survive as low banks in forest and field, and some positions have been marked or partly reconstructed, which makes this a good place to understand how the system worked.

Further north, near Neuwied, the large fort of Niederbieber housed a substantial garrison, and it forms part of the same frontier, with civilian settlements around it. Closer at hand, Bendorf has an unusual claim to industrial fame in the Sayner Hütte, an ironworks founded in the eighteenth century that became famous for its cast-iron buildings and decorative pieces in the nineteenth. The cast-iron hall, designed with slender arches and an elegant lattice, is an early example of an iron-framed building and still stands, a reminder that the region has been making things for a long time.

The riding is varied. Roads climb out of the Rhine valley through forest, with bends and some steeper gradients, then open onto the plateau, where fields and villages lie among low hills. Surfaces are mostly good, and traffic is light on minor roads, though the main routes near Koblenz and Bendorf are busy. The Rhine valley itself, with its castles and vineyards, is a classic ride, and the view from a height above the river is spectacular. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, and fog can fill the valley on cool mornings.

Bendorf has fuel stations, supermarkets and restaurants, and Stromberg and Weitersburg have smaller services. Try a bowl of Rhenish potato soup, or a plate of Sauerbraten with dumplings, and a glass of Riesling from the nearby slopes. If you have time, walk a short section of the Limes trail, where the banks are clearest, and notice how deliberately the engineers chose their line.
t.watchtowers wp 4 76 to 4 80 including th:
Echzell is a small town on the edge of the Wetterau with a very big Roman past. A large fort stood here, one of the main garrison points on the Upper Germanic Limes, and the civil settlement beside it grew into a busy town, with workshops, shops, baths and an inn for travellers. Little is visible above ground today, but the outline of the fort is known, and the watchtowers numbered 4/76 to 4/80 stretch away along the frontier line. The numbers belong to the old survey system, and the line of towers, ditch and palisade ran through fields that are now farmland.

The Wetterau was a prize for Rome: fertile loess soil, a mild climate and a river, the Nidda, flowing through it. Soldiers and settlers raised wheat and cattle, and the Roman army took much of the produce to feed the frontier. After the Romans left in the third century, Alemannic and Frankish peoples moved in, and the landscape gradually became the farmland of villages and small estates you see today. Not far away, at the Glauberg, a Celtic prince's tomb and hill fort from the fifth century BC show that the region was already rich before Rome.

Roads here are gentle and straightforward, making this a pleasant place for a relaxed ride. The Wetterau has long, open bends, small villages with timber-framed houses, and orchards of apple and plum, and the surface is usually good. The Vogelsberg hills, an old volcanic massif, rise to the east, with more winding roads and forest. Traffic is light apart from commuter times, and the best months are May to October. Fog can settle on the plain in autumn mornings, and the light after it clears is soft and golden.

Echzell, about four kilometres away, has fuel, shops and bakeries, and nearby Berstadt and Wohnbach have smaller services. The region is known for apple wine and for Handkäse mit Musik, a sour milk cheese served with onions and vinegar, a dish that tests the courage of visitors. Plan a short stop at the site, read the information board and look across the fields toward the line of the frontier, then continue to the next point on the ride.
t.watchtowers wp 5 13 to 5 14 including th:
The Main river is where the Roman frontier changes character. Coming down from the north, the Limes runs in a long arc through the Wetterau and then meets the river near Großkrotzenburg, and from there the Romans used the Main itself as the boundary, with towers and forts strung along its bank. The numbers 5/13 and 5/14 belong to that river line, and a fort and its civilian settlement sit close by. On the ground, expect a marker, a low rise and a view down toward the water rather than anything dramatic.

Großkrotzenburg's Roman fort was a solid one, with a garrison that controlled the river crossing, and the finds from it show soldiers from far afield. What you notice now, apart from the history, is how industrial the lower Main has become: a big power station stands on the riverbank, barges push upstream with gravel and containers, and the motorways and railway lines are never far. It is a landscape where Roman, medieval and modern Europe are laid on top of one another, and the contrast is oddly satisfying.

Ride away from the river and the country changes. The Spessart, one of the biggest continuous woodlands in Germany, begins a short distance upstream, and its oak and beech forests are famous for timber, once floated to the Dutch shipyards. The roads into the hills are smooth, with long bends, gentle gradients and little traffic on weekdays, and they make an excellent afternoon. On the plain, riding is easy but built-up, and commuters from Frankfurt fill the roads at rush hour. Spring and autumn are best, and morning mist on the river is lovely.

Hanau, five kilometres away, is the big town, famous as the birthplace of the Brothers Grimm, and it has stations, shops and plenty of cafés. Großkrotzenburg and Kahl am Main also have fuel and bakeries, so there is no need to carry spare. Local food is solid Hessian and Franconian, with schnitzel, potato dishes and apple wine. Spend a quarter of an hour at the marker, look across the river, and imagine the empire ending at the water's edge.
t.watchtowers wp 3 23@50.2,8.3:
Idstein sits in a bowl of the Taunus hills north of Wiesbaden, and its centre is among the best-kept half-timbered towns in Hesse. The Killinger House, a tall timber-framed building with elaborate carving, is the showpiece, and the Witches' Tower, a stone remnant of the old castle, stands above the old town as a reminder of a darker chapter. The Roman Limes passes through the hills just to the north, and Watchtower 3/23 is one of many positions on the ridge, part of the line that ran for about five hundred kilometres across Germany.

The Taunus section of the Limes is particularly rewarding for walkers, since the line follows the high ground, and nearby is the fort of Zugmantel, one of the larger sites in the area. Rome's soldiers here were watching a frontier of forests and farms, and the weather could be miserable: damp, cold and misty for much of the year. The local geology is slate and quartzite, giving the hills a dark, wooded character, and the streams are fast and clear.

For riders, the Taunus is one of the best playgrounds in the Rhine-Main area. Roads climb out of Idstein toward Niedernhausen and the ridge, with long, medium-fast bends, a few tight corners and good surfaces, and the forests close in with a sense of cool and shade. Weekends bring many bikes and cyclists, and speed limits are enforced, with cameras and police in some places, so ride with a margin. Early morning on a weekday is the nicest time, with mist in the valleys, and autumn colour on the beeches is outstanding. In winter, ice can linger on shaded roads until noon.

Idstein has fuel stations, supermarkets, a bakery on nearly every corner and several restaurants in the old town, and Niedernhausen and Waldems have smaller services. Hessian specialities include green sauce and apple wine, and a coffee and a cake under the timber-framed gables is a good reward. Walk a short section of the Limes path, notice the bank and ditch, and see how a straight line was laid out across the hills.
t.wadden sea@53.5,8.6:
Where the Weser river widens into the North Sea at Bremerhaven, the land and water merge into one of the strangest landscapes in Europe. The Wadden Sea, a shallow stretch of sand and mud flats running from the Netherlands past Germany to Denmark, is the largest unbroken system of tidal flats in the world, and UNESCO protects it as a World Heritage Site. Twice a day the sea retreats, leaving a gleaming plain that birds, seals and worms use as a feeding ground, and twice a day it comes back, quickly and quietly.

The living things here are what make it important. Millions of migrating birds, among them knots, oystercatchers and brent geese, stop to feed each year on their way between the Arctic and Africa, and seals rest on the sandbanks. The mud is full of worms, snails and shellfish, which make it one of the most productive habitats on earth. Bremerhaven itself is a port city, a place of docks, cranes, shipyards and emigrant history, and its museums include one on German emigration to America and one on the sea.

For motorcyclists, this is dyke country. The sea walls that protect the land form roads and tracks of their own, with grassy slopes, sheep and wide views, and the flat polder behind is crossed by straight country roads. The wind is the main character, often strong and cold, and rain can arrive quickly. Surfaces are generally good, though some dyke tracks are closed to motor vehicles, so follow the signs. Autumn can be wonderful, with huge skies and migrating geese, and summer evenings stay light until late.

Bremerhaven has fuel in plenty, along with supermarkets, restaurants and hotels, and ferries cross the Weser to Nordenham, which is useful if you want to explore the other side. Local food includes fish sandwiches, shrimp and the sailors' stew called Labskaus. Never walk out on the mudflats without a guide and tide tables, because the water returns faster than you can walk, and check the tides before planning a stop at the shore.
t.taereung cluster@37.6,127.1:
Korea's Joseon kings chose their tombs the way they chose a capital, with a geomancer. A good site needed a mountain behind, water in front and a gentle forest around, and the royal tombs scattered across the countryside around Seoul follow that rule, which is why many of them feel like parks. Taereung is one of the best known, on the north-east side of the city, a burial ground for Queen Munjeong and her son King Myeongjong in the sixteenth century. The forty tombs of the dynasty were listed by UNESCO in 2009, and walking among them is a calm contrast to the city outside.

Each tomb follows the same plan. A red-painted spirit gate and a stone path lead up to a grassy mound, with stone figures of officials, horses and sheep standing guard, and a T-shaped shrine hall where rites were held. The mound sits in a round embankment under pine trees, and the light through the branches makes the place feel unhurried.

The other half of this ride is Namhansanseong, a mountain fortress south-east of Seoul where King Injo took refuge in the winter of 1636 and 1637 when the Qing army invaded. He held out for about six weeks before surrendering and bowing to the Manchu emperor, one of the more painful episodes in Korean history, and the walls still follow the ridge for several kilometres. The fortress was listed in 2014, and a walk along the wall at sunset gives long views over Seoul's suburbs.

For a rider this is an urban Korean day with a few bright spots. The traffic in Seoul and Guri is dense and fast, the tolls come from electronic passes, and the roads are in excellent condition. Guri has nearly two hundred thousand people and Namyangju ninety thousand, so fuel is no trouble anywhere, and roadside restaurants serve kimchi stew, grilled pork and cold noodles. The better riding lies on the hill roads around Namhansanseong and further east along the Han river, where bends are tight and views open over wooded valleys. Autumn is the best season, when the maples turn red and the air is dry. Winters are cold and icy, and summers are humid, with sudden storms in July.
t.yugok ri and durak ri tumuli@35.5,127.6:
The people of the Gaya confederacy never built an empire, which is why they are overshadowed by the neighbouring kingdoms of Baekje and Silla. But in the fifth and sixth centuries they ran a loose group of small states in the south of the Korean peninsula, famous for iron, and the tumuli in Jangsu, on the high ground of Jeolla province, are evidence that this mountain county had its own ruler. The round grassy mounds of Yugok-ri and Durak-ri sit on ridges and in fields, and iron tools, horse gear and weapons have been dug out of them. They are part of the UNESCO listing for the Gaya Tumuli, added in 2023.

It helps to know that Jangsu is a plateau, around six hundred metres up, and one of the highest and coolest counties in the region. The county is known for apples, sweet, crisp and grown in cool nights, and for its beef, and in autumn you pass orchards with red fruit and farmers selling boxes by the roadside. The mounds are quiet and low, not showy, and the pleasure is the setting, a high green valley surrounded by ridges, where you can look around and see the same view the people who built them knew.

Jangsu itself is a small town of about twenty-six thousand, with fuel, convenience stores and restaurants, and the larger town of Namwon, further south on the edge of Jirisan, has more. The riding in the area is a delight, with narrow, smooth roads over passes and along valleys, thickly forested slopes, few cars and surfaces that are generally excellent, even in the countryside. Bends tighten as you climb into the foothills of Jirisan, the great mountain of southern Korea, and the weather can be much colder at height than in the plain.

Spring brings blossom, and autumn brings colour, but winter can bring ice and fog on the high roads, and some mountain passes get closed after snowfall. Eat local pork or beef, rice with mountain greens, and in Namwon try the catfish soup, which locals prize. Allow time for stopping, because the road invites it.
t.magoksa temple@36.6,127.0:
Magoksa sits in a fold of Taehwasan mountain in South Chungcheong, a short drive from the old Baekje capital of Gongju, and it is the sort of temple that makes a good argument for getting out of the car. A stream runs beside the approach, maples and zelkova trees close overhead, and the main buildings sit within a double compound, one for monks and one for the Buddha. Its tradition goes back to the seventh century, though most of the present wooden halls are much younger, and its five-storey stone pagoda with a metal finial on top is unusual, since the top part shows Tibetan influence, possibly from the Yuan dynasty.

It is one of seven mountain monasteries listed by UNESCO in 2018 as Sansa, Buddhist Mountain Monasteries in Korea, which were chosen because they are still living places of practice, not museums. The monks still chant at dawn and dusk, and visitors can join a temple stay for a night or two, sleeping on the floor and eating simple vegetarian meals. A path leads up through the forest behind the temple, and in autumn the maples glow red and orange.

Gongju is a town of more than seventy thousand, with fuel and cafes, and it has its own history, with the tomb of King Muryeong, one of the great finds of Korean archaeology, found intact in 1971. Yesan, another thirty-odd kilometres to the north-west, is apple country, and is also close to the temple of Sudeoksa. Both give you good places to eat and refuel before heading into the hills.

The riding is calm. Roads in this part of Korea wander through rice fields, orchards and low wooded hills, with views of small villages and farmhouses, few trucks outside harvest, and a road surface in good condition. Bends are mild, and the speed limits are strict, with cameras at regular intervals, so keep an eye on the signs. The Geum river flows past Gongju, and its banks are lovely for a late afternoon walk.

Come in spring for the new leaves or in October and early November for the maples. In summer it is hot, wet and buzzing with cicadas, and in winter the road may be icy. Arrive early to avoid the buses, and bring a small coin for the donation box.
t.uedem hochwald hochwald 2@51.7,6.4:
Flat is the word for the Lower Rhine, and the Hochwald is the exception that proves it. Near Uedem, on the German side of the Dutch border, a long low ridge of wooded hills pushes up from the plain, the leftover of ice-age glaciers that stopped here, dumping gravel and sand in a long arc. The ridge is not high, but in a landscape where a church tower is a landmark, it counts as a range. The forest is a mix of beech, oak and pine, with sandy paths and cyclists, and it is a favourite of weekend walkers. A scouting label like Hochwald 2 only tells me there are several viewpoints in the same area, so treat the forest as a whole.

The towns around are small and orderly. Uedem has about eight and a half thousand people, a church with a tall tower and, nearby, a NATO air defence base, while Kalkar, to the north, has about fourteen thousand and a market square lined with brick gables. The church of St Nicolai in Kalkar holds some of the finest late medieval carved wooden altars in Germany, made by local workshops, and is well worth a quiet half hour. A mile or two away, the unfinished nuclear power plant of Kalkar was converted into an amusement park, which is surely one of the great examples of German pragmatism.

For riders, the Lower Rhine is easy and gentle, with flat, straight roads between fields, windbreaks of poplars, old farmhouses of red brick and a lot of cyclists who ride three abreast. Surfaces are excellent, speed limits strict and speed cameras plentiful. Wind is the main challenge, and a headwind across open fields can be tiring. There are few curves, so the pleasure is in the pace and the scenery, the hedgerows, the cows and the long light of evening. Fuel is plentiful in Kalkar, Uedem and the larger town of Kleve, which has a castle on a hill, the Schwanenburg, and a fine view over the Rhine plain.

Asparagus season, from April to June, fills the local restaurants with white spears and ham, and autumn brings mist and geese flying in from the north. Spring is lovely, with blossom and fresh green, and mid-summer is warm and busy with cyclists. Winters are grey, damp and cold, but the air is clean and the forest is empty.
t.limessection between watchtowers wp 1 39:
Between Rengsdorf and Anhausen the Westerwald is open farmland and beech woods, and a Roman frontier ran straight through it. The Upper German-Raetian Limes, listed by UNESCO in 2005, started on the Rhine near Rheinbrohl and ran for hundreds of kilometres to the Danube, a line of timber towers, a palisade, and in places a ditch and bank. The code WP 1/39 a is not poetry, it is bookkeeping: the old German Reichs-Limeskommission numbered the frontier by section and then by watchtower, and archaeologists still use their numbers. Here, a section of the line survives as a low bank and shallow hollow in the grass, which you will walk past without noticing unless someone points it out.

That is the honest summary of most Limes stops. There is not a wall to climb, only a faint ridge and an information board, and the pleasure is in picturing a legionary or auxiliary soldier on a cold morning watching smoke rise from the next tower. The Romans chose their line carefully, along ridges and with views, so the ride here is a ridge ride in the soft sense, with long gentle gradients and farm lanes joining the main road. Surfaces are generally good but narrow, with tractors, cyclists and the occasional horse.

The towns nearby are all small, with Anhausen, Melsbach and Rengsdorf each a couple of thousand people or fewer, so for serious fuel and a proper lunch the answer is Neuwied, a short run down to the Rhine. Neuwied itself is a planned town, laid out by a count in the seventeenth century with a policy of religious tolerance that drew Moravian Brethren, Mennonites and others, and its streets are unusually regular for the region. The Rhine is the better backdrop for an afternoon, with ferries, barges and a gravel bank for sitting.

Plan this stop as a pause between bends rather than a destination. A local bakery coffee, a look at the board, a minute with the grass. The Westerwald weather changes fast, so check the sky, and note that autumn mist in the valleys makes the ridge top feel like an island. Spring, when the beech is bright and the farmers are out, is the nicest time.
t.watchtowers wp 2 2 to 2 4@50.3,7.7:
Bad Ems sits in a narrow bend of the Lahn river, and the hills above it are steep, wooded and cut by short valleys. The watchtowers listed here, from WP 2/2 to 2/4, belong to the second section of the Upper German-Raetian Limes, the Roman frontier that UNESCO added to its list in 2005. In this stretch the line climbed away from the Rhine and cut over the high ground of the Taunus and Westerwald fringes, and the Romans placed their towers where the view was best. What you see now are mostly foundations and low mounds, with a few reconstructed pieces nearby, so bring imagination and leave the high expectations at home.

The spa town below has a stronger story than the towers. Bad Ems was a favourite of European royalty and the Russian court in the nineteenth century, and in July 1870 it was the setting for the Ems Dispatch, a telegram whose edited text pushed France and Prussia into war. A walk past the Kurhaus and the colonnades shows the scale of the old spa trade, and the onion domes of the Russian Orthodox church on the slope are a surprise on a German hillside. Thermal springs still feed the baths. At around ten thousand people, the town has pumps, supermarkets and cafes, which makes it the logical base.

Riding around Bad Ems is a series of hairpins and short climbs, with the Lahn road below, the B260 up the valley, and quieter forest roads winding to Nassau and Dausenau. The nearby village of Dausenau has a leaning church tower and half-timbered houses that tilt into the street. The valley is narrow, so on busy days the main road becomes slow, and wet leaves in autumn make the shaded bends treacherous. Early morning in spring gives you mist on the river and almost no traffic.

Allow time to drop down to the water. A river cruise boat sometimes passes, and a bench by the Lahn with a bakery coffee makes a fair ending to a short walk. If you come in winter, remember that north-facing slopes stay icy longer than the weather forecast suggests.
t.fortsite and civil settlement of echzell:
Echzell is a village of a few thousand people in the Wetterau, the broad, fertile basin north-east of Frankfurt, where loess soil has been farmed since the Stone Age and the horizon rarely rises above a gentle swell. The Romans liked it for exactly that reason. They built a fort at Echzell in the later first century as part of their push into the Wetterau, and a civil settlement grew up around it in the usual way, with traders, craftsmen and families outside the gates. The fort later became part of the Upper German-Raetian Limes, which UNESCO listed in 2005. Almost nothing of the walls stands now, and the outline lies mostly under fields and houses, so the Echzell stop is about reading a landscape rather than visiting a monument.

That is not a bad thing for a rider. The Wetterau is easy country, with straight lanes between wheat and sugar beet, wind that you can feel in the open stretches, and a succession of small towns with half-timbered cores. The Horloff river meanders in the lowlands nearby, and in spring the meadows flood and bring in herons and, in some years, cranes on migration. The surface of the farm roads varies, with tractor mud on the verges in harvest time, and the best riding is in the morning when the air is cold and the light is long and low.

For practical needs you have what you want. Echzell has around six thousand people, so fuel, a bakery and a pharmacy are within reach, and Reichelsheim and Berstadt are close. Further south the ground climbs towards the Vogelsberg, a huge old volcano that is the largest basalt field in central Europe, which gives you a clean change of scenery if you want real corners. A few kilometres along, the Limes line itself runs on towards Butzbach and the Taunus.

Keep the stop short and honest. Read the board, stand on the field edge for a moment, and notice how flat the horizon looks to a soldier posted here from Italy or Gaul. Then go and find a village bakery, which in the Wetterau often sells excellent plum cake in late summer.
t.watchtower wp 1 61@50.4,7.6:
Höhr-Grenzhausen is clay country, and that decides almost everything about this part of the Westerwald. The hills hold a thick seam of fine, high-quality stoneware clay, and for centuries the area has been known as the Kannenbäckerland, the land of the jug makers. Grey salt-glazed pottery with blue decoration, called Westerwald stoneware, was exported across Europe from here, and workshops and a ceramics museum still keep the trade alive. It is a surprising backdrop for a Roman watchtower, but the Romans were here first, and WP 1/61 is one of the numbered posts of the Upper German-Raetian Limes, which UNESCO listed in 2005.

The site itself is modest, as most of the towers are. The limes ran over the forested ridge above the town, and the old numbering, section and tower, comes from the German survey of the late nineteenth century. You are looking at a mound, a possible reconstruction and a sign, in beech and spruce woodland that smells of damp needles in the morning. Do not make a long trip for the tower alone. Make the trip for the lanes.

The roads around Höhr-Grenzhausen are among the more rewarding in the region. The land is cut by little valleys, with climbs through woodland to open ridges and back down into villages with brick and slate roofs, and the surface is mostly sound. The Westerwald is a plateau with moody weather, so even in July a front can arrive from the Atlantic and drop the temperature by ten degrees. Take a layer. The smaller lanes between the villages give the best twisting, and they are quiet on weekdays.

If you have an extra half hour, a visit to the ceramics museum tells you more about the area than any watchtower. Local bakeries do a good plum tart, and the potters sell mugs that survive the journey home in a pannier far better than you would expect.
t.watchtowers wp 3 41 to 3 44@50.2,8.4:
The Taunus is the low, forested mountain range that closes in the north of the Frankfurt basin, and the Romans put their frontier along and over it. Here, near Glashütten, the line passes through high woodland at roughly four hundred metres above sea level, in an area that is cold and often foggy in winter. Towers 3/41 to 3/44 belong to the third section of the Upper German-Raetian Limes, the one that UNESCO recognised in 2005 together with the rest of the frontier. The Romans cleared a swathe through the forest, set up a palisade, and watched the open ground to the north, where tribes of the Chatti lived. The name Glashütten itself recalls glassmaking, once common in these forests because wood, sand and potash were all to hand.

The roads here are some of the best in the Frankfurt hinterland. From the town the B8 goes down to Königstein and the plain, while up above the Feldberg, the highest point in the Taunus at around 880 metres, a network of narrow lanes with decent asphalt offers long, easy bends and good visibility. Cars and cyclists crowd the Feldberg on dry Sundays, so if you can, come on a weekday. Early morning is gorgeous, with mist in the hollows and sun hitting the beech tops.

Walkers do the Limes trail through the woods, and you will see a line of mounds and a rebuilt tower at some places along the way. The Saalburg, the reconstructed Roman fort near Bad Homburg, is not far, and it is the best place to understand what these watchtowers were for. If the weather turns, Idstein to the north has a medieval centre with half-timbered houses and a witch tower. Look closely at the beams.

Glashütten and the neighbouring villages have enough people to keep a pump going, and Schmitten and Waldems both have fuel and bakeries. In winter the Taunus can hold ice on shaded corners long after the valley has thawed, and the Feldberg road sometimes closes for snow. Come in late spring or September, when the beech leaves are young or just starting to turn, and take a flask, because cafe stops are sparse between the villages.
t.watchtowers wp 1 78 to 1 81@50.4,7.7:
Kadenbach, Arzbach and Eitelborn are three small villages on the broad, wooded plateau of the Westerwald, a short way north of the Lahn valley, and the four watchtowers here sit in a short run along the Roman frontier. Numbers 1/78 to 1/81 belong to the first section of the Upper German-Raetian Limes, running from the Rhine towards the Taunus. The frontier was a palisade with towers placed within sight of one another, and the signal system relied on fire at night and smoke or flag by day. In this area the Romans picked ridges and shoulders of hills so the view ran for miles over land that was then forest and scrub.

Arzbach is a clay village, like its neighbours, and potters have worked here for centuries using the same pale stoneware clay that made the area famous. The land is gentle farmland with orchards and low hills, where the lanes between villages are well suited to relaxed riding. You can string together loops of fifty kilometres on small roads that ignore the main traffic, with just enough climb to make it interesting and long views north to the high plateau. The weather, as everywhere on the Westerwald, is changeable, and winter can bring black ice on the exposed ridges. Midsummer evenings are the kindest time.

Fuel is not available in the hamlets themselves in any dependable way, so aim for Bad Ems on the Lahn, a few kilometres to the south, or Höhr-Grenzhausen, which has enough people to support several pumps and an excellent range of bakeries. The ridge top itself has a quiet, open feel, with big skies and the odd buzzard turning slowly over the fields.

The tower mounds are low, and you will probably see the information board before anything else. It is worth treating the stop as a short pause, with a look along the line and a moment to think about how thin the frontier was in real life. A few hundred soldiers watched a long border, and the system depended on discipline and signals more than on force. Later in the day, drop down to the Lahn, where the road follows the river between wooded slopes and the air smells of water and old stone.
t.watchtowers wp 1 74 to 1 76@50.4,7.7:
Between Hillscheid, Neuhäusel and Kadenbach the land lifts into a low, rolling plateau of fields, beech copses and small clay pits, and the watchtowers 1/74 to 1/76 mark a tight cluster of Roman posts on the frontier. On paper it looks like a long list, but on the ground it is a gentle, almost domestic country where cows graze behind electric fences and church towers rise over village roofs. The frontier here was part of the Upper German-Raetian Limes, which UNESCO listed in 2005, and a map of the area shows a sequence of numbered towers a few hundred metres apart, each one in sight of the next.

This is the best part of the section for plain, easy riding. The little roads between Neuhäusel, Hillscheid and Höhr-Grenzhausen link up in loops, with moderate climbs and long views, and the traffic is local and mostly polite. Afternoon sun low across the fields makes the stone walls glow. It rains often, and hay or manure on the road is a regular hazard. If you like cobbled village centres, they are here as well, each with a tavern and a baker.

The nearby town of Höhr-Grenzhausen is the ceramics capital of the area. Its museum covers the craft of salt-glazed stoneware, which was shipped in huge quantities from the Westerwald to Britain and the Low Countries. In the town's workshops you can still see potters at their wheels, and a morning spent browsing mugs and jugs is a pleasure that fits well with motorcycle luggage if you wrap carefully. Fuel and supermarkets there are plentiful, and Hillscheid and Neuhäusel have small shops but no guaranteed pump.

The watchtower stop is brief. If you walk the sign-posted trail, you will see the line of mounds and perhaps a reconstructed timber tower, and you will notice how the ridge chosen by the Romans allows a clear sight line to the next one. These towers worked like a chain of lamps, and a message could cross a long distance in minutes. A cold windy day on this ridge makes you appreciate the soldiers who lived in them.

Take your time heading back. Evening is the best hour, with the fields turning gold and the smell of cut grass drifting from farms. The lanes here reward riders who slow down.
t.watchtowers wp 4 20 to 4 36 including th:
Near Butzbach the Wetterau starts to break against the Taunus, and the Roman frontier passes through that transition with a long series of numbered watchtowers, in this case 4/20 to 4/36. It is a longer run than most, and it reflects how carefully the Romans watched this side of the line, where the open plain makes a natural highway for anyone coming from the north. The Upper German-Raetian Limes, listed by UNESCO in 2005, crosses farmland here, and in places the old rampart survives as a low bank in a meadow edge or a stretch of forest.

Butzbach has a good Roman story on its own. A fort stood on the edge of the town, and the local museum and the nearby reconstructed bath complex tell you about life on the frontier, with bits of pottery, tombstones and tools. The medieval town is lovely, with a market square surrounded by half-timbered houses and a Gothic church, and Butzbach has about twenty-five thousand people, so it is the natural place to find fuel and a decent lunch. The nearby spa town of Bad Nauheim, a short ride south, is known for its Art Nouveau bathhouses.

The riding is excellent for an easy day. The landscape rolls with orchards, arable fields and small forests, and the B3 and its parallel back roads allow good progress, while the lanes towards Ober-Mörlen and Rockenberg offer calmer riding. The wind can be strong on open ground, and autumn fog sits in the hollows until mid-morning. If you want twisty roads, the Taunus is a short run to the south-west, and the ride up through beech forest to the Winterstein is the kind of climb that rewards patience.

At the stop itself you will not find much that rises above ankle height. Keep your expectations low, read the information board and imagine the gap in the trees that the Romans maintained on either side of the palisade. Then ask where the nearest cake is. In the Wetterau, a farm cafe is never far, and the local apple wine, Ebbelwoi, appears on menus in autumn. A short half hour is plenty, and an afternoon in the town is a better use of the day.
t.watchtower wp 1 39@50.5,7.5:
This single tower, WP 1/39, belongs to a stretch of the Upper German-Raetian Limes that runs close to Rengsdorf and Melsbach, on a gently rolling shoulder of the Westerwald. Unlike many of its neighbours it has been marked and reconstructed in a way that lets you see how it might have looked, with a timber tower over a stone base, and a cleared line of sight in each direction. The towers were usually just a few metres square, with a lookout floor on top and a ladder you could pull up. A handful of soldiers at most would have lived in one, which gives you a sense of scale: it was a sentry post, not a castle.

The country around it is farmland with patches of beech and spruce. Rengsdorf is a small town of the Westerwald with a spa tradition and a pleasant centre, and Melsbach and Anhausen are villages that give a sense of local life. The roads here are quiet and well surfaced, often with views that open suddenly over the Wied valley and the Neuwied basin. The Wied river itself has cut a pretty, winding valley with little mills, and the stretch downstream toward the Rhine is a good ride, with bends and shade.

For fuel and a proper meal, Neuwied is the answer, only six kilometres away, down a long descent to the Rhine. Neuwied has a good promenade and a flood wall painted with local history, and it also has the Roman fort at Niederbieber, which was one of the largest on the frontier, and the museum at Rheinbrohl, where the Limes began. If you want a short Roman circuit, the Limes visitor centre at Rheinbrohl makes a good start or finish.

The tower is easy to stop at, since it sits near a road with a small parking area, and the walk to it is short. It is worth looking at the view from the platform if it is open, because the reason for the site is the view. Mornings are best, with fresh light and quiet. In winter the tower is a cold, grey lump in the mist, which is, I suspect, much how the soldiers saw it.
t.yangdong cluster yangdong village@36.0,1:
Yangdong is a village that was never really meant to be seen. The Wolseong Son clan and the Yeogang Yi clan settled in this fold of hills north of Gyeongju in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, and over the next few hundred years the two families built the tiled mansions of the elite on the upper slopes and the thatched houses of everyone else below, all in careful relation to the hillside. It is one of the best preserved clan villages in Korea, and in 2010 it joined Hahoe, near Andong, on UNESCO's list of historic villages of Korea.

Walking through it, you notice how it works as a diagram of the old social order. Houses climb the ridges in four spurs shaped like the Chinese character for water, the main halls face the river with an eye to feng shui, and scholars' pavilions sit where the view is best. Dry stone walls, persimmon trees and kitchen gardens fill the lanes between. It is a living village, and residents still farm here, so keep your voice low and stay on the paths. Scholar-officials from these families served the Joseon court, and some of their descendants are still around.

On a motorbike, the area is a pleasant mix. The approach from Pohang or Gyeongju is on regular main roads with good surfaces and plenty of cameras, so watch your speed, and then the road narrows into the valley. The rolling country around Gyeongju is excellent for gentle riding, with rice terraces, ancient burial mounds and low pine ridges. Gyeongju was the capital of the Silla kingdom for nearly a thousand years, and the Tumuli Park belt just south, with its great grass-covered royal tombs, is worth an hour at least.

Fuel is easy at Yeonil and Pohang, and Pohang, a big steel city, is also known for its raw fish. Gyeongju itself serves a very good ssambap, with rice and grilled meat wrapped in lettuce. Spring cherry blossom is spectacular but crowded, and autumn is clear and dry, a better season for riding. Summer brings monsoon rains in July.
t.kleve reichswald west@51.8,6.1:
Kleve sits on the lower Rhine, a few kilometres from the Dutch border, in a landscape so flat that the one low hill outside the town counts as an event. West of it, the Reichswald is a big, dark forest of pine and beech, one of the largest wooded areas in this part of North Rhine-Westphalia, and for a rider coming from the Ruhr it feels like an exhale. The forest roads are straight and shaded, and the surrounding villages, Kranenburg among them, are neat, brick-built and utterly peaceful.

The history is heavier than the scenery suggests. In February 1945, the Reichswald was the scene of Operation Veritable, when British and Canadian troops fought their way through the forest and the flooded Rhine plain in some of the grimmest fighting of the war's final months. Kleve itself was almost completely destroyed, and its old town was rebuilt in the postwar style. Several thousand Commonwealth soldiers lie in the Reichswald Forest War Cemetery, a quiet and carefully tended place in the woods that is worth a few minutes of silence, and another large cemetery lies across the border in Groesbeek.

Before that, Kleve was the capital of the Duchy of Cleves, and one of the duke's daughters, Anne, became briefly the fourth wife of Henry VIII. The Schwanenburg, the Swan Castle, still stands on its hill over the old town, and is tied to the legend of the Swan Knight, Lohengrin, who arrived by boat drawn by a swan. A good way to see the castle is to climb the hill after parking in the lower town.

The riding is relaxed rather than exciting. Roads are flat and well kept, speed limits are enforced, and the cycle paths are as busy as the roads. The Rhine and its flood meadows make good riding in spring and autumn, with geese in huge numbers, and a ferry or two. Kleve has plenty of fuel, cafes and bakeries, and Dutch ones just over the border are just as easy. A day here is a gentle one, which is a pleasure of its own.
t.utrecht limes road veldhuizen@52.1,5.0:
This is a ride along an old frontier that is now a residential suburb. When the Romans held the lower Rhine, the river itself was the border of the empire, and a chain of forts, watchtowers and roads ran along its south bank. One of the forts stood where Utrecht is now, under the name Traiectum, and another, with a fine reconstruction, lies in the modern district of Leidsche Rijn. The whole frontier, the Lower German Limes, was added to the World Heritage list in 2021. Today it is hard to see anything of it, because the Rhine silted up and shifted, and the land is mostly polder, pasture and new housing estate.

The Utrecht-Limes road follows the line of the old river, now called the Oude Rijn, past Veldhuizen, Vleuten and De Meern. Here you find dyke roads, a neat line of willows, long narrow fields reclaimed from the peat, and in the distance the Dom Tower of Utrecht standing alone above the flat. A handful of finds have come to light as the district was built, including a Roman barge that was dug out of the mud nearby, and it is worth looking in a local museum if you want to see the real things.

The riding is flat, quiet, and entirely under the thumb of the Dutch traffic police. Speed limits are low, cameras are common, and cyclists use every road. A motorbike wins a quiet kind of pleasure here, in the smell of cut grass, the wind off the polders, and the low light on the water. Wind is the main weather issue, because there is nothing to stop it, and rain showers arrive suddenly from the west.

Veldhuizen and Vleuten have fuel and supermarkets, and Utrecht is only a few minutes away if you want something more substantial, with its canal wharves and cafes at water level. The pleasure is in taking it slowly and imagining the legions on the far bank, looking into the unconquered north.
t.spa@50.5,5.9:
The word spa comes from this town, and that is the kind of claim that most places make and few can prove. Here it happens to be true: Spa, in the Ardennes foothills of eastern Belgium, has been a place for taking the waters since the Romans, who are said to have noted its iron-rich springs, and from the sixteenth century it was a fashionable resort. Visitors have included the Russian emperor Peter the Great, who came in 1717 to cure his stomach, and the town's central spring, the Pouhon Pierre-le-Grand, is named after him. The bottled water that bears the town's name is sold worldwide, and the little town has a quiet, slightly faded charm, with grand hotels, a thermal baths complex on the hill and a casino.

It is also a motorcyclist's town, because of the nearby circuit of Spa-Francorchamps, a few minutes away, which hosts the Belgian Grand Prix and a famous round of the motorbike calendar, along with a road network that has been a favourite of riders for generations. The Eau Rouge corner and the Raidillon climb are some of the most famous in racing, and the public roads around the circuit are fast, wooded and fun. Stavelot, with its old abbey, lies a few kilometres to the east.

From Spa, the road climbs on to the High Fens, the Hautes Fagnes, a high plateau of peat bog, heather and stunted spruce that is the wildest landscape in Belgium. Boardwalks cross the wet ground, mists collect in the hollows and the wind is often sharp. On a clear day, the views over the moor are remarkable, and in autumn the colours go gold and rust. The road continues across the German border into the Eifel, where the old walled town of Monschau, with its half-timbered houses along the Rur river, is worth a stop.

Spa is a town of about eleven thousand people, with several fuel stations, bakeries, and restaurants, and Theux, a few kilometres away, has the same. This makes it a convenient place to fill up before the high country. Check the weather, because the Fens can be cold and wet even in June, and fog on the plateau is common in autumn.
t.songhak dong tumuli@35.0,128.3:
The little port town of Goseong, on the south coast of Korea, is best known to many Koreans for dinosaur footprints, but the green mounds on a ridge above the sea tell an older story. The Songhak-dong tumuli are burial mounds of the Gaya confederacy, a group of small city-states that flourished in the south of the Korean peninsula alongside the better-known kingdoms of Baekje, Goguryeo and Silla, and that were gradually absorbed by Silla in the sixth century. Goseong was the centre of one of these states, usually called Sogaya, and the big round mounds here, laid out in a line above the bay, were the graves of its rulers.

The Gaya were great ironworkers and traders. Their iron ingots and armour were exported to Japan and the Korean kingdoms, and their burial goods, such as elongated pots, horse armour, and finely made ornaments, show a culture linked to the sea routes. The Gaya Tumuli were inscribed on the World Heritage list in 2023, a series of seven sites across southern Korea, of which Songhak-dong is one. Today the mounds form a quiet park, with grass, pines, and a view across the water to the islands of the strait.

The riding along this coast is relaxed and scenic, with rias, islands and fishing villages. The roads wind around bays, climb over low headlands and drop to small harbours, with oyster rafts and nets drying in the sun. Traffic is moderate, with speed cameras common and limits strictly observed. Spring, with azaleas on the hillsides, and autumn, with clear light, are best. Summers are humid and typhoons can arrive in late summer, and in winter the south coast is mild compared with the interior.

Goseong itself has about twenty-seven thousand people, so fuel, food, and accommodation are no trouble, and the larger city of Tongyeong lies a short ride to the east, famous for its seafood and the admiral Yi Sun-sin, who defeated the Japanese navy in the nearby waters in the 1590s. Eat fresh fish, and if you get a chance, try the local sea squirt or oysters, which are part of the region's identity. The Goseong dinosaur museum is an easy side trip.
t.yangdong cluster oksanseowon confucian a:
In the green hills east of Gyeongju, where the old Silla capital gives way to the rice fields and pine woods that lead toward the East Sea, the Joseon dynasty left a different kind of monument. Oksanseowon is a Confucian academy, a seowon, built in the sixteenth century to honour the scholar Yi Eon-jeok, known by his pen name Hoejae, who lived from 1491 to 1553. It belongs to the Yangdong cluster, part of the Historic Villages of Korea inscribed by UNESCO in 2010 together with Hahoe, and it shows how the Neo-Confucian elite wanted to live, study and be remembered.

The academy is set at the foot of a hill beside a stream, and its layout is a lesson in discreet beauty. A tall pavilion, the Muoru, hangs over the water, its open floor designed so that scholars could sit and watch the seasons pass. Behind it are study halls, a lecture room, dormitories and a shrine, all in grey tile and unpainted wood, arranged on rising terraces according to rank. The point was to live in harmony with the landscape, and that is why the buildings seem to grow out of the hillside. Nearby, the Yangdong village itself has hundreds of tile-roofed and thatched houses on a hillside, many dating back centuries, and it is still lived in by the descendants of two clans.

The approach is through gentle country with pleasant, easy roads, rice and persimmon fields, and low hills. It is not demanding riding, but it is calm, with small villages, farm traffic and little else. Autumn, with orange persimmons and golden rice, is the best season, and spring brings cherry and plum blossom. The summer is hot and wet. The petroglyphs of the Bangucheon stream, to the south near Ulsan, are an unusual neighbour, carved with whales and hunters thousands of years ago.

Pohang, a steel city of about half a million people, lies eighteen kilometres to the east, and Yeonil, closer, is a small market town with fuel and food. In Gyeongju, to the south-west, the royal tombs, Bulguksa temple and Seokguram grotto are among the great sights of Korea. Take off your shoes where asked, speak quietly and look at the roofs. They are the best part.
t.uireung cluster@37.6,127.1:
Seoul is a city of ten million people, and it still has forested royal burial grounds on its edge. The Joseon dynasty, which ruled Korea from 1392 to 1910, buried its kings and queens in forty tombs scattered around the capital, each placed according to the rules of geomancy, with a hill behind, water in front, and a quiet clearing for ancestral rites. Nearly all of them survive, and in 2009 they were inscribed together as a World Heritage site. The cluster on this stretch of the map, east of the city towards Guri, belongs to that family of graves.

The layout is consistent and quite moving. A red-spiked gate marks the entrance, a stone-paved path leads to a hall where rituals were performed, and beyond, on a green hill, rises the grass-covered mound itself, ringed by a low stone fence and guarded by stone sheep, tigers and officials. Civil and military officials stand in stone on either side, patient for five centuries. The tombs were not for sightseeing, and that gives the groves their peaceful, almost private character. In the pine woods around the Donggureung group, to the east, nine tombs share a single enclosure of old trees, and one holds the founder of the dynasty, Taejo.

Reaching them on a bike means a short run out of the city that is a lot less romantic than the destination. Seoul's expressways are fast and busy, with cameras everywhere, so keep to the limits, and the final approach is through suburban streets of apartment blocks and shopping strips. Guri, a city of nearly two hundred thousand people, has fuel, restaurants and everything you need. The Han river runs across the plain below, and its cycle paths and parks are well used on summer evenings.

Better riding comes east of here, up the Han valley towards Yangpyeong and the hills of Gyeonggi province, where bends, forests, and river views make a fine day out. Autumn, with golden ginkgo and maple, and spring, with cherry and azalea, are the best times. In winter the cold is sharp and bridges can be icy. The summer monsoon from late June to July brings very heavy rain.

Join the Koreans in a slow walk on the forest paths of the tomb parks. They are open to visitors, with modest fees and a closing day each week, and they are a fine way to understand a country that looks forward and back at once.
t.koryo songgyungwan@38.0,126.6:
Kaesong was the capital of Korea for nearly five centuries, long before Seoul, and the Koryo Songgyungwan is the best reminder of that age. The compound began in 992 as the Gukjagam, the national academy, in the Goryeo dynasty, which gave Korea its Western name, and it was turned into the Songgyungwan in the late fourteenth century. The present buildings, with their curved tile roofs, wooden pillars and ancient ginkgo and zelkova trees, mostly date from the seventeenth century, after the Japanese invasions of the 1590s, and the site is now a museum of the Koryo period, with celadon, metalwork and printing blocks on display. Kaesong's historic monuments and sites were inscribed on the World Heritage list in 2013.

The city lies on the southern edge of North Korea, only a few kilometres from the demilitarised zone, and its old centre has a quiet, provincial feel. The town has long been famous for ginseng, and its cooking is considered among the finest in Korea, with elaborate dishes of many small bowls. A few kilometres away, the Sonjuk Bridge records one of the most famous stories in Korean history, the murder of the loyalist scholar Jeong Mong-ju in 1392, shortly before the dynasty fell.

This is not a place you can simply ride to. From the south, the route passes Munsan, about twenty-four kilometres away in South Korea, but the border there is closed to ordinary traffic, and foreign visitors to North Korea can only travel on an organised tour, with official guides, fixed itineraries and no independent movement. Private motorcycles, rental bikes and independent riding are not possible, so treat this as a place to read about, or to visit only through an arranged and approved tour, if that ever becomes possible and appropriate for you.

For the landscape, Kaesong lies among low hills at the foot of the Songak mountain, with rice fields, orchards and small villages around the town. The seasons are sharply marked, with a hot, humid summer, a cold, dry winter and a golden autumn. If you want to see something of the Goryeo world from the south, the museums in Seoul, Gyeongju and Ganghwa Island tell much of the same story, and Ganghwa, reachable by an easy ride from Seoul, was the refuge of the court during the Mongol invasions in the thirteenth century.
t.anak tomb no 3@38.4,125.5:
Some tombs hold their dead, and others hold a whole world. Anak Tomb No. 3 in South Hwanghae Province is one of the great painted tombs of the Goguryeo kingdom, which ruled much of Korea and Manchuria from the first century BC to 668 AD. The chamber, built of stone slabs and covered with plaster, is decorated with murals showing a kitchen, a stable, a smokehouse, musicians and a long procession of soldiers, officials and attendants, some two hundred and fifty figures by the usual count. An inscription dated to 357 AD names a man called Dong Shou, a refugee from the Chinese states, and for years that was taken to be the tomb's owner, though some scholars argue it may have belonged to a Goguryeo king.

The paintings are the reason the site matters. They show clothing, hairstyles, musical instruments, kitchen tools and architecture in a lively, colourful style, so they give historians a window into fourth-century life that few written sources match. The Complex of Koguryo Tombs was inscribed in 2004 as World Heritage, and the Anak tombs are among its main features.

Anak county lies on the rolling farmland of the Hwanghae plain, south-west of Pyongyang, a country of rice fields, apple orchards and low hills, with the Taedong and Jaeryong rivers feeding the soil. Villages line the road, and farmers work the fields by hand or with oxen. This is a region that holds a great deal of historical interest and also a great deal of bitter modern history, with the Korean War battles and later events of memory.

Practical advice must be blunt. North Korea does not allow independent travel, motorcycling or self-driving by foreigners, and visits to the Hwanghae sites are possible only on special arranged tours, if at all. The text of this entry is therefore for armchair travel. Towns such as Anak, with about twenty thousand people, and Chaeryong, with over fifty thousand, would have the basic services of a regional centre, but I cannot give reliable details about fuel, food or opening times for foreigners. If your interest is Goguryeo, the tomb murals at Jian in China and the museum collections in Seoul give a fine introduction.
t.anak tomb no 1@38.5,125.5:
A few kilometres north of Anak Tomb No. 3, the same farming plain holds another Goguryeo burial, Anak Tomb No. 1, and the contrast between them is a nice example of how varied these graves can be. The Goguryeo kingdom, whose people built great mountain fortresses and left thousands of stone tombs across what is now North Korea and north-east China, painted the walls of its aristocratic graves with scenes from life, belief and the afterlife. Tomb No. 1 belongs to the same early group, with a chamber of dressed stone slabs and plastered walls, and it is part of the World Heritage listing of Koguryo tombs that dates from 2004.

The paintings in these tombs gradually changed over time. The earliest ones, like those at Anak, show the owner at home, with attendants, guards and servants arranged in careful hierarchy. Later tombs, from the fifth to seventh centuries, tend towards the sacred, with the four guardian animals of the compass, the azure dragon, the white tiger, the red bird and the black tortoise entwined with a snake, painted on the walls with extraordinary elegance. Together the tombs form a visual record of a culture, with details of dress, tools and religious ideas that we can barely find elsewhere.

The landscape is gentle, broad and agricultural. The land between Anak and Chaeryong is largely flat, with rice paddies, maize and orchards, framed by low ranges on the horizon. In late autumn the fields are brown and gold, and in winter the cold air from Siberia brings snow and hard frost. Spring is quick and bright, with blossom and the first green shoots.

I must be plain about access. This is North Korea, where foreign visitors may travel only on tightly organised tours, with official guides, and cannot ride or drive their own vehicles. I do not know of any current route by which a rider could visit this tomb, and I would not want to suggest otherwise. If you are following the Goguryeo story, you can do so more freely in South Korea, with the Seoul museums and the fortress walls along the Han river, or in the Chinese city of Ji'an, where the royal tombs and the great stele of King Gwanggaeto stand.
t.el vizcaino@27.5,-113.6:
Baja California is a long, thin peninsula, and El Vizcaino is where it gets properly wide. The biosphere reserve covers a huge, dry belt of the central peninsula, from the Pacific lagoons on one side to the Sierra de San Francisco on the other, and it is named after Sebastian Vizcaino, the Spanish captain who sailed these coasts in 1602. Scattered over the desert are the strange plants that make Baja famous, the towering cardon cactus, the squat elephant tree, and the cirio or boojum, a tall tapering spike that looks like an upside-down carrot with a few frizzy branches. After a rare rain the ground is briefly green.

The reserve is a World Heritage site for two reasons. The first is whales. Every winter, grey whales travel thousands of kilometres from the Arctic to breed in the warm, shallow lagoons of Ojo de Liebre and San Ignacio, and from January to March small boats can take visitors close enough to touch a curious calf. The second reason is the rock paintings in the Sierra de San Francisco, huge, red and black figures of people and animals, up to several metres high, painted on canyon walls by an unknown people many centuries ago. They are reached with local guides and mules, and need a permit.

The riding is long and simple. Highway 1 crosses the peninsula in endless straight sections with huge views, a surface that is mostly good, and little traffic apart from the occasional truck. The dangers are not bends but distance, wind and sun. Strong crosswinds can push a bike across a lane, and in summer the heat is severe. The cooler months, from November to April, are much better. Cattle and sometimes burros wander on to the road, especially at dusk, so avoid riding after dark.

Fuel is the vital practical point. Stations are far apart, often more than a hundred kilometres, and sometimes run dry, so top up whenever you pass one and carry a spare can. Small towns such as San Francisco and Las Margaritas have little, and Guerrero Negro, on the Pacific side, and San Ignacio, an oasis town of date palms with an eighteenth-century Jesuit mission church, are the main services. San Ignacio is a lovely place to rest, shaded by palms beside a freshwater lagoon in the middle of the desert. Pack water, snacks and a good puncture kit, and let the quiet sink in.
t.culvert near offerhausweg@52.1,5.1:
The name tells you what is here, a culvert, a small tunnel for water under a path or a bank, and the humble nature of the place is its charm. The Netherlands is a country made of managed water, and this part of Utrecht, on the eastern edge of the city near the university campus of De Uithof, is cut by streams, ditches and old defensive works that were all designed to move water about, or to hold it back. A culvert is the kind of detail that engineers make a country work with, and that most travellers never see.

The area has a double history. Roman engineers built a road along the south bank of the Kromme Rijn, the Crooked Rhine, as part of the frontier, linking the fort of Traiectum, in the middle of modern Utrecht, with forts upstream, and traces of its line are still followed by the cycle paths and lanes east of the city. Much later, in the nineteenth century, the Dutch built a defensive barrier called the New Dutch Water Line, a series of forts and flooded fields stretching from the Zuiderzee to the south, designed to keep invaders at bay by drowning the land in a thin sheet of water. Fort Werk IV, one of the ride's other stops, belongs to that system, and its dams, sluices and culverts were its working parts.

For a rider, the roads around here are excellent for gentle, easy riding. The land is flat and green, the lanes are narrow, and there is a dense web of cycle paths, which are not for motorbikes and carry heavy cyclist traffic. Roads shared with bicycles require care at junctions and roundabouts, where cyclists have priority. Speed limits are low, often sixty or even thirty in built-up areas, and traffic is strictly policed. Rain showers pass quickly, and in autumn mist lies on the fields in the mornings.

Utrecht is a city of nearly three hundred thousand people, so fuel, food and everything else is plentiful, and the old centre is beautiful, with its canals, wharf cellars and the tall Dom tower. De Uithof, the campus area, has cafes and shops on the edge. A small detail such as a culvert becomes an excuse to look at the landscape more closely, and to think of the generations of Dutch who kept their feet dry.
t.utrecht hoge woerd@52.1,5.0:
The Romans left their ships behind. In the 1990s, when the new suburb of Leidsche Rijn was being built on farmland west of Utrecht, excavators found the remains of several Roman river barges buried in the clay at De Meern, flat-bottomed craft that carried supplies along the Rhine to the soldiers on the frontier. Close to them, archaeologists uncovered a fort, called Hoge Woerd, which is now one of the best-known pieces of the Lower Germanic Limes. Part of its walls and gate towers has been reconstructed on the original foundations, and it stands incongruously among the houses of a modern housing estate, with a museum and a field where people can see the layout.

That mix of old and new is what makes the place so Dutch. Leidsche Rijn is one of the largest new housing districts in the Netherlands, built from the 1990s onwards with its own canals, parks and cycle routes, and the fort has simply been absorbed into it, as a landmark among the new streets. Walking the walls, you can imagine auxiliary soldiers, recruited in far-off provinces, standing guard over a river that is now a sleepy waterway.

The ride into Utrecht from this side is simple. Roads are smooth, well signed and strictly regulated, and the district is a grid of residential streets and bike lanes, so the speed is low. The Vleuten and De Meern area, now merged into Utrecht, has an old village core with a church tower and small pubs. The motorway ring around Utrecht is busy and fast, with cameras, and in rush hours, it clogs completely, so time your arrival to avoid the peaks. A weekend morning is the quietest.

Veldhuizen and Oog in Al are neighbourhoods with several thousand people each, and fuel and food are no trouble anywhere in the city. The Old Rhine that once carried the Roman barges now runs in a modest channel, and the water meadows to the west, with their cows and reflections, still feel like open country. In spring and early summer, the air smells of cut grass, and in autumn the mists are thick over the fields. Nearby, the Haarzuilens castle and its park, a short ride west, make a quiet detour on a sunny day.
t.group shelter type p@52.1,5.2:
Concrete is not usually romantic, but a Dutch group shelter manages it. Type P was a standard design of bunker built in the 1930s along the New Dutch Water Line, the old defensive belt that ran in an arc around Utrecht, Amsterdam and the middle of the country. Each shelter was a small, low, rectangular box of reinforced concrete with a flat roof and a narrow door, designed to protect a squad of soldiers from artillery and aircraft while they waited for the real fighting to start. Hundreds were built, and when you find one, usually half hidden in grass or trees, it looks like a stout, silent animal.

The idea of the Water Line was typically Dutch. The country had learned over centuries that its best defence was water, and from the early nineteenth century engineers prepared a chain of forts and sluices that could flood a wide strip of land to a depth of about half a metre, too deep for troops to walk through and too shallow for boats. The shelters of the 1930s were a modernisation, reflecting the lessons of the First World War. In May 1940, though, the German army came by air and by tank, and the line did not hold for long. The whole system is now a World Heritage site, listed with the Defence Line of Amsterdam.

You reach this part of the country by gentle, tidy roads. The area east of Utrecht, near De Uithof and the Kromme Rijn, is a patchwork of meadows, hedges, small woods and country houses, with long straight cycle paths and a few lanes shared with bikes. Speed limits are low, often thirty or sixty, and cyclists are frequent and fast, so ride carefully. Weekends bring crowds of walkers and cyclists, and the quietest times are early morning or late evening. In winter the light is low, and fog often sits in the hollows.

De Uithof and Utrecht both lie within a couple of kilometres, so petrol, coffee and meals are easy to find. A walk along the old defence lines, with their embankments and ditches, is a nice break from the saddle. Note that some of the shelters are on private land or in nature reserves, so keep to paths and respect signs.
t.utrecht domplein@52.1,5.1:
Dig under the Domplein in Utrecht and you hit a Roman fort. That is not a figure of speech: when the city was rebuilt after the great storm that brought down the nave of the cathedral in 1674, the foundations were already sitting on the foundations of something much older. The Romans built a fort here around the middle of the first century, on a low sandy rise beside the Rhine, and called it Traiectum, the crossing.
