When the legions left, the name stuck, and a thousand years of sound changes turned it into Utrecht.

The square is the middle of the story. On one side stands the Dom Tower, at 112 metres the tallest church tower in the Netherlands, finished in the fourteenth century and still the thing you steer by from half the province. Beside it is the gap where the nave used to be, because the storm of 1674 took it away and nobody ever rebuilt it, so the tower and the choir now stand apart across an open square. The saint who started it all was Willibrord, an Anglo-Saxon missionary who arrived around 690 and became the first bishop here, and for centuries Utrecht was the religious capital of the Low Countries.

For a rider this is a place to park and walk. The old centre is a tangle of canals with wharf cellars, narrow lanes and one-way streets, with a lot of cyclists who have never heard of motorbikes, and parking is the real puzzle. Use a garage on the edge and cross the last few hundred metres on foot. The ring roads around the city are fast, camera-heavy and congested at rush hour, so aim for a mid-morning arrival or a weekend. Fuel and food are no trouble in a city of nearly three hundred thousand.

The Oudegracht, the old canal that runs through the centre below street level, is the thing to look at after the cathedral. Its quays sit two storeys below the pavement, with vaulted cellars that were once warehouses and are now cafes, so you drink your coffee at water level while the bicycles clatter overhead. Grey days suit it, and so does the carillon, which rings out over the rooftops. Rain is frequent and always short.

Cycle out of town in any direction and the land flattens into polder, but that is another story, and the way to the north leads to Schokland, the former island that is now a field.
t.bunnik vechten provincialeweg@52.1,5.2:
A modern fort and a Roman one stand within a couple of kilometres of each other here, and both exist because of the same river. Vechten, on the Kromme Rijn just east of Utrecht, was the Roman fort of Fectio, one of the best-known sites on the Lower Germanic frontier. It lay at a point where the Rhine split, with the branch that became the Vecht heading north, and that made it a perfect depot. Soldiers, grain, and building stone all went through here, and archaeologists have pulled a remarkable amount out of the ground, including altars, bronze statuettes and the debris of a busy harbour.

The soil explains the finds. Flood clay and river silt sealed everything in wet layers, so wood, leather and metal survived in conditions that would have rotted them elsewhere. The frontier line, the Limes, was inscribed on the World Heritage list in 2021, and Vechten is part of that story. Not much is visible, and part of the appeal is that you must imagine the fort from the shape of the land, a slight rise above the low meadows, with the river curving beside it.

The second fort is Fort bij Vechten, a nineteenth-century brick bastion that belonged to the New Dutch Water Line. Its low earth-covered walls and moat survive and the grounds house a museum about the Water Line, which tells how Dutch engineers planned to hold off invaders by flooding the fields. The coincidence of these two defensive structures, nearly two thousand years apart, on the same river bend makes the area a perfect, quiet lesson in how geography repeats itself.

The riding is mild. The Provincialeweg and the lanes around Bunnik run through flat green country with farms, orchards and the occasional old country house, and on a weekday you will have the roads mostly to yourself apart from cyclists. Weekends bring more people, with families and sporting cyclists out in numbers, and speed limits are low and enforced. A headwind on the open stretches can be tiring, and spring showers pass quickly.

Bunnik has about six thousand people, so fuel and a meal are easy, and Utrecht is a short ride west. A bakery in the village will sell you a sandwich and an apple tart, and the riverside paths are lovely in the soft light of late afternoon.
t.bad ems@50.3,7.7:
The most consequential telegram in German history was sent from a spa town on the Lahn. In July 1870, King Wilhelm I of Prussia was taking the waters at Bad Ems when the French ambassador came to ask him to promise that no Hohenzollern prince would ever take the Spanish throne. The king refused politely, and sent a report to Bismarck in Berlin, who edited the text to make it sound like a snub, and published it. The Ems Dispatch, as it is known, helped to provoke France to declare war, and the Franco-Prussian War led to the creation of the German Empire in 1871.

Ems was already one of the grandest spas in Europe. The hot springs rising in the narrow wooded valley were known to the Romans, and by the nineteenth century the town drew emperors, tsars, composers and writers. Tsar Alexander II came for his lungs, and Dostoevsky and Goncharov also took the cure. The Russian Orthodox church, with its gilded onion domes, is a reminder of how many Russian visitors came here. The Kurhaus, the colonnades and the promenade along the river are still elegant, and the town, together with ten other famous spa towns of Europe, was inscribed on the World Heritage list in 2021. Bad Ems also gave its name to the Emser pastilles, throat lozenges still sold in pharmacies.

The ride is part of the charm. The Lahn valley winds through steep, forested hills, with castles, vineyards and half-timbered villages, and the road from Koblenz follows the river for much of the way, with moderate traffic and good surfaces. Up on the plateau of the Westerwald and the Taunus, the roads are twistier, with bends, climbs and views, and popular with German riders at weekends. Autumn, with colour in the beech woods and mist on the river, is the best season, and summer weekends can be busy. Watch for speed cameras and for farm traffic.

Bad Ems has nearly ten thousand people, with petrol stations, shops, hotels and restaurants, and Dausenau, a few kilometres away, is a smaller village with a leaning church tower. The Roman frontier, the Limes, also ran through these hills, and traces of its watchtowers survive in the woods nearby. A glass of Riesling and a slice of Westerwald cake make a fine ending to the day.
t.fortlet ferbach@50.4,7.7:
The Limes was a frontier made of many small pieces, and Ferbach is one of the little ones. It was a fortlet, a small stone-and-timber post on the Upper Germanic frontier that ran from the Rhine into the hills of the Westerwald, and it housed a handful of soldiers who watched the ground in front of them. Nothing here is grand. What you find is a wooded plateau with traces of ditches and the outline of a small enclosure, and the interest lies in imagining the daily routine of men on a frontier posted far from Rome.

The Limes section here begins at the Rhine near Rheinbrohl and climbs into the Westerwald, a low, rolling upland of beech and spruce, meadows and small villages. Höhr-Grenzhausen, the nearest town with almost 10,000 people, belongs to the so-called Kannenbäckerland, the Jug Bakers' Land, where potters have worked the local grey clay for centuries to make stoneware, and a ceramics museum in town tells the story. Koblenz, where the Rhine and Moselle meet, is a short ride to the west and has the bigger shops and fuel stations.

The riding in the Westerwald is easy and satisfying: roads rise and fall through forest, with long curves, pleasant gradients and few steep sections. Traffic is light on the minor roads, and farms and wind turbines mark the ridges. Autumn colour is good, and in winter frost and fog can linger on the high ground, so take care on shaded bends. The weather is often cooler and wetter than in the Rhine valley below, so bring a waterproof.

If you are following the frontier, the Limes is marked in many places with signs and reconstructed towers, and a hiking route known as the Limes trail follows its line. The German Limes was inscribed by UNESCO in 2005 as part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire. The region is also known for its rich pottery, and you might pick up a small blue-grey stoneware piece as a souvenir. After a look at the fortlet, a slice of cake and a coffee in Höhr-Grenzhausen is a gentle way to finish.
t.watchtowers wp 4 72 to 4 73@50.5,8.9:
Behind the name is a number system, because the Limes archaeologists gave every watchtower a code. WP means Wachposten, a watchtower, and 4/72 means the seventy-second one on the fourth section of the frontier, the one that crosses the Wetterau. This pair of towers stands in farmland near Hungen, in central Hesse, and the Romans placed them on a gentle rise from which a watchman could see across the open plain and signal to the next tower along the line.

The Wetterau is a broad, fertile basin north of Frankfurt, with rich loess soil that has been farmed since the Neolithic. The Romans wanted it. They pushed the frontier out so that it looped around the basin in a great arc, instead of following the Taunus ridge, and farms and estates called villae rusticae fed the garrisons. The border here was marked by a palisade and, later, a ditch and rampart, with small stone watchtowers every few hundred metres. Today the line shows up mostly as a low bank, a row of trees or a faint ditch in the field.

Hungen is a small town of about 4,600 people, with a castle and a half-timbered centre, and Lich, about 8 km away with 13,500 people, is the better place for fuel and supplies, and also known for its brewery and for the Solms family's castle. The surrounding roads are quiet farm lanes between fields of wheat, sugar beet and rapeseed, with the Vogelsberg, an extinct volcano, rising to the east. This is easy, relaxed riding, pleasant in late spring and early autumn, though traffic on the main roads can be busy with commuters heading towards Giessen and Frankfurt.

The Upper German-Raetian Limes is a UNESCO site, but much of it is subtle on the ground, so it helps to read the information boards. In summer the wide fields give a long view, and in autumn mist lies in the hollows in the morning. There is a good chance of seeing red kites circling overhead, a bird that is common in this part of Germany. A coffee and a piece of Streuselkuchen at a bakery in Hungen make a comfortable break, and the church towers of the villages on the plain give you a sense of how the landscape is dotted with life.
t.watchtowers wp 1 89 to 1 92@50.3,7.7:
Bad Ems is the sort of town that makes you straighten your collar. It lies in the narrow, wooded valley of the Lahn river, where hot springs have been used since Roman times, and in the nineteenth century it became one of the great spa towns of Europe. Kings, tsars and writers came to take the waters, among them Kaiser Wilhelm I, who was at Ems in July 1870 when a diplomatic telegram was edited by Bismarck and helped trigger the Franco-Prussian War. The Kurhaus, the colonnades and the grand hotels along the river still show what the town was like in those days.

The watchtowers on the heights above belong to a much older story. The Roman frontier, the Upper Germanic Limes, crosses the Lahn here, and the code WP 1/89 to 1/92 refers to numbered watchtowers along this stretch. The Romans built timber towers first and later replaced them with stone, and there is a fort in the area as well. On the ridge above the valley the line of the frontier runs through forest, where a footpath follows the course of the old palisade, and the wooded hills give a feeling of how remote and exposed the posting would have been.

For riders, the Lahn valley is a pleasure. The roads along the river wind between steep, wooded slopes and vineyards, and the valley is narrow enough that the bends come naturally. The B260 and the side roads over the Taunus and the Westerwald offer more twists and climbs, with some tight hairpins. Traffic is moderate, and in summer there are many cyclists, so be patient. Spring and autumn bring the best colours, and winter fog can fill the valley.

Bad Ems has almost 10,000 people and has fuel, supermarkets and restaurants, while Dausenau, a small village two kilometres up the river, is famous for its half-timbered houses and a leaning church tower. Nassau, with its castle, is a short ride upstream, and Koblenz is a short ride downstream. Try the local wine, a dry Riesling, or a plate of Flammkuchen, and consider a walk on the river path. The spa tradition survives, and a short dip in the thermal baths is an option for a stiff rider.
t.fortlet dicker wald 1@50.5,8.7:
The Dicker Wald, the thick forest, is a good name for a place where a Roman fortlet once stood among trees. The fortlet was a small post on the Wetterau Limes, the frontier line that curves around the plain north of Frankfurt, and it sat just inside woodland that still covers much of the hill. What you find today are low earthworks and the outline of a small enclosure, but the surrounding forest gives a good sense of the lonely, damp setting soldiers would have known. The Limes was a frontier of watchtowers, small forts and larger garrisons, all linked by a path and a palisade.

The larger fort at Butzbach, only about 4 km away, was one of the main garrisons on this stretch, and the town has a museum and a well-preserved medieval centre with half-timbered houses and a market square. Butzbach has around 25,000 people and has fuel, supermarkets, bakeries and restaurants, so it is the natural base, as the town was a Roman garrison place. Langgöns and Rockenberg, closer to the forest, are smaller villages with a few shops.

The surrounding countryside lies at the foot of the Taunus, where fertile farmland gives way to wooded hills. Roads here are quiet and well surfaced, with gentle curves through fields and woods, and the climbs are modest. The A5 motorway runs close by, and its traffic noise can be heard in places, though minor roads are peaceful. This is not dramatic riding, but a pleasant, easy circuit that fits the spirit of a frontier trail, and the light through the beech leaves in spring is lovely.

The German Limes was inscribed by UNESCO in 2005, and this area is a good place to see how the frontier worked on the ground. Look out for signs along forest tracks, and bring a map or a phone with offline data, since the woods are large and signal can drop. In autumn mushrooms appear and the forest floor is thick with leaves. Wild boar and roe deer live in the woods, and you may see signs of them. A slice of apple cake and a coffee in Butzbach will make a good ending to a short, quiet outing.
t.koln praetorium@50.9,7.0:
Under Cologne's town hall there is a Roman palace, and you can walk through it. The Praetorium was the residence of the governor of the province of Lower Germany, a large building complex on the edge of the Rhine that dates from the first century and grew over the next few hundred years. The city, called Colonia Claudia Ara Agrippinensium, was founded in the first century AD and named for Agrippina, the mother of the emperor Nero, who was born in a camp nearby. The remains of the palace were found during rebuilding after the Second World War, and the cellars and corridors are now open as an archaeological site.

The Praetorium belongs to the Lower Germanic Limes, the Roman frontier that followed the Rhine to the sea, which UNESCO added to its list in 2021. Cologne was the capital and the largest city on that frontier. Close by you can find the Roman-Germanic Museum, beside the cathedral, where the Dionysus mosaic is on display in the room where it was found, and the Roman sewer and the stretch of Roman wall, which show how substantial the city was.

For a rider, Cologne is an urban visit and needs a different mindset. The old town is mostly pedestrian, with cobbles, trams and many one-way streets. Cars and bikes are numerous, and the city has a low-emission zone, so check whether your vehicle meets the rules before arriving. The ride in along the Rhine from Bonn or Düsseldorf is flat and broad, and the cathedral appears on the skyline long before you reach it. The twin spires of the Dom, a huge Gothic building begun in the thirteenth century and finished in the nineteenth, are best seen from the other side of the river, near the Deutz bridge.

With almost a million people, the city has fuel stations, supermarkets and bike parking in plenty, though a quiet side street is easier to find than a space in front of the cathedral. Weekdays are heavy with commuters, and Sunday mornings are calmer. The local drink is Kölsch, a pale, light beer served in tall thin glasses by waiters in blue aprons, and the local pub food, Halve Hahn, is a rye roll with cheese, which has nothing to do with chicken. Allow an hour for the Praetorium, and an evening for a stroll beside the Rhine.
t.kottenforst sud riesenweg@50.7,7.1:
South of Bonn the land rises into the Kottenforst, a big forest on a low plateau that the archbishops of Cologne once kept as a hunting ground. They cut long straight rides through it, many meeting at star-shaped junctions so that a hunting party could see the quarry and follow it, and the pattern survives. The woods are mostly beech and oak, with a few conifer plantations and damp hollows, and they cover a large part of the area between Bonn, Meckenheim and Wachtberg. The Riesenweg, the Giants' Way, is one of the paths that cross it, a name that suggests something older and bigger than the track you walk on.

This is also Roman country. The aqueduct that carried water from the Eifel to Cologne, a channel of about 95 km, ran along the edge of this region, and traces of it can be seen in the forest and the villages, in the form of a buried channel, an access shaft and a few preserved sections. The Romans needed their frontier city on the Rhine to have clean water, and this was their way of getting it. It is a modest remnant, but it makes you think about how much planning went into a city.

The roads through and around the forest are quiet and pleasant, if not dramatic. Narrow lanes cross open farmland and woods with gentle curves, with the Siebengebirge, the seven hills of the Rhine, rising to the east. Many forest tracks are closed to motor traffic, so stay on the public roads and respect the signs. At weekends the area is busy with walkers, cyclists and horse riders, and the Bonn region has plenty of traffic, so a weekday morning is best. Autumn colour is very good.

Wachtberg, with about 20,000 people three kilometres away, and Meckenheim, a larger place, have fuel, shops and cafés. Bad Godesberg, now part of Bonn, was the diplomatic quarter in the days when Bonn was the capital and is a stylish place for a coffee. The Rhine and the Ahr valley, famous for red wine from Spätburgunder grapes, are both within reach, and the Ahr, which was badly hit by floods in 2021, is still recovering, so a visit supports local businesses. Watch for deer at dusk.
t.hwangnyongsa belt@35.8,129.1:
Gyeongju was the capital of the Silla kingdom for nearly a thousand years, and it is often called a museum without walls, because the tombs, temple sites and palace ruins lie scattered through a modern provincial city. Hwangnyongsa was once the greatest temple in the kingdom, begun in 553, and its nine-storey wooden pagoda, built in the seventh century after the monk Jajang came back from China, was one of the tallest wooden buildings in East Asia. The temple was burned down when the Mongols invaded in 1238, and what is left is a wide field of foundation stones, where the outline of the great hall and the pagoda base can still be made out.

The belt around it, a historic area on the eastern side of the city, includes the royal palace site at Wolseong and the remains of other temples. Nearby, the temple of Bunhwangsa still has a pagoda made of brick-like stone from the seventh century. Silla was a sophisticated state that built observatories, gilded crowns, and elaborate tombs, and the UNESCO recognised the Gyeongju Historic Areas in 2000.

Riding here is easy and pleasant. Gyeongju is a flat basin ringed by low mountains, with wide boulevards, bicycle lanes and large grassy burial mounds, called tumuli, rising among the buildings. The road along Bomun Lake, to the east, is a gentle route, and the mountain roads toward Toham Mountain and Bulguksa wind through pine forests. Traffic is heavy at weekends and during the spring cherry blossom, when thousands of visitors fill the streets. In winter the basin is cold and dry.

Gyeongju has about a hundred and fifty thousand people, so fuel stations and food are plentiful, and there are many places to try the local Gyeongju bread, a small sweet bun filled with red bean, and ssambap, rice with a spread of leafy vegetables. Visit in the cool season of autumn and spring, and in the evening the lit-up ponds at Wolji, a short ride away, are a beautiful spot to end the day.
t.hongyureung cluster@37.6,127.2:
The Joseon dynasty lasted from 1392 until 1910, and its kings and queens were laid to rest in a scattering of forested tombs around Seoul, forty of which are on the World Heritage list. Hongyureung is the name for two of them close to Namyangju, Hongneung and Yureung, which belong to the last two rulers of Korea. Hongneung is the resting place of Gojong, who proclaimed the Korean Empire in 1897 and died in 1919, in mysterious circumstances, just before the great independence uprising of that year. Yureung holds his son Sunjong, the last emperor, who lost his throne when Japan annexed Korea.

These two tombs differ from the older ones in a way that tells a story. Because the dynasty had become an empire, the layout follows Chinese imperial custom more closely, with stone figures of horses, elephants and lions, and a Chinese-style hall for ceremonies, rather than the more modest Joseon style. Even so, the setting is typical: a gentle hill, a stream in front, trees behind, chosen according to geomancy, so the dead may rest well.

Namyangju lies on the Han River upstream from Seoul, in a region of wooded hills and reservoirs, and the roads to it are some of the pleasantest near the capital. The road along the river toward Paldang winds beside the water, with cafes and bridges, while the hills north and east offer tight, shaded bends. Weekends are crowded with cyclists, hikers and families, and the roads clog around the riverside cafes. In winter the hills ice up, and in the summer monsoon, the road can flood.

Namyangju, a city of about ninety thousand, has fuel stations and restaurants, and a short run takes you to the Dasan area, where the thinker Jeong Yak-yong lived, and to the Yangsu riverside gardens. Eat tteokgalbi, grilled rice-cake ribs, or a sundubu stew, followed by a coffee overlooking the river. The tombs have an entrance fee and are closed one day a week, so check before you set out. Spring and autumn are lovely.
t.shinan muan getbol@35.0,126.3:
At low tide the sea retreats a long way from the coast of Shinan, leaving behind a vast grey plain of mud, glittering with water and printed with the tracks of crabs and birds. Koreans call this getbol, and the south-west coast has some of the broadest tidal flats in the world, a landscape that is neither land nor sea. The Shinan-Muan group, inscribed by UNESCO in 2021, is a stretch of this system, with channels, salt marshes and sandbars, and it shelters hundreds of species, many of them rare, including migratory shorebirds that stop here on their long flights between Siberia, Alaska and Australia.

People have worked the flats for centuries. Women dig for clams and cockles, fishers net tiny octopuses, and salt farms boil seawater and dry it in shallow ponds. Shinan county is made up of more than a thousand islands, many of them linked by bridges, and the sight of white salt pans against the grey mud, with low islands in the haze, is unforgettable. Muan, fifteen kilometres from the point, is known for its lotus ponds and white sand beaches.

The ride from Mokpo, with its bridges and harbour, leads out onto the islands by causeway, through a landscape of salt flats, onion fields and rice paddies, with the sea always close. The roads are flat and good, but the coast is exposed to wind and sudden sea fog, particularly in spring. Summer brings heavy rain and humidity, and typhoons come in late summer. Time your visit with the tide table, since the flats look empty at high water, and never walk out on the mud without local guidance, because the tide returns quickly.

Muan has about seventy-five thousand people and offers fuel stations, shops and restaurants, and the speciality is nakji, the long-armed octopus, served raw and wriggling, or in a spicy stir-fry. Autumn is the best season, when the sky is clear and the migratory birds arrive. Bring a windproof jacket, and expect to share the narrow roads with farm trucks.
t.archeological site in gwanbuk ri and bus:
Buyeo was once Sabi, the last capital of the kingdom of Baekje, which flourished on the south-west of the Korean peninsula until it fell to Silla and Tang China in 660. The kingdom's kings moved here in 538, built a walled city beside the Geumgang river and made it a centre of Buddhism, craftsmanship and trade, sending monks and artisans to Japan, where Baekje taught the court the arts of temple building. At the site in Gwanbuk-ri, archaeologists have found the foundations of a palace and workshops, and near it the fortress of Busosanseong runs along the ridge above the river.

Busosan is the place to get a sense of the setting. The fortress wall winds along the hill, and a path climbs through pine woods to Nakhwaam, the Rock of Falling Flowers, a high cliff above the river where, according to legend, three thousand court ladies threw themselves to their deaths rather than be captured when the city fell. Whether the story is accurate or an invention of later centuries, the cliff is dramatic. Baekje's finest relic, a bronze incense burner with exquisite dragons and mountains, was found in a temple site not far off, and it is now in the national museum in Buyeo.

The riding here is mellow. The Geumgang river valley is wide and flat, with rice paddies, greenhouses growing melons, and low wooded hills, and roads follow the water for long straight stretches. A gentle climb to the fortress offers views of the river bends, and the old riverside road is pleasant at a slow pace. In the lotus season of July and August the ponds at Gungnamji are in flower. Winter is cold and dry, and in summer the monsoon can drench the valley.

Buyeo is a town of some thirty-two thousand, with petrol and restaurants close by. Try the local speciality, which is roasted rice and sweet lotus tea. Baekje's historic areas joined the UNESCO list in 2015. The best seasons are April for the blossom and October for clear air and gold light.
t.sonjuk bridge and phyochung monuments@38:
The Sonjuk Bridge is a small stone bridge in the Korean city of Kaesong, and it has the most bloodstained history of any bridge on the peninsula. In 1392, as the Goryeo dynasty collapsed and General Yi Seong-gye prepared to found the Joseon dynasty, his son Yi Bang-won invited the scholar Jeong Mong-ju, a loyalist of the old dynasty, to a meeting. On his way home Jeong was struck down on this bridge, and tradition says that the dark stains on the stone are his blood, and that bamboo grew from the spot. Jeong became a symbol of loyalty, and a stone memorial and pavilion were built beside the bridge in later centuries.

Kaesong was the capital of Goryeo for almost five hundred years, and it holds royal tombs, palace foundations, a famous academy and the remains of city walls. UNESCO listed the historic monuments in 2013. The city sits just north of the demilitarised zone, a short drive from the border, and it is known for ginseng, for its cuisine and for a long tradition of trade.

Here I have to be plain with you: Kaesong is in North Korea, and it is not somewhere a rider can simply turn up. Foreign access is tightly controlled, visits are only possible on organised tours when the authorities allow them, and individual travel by motorcycle is not possible. Even guided access has been suspended for long periods. Anyone with an interest in the place should check current government travel advice, and treat this stop as a piece of history rather than a plan.

Kaesong is a city of more than three hundred thousand, and the landscape around is wooded hills, rice fields and rivers, with pine forests on the ridges. The famous local dish is a banquet of many small plates in brass bowls, and the area was known in the past for its ginseng and for its roadside inns. For anyone curious about the story, the Goryeo Museum in the city, in the old Confucian academy, keeps the tradition of the dynasty alive.
t.berg en dal aqueduct louisedal@51.8,5.9:
The Romans were water engineers, and the Berg en Dal aqueduct, near Nijmegen, is a trace of that skill in the Dutch landscape. Nijmegen was a major Roman centre, called Noviomagus, with a legion fortress on the Hunerberg and a town that grew beside it, and it needed a good water supply. The solution was to tap springs in the hills to the east, in the hills around Berg en Dal, and carry the water in a channel for several kilometres. Remains have been found near Louisedal, in the form of stone foundations and traces of the channel.

The hills themselves are a surprise in this flat country. They are a push moraine, a ridge of sand and gravel shoved up by the ice sheet in the last ice age, and they rise to over a hundred metres, covered in beech and oak woods. Springs flow from the foot of the slope, which is why the Romans, and people before and after them, settled here. Today the area is a nature reserve with walking paths, and a small number of museums and old villas dot the slopes.

Riding here is delightful by Dutch standards. The roads climb gently through the woods in a series of curves, with speed limits that are often low, and the surfaces are smooth. On weekends the roads fill with cyclists and walkers, and drivers are used to sharing the space. In the autumn the leaves fall and the road gets slippery, and in winter frost lingers in the shade. Cameras are common, and fines are heavy. A ride to the viewing points and a coffee in a woodland cafe makes a good short outing.

Berg en Dal is a small village, and Nijmegen, the nearest city, has fuel stations, restaurants and shops, as well as the Valkhof and the Roman museum. The Waal is a short ride away, with long views from the dike. Come on a bright weekday in spring or autumn, and expect pancakes, which are a local speciality in the woodland tea houses.
t.utrecht limes road de balije@52.1,5.0:
The Romans built their northern frontier along the Rhine, and in what is now the Netherlands they built a road beside it, running on the natural levee of the river, which was the highest and driest ground. Today the Kromme Rijn, the Crooked Rhine, flows past Utrecht as a small, quiet river, but in the first century it was the main channel, and the road ran alongside it, linking forts and watchtowers from the sea to the Roman towns upstream. At Utrecht there was a fort, Traiectum, from which the city takes its name, and nearby at Vechten stood the larger fort of Fectio, one of the most important along the Dutch stretch of the frontier.

De Balije lies in the Utrecht district of Leidsche Rijn, on the western side of the city, and I should say that what remains above ground is slight, and the road is mostly a line under the modern streets and fields. The modern district is a vast new suburb built since the 1990s, with the Roman past commemorated by markers and a small museum. Archaeologists found the old road, a ship and parts of a bridge here, preserved in the wet soil.

Riding in and around Utrecht is easy but unexciting. Roads are flat and well kept, and the dike roads along the Kromme Rijn and the Vecht are charming, with old farmhouses, country estates and blossom in spring. The city has an extensive network of cycle paths, and cars are limited in the centre. Speeds are low, and cameras are everywhere. The wind blows steadily across the polders, and in winter, fog sits on the meadows.

Veldhuizen is a suburb with shops and cafes, and Utrecht proper has fuel, restaurants and the great Dom tower, the tallest church tower in the country, visible from miles away. The area is known for its castles and country houses, such as De Haar. Try a pannenkoek or a bowl of pea soup in winter. Come in May, with meadows green and long light on the water.
t.herwen de bijland@51.9,6.1:
At Lobith, a few kilometres east of here, the Rhine enters the Netherlands from Germany, and you can feel the river changing its mind about what it is. Within a short distance it splits into branches, the Waal, the Nederrijn and the IJssel, and spreads across a wide floodplain, the Bijland, of meadows, willow thickets and old river arms. In Roman times this was the frontier, and a fort at Herwen, called Carvium, guarded the river crossing with a garrison and a small settlement. The Roman road ran along the dike, and ships tied up at its harbour.

The floodplain is a different world from the rest of the country, because here the river rules. In winter and spring the water comes up and covers the fields, and sheep, cattle and wild horses graze in the uiterwaarden, the foreland meadows. Geese arrive in huge flocks, and white-tailed eagles and spoonbills have returned in recent years. Some of the old dikes have been moved back to give the river room, and the result is a patchwork of lakes, reedbeds and meadows.

The riding is calm and often beautiful. Dike roads run along the Pannerdensch Kanaal and the Waal, with views across wide water and fields, and farms sit on mounds above the flood line. The road surface is generally excellent, though narrow, and cyclists have priority. Wind blows from the west, and in winter the river fog is thick. During high water some roads in the floodplain can be closed, so check the local news after prolonged rain.

Lobith is a village of about three thousand with a couple of cafes, and fuel and supermarkets wait in Zevenaar. The border crossing into Germany is just beyond, and Emmerich on the German side has a long riverside promenade. Try a local asparagus dish in late spring, and coffee with a slice of vlaai. Early morning, with mist rising from the river and geese calling, is the finest hour.
t.nijmegen valkhof area valkhofpark@51.8,5:
Nijmegen calls itself the oldest city in the Netherlands, and it has a good case. The Romans founded a military camp on the hill here in the last years BC, and a town followed, which was given full town rights around AD 100. Many centuries later, on the same hill by the Waal, Charlemagne built a palace, the Valkhof, and Frederick Barbarossa rebuilt it in the twelfth century as a magnificent imperial residence. Little survives except for a chapel and a ruined apse, but the Valkhofpark, with its terraced slopes and view across the river, still marks the site of one of the most important places in the medieval empire.

The Waal, the broadest branch of the Rhine, flows below the park, and the great bridge that spans it was the scene of one of the famous episodes of the Second World War. In September 1944, during Operation Market Garden, American paratroopers crossed the river in canvas boats under fire to capture the bridge, which opened the road north towards Arnhem. The city was damaged by bombing in 1944, and much of it was rebuilt after the war. Every July, the Four Days Marches draw tens of thousands of walkers from around the world through its streets.

For riders, Nijmegen is a city to enjoy at an easy pace. The centre has restrictions on traffic, with narrow lanes, cobbles and cyclists everywhere, and parking is best done at the edge. A short ride to the hills of Berg en Dal and the Ooijpolder gives the nearest thing to curves in the region, and the dike roads along the Waal give wide views. Speed limits are low and cameras are common.

Nijmegen has a population of about one hundred and fifty-nine thousand, and fuel, food and cafes are plentiful. It is a student city, so evenings are lively. Spring and autumn offer the best light for viewing the river, and a stroll in the Valkhofpark at sunset gives a good view across the Waal.
t.limessection between watchtowzers wp 1 3:
The Roman frontier in Germany starts at the Rhine and heads off into the woods, and the Westerwald is where it first leaves the river. Near Rheinbrohl the Upper German Limes begins, and from there it climbs the hills to the east, a line of earth banks, ditches and watchtowers that once ran for about five hundred and fifty kilometres to the Danube. Between the towers numbered 1 and 30 it crosses the high ground behind Neuwied, through the area of Melsbach and Rengsdorf, and what remains today is mostly a low bank and a shallow ditch in the forest.

The towers were modest wooden and later stone structures, a few storeys high, built within sight of one another so that soldiers could signal along the line. The frontier was not a wall in this part, but a boundary that controlled movement, with a palisade of oak posts in places. It was built in the second century AD, and it held until the Alamanni broke through around 260. The whole line was listed by UNESCO in 2005 as the Upper German-Raetian Limes.

The country here is beech and oak forest on rolling hills, with meadows, small villages and old half-timbered farms. Rengsdorf and Melsbach are small and quiet, with a few thousand people between them. Roads wind up and down through the Westerwald with moderate bends, good surfaces in most places and very little traffic outside holidays. Weather is cool and damp, and fog and drizzle are common, but in autumn the colours of the beeches are rich.

For fuel, aim for Neuwied, a short way to the south on the Rhine, because the villages of the Westerwald are small and stations are not frequent. The Limes marker posts and information boards mark the path, and a trail follows the line for walkers. Expect to see the bank and ditch only as faint ripples in the leaf litter, and expect to use your imagination. A soldier on duty here would have been cold, bored and far from home, and the forest still has that feeling. Pack a rain layer, whatever the forecast says.
t.kottenforst nord durrenbruch 3@50.7,7.0:
The Kottenforst is a big woodland on a ridge west of Bonn, and for centuries it belonged to the prince-electors of Cologne, who used it as a hunting ground. Long straight rides, cut through the forest in the eighteenth century, radiate from hunting lodges, and they are still visible as avenues of beech and oak. The Elector Clemens August, who built the baroque palaces of Augustusburg and Falkenlust at nearby Bruhl, loved falconry, and the forest was part of that world. The palaces are UNESCO World Heritage, and they are a short ride away.

The northern part of the forest, near Alfter and Bornheim, lies on the edge of the Vorgebirge, the low ridge that separates the Rhine from the Cologne lowland. The soil is rich loess, and the area has long been orchard and vegetable country, famous for asparagus and strawberries in spring. The Romans knew it too. The great Eifel aqueduct, the Roman canal that carried water to Cologne from springs in the hills, ran along this side of the Vorgebirge, and traces of it survive. Cologne was a legionary base and the capital of the province of Lower Germany, and its Praetorium, the governor's palace, stood by the Rhine.

Riding here is gentle. The forest roads are narrow and quiet, with surfaces that vary from smooth to patched, and many of the forest tracks are closed to motor vehicles, so stay on the public roads. The lanes between villages run past orchards, farm shops and half-timbered houses. Traffic is heavier on the main roads between Bonn and Cologne, and on summer weekends the forest fills with walkers and cyclists. Wild boar and deer live in the woods, and you should take care at dusk.

Bornheim has nearly fifty thousand people, and Alfter more than twenty thousand, so fuel and food are not a problem. Local farm shops sell apples, plums and honey, and in spring you can buy asparagus straight from the field. Cologne and Bonn are both close, and you can slip out of the cities for a quiet afternoon. Autumn is lovely, with golden leaves and mist in the glades.
t.watchtower wp 1 87@50.4,7.8:
The Limes crosses the Lahn at Bad Ems, and this stretch of the Rhineland-Palatinate hills is where the Roman frontier meets one of Germany's prettiest river valleys. The Lahn runs through a deep, wooded gorge here, with vineyards and steep slopes, and old spa towns along the banks. Dausenau is a small medieval town of half-timbered houses that still has its town wall, and a church tower that leans, a result of an unstable foundation. Arzbach lies on the high ground to the north, known for pottery.

The watchtower marked on the Limes here is one of a chain that kept watch on the Roman side of the frontier. The Romans built the Limes in the second century AD, and it ran through forests and hills in a line that was not always straight. Towers were placed on high points with good views, and the one at this point was part of the section on the right bank of the Lahn. Little remains of the tower itself beyond a low mound and a marker, but the Limes path gives access.

The river valley is one of the best riding areas in the region. The road along the Lahn runs from Koblenz upstream, winding with the river through villages and past castles, with steep forested slopes above. The surface is generally good, with some tight bends, and traffic can be heavy at weekends. Bad Ems, a short way away, was a fashionable spa in the nineteenth century, visited by kings and emperors, and it was here in 1870 that a telegram, the Ems Dispatch, helped to start the Franco-Prussian War.

Arzbach and Dausenau are small, so for fuel plan on Bad Ems or Nassau, where there is more choice. Local food is hearty, with dumplings and sausages and good cakes, and the Lahn wines are light and fresh. Weather in the valley can be misty in the morning and warm by afternoon. In autumn the leaves turn red and gold, and the valley fills with woodsmoke. Take an hour to walk the lanes of Dausenau and look at the leaning tower. It is a small place with a great deal of character.
t.fort site and civil settlement of nieder:
Niederbieber was one of the biggest Roman forts in the German frontier country, and it sits on the edge of the modern town of Neuwied, on the river Wied, a few kilometres from where it flows into the Rhine. The fort was built in the second century as a base for a cavalry unit and later a larger garrison, and a large civilian town, the vicus, grew up around it. In the early third century it was rebuilt and expanded, and it had stone walls, towers and a commander's residence, with a large bathhouse and shops outside.

The end of this fort is a dramatic story. In about 260, the Alamanni, a federation of Germanic peoples, broke through the Limes, and the Romans abandoned the whole region east of the Rhine. Niederbieber was left empty, and many of the inhabitants may have fled with whatever they could carry. Archaeologists found coins and hoards of metalwork that were hidden and never recovered, which tells of fear and haste.

The place is on the list of UNESCO's Upper German-Raetian Limes, which recognised the frontier in 2005. Most of the fort lies under fields and housing, but excavations have mapped its layout, and a small museum and information boards in the area explain the story. The finds from the site are shown in the Roman museum in the Rhineland region, and you can see weapons, jewellery and pottery that were found in the vicus.

Neuwied, a town of about sixty-seven thousand people on the Rhine, has fuel, food and rooms, and Melsbach is a small village close to the fort. The riding here is gentle, with the Rhine valley to the south and the Westerwald hills to the east. Quiet roads wind through orchards and fields, and the Wied valley is pretty, with old mills and pleasant stretches of woodland. The Rhine itself is a busy waterway, with long barges and cruise ships. Spring and autumn are lovely, and summer weekends are busy.
t.st mary s cathedral and st michael s chu:
Hildesheim is a town that was destroyed and put back together. On 22 March 1945, bombers flattened most of the old town, and the cathedral and the church of St Michael were left as burnt shells. After the war, the people rebuilt them, stone by stone, and both are now UNESCO World Heritage, listed in 1985. They are among the finest examples of Ottonian architecture in Europe, from the years around the year 1000.

The man behind them was Bishop Bernward, a scholar and artist who ruled the diocese from 993 to 1022. He built St Michael's as his own burial church, with a clear, geometric plan, two choirs and a nave with alternating columns and pillars, and he commissioned bronze doors for the cathedral, cast in one piece, with scenes from Genesis and the life of Christ. The doors, which now stand at the entrance, are a remarkable survival, and so is a bronze column that spirals with scenes from the life of Christ. The painted wooden ceiling in St Michael's, from the thirteenth century, was taken apart and stored during the war, and then put back.

The cathedral courtyard holds a famous rose bush, the Thousand-Year Rose, said to be as old as the cathedral itself. According to legend, Louis the Pious, hunting in the forest, hung his reliquary of the Virgin on a wild rose, and when he returned the rose had grown so that the relic could not be moved, and he took it as a sign to found a church here. In 1945 the rose burned with the cathedral, but new shoots appeared from the roots and it bloomed again.

Hildesheim has about a hundred thousand people, so fuel and food are easy, with the old market square rebuilt in its medieval form and cafes under the half-timbered fronts. The countryside around is the gentle hill country of Lower Saxony, with the Harz mountains to the south, and the roads are quiet and well kept. Spring is the time for the rose, which usually blooms in late May. Early morning is best for the courtyard.
t.limessection between wp 4 37 and 4 39@50:
The Wetterau is a broad, fertile basin north of Frankfurt, and the Limes crosses it on its way from the Taunus hills towards the Main. Near Butzbach, the frontier runs through farmland and low wooded ridges, with a line of watchtowers, and the stretch between towers 4/37 and 4/39 is a quiet piece of it. The Saalburg, the reconstructed Roman fort in the Taunus, lies a short distance to the south, and it makes the best starting point for understanding what the frontier looked like.

The Upper German Limes was built by the Romans in the second century, and it runs from the Rhine to the Danube. In this part, it consisted of a wooden palisade, a ditch and a bank, with towers set a few hundred metres apart. Soldiers living in forts behind the line signalled by fire or horn if anything happened. The fort at the Saalburg was rebuilt in the early twentieth century on the orders of Kaiser Wilhelm II, and it includes gates, a headquarters building and a granary. UNESCO listed the Limes in 2005.

The country is open, rich farmland, with fields of wheat, barley and sugar beet, and villages of old half-timbered houses. Butzbach, a town of about twenty-five thousand people, has a pretty market square with a Renaissance town hall and a medieval centre. It has fuel, food and rooms, and Langgons, to the west, is a smaller place. Riding here is relaxed, with modest bends, good surfaces and little traffic outside the main roads. The Taunus hills to the south offer more fun, with winding roads through beech forest and a few steep climbs.

Weather in the Wetterau is mild by German standards, with early springs and warm summers, and the autumn is long and golden. Wind can blow across the open fields, so wear a layer. The Limes in this stretch is mostly a gentle swelling in the field, but information boards mark the route. Allow an hour or two to walk a short section, then ride on for lunch. The country does not ask for much attention, and it gives back more than you expect.
t.north wall areas 1 to 2@54.5,9.5:
The Danevirke is a wall that has been in the news for a thousand years. It stretches across the base of the Jutland peninsula, where the land narrows between the Baltic inlet of the Schlei and the marshes of the Treene and Rheide rivers, and it was built, extended and rebuilt from about the eighth century by Danish kings. It protected the southern border of the Danes against the Franks and later the Saxons, and its earthen banks, once topped by timber palisades, ran for some thirty kilometres. UNESCO listed it together with the Viking trading town of Hedeby in 2018.

The North Wall, near the village of Dannewerk, is among the best-preserved sections. A low green bank, several metres high in places, runs across fields and woods, and in the middle you find the Crooked Wall, a curved stretch that was built in the tenth century. Excavations have shown several building phases. Nearby, the remains of a brick wall from the twelfth century, built by King Waldemar the Great, show how important the barrier remained.

The wall's story has a modern echo. In 1864, during the war between Denmark and Prussia, the Danes abandoned the Danevirke without a fight, retreating to Dybbol, and the loss became a Danish trauma. Today the border lies further north, and the Danevirke Museum explains the history to visitors. Hedeby, the Viking town on the Schlei, was a major trading centre, and its reconstructed houses can be visited.

The landscape is flat and open, with farmland, hedgerows, and low ridges, and the Schlei, a narrow arm of the Baltic, lies a short ride to the east. The roads are straight, with good surfaces and little traffic, and the wind blows steadily from the west. Schuby is a small village nearby, and Schleswig, a historic town on the Schlei, is the place for fuel and food. Fish is the thing to eat, served smoked or fried. Weather is cool and changeable, and a windproof layer is a good idea even in summer. Autumn is crisp, and the light on the water is lovely.
t.kottenforst sud villiprot@50.6,7.1:
South of Bonn the Kottenforst climbs onto the same ridge that carries the villages of Wachtberg and the town of Meckenheim, and the woods here feel older and quieter than the suburbs around them. Beech and oak stand over a floor of leaf mould, with springs and small streams that gather in damp hollows, and the old hunting rides still run ruler-straight through the trees. The name Villiprot is one of those forest place names that sounds Roman, and the forest does carry Roman traces: the Eifel aqueduct, which brought spring water to Cologne over about ninety-five kilometres, crossed this country, and parts of its line can be followed on walking trails.

That aqueduct is one of the great Roman engineering works north of the Alps, built in the first century AD and carrying water mostly in a buried channel with a very gentle fall. Along the way it passed under hills and over valleys, and the arched bridge sections that crossed valleys have long since disappeared. Mineral deposits from the water built up inside the channel as limestone, and the stone was later cut and used for church and house decoration. A visit to the section in the forest is quiet and modest, but the story of Cologne's thirst is quite something.

Wachtberg and Meckenheim have between them nearly fifty thousand people, so fuel and food are straightforward, with bakeries, supermarkets and small restaurants in every village. The riding is a mix of forest lanes and open ridge roads, with good surfaces, easy bends and modest traffic. To the south the land drops into the Ahr valley, a wine region known for red Spatburgunder, and a bit east the Siebengebirge rises over the Rhine, with the castle ruin of Drachenfels. These make a good day out from the forest.

The best seasons are spring, when the beeches come into leaf, and autumn, when the woods turn copper. Summer weekends bring walkers and cyclists, so take care on the forest roads. Deer and wild boar are common at dusk. Orchards on the edge of the forest sell apples and cherries from stalls, usually on an honesty system, so keep some coins in your pocket.
t.uedem hochwald hochwald 8 2@51.7,6.4:
The Hochwald is a long wooded ridge on the left bank of the Lower Rhine, between Uedem and Xanten, and it stands out because everything around it is flat. It is a terminal moraine, a pile of rubble pushed up by an ice sheet in the last ice age, and its slopes carry beech and oak and pine, a cool green island in a plain of fields and pastures. Near Uedem, the Hochwald runs for some kilometres in a line, and walkers use the forest paths.

Close by lies the old Roman world. Xanten, about seven kilometres away, was the site of a Roman city, Colonia Ulpia Traiana, and of the legionary fortress of Vetera, and today it has one of the biggest archaeological parks in Europe, with reconstructed gates, temple, amphitheatre and a large museum. The Lower Germanic Limes, the frontier along the Rhine, was listed by UNESCO in 2021, and the ridge near here was a place of military interest, with camps and roads on the high ground that gave a view over the river plain.

The Lower Rhine is a peaceful stretch of Germany, close to the Dutch border. The roads run straight across a plain of fields, hedgerows, poplars and farms, and the sky seems huge. The riding is easy but can be monotonous, with gusty wind from the west, and a few shower clouds are normal. Spring brings asparagus stalls along the road, and autumn brings geese in their thousands from the north, which feed in the fields. Cyclists are numerous.

Uedem is a small town of nearly nine thousand people, and Xanten, about twenty-one thousand, has fuel, hotels and restaurants. Xanten also claims to be the home of Siegfried of the Nibelung legend, and the name of the legendary hero shows up on the signs. The Rhine itself is not far away, a wide, slow, brown river with barges, and it is a good place to watch the evening light. Take a waterproof layer, because this part of Germany is rarely completely dry.
t.fort site and civil settlement of arzbac:
Arzbach sits a few kilometres north of the Lahn, in the wooded Westerwald hills behind Bad Ems, and it is one of those places where the Roman Empire left a mark you have to squint to see. The fort and its civil settlement belonged to the Upper German-Raetian frontier, the Limes, which ran for hundreds of kilometres from the Rhine near Rheinbrohl all the way to the Danube. Here it was a ditch, a rampart and a timber palisade, studded with watchtowers within sight of one another. Nothing grand survives above ground in the village itself. What you get is the lie of the land: a ridge chosen because a sentry could see from it, and a settlement that grew beside the soldiers because soldiers need bread, boots and beer.

The riding is the reason to link it with the rest of the Limes sections. Roads here are the quiet kind that Rhineland-Palatinate does so well, narrow ribbons through beech and spruce, with tight little bends where a stream has cut a fold into the slope, and then a short open stretch over farmland where you can see the next ridge. Surfaces are generally decent, though forestry trucks leave mud and gravel at junctions, and leaves lie thick in autumn. Mornings are best, before the Sunday walkers appear at the car parks.

The nearest proper town is Bad Ems, about five kilometres away, a nineteenth-century spa on the Lahn. It is where the famous telegram of 1870 was drafted that helped tip France and Prussia into war, and where Kaiser Wilhelm took the waters. It has fuel, cafes along the river and a handful of grand, faintly faded bathing halls. Arzbach itself, with under two thousand people, and its neighbours Kadenbach and Eitelborn are small enough that I would not count on a pump after dark; fill up in Bad Ems or Montabaur direction before heading into the woods.

This is also the gateway to the Limes the way many riders meet it, a series of numbered watchtower positions marked by small signs, a reconstruction here, a low mound there. The mood is pastoral, slightly eerie, and quiet enough that you can hear the engine tick as it cools. If you like places where you have to supply the imagination, stop, turn the engine off, and look along the ridge line the way a legionary would have.
t.civil settlement of butzbach@50.4,8.7:
Butzbach is the sort of town that gets overlooked because it sits beside the motorway and the Frankfurt sprawl, and that is a pity, because the old centre is a proper half-timbered market town with a square worth a coffee. About a kilometre from the middle, the Romans once had a fort on the Limes, and the civil settlement, the vicus, grew up beside it. That is the story behind the label: soldiers first, then traders, wives, craftsmen and innkeepers who followed the pay.

The landscape explains why. Butzbach lies on the northern edge of the Wetterau, a broad, fertile plain of loess soil, one of the best farming country in Hesse, with the Taunus rising to the south and the first low hills of the Vogelsberg and the Lahn country beyond. The frontier here ran along the edge of the plain, taking in the rich land that Rome wanted inside its boundary. Today the plain is wheat, beet and rapeseed, with wind pushing across it, and the roads are straight and fast, which is a different pleasure from the hill lanes elsewhere on the same Limes. Early light on a clear spring morning, with the fields green and the church towers sharp, is as good as it gets.

For a rider this is a practical stop. The town has about twenty-five thousand people, so fuel, food and a bakery are all within a few minutes, and Langgöns and Rockenberg, a little farther out, can offer the same on a smaller scale. Parking near the market square is easy on a motorbike, and the pedestrian lanes are pleasant to walk. The wall of half-timbering around the market, with its fountain and stepped gables, is the thing to look at while you eat.

The Limes itself is now a World Heritage line, and the route here threads watchtower positions numbered in the surveyors' system that the frontier researchers used, with a few reconstructions along the way. Be ready to read little information boards rather than gape at ruins. It rewards a patient rider, and anybody who enjoys the quiet satisfaction of standing where an empire simply stopped.
t.limessection between watchtowers wp 1 67:
There is no spectacle at this section of the Limes, and that is exactly its character. It lies in the hills of the lower Westerwald, between Hillscheid, Höhr-Grenzhausen and little Simmern, about the point where the Roman frontier crossed from the Rhine side towards the Lahn. The Romans marked it with watchtowers, numbered by archaeologists in a long sequence from the Rhine eastwards, and this is watchtower position 1/67 on the first section of the frontier. Between them ran a palisade and a ditch. Today you meet it as a faint line in the woods, a bump in a field, a reconstruction here and there, and a sign with a map.

What makes the area rewarding for riders is the country around it. These are low forested hills with small valleys, and the roads that connect the villages are tight, narrow and often twisty, with a sprinkling of hairpin-ish bends where they drop to a stream. Surfaces vary; some are smooth, some patched, and forestry traffic leaves gravel on corners. Be gentle on damp mornings under the trees. The Westerwald weather is quick to change, cool and wet more often than the Rhine valley down below, and a thin jacket liner is a good idea even in summer.

Höhr-Grenzhausen is the town to know. With nearly ten thousand people it has fuel and food, and it sits at the heart of the Kannenbäckerland, the Jug Bakers' Land, a district famous for centuries for its grey stoneware with cobalt blue decoration. The clay lies right under the hills, and potters have worked here since the Middle Ages. There is a ceramics museum in the town, and the shops sell salt-glazed mugs and jugs that make surprisingly sensible souvenirs for riders with a pannier.

Hillscheid and Simmern are small, with just a couple of thousand people at most, so do not rely on them for fuel late in the day. It is a pleasant, unshowy corner, the sort of place for a slow pass through the woods, a pause at a watchtower sign, and then a coffee in a town that still makes jugs.
t.limessection between watchtower wp 1 87:
Along this part of the Limes, between Arzbach, Dausenau and Kadenbach, the Roman frontier cuts across the hills above the Lahn valley, and the numbered watchtower positions, here around the 1/24 to 1/26 group, give the section its identity. A watchtower was small, a stone base with a timber upper room, and signalled by fire or horn to its neighbours. The point of it all was surveillance rather than defence; if trouble came, the troops in the forts behind would be told. Standing at one of these positions now, in forest rather than the open ground the Romans cleared, you have to remind yourself that the trees are a later gift.

The riding is quiet and pleasant. The lanes run through the Westerwald edge, climbing out of the Lahn gorge in tight bends and then settling into easy curves among the beech woods, with plenty of places where a clearing opens onto a slope of fields and a church spire. Traffic is light, apart from the odd tractor, and the roads are narrow enough that a moderate pace is the right one. Early in the day, when the air is still cool and smells of damp leaf-mould, is the best time. Autumn is gorgeous but slippery.

Dausenau, down on the Lahn, deserves a stop in its own right. It is a tiny walled town of about thirteen hundred people, and its church tower leans noticeably out of true, the result, so the story goes, of the foundations settling on soft ground. Half-timbered houses crowd along the river, and the Lahn valley road gives you gentle, scenic riding when you want a change from the woods.

For fuel, the better choice is Bad Ems, a few kilometres east, a spa town of around ten thousand people with several stations and plenty of cafes beside the river. Arzbach, Kadenbach and Dausenau are small, so treat them as places for a bakery stop. The area is gently historical rather than dramatic, rewarding anyone happy to read a sign, look along a ridge, and enjoy the lane.
t.sansong@35.8,129.2:
Sansong is a name I cannot pin to a single stone, so let me tell you about the country around it. The coordinates put you in the Gyeongju basin in the southeast of South Korea, a flat valley ringed by low mountains that served as the capital of the Silla kingdom for nearly a thousand years, from the first century BC until 935. The nearest town is Gyeongju itself, a city of about a hundred and fifty thousand with fuel stations, noodle shops and a reputation as a museum without walls.

Silla was one of the Three Kingdoms of Korea, and its capital grew rich on gold, Silk Road trade and the Buddhist faith. The evidence is all around. Huge grass-covered royal burial mounds rise right in the middle of the town at Daereungwon, and from the roadside they look like green soft hills. Cheomseongdae, an observatory tower dating from the seventh century, stands in a field of cosmos flowers. On the slopes of Mount Toham above the city, Bulguksa temple and the Seokguram grotto, with its serene stone Buddha facing the dawn over the East Sea, are some of the finest Buddhist works in Asia.

The riding is better than you might guess. A road climbs through pines to the temples, with lazy bends and cool air, and east of the city you drop to the coast near Gampo, where a rocky shoreline holds the offshore resting place of King Munmu, who vowed to guard Korea as a dragon after his death. Expect speed cameras, which are numerous and enforced in South Korea, and bus drivers who rule the road.

Food is a pleasure. Gyeongju is known for hwangnam-ppang, small round pastries filled with sweet red bean paste, and for ssambap, rice served with a spread of vegetable side dishes. Try them in the old market streets.

April, when cherry blossoms line the roads around Bomun Lake, and October, when the ginkgo leaves turn the colour of old gold, are the best times. Summer is hot and humid, and winter brings sharp, dry cold with clear light.
t.hwasun dolmen site@35.0,126.9:
Walk through the rice fields near Hwasun and you can lose count of the dolmens. Nearly six hundred of them lie scattered across the slopes at Hyosan-ri and Daesin-ri in South Jeolla, the biggest concentration in a trio of Korean sites that were listed as a World Heritage landmark in 2000. They are huge flat capstones balanced on smaller upright stones, some of them over a hundred tonnes, built roughly three thousand years ago in the Bronze Age by a society that left no written word. Korea has more dolmens than anywhere else in the world, perhaps around forty percent of all that exist, and this valley is where you feel it.

What makes Hwasun special is that you can see the quarry. A mountainside behind the site still holds the rock from which the capstones were split, and the cutting marks tell you how people did it, with wedges and water and fire. The dolmens sit along a stream, and a path winds between them. Some are table-shaped and some squat like boulders; you will find a few lying half in the grass, as if resting.

The area is farmland, and the setting is gentle. The nearest town, Hwasun, is a place of about sixty thousand people with petrol stations and restaurants, and the city of Gwangju is not far away if you need serious supplies. The riding in this part of Korea tends to be rural and calm, along narrow roads between paddy fields with mountains in the distance. Mudeungsan, the big granite massif by Gwangju, is a short ride away, with winding roads and a national park. Unjusa temple near Hwasun is known for its legend of a thousand stone Buddhas and pagodas, and there are impressive red sandstone cliffs by the reservoir.

Expect speed cameras, which are common and strictly enforced, and little English signage away from the main roads. Spring brings the cherry and plum blossoms, and in October the rice turns gold around the stones, which makes the best photographs. Summers are hot and humid with heavy monsoon rain in July.

This is the sort of place where an hour feels like a century, and that is exactly how the builders would have wanted it.
t.seowon@36.7,128.8:
Dosan Seowon is a school, and it is the school of a man who is still on the thousand-won note. Yi Hwang, better known as Toegye, was the greatest Neo-Confucian philosopher of Korea's Joseon dynasty, and after he died in 1570 his students built this academy beside the Nakdong river where he used to teach. It opened a few years afterwards and became the model for hundreds of others. The site was listed as one of nine Neo-Confucian academies of Korea on the World Heritage list in 2019.

The buildings are plain and beautiful: low tiled roofs, wooden floors, open halls where students sat in rows to read the classics, a shrine behind, and a library of old woodblock prints. A dormitory lies to one side and a small pavilion looks out over water. Everything is deliberately modest, because the Confucian ideal was learning without luxury. The setting does the rest, with the river below, the hills behind and a stand of old trees in front, so that the scholars could study in the company of landscape.

The approach is the best part for a rider. From the city of Andong, famous for its mask dances and its food, the country roads run north through orchards, rice terraces and small farming villages, then wind up along the shore of a reservoir formed by a dam on the Nakdong. Traffic is light, the bends are gentle and the scenery changes with the seasons. Andong has plenty of fuel, and the smaller villages have little else, so fill up in town.

Andong is the place to eat. The local dish is jjimdak, braised chicken with glass noodles and vegetables, and Andong soju is a stronger, older kind of liquor than the clear green-bottle stuff. Salted mackerel, ganjaengi, is another local pride.

Come in autumn when the leaves turn on the slopes, or in spring when the plum and cherry blossoms scatter. The site is quiet, so you may have the whole courtyard to yourself. Take off your shoes where signs ask, and keep your voice low, as the place expects.
t.hahoe cluster byeongsanseowon confucian:
Byeongsan Seowon looks across the Nakdong river at a cliff that is, quite literally, the best view in the neighbourhood. The academy stands in a bend of the river a short ride from the famous village of Hahoe, and its old lecture hall, called Manhyudae, was built with one aim: to frame the opposite cliff like a painting. Students sat on the open wooden floor and read the classics while the river slid past below. That is the Korean idea of education, a mind sharpened by the best possible landscape.

It belongs to the Ryu family of Andong, the same clan that built Hahoe. The most famous scholar here is Ryu Seong-ryong, who served as prime minister during the Japanese invasions of the 1590s and wrote the Jingbirok, a memoir of the war that is still read as a classic. The academy grew from a smaller school into a larger one in the sixteenth century and was one of the few to survive the nineteenth-century purge of academies, a political crackdown that closed hundreds. Together with eight others, it was listed as a World Heritage site in 2019.

The buildings are low, tiled and quiet, set on a slope with a gate at the bottom and rising courtyards behind. A massive zelkova tree grows near the lecture hall, and old pines line the paths. The whole thing takes about an hour to enjoy, and you will probably share it with only a handful of other people.

Getting here is easy from Andong, a city of about a hundred and thirty thousand with all the fuel, food and repair you might need. The roads east and south of the city follow the river through farm country, with some gentle bends and good views. The best riding is on the quieter local roads, not the main highway. Speed cameras are common in Korea, so keep an eye on limits.

Visit in early autumn, when the cliff turns russet and the rice is ripe, or in spring when the river is high and clear. A good lunch is heotjesabap, a ceremonial rice dish traditional in the region, and the local soju will keep you warm. Be prepared to walk, as the car park is some way from the gate.
t.area 1@37.5,127.2:
Seoul is a city of ten million, and a fortress sits just above its south-eastern edge. Namhansanseong is what the ride calls Area 1, and it is where the Joseon kings used to run when invaders arrived. The wall, about twelve kilometres of stone and earth following the ridge line, was built in the early seventeenth century on the foundations of older fortifications, and the whole enclosure sits on Mount Namhan, a granite hill just beyond Seongnam. It was listed by UNESCO in 2014.

Its story is a bitter one. In the winter of 1636, the Qing army invaded Korea and King Injo fled here with thousands of soldiers and officials. The siege lasted about forty-five days in appalling cold, with food running out, and in January 1637 the king gave up. He walked down to a ford on the Han river called Samjeondo and bowed to the Manchu emperor, an act of submission that Koreans still remember as one of the most humiliating moments in their history. Standing on the wall you can see why it was such a good refuge and why it failed, as the ridge is lovely and the supplies were not.

The area today is a provincial park, wooded and well kept. Roads climb from the plain to the gate, with hairpins and tight bends. At weekends it fills with hikers, cyclists and families, and the car parks, restaurants and chicken-porridge houses are packed. For fuel, Seongnam is one of Korea's bigger cities, with a million people and a station at every junction, so you will not be stuck.

A practical note: motorcycles are barred from Korean expressways, so you will use the national roads, which can be busy but are well surfaced. Speed cameras are everywhere. In this region, an early start on a weekday is the way to find a quiet road.

Spring brings cherry blossoms along the lower road and autumn colours are spectacular on the wooded ridges. Winter is cold and the air is clear, with views over Seoul on good days. Walk a section of the wall if you can; the stones are warm in the afternoon sun.
t.jangneung cluster@37.2,128.5:
Danjong was a boy of twelve when he became king, fourteen when he was forced off the throne, and sixteen when he died in exile, and the place where they buried him is Jangneung. In 1455 his uncle, later King Sejo, seized power, and two years later the boy was sent to Yeongwol, a remote valley in the mountains of Gangwon province, surrounded on three sides by river and on the fourth by cliffs. He died there in 1457, reportedly by poison and local tradition says a village official buried him secretly at night. His tomb was only restored to royal rank in 1698, centuries later, when a later king gave him the name Danjong.

That story is why this tomb, one of forty royal Joseon tombs listed as World Heritage in 2009, is the only one far from Seoul. It sits on a wooded slope, with a stone-lined path leading up to a mound guarded by stone sheep and tigers. A pavilion nearby holds records and ceremonies, and every spring a memorial festival remembers the boy king.

The setting is among the loveliest in Korea. Yeongwol lies deep in the Taebaek mountains, along the Dong river, with limestone peaks, forests and a famous bend in the river at Seonam village that looks like the outline of the Korean peninsula. The roads wind through valleys, with gradual bends and forested ridges, and are quieter than the expressway country near Seoul. Yeongwol itself is a small town of around twenty-five thousand and has fuel, food and basic repairs, and you should fill up there before heading into the hills.

Local pride includes buckwheat, which grows well in the cold climate; try memil-jeon, buckwheat pancakes, or noodles. The poet Kim Sat-gat, a wandering figure of the nineteenth century, is also buried in the area and celebrated at a small museum.

Autumn colours here are superb, and spring brings the scent of cherry and apricot blossoms. Winters can be severe, with ice on the passes, so check conditions before travelling. The air is cold and clean, and the dawn mist from the river lifts slowly, as if reluctant to reveal the grave.
t.hahoe cluster hahoe village@36.5,128.5:
Hahoe means something like river-wrapped, and the village earns its name. The Nakdong river makes an S-shaped bend around a sandy spit, and the Ryu clan built a settlement of tile-roofed noble houses and thatched farm cottages inside the curve. It has been continuously lived in for more than five hundred years, and the old layout, with its pine groves, stone walls and narrow lanes, is intact. Together with Yangdong village near Gyeongju, it was inscribed on the World Heritage list in 2010 as a model of Joseon-era clan life. Villagers still live here, farm here and run guesthouses, so remember that you are walking through a village, not a stage set.

The cliff across the river, Buyongdae, is the best viewpoint. You cross by a small ferry or take the path through the pines, then climb for a view down onto the whole bend with the village laid out like a map. The village is also home to Hahoe masks, the carved wooden masks used in a traditional dance-drama, with a museum nearby. Visitors are often struck by how comic the masks are, with big jaws and mocking grins aimed at pompous aristocrats. Queen Elizabeth II visited in 1999 on her seventy-third birthday, a fact local guides will mention within a minute of meeting you.

Cars are not allowed into the village itself, so you park at the car park and walk or take a shuttle. Andong, the city about twenty kilometres away, has the fuel, food and everything else, and the roads between are gentle farm country, with tidy rice fields and apple orchards. This is not hardcore riding country, but the bends along the river are pleasant, and the back roads are pretty and quiet.

Try Andong's jjimdak and a bowl of heotjesabap, then a cup of local soju if you are not riding on.

The best seasons are autumn, when the persimmon trees are bright orange, and spring, when the river runs clear. Summer rain can make the lanes muddy, and in winter the river freezes on the edges. Leave early; the day-trippers arrive from mid-morning.
t.sungyang sowon@38.0,126.6:
Jeong Mong-ju was a scholar and loyal official of the Goryeo dynasty, and on the evening of April 1392 he was killed on a stone bridge in Kaesong by henchmen of Yi Seong-gye, the general who was about to found the Joseon dynasty. Jeong had refused to switch sides. Legend says that his blood stained the stone of the bridge, Seonjukgyo, and that it is still visible, and that bamboo grew from the spot, which gave the bridge its name. Sungyang Seowon, the academy beside it, was built to honour him. It was originally his house and became a shrine and school, and still shows Korean loyalty as a theme: a dead man whose refusal made him a hero.

Kaesong was the capital of Goryeo, the dynasty that gave Korea its name, from the early tenth century until 1392. Its old centre is a cluster of historic monuments listed on the World Heritage list in 2013, including palace foundations, tombs, a former Confucian academy and city walls. The setting is a ring of low hills, Songak mountain behind, with old pines and tile roofs among modern streets.

This is not a place a rider can simply turn up. Kaesong lies in North Korea, about eight kilometres from the border, and visits are only possible on arranged tours, with guides and fixed routes. That makes the question of fuel, food and roads academic, so I will tell you what I can instead of pretending to knowledge I do not have. The city is large, about three hundred and thirty thousand inhabitants, and was historically known for its ginseng, which is still its famous product. Kaesong cuisine has a high reputation in Korea, with elaborate rice meals served in brass bowls and a distinctive wrapped kimchi.

If you are reading this on the Korean peninsula's southern half, you can look across toward Kaesong from observation points near the border, and the imagination can do the rest. The old academy buildings, the bridge and the quiet wooded grounds belong to the Goryeo story as much as to any modern border.
t.kaesong walls@38.0,126.5:
The walls of Kaesong tell you what a medieval capital thought about safety. Goryeo's rulers lived behind several rings, an inner enclosure around the palace, a middle wall and an outer wall of earth and stone running around the hills for kilometres. The outer wall was begun in the early eleventh century, partly in response to Khitan invasions from the north, and was rebuilt and extended later. Parts are still visible along the ridge lines, with gates at key points, and they are now part of the World Heritage listing of historic monuments and sites in Kaesong, inscribed in 2013.

You will not find a road sign for them. Kaesong is in North Korea, close to the border, and the city is only open to foreign visitors on controlled tours with guides.
