I can write about the wall but not about how to ride to it, and I would rather say so honestly than invent a route. If you are ever in a position to visit, the main landmarks are the palace site at Manwoldae, the old Confucian academy, the royal tombs in the hills and the bridge where Jeong Mong-ju died.

What interests historians is the idea of Kaesong as a trading capital. The dynasty traded with Song China and with Arab merchants, and the name Korea is said to come from Goryeo as foreigners first heard it. The city grew rich on ginseng, celadon pottery and printing. Goryeo produced some of the finest celadon ever made, with a delicate blue-green glaze, and the world's first movable metal type was probably used in Korea during this age.

The surrounding landscape is wooded hills and rice fields, with the long Songak mountain looming over the city. The climate has four distinct seasons, with a hot, humid summer, a brilliant autumn and a cold, dry winter.

For fuel and food in practice, a tour looks after everything for you. Meals tend to be long, ceremonial affairs, and the local cooking is regarded as among the best in Korea. If you want a sense of the place without crossing the border, museums in Seoul hold excellent Goryeo celadon. Treat this entry as a story, not a route.
t.islands and protected areas of the gulf:
Jacques Cousteau once called the Gulf of California the world's aquarium, and the number backs him up: more than two hundred and forty islands and a protected stretch of sea, listed by UNESCO in 2005, hold about a third of the world's marine mammal species. Blue whales and fin whales come into the gulf to feed in winter and spring, sea lions haul out on island rocks, dolphins ride the bow waves of boats, and whale sharks cruise in warmer months. The water is a startling turquoise against cactus-covered desert islands in the colours of rust, ochre and bone.

I do not know the exact spot this label points to, so I will tell you about the coast it belongs to. The coordinates fall on the gulf side of the Baja California peninsula, in the stretch between Santa Rosalia and the lagoon country to the northwest, one of the emptiest and most beautiful parts of Mexico. Santa Rosalia itself, to the south, is a curious town: it was built by a French mining company in the 1880s to work copper, and it still has wooden houses with deep verandahs, a bakery famous for French bread, and an iron church that, according to local legend, was designed by Gustave Eiffel.

Riding here means Mexican Highway 1, the Transpeninsular, a two-lane road that runs the length of Baja. It crosses desert, with giant cardon cacti, boojum trees and sudden glimpses of blue water, and the gulf stretch south toward Mulege and Bahia Concepcion is among the best motorcycle roads in North America. Distances between fuel stops can be very long, so fill whenever you can, and carry extra water. Watch for cattle at night, hard crosswinds and slow trucks on the curves.

The gulf is cold for swimming in winter and exhilarating in autumn. Summer is intensely hot and humid, with hurricane season from August to October, so the best months are November to April, when whale-watching is at its peak.

Pack sunscreen, spare tubes and a good sense of humour, and let the desert and sea do the rest.
t.nijmegen kops plateau east@51.8,5.9:
Under the suburbs of Nijmegen lies the oldest town in the Netherlands, at least according to Nijmegen, and on the Kops Plateau you can see why they say it. In the first century, the Romans chose this long ridge above the river Waal as a base for their legions. It was the perfect spot, a high sandy plateau with the broad river at its feet and a clear view across the flat country to the north. Their camp here, with ramparts, ditches and barracks for thousands of soldiers, was one of the largest military bases on the northern frontier of the empire.

The east side of the plateau has a dramatic story attached. In AD 69 and 70, a Batavian officer called Civilis, who had served in the Roman army, led his own people in a revolt against Rome. Nijmegen was one of his main targets, and the legionary camp was burned. Rome sent a large army to put the revolt down, then rebuilt on the nearby Hunerberg a new fortress, which later grew into a city. What you see on the Kops Plateau today are the traces: banks, ditches and a landscape shaped by army engineers two thousand years ago, now a part of the Lower German Limes listed by UNESCO in 2021.

The ride here is a Dutch one. Roads are smooth and well signed, with cycle lanes beside nearly every road and cyclists behaving as if they own it. Speed limits are strict, with cameras and police who do not forgive, and there are roundabouts every few hundred metres. You will find plenty of fuel in Nijmegen, a lively university city of some one hundred and seventy thousand people, and the nearby suburbs.

Nijmegen is the oldest city in the country, and locals will tell you so with pride. In July the city hosts the Four Days Marches, a walking event that draws tens of thousands of walkers from around the world and fills the streets with flowers and music. Visit a cafe on the market square and sample a local pastry or a Dutch coffee.

Spring brings blossom and tulips, and late summer brings cool, soft light. Winters are grey and damp. Expect wind on the open stretches.
t.nijmegen kops plateau north@51.8,5.9:
Climb to the northern edge of the Kops Plateau and the land falls away to a wide green river valley, the Waal, the Rhine's biggest arm, and beyond it the flat polders of the Betuwe stretch toward the horizon. The ridge you stand on is a relic of the Ice Age. About a hundred and fifty thousand years ago an enormous glacier pushed ahead of itself a wall of sand and gravel, and the hills around Nijmegen, which locals call the seven hills even though nobody agrees which seven, are its leftovers. For the Dutch, who live mostly below sea level, this is genuinely high ground.

The Romans noticed. A high place beside a navigable river at the edge of an empire was irresistible, and the north slope of the plateau was part of their legionary camp, a position from which they watched the Rhine frontier. This point on the plateau is included in the Lower German Limes, the frontier of the Roman Empire along the Rhine, listed by UNESCO in 2021.

Below the slope runs the Waal and the great bridge at Nijmegen, which became famous in September 1944. During Operation Market Garden, American paratroopers crossed the river in canvas boats under heavy fire, and then British tanks and American infantry seized the bridge. The story is well documented and the memorials are numerous, the most evocative being a quiet riverside walkway near the bridge.

Riding here is flat, tidy and polite, a landscape for easy touring rather than for bends. The roads along the dikes, the embankments that hold back the river, make a charming ride when the traffic is light, with views over water meadows, willows and cows. Wind is the real hazard, because there is nothing to stop it, and a headwind on a dike road can be hard going. Nijmegen has all the fuel, food and repair you need.

Take a stop in one of the riverside cafes, with a view of the bridge and the barges, and try a bitterbal or a slice of apple pie. The best seasons are late spring, when the meadows are green and the light is long, and early autumn. In winter the river can flood the water meadows, and the dikes become high ground in the oldest sense.
t.nijmegen kops plateau kopse hof north@51:
Kopse Hof is the name given to this northern corner of the plateau, and the first thing to say is that the Roman layer is under your feet, not in front of you. For the last few decades Dutch archaeologists have dug across this ridge ahead of every new street and housing block, and what they found was astonishing: ditches, postholes, the outlines of timber barracks, pits and graves, pottery, coins, tools and shoe soles preserved in the wet. A city sits on top of a legionary camp, and the modern streets of Nijmegen run over the old Roman roads.

The Roman town that grew here after the soldiers left was called Noviomagus, which means new market, and the modern city's name descends from it. It was the capital of the Batavian people and one of only two Roman cities in what is now the Netherlands. The Valkhof museum in town shows what has been dug up, from everyday pottery to fine glassware, and is a good way to make sense of the empty fields.

The ride is Dutch in the best sense. Cycle paths give way to quiet streets, then to country lanes between orchards and the gentle hills that mark the edge of the Ice Age moraine. There is almost no gradient in the Netherlands, so the pleasure comes from the changes in scenery, from river to woodland to bulb fields. Fuel is easy throughout. Speed limits are low and enforced, and cameras are common, so ride at the limit and enjoy it.

Locals have a tradition of eating pancakes, pannenkoeken, which you can order savoury with bacon and cheese or sweet with syrup, and which fit well into a tour. Nijmegen is also a student town, so the cafes are lively and cheap.

Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with fewer tourists and softer weather. Rain can arrive suddenly and waterproofs are wise in any month. In the evening, when the light turns gold, the plateau seems to hold its breath, and you can almost imagine the sound of marching feet.
t.zilveren schaats@52.1,5.1:
The Dutch are proud of skating, and Utrecht's Silver Skate is the sort of name that makes sense only here: a country of canals that freezes about one winter in ten, where the whole nation drops its work when the ice holds and goes out to skate. I cannot tell you what exactly the label points to, so let me talk about the place it sits in. The coordinates are in the middle of Utrecht, a city of about three hundred thousand that is the geographic heart of the Netherlands, and in the story of the Dutch Water Defence Lines, which UNESCO listed in 1996 and extended in 2021, Utrecht is the keystone.

The idea was ingenious. Instead of building a wall, the Dutch simply let in the water. Starting in the seventeenth century, they developed a belt of land from the Zuiderzee down to the Biesbosch that could be flooded to a depth of about forty centimetres, too shallow for boats and too deep for marching soldiers, and defended the dry spots with forts. The New Dutch Waterline ran right past Utrecht, which was kept inside its protection. Locks, sluices and culverts controlled the water, and forts like Rijnauwen and Vechten stood on the high points.

A modern rider enjoys the city differently. Utrecht's old centre has canals with wharf cellars, which sit below the street level and now house cafes, and the Dom Tower, which at 112 metres is the tallest church tower in the country. Motorbikes are tolerated in the centre but parking is tight, so leave the bike at a garage on the edge. Fuel is easy in a city of this size, and the ring roads connect to the A2 and A12 motorways.

Surrounding country is flat and green, crisscrossed with cycle paths, windmills and small villages. For a ride, aim for the Vecht river to the north, with its string of old country houses, or the polders south of the city.

Eat a stroopwafel warm from a market stall and look for a cafe on the canal. The best months are May to September, but the real magic is a hard winter, when the canals go solid and the city gets out its skates.
Nijmegen sits on the first real hills that the Rhine delta meets, and on the Hunerberg, now a leafy suburb with a park, the Romans built a fortress. From about the year 70, after the Batavian revolt had been crushed, the Tenth Legion, Legio X Gemina, was stationed here, some five thousand men in a stone-walled camp. It was a serious piece of engineering, a mini-city of barracks, workshops, a hospital and a commander's house, and the legionaries were here for about thirty years. The civilian town that grew beside it later became the first in the Netherlands to receive Roman town rights.

The area labelled Hunnerpark on the ride and the neighbouring Valkhof are where the story keeps going. Valkhof means falcon court, and a palace stood there under Charlemagne in the eighth century. Frederick Barbarossa rebuilt it in the twelfth century, and today you can see a small round chapel from that era, the Saint Nicholas chapel, among the trees of the Valkhof park, which looks out over the Waal river. The rest was demolished in the seventeenth century. It is a lovely park to rest in with views of bridge and barges.

Riding here is typical of a Dutch city of a hundred and sixty thousand: bike lanes on every road, trams of cyclists, roundabouts, narrow brick streets, and speed limits that are rigidly kept. The centre is partly pedestrian and parking is hard, so use a garage and walk. Fuel and repairs are no problem, and the city has a large student population that makes cafes lively and affordable.

Nijmegen was badly bombed by mistake by American planes in February 1944, and fought over again in September, but it has been rebuilt with a pleasing mix of old and new. The tall Waal bridge is the symbol of the city, with a modern second crossing nearby.

Try a plate of local apple pie, a coffee on the Grote Markt and a glass of beer from one of the town's craft brewers. April to October is ideal for riding, while the summer Four Days Marches in July fill the streets with walkers. Ask at the tourist office for the Roman route, which links the key sites on foot.
t.berg en dal aqueduct cortendijk@51.8,5.9:
Water is the oldest luxury a city can have, and Roman Nijmegen insisted on it. A legion and a town of thousands needed clean drinking water, and the springs in the foothills at the edge of the plateau, near what is now Berg en Dal, provided it. The Romans built an aqueduct to carry it down to the fortress, a gently sloping channel which ran for several kilometres. Most of it was buried or built at ground level, so the remains are traces in the soil rather than tall arches, and archaeologists have followed it by digging and mapping, with a few sections uncovered and marked. It is one of the few places in the Netherlands where you can walk the line of a Roman water supply, and it forms part of the Lower German Limes on the UNESCO list.

The Cortendijk part sits in a landscape that makes the engineering feel sensible. At the foot of the wooded hills the springs still rise, and the land slopes gently down to the plain. The hills are the push moraine left by the glaciers of the last Ice Age, and the springs come from the water that percolates through the sandy slopes. Roman engineers simply used what nature had arranged.

The riding here is the Dutch version of hill country: low, wooded ridges, small climbing roads and sunken lanes, with views toward the Rhine delta. Villages like Berg en Dal have large villas set among beech trees, a legacy of the nineteenth-century rich who came to escape the city. The Afrika Museum there is one of the most unusual in the country. Roads are narrow and signed with low speed limits, and there is a constant flow of cyclists, especially at weekends.

Fuel and food are best found in Nijmegen, a short ride away, although the villages have cafes and small shops. Local fare includes asparagus in spring, and pancakes in any season.

If you want to stretch the day, the Ooijpolder to the north has bird life and wide views, and the woods of Groesbeek to the south are good for quiet lanes. Spring and autumn are the best times, with leaf colours in October, and the rain can come suddenly, so pack a waterproof.
t.berg en dal aqueduct marienboom@51.8,5.9:
The hills south-east of Nijmegen have a second history that has nothing to do with Rome. On Sunday 17 September 1944, thousands of American paratroopers of the 82nd Airborne Division landed on the heath and fields around Groesbeek, as part of Operation Market Garden, to seize the high ground and the bridges over the Maas and Waal. They succeeded in many things, but the push to Arnhem failed, and the front line stayed near here through a bitter winter. Nijmegen was liberated only partially, and fighting went on across the Reichswald forest just over the German border until the spring of 1945. The National Liberation Museum in Groesbeek tells the story, and the Canadian War Cemetery, with over two thousand graves, set among beeches, is one of the most moving places in the area.

The Marienboom section of the Berg en Dal aqueduct, though, is Roman. The aqueduct that fed the legionary fortress ran along the foot of these hills, and this part of the route belongs to the group listed by UNESCO as the Lower German Limes. It is easy to see how the two histories overlap here: the high ground with its water and its view has been valuable to every army for two thousand years.

For a rider the area is an attractive mix of heath, woodland and low hills, with quiet roads and fewer cyclists than the city. The Groesbeek forest and the Mook heath are good for relaxed touring, and the road along the ridge gives views over the Maas and the German border. Speed limits are low, and police do check them.

Fuel is not available in the villages, so fill up in Nijmegen or Groesbeek. There are cafes and small restaurants in the larger villages, and the local speciality is the pancake, which comes in dozens of varieties.

Spring brings wild flowers to the heath, and the autumn colours are good in the beech woods. Winter fog is common, and the days are short. If you visit in September, you may catch ceremonies marking the anniversary of the landings.
t.culvert bridge kromme rijn@52.1,5.1:
A river that has lost its job is a curious thing to ride beside. The Kromme Rijn, the crooked Rhine, was once the main channel of the Rhine through the middle Netherlands, and the Romans used it as their northern frontier. They built forts along it at intervals, among them one at Vechten, just east of Utrecht, and another at Bunnik, and the river served as a road for supply boats. In the Middle Ages the Rhine silted up and shifted, and what is left is a gentle, winding stream with willows and farm bridges, in a landscape of meadows and moated estates.

The culvert and bridge here belong to the later story of the Dutch Water Defence Lines. As far as I can tell, this is one of the structures used to manage the water in the New Dutch Waterline, where the idea was to flood a belt of land in wartime, and sluices and culverts allowed the engineers to let water in or hold it back. Modest in appearance, it is an example of how much of the line's strength lay in plumbing.

The area lies just east of Utrecht, near the suburb of Lunetten, whose name comes from a ring of small forts called lunettes. The surrounding countryside is a favourite with Dutch cyclists, and the lanes through the polders and past old farmsteads make a gentle ride. Roads are narrow and often shared with riders on bicycles, so keep speeds low. Fuel is no problem in Utrecht, and there are petrol stations along the roads to Houten and Bunnik.

Fort Vechten, nearby, houses a museum about the Waterline, with exhibitions on the engineering and the military ideas. In a flat country, a modest earth bank was sometimes the best defence, and the surprise is how well the system worked in theory and how rarely it was tested in practice.

Spring brings blossom in the orchards around Bunnik, and autumn brings mist on the meadows. The best time to ride is early morning, when the air is cool and the light is low and gold. Winters are damp, and in cold years you might see skaters on a flooded field.
t.nijmegen kops plateau west@51.8,5.9:
Go west from Nijmegen along the river and you are following the northern frontier of the Roman Empire. The Lower German Limes ran for about four hundred kilometres along the Rhine, from near Bonn to the North Sea at Katwijk, and for roughly three hundred years it marked the edge of the empire. It was never a wall. It was a line of forts, watchtowers, roads, harbours and ports along a river, defended by auxiliary troops and patrolled by boat, and almost all of it lies buried under fields, villages and dikes. In 2021 it was added to the World Heritage list.

The west side of the Kops Plateau is a good place to understand this. From here the old fortress looked out across the river valley, and the road west ran along the south bank of the Waal and then the Rhine. Today there is a modern equivalent: dike roads and country lanes run along the old river line through Arnhem, Wijk bij Duurstede, Utrecht, Leiden and the dunes at the coast. Riding it is a Dutch pleasure, with polder views, windmills, farms with thatched roofs, and the river never far away.

Do not expect hills or hairpins. This is a gentle country that rewards patience, with low speed limits, cameras and roundabouts at every junction. Wind off the North Sea is the main challenge, and a headwind on an exposed dike can be tiring. Fuel is easy in the towns, and Nijmegen itself has every service you could want.

Along the way you can visit small museums in places such as Wijk bij Duurstede and Vechten, which show Roman finds and explain the frontier. The Kops Plateau is a good beginning for the journey, because it tells you who these soldiers were, where they came from and why they stayed.

Spring is the best season, with fruit blossom in the Betuwe, followed by the long light evenings of early summer. Autumn brings migrating geese, and winter can bring floods, which in a way is the Rhine reasserting its old rights. Bring waterproofs, because rain arrives without warning, and a thermos for the cold dike tops.
The Swartendijk stretch lies on the quiet side of the hills, away from the villas and museums of Berg en Dal. This is where the Heilig Land Stichting, the Holy Land Foundation, was set up in the nineteenth century by Dutch Catholics, who built an enormous religious theme park with replicas of biblical sites, a Golgotha, a Jordan river and a Holy Sepulchre, in the woods and hills near the German border. It still exists, though it now has the air of a very large and slightly surreal garden, and it stands as a reminder that these slopes have been a place of pilgrimage as well as war.

The Roman aqueduct belongs to this landscape too. The springs on the hillside near here fed the water channel that ran to Nijmegen's fortress, and the line of the water supply is a part of the Lower German Limes UNESCO listing. The Duivelsberg, the devil's hill, rises near the border and is one of the highest points in the area, with a legend of the devil living in it. The hills are the sandy leftovers of an Ice Age glacier and the woods are mostly beech and oak.

Riding here is pleasant in a modest way. Narrow roads wind through the forest, with sunken lanes and short climbs that count as serious hills in the Netherlands, and crossing into Germany at Beek takes you to the Reichswald with its long straight forest roads. Road surfaces are generally good, though autumn leaves can be slippery and farm tractors are common. Keep to the speed limits, as police here are diligent.

For fuel, go back toward Nijmegen or to Groesbeek, because the hill villages do not offer much. Cafes and small restaurants offer pancakes and local beer, and the Dutch concept of gezelligheid, a kind of warm cosiness, is at its best on a damp afternoon in a wood-panelled cafe.

Spring is the best time, when the beech leaves emerge a luminous green, followed by golden October. Summer weekends can bring crowds, especially on the cycling routes. In winter the fog sits in the hollows, and the whole area becomes still and grey. Leave the bike at the foot of a lane and walk a while, because the slopes deserve it.
t.hannover@52.3,9.8:
Hannover is not the first name that comes to mind when riders talk about great destinations, and it would probably say that is fine. It is a big, calm, practical city of half a million people on the northern edge of the German hills, where the flat North German Plain begins to roll up toward the Deister and the Weser Uplands. The coordinates here are on its southern fringe, close to the exhibition grounds, the Messe, which hold the world's largest industrial fair and hosted Expo 2000.

The city was rebuilt after heavy wartime bombing, so much of the centre is plain postwar architecture, but there are good pockets. The Herrenhausen Gardens, a baroque garden laid out for the electors of Hanover, are lovely, and the royal family of Hanover became the kings of Great Britain in 1714, which is why English monarchs from George I to Victoria share a German city's name. The New Town Hall, with its green dome and an inclined lift that climbs inside it, offers a view across the whole city. Look out for the red thread painted on the pavement that leads you through the sights.

As a ride base, the city is excellent. Within an hour you are in the hills: the Deister, with its wooded ridges and little roads, the Extertal and Lippe uplands to the southwest, and the Oker valley and Harz mountains to the southeast. The terrain is rolling rather than mountainous, with bends through beech and oak woods and open views over farmland. Weekdays are quiet, while summer weekends bring crowds of other bikes. Roads are well surfaced, though speed cameras are common near villages and on straight stretches.

You will find fuel stations everywhere, including on the road to Laatzen and Pattensen, and excellent bakeries for an early start. Food here is straightforward, with Hannoveraner sausage and bread, and in spring there is asparagus on every menu. A stop in the old town near the Marktkirche gives you cobbles, half-timbered houses and a coffee.
t.liege@50.6,5.6:
Liège is a hard-working Walloon city on the Meuse, where steelworks once glowed along the river and the people have a reputation for warmth and bluntness. It has none of the polished prettiness of Bruges, and that is part of its appeal. The old centre is a tangle of lanes and courtyards under the hill called the Citadelle, with the grand Palace of the Prince-Bishops standing on a vast square, a reminder that this was an independent church state for nearly eight centuries.

You see the city's character in small things. On Sunday mornings the Batte market runs for a kilometre along the river, selling everything from cheese to clothes to live chickens. The Montagne de Bueren, a staircase of 374 steps, climbs up from the old town to the hillside, and people run it for training. The Liège waffle, dense and chewy with pearl sugar caramelised in the dough, is sold from every corner, and the writer Georges Simenon, creator of Inspector Maigret, was born here in 1903. The sleek white station at Guillemins, designed by Santiago Calatrava, opened in 2009 and looks like a ship's keel, tying the city to the modern rail network.

As a starting point for the Ardennes, Liège is ideal. Within half an hour of leaving town you are in rolling forest, following the Ourthe or Amblève valleys, with their long bends and stone villages. Further on lie Spa and the motor racing circuit at Francorchamps, then the high moors of the Hautes Fagnes, where the road crosses peat and heather. The Ardennes were the scene of the Battle of the Bulge in December 1944, and war museums, memorials and tanks by the roadside tell that story in Stavelot, La Gleize and elsewhere. Roads are well surfaced but speed cameras are common, and fog or ice can appear quickly in the cooler months.

Liège has fuel at every turn and a range of hotels. The Saint-Nicolas area nearby is also well served. Try boulets, meatballs in a sweet and sour sauce, with chips, and a local beer in one of the city's cafes. Autumn colour in the Ardennes is a highlight, so plan a loop in October.
t.waterton glacier international peace par:
Waterton Lakes National Park is where the Canadian prairies slam into the Rocky Mountains with hardly a foothill to cushion the blow. Flat grassland stretches all the way to the base of the peaks, which rise abruptly above the lake, and the effect is dramatic. The park occupies the southwest corner of Alberta, and together with Glacier National Park across the border in Montana it forms the Waterton-Glacier International Peace Park, created in 1932 as the world's first such park, and a symbol of friendship between the two countries.

The small townsite sits on the shore of Upper Waterton Lake, which extends across the border, and is dominated by the Prince of Wales Hotel, a Swiss-chalet-style building with a steep roof, built by the Great Northern Railway in 1927 on a bluff above the lake. Wildlife roams freely here: bighorn sheep and mule deer walk the village streets, and black bears and grizzlies are present in the park. Waterton is also famous for wind, which is strong enough to knock cyclists off their bikes and has shaped the trees into leaning flags.

Roads in the park are short but memorable. The Akamina Parkway climbs into the mountains to Cameron Lake, at the base of a steep-sided cirque on the border, and the Red Rock Parkway follows a valley to a canyon of red and green rock. Both are narrow and winding, with speed limits that are rightly low, and you should watch for wildlife on the road. Weather changes quickly, with snow possible in any month, and wind can be fierce on exposed stretches. The best time is July to September, though the park is quiet and clear in early autumn. Many facilities close from October to May.

A park pass is needed for entry. The townsite has fuel and basic services, plus restaurants and shops, though the choice is narrower than in bigger towns, and Pincher Creek, to the north, offers more. In summer, book rooms early. Stroll along the lake front and take the boat trip to Goat Haunt, Montana, if you have the time and the right documents.

The southern half of the Peace Park is Glacier National Park in Montana, a rugged expanse of peaks, lakes and valleys carved by ice, with the Continental Divide running through its core. The park was established in 1910 and covers more than a million acres, and in its heyday it held about a hundred and fifty glaciers. Climate change has reduced that to a few dozen, and the shrinking of the ice is one of the park's central stories.

Its great road is the Going-to-the-Sun Road, a narrow, spectacular route built in the 1920s and finished in 1933, which crosses the mountains at Logan Pass, at about 2,025 metres. It clings to cliffs on the western slope, passes through a rock tunnel and a long arched gallery, and runs beside waterfalls and meadows. Because snow lingers, the full road usually opens only around late June or July and closes in October, and in recent summers the park has sometimes required advance vehicle reservations, so check the current rules. Vehicle size limits also apply on the narrow western section.

Wildlife is part of the magic: mountain goats and bighorn sheep appear near Logan Pass, and grizzly and black bears wander the valleys, so carry bear spray if you hike, and never approach animals. The park lies on the traditional lands of the Blackfeet people, whose reservation borders it on the east, and their cultural centre and events add depth to a visit. The weather is unpredictable, with cold, rain and even snow at the pass in midsummer, and the road can get very busy.

Services in the park are seasonal and fairly simple, with lodges and restaurants that close in autumn. Early morning gives the best light and fewest crowds, and the east side tends to be windy. Bring layers, a good rain jacket and plenty of patience for slow traffic and roadworks.
t.uedem hochwald hochwald 11@51.7,6.4:
Lower Rhine forests do not announce themselves, and the Hochwald between Uedem, Xanten and Kalkar is no exception: a dark block of beech, oak and pine on a low ridge, with flat farmland on every side. Point 11 is a spot somewhere inside that woodland, about six kilometres from Uedem, so think of it as a way into the forest rather than a particular junction or bench.

The ground is quiet now, which is the odd thing about it. In February and March of 1945 this was one of the nastiest pieces of the Rhineland campaign. The Germans held the Hochwald as a fortified gap on the way to the Rhine, and Canadian and British troops fought through it in cold, mud and flooded fields. You will not find much that shouts about it from the saddle, but the straight rides and the regular lines of trees make more sense when you know the forest was shelled and then replanted. Smaller memorials and war graves are scattered around the district, and the larger cemeteries across the Reichswald near Kleve are worth a short detour if you like your history sober.

For riding, expect the Niederrhein in its plainest form. The roads are flat and mostly straight, with sudden right-angle bends where a field boundary or a drainage ditch once decided the route. Surfaces are generally fine, though forest tarmac gets strewn with needles, wet leaves and the odd sandy patch where a tractor has crossed, so brake early on the shady bends. Cyclists are everywhere here, in pairs and in families, and many rural roads have a limit of 70 or 100 that is easy to forget on a Sunday and actually enforced in places. The pleasure is rhythm rather than drama: long even stretches, birdsong when you kill the engine, and the resinous smell of warm pines.

Fuel is not a problem if you plan it. Uedem itself, a town of roughly eight and a half thousand, has what you need, and Xanten and Kalkar are bigger still. Inside the forest there is nothing, so top up before you go in. For a coffee and something sweet, the market squares of Xanten and Kalkar are both worth the extra few kilometres, and Kalkar's brick Gothic town hall is a good excuse to lean on the bike and look up.

Come on a weekday in late spring or early autumn, when the light slants low through the trunks and the car and bicycle traffic thins. In deep winter the same place is wet, grey and frankly a little grim, which is, in its way, honest.
t.culvert bridge near minstroom@52.1,5.1:
A culvert is not the stuff of travel posters, but on the eastern edge of Utrecht it tells you exactly how this country works. The spot lies near the stream called Minstroom, less than two kilometres from the middle of Utrecht and next to the university district of De Uithof. Here water is steered, held back, sent under roads and, when the army needed it, spread across the fields on purpose.

That last part is the point. East of the city runs a chain of forts and sluices that belonged to the New Dutch Waterline, the old defensive system built to flood a broad belt of land so that an enemy would find it too wet to march across and too shallow to cross by boat. A culvert or small bridge like this was part of the plumbing: open the right gates and the water went where the planners wanted. The line is now listed among the UNESCO Dutch Water Defence Lines, and the whole idea of defending a country with a plug and a polder is wonderfully Dutch.

On a motorcycle you come at this from the city, which means low speed limits, bike lanes on both sides, traffic lights and streams of students on bicycles. It is not a place for corner carving. What it offers is a short, easy contrast: five minutes from the Dom Tower and the canal wharves you are among hedgerows, horse paddocks, the wooded Amelisweerd estate and a slow stream with herons standing in it. Mind the cyclists at junctions, since in the Netherlands they have right of way far more often than visitors expect, and parking a motorcycle on a pavement in a residential street can earn a fine.

Utrecht is a proper city, so fuel, food and coffee are all easy; you will find petrol stations on the ring roads and plenty of cafés along the Oudegracht, the old canal with wharf cellars below street level. De Uithof itself is a campus with canteens that feel a little institutional but are cheap and quick. Morning is the best time, before the commuters, and late summer evenings give a soft light on the water.

If you are hungry for more forts, the nearby Fort Vossegat and its neighbours are only minutes away on a bike or a quiet lane.
t.uedem hochwald hochwald 9@51.7,6.4:
Come in late October and the sky over this corner of the Lower Rhine fills with noise. Tens of thousands of geese, mostly white-fronted and bean geese from the Arctic, winter on the wet meadows along the Rhine between Xanten and the Dutch border, and in the evening they stream in over the fields in long, restless skeins. Hochwald 9 sits in the forest just east of the flat farmland where they feed, about seven kilometres from Uedem, so you may well hear them before you see them.

The forest itself is a modest affair, a ridge of mixed woodland that was left standing while everything around it was drained and ploughed. That is why it feels so enclosed: you leave open polder country, cross a belt of oak and pine, and the sky closes over you for a few minutes. Roads in the Hochwald are narrow and often lined with a drainage ditch, so there is little room for error if a tractor appears. The surface is mostly good with the odd patch of heave where roots push up beneath the tarmac.

For a rider the pleasure here is very specific. There are no gradients to speak of, the visibility on the straights is long, and the real hazards are agricultural: mud on the road after beet or maize harvest, slurry smells in spring, and the cyclists who treat every country lane as a shared living room. Wind is the one thing that can really make itself felt, because nothing stops it between here and the North Sea. A headwind on an open stretch can make a small bike feel like it is climbing a hill.

Uedem is the nearest sizeable place, with fuel, bakeries and a few cafés, and Xanten, a larger town with a Roman past, is about the same distance away. If you are visiting for the geese, bring binoculars and stop on a verge well off the carriageway, since the birds spook easily and the drivers do not expect you.

Dusk in November, with the engine off and a thermos in your hand, is the best reason to be here.
t.shelter@52.1,5.2:
Pull up near the shelter and you are in the southeastern part of Utrecht, a stone's throw from the university campus of De Uithof and a short ride from the city's canals. The label does not say which shelter, and in this district there are several, so treat it as an introduction to the countryside along the Kromme Rijn, the old Rhine course that once carried the river's main flow past Utrecht before it silted up and moved south.

That old river is the key to the place. Romans had a frontier along it, medieval bishops cut it into the landscape of estates and bridges, and a series of country houses was strung along its banks. When the Dutch decided in the nineteenth century to defend their heartland with water rather than walls, they pegged the Waterline to the same low ground, and the forts and bunkers that dot the eastern side of Utrecht grew out of that decision. A shelter in this area is likely to be part of that story, whether it was a bus stop, a picnic hut or a bunker.

Riding here is slow and civilised. The roads are narrow and often shared with riders on cycle tracks, and the speed limits are low, especially close to the campus. Treat it as a rolling museum rather than a motorway. If you want a few relaxed kilometres between city and country, the lanes toward Bunnik and Rijnsweerd are pleasant, bordered by hedges and old trees, and Amelisweerd, the wooded estate beside the river, is lovely when the beech leaves turn.

Fuel is easy in Utrecht, a city of nearly three hundred thousand, and you will find it on the ring roads. Food is better in town: cafés fill the canal wharves along the Oudegracht, and a coffee near the Dom, the 112-metre cathedral tower that still dominates the old city, is a good way to finish. Weekday mornings avoid the worst of the student traffic, and spring blossom in the fruit orchards south of the city is gentle and lovely.

The wind off the polders can be sharp, so a windproof layer helps even in summer.
t.group shelter type p@52.1,5.1:
Concrete has a way of outlasting the fear that poured it. Type P group shelters belong to the Dutch defences of the late 1930s, small low bunkers designed to give a section of soldiers somewhere to sit out shelling while they waited for an attack. This one is on the eastern fringe of Utrecht, beside the university quarter of De Uithof, in a belt of land that was meant to be flooded rather than fought over.

The idea behind the Waterline was simple and a little unnerving. Open the sluices, let the fields fill to knee depth, and an advancing army finds roads submerged, ditches hidden and boats unable to float. Forts and shelters stood on the dry spots to cover the approaches. In practice, in May 1940 the line was not tested in the way its planners hoped, since the Dutch army capitulated after the bombing of Rotterdam and the German advance was fast; but the shelters are still here, mossy and strangely small, grass growing on their roofs.

Getting to them by motorcycle is easy and slightly comic. You leave the busy ring and the clatter of the university, then slip along lanes where bicycles outnumber cars twenty to one, past pollarded willows, drainage ditches and the odd riding school. Keep your speed polite. The cycle lanes are painted red, the surfaces are good, and the Dutch signs mean what they say. Windy days off the polder are common; autumn mornings often bring ground fog that hangs low over the fields until nine or ten.

Fuel is no trouble, because Utrecht lies just next door with stations on the ring road, and a city of this size has coffee in every direction. The Oudegracht is the place for a proper stop, with its sunken wharves and cafés tucked in under the arches, and the Dom Tower, rising 112 metres, is a pleasant landmark to steer by. Most bunkers in this area are fenced or locked, so take photographs from the path and leave them be.

The best moment is a dry weekday evening in late summer, when the light is low and gold on the grass and the last students have gone home.
t.watchtower at the reduit of fort vossega:
Fort Vossegat stands at the eastern edge of Utrecht, close to the university campus of De Uithof, and its watchtower tells you a lot about how this country once planned to survive. A reduit is the central stronghold of a fort, the last place you fall back to when the outer works are gone. At Vossegat it is a tough brick block rising out of a moat, with a tower from which a sentry could see over the flat land toward the approaches east of the city.

The fort belongs to the New Dutch Waterline, a nineteenth-century defensive belt that ran from the Zuiderzee down to the Biesbosch. The plan was to protect Holland, the economic heart of the country, behind a sheet of shallow water, with forts like Vossegat guarding the dry crossing points. By the time it was finished, rifled artillery and then aircraft had already made much of it obsolete, and it was never used as intended on a large scale. What survives is a surprisingly intact system of forts, sluices and bunkers, now recognised as part of the UNESCO Dutch Water Defence Lines.

Riding to the tower means threading through suburban Utrecht: roundabouts, bus lanes, cycle tracks and speed bumps. It is not an exciting stretch, but it is easy, and the final approach is lovely, with low earthworks, a ring of water and tall old trees. Park where the signs allow and walk. Forts like this are often open for events or guided tours rather than all the time, so a quick check of local listings is wise if you want to go inside; otherwise the exterior and moat are the draw.

The city of Utrecht, only two kilometres away, has everything you could want. Fuel is on the ring roads, and a coffee and an apple pastry at a café on the Oudegracht makes a nice contrast with the military severity of the fort. Utrecht's Dom Tower, 112 metres tall, is the tallest church tower in the country, and climbing it is a good way to see how the Waterline's flooded plains once spread to the horizon.

Choose a bright October morning, when the moat reflects the red brick and the leaves on the earthworks have turned.
t.uedem hochwald hochwald 13@51.7,6.4:
The Hochwald is the sort of place that NATO likes, and the reason is the sky. Uedem, six kilometres from Hochwald 13, hosts a major air defence and control site, a Luftwaffe installation that sits beside the forest and helps monitor air traffic across northern and central Europe. You will not see much of it from the road beyond fences and the odd radome, but it explains why the ridge, which stands higher than almost anything else on the Lower Rhine plain, was such a useful place to put a radar.

The forest itself is a mix of pine, beech and oak on sandy, glacially shaped ground. It stretches between Uedem, Kalkar and Xanten, and the roads cut through it in straight lines as if drawn with a ruler. The ride is gentle, with long, level stretches and the occasional gentle bend where an old estate boundary once ran. There is not a hairpin within fifty kilometres, so if you want a technical challenge you are in the wrong district, but the quiet and the predictable surface make it a restful place for an easy touring day.

Be aware that military zones sit in the district and photography near fences can attract attention from guards, so keep your camera aimed at the trees. Hunting also goes on in the forest in autumn and winter, and the rides are well marked with signs telling you when parts of the forest are closed. Fallen branches after a storm can block the lanes, and in autumn the leaves are slippery after rain.

Uedem has fuel and a few cafés, and Kalkar and Xanten both offer larger selections. If you want a proper meal after a ride, an old-fashioned Niederrhein inn in any of these villages will happily feed you pork schnitzel with fried potatoes and a glass of the local Altbier, a dark, bitter beer in the Düsseldorf style.

For the best of the forest, aim for a still morning in April, when the beech leaves are new and the light is green and thin, and when the ground is still soft after the winter.
t.uedem hochwald hochwald 4@51.7,6.4:
Kalkar is where the Hochwald roads lead you if you let them, and Kalkar is full of surprises. It is a small brick town of fourteen thousand on the Lower Rhine plain, and its market square is a model of late medieval civic pride, with a stepped-gable town hall from the fifteenth century facing the church of St Nicolai, where a set of carved wooden altars made in the town's own workshops around 1500 draw art historians from far away. Hochwald 4 itself lies in the forest about seven kilometres from the centre, so you come to the town after the woods.

Then there is the reactor. On the town's edge stands a nuclear power station that was never switched on, a fast breeder built in the 1970s and 1980s at enormous cost, then abandoned after political opposition and doubts over safety, without ever producing a kilowatt for the grid. It has since become an amusement park, and the cooling tower is painted and now holds a carousel. It sounds like a joke, but it is true, and the sight of children's rides under a tower built for plutonium is oddly memorable.

For the ride itself, the Niederrhein delivers what it always does: broad skies, fields of maize, potatoes and sugar beet, and straight or gently bent roads that can be taken with a relaxed hand. The woodland roads near Hochwald 4 are narrower than the farm roads, with mixed tarmac and a few sandy edges, and they often have 70 km/h limits through the trees. The wind can be a nuisance, as there is almost nothing to block it, and a spring rain shower is quickly followed by sun.

Fuel is easy in Kalkar, Uedem and Xanten; all three have stations on the main roads. Coffee and cake are best in Kalkar's square, where terraces fill in warm weather. If the church is open, the altars are worth ten minutes in the cool dark, and the carved details, from small sheep to wrinkled saints, reward a slow look.

A weekday in September, when the harvest traffic has not yet peaked, is a good time to come.
t.uedem hochwald hochwald 6@51.7,6.4:
The Romans got to Xanten first, and the forest roads of Hochwald 6 lead you to the town they left behind. About seven kilometres from the point, on the Rhine plain, lies the site of Colonia Ulpia Traiana, a Roman city founded in the early second century under Trajan. Most of it was later quarried for building stone, which is why the Archaeological Park today can rebuild the amphitheatre, a gate and some of the city walls on their original footprints, and why you can stand in a reconstructed temple and imagine the Rhine frontier at its busiest.

Xanten has older layers too. The cathedral of St Viktor, a long Gothic church with a forest of pillars, commemorates a martyr said to have died here with his comrades in the Roman army; the town's name comes from the Latin for holy ones, sanctos. And the Nibelungenlied, the medieval German epic, places the hero Siegfried's birth in a city it calls Santen, so Xanten leans on that too, with a Siegfried museum and the occasional dragon on a shop sign.

Out in the Hochwald itself the riding is quiet, flat and straightforward, and there is little to do but watch the tree trunks flick by. The roads are narrow, hemmed by ditches, and the surface is often patched where the heavy farm machinery tears at the edges. In summer the woods are a relief from the heat of the plain; in winter, fog and frost can settle among the trunks and hold the tarmac slick until midday. Keep an eye out for deer at dusk, and expect cyclists even on gloomy afternoons.

Xanten, a town of over twenty thousand, has fuel, supermarkets, cafés and a market square where you can sit under the cathedral's towers with a coffee and a slice of apple tart. The lakes south of the town, flooded gravel pits turned into sailing and swimming water, are good for a break on hot days. Uedem and Kalkar are close alternatives for petrol.

Pick a clear day in May, when the Archaeological Park is green and the forest is fresh, and give the Roman town an hour or two before you turn back.
t.uedem hochwald hochwald 3@51.7,6.4:
Rivers are the border here, and Hochwald 3 sits on the ridge that looks across the plain toward both the Rhine and the Netherlands. About six kilometres from Uedem, the forest road passes through a country where the nearest big water is a short ride to the east: the Rhine, wide, brown and busy with barges, with a few small cable ferries still carrying people, cyclists and sometimes motorcycles from bank to bank. The Dutch frontier is not far to the west, and the city of Nijmegen, old and hilly by Dutch standards, lies a short day's trip beyond.

That mixture of Germany and the Netherlands is the real flavour of the Niederrhein. You see it in the architecture, the red brick and white window frames; in the bikes, which outnumber cars on small roads; in the food, where cheese and sweet syrup on bread are as common as sausage. Cleves, the next town of consequence to the north-west, was once the seat of dukes whose daughter Anne was married to Henry VIII of England in 1540 and divorced within months.

Riding in the Hochwald is calm to the point of drowsiness. The roads run level and the bends are gentle, with the occasional off-camber crown where the tarmac has been resurfaced. Traffic is light on weekdays and heavier on Sundays, when families head out on bicycles and motorcyclists arrive from the Ruhr. Watch for the junction priorities, since many minor roads give way to the right, and for farm vehicles that may take up the whole width.

Uedem has fuel, bakeries and a small supermarket, and larger towns such as Kalkar, Xanten or Goch offer more choices. If you plan to cross the Rhine by ferry, check the timetable first, because services change with the season and the water level, and don't count on them running in very low water or ice.

A late afternoon in September, when the sun drops over the plain and the woods smell of resin and damp earth, suits this spot best.
t.uedem hochwald hochwald 10@51.7,6.4:
Ice made this ridge. Hochwald 10 lies in a belt of low hills between Xanten, Uedem and Kalkar that the glaciers of the Saale ice age shoved up from the floor of the Rhine valley, a pile of sand and gravel pushed into a long arc that now stands a few dozen metres above the plain. That is not much, but on a landscape this flat it is enough to hold a forest and give the whole area a different character, with drier soil, pines, birches and oaks, and views that open suddenly where a clearing allows.

Geologists call it a push moraine, and for a rider that means the ground does something unusual for the Niederrhein: it rises and falls. Do not expect mountains. A few gentle climbs, a bend through a cutting where the sandy soil is exposed, a slow descent to a fringe of fields: that is the scale of it. But after kilometres of ruler-straight farm roads, the sensation is welcome, and the woodland air is a degree or two cooler in summer.

The ground is sandy and well-drained, which is good for walking, mushrooms and horses, and less good for riding off the tarmac, so stay on the road. Loose sand blows across the carriageway at junctions after dry spells, and in spring pollen from the pines coats everything yellow. Birdlife is rich: buzzards circle over the clearings, woodpeckers knock in the old beeches, and in dusk light you can sometimes catch a roe deer stepping out of the shade. Wild boar are present in the Lower Rhine woods too, and a collision with one is no joke, so take care at twilight.

Fuel is easy in Uedem, about seven kilometres away, and Xanten and Kalkar are each a few minutes further. For a hot drink and a hearty plate, a Gasthof in any of the surrounding villages will serve you a plain Niederrhein meal without fuss, and nobody will mind riding gear. There is no water or shelter in the forest itself, so bring what you need.

October, with the beech leaves copper and the first mist drifting through the trunks, gives the best light and the least traffic.
t.uedem hochwald hochwald 5@51.7,6.4:
Between April and midsummer, the Niederrhein belongs to asparagus. Farms around Uedem, Xanten and Kalkar sell white spears from roadside stalls and serve them in restaurants with new potatoes, ham and butter or hollandaise, and the season officially ends on the feast of St John, the twenty-fourth of June, when the growers let the plants rest. Hochwald 5 is a forest spot, about seven kilometres from Uedem, but it sits in a region where the fields that border the trees have the sandy, well-drained soil that white asparagus loves.

So eat well on this ride, and plan it around the harvest. In season you will smell the fresh straw and see the black foil of the raised beds running across the fields like long dark ribbons. Pickers work early, so mornings can be busy with vans and tractors, and the narrow lanes are lined with parked cars outside the best-known farm shops. Later in the year the same fields give way to maize, potatoes and beet, and the roadsides fill with Rhineland apples and pumpkins.

The forest road itself is quiet, shaded and plain, with long flat sections and the odd low rise. Surfaces are generally good, though tractors drag mud and sand onto the road at field entrances. The speed limits are often lower than you expect and are checked from time to time. In wet weather, take extra care on the leaf-strewn bends, and in hot weather, remember that there is neither water nor shop inside the woods.

Fuel is available in Uedem and in larger Xanten and Kalkar, and bakeries in each open early. Many farm shops sell homemade jam, fruit schnapps and fresh eggs; a few have a small café corner for coffee and cake. A heavy lunch on a motorcycle can make you sluggish, so go for a light plate or share one.

Aim for mid-May on a weekday, when the weather is usually kind and the harvest is at its peak but the crowds are small.
t.uedem hochwald hochwald 8 1@51.7,6.4:
Wind is the main character on the Lower Rhine plain, and Hochwald 8.1 is the place where you can feel what it does. Standing in the forest roughly seven kilometres from Uedem, the trees give you a rest from it, but a few minutes in either direction and you are out on open polder with nothing between you and the sea but a few hedges and the odd church tower. Riders from the hills learn quickly that flat does not mean easy.

The area is also bicycle country, with a network of signed cycle routes joining villages, farms and forests, and the landscape has been shaped by it. Wide cycle tracks run beside most roads, drivers expect cyclists to be everywhere, and the locals often ride in rows of two or three at a time, chatting. As a motorcyclist you share the lanes rather than own them. A calm, patient style suits the place, and slow overtakes with plenty of space are the norm; a loud, fast approach will get you a frown or worse.

Weather comes in from the west and is mostly mild and damp. Light rain on a summer afternoon is common, followed by a clear evening and a low golden sun, and thunderstorms can build quickly on hot days. The forest roads stay wetter than the open ones, since the leaves block the sun. Autumn brings fog in the early morning and slippery roads after leaf fall, and winter can bring black ice in the shaded patches.

Uedem has fuel, bakeries, and a market on certain weekdays, and Xanten and Kalkar are close enough for anything further. If you have a few hours, the Rhine itself, with its dikes, meadows and barge traffic, is a good short detour to the east, and walking up onto the dike on a clear day gives a wide view of the river and the plain.

Late summer evenings, when the heat has left the air and the sun is low, are my pick for this spot.
t.itzehoe@53.9,9.5:
Itzehoe does not have a famous skyline, and that is rather the point. It is a solid town of about thirty thousand on the Stör river in the flat marshland of Schleswig-Holstein, and its job in this ride is that of a gate, the last reliable fuel and breakfast before the open country of the North Sea coast. The town sits some sixty kilometres northwest of Hamburg, and the name goes far back, with a fortress called Esesfeld said to have been built here in the early ninth century during the wars of Charlemagne against the Saxons.

The Stör is small but important, a tidal river that winds toward the Elbe, and it gave Itzehoe a role as a trading and market town in the Holstein region. The old town has several brick churches, a former convent that is still used, and a few quiet squares. It is not a place of must-do sights, but the people are friendly, and the bakeries open early, so a cup of coffee and a roll before the day's ride is a pleasant start.

The riding that leads out is flat, open and honest. West of town the roads cross Dithmarschen, a landscape of dikes, drainage ditches, sheep and wind turbines, and the horizon is huge. There are no hills, no real corners, and the main variable is the wind, which on the North Sea coast can be strong enough to push a bike sideways. Check the forecast, and lean into it. The dikes, built over centuries to keep the sea out, are a quiet and slightly eerie part of the scenery. Roads along them are narrow, and sheep graze on the slopes, so take care and obey signs that restrict access.

In summer the weather is mild but changeable, with sun, showers and cloud sweeping across the sky within an hour. In autumn the wind brings clear light, and in winter the roads can be icy. Ride out early to avoid the traffic heading to the beach resorts at St. Peter-Ording. Itzehoe itself has plenty of fuel stations, supermarkets and a few simple restaurants, and the mix of fish rolls and rye bread is the local taste. Fill the tank here, because stations get thinner as you head toward the coast.
t.hameln@52.1,9.4:
Everyone knows the story, and Hameln has not tried to hide it. According to the legend, in 1284 the town was overrun by rats, and a stranger in colourful clothes offered to rid it of them in return for payment. He played his pipe, the rats followed him into the Weser and drowned, and the town refused to pay. So he played again, and this time the town's children followed him out of the gate and were never seen again. The Brothers Grimm wrote it down, Robert Browning wrote a poem, and the Pied Piper became one of the best-known figures in European folklore. The historical record does record some tragedy in 1284, though what actually happened is still a mystery.

The town deals with it cheerfully. Rat motifs decorate bakeries and shops, a rat-catcher's house with a carved front stands in a street that is closed to music, and on summer Sundays actors perform the tale in front of the Hochzeitshaus, the old wedding house. Apart from the legend, Hameln is a fine example of Weser Renaissance architecture, with ornate gabled houses of stone and timber, richly carved, standing along the main streets and lanes. The town lies on the Weser river, which has carried goods and people through the region for centuries, and the old centre is a pleasant place for a walk.

For the rider, Hameln is the practical kind of stop. It has about fifty-eight thousand people, so fuel, groceries, and repair services are all available, and cafés on the old town squares are well suited to a long coffee break. The countryside around is gentle hill land, with the roads leading toward the Lippe hills and the Harz mountains winding through woods, villages and fields. The surface is generally good, with some bumpy patches, and traffic can be heavy in town at midday. Weekends in summer bring tourists and cyclists on the river path.

Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with fresh green or golden colour in the hills, and clear air. Summer is warm, with the occasional thunderstorm. Try the local sausage and potato dishes in the old town, and leave time for a stroll along the Weser embankment in the evening, when the light turns the river gold.
t.bad nenndorf@52.3,9.4:
Bad Nenndorf is a spa town that never grew into a resort, and that suits it. It sits in the Schaumburg countryside west of Hanover, at the foot of the low wooded ridge of the Deister, and its trade is sulphurous water. Springs here were developed as a bath in the late eighteenth century under the rulers of Hesse-Kassel, and a park of old trees, colonnades and bathhouses survives from that period. The smell of the water is distinctive, and the baths are still used for health treatments, particularly for joint and skin complaints. The town is quiet, tidy and slightly formal.

There is a darker chapter in its past. After the Second World War a British interrogation centre operated in the town, and the treatment of prisoners there caused a scandal back in Britain. It is a reminder that even peaceful spa towns have layers of history. Today the town is calm, and the surroundings, with farmland, small villages and castles such as the one at nearby Rodenberg, are good for relaxed riding.

The road system around Bad Nenndorf is a web of secondary roads that run through the lowland between the Deister and the Weser hills. The surface is generally smooth, and bends are gentle, passing through villages with half-timbered houses and brick churches. Traffic is light outside commuter hours, and the main risk is agricultural machinery in the harvest season. To the south, the Deister ridge, about twenty kilometres long, offers forested roads and walking trails, while to the north the Steinhuder Meer, the largest lake in Lower Saxony, is a popular day out.

For the rider, the town is a handy break. It has about ten thousand people, so fuel stations, bakeries and cafés are plentiful, and it is a good place for a coffee or a late breakfast before heading on. A walk through the spa gardens takes ten minutes and is an easy way to loosen up. Spring and early autumn are the best times for the ride, when the fields are green or golden and the light is soft. In summer, cafés set tables in the park, and in the evening the town falls quiet, so there is no need to hurry.
t.head smashed in buffalo jump@49.7,-113.7:
Imagine a wall of sandstone, ten metres high, with the plain falling away beneath it. For about five thousand years the Blackfoot and their ancestors used cliffs like this one, in the foothills of the Porcupine Hills in southern Alberta, to hunt bison. Hunters spent days guiding a herd, gently and patiently, along lines of stone cairns called drive lanes, until the animals were running without knowing it, and then the lead animals went over the edge. Below, the whole community waited with knives, and the meat and hides of one successful drive could see a band through the winter. UNESCO lists the site as one of the oldest and best-preserved examples of the method anywhere in the world.

The name sounds like a joke and is not. In the tale that has come down, a young man wanted to watch the bison fall from beneath the cliff, and the animals piled up so deep that he was killed, his head crushed under the weight. Whatever the truth, the name stuck. The interpretive centre is built into the cliff itself, with five floors of exhibits climbing through the rock, and the story is told partly by Blackfoot guides, which makes all the difference. At the top, you walk along the cliff edge and look across a sea of grass toward the Rockies, and the wind pulls at your jacket, the same wind that carries the scent of sage.

The roads here are prairie roads: wide, empty and straight for long distances, then gently rolling where the land lifts toward the mountains. Wind is the main theme. Chinooks, the warm, dry winds that roll down the eastern slopes of the Rockies, can gust hard enough to push a loaded motorcycle across a lane, and the whole region is dotted with wind turbines. Keep an eye on the grass verge for prairie rattlesnakes in warm weather, and for deer and pronghorn at dawn and dusk. Summer afternoons bring thunderstorms that build over the mountains, hail included, so plan your day to arrive early.

Fort Macleod, about seventeen kilometres away, has fuel and a few places to eat, and a museum of the old Mounted Police fort founded in 1874. Pincher Creek is the next bigger stop on the way to Waterton. Bring water and a layer for the wind. Late May to September is the usual season, though the roads can be clear in the shoulder months if you keep an eye on the forecast.
t.rendsburg canal@54.3,9.7:
Rendsburg is a town made by a ditch, and what a ditch. The Kiel Canal, known in German as the Nord-Ostsee-Kanal, was opened in 1895 as the Kaiser-Wilhelm-Kanal, cutting across the base of the Danish peninsula so that ships need not sail all the way around Skagen. It is still the busiest artificial seaway in the world by number of ships, and standing on the bank at Rendsburg you can watch container vessels, tankers and ferries glide past at what looks like walking pace, a few metres from the road. A quiet fact makes it more striking: the surrounding land is so flat and low, only a few metres above sea level, that the ships seem to be sailing through meadows.

The landmark is the high railway bridge of 1913, a great steel loop that lifts the line high enough to clear the shipping, and beneath it hangs a transporter ferry, a platform on cables that carries cars and bikes across the canal. It is one of very few still working in the world, and riding onto it is a genuine curiosity. The old road tunnel under the canal, from 1961, is the other crossing, and several ferries operate free of charge along the canal. Beside the water is the old town on the Eider river, a tidy mix of garrison buildings and brick houses dating to the time when the Danish crown fortified the place.

The riding in this region is gentle, flat and often windy, a world of long straight roads, hedge-lined fields called knicks, reed beds and quiet villages. It is not a place for hairpins, but it has a generous, slow rhythm, and the canal-side roads on both banks are very pleasant on a bike, with the ships alongside. Wind from the North Sea can be strong, and cross-winds on the bridges can surprise you.

Rendsburg has nearly thirty thousand people, so you will find fuel, bakeries, fish sandwiches and cafes, and the neighbouring town of Büdelsdorf has the old iron works turned into an art venue. Try a Fischbrötchen by the water on a sunny afternoon, and watch for the big ships, which announce themselves with a deep horn.
t.nortorf@54.2,9.9:
Nortorf will not make anyone's list of great European destinations, and it does not pretend to. It is a farming town of about six thousand people in the middle of Holstein, set on the edge of the Geest, the sandy, gently rolling ridge of central Schleswig-Holstein, halfway between Neumünster and Rendsburg. Its job, in a riding day, is a useful one: a place to fill the tank, get a decent breakfast, and set off along quiet back roads.

What you find here is practical northern Germany. The market square is small and tidy, there are bakeries that open early, supermarkets, and a good number of cafes, and the main road makes for easy access from the A7 motorway. Beyond the town the landscape is classic Holstein, with fields enclosed by knicks, the old earth banks planted with hazel and oak that farmers have used as hedges for centuries. The land is low and rolling, and the sky is huge, with big cloud formations that cross the horizon in slow processions. The Naturpark Aukrug lies just to the south, with a mixture of woodland, heath and lakes that make for winding, shaded riding.

The roads around Nortorf are mostly flat to gently undulating, with long bends and short straights between villages. The surface is generally good, but tractors and farm vehicles are common during harvest, and the occasional gravel or mud patch can appear at field entrances. Wind is a feature all year, as the North Sea and the Baltic are both only a short distance away, and rain squalls move through quickly. Mornings in early summer are lovely, with mist in the hollows and cows grazing, while October brings the smell of woodsmoke and ploughed earth.

The Kiel Canal is only a few minutes north, and crossing it by ferry or bridge is a pleasant part of any loop. Fuel is easy here, and a town of this size also has banks and pharmacies, so it is a good place to take care of the small things before heading out. In the shops you will find the staples of Schleswig-Holstein: smoked fish, rye bread and strong black coffee, so a slow breakfast is a good way to begin.
t.hannover west@52.4,9.6:
Hannover has a gate in every direction, at least in this ride's plan, and the one in the west lies near Seelze, a town on the Leine river a few kilometres outside the city. The Leine is a quiet and rather muddy stream that winds through flat country, and from here the ride sets off west, into the Weser hills, toward Bückeburg and onward into the Harz foothills. For a rider the gate is simply a convenient place to start with a full tank, light traffic and an easy road out, and it avoids the knot of the city centre.

The city itself deserves more than a glance. Hannover is better known for trade fairs than for beauty, and the Messe, the biggest exhibition ground in the world, fills the south-east of town, but the older story is more interesting. In 1714 the elector of Hannover became King George I of Great Britain, and for more than a century the two countries were linked under one crown. The Herrenhausen Gardens, laid out for the electors in the baroque style, are one of the finest in Europe, with clipped hedges, fountains and a long avenue of lime trees. Hannover is also the home of the Bahlsen biscuit and a well-known school of industrial design.

The landscape west of the city is the north German plain turning into the first low ridges of the uplands. Roads are generally straight and fast across the flat sections, then wind through villages and over low ridges in the Weser and Deister hills, with brick farmhouses and half-timbered barns. Tree-lined lanes shade the road in summer, and the surface is generally good, though mud from farm vehicles can be slippery. Wind can be strong on open stretches.

Seelze, with about thirty-three thousand people, has fuel stations, supermarkets and bakeries, and the larger city of Hannover supplies anything else. A good coffee and a slice of cake in a local bakery is the standard German start to a ride. Spring and autumn offer the best light, while winter brings fog and ice, and in summer weekends the roads of the Weser hills fill with motorcyclists, so choose a weekday when you can.
t.hannover south@52.3,9.8:
South of Hannover the flat plain starts to fold, and the small town of Pattensen, on the Leine, marks the place where the ride leaves the city for the hills. The land here is the Calenberger Land, a fertile farming country of wheat and sugar beet, with big brick farmhouses and low ridges on the horizon. Beyond it rise the limestone ridges of the Leinebergland, the Ith and the Hils, long, forested crests with cliffs and old quarries, and they are the reason the ride exists.

The Ith is a thin ridge about twenty kilometres long, with limestone cliffs, beech woods and caves, and its roads climb from the valley in a series of bends and hairpins that are a pleasure on a quiet morning. The Hils is a wider, wilder upland, with dense forest and few villages, and the roads that cross it are often narrow, shaded and damp. Surfaces vary, with sections of smooth asphalt and others scarred by forestry lorries, and leaves and mud can make corners slippery in autumn. Watch for deer at dawn and dusk, and for cyclists on sunny weekends.

Near Pattensen stands a very odd building indeed, the Marienburg, a fairy-tale Gothic Revival castle with turrets, battlements and a courtyard, built in the 1860s by King George V of Hanover as a gift for his wife, Queen Marie. The kingdom was annexed by Prussia soon after, and the royal family never really lived there, which gives the whole place a slightly melancholy air. The castle sits on a hill above the Leine valley and can be seen from the road for some distance.

Pattensen has nearly fourteen thousand people and offers fuel stations, bakeries and a couple of restaurants serving German standards such as schnitzel and asparagus in season, from late April to June, when the whole region is mad for it. The larger city of Hildesheim lies to the south-east, with a Romanesque cathedral and famous rose bush, and Hannover is close behind you. Ride on a weekday if you can, because the best roads get busy with motorcyclists on Saturdays and Sundays. Spring and autumn are good, and the first frosts bring a dangerous sheen to shaded bends.
t.east wall area 2e to 2f@54.5,9.8:
The Danevirke is a wall, or rather a series of walls, that once stretched across the neck of the Jutland peninsula, and this stretch is the eastern end, near the Windeby lake and the shore of the Baltic. The first earthworks went up in the seventh century, and later kings of Denmark extended them in several phases, culminating in a brick-faced wall built in the twelfth century under Valdemar the Great. The purpose was to protect the southern border against the Franks and the Saxons, and it worked more or less for several hundred years. A few steps along the grassy bank, and you can see a low ridge and a ditch, easily mistaken for a hedgerow.

Hedeby, the great Viking trading town at the end of the Schlei inlet, lay just behind the wall and was one of the largest settlements in northern Europe in the ninth and tenth centuries, with merchants, craftsmen and ships from Scandinavia to the Arab world. UNESCO lists the wall and the town together as the Archaeological Border Complex of Hedeby and the Danevirke, and a museum near the site shows reconstructed Viking houses and a warship. Windeby, a village nearby, is known for a bog body, a young person from the Iron Age found in a peat bog in 1952 and long called the Windeby Girl, though more recent research has made the identification uncertain.

The riding is gentle. The roads around Eckernförde and the Schlei run through rolling farmland, with fields of rapeseed and wheat, dark beech woods and brick-built villages with thatched roofs, and the Baltic is never far. The surface is generally good, and the traffic is light outside the holiday season. Wind from the sea can be strong, particularly in spring and autumn, and sudden showers are likely at any time of year. Look for storks in the villages in summer and for wild geese in winter.

Eckernförde, with about twenty-three thousand people four kilometres away, has fuel, bakeries and fish restaurants, and its harbour is a pleasant place for a coffee. Try a smoked sprat, a local speciality, or a fish roll from a stall. Summer weekends are busy with holidaymakers, and midweek is calmer. The best times are late spring and early autumn, when the light is golden, and winter brings a cold, grey beauty to the whole coast.
t.lemgo old town@52.0,8.9:
Lemgo is one of those German towns where the old centre survived intact, a mass of half-timbered and stone gabled houses in the Weser Renaissance style, grouped around a market place and a clutch of churches. The town of about forty-two thousand people lies in the Lippe region in eastern North Rhine-Westphalia, on the edge of the Teutoburg Forest, and was once a member of the Hanseatic League, which explains the wealth of building from the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

The most famous house is the Hexenbürgermeisterhaus, the witch mayor's house, with an elaborate facade of carved stone, built by a wealthy family in 1571 and later home to a mayor who presided over witch trials in the seventeenth century, when dozens of people in Lemgo were executed. The house now holds a museum that explains the period, and it is an interesting if sombre stop. The Rathaus, the town hall, is also remarkable, with a row of oriel windows and an arcaded apothecary wing, and the market square in front is the heart of the town, with cafés spilling outdoors on warm days.

For motorcyclists, Lemgo is a cultural stop and a place to refuel, since it has everything: petrol stations, restaurants, bakeries and supermarkets. The old centre is largely pedestrianised, so park at the edge and walk in. The roads surrounding it, through the Extertal and across the hills of the Lippe uplands, are quiet and winding, with forest and farm views, and short, steep climbs that give some of the best riding in this part of the country. Surfaces are generally good, and speed limits in the villages are checked.

The region is known for its asparagus in spring, for pumpernickel, ham and Pickert, a local potato bread, and for the beer from small breweries. Summers are warm and green, and autumn brings misty mornings with wood smoke in the air. Be careful with tram-style cobbles in the centre, which are slippery after rain, and with farm vehicles on the narrow lanes. A short walk along the old town streets in the evening, once the day trippers have gone, is worth the effort.
t.koblenz@50.4,7.6:
Two rivers meet at the tip of Koblenz, and a gigantic bronze-and-stone monument marks the spot. The German Corner, the Deutsches Eck, is a green point of land where the Moselle slides into the Rhine, with a copy of an equestrian statue of Emperor Wilhelm I standing on a high plinth at the end. The Romans called the place Confluentes, the confluence, and the name has worn down over two thousand years into Koblenz.
