Across the Rhine, the fortress of Ehrenbreitstein sits on a rocky ridge above the water, reached by cable car, and the view from the walls takes in both rivers and the whole old town.

For riders, Koblenz is the doorway to two of Germany's best valley rides. Upstream along the Rhine, the Upper Middle Rhine Valley, a World Heritage landscape since 2002, runs for about sixty kilometres to Bingen, through a steep gorge lined with vineyards, half-timbered villages and more than thirty castles. The road follows the river on either bank, with pleasant bends, sudden views and the freight trains rattling along the opposite side. The Loreley rock, a slate cliff of about a hundred and thirty metres, was a feared bend for boatmen and is the home of a legendary siren in a poem by Heinrich Heine. Traffic can be heavy in summer and at weekends, so a weekday morning is calmer.

The Moselle Wine Route heads in the other direction, southwest toward Trier, along a river that twists in great loops between steep slate slopes planted with Riesling. The road is narrower, quieter and more intimate than the Rhine, with pretty towns such as Cochem, topped by a neo-Gothic castle, and Bernkastel-Kues, with a crooked market square of timbered houses. Sudden speed limits and cameras catch the unwary in every village. The best months are May to October, and the harvest in autumn, when vineyards turn gold and red, is superb, though wine festivals fill the villages.

Koblenz itself is a city of about a hundred thousand, so it has everything needed: fuel stations on the main roads, repair shops, hotels and plenty of cafes. The old town is compact, and a Riesling in a courtyard is a pleasant way to end the day, though the motorcyclist might prefer the Rhenish potato pancakes called Reibekuchen with apple sauce. Rain is possible at any time, so carry a waterproof, and leave extra time at weekends, when the river valleys fill with tourists.
t.hannover north west edge@52.4,9.6:
Garbsen is a big, flat suburb of Hannover, made mostly of new housing, shopping streets and industry, and it has no pretensions beyond being a practical place to start. The Mittelland Canal runs close by, carrying barges between the Rhine and the Elbe, and the whole area lies on the edge of the North German Plain, where the sky takes up most of the view. That, however, is the point. Within twenty minutes you are among fields, woods and moorland, and the city has gone.

The goal is Steinhuder Meer, the largest lake in Lower Saxony, which lies about thirty kilometres to the north-west. It is wide, with a surface of some thirty square kilometres, and astonishingly shallow, only about three metres deep at the most, so that on a calm day it looks like a large silver dish laid on the land. In the middle sits Wilhelmstein, a tiny artificial island with a fortress that Count Wilhelm of Schaumburg-Lippe built in the 1760s as a military school, one of the odd little relics of German princely life. Boats cross to it from the village of Steinhude, whose narrow lanes of low houses are full of smokehouses selling eel, the local speciality, which you may like or loathe.

The riding is gentle. The roads around the lake run through reed beds, birch woods and bog, with plenty of long, flat straights and the occasional bend. Further west, the Rehburg Hills rise to a modest height, a ridge of forest with a few sweeping gradients and quiet roads through beech woods, an unexpected relief after the flatlands. This is relaxing country rather than a technical challenge. The best months are May to September, with wind off the lake a constant, and early morning mist over the moor in autumn.

The moors around the lake are a nature reserve, and in spring and autumn the birdlife is remarkable, with cranes, ospreys and great numbers of geese passing through. Garbsen and nearby suburbs offer all the fuel stations, supermarkets and bakeries you could want, so fill the tank here, since the villages near the lake are small. On sunny weekends the shores and lanes are full of cyclists and families, so allow time. A plate of smoked eel or a simple Matjes herring with potatoes, eaten by the water, is a fitting reward.
t.hannover north@52.5,9.8:
Langenhagen, on Hannover's northern edge, is known for its airport, and the occasional rumble of jets overhead is a reminder that this is the city's door to the outside world. The district's flat suburbs, business parks and long, straight roads belong to the plain, but Hannover itself has more to offer than most visitors expect. Between 1714 and 1837 the rulers of this small German electorate were also kings of Great Britain, from George I onward, and the baroque gardens at Herrenhausen, once their summer residence, are among the grandest in Germany, with a spectacular fountain that shoots up to about seventy metres.

The city also has the philosopher Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, who served the court and is commemorated by a famous biscuit named in his honour, and the New Town Hall, a huge building of 1913 with a dome and a model of the city in the lobby. Much of Hannover was destroyed in the Second World War, which explains its modern look, and the surviving old streets are a small fraction of the earlier town.

North of the city, the land opens into the Südheide, a region of pine forest, heath and sandy soils that stretches toward Celle. The roads here run between pines in long, easy lines, with gentle bends and an occasional dip over a stream, and in late summer the heather blooms in purple patches. This is quiet riding, good for relaxed days and for a rhythm without hurry. Surfaces are mostly good, with some patched sections, and deer and wild boar cross at dusk, which is a real hazard. Autumn mist and winter ice make the heathland roads treacherous in the early hours. May to September is best.

In the other direction, a long day takes you toward the Teutoburg Forest and the Externsteine, a group of tall sandstone pillars near Detmold that have been a sacred and mysterious place for centuries. Nearby stands the Hermannsdenkmal, a giant copper statue completed in 1875 to commemorate the Germanic leader Arminius, who defeated three Roman legions in the forest in AD 9. The ridge road along the Teutoburg is lovely, with curves through beech forest and wide views over the plain.

Fuel and services are abundant near the start, with Langenhagen and the surrounding suburbs offering stations, bakeries and supermarkets. Fill up before heading into the heath, where villages are small and stations are far apart. Check the speed limits, because Lower Saxony has many fixed cameras, and carry a layer for chilly mornings.
t.ganghwa island coastal ride photo pull o:
Where the Yellow Sea meets the Korean coast the tidal range is among the biggest in the world, and the pin sits on the shore of it, at the edge of a landscape that changes twice a day. At low tide the water retreats for kilometres, leaving a vast grey expanse of mud and sand, crossed by channels and dotted with fishing boats waiting for the water to return, and at high tide the sea sweeps back in. The range near Incheon can reach about nine metres, a fact that strikes you more clearly when you see boats lying on their sides in the mud.

The pin lies on the coast of Gyeonggi province, close to Daebudo, an island joined to the mainland by a long seawall. The nearby Sihwa dike, a dozen kilometres long, closed off a bay in the 1990s, and its tidal power station, which generates electricity from the flow of water through the dam, is the largest of its kind in the world. The dike road is a straight, flat route with water on both sides and views over the sea, popular with cyclists and riders. Daebudo itself has beaches, seafood restaurants and a long coastline of pine trees and mud flats, with a popular spot for sunsets over the water.

The Ganghwa label refers to a large island to the north, which has dolmens, forts and a long history of resistance to foreign invasion, but this stop belongs to a different part of the coast. The riding along the shore is easy and scenic, with mostly flat roads, good surfaces and plenty of traffic at weekends, as Seoulites head for the sea. The wind off the water can be strong, and it often carries a salty haze that softens the light.

For fuel and food, Ansan, a big city a short ride inland, has everything, and the island has seafood restaurants serving raw fish, grilled shellfish and the local specialty of kalguksu, a noodle soup with clams. Fuel on the island is limited, so fill up in Ansan or Hwaseong before crossing.

Plan to arrive an hour before sunset. The sky turns orange and the mud flats shine like a mirror, with silhouettes of fishing boats and wading birds. It is a lovely and unexpectedly peaceful place so near to a megacity.
t.yangpyeong mountain roads photo pull off:
Hwaseong is not one town but a sprawl of villages, factories and farmland on the edge of the Seoul metropolitan area, and the pin sits among them. With nearly half a million people, the city has grown enormously in recent decades, and it is home to big research campuses and car plants, including the research centre of one of South Korea's biggest car makers. Yet between the factories, there remain rice paddies, orchards, greenhouses and small hills, and a short ride can take you into a rural landscape that feels far from the capital.

The best-known historic site nearby is the Hwaseong Fortress in Suwon, built in the 1790s by King Jeongjo, a long wall with gates, towers and a beautiful design, which is on the UNESCO World Heritage list. It lies about twenty kilometres away, and a stroll along its walls is a pleasant way to spend an afternoon. Closer by, the area around the Sihwa reservoir has a site of fossilised dinosaur eggs, which is one of the most important in Korea.

The label refers to Yangpyeong, a river valley east of Seoul with mountains and forests, but it lies far from here, and this is a different kind of place: an agricultural fringe, with straight roads, bridges and traffic. The riding is mostly urban or suburban, with long stretches of dual carriageway, and speed cameras are extremely common in South Korea, so keep within the limits. For a better ride, head toward the hills near Suwon and the coast, where quiet lanes wind through farmland.

Fuel and food are everywhere. Hwaseong and Suwon have convenience stores, restaurants and petrol stations, and the food is excellent: galbi, grilled marinated ribs, is a speciality of Suwon, and a bowl of hot soup after a cool morning is worth finding. Rest areas on the expressways are surprisingly good, with food courts and regional snacks.

The stop is a photo pull-off, and a good one is a little rise among the fields, where you can see the paddies and the distant shape of the apartment blocks. Dawn and dusk are the best times, when the light is soft and the traffic is light. It is not a remote spot, but it has an honest, working feel that tells you something about modern Korea.
t.kassel@51.3,9.5:
Kassel is a city that rebuilt itself after being flattened by wartime bombing, so the first impression from the ring road is more concrete than fairy tale. Give it an hour and the other Kassel appears. This is where the Brothers Grimm lived and worked for years in the early nineteenth century, collecting the tales that would make them famous, and the city is the start of the German Fairy Tale Route to Bremen. A museum in the city, the Grimmwelt, tells their story and shows original manuscripts.

The real jewel is the Bergpark Wilhelmshöhe, a huge hillside park laid out by the landgraves of Hesse-Kassel in the baroque era, crowned by a giant copper statue of Hercules standing on an octagonal base. On summer afternoons, water cascades down a long staircase of stone steps in a spectacular show, with the water running for about half an hour and taking time to reach the bottom. UNESCO added the park to its World Heritage list in 2013. The park is at the western edge of the city, and the road up to it is a pleasant, gently curving climb.

Kassel is also known for the documenta, a major contemporary art exhibition held every five years, which fills the city with strange installations. The city sits in the valley of the Fulda, with the wooded hills of northern Hesse all around, and the roads out of town are good: quiet, rolling, forested and mostly well surfaced, with the Reinhardswald and the Habichtswald offering a day's riding in either direction. The traffic is heavy on the motorway interchange, and the city centre is a tangle of one-way streets, so use the ring road if you can.

Fuel is easy here, as it is a big city with plenty of stations, and there are good places to eat in the Vorderer Westen district. A speciality is Ahle Wurst, a hard dried sausage from northern Hesse, and a local dish called Weckewerk, a kind of savoury pudding. The ride towards Bremen goes up the Weser valley, through forests and half-timbered villages, so you will hear plenty about Hansel and Gretel and Sleeping Beauty before you reach the sea.
t.bremen@53.1,8.8:
Bremen is the city of four animals, and you will meet them before you have parked: a donkey, a dog, a cat and a rooster standing on each other's backs in bronze beside the town hall. In the Grimm tale they set out to become musicians in Bremen, but they never actually get there, finding a robbers' house on the way, so the city is the destination of a story whose characters stopped short. The statue's front legs are polished gold by visitors rubbing the donkey's hooves for luck.

Bremen is a free Hanseatic city, a city-state in its own right with about half a million inhabitants, and its centre has the confidence of a place that has been rich for a very long time. The town hall and the huge stone Roland statue on the market square, dating from 1404, are on the UNESCO World Heritage list. The Schnoor quarter, a tangle of small lanes with tiny houses, is a favourite for browsing and a coffee, while Böttcherstraße is a short, brick-built street from the 1920s with a distinctive, slightly eccentric character, and a carillon of Meissen bells that plays at midday.

This is also coffee country. Bremen has been a major coffee port for more than a century, and the smell of roasting beans still drifts over the city on some mornings. The Beck's brewery sits beside the Weser, and a cold glass of it is a fitting end to a ride. Fish and kale are traditional, and a proper Bremen dish is Kohl und Pinkel, cabbage with smoked sausage, which is more of a winter proposition.

For a rider, Bremen is the end of the Fairy Tale Route and a place for fuel, a meal and a stroll, but not for the riding itself. Roads around the city are flat, busy and straight. Stuhr, just to the south, has plenty of stations and supermarkets, and the road network is dense. The best part of arriving is the approach along the Weser, with its green banks and sea breeze. Park near the market, as the old centre is largely pedestrian, and explore on foot. Allow some time for the trams, which are many and efficient, and give them room.
t.hamburg south west edge@53.4,9.9:
Hamburg does not end so much as thin out, and this is where it happens. Out here on the south-west edge, between the Elbe and the heath, the port's industrial yards give way to a landscape of commuter villages, motorway interchanges, fields and low wooded hills, and the town of Neu Wulmstorf, with about twenty thousand people, is the nearest place of any size. Behind you lies Harburg, once a separate town on the south bank of the river, and ahead is the flat green country of Lower Saxony.

The ground is a glacial one, a sandy ridge of moraine left by the ice age, called the Harburg Hills. Pine and beech woods, heathland and old sand pits cover the slopes, and on a clear day you can see the cranes of the harbour from the top of the ridge. To the west lies the Altes Land, the largest continuous fruit-growing area in Northern Europe, a strip of apple and cherry orchards along the Elbe marshes, and in late April the blossom turns the whole district white and pink. The old farmhouses, with their half-timbered fronts and carved gate arches, are among the finest in northern Germany.

A ride from here to the Weserbergland is a long sweep south through the plain. The first stretch is the busy road out of the city, with traffic lights, roundabouts and a lot of lorries heading for the port, and then the pace eases as the fields open up. The roads across the heath are long and straight, with tree-lined avenues and farms, and wind can be a nuisance on exposed sections, particularly from the west. The hills of the Weser, with their gentler curves, are a day's ride away.

Fuel and food are no problem in Neu Wulmstorf and the surrounding villages, and the supermarkets and bakeries here open early, which suits an early start. Try a Franzbrötchen, Hamburg's cinnamon pastry, from a bakery on the way out, and a fish roll if you have time. Late spring and early autumn are the best times, and the Altes Land is a fine detour. Check the weather, because the north German coast is changeable, and a sharp shower can arrive with little warning.
t.rotenburg@53.1,9.4:
Rotenburg an der Wümme is a quiet district town of about twenty-two thousand people on the river Wümme, halfway between Hamburg and Bremen, and a convenient place to fill the tank on the way south. The pin lies on the edge of town, less than a kilometre from the centre. The landscape here is typical of northern Lower Saxony: flat or gently rolling, with heath and pine, wet meadows and the dark, boggy ground of the moors. Everything is green, and the sky is large.

The Wümme runs north-west through broad meadows to join the Lesum and then the Weser near Bremen, and the countryside around it is a mosaic of meadows, small woods and farms. The Wümmewiesen are a protected area with wet grassland, rich in birds, and storks and cranes are not unusual. The Teufelsmoor, the Devil's Moor, lies further west, and was settled in the eighteenth century by colonists who drained the peat bogs, cut turf and built long, low farmhouses along straight canals. The moor later attracted a school of painters, the Worpswede artists, who found something strange and beautiful in its misty light.

The riding is easy and pleasant rather than exciting. Roads run straight through the pines, with occasional bends around villages, and the surface is mostly good. Wind is the main variable, and it can be strong on the open land. The best time is spring, when the heath is waking up, or late summer, when the heather blooms purple. Early morning mist hangs over the meadows and gives the scene an almost Dutch air.

Rotenburg itself has a pleasant old church and a small museum, and the town is known for a large hospital and care foundation. Its position on the railway and the main road between the two big cities means that traffic is dense on the through roads, so leave them for the quiet lanes as soon as you can. There are plenty of cafes and bakeries around the market, and the fuel stations on the main roads are open late. Hemsbünde, a village a few kilometres away, has little more than a pub.
t.nienburg river road@52.6,9.2:
Nienburg lies on the Weser at the point where the river enters its flat, meandering lower course, and the pin sits right on the town at the edge of the water. With some thirty thousand people, it is a proper town with fuel, supermarkets and cafes, and with a pleasant, slightly sleepy old centre of brick and half-timber. The river here is broad and slow, lined with willows and meadows, and it makes a good place for a stop and a flask of coffee.

The Weser is the great river of this part of Germany, formed at Hannoversch Münden by the meeting of the Werra and the Fulda and flowing north to the North Sea at Bremerhaven. Along the way it passes through a string of attractive towns, and Nienburg is one of the most relaxed. The region is famous for asparagus, and from April to the end of June, the traditional end of the season, restaurants all over the area serve it with ham and new potatoes. The German Asparagus Route passes right through here, and you will see roadside stalls selling the white stalks by the kilo.

The riding here is flat and easy, along the river through fields and small villages. The dike roads are quiet and the surface is generally good, with long, straight stretches and gentle bends. There is not much shelter, so wind can be a factor, and the wide views over the meadows and the river are lovely in the evening, with the light low and golden. A cycle path follows the Weser for most of its length, and cyclists are common, so give them room.

Drakenburg, a village about five kilometres away, is on the river, and the surrounding area has a number of lakes and gravel pits, some of which are used for swimming. Look for signs before you plunge in, as the Weser itself has currents and shipping, and is not recommended for swimming. The Steinhuder Meer, Lower Saxony's biggest lake, is a short ride to the east, and offers beaches, sailing and a good place for smoked eel.
t.rinteln weser bends@52.2,9.1:
Rinteln is a small Weser town of about twenty-eight thousand people, set where the river swings in a series of wide bends between the hills of the Weserbergland. The pin lies almost in the centre, so everything a rider needs is within a short walk: fuel, a bakery, a market square and a decent place to eat. The old town is full of half-timbered houses and handsome buildings in the Weser Renaissance style, a distinctive form of gables, bay windows and decorated stonework that spread along the river in the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries.

The Weser here is slow and wide, flowing past wooded hills on either side, and the landscape is soft and green, with orchards and small villages tucked into the valleys. Luhden, four kilometres away, sits in the hills, and the road up to it climbs in a series of gentle bends. The Weserbergland is not high, but it is lively, with hills, forests and ridgeline roads that offer long views over the valley. The traffic is light, apart from the weekend crowds, and the road surface is generally good.

Hameln, twenty-five kilometres upstream, is the town of the Pied Piper, the legendary rat-catcher who, when the town refused to pay him, led its children away. The story, which the Brothers Grimm included in their collection, is said to relate to a real event in 1284. Hameln has a pleasant old centre with a daily show on the town clock and rats on every souvenir. Rinteln makes a quieter alternative for a rest, with fewer coach parties.

The river is the thread, and a ride along its banks is a gentle way to pass an afternoon. Ferries still cross in a few places, and the old road along the foot of the hills passes small villages and chapels. In autumn, the beech woods turn gold and the river mist lingers in the morning. The weather in this region is mild, with frequent showers, so a waterproof layer is a good idea. A glass of Weser region beer in a small inn makes a good end to the day.
t.marburg@50.8,8.8:
Marburg climbs a steep hillside above the Lahn river, with a castle at the top, a Gothic church on the slope and a student at nearly every corner. It is a university town in the real sense: the university was founded in 1527 as the first Protestant university in the world, and roughly a quarter of the population is made up of students. That gives the narrow lanes of the old town an energy that few places in Hesse can match, with bookshops, cafes and bars crowded into every nook.

The Elisabethkirche, built in the thirteenth century to honour Elizabeth of Hungary, a landgravine who gave away her wealth to the poor and died young, is one of the first purely Gothic churches in Germany. It is a tall, pale building with two spires, and its interior holds Elizabeth's shrine, a golden reliquary that drew pilgrims from across Europe. The Landgrafenschloss above it, a mixture of medieval and later buildings, offers a fine view over the town and the valley, and the walk up is steep and worthwhile.

The Brothers Grimm studied here in the early nineteenth century, and the town forms part of the German Fairy Tale Route. In 1529 Marburg hosted a famous debate between Martin Luther and Huldrych Zwingli about the Eucharist, which failed to settle their differences but shaped the Protestant world. In the late nineteenth century, Emil von Behring developed his diphtheria antitoxin here, work that earned him the first Nobel Prize in medicine and gave Marburg a lasting reputation in medical research.

The riding between Hanau and Kassel on the fairy tale route is gentle, through the Vogelsberg and the Lahn valley, with wide roads and long, easy bends. Marburg itself has narrow streets and heavy traffic, so park outside the old town and walk up. Fuel is easy in the lower town, and Cölbe, five kilometres north, has more. Evenings are lively and the cafes are open late, so it is a fine place to stop for the night.
t.hannover south east@52.2,9.9:
This is the flat, fertile ground south-east of Hannover, where the city's suburbs give way to the Hildesheimer Börde, one of the richest farming landscapes in Germany. The soil is loess, a fine, wind-blown dust laid down in the ice age, and it is so deep and so good that sugar beet, wheat and rapeseed grow in enormous fields stretching to the horizon. Sarstedt, a town of nearly nineteen thousand people on the Innerste river, is the largest place nearby, with Giesen and Harsum close by, and the villages are neat and prosperous with brick houses and big farms.

The geography is quiet but not dull. The Leine and the Innerste rivers wind through the plain, lined with willows, and on a clear day the blue line of the Harz mountains is visible on the southern horizon, with wind turbines standing in rows across the fields. Hildesheim, about fifteen kilometres to the south, has two Romanesque churches on the UNESCO list, the cathedral and St Michael's, and a rebuilt market square with a famous timber-framed Knochenhauer-Amtshaus, the butchers' guild hall, that is worth a detour.

For the rider, this is the starting gate for a longer journey to the Kyffhäuser, a low, wooded ridge in Thuringia with a huge monument to the emperor Barbarossa, who legend says sleeps inside the mountain until the ravens stop flying round it. The first part of the road crosses the Börde on straight, quiet lanes, with views across the fields and the occasional bend around a village, and the pace is easy. The wind can be strong, particularly from the west, and in harvest time, tractors and sugar beet lorries on the road are a hazard.

Sarstedt has fuel stations, supermarkets and several bakeries, so fill up here before the long run south-east. Look for a coffee and a slice of cake in a village bakery, or a plate of Braunschweiger sausage and potatoes at a country inn. Spring and early autumn are the best seasons, when the fields are green or golden and the air is clear, and in winter fog and frost can make the roads slippery. Check the forecast before setting out for the hills.
t.rendsburg bridge@54.3,9.7:
The Rendsburg High Bridge is a railway viaduct that does something unusual: it hangs a gondola from its steel framework, a transporter ferry swinging just above the water of the Kiel Canal. The bridge opened in 1913, built so that trains could climb high enough for ships to pass underneath while the town below stays connected across the canal. The railway loops around the town to gain height, so the whole structure reads like a giant iron ribbon laid over the landscape. It is the sort of engineering that makes people stop and stare, and bikers are no exception.

The canal itself is the busiest artificial waterway in the world by number of ships, linking the North Sea at Brunsbüttel to the Baltic at Kiel and sparing vessels the long trip around Denmark. Standing on the bank you can watch container ships, tankers and the occasional yacht glide past at walking pace, close enough to hear the engines. The ferry that runs under the bridge, the Schwebefähre, still carries pedestrians and cyclists, and a few vehicles; check before you ride on, because it is a small deck and a motorcycle is not what it was designed for. Its schedule and capacity are best confirmed on the spot.

Rendsburg is a proper town of twenty-eight thousand people, with fuel, food and a pleasant old quarter, the Altstadt, and a fortress district of cobbled streets in the old garrison part. Büdelsdorf lies just across the water and has plenty of supermarkets and petrol stations. The riding in the flat country is gentle and honest: long straights, a lot of wind coming off the plain, and the occasional canal crossing by ferry that adds a bit of theatre to the day. Northern Germany is not for hairpins, but it is for rhythm, and the bridge is a good place to find it.

Approach from either bank on a quiet morning and you get the best view of the structure with the sun behind you. Gulls follow the ships, the air smells of diesel and brackish water, and the whole place hums with the low drone of engines that you stop noticing after a while. It is a good end to a ride, or an excellent excuse for a coffee break, with the steel girders overhead and the canal sliding by.
t.hannover west escape@52.3,9.5:
Hannover has a reputation for being flat, grey and efficient, which is mostly unfair, though to be honest the first twenty kilometres west of town will not change your mind. The starting point here sits on the Calenberg lowland, a farming plain of big fields, hedgerows and straight roads, just outside the built-up edge and close to the villages of Großgoltern and Egestorf. The Deister ridge lies not far to the south-west, and that low range of wooded hills is the first real promise of curves for anyone leaving the city in that direction.

What makes this a good escape is how quickly the traffic thins. Within minutes of leaving the ring road you are on quiet country roads that link small villages with church towers and brick farmhouses, most with a barn big enough to swallow a bus. The surface is mostly decent, though the plain gets muddy at harvest and the cross-winds can be annoying. It is not dramatic riding, but it is the smooth kind, good for warming up before the route heads toward the hills. Early morning is best, when the mist lies in the fields and the light comes in low and gold.

The region has a long history as a crossing point. The old trade roads between the Rhine and the Elbe ran through here, and the Hanoverian dynasty that later gave Britain its Georgian kings started from this modest city. The Leine and the Deister coalfields shaped the area's economy for centuries, and the old mining towns on the ridge still carry the memory. Local food is hearty; in the villages you are more likely to find a bakery with a cake counter than anything exotic.

Egestorf is the nearest sizeable place, with nearly eight thousand people, so you will find fuel and a supermarket there, and Hannover itself has every service you can imagine behind you. Small places like Großgoltern are quieter, so fill up beforehand. In the cool part of the year the air smells of damp earth and woodsmoke, and the wind off the plain can be sharp, so bring a layer. Treat this stop as the start of the day, a place to check your tyres, eat something solid and look south at the hills.
t.buckeburg@52.3,9.1:
Bückeburg is a small residential town in Schaumburg-Lippe, the little princely state that survived as a sovereign territory until 1918, and the pin sits right in the centre, with all the services you would expect in a town of twenty thousand. Fuel is available here and in the neighbouring villages, and the main street has bakeries and cafes. The country around it is flat and fertile, with the Weser some kilometres to the west and the low ridge of the Bückeberge to the south.

This is also an army town of a quiet sort. The German army's aviation school and a helicopter museum are based here, and the Hubschraubermuseum, a collection of rotary-wing aircraft from many countries, attracts visitors. The sight of helicopters clattering over the fields is a common one, and the museum has a decent collection, including some oddities from the Cold War.

The riding in the area is relaxed and rural, over small roads that run through villages and past fields of wheat and sugar beet. The surface varies, and bends are gentle, with the Bückeberge and the Weser offering a few hills. Traffic is light on the minor roads, though the main road to Hannover can be busy with trucks. The best times are spring, when the rapeseed is in bloom, and early autumn, when the beech woods turn red.

Bückeburg's town church, finished in 1615, was one of the first major Protestant churches built in Germany, and its Baroque facade is worth a look. The town is a pleasant place for a coffee, and the market square has a few attractive buildings. Ahnsen, a village three and a half kilometres away, has a quiet lane and a pub, but little else. If you intend to push on towards the Weserbergland or the Teutoburg Forest, fill up here, as services thin out in the hills. A short walk through the town park offers shade and a quiet bench.
t.bad iburg forest@52.2,8.0:
Bad Iburg lies on the northern slopes of the Teutoburg Forest, a long wooded ridge that runs across north-west Germany, and the pin sits in the town, a spa and holiday place of about twelve thousand people. The hills here are not high, no more than three hundred metres or so, but they are steep, well wooded and cut with small valleys, and the road in from the plain climbs through beech forest with a satisfying series of bends. The town has fuel, bakeries and several inns, and it is a pleasant place for a late lunch.

Above the town stands the castle of Iburg, once a Benedictine abbey and later the residence of the prince-bishops of Osnabrück. It is a large and handsome complex, with a mix of medieval and baroque buildings, and it is open to visitors. In 1668 Sophie Charlotte, later the first queen of Prussia, was born here, and the rooms hold a small museum about her. The castle stands on a ridge, with a fine view over the town and the forest, and the walk up from the market takes about ten minutes.

Bad Iburg is a Kneipp spa, a place where the water cure promoted by the Bavarian priest Sebastian Kneipp is practised, and you will see small pools in the park where visitors stand in cold water up to their knees. The air is clean, the forest paths are well marked, and the Hermannsweg, a long-distance trail, runs along the ridge. The ridge road offers good riding, with gentle climbs and descents, long views to the north and a surface that is generally smooth. Traffic is heavy on summer weekends, when families come to walk.

Lienen, four kilometres away, has a quiet centre and a fine church. For food, look for the regional dishes of Westphalia: Pfefferpotthast, a spicy beef stew, and Pumpernickel, the dense dark rye bread, served with ham and good butter. In the evening, the light is soft over the forest, and the air smells of pine and woodsmoke. It is a sensible place to stop for the night, and an even better place to finish a day.
t.hannover north edge@52.5,9.8:
The northern fringe of Hannover is where the city gives up and the Wedemark begins, and the landmarks that matter are small. Isernhagen and Langenhagen sit side by side, the first a strung-out village-suburb with a great many gardens and horse paddocks, the second a proper town that happens to host the city's airport. The coordinates here fall between them, on the flat sandy plain that the Leine and Aller rivers have been working on for millennia. The sandy soil is why pine and birch woods start creeping in as you head north.

The riding that follows is a calm and steady introduction to the Lüneburg Heath region, with long, gently curving roads through fields and forest, the occasional oak avenue and plenty of horses in the paddocks. It is easy cruising rather than a technical challenge. Traffic is heavier near the city and the airport, and you will meet cyclists on the lanes in summer, but the further north you go the quieter and more rural the roads become. Weekday mornings are good; Sunday afternoons can get busy with people heading out to the heath.

Isernhagen has a distinct history as farming land with large estates, and the area is known for asparagus in late spring, which German restaurants celebrate fanatically between April and June. If you see a roadside stand with white spears and a handwritten sign, it is worth a stop. The soil here suits it. Langenhagen gives you everything practical: fuel, supermarkets and cafes, and with fifty thousand inhabitants it will have what you need. Hannover's centre, with its cultural quarters and the huge city forest of the Eilenriede, lies about twelve kilometres south, but this edge of town is better suited to a quick coffee than a long visit.

The beauty of starting here is the speed with which the landscape opens. You can be among pines and heather within half an hour, with the sandy tracks and low sunlight that make northern Germany special in the early autumn, when the heather turns purple. The air has a resinous, dusty smell on a warm day, and the wind brings that mix of grass and diesel that belongs to every flat country. Check your fuel before leaving; the first few villages are small, and the roads toward the heath are quiet in every sense.
t.harburger berge forest@53.4,9.9:
South of Hamburg, on the far bank of the Elbe, a ridge of low, wooded hills rises to a little over a hundred metres, and Hamburgers treat it as their mountains. The Harburger Berge are what is left of a glacial moraine, covered in beech, oak and pine, with patches of heath and sandy soil. The highest point, the Hasselbrack, reaches 116 metres, which makes it the highest natural point in the whole city state of Hamburg, a fact that Hamburgers recite with a mixture of pride and self-mockery. The pin lies in these woods, four kilometres from the centre of Harburg and under five from Seevetal.

The country here is a surprise after the flat marsh of the Elbe. Roads climb and dip through forest in gentle bends, with the surface generally good and the speed limits strict, because this is a commuter zone with a lot of cyclists and walkers. In the middle of the hills the Wildpark Schwarze Berge, a wildlife park, keeps native animals in large enclosures, and families come at weekends for the native animals. Dog walkers and joggers fill the forest paths on dry mornings, so ride with care.

Harburg itself has been a separate town for much of its history, and only became part of Hamburg in 1937. It has an old harbour on the Elbe, a former industrial area of rubber and oil mills, and a university of technology. The big cities of the Elbe, Hamburg to the north and Lüneburg to the south-east, have spread into the villages, and Seevetal is a patchwork of residential settlements of over forty thousand inhabitants. Fuel and shops are plentiful on the main roads, and a coffee in Harburg's old streets is a good start.

For a rider, this is the gentle beginning or end of a longer day, the transition between city and heath. A short ride south brings you to the Lüneburg Heath, with its open, sandy landscape, junipers and heather, and the roads there are quieter and flatter than here. In late summer, the heath is purple, and the light is lovely. If you want a short ride before dinner, loop through the Harburger Berge on a weekday evening, when the woods smell of resin and the light filters low between the trunks.
t.buckeburg palace sight@52.3,9.1:
Bückeburg is a town to be seen from the inside of its palace, and the palace does not disappoint. Schloss Bückeburg, a Renaissance and Baroque complex surrounded by a moat, has been the seat of the princes of Schaumburg-Lippe for four hundred years, and the family still lives in part of it. A series of interiors are open to visitors, among them the Golden Hall, a magnificent room with an ornate, gilded ceiling. The gate and gardens are free to walk through, and the park around it is pleasant.

The town and palace had a surprising cultural life. Johann Gottfried Herder, the philosopher, served as court preacher here in the 1770s, and Johann Christoph Friedrich Bach, a son of Johann Sebastian, spent most of his career as a court musician in Bückeburg. His music is occasionally played in the palace, and a small museum recalls the family. Another sight is the princely mausoleum, a neo-Romanesque building in the park with a vast golden mosaic dome that gleams as you step inside, one of the most striking interiors in Lower Saxony.

For the rider, Bückeburg is a short stop and a gentle one. The palace sits right in the town, so park nearby and walk, and the surrounding streets are pleasant and quiet. There are cafes on the market square, including a good one for cake, and fuel is available on the edge of town. The ride from here goes through the Weser Hills or towards Minden, over small roads with a few bends and not much traffic.

On a fine afternoon, sit by the moat and look at the reflection of the palace in the water. In early summer the garden is full of roses, and the trees are in full leaf. The area around Bückeburg is rich in small museums and manor houses, and a visit to any of them offers a glimpse of the old, small German states, with their courts, orchestras and eccentric rulers, before unification swept them away. It is a quiet history, and it fits well with a quiet town.
t.minden river@52.3,8.9:
Minden sits at the point where the Weser leaves the Weserbergland through the Porta Westfalica, a gap in the hills that has been a crossing point for centuries, and the pin lies on the river bank in the middle of the old town. With about eighty thousand people, it is a real city, with fuel, restaurants, shops and a railway station. The Weser here is wide and calm, with a promenade and a few cafes, and the old cathedral stands on a terrace above the water.

Minden is the place where one great waterway crosses another. The Mittelland Canal, which links the Rhine and the Elbe, runs across the Weser on a huge aqueduct, so that ships pass over the river high above the heads of anyone on the bank. The first bridge dates from 1914, and a second one was built in the 1990s, and a visit to the site on a weekday often means a glimpse of a barge sailing across. The Weser itself is a busy waterway, and the lock and the old harbour are worth a walk.

The cathedral is a fine Gothic hall church, rebuilt after the war, and the old town has a fair number of historic buildings, including the Rathaus and several handsome houses on the Weser embankment. Just north of the city, the Porta Westfalica, a narrow gorge between the Wiehengebirge and the Weser Hills, is marked by a monument to Kaiser Wilhelm I, standing on a hilltop and visible from far away. The colossal figure inside a stone canopy dominates the gap, and the view from the terrace is excellent.

The ride from Minden is gentle and pleasant, along the river or over the hills. The road to the Porta passes through woods, with a few bends and a smooth surface. There are bathing places on the river and the lakes nearby, but the Weser itself is not clean enough for swimming and has strong currents. Pick a designated spot and read the signs. A stop at the river terrace with a coffee, watching barges and cyclists drift by, is a pleasant way to pass the time before moving on.
t.buxtehude@53.5,9.7:
Buxtehude is the town of the hare and the hedgehog. In the Low German fairy tale collected by the Brothers Grimm, the hedgehog challenges the hare to a race, and wins by tricking him, with his wife waiting at the finish line looking just like him. The story is set on the heath near Buxtehude, and the town celebrates it with statues and a fountain. The name has also become a German byword for a remote place, as in the saying that someone is living in Buxtehude, which is a bit unfair to a lively Hanseatic town of nearly forty thousand.

The pin lies a kilometre and a half from the centre, close enough that you can reach the old town in a few minutes. The old centre is built around the Fleth, a small canal that once brought boats right up to the merchant houses, and many of the half-timbered buildings and brick warehouses have been restored. The market square has a handsome town hall, and there are cafes and restaurants beside the water. Fuel and supermarkets are on the outskirts, and coffee is available on every corner.

Buxtehude is the gateway to the Altes Land, the vast orchard country along the south bank of the Elbe, and this is the reason many riders come. In late April and May, when the apple, cherry and pear trees bloom, the whole landscape is covered in white and pink, and the old farmhouses with their brick-patterned gables and ornate doorways stand among the blossoms. The roads run along the dikes and canals, flat and gentle, with a few sharp bends, and the blossom festival draws huge crowds. Jork, six kilometres away, is the centre of the region, with a fine church and a number of attractive old houses.

In autumn, the orchards are heavy with apples, and farm stalls sell them by the crate, along with cider and jams. The wind off the Elbe can be strong and cold, and the sky is wide and bright. At the weekend the roads fill with cyclists, and it is wise to ride early. After a day among the trees, a coffee and a slice of apple cake in Buxtehude make a welcome end.
t.kappeln schlei bridge@54.7,9.9:
Kappeln lies on the Schlei, a long narrow inlet of the Baltic that reaches forty-odd kilometres inland, like a fjord that forgot to be steep. The pin sits at the town's centre, at the bridge, and Kappeln has about ten thousand people, fuel, bakeries and a harbour full of old boats. The bridge itself is the town's emblem: a lifting bridge from the 1920s that opens to let ships through, so be prepared to wait a few minutes while the roadway rises and the sailing boats glide past.

Kappeln is the capital of Angeln, the rolling, hedge-patterned peninsula between the Schlei and the Flensburg Fjord that gave England its name. The Angles, a Germanic tribe who migrated to Britain in the fifth century, are said to have come from this region, and you will see the name on signs and shops. The country is a landscape of low hills, farms and thatched cottages, with winding lanes under old trees and hardly any traffic. The surface is generally good, and the bends are gentle, making it a very pleasant place to ride slowly.

On the water, the Heringszaun is the unique sight. This is the last herring fence in Europe, a long line of stakes and nets in the shape of a funnel that traps herring as they swim in during spring, and it has been used for centuries. Fresh and smoked herring are sold from stalls and small restaurants nearby, and a roll with smoked fish and onion is the thing to eat while watching the boats. A Dutch-style windmill stands on the harbour, and there are cafes along the waterfront.

Gelting, ten kilometres away, is the gateway to the Geltinger Birk, a nature reserve of heath, dunes and grazing cattle on the Baltic coast, where the land is flat and the wind is steady. Go in the morning, when the air is bright and the reeds shine. The old harbour and the maritime atmosphere make Kappeln a good stop for a long lunch, and for an excursion boat down the Schlei.
t.hamburg west edge@53.6,9.9:
Altona was Danish until 1864, a fact that surprises many visitors, and the quarter still feels a little apart from the rest of Hamburg. The coordinates here fall on the high bank of the Elbe at Ottensen and Altona, where the city looks out over the widest part of the river and the container cranes of the port sit on the opposite shore. The water is just ten metres or so below the street at this point. It is the part of Hamburg most closely tied to ships and the sea, and you can smell it: tar, diesel, wet rope and fish.

Altona's Fischmarkt is famous for its Sunday morning gathering, which starts before dawn and draws everyone from party-goers on the way home to families buying eels and bananas by the crate. If your ride starts at the weekend, it is an extraordinary place for a pre-ride breakfast. The Elbchaussee, the long road that runs west along the river high above the water, passes grand merchants' villas and white mansions with gardens sloping down to the shore. It is lovely but slow, with many traffic lights and a low speed limit, and the cobbled and tram-free surfaces in the old quarters are better treated with respect when wet.

From here the way west is a gentle transition. Past Blankenese, where stepped lanes climb a wooded hillside, the road stays near the river, and the ferries that cross the Elbe, among them the passenger boats on the public transport network, give a flavour of the harbour city. Cafes and bakeries are plentiful in Ottensen, with its converted factories and independent shops, and the Altona district has fuel stations on the main routes, so the practical side of a start here is easy. Do be careful in the old streets, where delivery vans, cyclists and trams create a puzzle every few hundred metres.

The best light is early morning or late afternoon, when the sun picks out the river and the cranes. Spring and autumn are nicest, with fewer crowds and clearer air, and winter has its own raw beauty when the wind brings sleet off the water. Take a moment on the bank before you ride away: watching a container ship the size of a small town slide silently past makes the road ahead seem pleasantly modest.
t.main wall area 1@54.5,9.5:
The Danevirke is the longest and most important archaeological monument in northern Europe, a network of earthworks and walls that stretches across the neck of the Jutland peninsula, and the Main Wall is its backbone. At this spot, close to the village of Dannewerk near Schleswig, you are standing on a grassy ridge that looks like nothing much until someone tells you it was built to stop armies. It runs for kilometres through fields and woods, and over a stretch of centuries it was raised, repaired and extended by Danish kings, from the early Viking age into the twelfth century.

The landscape explains why the wall is here. The peninsula narrows between the marshy valleys of the Treene and Rheide on the one hand and the long inlet of the Schlei on the other, leaving a land bridge only a few kilometres across. Anyone travelling overland between the Danes in the north and the Saxons and Franks in the south had to pass this gap, and the Danevirke closed it. A later brick section, usually credited to King Valdemar in the 1100s, is among the earliest medieval brick structures in the region, and a good example of how the building style came north. The monument was inscribed by UNESCO in 2018 together with Hedeby, the Viking trading town nearby.

For a rider, the interest is in how quiet and gentle the surrounding roads are. Small lanes follow the line of the wall through arable land, with gentle curves and fine views over flat farmland and the occasional wood. The surface is mostly fine but narrow, and there are few places to pull in on the busy stretches, so choose your stopping point with care. Traffic is light except on the main road to Schleswig. A museum near the wall explains the history with models and excavation finds, and walking paths along the earthwork give you the sense of scale that a road cannot.

Dannewerk itself is tiny, so for fuel and food head into Schleswig, about five kilometres away, where there are stations, supermarkets and a nice old town by the Schlei. The area smells of grass and wet earth, and the wind is rarely absent. Come on a clear spring day when the larks are singing above the ramparts, and you will find the whole thing remarkably peaceful for a place that was designed around fear.
t.offshore work@54.5,9.6:
The word on the sign suggests a ship, but the offshore work here is a piece of earthwork, an outlying defence belonging to the old Danevirke system. The ground is south of the Schlei, the long narrow fjord that cuts inland from the Baltic to Schleswig, between the villages of Fahrdorf, Schaalby and Fleckeby. In practice, for a rider, the label is a pointer to a landscape rather than a single monument: low farmland, hedged fields, small woods and quiet lanes that run down to the water.

The Schlei is the best thing about this district. It is a drowned glacial channel about forty kilometres long, so narrow in places that it looks more like a river, and its banks are lined with reeds, small harbours and red-roofed villages. Fleckeby sits on one of the fjord's inlets, and Fahrdorf lies close to the old bridge that crosses toward Schleswig. Historically this was a frontier area, where Danish and German-speaking communities mixed, and the region changed hands several times before the borders settled after the plebiscites of 1920. That mixed heritage still shows up in the village names and in the food, which includes smoked herring and rolls with pickled fish.

The roads here are quiet and good for steady, relaxed riding. They are mostly straight with occasional bends where a stream or a patch of woodland interrupts the fields, and from time to time a gap in the hedge opens a view across the water. The wind off the fjord can be cool and stiff even in midsummer, so a spare layer is sensible. Cyclists and tractors are the main hazards. In late summer, when the fields are being harvested, you will find straw and mud on the road and a smell of dust and cut grain in the air.

For fuel, Schleswig, about ten kilometres away, has plenty of stations and supermarkets, and the villages here have bakeries and a few cafes that open mostly in the season. Eckernförde lies to the east on the coast. If you only have time for one thing, walk down to the water's edge at a quiet spot and watch the reeds move in the wind: the Schlei always seems to be thinking about something.
t.frankfurt@50.1,8.7:
Frankfurt is the one German city with a skyline, and the locals have a nickname for it: Mainhattan. A cluster of glass towers rises from the north bank of the river Main, the banking district, and you can see it from the Taunus hills on clear days. The rest of the city is more modest than the towers suggest. The old centre was heavily bombed in the war and has been rebuilt in places, with the Römer, a medieval town hall with stepped gables, restored on its square and the Cathedral of St Bartholomew, where emperors were crowned, still standing by the river.

History is surprisingly rich. Goethe was born here in 1749 and his house is a museum, and the Paulskirche, a round church near the Römer, was the seat of the first freely elected German parliament in 1848. The south bank, Sachsenhausen, is the place for apple wine, called Apfelwein or Ebbelwoi, served in grey jugs with a patterned glaze in old taverns, and it is an acquired taste worth acquiring. Frankfurt is also the home of one of the busiest airports in Europe, and the sound of planes comes and goes on the western side.

For a rider the city is a base rather than a destination. The roads are busy, with trams, one-way systems and a lot of traffic lights, and low-emission zones apply in the centre. Once you break through the commuter belt, the Taunus to the north-west rises into forested hills with the Feldberg at around eight hundred and eighty metres, and the roads there are among the best near the city, with bends, gradients and good surfaces. Weekends bring a lot of other bikers, so early starts help. The Limes, the old Roman frontier, runs through this country too, and the fortlet at Lochmühle is one of its small outposts.

Fuel is no problem at all. Stations are on every main road, and the city has bakeries and cafes in every neighbourhood. Parking a motorcycle in the centre is possible with a little patience, and a stroll along the riverside paths is a pleasant way to wake up before the ride. Late autumn can bring thick river fog that lingers until midday, so give yourself time and visibility.
t.dusseldorf@51.2,6.8:
Düsseldorf has two reputations that do not always sit comfortably together: fashion and beer. The Königsallee, a wide boulevard with a tree-lined canal down the middle, is lined with expensive shops, and the city is a hub for advertising, trade fairs and business. Yet the old town, the Altstadt, is crammed with traditional brewery pubs serving Altbier, a dark copper top-fermented beer poured fresh from the barrel into small glasses by waiters called Köbes. The stretch is often called the longest bar in the world, and on a Friday night it seems like it.

The city sits on the right bank of the Rhine, and the riverfront promenade is a favourite place to walk and watch the barges. The Rheinturm, a television tower with a clock made of lights, gives views over the river, and the Medienhafen, an old port converted to offices and restaurants, has odd buildings by Frank Gehry that look like crumpled paper. The poet Heinrich Heine was born here in 1797. There is also a large Japanese community, and you will find excellent ramen and sushi in the streets near the station.

The riding starts in the middle of Germany's most densely populated region, and the first part is a matter of patience. Motorways, ring roads and industrial areas fill the horizon, and traffic is heavy at rush hour. The Rhine valley itself is flat, though a short ride east brings you to the Bergisches Land, with wooded valleys, reservoirs and twisting roads, and to the north-west the lower Rhine has its own gentle rural charm. Low-emission zones apply in the city, and the speed cameras are many. Do not underestimate the distances either: the Ruhr area, with the Zollverein coal mine, is only about forty kilometres to the north-east.

Fuel is plentiful in a city of over five hundred thousand, and breakfast cafes and bakeries are everywhere. It is a good place to start early, to be out of the urban sprawl before the commuters arrive. If you finish here in the evening, a glass of Altbier in the old town is the right way to close the day. The smell of the place is a mixture of river water, malt and exhaust, which is oddly comforting.
t.main wall areas 2 to 3@54.5,9.5:
Start with the ground, because the ground is the whole reason this wall exists. Between the Baltic inlet of the Schlei and the North Sea marshes, the Jutland peninsula pinches to a corridor of firm, sandy land, and for more than a thousand years every army, trader and pilgrim travelling between Scandinavia and the rest of Europe had to squeeze through it. The Danes built their great barrier across this corridor, and at these coordinates, a short way from the village of Dannewerk, you are on a section of the Main Wall where the ramparts are especially legible, with the bank rising above the field and a ditch alongside.

Archaeologists have found that the wall was not built once but many times, with timber, turf, clay and eventually brick used in successive centuries. The oldest dated phases go back to the early 700s, and the big expansions came under King Godfred in the early 800s and Harald Bluetooth in the later 900s. Later still came the brick facing of the twelfth century, which gave the monument the look of a medieval castle wall stretched across the countryside. Walking along it today, you read the rise and fall of kingdoms in the profile of a grass-covered bank.

The lanes nearby are the kind you want when you are looking for quiet. They run through arable fields and low woods, with little traffic except local farmers, and the surface is good if narrow. Corners are gentle, visibility is usually decent, and the horizon is wide. I would choose an overcast morning or a low-sun evening, when the shape of the earthwork stands out best. Dannewerk and Schuby are villages, with limited services, so fuel and food are best found in Schleswig, a short ride away, where there is a pretty old town and a lakeside promenade.

Nature has reclaimed much of the wall, and the banks are now home to wild flowers, rabbits and, in spring, skylarks that rise from the grass in a continuous trill. In winter the wind sweeps across the open land and the air smells of frost and ploughed clay. A short walk from the roadside, with the dull thud of boots on turf, lets you feel the size of the thing. It is a place for stopping and looking rather than for racing, and it rewards patience.
t.connection wall areas 5 to 7@54.5,9.5:
Schleswig is a town that stretches along the head of the Schlei like a ribbon, and the section of the Danish defences marked here lies on its southern and western side. This is where the long Main Wall met the edge of the water and the Viking harbour town of Hedeby, and the connecting wall was built to link the two so that no one could slip through the gap. On the ground it appears as a low, grassy bank crossing meadows and the edges of woods, only a few kilometres from the old town.

The town of Schleswig itself is well worth the time. The fishermen's quarter, called Holm, is a tiny village of low cottages on a former island in the Schlei, with its own small chapel and a cemetery on a spit of land, and the narrow lanes smell of smoke from the herring smokehouses. The cathedral, St Peter's, has a brick tower more than a hundred metres tall and houses a carved wooden altarpiece by Hans Brüggemann from 1521, a huge piece of late Gothic woodwork. On the north side of the town, Gottorf Castle stands on its island, once the seat of the dukes of Schleswig-Holstein-Gottorf and now a museum.

Riding here is gentle. The roads wind around the end of the fjord with small ups and downs, passing through villages and between hedged fields, and the surface is generally good. The traffic in Schleswig can be busy at midday, particularly near the bridge, and weekends in summer bring day visitors. A pleasant way to link the sights is to ride along the Schlei shore on the quieter side roads, stopping at small harbours where boats are tied up and the reeds rustle.

For fuel, Schleswig has all the stations and supermarkets you need, and Fahrdorf, a short way along, has smaller shops and a bakery. The smell of smoked fish is a good clue about lunch, since a bread roll with smoked herring or a plate of fried fish is easy to find near the water. The best light is in the evening, when the fjord turns pink and the towers of the town stand out against the sky.
t.east sea coastal long day photo pull off:
The pin sits in the hills just north of Seoul, close to Soyosan, a mountain of granite ridges and thick forest above the city of Dongducheon. Though the label speaks of the East Sea, which is on the other side of the peninsula, this is an inland spot, a quiet start or finish point for riders leaving the capital to the north. The border with North Korea lies thirty kilometres or so farther up the road, and the presence of the military is a part of everyday life, with check posts, training areas and the occasional tank crossing sign.

Soyosan has a long history as a place of Buddhist retreat. The monk Wonhyo, one of the great figures of Korean Buddhism in the seventh century, is said to have meditated at a hermitage on its slopes, and a small temple, Jajaam, still stands there. The mountain is popular for day hikes, and in autumn the maples draw visitors. Dongducheon, the town below, grew around a large American army base, Camp Casey, and still has a patchwork of Korean and American influences, with burger shops and army-surplus stores next to noodle restaurants.

Riding in this part of Korea has its own rules. Motorcycles are banned from expressways, so you travel on national routes, which are busy, well signed and often fast, with frequent speed cameras and traffic lights. The scenery is mountainous and wooded, with narrow valleys and rice fields, and secondary roads wind in good, tight curves. Helmets are mandatory, and many roads are thick with trucks. Weekday mornings are the quietest, and early autumn offers cool air and clear skies.

Fuel is easy, since stations are common even in small towns, and Yangju and Uijeongbu are both big enough for everything you need. Pocheon, a little to the north-east, is famous for its makgeolli, a milky rice wine, and for grilled pork ribs, which are an excellent reason to stop after the ride. Bring a little cash and a phone with a Korean map app, since navigation in English can be unreliable, and keep to the speed limits, as police are alert.
t.ganghwa island coastal ride@37.9,126.5:
Let me be straight about this pin: the coordinates sit across the water on the North Korean side of the Han river estuary, close to the city of Kaesŏng, and no rider is going to reach them. It is shown on the ride as the finish and food stop of the Ganghwa island route, and what it really stands for is the island's north coast, from which you can see the opposite shore a couple of kilometres away. That view, of ordinary hills and fields on the far bank, is one of the oddest sights in Korea.

Ganghwa is a place that has been a refuge and a frontier for centuries. During the Mongol invasions of the thirteenth century, the Goryeo court moved its capital here and held out for nearly forty years, and the monks carved a great set of woodblocks of the Buddhist canon on the island. In the nineteenth century, French and American naval forces landed here, and in 1876 a treaty with Japan was signed that opened Korea to the outside world. Prehistoric dolmens, among the finest in Korea and listed by UNESCO, stand in the fields, and Mount Manisan has an altar said to have been built by the mythical founder of the Korean nation.

The riding on Ganghwa is relaxed. Roads run along dikes and across reclaimed land, with wide views of tidal flats, and the coast road passes military posts and wire fences, where you may be asked to slow and show your passport. Photography is restricted at some points. The tide here is among the biggest in the world, and the sea retreats for kilometres, leaving a shining plain of mud that birds cover by the thousand.

For lunch, the island offers good seafood, sweet potatoes, ginseng and the local turnip, usually served in modest family restaurants with floor seating. Ganghwa town has fuel and a cluster of cafés. Bring your passport for the military checkpoints near the border, and be polite. Weekends bring heavy traffic from Seoul, so a weekday ride is a better choice.
t.yangpyeong mountain roads@37.7,127.2:
Namyangju is the green lung on the north-east edge of Seoul, and this pin sits among its hills, a short ride from Uijeongbu and the Hwado district, with the granite hump of Suraksan to the west and the long ridge of Cheonmasan to the east. The mountains here are small by Korean standards, but they rise abruptly from the suburbs, and within ten minutes of the apartment blocks the road is running through oak woods and past orchards. It is a good place to begin a ride, with fuel, coffee and a quick exit to quieter roads.

The district has some of the best-preserved royal forest in the country. Gwangneung, just to the north, holds the tomb of King Sejo, a fifteenth-century Joseon ruler, and the woods around it were closed to the public for centuries and have grown into an exceptional broadleaf forest, now a biosphere reserve and part of a UNESCO group of royal tombs. The Korea National Arboretum is nearby, and the air under the trees smells of damp earth and resin. Namyangju was also the home of Jeong Yakyong, known as Dasan, a great scholar of the late Joseon period who wrote much of his work in exile and is remembered by a museum on the Han river.

Riding in Korea comes with a few rules that are worth knowing. Motorcycles are banned from expressways and some motorways, so your route is on national and local roads, which are plentiful but busy, with many speed cameras and frequent lights. In the hills, the secondary roads are narrow and winding, with tight bends, and in autumn they are lined with colour. Wet leaves can be slick. Weekend traffic from Seoul is heavy, particularly in the afternoon, so mornings are best.

Fuel is easy. Stations are everywhere in this part of Gyeonggi, and many have attendants who will fill the tank for you. Cafés cluster along the roads leading into the hills, some with terraces and views, and restaurants serve grilled meat, noodles and stews. Keep a small amount of cash, though cards are widely accepted. Helmets are required, and so is a licence valid in Korea, so check your documents before you set off.
t.yangpyeong mountain roads scenic road@37:
This pin lies where two rivers become one. A few kilometres east of here, at Dumulmeori, the Bukhan and Namhan rivers meet to form the Han, and just downstream, the Paldang dam holds back a long lake that supplies drinking water to much of the Seoul region. The water is wide, calm and often silvery, and the road that runs beside it is one of the most pleasant escapes from the capital. Hanam and Wabu are the nearest towns, and the whole area feels like a very long lakeside suburb.

The scenery is gentle. Low hills covered in oak and pine drop to the water, with small farms and boat docks along the shore, and cafés and restaurants with terraces take advantage of the views. At Dumulmeori, an ancient tree stands beside the confluence, and the mist in the early morning gives the water a dreamlike look. A cycle path follows the old railway line along the Namhan river, and it is busy with cyclists on weekends, so watch for them at junctions and bends.

The riding is easy rather than thrilling. The road along the Paldang lake has moderate curves, plenty of traffic lights, and a steady stream of cars, particularly on weekend afternoons, when the whole of Seoul seems to head here for lunch. Midweek or early morning is a different place, with an empty road and a soft light. Spring brings cherry blossoms along the roadside, and autumn brings mist and colour. Speed cameras are frequent.

For practicalities, fuel is easily found in Hanam and Wabu, and the small towns along the lake. The local speciality is river fish stew and, in the cafés, a wide choice of coffee and pastries. Parking can be a problem at the most popular spots on weekends, so go early. A walk along the water for ten minutes is a pleasant way to rest before the next stretch.
Gwangju here is the Gyeonggi one, not the big southern city of the same name, and the confusion is a regular source of jokes in Korea. The pin sits in its hills, a few kilometres from the town, about halfway between Seongnam and Icheon, in rolling country of low wooded ridges, small reservoirs and scattered villages. The high point is a modest pass that a lorry takes in its stride, but for a rider leaving the city it feels like a first proper climb. In winter, there is ice on the shaded side.

The area has a place in ceramic history. During the Joseon dynasty, the royal court's white porcelain was fired in kilns around Gwangju, which were established in the fifteenth century and supplied the palace with its finest tableware for centuries. The clean white ware with its faint blue tint is one of Korea's best-loved craft forms, and the district still has potters and a ceramics museum. Nearby, a ski resort at Gonjiam brings crowds in winter, and the same roads that are empty in summer fill with cars carrying skis.

The roads are a mixture of wide, fast national routes and narrow, winding country lanes, and the best riding is on the latter, where they climb through forest and over small passes. Motorcycles cannot use expressways in Korea, so the national roads take the traffic, and they are busy with trucks. Avoid weekend afternoons if you can. Dawn rides are rewarded with mist in the valleys and a clear light on the ridges.

Fuel is easy: Gwangju and Icheon are large enough to have plenty of stations and restaurants, and Seongnam, a city of a million, is not far. Food is hearty, with rice dishes and stews, and Icheon is famed for its rice, which is served steamed in an iron pot. Carry a little cash for small restaurants, and keep your documents handy for police checkpoints, which do occur on some routes.
t.yangpyeong mountain roads@37.6,126.4:
Ganghwa has a west coast that most visitors miss. The pin lies on the western side of the island, a little south of its centre, where the land runs down to wide tidal flats and the sea retreats for kilometres at low water. The village roads are narrow and quiet, farms grow rice and ginseng and the famously good turnips, and the air smells of salt, mud and woodsmoke. It is a landscape that feels far from Seoul, though the capital is only an hour or so away.

Ganghwa's turnips, called sunmu, are a local pride, rounder and sweeter than ordinary ones, and they feature in the island's kimchi. Seafood is the other great asset. In the harbours, you can eat crab, clams and sea bass fresh from the boats, and at the beaches near Dongmak the evening sun sinks into the sea in a long, orange blaze. The tide here is among the greatest in the world, and the tidal flats are an important stopping place for migrating birds, including some rare waders.

The island's riding is calm. Dikes and coastal roads run for long distances with almost no traffic on weekdays, and the sea is always at the edge. There are few steep hills, but wind can be strong, and in summer, the heat on the exposed stretches is intense. At weekends, the main roads fill with cars from the city, so the quiet lanes are the better choice. The bridges to the mainland, Ganghwa and Chodae, are easy to use on a motorbike, and the toll is low or nonexistent.

For fuel, the island has stations in Ganghwa town and a few of the larger villages, but nothing in the quiet corners, so fill the tank before you go exploring. Simple restaurants serve seafood stews and grilled fish, usually with a large number of side dishes, and prices are modest. Cards are accepted in most places, but a little cash is helpful. If you can, time your visit for sunset, and stay until the last colour fades.
t.ganghwa island coastal ride@37.6,127.3:
Hwado sits on the north-eastern edge of Seoul's sprawl, where Namyangju's streets begin to run out and the hills close in. The pin lies a few kilometres from the town, among the roads that head up to the Bukhan river and the mountain country of Gapyeong. For a rider setting out on a day that will end on Ganghwa island in the far west, it is the start of a long arc, so fuel and food matter. Hwado and Wabu have plenty of both.

The area is known for furniture. Along a road in nearby Maseok, dozens of workshops and showrooms sell everything from plain pine tables to hand-carved chests, and the smell of sawdust and varnish hangs over the district. It is a small but telling sign of how the hills around Seoul have turned into a service area for the capital. Above the town, Cheonmasan rises in a wooded ridge popular with weekend hikers, and the old railway line along the river has become a cycle path.

The road north-east along the Bukhan, Route 46, is a classic Korean riding route. It passes through a series of small towns and riverside resorts on the way to Gapyeong and Chuncheon, with long views of the water and the hills. In Chuncheon, the local speciality is dakgalbi, spicy stir-fried chicken cooked on a hot plate, which draws visitors from Seoul. The road is busy at weekends, with heavy traffic and many cafés, but the scenery is good and the corners are pleasant.

Be aware of traffic. Weekends see long queues on this corridor, and the roads that carry motorbikes are the national routes, since motorcycles are banned from expressways. Start early, before seven, and you will be through the worst before the cars wake up. Fuel is easy at Hwado, and many stations offer help at the pump. Check your route and your tank before you leave, because the day ahead has many kilometres, and the tidal marshes of Ganghwa feel a long way off.
t.ganghwa island coastal ride scenic road@:
Between Gwangju and Icheon, the land of Gyeonggi turns from suburb to countryside, and the pin lies in this softer part of the map, in a landscape of rice paddies, reservoirs and low wooded hills. Seongnam and Seoul are less than an hour away, but the traffic thins, the villages are small and the fields are neat and flat in the valleys. The roads here are national and provincial routes that bend easily from village to village, and a ride along them has an unhurried, pastoral quality.

Icheon has a name that every Korean knows, and it comes from rice and ceramics. The local rice was once sent to the royal court, and it is still prized as the best in the country, with a slightly sticky, sweet quality that is served steamed in an iron pot. The town is also a major centre for pottery, with a village of kilns and workshops where modern potters work in traditional styles, and an annual ceramics festival in spring. There is a hot spring spa as well, which is a good place to ease tired shoulders after a day on the road.

For the ride, expect mixed conditions. Roads are generally good, with moderate bends and occasional heavy trucks, and the scenery varies from forest to farm. In autumn, the rice turns gold and the persimmon trees are loaded with orange fruit, and the colours are excellent. Spring brings blossom and a soft haze. Summer can be hot and humid, and winter is cold, with a risk of ice on the shaded bends.

Fuel and food are easy in Gwangju and Icheon, which have many stations and restaurants. Try the Icheon rice at a local restaurant, usually served with a spread of side dishes. A cash reserve is useful for village cafés that do not take cards. Be careful at crossings in the farm villages, where tractors and elderly pedestrians may appear. Remember that motorcycles are not allowed on expressways, so stick to the national roads.
t.ganghwa island coastal ride high point@3:
The pin lies in the countryside between Icheon and Yongin, a few kilometres from the border of Gwangju, in a landscape of low hills, reservoirs and farmland that fills the space between the Seoul metropolitan area and the southern provinces. The label calls it a high point, and the hills here do rise to a couple of hundred metres, enough for a view across paddy fields and plastic greenhouses to the next ridge. The land is hardworking, and few visitors stop, which is part of the charm.

This was farm country long before it was suburban. The Joseon dynasty's kings relied on the rice of this region, and the fruit orchards and greenhouses of the area still send produce to Seoul's markets. Strawberries, peaches and pears are the main crops, and in season, roadside stands sell them at modest prices. A few kilometres south, Anseong is known for its traditional performing troupe, the Namsadang, a travelling band of acrobats and musicians whose art is on UNESCO's intangible heritage list, and for a famous breed of beef cattle.

The roads here are mostly national routes and provincial lanes, with long straights and moderate curves. Because motorcycles cannot use expressways, they serve as the main routes, and truck traffic can be heavy near the industrial estates. The minor roads between the villages are quieter and more rewarding, with narrow bridges and little climbs, and the air smells of hay and fertiliser. Weekday mornings have the least traffic. In winter, watch for frost on bridges and in shaded sections.

Fuel is easy, with stations in Icheon, Osan and Gwangju, and small restaurants serve soup, noodles and grilled meat, often with unlimited side dishes.
