Carry a little cash for places that do not take cards. If you are riding at the end of a long day, be careful, as the country roads have few lights and farm vehicles move slowly. A stop for a hot drink from a vending machine or a café is a good idea, particularly in the cool months.
t.gyeongju@35.9,129.2:
For almost a thousand years, from 57 BC to AD 935 by the traditional count, Gyeongju was the capital of the Silla kingdom, and the city still behaves like a place that remembers it. The old centre is flat and green and quiet, with the great grass-covered burial mounds of Silla kings and queens rising among the houses and shops like a row of soft hills. Nothing in the city is allowed to climb too high, which keeps the skyline low and lets the mountains behind it stay visible.

The tombs are the signature. Daereungwon, the tumuli park, holds large mounds in rows, and one of them, Cheonmachong, the Heavenly Horse Tomb, can be entered, revealing the timber and stone layers of the construction and a display of gold crowns and ornaments. These crowns, slender and hung with jade, are among the finest of their age. Nearby the stone observatory Cheomseongdae, thought to date from the seventh century, stands in a field like a bottle, and Anapji, a pond with pavilions, is lit in the evenings and reflects the lights beautifully.

In the hills east of the city rise Bulguksa temple and the Seokguram grotto, built in the eighth century, with a granite Buddha gazing out toward the sea, and both are UNESCO sites. The road up Tohamsan to the grotto is narrow and winding, with fine views and a cool breeze, and it is a pleasant short ride, best before the tour buses arrive. Autumn brings red maples and ginkgo, and spring has cherry blossom in the park by Bomun Lake.

Gyeongju is also famous for Gyeongju bread, a small pastry filled with red bean paste, and for ssambap, rice with leaf wraps and a dozen side dishes. Fuel and meals are easy, and bike parking is straightforward outside the tomb area. Cycling is popular here, and rental shops line the streets, a sign of how gentle and walkable the town is. Spend a slow morning among the mounds and an unhurried evening by the pond.
t.busan@35.2,129.1:
Busan is Korea's great port, a long, steep city of more than three million squeezed between mountains and sea in the south-east corner of the peninsula. Container cranes line the harbour, ferries leave for Japan and fishing boats unload at Jagalchi market, where women in rubber aprons sell live octopus, eels and fish from tanks. The city has the energy and sharp tongue of a seaport, and its dialect is distinctly rougher than Seoul's.

It is also surprisingly beautiful. Haeundae beach, with towers behind it, fills with swimmers in summer, while on the other side of the city the Gamcheon culture village climbs a hillside in terraces of pastel houses. The Gwangandaegyo bridge, strung with lights, curves across the bay, and the Taejongdae park on the southern tip has cliffs, pines and a lighthouse. Busan also holds the UN Memorial Cemetery, where soldiers who died in the Korean War are buried, a moving place that takes an hour of quiet.

Riding here is mostly about the coast. The road from Busan northeast toward Ulsan and Gyeongju follows the shoreline, with views of fishing harbours and rocky bays, and the old petroglyphs of Bangudae near Ulsan, carved on a cliff above a river, are among the oldest depictions of whales and hunting in the world. Within the city, traffic is heavy and the many tunnels and bridges can confuse a navigator, so follow the lane markings. Speed cameras are plentiful. Typhoons strike in late summer.

Food is a main reason to go. Dwaeji gukbap, a pork and rice soup, is the local comfort dish, milmyeon is cold wheat noodles in tangy broth, and hotteok, sweet pancakes with nuts and syrup, are sold on the street. Fresh raw fish dinners by the sea are famed. Fuel is easy to find, and parking for bikes is available at many car parks. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with clear skies and moderate temperatures. Give yourself an evening at the harbour as the lights come on.
t.islands of the gulf of california@29.0,-:
There is no road here. The pin sits out on the water of the Gulf of California, a long narrow sea between the Baja peninsula and mainland Mexico, close to Isla Tiburón, the largest island in the country. This is a protected area, listed by UNESCO in 2005 as the Islands and Protected Areas of the Gulf of California, and its coastline is mostly empty cliff, cactus and sand. The ride attached to it is really a ride to the edge of it, and it makes sense to be clear about that.

Tiburón belongs, in a cultural sense, to the Seri people, the Comcaac, who have lived along this coast for centuries as fishers, hunters and gatherers, and whose territory faces the island across a narrow channel. Their basketry, woven from desert plants, and their carved ironwood animals are known well beyond the region. The island itself holds mule deer and a population of bighorn sheep, and its shores attract sea lions, pelicans and frigatebirds.

The sea around is the real wonder. The Gulf is rich in nutrients, and whales come to feed, including fin and blue whales and sometimes grey whales in the cooler months. Dolphins ride the bow waves of fishing boats. The water is warm, clear and green, and the desert comes right down to the shore, so you see saguaro cactus standing within sight of surf.

For a rider, the useful places lie on the mainland. Bahía de Kino, on the Sonora coast, sits in front of Tiburón and is reached by a long straight road from Hermosillo through desert flats and mesquite; the surface is usually decent, but the heat in summer can be extreme, and you should carry plenty of water and avoid the midday hours. Fuel is available in towns along the way, but stations can be far apart in remote stretches, so fill up whenever you can. Boat trips depend on permits and local operators, and some areas of the islands are off limits, so ask in town and respect the rules. Winter and spring are the kindest seasons here.
t.east sea coastal long day@37.4,126.8:
Incheon is a vast port city on the western coast of South Korea, with over two and a half million people, and the fuel gate sits on its eastern edge, close to Bucheon and the sprawl that links the city to Seoul. The two cities have grown together, and the landscape is a dense mix of apartment towers, factories, shopping streets and elevated roads. Petrol stations are plentiful, and at this hour the first challenge is to escape the traffic.

Incheon has a notable place in history. In September 1950, in the middle of the Korean War, General MacArthur ordered a bold amphibious landing here, and its success reversed the course of the war, pushing the North Korean army back and leading to the recapture of Seoul. A memorial park in the city commemorates the landing. The port was also one of the first to open to foreign trade in the 1880s, and the Chinatown near the harbour, the only official one in Korea, is a lively place famous for jjajangmyeon, noodles in a thick black bean sauce, which was invented here and is now a national dish.

The ride is named for the East Sea, the body of water on Korea's eastern side, which most of the world calls the Sea of Japan. To reach it, you have to cross the whole peninsula, passing over the Taebaek mountains, which is a long day. The first part of the route runs through the suburbs and along expressways, which are well maintained, with speed cameras everywhere and strict limits. Starting early helps avoid the rush hour, and many riders pick the quieter Sunday mornings.

Korean petrol stations are mostly full service and efficient, and many have small convenience stores. If you need a quick breakfast, a gimbap roll or a bowl of soup is cheap and filling.

Check your tyres, fill up and eat something. After the grey suburbs and the cranes of the harbour, the mountains will feel like a different country.
Yeongjong is a flat island off the coast of Incheon, in the Yellow Sea, and it is where Korea's main international airport stands. The coordinates here fall at the edge of the island, close to the tidal flats and the sea, and the label's high point is a joke of sorts: the landscape is flat, with just a few small hills. The tides on this coast are among the largest in the world, with a range of up to nine metres, so at low tide the sea retreats for a kilometre or more, leaving vast expanses of grey mud.

Those tidal flats are alive. Clams, crabs and mudskippers burrow in the mud, and thousands of migrating shorebirds stop here in spring and autumn on their journey between Australia and Siberia. People walk out to dig for clams, and seafood restaurants along the shore serve grilled shellfish and spicy noodles. The island is joined to the mainland by two long bridges, including the Incheon Bridge, over twenty kilometres long, which links the island to the new city of Songdo and sweeps across the bay in a pair of tall pylons.

The beaches on the island, such as Eurwangni, which is close to the airport, are a popular place to sit and watch the planes landing against the sunset, and there are plenty of cafes and restaurants. In summer the water is warm enough for a dip at high tide, but the mud and the strong currents mean you should be careful. Out of season, the beaches are wide, windy and almost empty.

For riders, it is a flat and easy place, with straight coastal roads, plenty of traffic and constant wind. The bridges have wind limits and may close in storms. Fuel is easy to find on the island and in Incheon, which is only ten kilometres away.

Take a break by the shore and watch the tide, then head back toward the city. The mudflats, with the light on the water, are strangely beautiful.
t.east sea coastal long day scenic road@37:
Yangju sits north of Seoul, in the hills that lead toward the border with North Korea, and the coordinates here are in a part of Gyeonggi province where the sprawl of the capital begins to thin out into valleys, farms and forest. To the south lies Bukhansan, the granite mountain park that rises above Seoul, and to the east the long peak of Dobongsan, nearly 740 metres high, with its sharp granite summits visible across the plain.

Uijeongbu, the larger city next door, has an unusual claim to fame. After the Korean War, when food was scarce, people near the American army bases made a stew from surplus ingredients, such as sausages, ham and canned beans, boiled with kimchi and noodles in a spicy broth. The dish, called budae jjigae, or army base stew, was invented here and has become a comfort food all over Korea. Several restaurants in Uijeongbu claim to serve the original.

The riding here is a mixture of busy highways and good mountain lanes. Route 3 runs north through Yangju, carrying heavy traffic, but side roads wind up into the hills, with bends and fine views over the valleys. The roads are generally well surfaced and signed, though the traffic cameras are everywhere and enforcement is strict, so keep to the limits. Military installations are common in this area, and photography near them may be restricted, so respect any signs.

Both Yangju and Uijeongbu have plenty of petrol stations and convenience stores, and you can eat well in the many roadside restaurants. In summer, the valleys with streams are popular with picnickers, who set up tents and cook meat on small grills, and it is a lively scene on weekends.

Autumn is superb in these hills, with maples turning red and yellow, and the air is crisp and clear. Start early, avoid the weekend crowds and enjoy the quiet back lanes.
t.east sea coastal long day@37.2,127.3:
Icheon is a city of nearly two hundred thousand people in the farming and ceramics country south-east of Seoul, and as a food stop it is hard to beat. The place is famous for its rice, which was grown for the royal court in the Joseon period, and the traditional way to eat it is a ssalbap jeongsik, a feast of rice cooked in a stone pot, served with dozens of small dishes of vegetables, fish and meat. The rice is sticky, fragrant and slightly sweet, and the scorched crust at the bottom of the pot is turned into a tea at the end of the meal.

Ceramics are the other tradition. For centuries Icheon has been a centre of pottery, and several villages have kilns, workshops and galleries where you can see potters at work and buy bowls, cups and vases. A ceramics festival is held in the spring, and attracts large crowds. The city also has hot springs, and the spa resorts and public baths are a fine way to relax after a long ride, with warm mineral water and steam rooms.

The surrounding country is gentle, with rice paddies, orchards and low hills, and the roads are well surfaced, with moderate traffic. It is not dramatic riding, but a pleasant, relaxed way to finish a long day, particularly in autumn, when the rice fields turn golden and the persimmons ripen. Spring brings pear and peach blossom, and the whole area is bright with colour.

Fuel is easy to find in the city, and in the larger villages, and there are many roadside restaurants, some of which serve food of excellent quality. A meal here can be surprisingly inexpensive, and the portions are large, so come hungry.

After a long journey from the East Sea, this is a fitting finish. Sit down, take off your helmet and let the dishes arrive one by one. You will have earned them.
t.ganghwa@37.6,127.3:
Hwado sits in the foothills of Mount Unjong, a mountain of around six hundred metres in the north of Namyangju, and the pin lands in the town, with the Han river a few kilometres to the south. Namyangju, to the south-east, is a large satellite city of Seoul, with a mix of apartments, farmland and woods. The town has a quiet, semi-rural feel, with vegetable fields and small restaurants strung along the roads.

The ride that ended here came from Ganghwa Island, and the last stretch passes through the green belt of the capital's north-east. The roads are narrow and winding in the hills, wider and busier along the main routes, with a surface that is generally good. Bends are frequent, and the views over the river valley are pleasant, especially in autumn, when maples and ginkgo trees turn red and yellow. Weekend traffic builds on the roads from Seoul, so a weekday or early start is better.

Namyangju has some famous names. Dasan Jeong Yak-yong, a great scholar of the late Joseon dynasty, was born here and wrote a vast body of work on government, science and agriculture, and his house and a memorial hall stand beside the river. Unjongsa, a Buddhist temple on the mountain, is known for its old trees and a bronze bell and for a rocky hillside with Buddha figures. The Han river, here wide and slow, has bike paths on both banks and views of wooded hills.

Fuel and food are easy, with stations along the main road and many restaurants. The valley is known for its duck and for traditional Korean dishes served in garden settings, and the cafes by the river have long terraces. A plate of grilled duck, with vegetables and rice, is a traditional meal, and the restaurants here keep long hours at weekends.

Take a walk beside the river if the light is good. The Han here is calm and wide, and the hills across the water are soft in the evening.
t.seoraksan@37.5,127.4:
Gonjiam is known for a ski resort and a horror film, but the pin lands a little to the south-east, in the rolling hills of Gwangju, Gyeonggi province, with the town of Docheok and the long lake of Paldang to the north. Yangpyeong is about ten kilometres to the north-east, and the city of Gwangju, about thirteen kilometres south-west, has about eighty thousand people. The valleys here are green, with small farms, orchards and pine woods on the slopes.

The road from here leads to Seoraksan, the mountain park on the east coast, and this is the first or last part of a weekend ride. The roads are winding and quiet in the hills, with bends, short climbs and wide views, and the surface is good. Autumn is the best season, when the leaves turn and the air is crisp, and winter has ice on the shaded roads. Traffic is light on weekdays, but on sunny weekends the lanes fill with cyclists and cars heading to restaurants.

This part of Gwangju has a lot of history. The Joseon kings drew their porcelain from kilns at Bunwon, in the Gwangju hills, and the royal ceramics produced there are among the finest in Korean art. A museum and kiln site near Gwangju tell the story. Nearby, Namhansanseong, a mountain fortress on the ridge, is a UNESCO site, with a long wall and gates, where King Injo took refuge during the Manchu invasion of 1636.

Fuel and food are easy enough, with stations in Gwangju and Docheok, and many restaurants in the valleys. The area is known for its country cooking, with stews, pancakes and grilled fish, often served in a traditional house with floor seating. A bowl of hot soup on a cool day is a joy.

Stop if you see a kiln chimney or a pottery sign. The craft here is old, and a bowl made by hand is a lasting souvenir.
t.seoraksan weekend@37.5,127.4:
Yangpyeong is a quiet county town east of Seoul, where the two arms of the Han River come together, and the confluence is one of the most beautiful spots in the region. At Dumulmeori, a name meaning two waters head, the North Han and the South Han merge into a broad, still stretch of water, with a famous old willow tree standing on the bank and wooden boats resting among the reeds. It is a favourite place for photographers, especially in the mist of early morning, and it appears in many Korean films and television dramas.

The county has a relaxed rural feel, with orchards, small farms, riverside cycle paths and mountains rising to the north and east. Yongmunsan, a mountain to the east, has a large old temple, Yongmunsa, with a ginkgo tree said to be well over a thousand years old, which turns a brilliant gold in October. Gwangju, the neighbouring city on the southern side, is smaller than its namesake in the south, but has a good number of restaurants and cafes by the water.

The ride to Seoraksan begins here, with a long run eastward along the river valley, past lakes and through hills, before climbing into the Taebaek mountains. The roads in this area are well surfaced, with moderate traffic and plenty of bends. Weekends are busy, as city dwellers head to the countryside, and the riverside roads fill with cyclists, so a weekday start is better. Speed cameras are frequent.

Yangpyeong has more than eighty thousand people, so fuel and convenience stores are easy to find. Local food includes mountain vegetables, grilled river fish and noodle soups, and several restaurants near the water have outdoor tables. A pot of hot tea at a riverside cafe is a calm way to begin the day.

The light on the river at dawn is soft and silvery, and the mist rises slowly. It is a good moment to leave the city behind and head for the mountains.
t.seoraksan weekend high point@37.1,127.1:
Osan is a city south of Seoul, in the middle of Gyeonggi province, with about a hundred and sixty thousand people, and it has a special place in the modern history of the country. On 5 July 1950, a few days after the North Korean invasion, a small American force known as Task Force Smith fought its first battle with the North Korean army near here, and a memorial now stands on the hill where they made their stand. It was the first engagement between American and North Korean troops, and it showed how unprepared the defenders were. A large American air base still lies on the edge of the city.

The label says high point, but the terrain is gently rolling, with low hills and farmland. On one of the hills stands the old fortress of Doksan, which was important in the Joseon period and the scene of a famous siege in the sixteenth century. The walls and a pavilion can still be visited, with good views over the surrounding plain. Anseong, to the south-east, is known for its traditional brassware, made by hand into bowls, and for the wandering performers called namsadang, who travelled from village to village with music, acrobatics and plays.

For riders, the roads here are mixed. Highways are busy and fast, with strict speed enforcement, but quieter local roads wind through the hills and fields, with farms, orchards and small villages. The surface is generally good, though narrow in places, and the bends are gentle. Autumn is a lovely time, with golden rice paddies and persimmons ripening on the trees.

There is plenty of fuel in Osan, as well as convenience stores, restaurants and cafes in every neighbourhood. Many serve classic Korean dishes such as bibimbap, stews and grilled meat, and portions are generous. Anseong has a number of restaurants specialising in beef.

It is an unpretentious place, but with some real history, and a good rest stop on a long run through Korea's central plain.
t.seoraksan weekend scenic road@37.1,126.9:
Hwaseong is a large and spread-out city on the western edge of Gyeonggi province, with an irregular coastline of tidal flats, small ports and farmland, and the coordinates sit inland, among the villages and fields south of the old walled city of Suwon. It is not a polished tourist area, but it holds some serious history. The royal tombs of Yungneung and Geolleung, listed by UNESCO among the Joseon royal tombs, lie in the wooded hills here. Yungneung is the tomb of Prince Sado and his wife, and Geolleung is that of King Jeongjo, Sado's son, who built the great fortress at Suwon.

The story of Prince Sado is one of the most dramatic in Korean history. He was the crown prince in the eighteenth century and was confined by his father in a wooden rice chest, where he died after eight days. His son, Jeongjo, later became king, and spent his reign honouring his father's memory, moving his tomb to this hillside and building the fortress at Suwon to protect it. The tombs stand peacefully among old pines, with stone figures of officials and animals.

The riding here is mixed. The main roads are busy with heavy traffic, trucks and commuters, and there are speed cameras at frequent intervals, but small roads thread through rice fields and orchards, and the coast has long, straight stretches beside the mud flats. Wind comes strongly off the Yellow Sea, and fog can settle on the plain in the early morning.

Hwaseong has nearly half a million people, so petrol stations and restaurants are easy to find, though they are spread across a large area. Seafood restaurants near the western ports serve grilled shellfish, raw fish and spicy fish stew. The area around Suwon, a short ride north, has more to see, including the fortress walls, which run for about five kilometres around the old city.

Take some time to visit the tombs, if you can. They are quiet, peaceful places, and they tell a story that every Korean child knows.
t.pocheon lake and forest photo pull off@3:
The coordinates here fall in the Yellow Sea, off the west coast of Korea, close to the border with North Korea, so the real place behind the label is the island of Ganghwa and the coast around it, some thirty kilometres away. The label talks about the lake and forest of Pocheon, which lies far to the east, but this point has nothing to do with it. This is the estuary of the Han River, where it meets the sea, a strip of tidal flats, marshes and low islands that forms part of the frontier.

Ganghwa has one of the richest histories in Korea. In the thirteenth century, when the Mongols invaded, the Goryeo court moved here and held out on the island for nearly forty years, thanks to the narrow, tidal channel that separated it from the mainland. The island has ancient dolmens, huge stone tombs from the Bronze Age, which are among the largest and best preserved in the country and are listed by UNESCO. Old temples, fortresses and a ginseng market add to the interest.

The coast of the island is a haven for birds, and the tidal flats are a feeding ground for migrating waders, including some endangered species. From a peace observatory on the north shore, you can look across the narrow water to North Korea, a strange experience on a clear day. Because of the border, the shoreline is lined with wire fences and watchtowers, and photography is restricted in places, so respect the signs.

The roads on the island are flat and quiet, with bridges linking it to the mainland, and farmland, rice fields and orchards. The traffic can be heavy at weekends, with day-trippers from Seoul, but weekdays are calm. Fuel is available in Ganghwa town and on the main roads, and many restaurants serve local specialities such as sweet potatoes and fresh seafood.

Pocheon, the place the ride is named for, is a mountain county with lakes, art galleries and rice wine, but this stop is a different thing: a quiet corner of the western coast, full of history.
t.yangpyeong@37.7,127.2:
Gwangneung is the forest of kings. The royal tomb of King Sejo, the seventh king of Joseon, and his queen lies on a wooded hillside in the northern part of Namyangju, and the surrounding forest, protected for more than five hundred years, is one of the best-preserved old woods in Korea. The pin lands in the same district, near Jinjeop, with the roads that lead north to Pocheon and the Korea National Arboretum close by.

The ride that ends here is the second part of a mountain tour, and the hills of Yangpyeong are not far to the east. The roads are winding and quiet, with bends through oak and hornbeam woods, and the surface is generally good, though patched in places. Traffic is light on weekdays, and the lanes between the villages are pleasant. In autumn, the red maples and golden ginkgoes draw crowds to the arboretum, so a weekday or early start is best.

The forest has an unusual status. Its trees, among them old hornbeams and oaks, shelter a wide range of wildlife, including the rare black woodpecker, and the whole area is a biosphere reserve. The royal tombs of the Joseon dynasty, including this one, are a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and they are laid out according to the geomantic principles of Korea, with a mountain behind and water in front. A stone path leads past the figures of civil officials, horses and sheep, which guard the tomb.

Fuel and food are available in Namyangju and Pocheon, and several restaurants stand along the roads, serving hearty country food. Pocheon is known for its makgeolli, a rice wine, and its galbi, grilled beef ribs. Cafes near the arboretum are open in the daytime.

Walk slowly beneath the trees if you stop. The quiet of the forest is the same silence that kings once demanded.
t.loreto@26.0,-111.3:
Loreto has a claim that no other town on the peninsula can match: in 1697 the Jesuit Juan María de Salvatierra founded the mission here, Nuestra Señora de Loreto, and it became the first permanent European settlement in the Californias. The town served as the capital of the whole region for decades, until the seat of government moved north, and the old mission church with its stone front still stands on a quiet street in the centre. Today it is a laid-back place of fourteen thousand people with a seafront promenade, a small harbour and a lot of fishing boats.

The setting does the rest of the work. Loreto looks east over the Sea of Cortez, and the islands of Isla Coronado and Carmen sit offshore inside a national marine park, so the water in front of town is flat and a deep blue in the mornings. Behind the town the Sierra de la Giganta rises in dry, jagged ridges, and a road leads up into the mountains to the old mission at San Javier, a stone church built in the eighteenth century, a good half-day detour if the bike and your nerves are up to the gravel.

On Highway 1 the stretch to reach Loreto from the north is memorable, running along the shore of Bahía Concepción with beaches below the road, then crossing dry hills and cactus flats. South of Loreto the road climbs through the mountains and descends toward Ciudad Constitución. Traffic is light, but lorries are slow and the shoulders are narrow, and animals do sometimes wander onto the tarmac, particularly at dusk. Ride in daylight.

Loreto has fuel at a Pemex in town and enough restaurants for any appetite, with seafood and tacos as the obvious choices. From June to October it is very hot and humid, and this is also hurricane season, so check the forecast. The cooler months from November to April are the best time, with warm days and pleasantly cool evenings, and an evening beer on the waterfront is the kind of thing that makes the long Baja miles feel entirely reasonable.
t.la roche en ardenne@50.2,5.6:
La Roche-en-Ardenne is a town of about four thousand folded into a tight loop of the Ourthe river, with the ruins of a medieval castle on a rock above the rooftops. The Ardennes here are not high, but they are steep: wooded ridges cut by deep, winding valleys, with fast clear rivers, slate roofs and stone farmhouses. The town was a tourist favourite long before the motorcycle, and it fills on summer weekends with riders from Belgium, the Netherlands and Germany, who come for the roads.

The town also has a heavy history. In December 1944, during the Battle of the Bulge, La Roche stood on a key road in the German offensive and was heavily bombed by the Allies, and much of the old centre was destroyed. It was rebuilt after the war, and a museum in the town tells the story. The castle above, which was a fortress in the Middle Ages, has been ruined for much longer, and a walk up gives a fine view over the loop of the river. Nearby, a number of memorials and tanks stand along the roads, remnants of the winter of 1944.

The roads from La Roche are the point. The N89 and its neighbours climb from the Ourthe valley over wooded plateaus and down again in series of bends, some tight and some wide, with a surface that is generally good but can be slippery with mud or leaves in the forest. The valleys fill with mist in the early morning, and by the afternoon on warm weekends the road is busy, so the quiet hours are the best. Be careful on the long downhill sections, where trucks or tractors sometimes appear, and in winter ice persists in shaded corners long after the sun has risen.

For food, the Ardennes are known for ham, smoked and dried in the old way, and for pâté de gibier, game pâté, along with boar and trout from the rivers. Local cafes serve Belgian beer with a plate of chips and mussels in season. The town has fuel stations, and Marche-en-Famenne, seventeen kilometres to the west, has more. Rendeux is a smaller village nearby on the Ourthe with a bridge and a riverside walk. Late spring and early autumn are the best times, when the forests are fresh or golden and the traffic is lighter.
t.jeonju@35.8,127.1:
Jeonju is the city that Koreans go to for food, and the reason has a name: bibimbap. The dish of rice, vegetables, egg and chili paste is made in many places, but Jeonju claims it as home, and the local version comes in a heavy brass bowl, with dozens of small side dishes, beautifully arranged. The city also has a tradition of makgeolli, the milky rice wine, served in some neighborhoods with a lavish table of snacks for the price of a single drink.

The Hanok Village, a district of more than seven hundred traditional houses with curved tile roofs, sits at the heart of the city, and wandering its narrow lanes is a pleasure, particularly in the evening when lanterns light up. Nearby stands Gyeonggijeon, a shrine that houses a portrait of Taejo, the founder of the Joseon dynasty, whose family came from Jeonju. The Pungnammun, a handsome old city gate, stands at the edge of the old town, and the city is known for its paper, hanji, still made by hand. A film festival in spring brings a younger crowd.

As the start of a mountain ride, Jeonju is a convenient point. The city lies on the Honam plain, with the long Jirisan range to the southeast, and expressways and national roads lead south through Namwon, a town linked to the folk tale of Chunhyang, toward Jirisan, Korea's first national park, whose highest peak, Cheonwangbong, is nearly two thousand meters. The roads over the mountain passes are among the best in the country, with long climbs, tight bends and sweeping views. They are closed or icy in winter, so spring to autumn is the season.

Jeonju is a big city with almost three-quarters of a million people, so fuel, food and hotels are everywhere. Traffic in the city is heavy, and the expressway exit onto the mountain roads is well signed. The best months are April, with cherry blossoms, and October, when the maples turn. Summer brings heat, monsoon rain in July and the risk of typhoons. Korean drivers can be aggressive, and motorcycles are restricted on some expressways, so plan your route to use the national roads, which are more pleasant anyway.
t.hadong@35.1,127.8:
Hadong, in South Gyeongsang's far western corner, is where Korean tea began, or so the story goes. In the ninth century, according to the old chronicles, an envoy named Daeryeom brought tea seeds back from Tang China, and King Heungdeok ordered them planted on the slopes of Jirisan, the great mountain that rises above the town. The wild tea terraces of Hwagae, in the hills north of Hadong, are still tended, and spring brings the first harvest, an event the area celebrates with a tea festival.

The Seomjin River, one of the cleanest in the country, runs through a broad, sunlit valley below, with white sand banks, pine groves and clam beds. The river is famous for its freshwater clams, served in soup, and for its spring cherry blossom: the road from Hwagae to the temple of Ssanggyesa, lined with thousands of cherry trees, is known as the ten-ri cherry blossom road, and in early April the petals fall like snow. Ssanggyesa, a temple in the mountain forest, is one of the oldest in the country, its stone paths shaded by tall trees.

The rider's interest is the mountain road. The roads through the Hwagae valley climb the slopes of Jirisan in a series of bends, with views over the river and farmland, and the road toward Gurye and Namwon passes through forested valleys. The surface is mostly good, but the roads are narrow, with guardrails and tight blind curves. At cherry-blossom time, traffic is heavy and slow, and on spring weekends the river road can be gridlocked. The park roads at high elevation are closed in winter.

Hadong has fuel and food, with Hwagae a village with a market of tea shops, restaurants and bakeries, while Gwangyang, about eighteen kilometers south, has the bigger supermarkets and stations. Novelist Park Kyung-ni set her epic novel Toji in the nearby village of Pyeongsa-ri, and the house used in the television drama is now a tourist site. The best months are April for blossom and tea, and October for the mountains' color, while the rainy season in July can cause landslides.
t.aschaffenburg@50.0,9.2:
Aschaffenburg stands where the river Main swings north out of Franconia and the forested ridges of the Spessart close in on the south bank. It is the north-western corner of Bavaria, and the Bavarians once nicknamed it their Nice for the mild climate that lets chestnuts and vines thrive. The sandstone is red, the river is broad and slow, and the town of sixty-eight thousand has the unhurried look of a place that has been pleasant for a long time.

The great building is Schloss Johannisburg, a huge red-sandstone palace built in the early seventeenth century for the archbishops of Mainz, who used the town as a second seat. Below it, along the river, King Ludwig I of Bavaria had the Pompejanum constructed in the nineteenth century, a full-scale replica of a Roman villa from Pompeii, because he adored classical Italy and could not be there often enough. Both are worth a short stop, and the gardens give a fine view over the water.

For riders, the real prize is the Spessart itself, one of Germany's largest unbroken forests, famous for its ancient oaks that once supplied the timber for Dutch shipyards. The country roads here wind in easy, flowing bends through beech and oak, climbing and dipping across valleys with half-timbered villages, and traffic is light on weekdays. There are old forest inns where you can sit under chestnut trees and order a schnitzel with a glass of local apple wine or beer. Sun-dappled and shaded in turn, the tarmac can stay damp after rain and leaves are slippery in autumn.

Fuel and food are easy in a town of this size. Several stations lie around the ring and along the Main. The town can be congested at commuter hours, since Frankfurt is just up the river, so ride out before eight or after six if you can.

Come in late spring or early autumn, when the forest is fresh or golden and the afternoons are still long enough for a loop through the trees and back to the river by evening.
t.wiesbaden@50.1,8.2:
Wiesbaden is a spa town that kept its manners. Its hot springs, around two dozen of them, rise at the foot of the Taunus and were prized by the Romans, who called the settlement Aquae Mattiacorum. In the nineteenth century the dukes of Nassau and then the Prussians made it one of Europe's fashionable bathing resorts, and the grand white facades and the stately Kurhaus, with its colonnade and casino, still hint at the days when Dostoevsky lost his money here at roulette.

Today Wiesbaden is the capital of Hesse and a city of almost three hundred thousand, with all the traffic that implies. Its best-loved quirk is the Nerobergbahn, a funicular opened in 1888 that runs on water: the descending car is filled with water ballast and pulls the other one up, and it is still working. At the top, the Greek Chapel's golden domes shine over the vineyards and the whole Rhine-Main valley lies below. The Russian church, built for a duchess from the czar's family, is another surprise.

For riding, the city sits between two good landscapes. North, the Taunus rises in beech forest with winding roads toward the Platte and Idstein, a region of smooth surfaces and long, flowing bends that is popular at weekends. West, the Rheingau opens along the river, where Riesling vineyards cover the south-facing slopes and small wine villages like Eltville and Rüdesheim sit under castle ruins. The river road is slow and scenic but busy with tour coaches and cyclists on sunny days.

Come in autumn if you can: the grape harvest colours the hills, the new wine appears, and the weekday roads are quiet. Summers can be warm and hazy in the valley. Winter is mild but wet.

Fuel stations are everywhere, including along the Rhine road. City centre parking is expensive, so leave the bike in a garage at the edge. Order a glass of Riesling with Handkäse, the local sour-milk cheese, to understand why the locals are so fond of their region.
t.maastricht@50.8,5.7:
Maastricht curls around the Meuse at the narrow waist of the Netherlands, closer to Belgium and Germany than to the rest of its own country. Locals sometimes joke that it feels more Burgundian than Dutch, and the evidence is on the plate and in the glass: vlaai, a fruit pie from Limburg, and cafes that stay lively long after midnight. It is the oldest city in the Netherlands, founded by the Romans as Trajectum ad Mosam, the crossing of the Meuse, and the stone bridge that replaced theirs still carries pedestrians.

History is layered here. The Basilica of Saint Servatius holds the relics of an early bishop, and the Basilica of Our Lady, Romanesque and calm, sits a short walk away. A medieval Dominican church has become one of the world's most photographed bookshops, with shelves climbing the nave. In 1992 the Maastricht Treaty, which created the European Union as we know it, was signed in the city. Under Sint Pietersberg, the hill to the south, old marl quarries form a labyrinth of tunnels that has sheltered both people and art in war.

Riding here is gentle but charming. The Netherlands is flat almost everywhere except this corner, where the land lifts into the Heuvelland, a rolling region of orchards and sunken lanes around Valkenburg. The Cauberg there is known to cycling fans from the Amstel Gold Race. The roads are narrow, tidy and well signed, and the bends are easy. Dutch police are strict and speed cameras are frequent, so keep the throttle polite and enjoy the view of half-timbered farms and fields of fruit.

From Maastricht you can slip across to the Belgian Ardennes or the German Eifel within an hour. Fuel is easy: the city is large and stations sit around the ring road and the motorway. In town, park in a garage and walk; the centre is a maze of one-way streets, and bikes can be tricky to park on cobbles.

The best months are May and September, when terraces are open and the hills are green.
t.arnhem@52.0,5.9:
Arnhem lies on the lower Rhine, with the green slopes of the Veluwe rising immediately to the north, and it is a city that most people know from a single week in September 1944. Operation Market Garden was meant to seize a string of bridges and speed the end of the war; the British First Airborne Division was dropped at Arnhem to hold the last of them, and for nine days a small force fought a hopeless battle against German armour. The film A Bridge Too Far made the story famous. The bridge there was later renamed after Colonel John Frost, who led the troops that held its northern end.

The history is easy to follow. In nearby Oosterbeek the Airborne Museum occupies the old Hartenstein hotel, which was the divisional headquarters, and the Airborne Cemetery has rows of white stones in the quiet. Every September, veterans and their families return for the commemoration, and the town fills with visitors.

For riding, the real treat is behind the city. The Veluwe is the largest forest and heath area in the Netherlands, and Hoge Veluwe National Park, a short run away, has deer, wild boar, purple heather in late summer, and the Kröller-Müller museum with a large collection of Van Gogh. The lanes through the woods are quiet and shaded, and the roads are well-surfaced, but the corners are gentle rather than exciting. Enforcement is serious in the Netherlands, and the limit on many forest roads is low, so ride slowly and enjoy the trees.

Weather swings from bright to showery within the hour, so pack a rain layer. The best months are May to early June and September. In midsummer cyclists multiply on the forest tracks.

Arnhem is big enough for every kind of fuel and food, and its university gives it a good selection of cafes. Park near the riverside and walk to the bridge if you want to stand where the story happened.
t.hongcheon@37.7,127.9:
Hongcheon sits in the heart of Gangwon Province, a county town of around seventy thousand people in a valley of the Hongcheon River, ringed by the first big mountains east of Seoul. About two hours from the capital by road, it serves as a gate to the hills, and for riders heading east to the coast it is the place to be sure your tank is full before the mountain roads begin. The town has plenty of fuel stations, convenience stores open all night, and restaurants that specialise in the local speciality, Hongcheon beef, which is raised in the cool uplands and is highly regarded for its marbling.

The surrounding landscape is steep and green, with forested ridges, terraced fields in the valleys, and clear streams running beside the road. Korea's mountains are often much steeper than their height suggests, and the road network follows the valleys closely, with a lot of curves and the occasional tunnel. Route 44 runs east from here toward Inje and the east coast, past the foothills of the Sorak range, a long and well-surfaced road that twists through the Gangwon ranges. Other routes lead off through Palbong Mountain and along the river, offering rewarding riding for those who like bends. The expressway from Seoul to Yangyang, with its long tunnels, has also cut journey times, and the old roads are now pleasantly quiet.

Culturally, the area is a rural heartland. Gangwon has long been known as a place of potato farmers, mountain herbs and, on the coast, fish. Chuncheon, twenty-four kilometres west, is famous for dakgalbi, spicy stir-fried chicken cooked at the table, and for its lakes. Hongcheon itself has its own pride in its produce, and in autumn, the roadsides have stalls selling chestnuts, apples and sweet potatoes.

The weather varies sharply with the seasons. Summers are hot and humid, with a rainy monsoon in July that can bring landslides and slick roads. Autumn is the best time, when the leaves turn in October and the air is crisp and clear. Winters are cold and snowy, and mountain roads may be icy and closed, so most riders stay home from December to March.

Traffic on Korean roads can be fast and sometimes aggressive, with speed cameras widespread, so watch the signs and keep to the limits. Convenience stores make an easy stop for hot drinks, noodles and snacks.
t.veluwe forest roads@52.1,5.8:
The forest here is the Veluwe, the biggest unbroken stretch of woodland, heath and drifting sand in the Netherlands, a raised plateau in the province of Gelderland that was pushed up by glaciers in the last ice age. It is odd to think of the flat country having a ridge at all, but the Veluwe rises to a hundred metres or so in places, and the roads wind between pines, oaks and beeches in a way that feels almost un-Dutch. The nearest villages are Otterlo, Harskamp and Wekerom, small and tidy, and the town of Ede is the bigger place with fuel and supermarkets about twelve kilometres away.

Nearby is the Hoge Veluwe National Park, which charges at the gate and is known for its free white bicycles. It contains the Kröller-Müller Museum, with one of the finest collections of Van Gogh's work in the world, and a sculpture garden in the woods. The museum was created by Helene Kröller-Müller and her husband Anton, who bought the surrounding land for hunting and then opened it to the public. Riders can park at the entrance and walk or cycle in, which is a pleasant change of pace.

The forest roads around the park are quiet and smooth, with a mixture of brick and asphalt, and cycle paths running alongside. Speed limits here are strictly enforced, and eighty kilometres per hour is the usual limit on roads outside built-up areas, with some sections lower. Cameras are common, and the police take noise seriously, so ride calmly and enjoy the forest rather than racing through it. The bends are gentle and long, not tight, and the pleasure is more about atmosphere than technical riding: golden light through pine trunks, heather in bloom in late summer, and a smell of resin and warm sand.

Wildlife is plentiful. Red deer, roe deer, wild boar and the mouflon, a wild sheep, live in the woods, and they cross roads at dawn and dusk. In autumn, the rutting season brings the bellowing of stags across the heath, which is quite a sound in the early light. Sand drifts, among the largest areas of inland dunes in western Europe, appear in clearings, and can blow onto the road in dry weather.

There is little in the way of services in the forest, so fill up and eat before you go. Otterlo has a few cafes and bakeries, and the museum has a cafe too.
t.deventer river@52.3,6.2:
Deventer is one of the oldest towns in the Netherlands, a Hanseatic city on the IJssel river that grew rich on trade in the Middle Ages and has kept its look. The river runs broad and slow beside the old harbour, with brick warehouses, churches and the long quay lined with cafes, and the centre is full of narrow lanes, towers and crooked gables. A town of nearly a hundred thousand people, it is large enough to have everything a rider needs, with fuel stations on the main roads and a good choice of places to eat in the old town.

The best-known local food is Deventer koek, a spiced gingerbread cake whose recipe goes back centuries, and which you can buy in bakeries and the old shops by the Brink, the main square. The square is also home to the Waag, the weigh house, a handsome medieval building with a tall tower, and the Bergkerk and Lebuinus church keep watch over the roofs. In the late Middle Ages, the town was a centre of learning and a home to the Modern Devotion movement, started by Geert Grote, whose ideas of simple, personal religion influenced writers like Thomas à Kempis. The town's old library, the Athenaeum, is among the oldest in the country.

On a motorbike, the town is better as a place to stop than to ride through. The centre has cobbles and one-way streets, and tram-like crowds of cyclists, so go slowly, and park on the edge or by the river. Out on the IJssel, the roads along the embankments are the thing, flat and quiet, with water and willows on one side and farmland on the other. The surface is mostly smooth asphalt, with sudden bends where the road follows the river.

The IJssel rises when meltwater and rain push the Rhine up, and the quay walls show it, with old flood marks and steps that lead straight into the water. Walking along them on a summer evening, you see why people love the place.

Come in late spring or early autumn for the best light, and a stop at one of the riverside terraces is a good way to end the day. Food ranges from pancakes to modern kitchens, and the gingerbread makes a fine souvenir.
t.ijssel dike roads@52.3,6.1:
Along the IJssel between Deventer and Zwolle, the road runs on top of the dike, with the river on one side and the low green polder on the other, and the whole of the Dutch relationship with water is laid out in a few kilometres. The IJssel is a branch of the Rhine that splits off near Arnhem and carries a good share of its water north to the old Zuiderzee, now the IJsselmeer. Along it lie wide floodplains, called uiterwaarden, where cattle graze in summer and where the river spreads out when it rises.

Riding on the dike is an easy business. The road is narrow, usually with a low speed limit, and it follows the river in long gentle curves, with the occasional sharp bend at a farm or a ferry landing. The surface can be uneven, and farm traffic, cyclists and walkers share the space, so take it calmly. From the top of the dike, you see over the floodplain to the river, with barges slowly passing, and on the other side to farms and red-roofed houses sheltering behind the embankment. On a clear day, the sky seems to take up three quarters of the view. Wind can be strong along the open stretches, and it is worth remembering that a headwind in the Netherlands feels like a personal insult.

The villages nearby, Olst and Epe among them, are small, and they have what you need. Olst has a ferry crossing, and Epe, in the woods on the edge of the Veluwe, is a larger town with fuel and supermarkets about six kilometres away. The river towns of Hattem and Zwolle, further north, are old fortified places, with city gates and canals, and Zwolle has the Hanseatic charm of its neighbour Deventer.

The history is the history of defence. For centuries, the people living along the river have fought the water, and the dikes are the result, each one higher than the last. In the winter of 1995, high water in the Rhine led to the evacuation of a quarter of a million people in the Netherlands, and the dikes held. Since then, the government has widened parts of the floodplain to give the river more room.

Spring and autumn are the best times to ride here, with mist on the water in the early morning and flocks of geese overhead. In summer, the dike gets crowded with cyclists, so choose a weekday.
t.high fens roads@50.5,6.1:
The High Fens, the Hautes Fagnes, are the great wet moorland of eastern Belgium, a high plateau of peat bogs, heather and stunted spruce that stretches toward Germany. It has a feeling unlike anywhere else in the Benelux, empty, windswept and slightly lunar. The highest point in Belgium, Signal de Botrange, stands here at 694 metres, which is not very high, but on a cold day with the wind blowing it feels more like the Scottish Highlands.

The fens themselves are a nature reserve, and the rules are strict. In many parts, walkers have to stay on boardwalks to protect the fragile peat, and the wooden planks wind out across the bog toward distant stands of birch. The area is home to black grouse, curlews and rare plants, including sundews, which catch insects, and cotton grass, which turns whole patches white in early summer. The bogs hold water like a sponge and, in a dry spell, they can burn, as they did in 2011, when a large fire swept across the plateau.

The roads that cross the fens are some of the best in the region. They run over the open plateau and down into river valleys through spruce forest, with long curves, short climbs, and views across the empty moor. The surface is mostly good, though frost heaves and potholes appear after winter. Wind is a constant, and can be strong on the open stretches. The weather changes quickly, with fog common in autumn and winter, and snow on the plateau well into spring.

Nearby is the world-famous racing circuit of Spa-Francorchamps, which hosts Formula One and motorbike races, and the old town of Spa, which gave its name to all spas, is only a short ride away. Malmedy, with its Carnival and its old abbey, lies to the south, and Eupen, with a German-speaking community, to the north. Language signs can switch from French to German in a few kilometres, which adds to the sense of crossing a border.

Malmedy and Jalhay both have stations, and the larger centres are Eupen and Verviers. Cafes and small restaurants in the villages offer waffles, hot chocolate and hearty Ardennes food, and on a cold day, they are very welcome.
t.monschau old town@50.6,6.2:
Monschau is a town squeezed into a narrow valley of the Rur river in the northern Eifel, so tightly that its half-timbered houses seem to lean over the water and over each other. It sits right on the German border, near Belgium's High Fens, and its steep roofs and dark slate walls give it a look straight from a fairy tale. A ruined castle stands on the hill above, and the main sights are small and close together, which makes the town easy to explore on foot.

The town grew rich in the eighteenth century from cloth, and the wealthy merchants built grand houses, the finest of which is the Red House, a clothier's mansion with a spectacular staircase. The old mustard mill, which still produces mustard in the traditional way, is another stop, and you can buy jars in several flavours. In the autumn, the smell of spices from the Printen bakers, who make a hard, spiced gingerbread, drifts along the lanes. Monschau also holds a lovely Christmas market, which draws large crowds, and a classical music festival in summer.

The roads in and out are the reason bikers come. From the Belgian side, the road crosses the High Fens, a wild plateau of heath and peat, and descends into the Rur valley in a series of bends. The B258 and B399 wind through forest and meadow, with good surfaces and attractive scenery, and the surrounding Eifel is a favourite for motorcycle tours. The roads are popular at weekends, and speed cameras and police checks are common, so keep to the limits and be considerate in the villages. Monschau's own streets are narrow and cobbled, and the centre is largely pedestrian, so park at the edge and walk in.

Nature is close at hand. The Rur valley is steep and wooded, and the High Fens nature reserve lies just across the border. The Eifel is old volcanic country, with crater lakes, called maars, to the south. Spring brings fresh green and abundant wildflowers, and autumn colour is excellent.

Food and drink is easy to find. There are cafes, bakeries and restaurants in the old town, and a slow lunch with a view of the river is a good idea. Fuel is available at Simmerath and Roetgen, a short distance away, but the village has little, so fill up beforehand. Weekends in summer and the Christmas season are busy, so arrive early.
t.eupen return roads@50.6,6.0:
Eupen is the capital of the German-speaking community in the east of Belgium, a small town of about eighteen thousand in the valley of the Vesdre, and a place where borders have moved more than once. For centuries it belonged to the Duchy of Limburg and then to Prussia, and only after the First World War, under the Treaty of Versailles, was it transferred to Belgium. People here speak German, and shop signs, church services and the local radio all use it, though French and Dutch are also heard. It is also the home of a well-known chocolate factory.

The pleasures of Eupen lie in what surrounds it. To the south, the Hautes Fagnes, or High Fens, rise to a wide plateau of peat bog, heather and stunted spruce. The highest point in Belgium, the Signal de Botrange, stands at six hundred and ninety-four metres, hardly an alp, but the landscape feels remote, with boardwalks over the moor, cotton grass in spring and mist most of the year. Parts of the fens are closed to motor traffic to protect the fragile habitat, and in dry spells there is a serious risk of peat fires, so follow the signs. To the east, the border town of Monschau, just across the line in Germany, is a gem of half-timbered houses.

Riding the return roads from the Eifel and the High Fens into Eupen is a joy at the end of a day. The road drops through forest and pasture, with wide curves, long views and a smooth surface, and the weather can change in minutes, from clear to fog to rain, so carry a waterproof. In autumn the beech woods are golden, and in winter frost and snow can lie on the heights when the valley is clear.

Fuel is easy in Eupen, with several stations and supermarkets, and the old town has cafes and bakeries serving waffles and heavy cakes. It is a convenient place to top up before the border.
t.aldan@58.6,125.4:
Aldan is a gold town. It began in the 1920s, when prospectors found rich deposits in the hills of southern Yakutia and thousands of people arrived in what became known as the Aldan gold rush, and it has been shaped by mining ever since. Today about twenty-four thousand people live here, in a mix of Soviet blocks, wooden houses and newer buildings, spread across a hilly site at the edge of the Aldan Highlands. The surrounding land is a patchwork of taiga, old mine workings and clear, cold rivers.

For a rider on the Lena Highway between Yakutsk and Neryungri, Aldan is a welcome stop with proper services. There are fuel stations, supermarkets, banks, restaurants and several hotels, and the town makes a good base for resting, repairing and stocking up. Smaller places along the road, such as Leninskiy and Lebedinyy, have fewer supplies, so fill up here. Local cafes serve filling Siberian food, including meat dumplings, soups and the Yakut speciality of frozen raw fish, though it is not for everyone.

The road itself is a long, demanding ribbon through the forest. The surface alternates between good asphalt and rough, broken sections, with gravel and mud in places, and gradients that are gentle but frequent. Bends are wide, and the main hazards are trucks, wildlife and weather, as rain and fog can arrive without warning. In winter, the cold is extreme and ice is common. June to September is the sensible window, with long light and mild temperatures.

The town's museum tells the story of the gold rush and the people who took part in it, and it is worth an hour if you have time. The hills around town are full of reminders, from piles of waste rock to rusting machinery, and some of the old workings are still active. Nature remains the greater presence, though, with larch forest running in every direction and the sky arching over the highlands. In the long evening light of summer, the hills glow gold, and it is easy to see why people once rushed to this spot.
t.fort site and civil settlement of ruckin:
East of Frankfurt, on the low ground where the Kinzig valley opens toward Hanau, the Romans pushed their frontier forward in the late first century AD. Rückingen, today a part of Erlensee, was the site of a fort with a civil settlement around it, part of the Wetterau section of the Upper German-Raetian Limes, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Limes here ran south toward the Main, and the forts guarded crossings and roads leading into the Roman province. As with most of the frontier in this area, there is little to see above ground, but the line of the Limes is marked and explained along cycle and walking routes.

The area is suburban and busy, crossed by motorways, railway lines and the flight paths of Frankfurt airport. It is not a place for scenic riding, but it is a good starting point for some excellent roads. To the north, the Vogelsberg, an old volcanic massif, offers winding roads through forests and meadows, and to the east, the Spessart is a large, quiet forest with twisting roads and small villages. The Saalburg, a reconstructed Roman fort in the Taunus, is the obvious next stop for anyone interested in the Limes, with a museum and reconstructed buildings.

Hanau, a few kilometres away, is the birthplace of the Brothers Grimm, and the German Fairy Tale Route begins there. A statue of the brothers stands in the market square. Its goldsmithing tradition is also old, and the town still has a school and museum devoted to the craft. The town was badly damaged in the Second World War, but the Philippsruhe palace and the old town of Steinheim survived.

Erlensee has fuel, shops and services. The Wetterau and Main-Kinzig area is known for apple wine, Ebbelwoi, served in ribbed glasses with hearty food like Handkäs mit Musik, a sour milk cheese with onions. Traffic is heavy around Hanau and Frankfurt, so ride early or at weekends, and expect speed cameras.
t.tongdosa temple@35.5,129.1:
Most Korean Buddhist temples have a statue of the Buddha in their main hall. Tongdosa does not. Instead, a window behind the altar looks out onto a stone stupa that is said to contain relics of the historical Buddha, brought back from China by the monk Jajang, who founded the temple in 646. That makes Tongdosa one of the Three Jewel Temples of Korea, representing the Buddha himself, alongside Haeinsa, representing the teaching, and Songgwangsa, the community of monks. It is part of the UNESCO-listed Sansa, Buddhist Mountain Monasteries in Korea, inscribed in 2018.

The temple lies at the foot of Yeongchuksan, a mountain north of Busan, and the approach is a long walk along a stream through pine forest, past stone inscriptions and small bridges. The temple complex is large, with dozens of halls, pavilions and hermitages, colourfully painted in the dancheong style, and a museum with Buddhist art. In spring, the plum blossoms in the courtyard are famous, and in autumn, the maples on the mountain turn red.

The area around is a mix of urban sprawl and mountains. Yangsan and Ulsan are industrial cities, while the Yeongnam Alps, a group of peaks over a thousand metres high, rise to the north-west, with winding roads, hiking trails and high grasslands that turn silver with silver grass in autumn. Riders should know that motorcycles are banned from Korean expressways, so you will use national roads, which are generally good but busy around the cities.

Fuel and food are easy to find in the towns. Temple food, vegetarian and simple, is offered at some temples, and Templestay programmes allow visitors to spend a night and join the monks' routine. Try bibimbap, Korean barbecue, and the seafood of Busan and Ulsan. Spring and autumn are the best times to visit, when the weather is mild and the colours spectacular.
t.dodong seowon@35.7,128.4:
The ginkgo tree in front of Dodong-seowon is over four hundred years old, a massive trunk with branches spreading wide, and in early November it turns a brilliant yellow and sheds its leaves into a golden carpet that photographers come from all over Korea to see. Behind it, the academy itself climbs a gentle slope in a series of courtyards and wooden halls, with a view over the Nakdong river. Dodong-seowon was founded in the sixteenth century to honour Kim Goeng-pil, a Neo-Confucian scholar executed in a political purge, and it is one of the nine Seowon, Korean Neo-Confucian Academies, inscribed on the UNESCO list in 2019.

Seowon were private academies where young men studied Confucian classics, prepared for state examinations and honoured the memory of great scholars with rituals. They were usually built in quiet places, close to nature, to encourage reflection. Dodong-seowon is known for its stone walls, decorated with patterns, and for the careful layout of its buildings, from the lecture hall to the shrine at the top.

The area is in Dalseong county, on the south-western edge of Daegu, a city of over two million. The countryside around is a mix of rice fields, orchards, hills and small villages, with the Nakdong river flowing south toward Busan. The river is lined with cycle paths, and the roads along it are pleasant, with little traffic. To the west, Gayasan, a mountain national park, is home to Haeinsa temple and the Tripitaka Koreana, a collection of more than eighty thousand wooden printing blocks, also on the UNESCO list.

Riders should note that motorcycles are banned on Korean expressways, so use national and local roads, which are generally good. Fuel and food are easy to find in Daegu and the towns around. Try the local specialities, such as makchang, grilled pork intestines, a Daegu favourite, and the apples for which the region is famous. Autumn is the best time to visit, for the ginkgo and the mild weather.
t.jangneung cluster@37.8,126.7:
North-west of Seoul, close to where the Imjin river flows into the Han and the demilitarised zone cuts the Korean peninsula in two, lies a royal tomb: Jangneung, the resting place of King Injo, who ruled Joseon in the seventeenth century, and his queen. Injo's reign was marked by invasions from the Manchu, and he was forced to humiliate himself before the Qing emperor in 1637, a defeat that still resonates in Korean memory. His tomb, like the other Royal Tombs of the Joseon Dynasty, inscribed on the UNESCO list in 2009, is a grassy mound on a hillside, guarded by stone figures of officials, warriors and animals, with a T-shaped shrine below.

The Joseon tombs were placed according to the principles of pungsu, Korean geomancy, with mountains behind and water in front, and their settings are peaceful, with pine forests and lawns. Jangneung is in Paju, a city that has grown rapidly in recent decades, with publishing towns, outlet malls and new housing, but the tomb area remains calm.

Paju is also the gateway to the DMZ. Imjingak, a park on the Imjin river, has memorials, a railway bridge and views toward the North, and tours to the Joint Security Area at Panmunjom and the infiltration tunnels start from here, though access depends on the security situation and requires booking. Munsan, twelve kilometres away, is the local centre, with fuel and services.

For riders, the roads north of Seoul are busy and urban, but they open up toward the DMZ, where military checkpoints and restricted areas limit where you can go. Motorcycles are not allowed on expressways. Ganghwa Island, to the west, is a good destination, with dolmens, fortresses and temples, and roads along the coast with views over the mudflats. Spring and autumn are the best times, when the weather is mild and the light clear.
t.piram seowon@35.3,126.8:
Piram-seowon sits on flat land among rice fields in Jangseong county, in South Jeolla province, its gates opening onto a courtyard with wooden pavilions and a shrine. It was founded in the late sixteenth century to honour Kim In-hu, a Neo-Confucian scholar from the region known for his integrity and his poetry, and it is one of the nine academies inscribed on the UNESCO list in 2019 as Seowon, Korean Neo-Confucian Academies. Unlike many seowon, which were closed by the government in the nineteenth century, Piram survived, and rituals are still held there.

The Jeolla region is the breadbasket of Korea, with vast rice fields and a reputation for the best food in the country. Gwangju, the regional capital, is less than an hour away, and it was the site of the 1980 uprising against military rule, now commemorated as a turning point in Korea's democratic history.

Nearby, Gochang has one of the largest concentrations of dolmens in the world, megalithic tombs from the first millennium BC, part of the UNESCO-listed Gochang, Hwasun and Ganghwa Dolmen Sites. Hundreds of them stand on a hillside, some huge, some small, in a landscape of fields and woods. Gochang also has a walled fortress, Gochang Eupseong, where women traditionally walk the walls with stones on their heads to ensure good health. Seonunsa, a temple in the mountains to the west, is famous for its camellias in spring.

The roads in this area are good, with gentle curves through rice fields, hills and forests, and little traffic outside the towns. Motorcycles are banned from expressways, so use national roads. Naejangsan national park, to the north, is famous for its autumn colours, which draw crowds in late October and early November. Yeonggwang, on the coast, is known for gulbi, salted and dried yellow croaker. Fuel and food are easy to find in Jangseong, Gochang and Gwangju.
t.dormagen@51.1,6.8:
Dormagen is not the sort of place that ends up on postcards, and it does not try to be. It is a working town of some sixty thousand on the left bank of the Rhine between Cologne and Düsseldorf, dominated on its northern side by a huge chemical park whose pipes and stacks glow at night. Yet the name itself comes from Roman times: Durnomagus was a fort on the Lower German Limes, the Rhine frontier that UNESCO listed in 2021, and a cavalry unit was stationed here to patrol the river and the road along it.

The remains are modest, largely buried under the town, with some foundations and finds displayed locally. But the riverbank tells the bigger story. For centuries the Rhine was a frontier, then a trade route, and then the backbone of German industry, and from the dykes here you can watch barges sliding past loaded with containers, coal and gravel. Just upstream, the walled town of Zons is the opposite of Dormagen's industrial face: a medieval customs town with towers, gates and a windmill, where the archbishops of Cologne once collected tolls from every ship that passed.

The riding is short and flat. Dyke roads and farm lanes along the Rhine meadows give easy cruising with river views, and a car ferry links Zons with Düsseldorf-Urdenbach across the Rhine, a pleasant way to avoid the city traffic. The region is dense with motorways, roundabouts and industrial estates, so plan your route around rush hours. For curves, head east into the Bergisches Land beyond the river, where the hills, valleys and dams begin almost immediately, or south into the Eifel for a full day out.

Dormagen has everything you need for fuel, food and parking. Zons is the nicer place for a break, with cafés in the old lanes and a sunny riverside terrace. If you are hungry, the Rhineland favourite is Himmel und Ääd, black pudding with mashed potato and apple, and a small glass of Kölsch from nearby Cologne goes with it nicely, ideally once the bike is parked for the night.
t.seosan getbol@37.5,126.6:
Korea's west coast has some of the largest tides on earth. Twice a day the Yellow Sea pulls back for kilometres, exposing vast shining mud flats, the getbol, laced with channels and alive with crabs, mudskippers, worms and shellfish. UNESCO has listed a series of these Korean tidal flats for their extraordinary biodiversity and for the millions of migratory shorebirds that stop here to feed on their way between Siberia and Australia. These coordinates sit at the edge of Incheon, where the great estuaries of the Han and its neighbours meet the sea.

Incheon is a city of millions, home to Korea's main airport and one of its biggest ports, and much of its coastline has been reclaimed from the mud over the decades. That makes the remaining flats all the more precious. When the tide is out, you might see people bent over the mud gathering clams, and when it comes back in, it moves frighteningly fast across the flat ground, so stay off unless you are with someone who knows the tides. Herons, egrets and spoonbills feed along the edges, and the sunsets over the Yellow Sea, with the mud reflecting the sky, can be extraordinary.

Riding here has one important rule: motorcycles are not allowed on Korean expressways, so you will be on national and local roads, which can be congested around Incheon and Seoul. Traffic is dense and fast, with delivery scooters darting between lanes and frequent speed cameras. The best riding is out on the coastal roads and islands linked by bridges, such as Ganghwa and Yeongjong, where traffic thins and the views open across the flats.

Fuel stations are everywhere, often with attendants, and payment by card is easy. Incheon's Chinatown, the oldest in Korea, is said to be the birthplace of jajangmyeon, noodles in black bean sauce, which makes for a fun stop. Along the coast, seafood restaurants serve grilled clams, raw fish and spicy fish stew. Spring and autumn bring the best weather and the bird migrations; summer is hot and wet with the monsoon, and winter can be bitterly cold.
t.beguinage de sint truiden@50.8,5.2:
At the edge of Sint-Truiden, a market town in the fruit country of Haspengouw, a ring of low brick houses surrounds a large grassy courtyard with trees and a Gothic church in the middle. This is the béguinage, one of the Flemish béguinages listed together by UNESCO, where for centuries communities of laywomen lived devout lives of prayer and work without taking permanent vows. It is one of the largest and best preserved in the region, and it has a calm, almost village-like feel.

Step into the church, now a museum, and you will find medieval wall paintings covering pillars and walls, with saints, angels and scenes from the Bible, many of them remarkably vivid. Nearby is the Festraets Studio, home of a monumental astronomical clock built by a local clockmaker in the twentieth century, with dials and mechanisms that fascinate anyone who likes machines. The town itself grew up around a Benedictine abbey founded in the seventh century by Saint Trudo, and its skyline of towers, including the abbey tower and the belfry on the market square, rises over a flat landscape of orchards.

Haspengouw is famous for its fruit, especially apples, pears and cherries, and in April the whole region turns white and pink with blossom, a spectacle that draws visitors from all over Belgium. The roads here are generally gentle, rolling through orchards, farmland and small villages with castle farms and chapels. They are narrow and often shared with tractors, cyclists and the occasional heavy truck loaded with fruit. Wind can be strong on the open plateau, and autumn brings mud on the roads from harvest machinery.

Sint-Truiden has more than thirty-five thousand people and all the fuel, food and parking you need. The town square, one of the largest in Belgium, is lined with cafés and restaurants. Look for local fruit products, including stroop, a thick syrup made from apples and pears, delicious on bread, as well as fruit tarts and cider. In spring, plan a loop through the orchards when the blossom is at its peak.
t.watchtowers wp 3 45 to 3 52 including th:
High in the Taunus hills northwest of Frankfurt, the Upper German Limes runs along the main ridge, and here, between Glashütten and Schmitten, a series of watchtower sites and the remains of a small fort follow the frontier through dense beech and spruce forest. The bank and ditch of the Limes are still clearly visible, winding over the hills like a long scar, and the area is part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire World Heritage site. Nearby, on the Kleiner Feldberg, lie the remains of a Roman fort, and a few kilometres east, the Saalburg near Bad Homburg is a fully reconstructed fort with a museum, the best place in Germany to imagine life on the frontier.

The real draw for motorcyclists, though, is the Großer Feldberg, the highest point in the Taunus at 881 metres, which rises just to the east. Its summit, with a tower, a viewing platform and a few kiosks, has long been a gathering point for riders from the whole Rhine-Main region, and on a sunny weekend the car park is full of bikes of every kind. From the top, on a clear day, you can see the skyline of Frankfurt, the Rhine valley and the Odenwald.

The roads that climb to the Feldberg and cross the Taunus are among the most popular in the area, with flowing bends, hairpins and steep climbs through the forest. Their popularity has a downside: heavy weekend traffic, frequent police checks and speed limits, and over the years some stretches have seen extra restrictions aimed at motorcycles because of noise and accidents. Ride with care and consideration, especially in the villages. In winter, the high Taunus can be snowy and icy.

Glashütten and Schmitten are small towns with fuel and some services, and Königstein, with its castle ruin and elegant villas, has more choice. The Feldberg summit offers snacks and drinks, and the villages of the Taunus have traditional inns serving Hessian specialities like Handkäse mit Musik, a sour milk cheese marinated in vinegar and onions, and Grüne Soße, a cold herb sauce served with eggs and potatoes, especially in spring.
t.neuss koenenlager@51.2,6.7:
On the southern edge of Neuss, in a residential area near the Rhine, lies one of the most important Roman military sites in Germany, though you would hardly know it from the surface. This was Novaesium, a legionary fortress that housed thousands of soldiers for much of the first century, and it is known as the Koenenlager after Constantin Koenen, the local archaeologist who excavated it systematically in the late nineteenth century. His work revealed the layout of an entire legionary camp, with headquarters, barracks, granaries and a hospital, and it became a model for Roman military archaeology. The site is part of the Lower German Limes, listed by UNESCO in 2021.

Today most of the fortress lies under houses and gardens, with a few information boards and markers, but the Clemens Sels Museum in the town centre displays finds from the excavations, including weapons, pottery and jewellery. Neuss itself is one of the oldest cities in Germany, founded in Roman times, and its old town has a Romanesque basilica dedicated to St Quirinus, a fine market square and remnants of medieval walls. The Rhine harbour, one of the largest inland ports in Europe, keeps the town busy.

Riding around Neuss means dealing with urban traffic, motorways and industrial areas, as it sits right across the river from Düsseldorf in one of the most densely populated parts of Germany. Speed cameras are frequent, and traffic jams are common at rush hours. Still, the Rhine meadows offer pleasant, flat riding along the dykes and through villages, and the area south towards Dormagen and Zons has quiet lanes. For hills and curves, head into the Bergisches Land on the other side of the Rhine or to the Eifel for a longer day out.

Neuss has everything a rider needs in the way of pumps and places to eat. The local brewery tradition includes Altbier, a dark top-fermented beer also brewed in Düsseldorf, served in small glasses. Try a Rhenish speciality such as Sauerbraten, marinated pot roast with red cabbage and potato dumplings, or a snack of Halve Hahn, a rye roll with a thick slice of cheese, which despite its name contains no chicken at all.
t.watchtower wp 3 4@50.2,8.1:
