In the western Taunus, between Bad Schwalbach and Taunusstein, the forest is thick and the hills roll gently, and the Upper German Limes runs along the ridge here as a still visible bank and ditch. The site labelled Watchtower WP 3/4 is one of the many small posts along this section, and a few kilometres to the east, near Taunusstein-Orlen, the fort of Zugmantel guarded a crossing of the frontier on an old trade route into Germanic territory. These remains are part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire World Heritage site, and a walk along the Limes trail through the forest here is peaceful and atmospheric.

Bad Schwalbach, a few kilometres away, was once one of the most fashionable spa towns in Germany, visited by aristocrats and royalty who came to drink its iron-rich waters. Its spa park, elegant bath houses and old hotels still give it a nineteenth-century air. Nearby Schlangenbad, which takes its name from the harmless Aesculapian snakes that live in its woods, is another historic spa. To the south, the hills drop towards the Rheingau, one of Germany's most famous wine regions, with vineyards stretching down to the Rhine.

For riders, the area offers a rich network of quiet roads. The Bäderstraße, the historic spa road, links Bad Schwalbach and the other spa towns with Wiesbaden and the Rhine, with long sweeping sections through forest and valleys. Smaller roads wind through the Aar valley and over the hills, with good surfaces and little traffic. Roads descending to the Rhine through the Wisper valley and towards Lorch on the river are especially enjoyable, with tight bends and wooded slopes. Beware of wildlife at dusk and wet leaves in autumn.

Bad Schwalbach and Taunusstein both have fuel stations, cafés and restaurants. The Rheingau, a short ride south, is perfect for a meal and a glass of Riesling, ideally at one of the seasonal wine taverns, the Straußwirtschaften, which open only for a few weeks each year. Try Rheingauer Spundekäs, a creamy cheese dip with pretzels, or a plate of local game in autumn.
t.kleve reichswald east@51.8,6.1:
South of Kleve, near the Dutch border, the Reichswald is one of the largest forests in the Lower Rhine region, a mix of oak, beech and pine on a low ridge of sand and gravel left behind by the glaciers of the Ice Age. On its edge, the Romans built military installations as part of the Lower German Limes, the frontier along the Rhine, and the remains in the Reichswald, including traces of camps, are part of the World Heritage site listed by UNESCO in 2021. There is little to see above ground, but the forest itself is a quiet, beautiful place to walk.

The Reichswald also bears the scars of a much more recent conflict. In February 1945, the Allies launched Operation Veritable through this forest to clear the way to the Rhine, and the fighting was brutal, in mud, flooded fields and dense woods. The Reichswald Forest War Cemetery, the largest Commonwealth war cemetery in Germany, contains the graves of thousands of soldiers, mostly British and Canadian, and it is a deeply moving place to visit. Kleve itself was heavily damaged in the war and has since been rebuilt around its castle, the Schwanenburg, which according to legend was where Lohengrin, the swan knight, arrived on the river.

Riding in this corner of Germany is mostly flat and gentle, with long straight roads through farmland, villages and forest, and dyke roads along the Rhine with wide views across the river meadows. Wind can be strong, and fog is common in autumn and winter. The roads are generally in good condition, and traffic is light outside the towns. It is easy to cross into the Netherlands, where roads are well marked and often have separate cycle lanes, and the Dutch town of Nijmegen, one of the oldest in the country, is just a short ride away.

Kleve, with around fifty thousand people, covers fuel and food without fuss. On the plate, expect Lower Rhine comfort: Reibekuchen, potato pancakes with apple sauce, and asparagus in season. The Schwanenburg has a museum and a tower with views across the flat land to the Netherlands.
t.marisan tumuli@35.3,128.4:
In Haman county, in the south of Korea, a long ridge rises above the town of Gaya, and along its crest lies a line of large burial mounds, grassy domes that seem to ripple across the hills. These are the Malisan, or Marisan, tumuli, the royal tombs of Ara Gaya, one of the states of the Gaya confederacy that flourished in the south of the Korean peninsula from roughly the first to the sixth century. In 2023, they were listed by UNESCO together with other Gaya tumuli across the region.

Gaya was a confederation of small kingdoms, famous for its ironwork and trade with China and Japan, before it was absorbed by the kingdom of Silla in the sixth century. Excavations in the tombs have revealed iron armour, weapons, horse gear and pottery, as well as evidence of human sacrifice, and a museum at the foot of the ridge displays many of the finds. A path runs along the crest among the mounds, with views across the town and the surrounding rice fields, and it is especially beautiful at sunset, when the low light picks out the shapes of the tombs.

Riding in Korea means avoiding expressways, which are closed to motorcycles, and using national and local roads, which are generally in good condition but can be busy around towns. The countryside around Haman is a mix of rice paddies, greenhouses, forested hills and small towns, with gentle curves and occasional climbs. The coastal areas to the south, around Changwon, Tongyeong and Namhae, offer more scenic roads, with islands, bridges and views of the sea.

The town of Gaya in Haman has fuel, shops and restaurants, and larger cities like Changwon and Jinju are within easy reach. Korean food is a highlight: try bibimbap, a mixed rice dish with vegetables and egg, or a meal of grilled pork belly with side dishes, the banchan, which always arrive in generous numbers. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, while summers are hot and humid and winters cold.
t.mireuksa temple site@36.0,127.0:
On a wide plain near Iksan, in the south-west of Korea, a large stone pagoda stands beneath a mountain, slightly incomplete and all the more striking for it. This is the west pagoda of Mireuksa, once the largest Buddhist temple of the Baekje kingdom, founded in the early seventh century by King Mu. The pagoda is the oldest and largest surviving stone pagoda in Korea, and after decades of collapse and a cement repair in the early twentieth century, it was carefully dismantled and restored in a project that took around twenty years, finishing in 2019. The temple site is part of the Baekje Historic Areas, listed by UNESCO in 2015.

According to legend, King Mu, as a young man known as Seodong, won the hand of Princess Seonhwa of the rival kingdom of Silla with a cunning song, and the temple was built at her request after the couple saw a vision of the Maitreya Buddha emerging from a pond. During the restoration, however, an inscription was found in the pagoda that named a different queen as the donor, adding a twist to the story. A reconstructed east pagoda and a museum displaying finds, including gold reliquaries, complete the site.

The riding around Iksan is easy, with flat to rolling roads through rice paddies, farmland and small towns. Motorcycles are not allowed on Korean expressways, so the national routes do the work here; they are well kept, if crowded near the cities. Further afield, the mountains of Jirisan and Deogyusan national parks offer more challenging and scenic roads, and the coast to the west has tidal flats and islands.

Iksan, a city of over a quarter of a million people, has plenty of fuel, shops and restaurants. Jeolla province, where Iksan lies, is famous throughout Korea for its food, with generous spreads of side dishes and dishes like Jeonju bibimbap from the nearby city of Jeonju. Visit the temple site in the late afternoon, when the light warms the stone and the mountain behind turns blue.
t.heolleung cluster@37.5,127.1:
In the south of Seoul, wedged between highways, apartment towers and the Daemosan hills, a forest of oak and pine hides two royal tombs of the Joseon dynasty. Heolleung is the tomb of King Taejong, the third king of Joseon, who ruled in the early fifteenth century, and his queen Wongyeong, and nearby lies Inneung, the tomb of King Sunjo and his queen from the nineteenth century. Together they form one of the clusters of the Royal Tombs of the Joseon Dynasty, listed by UNESCO in 2009.

The Joseon royal tombs follow a strict layout, shaped by Confucian ritual and the principles of geomancy. A path of stone leads from a red gate to a T-shaped shrine where rituals were performed, and behind it, on a slope, the burial mound is guarded by stone statues of officials, warriors, horses, sheep and tigers. Taejong, the father of King Sejong, who created the Korean alphabet, was a ruthless and effective ruler who consolidated the young dynasty, and his tomb is one of the grandest. The forest around the tombs is a quiet refuge from the city, with walking trails, birdsong and, in autumn, glowing red and yellow leaves.

Riding in Seoul is not for the faint-hearted. Traffic is dense and fast, with delivery scooters weaving everywhere, and motorcycles are banned from expressways and from the city's motor-vehicle-only urban highways, including the fast riverside roads along the Han. Navigation can be complex, and parking is tight. Outside the city, the mountains and valleys of Gyeonggi and Gangwon provinces offer much better riding, with curvy roads through forests and along rivers, reachable on national roads.

Seongnam and the surrounding districts have plenty of fuel stations, shops and restaurants. Korean food is everywhere, from simple noodle shops to barbecue restaurants where you grill meat at the table. Try naengmyeon, cold buckwheat noodles in a tangy broth, perfect on a hot summer day, or a steaming bowl of samgyetang, chicken soup with ginseng, said to restore energy. Visit the tombs in the early morning or late afternoon, when the light filters through the trees and the crowds are small.
t.dosan seowon@36.7,128.8:
If you have handled a Korean thousand-won note, you have already seen Dosan Seowon. The building on the back of the note is this Confucian academy, and the scholar on the front is Yi Hwang, known by his pen name Toegye, one of the most influential Neo-Confucian thinkers of Korea. He set up a small study hall here in the sixteenth century, on a quiet slope above the Nakdong river, and after his death in 1570 his disciples expanded it into a full academy, a seowon, where students came to study the classics and honour his memory. It is one of the nine Korean Confucian academies listed by UNESCO in 2019.

The academy is a group of simple wooden buildings arranged on terraces, with lecture halls, dormitories, a library and a shrine, surrounded by trees and gardens. The setting is peaceful and beautiful, with views over the river, which has been widened into the Andong Dam reservoir. Across the water, on a small island, stands a pavilion marking the site where a special state examination was held in Toegye's honour in the eighteenth century.

The riding around Andong is varied and enjoyable. The roads follow the river valleys and climb over low mountains, with gentle bends, good surfaces and light traffic outside the cities. The countryside is green and wooded, with rice fields, orchards and traditional villages. The Hahoe Folk Village, also on the UNESCO list, lies to the west of Andong, a traditional village of tile-roofed and thatched houses in a bend of the Nakdong river, famous for its mask dance drama.

Andong, about twenty kilometres away, is a city of more than a hundred thousand people, with fuel, shops and restaurants. It is known as the capital of Korean spiritual culture, and its food is distinctive: Andong jjimdak, a braised chicken dish with noodles and vegetables in a sweet and spicy sauce, and Andong soju, a strong traditional spirit with a long history. The summers in Korea are hot and humid, with the monsoon rains in July, and winters are cold. Spring, with cherry blossoms, and autumn, with brilliant colours, are the best seasons for riding.
t.arnhem meinerswijk@52.0,5.9:
The Rhine has always been a frontier here. In Roman times, the Lower Rhine marked the northern edge of the empire, and the Romans built a chain of forts, watchtowers and roads along its banks to guard it. At Meinerswijk, on the southern bank of the river opposite Arnhem, the remains of one of those forts lie buried in the floodplain. It is part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire, Lower German Limes, listed by UNESCO in 2021. There is little to see on the surface, but the floodplain itself, a wide expanse of meadows, ponds and willows, is a pleasant place to walk, and markers explain the history.

The Rhine was a frontier again in 1944, during Operation Market Garden, when Allied paratroopers tried to seize the bridges over the rivers of the Netherlands to open a route into Germany. British airborne troops reached the road bridge at Arnhem, just across the river from Meinerswijk, and held it for several days against fierce German attacks before being overwhelmed. The bridge, rebuilt after the war, is now named after John Frost, the officer who led its defence. In Oosterbeek, a few kilometres to the west, the Airborne Museum and the war cemetery tell the story of the battle.

Riding in the Netherlands is flat and orderly, with good roads, clear signs and plenty of cyclists, who have priority in many situations. North of Arnhem lies the Veluwe, a large area of forest, heathland and sand dunes, with quiet roads winding through the trees and the Hoge Veluwe National Park, home to the Kröller-Müller Museum and its collection of paintings by Van Gogh. To the south, the river landscape between the Rhine and the Waal offers roads along the dykes, with wide views over the water and the meadows.

Arnhem is a city of more than a hundred and fifty thousand people, with fuel, shops and restaurants. The floodplain at Meinerswijk can flood in winter and spring, when the river is high, so paths may be closed. The weather is mild and often damp, with wind blowing across the flat land, and the light in the evening, over the river and the meadows, can be beautiful.
t.fort along the pampus@52.4,5.1:
Out in the open water of the IJmeer, a few kilometres off the old fortified town of Muiden, a low circular fortress sits on an artificial island. This is Pampus, one of more than forty forts that make up the Defence Line of Amsterdam, a ring of fortifications built around the city in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. The idea was simple and very Dutch: in case of attack, large areas of land around the city would be flooded to a depth that was too shallow for boats and too deep for soldiers to wade, and the forts would guard the roads, railways and dykes that crossed the flooded zone. Pampus guarded the approach to Amsterdam by water. The line was listed by UNESCO in 1996.

The fortress was never tested in battle, and by the time it was finished, advances in artillery and aviation had already made it obsolete. Today it is a museum, reached by ferry from Muiden, with exhibitions, tours and a restaurant, and the walk around the island gives fine views over the water and the skyline of Amsterdam in the distance.

Muiden itself is a charming little town, with a busy harbour full of sailing boats, and the Muiderslot, a moated castle from the thirteenth century, one of the best-preserved in the Netherlands. In the seventeenth century it was the home of the poet and historian P.C. Hooft, who gathered a circle of writers, artists and scholars there, known as the Muiderkring.

For riding, the area offers a mix of busy motorways and quiet dyke roads. The roads along the IJmeer and the Vecht river are pleasant, with views over the water and the meadows, and the Vecht, lined with grand country houses built by wealthy Amsterdam merchants, is especially beautiful. Weesp, a fortified town with canals and windmills, is a few kilometres away, and the area around Naarden, with its star-shaped fortress, is another fine destination. Muiden has fuel, shops and restaurants, and the ferry to Pampus runs on a seasonal timetable worth checking in advance. The weather can be windy on the water, and crossings may be cancelled in rough conditions.
t.watchtower wp 1 64@50.4,7.7:
Höhr-Grenzhausen smells of clay and fire. The town, in the Westerwald hills north east of Koblenz, is the heart of the Kannenbäckerland, the jug-bakers' land, where potters have been making salt-glazed stoneware for centuries, with its characteristic grey body and cobalt blue decoration. Westerwald stoneware jugs, mugs and pots were exported across Europe and beyond, and the craft is still alive today, with workshops, a ceramics museum and a college for ceramic design. The Roman frontier ran right past the town, and the site of watchtower WP 1/64, near Höhr-Grenzhausen, is one of the many traces of the Upper German Limes, part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire World Heritage Site.

The Limes began on the Rhine at Rheinbrohl, a short distance to the north west, and ran south east through the hills, a line of watchtowers, forts and a palisade with a ditch behind it. The watchtowers were spaced within sight of each other, so that signals could be passed along the frontier, and the remains of some have been excavated and marked, while others survive only as low mounds in the forest. A walking trail, the Limeswanderweg, follows the line of the frontier through the hills.

The Westerwald is a rolling upland of forests, meadows, small villages and lakes, cut by deep valleys that run down to the Rhine and the Lahn. The riding is enjoyable, with quiet roads winding through the hills, plenty of bends and occasional steep climbs and descents. The surfaces are generally good, and traffic is light outside the towns. To the south, the valley of the Lahn offers a beautiful ride, with the river winding between wooded slopes, castles and old towns, and to the west, the Rhine gorge, with its castles and vineyards, is one of the great rides of Germany, though the roads along the river can be busy.

Höhr-Grenzhausen, a town of nearly ten thousand people, has fuel, shops and restaurants, and the ceramics shops are well worth a look, though a large jug is awkward to carry on a bike. Koblenz, at the meeting of the Rhine and the Moselle, is a short ride away, with everything you could need. The weather in the Westerwald is cooler and wetter than in the river valleys, with fog in autumn and snow in winter.
t.kottenforst nord domhecken 5@50.7,7.0:
Between Bonn and the Eifel lies the Kottenforst, a broad, flat forest of oak, beech and hornbeam on the plateau of the Ville, once a hunting ground of the Electors of Cologne, who laid out long straight rides through the trees for their stag hunts. Hidden in the woods are the faint outlines of Roman camps, earthworks left by soldiers who trained or camped here when Bonn, then called Bonna, was the base of a Roman legion on the Rhine frontier. The site at Domhecken, in the northern part of the forest, is one of the components of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire, Lower German Limes, listed by UNESCO in 2021. Like many such sites, it is subtle, a low bank and ditch among the trees, but it adds a layer of history to a walk or a ride through the forest.

The Romans left another, more visible mark on this region: the Eifel aqueduct, one of the longest in the Roman world, which carried water from springs in the Eifel hills to Cologne, a distance of nearly a hundred kilometres. Sections of the aqueduct can still be seen in several places, and the hard lime deposits that formed inside it were later quarried and used as a kind of artificial marble in churches across the Rhineland. At Iversheim, to the south, the remains of Roman lime kilns have been excavated and can be visited.

The riding around the Kottenforst is gentle, with roads crossing the forest and running through the farmland and villages of the Vorgebirge, the foothills between Bonn and Cologne, known for fruit and vegetable growing. The roads are good but can be busy, especially near Bonn and the motorways. To the south, the Eifel offers some of the best riding in Germany, with winding roads through volcanic hills, crater lakes and valleys, and the famous Nürburgring racetrack, which is open to the public on certain days for laps of the Nordschleife, a legendary and demanding circuit.

Alfter, about four kilometres away, and Bornheim are small towns with fuel and shops, and Bonn, the former capital of West Germany and the birthplace of Beethoven, is a lively city with everything you could need. The weather is mild, with rain likely at any time of year, and the forest roads can be slippery with wet leaves in autumn.
t.limessection between watchtowers wp 2 13:
Up on the plateau of the Hintertaunus, north of the Rhine gorge, the Roman frontier crossed a quiet landscape of fields and forest near Singhofen, and a section of it between two watchtowers survives here as a faint bank and ditch running through the woods. This is the Upper German Limes, which ran for more than five hundred kilometres from the Rhine to the Danube, marking the boundary between the Roman Empire and the free Germanic tribes from the second century until the Romans withdrew in the third. It was not a great wall like Hadrian's in Britain, but a line of watchtowers, forts and a timber palisade, later strengthened with a ditch and bank. Together with the Raetian Limes, it was listed by UNESCO in 2005.

The town of Nassau, about six kilometres away in the valley of the Lahn, gave its name to one of the great dynasties of Europe. The House of Nassau, which took its name from the castle above the town, produced counts, princes and eventually the royal families of the Netherlands and Luxembourg. Nassau was also the home of the Prussian reformer Baron vom Stein, who was born in the family house that still stands in the town.

The riding around Singhofen and Nassau is excellent. The Taunus plateau is crossed by quiet roads through fields and forests, with long views over the hills, and the roads that drop into the Lahn valley are steep and winding, with tight bends and fine views over the river. The Lahn itself winds between wooded slopes, past castles, old towns and spa resorts such as Bad Ems, where the elegant spa buildings recall the days when emperors and kings came to take the waters. Further south, the Rhine gorge, with its castles, vineyards and the Loreley rock, is one of the most famous landscapes in Germany.

Singhofen and the surrounding villages are small, with limited services, so it is best to fill up in Nassau or Bad Ems. The local food is hearty, with Rhineland specialities such as Reibekuchen, crisp potato pancakes, and plenty of sausage, and the wines of the Rhine and the Lahn valleys are excellent. The weather on the plateau is cooler and windier than in the valleys, and fog can linger in the mornings in autumn.
t.watchtowers wp 2 14 to 2 16@50.3,7.8:
Imagine standing in a small timber or stone tower on a cold winter night, looking out over the dark forest for signs of movement, with a fire ready to signal to the next tower along the line. That was the life of the soldiers who manned the watchtowers of the Roman frontier, and the remains of three of them, numbered 2/14 to 2/16 by archaeologists, lie in the woods between Singhofen and Miehlen, on the plateau above the Rhine and the Lahn. Their foundations survive as low mounds and traces in the ground, and the line of the frontier, the ditch and bank, can be followed between them. They are part of the Upper German-Raetian Limes, one of the components of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire World Heritage Site.

The watchtowers were usually placed at intervals of a few hundred metres to a kilometre, depending on the terrain, so that each could see its neighbours. The early towers were made of wood, later replaced by stone, and they were usually two or three storeys high, with a lookout platform at the top. Behind them, larger forts housed the main garrison units, ready to respond to any threat. Reconstructions of watchtowers can be seen in several places along the Limes, giving an idea of what they looked like.

The area between Singhofen and Miehlen is a quiet rural plateau, with fields, meadows and patches of forest, and the roads are narrow, winding and almost empty. To the west, the land drops steeply into the Rhine gorge, and the road down to St. Goarshausen and the Loreley is a spectacular ride, with tight hairpins and views over the river, the castles and the vineyards. The Loreley rock, made famous by the poem of Heinrich Heine about the siren who lured boatmen to their deaths, rises high above the river, and there is a visitor centre and viewpoint at the top.

Miehlen and Singhofen are small villages with few services. Nassau, about six kilometres away, has fuel and shops, and the towns along the Rhine have plenty of restaurants and hotels. A car ferry crosses the Rhine at St. Goarshausen, as there are no bridges for long stretches of the gorge. The weather is mild, with warm summers and cool, damp winters, and the river valleys can be foggy in autumn.
t.frederiksoord wilhelminaoord@52.9,6.2:
In 1818, after years of war, famine and poverty, a former general named Johannes van den Bosch founded the Society of Benevolence in the Netherlands, with a radical idea: to take poor families from the cities and give them a new life as farmers in the empty heathlands of the north east. The first colony was established at Frederiksoord, in the south of Drenthe, and others followed at Wilhelminaoord, Willemsoord, Veenhuizen and elsewhere. Each family was given a small house, a plot of land and training in farming, and children were educated in schools, an unusual provision for the time. The Colonies of Benevolence, in the Netherlands and Belgium, were listed by UNESCO in 2021.

The experiment had mixed results. The free colonies at Frederiksoord and Wilhelminaoord became established communities, but the land was poor and the colonists struggled to make a living, and the society later took on more coercive roles, with institutions for beggars, vagrants and orphans at Veenhuizen, which later became a prison village. Today, the landscape of the colonies, with long straight roads lined with trees, small farmhouses, and fields laid out in a regular pattern, is a remarkable reminder of this social experiment. The museum at Frederiksoord tells the story, and a gardening school established by the society still operates.

The riding around Frederiksoord is flat and peaceful, through a landscape of fields, woods, heathland and small villages. The roads are well surfaced and quiet, with long straight stretches and gentle bends. To the west lies the Drents-Friese Wold, a national park of forests, heaths and drifting sand dunes, with quiet roads through the trees, and to the east, the Dwingelderveld, another national park, with one of the largest wet heathlands in western Europe. The area is popular with cyclists, so ride carefully and give them space.

Vledder and Noordwolde are small villages with basic services, and Steenwijk, about eight kilometres away, is a small fortified town with fuel, shops and restaurants. The local food is simple and hearty, with pancakes, soups and stews, and the cafes in the villages are good places to stop for coffee and apple pie. The weather is mild but often windy and wet, and the heathlands are at their most beautiful in late summer, when the heather blooms purple.
t.fort site and civil settlement of markob:
Marköbel is a village in the eastern Wetterau, the fertile plain north east of Frankfurt, and it stands on the site of a Roman fort that guarded the frontier where it crossed this open country. The fort, with its civilian settlement, the vicus, where merchants, craftsmen and soldiers' families lived, was part of the Upper German Limes, and today little remains above ground, but the village streets still follow parts of the old layout, and a reconstructed section of the frontier and markers explain the history. It is part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire World Heritage Site.

The Wetterau was valuable to the Romans for the same reason it is valuable today: its rich soils, which produce wheat, sugar beet and vegetables in abundance. The frontier made a wide loop here to include the plain within the empire, and the remains of forts, watchtowers and villas are scattered across the area. The Saalburg, a reconstructed Roman fort in the Taunus hills to the west, gives a vivid picture of what these frontier forts looked like, with walls, gates, barracks and a museum.

The riding in the Wetterau is gentle and open, with straight roads through fields and villages, and little traffic outside the towns. To the east, the land rises towards the Vogelsberg, the largest volcanic massif in central Europe, a broad dome of basalt covered in forests and meadows, with winding roads that are popular with riders, especially on summer weekends. The Vogelsberg roads have bends of every kind, good surfaces and fine views, but they are also watched closely by the police, and in the German uplands some popular routes carry weekend restrictions for motorcycles because of noise and accidents, so read the signs.

Nearby, the walled town of Büdingen is one of the best-preserved medieval towns in Hesse, with half-timbered houses, a castle and a complete ring of walls. Hammersbach and Langenselbold have fuel and shops, and the larger town of Hanau, birthplace of the Brothers Grimm, is a short ride to the south. The local drink is Apfelwein, a dry, sour cider served in grey stoneware jugs, best enjoyed with hearty Hessian food such as Handkäse mit Musik, a sour cheese marinated with onions. The weather is mild, with warm summers and cool winters.
t.buseoksa temple@37.0,128.7:
The name Buseoksa means temple of the floating stone, and the legend behind it involves a monk, a princess and a dragon. When the monk Uisang founded the temple in 676, after returning from studies in China, a young woman named Seonmyo who had fallen in love with him there is said to have followed him in the form of a dragon, and when local bandits opposed the new temple she lifted a huge rock into the air to frighten them off. A large boulder behind the main hall is still pointed out as the floating stone, and you will be told that a thread can be passed beneath it.

The main hall, the Muryangsujeon, is one of the oldest surviving wooden buildings in Korea, dating from the Goryeo period, and its columns swell gently at the middle in the manner that architects call entasis. Standing on its terrace at sunset, with the ridges of the Sobaek mountains fading blue into the distance, is one of the great quiet moments of Korean travel. Buseoksa is one of the seven mountain monasteries inscribed together by UNESCO as the Sansa, Buddhist mountain monasteries of Korea, and it remains a working temple.

The approach road climbs from Yeongju through orchards: the area is famous for its apples, and in autumn the road is lined with stalls selling them, while the avenue of ginkgo trees leading up to the temple gates turns brilliant yellow. The roads in the Sobaek mountains are generally well surfaced, with some lovely twisting stretches and moderate traffic. One crucial detail: motorcycles are banned from Korean expressways, so you will be using national and local roads, which is no hardship here. Spring blossom and autumn colours are the peak seasons, and weekends bring crowds.

Yeongju, about twenty kilometres down the valley, is where you top up the tank and find a bed, while the lane below the temple gate has restaurants serving mountain vegetables and bibimbap. Nearby, the Sosuseowon Confucian academy and the old village of Seonbichon offer a glimpse of another side of Korean tradition. Wear comfortable shoes for the walk up the stone stairs, which are steep, and keep your voice down within the temple grounds.
t.tokhung ri tomb@39.0,125.4:
Beneath a low grassy mound in the countryside south-west of Pyongyang lies one of the finest painted tombs of the ancient kingdom of Koguryo. Tokhung-ri was built in 408 for a high-ranking official, and its walls are covered in murals showing his life: processions, hunting scenes, officials paying respects, mythical creatures and a starry sky with the sun and moon. Unusually, it carries a long ink inscription giving the man's titles and the date, which makes it an important anchor for the history of the whole kingdom. It is part of the Complex of Koguryo Tombs inscribed by UNESCO in 2004.

Koguryo was one of the Three Kingdoms of ancient Korea, a powerful state that at its height stretched deep into what is now north-east China. Its tombs, built of stone chambers covered with earth, preserve paintings of remarkable liveliness, with flowing lines and bright colours, and they are among the most important sources for understanding life and belief in the region at the time. The countryside around is flat and agricultural, with rice paddies and villages in the plain of the Taedong river, which flows past Pyongyang to the sea at Nampo.

It needs saying plainly: independent riding here is not possible. Foreign visitors to North Korea can only travel on organised tours with official guides, and access to particular sites depends on government permission. The roads in the area are generally wide but uneven, with little traffic except for military vehicles, trucks and the occasional bicycle. If you are ever able to visit, it will be by bus or minibus as part of a tour group, and the murals themselves are often protected, with visitors shown replicas.

There are no services for independent travellers, and fuel, food and accommodation are arranged by tour operators. Nampo and Pyongyang are the nearest cities. Anyone considering a visit should consult current government travel advice, which for many countries strongly advises against all travel to North Korea, and take very seriously the legal risks involved. For most people, Tokhung-ri will remain a place to know through books and photographs.
t.museong seowon@35.6,127.0:
Just outside Jeongeup, in a village of low houses and persimmon trees, stands Museong-seowon, a Confucian academy that has served its community for centuries. It honours Choe Chi-won, the great ninth-century scholar of the Silla kingdom who served as magistrate in this area and whose poems and essays made him one of Korea's most celebrated writers. Seowon were private academies where young men studied the Confucian classics and the memory of revered scholars was honoured with rites, and Museong is one of nine inscribed together by UNESCO in 2019.

What makes Museong special is its closeness to ordinary life. Many seowon were built in secluded valleys; this one sits in the middle of a village, and it was one of the few that survived when the regent Heungseon Daewongun ordered most academies closed in the 1870s. The buildings, a lecture hall and a shrine set behind simple gates and walls, are modest and elegant, with wooden floors and tiled roofs. The region has another claim to history: the Donghak peasant uprising of 1894, which began near Jeongeup, shook the Joseon dynasty and helped trigger the war between China and Japan.

The riding around Jeongeup is gentle and rural, through rice fields, villages and low hills, with the Naejangsan mountains rising to the south. Naejangsan national park is one of the most famous places in Korea for autumn colour, with its maple trees turning crimson in late October and early November, and the roads into the park are beautiful but crowded in that season. As elsewhere in Korea, motorcycles are kept off the expressways, so you will be on national and local roads, which are well surfaced and suit relaxed touring.

Jeongeup, a city of well over a hundred thousand people, is six kilometres off and takes care of petrol and beds without fuss. Local cooking in the Jeolla provinces is famous across Korea for its rich flavours and the generous number of side dishes, and a meal here is part of the pleasure. The academy is often quiet, and you may have the place to yourself; respect the buildings, which are still used for ceremonies, and take off your shoes if you step onto the wooden floors.
t.getbol@35.7,126.7:
On Korea's west coast the sea goes out a very long way. The Yellow Sea has big tides, and when they drop they expose huge plains of mud, the getbol, glistening and grey and full of life. The Korean tidal flats were inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 2021, covering stretches from Seocheon in the north to Gochang, Shinan and Boseong-Suncheon in the south, and they are among the most important feeding grounds on Earth for migratory shorebirds travelling between Siberia and Australia. Crabs, mudskippers, worms and shellfish swarm in the mud, and people have harvested them for centuries.

Buan, the nearest town, sits at the base of the Byeonsan peninsula, which juts into the sea with a rugged coastline of cliffs and coves. At Chaeseokgang the rock has been weathered into layers that look like stacks of books, a favourite spot at low tide and sunset. To the north stretches the Saemangeum seawall, one of the longest in the world, which closed off a vast estuary for reclamation and became a symbol of the debate between development and conservation. Gochang, a little to the south, has some of the protected mudflats along with one of the densest concentrations of prehistoric dolmens anywhere.

The riding here is easy and scenic, along coastal roads that follow the shore around the peninsula, with views over the sea and the mudflats and the islands offshore. The roads are generally well surfaced, traffic is moderate except at weekends and holidays, and the wind can be strong off the sea. Motorcycles cannot use the expressways, but the national roads are a pleasure. Come in April or September, ideally when the migratory birds are passing through, and sunsets over the Yellow Sea are famous.

Buan, nine kilometres inland, covers petrol, motels and a market. The seafood is the real reason to linger: try the grilled clams, the raw fish, and the jukkumi, small octopus, in spring. If you walk out onto the mudflats, check the tide times carefully, since the sea comes back quickly, and never go out alone. Wear old shoes or boots you do not mind getting muddy, because you will get muddy.
t.fort site and civil settlement of marien:
Marienfels is a small village in the hills of the western Taunus, between the Rhine and the Lahn, and it sits on the site of a Roman fort and its civilian settlement, part of the Upper Germanic-Raetian Limes World Heritage listing. The frontier wall ran through these hills, and the fort housed a garrison that guarded the frontier and the roads that crossed it. Little remains above ground, but excavations have revealed the outline of the fort and the settlement, with houses, baths and workshops.

The surrounding landscape is the Blue Land, as the Rhein-Lahn district calls itself, a region of rolling hills, forests and small villages, cut by deep valleys that lead down to the Rhine and the Lahn. The Middle Rhine gorge, with the Loreley rock, castles and vineyards, is a few kilometres to the west, and the Lahn valley, with Bad Ems, Nassau and its castle, lies to the north. Nastätten, the nearest town, is a small market centre in the hills.

For riders, this area is a playground. The B260, known as the Bäderstraße, the spa road, runs from Bad Ems through Nastätten towards Schlangenbad and Wiesbaden, with endless curves through forests and over hills, and it is popular with motorcyclists, so expect speed limits and police checks. The Wispertal, to the south, is another famous motorcycle road, winding through a narrow forested valley. The roads down to the Rhine, with hairpins and views over the river, are spectacular.

Nastätten, six kilometres away, and Nassau on the Lahn have fuel and shops, and the Rhine towns below, St. Goar and St. Goarshausen among them, have plenty of restaurants and wine bars. In autumn, look for Federweißer, the cloudy, half-fermented new wine, served with onion tart, and in summer for Riesling from the steep slate slopes of the gorge. The Loreley rock, where the legendary siren lured boatmen to their deaths, has a visitor centre and a terrace with a superb view down the river, reached by a winding road that is a pleasure in itself.
The Kottenforst is a big, flat, rather mysterious forest on the plateau south-west of Bonn, crossed by long, dead-straight avenues laid out by the Electors of Cologne in the eighteenth century as hunting rides. The Bellerbuschallee is one of them, and walking or riding along it you pass oak and beech, wet hollows and the occasional deer. Under the trees, though, lie traces much older than the Electors: the low ramparts of Roman practice camps, where legionaries from Bonn learned to dig defences quickly. These camps form part of the Lower German Limes World Heritage listing inscribed in 2021.

Bonna, on the Rhine below, was a full legionary fortress, and the river itself was the frontier here. The Romans also built one of their greatest engineering works nearby: the Eifel aqueduct, which carried spring water over ninety kilometres to Cologne, and fragments of it, with their thick crusts of limestone sinter, turn up across the region. On the far side of the Rhine rise the volcanic cones of the Siebengebirge, with the ruined castle of the Drachenfels on top, where legend says Siegfried killed the dragon and bathed in its blood.

Inside the forest itself the avenues are for walkers, cyclists and horses, not engines, so treat this as a place to park and wander. The riding is all around it. South through Wachtberg the lanes roll over open farmland with views to the Siebengebirge, and from there the Ahr valley, with its steep vineyards and twisting road through Altenahr, is half an hour away, as are the volcanic lakes and curving roads of the Eifel. Across the river, the climbs in the Siebengebirge are short but tight. Weekends bring plenty of fellow riders and some local speed controls.

Wachtberg, four kilometres away, covers fuel and basic shopping, and Bonn has every service you could ask for. In town, Beethoven's birthplace on the Bonngasse is a fine detour, and the beer gardens along the Rhine promenade are a good place to watch barges go by. In the forest, carry water, keep to the paths in the protected areas, and listen for woodpeckers drumming in spring.
t.watchtower wp 1 77@50.4,7.7:
In the hills of the Westerwald, east of Koblenz, the Roman frontier ran from the Rhine up across the high ground towards the Taunus, and archaeologists have numbered every tower site along it. Watchtower WP 1/77, near the villages of Kadenbach and Arzbach, is one of them, now marked by a low mound or reconstructed foundations in the woods. The frontier here was a palisade of timber and later an earth bank and ditch, with towers every few hundred metres, and the whole system is part of the Upper German-Raetian Limes World Heritage listing.

The surrounding area is the Kannenbäckerland, the land of the jug makers, where grey stoneware with blue decoration has been made for centuries from the rich clay deposits of the region. Höhr-Grenzhausen, the main town, has a ceramics museum and many potteries, and salt-glazed jugs, mugs and crocks from here were once exported across Europe. The Westerwald itself is a landscape of rolling hills, forests and small villages, cooler and wetter than the Rhine valley below.

For riders, the Westerwald offers quiet, flowing roads through forests and villages, with gentle climbs and views over the hills. The roads down to the Rhine and the Lahn are steeper and twistier, with hairpins and lovely views over the river valleys, and Koblenz, where the Moselle meets the Rhine at the Deutsches Eck, is a short ride away. On the minor roads you will mostly share the tarmac with tractors and the odd post van.

In Höhr-Grenzhausen, six kilometres away, you can refuel and then browse a ceramics museum and potteries welcome visitors; you might take home a grey and blue stoneware jug as a souvenir. The villages have inns serving Westerwald food, potato dishes, game in season and Döppekuchen, a hearty potato cake with bacon. Koblenz, a short ride away, has the dramatic Deutsches Eck at the confluence of the Rhine and Moselle, and a cable car up to the Ehrenbreitstein fortress, one of the largest in Europe, with a view that makes the ride worthwhile.
t.signaltower johannisberg@50.4,8.7:
On a hill above Bad Nauheim, the Johannisberg, the Romans built a signal tower that could communicate with the frontier forts of the Wetterau, the fertile plain that bulges north of Frankfurt and was protected by a long loop of the Limes. The site, with a later medieval chapel and a modern observation tower, gives wide views over the plain and the Taunus hills, and it is part of the Upper German-Raetian Limes World Heritage listing. On a clear day you can see the towers of Frankfurt on the horizon.

Bad Nauheim is a spa town with a remarkable ensemble of Art Nouveau buildings, the Sprudelhof, built in the early twentieth century around the springs, with tiled bathhouses and courtyards. Its salt springs were also used for salt production, and the graduation towers, where brine trickles through bundles of brushwood, still stand in the park. In 1958, a young American soldier named Elvis Presley was stationed at nearby Friedberg and lived in Bad Nauheim, and the town remembers him with a statue and an annual festival.

The riding around Bad Nauheim offers variety. The Wetterau itself is flat and agricultural, with straight roads and villages, but to the west, the Taunus hills rise, with winding roads through forests and up to the Großer Feldberg, the highest point in the range, a popular meeting point for motorcyclists. To the north-east, the Vogelsberg, an extinct volcano, offers some of the best roads in Hesse, with endless curves and little traffic.

Bad Nauheim is a town of thirty thousand people and has fuel, shops, restaurants and hotels. The spa park and the Sprudelhof are pleasant places for a stroll, and the cafés in the town centre serve cakes and coffee in the best spa tradition. Try the local apple wine, Ebbelwoi, with Handkäs mit Musik, a sour cheese marinated with onions, the regional speciality, and if you are an Elvis fan, look for the statue and the house where he lived. The Feldberg, an hour's ride away, is a classic Sunday meeting point for riders.
t.watchtowers wp 1 23 to 1 24@50.5,7.4:
The Upper German-Raetian Limes began at the Rhine, at Rheinbrohl, and climbed into the hills on the east bank, and towers WP 1/23 and 1/24, near the wine village of Leutesdorf, are among the first along its route. They are now marked by foundations or mounds in the forest above the river, and they are part of the World Heritage listing. From here the frontier ran for more than five hundred kilometres to the Danube, and it is fascinating to stand at the very beginning of such an enormous undertaking.

Across the river, Andernach is one of the oldest towns in Germany, with a well-preserved medieval centre and walls, and it is famous for its cold-water geyser, which erupts to a height of around sixty metres and is said to be the highest cold-water geyser in the world. Further west, the Laacher See, a volcanic crater lake, is surrounded by forests and dominated by the Romanesque abbey of Maria Laach, one of the finest in Germany. The Eifel volcanic landscape stretches beyond, with craters, lakes and mineral springs.

The riding here is excellent. The roads along the Rhine, on both banks, offer views of castles, vineyards and river traffic, although they are busy at weekends. The roads up into the hills, through the Westerwald and the Eifel, are winding and fun, with forests and villages, and the routes around the Laacher See and the Eifel volcanoes are popular with motorcyclists. Ferries cross the Rhine at several points, offering a pleasant break.

Andernach, four kilometres away across the river, has fuel and shops, and Leutesdorf has wine taverns and inns where the local Riesling is poured generously. The cold-water geyser at Namedy, reached by boat from the Andernach waterfront, erupts at intervals and is a spectacle worth seeing. In the Eifel, try Reibekuchen, crispy potato pancakes with apple sauce, and trout from the clear streams. Maria Laach abbey, with its Romanesque church and lakeside setting, is a peaceful place to stop, and its bookshop and café are excellent.
t.mt namsan belt@35.9,129.2:
Namsan, the southern mountain of Gyeongju, is a modest granite ridge rising just under five hundred metres above the old capital of the Silla kingdom, and it is crammed with more Buddhist art than almost any mountain in Korea. For centuries the monks and craftsmen of Silla, which unified much of the Korean peninsula in the seventh century and ruled from Gyeongju until the tenth, carved Buddhas into its boulders, built stone pagodas on its ridges and placed temples in its valleys. UNESCO took in the whole mountain when it listed Gyeongju's historic areas, and walking its trails is like moving through an open-air museum among the pines.

Some of the highlights are the seated Buddha in Samneung valley, the carved rock faces at Chilburam, where seven Buddhas emerge from the granite, and the slightly smiling Buddha of Bulgok, sitting in a niche like a person sheltering from the rain. At the foot of the mountain lies Poseokjeong, a curving stone water channel where, legend says, Silla nobles floated cups of wine and recited poems. Nearby are royal tombs, great grassy mounds that dot the landscape of Gyeongju itself.

Gyeongju is a pleasant, low-rise city, more relaxed than most in Korea, with its central area of royal tumuli, the Cheomseongdae observatory tower and the lovely Donggung palace with its pond lit up at night. Bulguksa temple and the Seokguram grotto, both on the slopes of Tohamsan to the east, are among the most celebrated Buddhist sites in Asia.

The riding is relaxed. Roads around the base of Namsan are quiet and lined with fields and small villages, and the climb up Tohamsan to Seokguram is a good twisty road through forest. Further east, the coast near Gampo and Yangnam has cliffs and fishing harbours. Korean roads are well maintained, but watch for speed cameras, which are everywhere and usually announced with signs, and for slow farm vehicles on minor roads. Gyeongju has plenty of fuel stations and restaurants; try the local ssambap, rice with a spread of leaves for wrapping, and Gyeongju bread, small pastries filled with red bean paste. Spring cherry blossom season is spectacular and crowded.
t.tomb of king tongmyong and jinpha ri gro:
This is one of the few places in a ride collection that you almost certainly cannot ride to on your own, and it is worth saying so plainly. The Tomb of King Tongmyong lies in North Korea, southeast of Pyongyang, and the country admits foreign visitors only on guided tours, with fixed itineraries, official guides and no independent driving, let alone motorcycling. Still, it is a remarkable place, and knowing about it adds a layer to understanding the Korean peninsula.

The tomb is traditionally attributed to Tongmyong, also known as Jumong, the legendary founder of the Goguryeo kingdom, which ruled much of northern Korea and Manchuria from around the first century BC to 668 AD. Goguryeo moved its capital to Pyongyang in the fifth century, and the tomb was probably built around that time. It was heavily restored and enlarged in the 1990s as a showpiece of national heritage. The nearby Jinpha-ri group consists of about fifteen tombs, some of them decorated with wall paintings, and together they are inscribed as part of the complex of Koguryo tombs. The paintings in these tombs, showing the four guardian animals, stars, hunting scenes and daily life, are among the finest early art in East Asia.

The landscape around is typical of the lowlands near Pyongyang: rolling hills, pine woods and rice paddies, with villages and cooperative farms. The roads are generally empty of private traffic, and travel is slow and controlled. Chunghwa is the nearest town, and Pyongyang, the capital, is the starting point for all tours.

If you are interested in Goguryeo history and want to ride, the better option is the Chinese side of the border, around Ji'an in Jilin province, where the earlier Goguryeo capital and its tombs are also on the UNESCO list and accessible, though China has its own rules about foreign drivers and motorcycles. In South Korea, museums in Seoul exhibit replicas and artefacts. For now, the Tomb of King Tongmyong remains a place better understood through books, photographs and imagination than from the saddle.
t.watchtowers wp 3 15 to 3 19 including th:
In the hills of the Taunus north of Wiesbaden, the Roman frontier ran along the ridges through dense forest, and between watchtowers 3/15 and 3/19 near Idstein, its line can still be traced on the ground. The Romans built an earth bank and ditch, topped with a wooden palisade, with stone watchtowers at regular intervals, close enough to see each other and signal along the line. In the forest, the bank and ditch survive as a long, low ridge and hollow, and the foundations of watchtowers appear as low mounds, sometimes with a few stones visible. The Upper Germanic and Raetian Limes, more than five hundred kilometres long, has been a World Heritage site since 2005.

The Limes walking trail follows the line through the forest, marked with signs and information boards, and walking a stretch of it gives a feel for the life of the Roman soldiers who manned the towers, watching the forest for movement, in all weathers, far from home.

Idstein, five kilometres away, is a delightful old town with one of the finest collections of half-timbered houses in Hesse, including the extravagantly carved Killingerhaus. The Hexenturm, the witches' tower, is a medieval keep that was used as a prison during the witch trials of the seventeenth century, and the Unionskirche, plain outside, has a lavishly painted baroque interior. The castle, once the residence of the counts of Nassau-Idstein, now houses a school.

The riding in the Taunus is very popular, with quiet roads winding through forest and over hills, linking small villages and old castles. Surfaces are generally good, but watch for cyclists, walkers and other riders, especially at weekends, and for deer at dawn and dusk. Some roads in the Taunus have weekend restrictions or speed limits for motorcycles because of noise and accidents, so check the signs. Idstein is the supply stop; Taunusstein and Niedernhausen nearby also have services. Wiesbaden, the state capital, with its spas and elegant boulevards, is about twenty kilometres south. Try Hessian specialities like grüne Soße, a cold herb sauce served with boiled eggs and potatoes.
t.watchtowers wp 1 3 to 1 10@50.5,7.4:
Rheinbrohl is where the Roman frontier of Upper Germany began. Here, on the east bank of the Rhine between Bonn and Koblenz, the Limes left the river and struck off inland, running across hills and valleys for more than five hundred kilometres to the Danube near Regensburg. The first watchtowers, numbered 1/1 onwards, stood in the hills above the town, and the stretch from 1/3 to 1/10 climbs from the Rhine valley into the forests of the Westerwald. The Römerwelt museum in Rheinbrohl, at the start of the Limes, brings Roman frontier life to life with reconstructions, hands-on exhibits and a reconstructed watchtower nearby.

The line of the frontier is visible in places as an earth bank and ditch running through the forest, with the remains of watchtowers as low mounds. The upland frontier has been on the World Heritage list since 2005, and the Lower Germanic Limes, which ran along the Rhine to the North Sea, was added more recently.

The Rhine valley here is wide and beautiful, with vineyards, orchards and forests on the slopes, small towns along the river, and castles perched on the hills. Across the river, the Brohl valley leads to the volcanic Eifel and the Laacher See, a crater lake with a Romanesque abbey on its shore. Bad Hönningen, three kilometres away, is a spa town with thermal baths, fuel and shops, and Linz am Rhein, a little further north, has a colourful old town of half-timbered houses.

The B42 follows the east bank of the Rhine, flowing and scenic, though busy at weekends and with trains running right alongside. For better riding, head up into the Westerwald or across the river into the Eifel, where the roads twist through forests and over hills, with little traffic and plenty of curves. The Nürburgring is about an hour away. Ferries cross the Rhine at several points, a pleasant break on a hot day. Watch for speed cameras in the villages. Try a glass of local wine from the Middle Rhine, Rhine fish, and Reibekuchen, potato fritters often served with apple sauce, a Rhineland favourite.
t.watchtower wp 3 42@50.2,8.4:
Glashütten takes its name from the glass huts that worked in these forests in the Middle Ages, when the endless beech and oak of the high Taunus supplied fuel for the furnaces and potash for the glass. Today it is a quiet village spread over a saddle below the Großer Feldberg, at around 880 metres the highest summit in the Taunus, and the Roman frontier passes right by it. Watchtower 3/42 stood on this stretch of the Limes, where the bank and ditch run through the forest along the ridge; near the Feldberg summit, the remains of a small Roman fort, the Feldbergkastell, show where a garrison guarded a pass through the mountains.

The Feldberg is the Frankfurt region's mountain. On a clear day you look south across the Rhine-Main plain to the towers of Frankfurt, the Odenwald and, in exceptional conditions, the hills of the Palatinate. The summit has a transmitter tower, a viewing platform, a restaurant and a crowd of walkers, cyclists, families and riders on weekends; in winter, it is one of the few places near Frankfurt where you can sledge.

The roads around the Feldberg are known to every rider in the region, which is both the attraction and the problem. They are steep, twisty and scenic, but they have a long history of accidents and noise complaints, and parts of them now carry speed limits, overtaking bans and, at times, weekend restrictions for motorcycles, as well as regular police checks. Ride them on a weekday morning with respect for the limits and they are a pleasure; on a sunny Sunday, the crowds and controls can spoil the fun. Watch for cyclists climbing slowly, deer in the forest and damp, leaf-covered corners in autumn.

Glashütten has basic shops; for fuel and a bigger choice, Königstein im Taunus, six kilometres away, is the obvious stop. It is a charming small town dominated by the ruins of a huge castle, blown up by French troops in 1796, with cafes and restaurants on its pedestrian streets. Schmitten, on the other side of the Feldberg, is a village with a few inns. The Taunus is cooler than the plain, often by several degrees, which makes it a welcome escape on hot summer days, but fog can roll in quickly, especially in autumn.
t.watchtowers wp 2 7 and 2 13 including fo:
Between the Lahn and the Rhine, the Roman frontier crossed a high, wooded plateau known locally as the Einrich, and the watchtowers from 2/7 to 2/13 stood on this stretch, near the village of Dachsenhausen. In the forest, the earth bank and ditch can still be followed, and small forts, built to house the soldiers who manned the towers, have left their outlines in the ground. Here, as elsewhere in Germany, the Limes belongs to the frontiers of the Roman Empire on the World Heritage list, but the forest is quiet, and you may walk the line for an hour without meeting anyone.

Below the plateau, the Lahn winds through a deep, wooded valley, and the little town of Nassau sits on its banks, overlooked by the castle that gave its name to one of Europe's great dynasties. The counts of Nassau built it in the twelfth century, and their descendants went on to rule in the Netherlands, where the royal house of Orange-Nassau still bears the name. Nassau was also the birthplace of Karl vom Stein, the Prussian statesman who reformed the state in the early nineteenth century; his family's town house stands in the centre.

Upstream, Bad Ems is an elegant spa town, where emperors and kings once came to take the waters, and where in 1870 the Ems Dispatch, a telegram edited by Bismarck, provoked the Franco-Prussian War. Bad Ems is part of the Great Spa Towns of Europe on the World Heritage list. Dausenau, between Bad Ems and Nassau, has a leaning medieval tower and an old inn.

The riding is varied and excellent. The Lahn valley road follows the river through forests and past castles, with gentle curves and lovely views, while the Bäderstraße, the B260, climbs from Bad Ems over the Taunus towards Wiesbaden, a road popular with riders for its curves and scenery. Smaller roads on the plateau link quiet villages through farmland and forest. Watch for cyclists, campervans on the Lahn and deer at dusk. Nassau, with about five thousand people, has fuel and shops; Bad Ems has more choice. The Lahn is popular for canoeing in summer, and a riverside beer garden is a fine place for a break.
t.fortlet adolfseck@50.2,8.1:
The Aar is a small river that winds north from the Taunus towards the Lahn, through a narrow, wooded valley that has served as a route through the hills since ancient times. Where the Roman frontier crossed the valley near Adolfseck, today a district of Bad Schwalbach, the Romans built a fortlet to control the crossing, a small, square fortification with a garrison of a few dozen soldiers. The remains have been excavated and are marked on the ground, and the stretch of frontier nearby is part of the World Heritage frontiers of the Roman Empire. Above the valley, the ruins of a medieval castle, also called Adolfseck, add another layer of history.

Bad Schwalbach, two and a half kilometres away, is a spa town that became fashionable in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, when the iron-rich waters of its springs drew visitors from across Europe. Its spa park, with old trees, pavilions and the elegant buildings of the Kurhaus, has a faded charm. The town was formerly known as Langenschwalbach, and it has a pleasant old centre of half-timbered houses.

Downstream, the Aar valley narrows, and the ruins of Hohenstein castle stand on a rocky spur above the river, one of the most dramatic castle settings in the Taunus. In summer, open-air theatre and music performances are held in the castle courtyard. To the south, across the ridge, the Rheingau slopes down to the Rhine in a sea of vineyards, producing some of the finest rieslings in the world, with villages like Eltville, Kiedrich and Rüdesheim.

The B54, the Aartalstraße, follows the valley with flowing curves through the forest, though it can be busy with traffic heading to and from Wiesbaden. Smaller roads climb out of the valley over the ridges to Schlangenbad, another spa town, and down into the Rheingau, with views across the Rhine. Watch for cyclists, deer and speed cameras. In Bad Schwalbach you can fill up and eat well; Taunusstein, a few kilometres to the east, also has services. A glass of Rheingau riesling at a wine tavern overlooking the Rhine is the perfect end to a ride in this area.
t.building remains southwest of saalburg@5:
If you want to know what a Roman fort on the German frontier really looked like, the Saalburg is the place, and these building remains lie in the forest just southwest of it, part of the civilian and military landscape that grew up around the fort. The Saalburg itself was rebuilt at the beginning of the twentieth century on the orders of Kaiser Wilhelm II, who was fascinated by Roman history and keen to present the German empire as the heir of Rome. The walls, gates, headquarters building and granaries were reconstructed on the original foundations, based on the archaeology of the time, and today the fort houses a museum full of finds from the frontier, along with workshops, a Roman garden and regular events with reenactors.

Around the fort, the remains of the civil settlement, the bath house, temples and other buildings are scattered through the forest, along with the earth bank and ditch of the frontier. The Limes runs along the ridge of the Taunus here, and the Saalburg guarded an important pass, still used by the B456, the road from Bad Homburg to Usingen. The whole frontier is a World Heritage site.

Bad Homburg, six kilometres away, is a spa town with a long history of elegance. It was the summer residence of Kaiser Wilhelm II, who stayed in the castle, and its casino and spa park attracted the aristocracy of Europe; the Homburg hat, made famous by Edward VII, is named after the town. Nearby, the Hessenpark open-air museum near Neu-Anspach shows rural buildings from across Hesse, moved and reconstructed in a village setting.

The B456 over the pass is a fast road through the forest with a few good curves, but it carries a lot of traffic, especially at rush hour and on weekends, when the Saalburg and the Taunus attract crowds. Smaller roads through the forest and the villages of the Usinger Land north of the ridge are quieter and more scenic. Watch for cyclists, walkers, deer and speed cameras. Wehrheim, about four kilometres away, has fuel and basic services; Bad Homburg and Oberursel have everything. Try the local apple wine and Hessian dishes in one of the traditional inns, and allow time to explore the fort properly.
t.watchtower sp 3 5@50.2,8.2:
Taunusstein did not exist as a town until 1971, when ten villages on the high plateau north of Wiesbaden were merged into one municipality, and so it has no old centre, just a cluster of former villages, each with its church, its half-timbered houses and its fields. One of them, Wehen, gave its name to the football club SV Wehen Wiesbaden, which started here before moving to the city. The Roman frontier ran along the edge of this plateau, and watchtower SP 3/5, close to the line, is one of the many small sites that mark it in the forest between Taunusstein and Idstein.

What makes this stretch of the Limes interesting is the way it uses the landscape. The Romans ran the frontier along the high ground of the Taunus, the watershed between streams flowing south to the Rhine and those flowing north to the Lahn, giving the soldiers in the towers long views over the land beyond. Each tower was within sight of its neighbours, and signals, probably with torches, flags or horns, could be passed along the line. The soldiers lived in small forts nearby and took turns on watch, in summer heat and winter snow. A walk along the Limes trail here, through beech and spruce forest, gives a sense of their isolation.

Modern engineering crosses the same ridge. The A3 motorway and the high-speed railway line between Cologne and Frankfurt both cut through the Taunus near Idstein, the railway in tunnels and on viaducts, and you will see the trains flash past at up to three hundred kilometres an hour.

For riders, the roads on the plateau and down into the valleys are pleasant and varied, with forest stretches, open farmland and small villages. The B275 runs north from Taunusstein towards Idstein and the Lahn, and smaller roads link the villages through the forest. Weekend traffic can be heavy with day-trippers from the Rhine-Main area. Watch for cyclists, deer and speed cameras. Idstein, about five kilometres away, has fuel, shops and a fine old town; Taunusstein and Niedernhausen also have services. The plateau is often cooler and windier than the Rhine valley, and fog can linger in autumn.
t.fort schrenzer@50.4,8.7:
Butzbach sits at the northern edge of the Wetterau, a broad, fertile plain north of Frankfurt, where the Taunus ends and the land opens out into fields of wheat, sugar beet and rapeseed. The Romans prized this land, and their frontier made a long detour around it, swinging east and then south to include the Wetterau within the empire. Near Butzbach, on the Schrenzer hill, they built a small fort, the Kastell Schrenzer, to guard the frontier where it left the Taunus and began its loop around the plain. The fort and the frontier nearby are part of the frontiers of the Roman Empire World Heritage site, and the remains, low earthworks in the woods, can be visited on foot.

Butzbach itself is a pleasant small town, with one of the most beautiful market squares in Hesse, surrounded by half-timbered houses and the old town hall. The Landgrafenschloss, a former residence of the landgraves of Hesse-Darmstadt, stands at the edge of the old town. Above the town, the Hausberg rises to almost five hundred metres, crowned by the remains of a Celtic hillfort, a reminder that people lived here long before the Romans.

Nearby, Bad Nauheim is a spa town with beautiful Art Nouveau bath buildings, where Elvis Presley lived while he was stationed with the US Army at Friedberg in the late 1950s. Münzenberg castle, a twelfth-century Hohenstaufen fortress with two tall towers, stands on a hill in the plain, nicknamed the inkwell of the Wetterau because of its shape.

The riding here is a mix of open plain and wooded hills. The Wetterau roads are straight and fast, with long views across the fields, while the roads into the Taunus to the west climb through forests with good curves. The roads around the Hausberg and towards Usingen are popular with riders. Watch for agricultural traffic, cyclists and speed cameras, which are common in Hesse. Butzbach, with about twenty-five thousand people, has all the services you need. Rockenberg and Ober-Mörlen are smaller villages nearby. Try the Wetterau's apple wine, served in a ribbed glass, and green sauce, made from seven herbs, a regional specialty.
t.xanten furstenberg@51.6,6.5:
The Fürstenberg is a low hill on the edge of the Lower Rhine plain, just south of Xanten, and two thousand years ago it was one of the most important military bases in the Roman Empire. Here the Romans built Vetera, a legionary fortress that housed up to two legions and served as a springboard for campaigns into Germania under Augustus. In AD 69 and 70, during the Batavian revolt, Vetera was besieged, starved into surrender and destroyed, and a new fortress was built nearby. The site on the Fürstenberg is part of the Lower German Limes, the Roman frontier along the Rhine from the Alps to the North Sea, which was added to the World Heritage list in 2021. On the ground there is little to see, mostly fields and woods, but the elevated position, with views over the river plain, explains why the Romans chose it.

Xanten, two and a half kilometres away, is a charming small town with a lot of history. The LVR Archaeological Park, on the site of the Roman city of Colonia Ulpia Traiana, has reconstructions of the city walls, a temple, an amphitheatre and houses, along with an excellent museum built over the remains of the Roman baths. The town's Gothic cathedral of St Victor is one of the finest churches on the Lower Rhine, and according to the Nibelungenlied, the hero Siegfried was born in Xanten.

The landscape of the Lower Rhine is flat and green, with wide meadows, dikes, old river arms, windmills and farms, and a big sky that changes with every shift of the weather. Wild geese spend the winter here in huge numbers, and the meadows along the river are important nature reserves. The Rhine itself is wide and busy with barges.

The riding is gentle and relaxing, on quiet roads along the dikes and through the villages, with few curves and lots of space. Wind can be strong, and rain is frequent. The roads are popular with cyclists, so share them with care. Xanten, a town of about twenty thousand people, has fuel, shops, cafes and restaurants; Alpen and Sonsbeck are smaller towns nearby. Try the Lower Rhine specialities, such as asparagus in spring, and a glass of local beer. The Dutch border is only half an hour away.
t.jisan dong tumuli@35.7,128.3:
Above the small county town of Goryeong, in south-eastern Korea, a line of grassy burial mounds runs along the ridge of Jusan mountain like the knuckles of a giant hand. These are the Jisan-dong tumuli, tombs of the rulers and elite of Daegaya, the most powerful member of the Gaya confederacy, a group of small kingdoms that flourished in the south of the peninsula until they were absorbed by Silla in the sixth century. The largest mounds are huge, and excavations found not only rich grave goods, iron weapons, armour, gold crowns and pottery, but also evidence that attendants were buried with their lords. Together with other Gaya tomb groups, the site was added to the World Heritage list in 2023.

Walking along the ridge between the mounds at sunset, with the town below and the hills folding away in every direction, is one of the quiet pleasures of Korea. A museum at the foot of the hill explains the culture, including a reconstruction of one of the sacrificial burials. Gaya is also remembered for music: the gayageum, the twelve-stringed zither that is still the classic Korean instrument, is said to have been created here, and Goryeong has a museum devoted to it.

A crucial piece of local knowledge for riders: motorcycles are not allowed on Korean expressways. That means you will be travelling on national and provincial roads, which in this part of the country is no punishment. West of Goryeong the roads climb into the Gayasan mountains towards Haeinsa, the great temple that holds the Tripitaka Koreana, more than eighty thousand wooden printing blocks carved in the thirteenth century. The route there twists through forest and along valleys, especially beautiful in autumn when the maples turn red. Expect speed cameras, sudden speed bumps in villages and the occasional bus taking more than its share of the road.

Goryeong town, at the foot of the tombs, has fuel, convenience stores and restaurants, and Daegu, one of Korea's largest cities, is only a short ride north-east if you need more. Korean roadside food is excellent and cheap: try a bowl of hot soup with rice and side dishes at any small restaurant, or a set of grilled pork with a mountain of fresh leaves to wrap it in.
t.seooreung cluster@37.6,126.9:
Joseon kings chose their final resting places with the same care they gave to their palaces, and the Seooreung cluster in Goyang, just north-west of Seoul, shows how. The name means the five tombs of the west, and the forested grounds contain the burial mounds of several Joseon kings and queens from the fifteenth to the eighteenth centuries. Each tomb follows the principles of pungsu, the Korean form of geomancy: a mountain behind for protection, open land in front, ideally with water flowing past. The mound sits on a terrace, surrounded by stone figures of officials, warriors and animals standing guard, and below is a T-shaped shrine where rites were held. The forty Joseon royal tombs were added to the World Heritage list together in 2009.

Walking through Seooreung on a weekday feels like stepping out of the city entirely. Paths lead through old pine and oak forest, the noise of traffic fades, and the stone figures watch over the hillside as they have for centuries. The royal rites are still performed at the tombs on certain days by descendants of the Yi family. In autumn the colours are spectacular, and in spring the forest floor fills with wildflowers.

Riding here means riding in the Seoul metropolitan area, which is to say traffic, traffic lights and very dense city streets. Remember that motorcycles are banned from expressways throughout Korea, so you will use ordinary roads, which in the city means a lot of stopping and starting. The real reward lies a short way out of town. Bukhansan National Park rises immediately north-east, granite peaks visible from much of the city, and beyond Goyang the roads into Paju and Yangju lead into hills and farmland towards the demilitarised zone, a strange and sobering landscape of military posts and fences along the Imjin River.

Goyang is a city of over a million people, so fuel, food and accommodation are no problem at all. There are small restaurants near the tomb entrance serving traditional dishes, and Ilsan, the newer part of Goyang, has a large lake park. If you have time, combine the visit with a trip to the Joseon palaces in central Seoul, like Gyeongbokgung, to see where the kings buried here actually lived.
t.area 2@37.5,127.2:
The label gives almost nothing away, but the coordinates place you in the wooded hills on the south-east edge of Seoul, where Seongnam, Gwangju and Hanam meet, and the mountain that dominates this area is Namhansan, crowned by the fortress of Namhansanseong. Built and expanded as an emergency capital in the early seventeenth century, its walls run for kilometres along the ridges, with gates, command posts and temples inside, and it became a World Heritage site in 2014. The fortress is remembered for a bitter episode: in the winter of 1636 to 1637, King Injo fled here as the armies of the Qing invaded, and after a siege of more than forty days in the cold, he came down and submitted, kneeling before the Qing emperor. Koreans still regard it as a moment of national humiliation and resilience at the same time.

Today the area inside the walls is a peaceful place of pine forests, restored buildings and trails along the ramparts, with views over the whole of Seoul on clear days. At weekends the hills fill with walkers in bright outdoor clothing, and the restaurants near the centre of the fortress specialise in dishes such as chicken boiled with herbs and rice, eaten after a long hike.

The road up to the fortress from Seongnam winds up the slopes of the mountain in a series of bends and is popular with local riders and drivers on fine days, which also means traffic, cyclists and pedestrians at weekends. The other access roads, from the Gwangju side, are quieter. As everywhere in Korea, motorcycles are not allowed on expressways, so the approach from Seoul uses ordinary roads, which can be slow in rush hour. South and east of the city, beyond Gwangju, roads lead into the hills around Paldang Lake and the Han River, which are well worth exploring on a free afternoon.

Seongnam, with over a million inhabitants, is right next door and offers all services, and fuel is easy to find along the main roads. If you visit in autumn, the colours on the fortress walls are wonderful; in winter, the roads up the mountain can freeze, so check the conditions before you go. Bring water for the walk along the walls, as the climbs are steeper than they look.
t.utrecht limes road zandweg@52.1,5.0:
Two thousand years ago the Rhine marked the northern edge of the Roman Empire here, and along its southern bank the army built a chain of forts, watchtowers and a road to link them. In the western suburbs of Utrecht, in the new district of Leidsche Rijn and the old village of De Meern, that road has been found again under the fields, a gravel and clay embankment with ditches either side, and part of it can be traced along the street called Zandweg.
