Nearby, at Castellum Hoge Woerd, the outline of a Roman fort has been rebuilt in a modern form, with a museum, a theatre and an observatory, and a flat-bottomed Roman river barge, found here in 1997 almost intact and complete with the cargo and personal belongings of its skipper, is on display. The Lower German Limes became a World Heritage site in 2021.

The Rhine has since moved its course, and the old Roman river is now a modest stream called the Oude Rijn, but the landscape still tells the story if you look closely: slightly higher, drier ground along the old riverbanks, where villages and farms were built, and lower, wetter land in between. Utrecht itself grew out of a Roman fort on the river, and the medieval city later developed around the cathedral, whose Dom tower, more than a hundred metres high, is still the tallest church tower in the country.

Riding in the Netherlands is flat, orderly and often windy. Cyclists have the priority almost everywhere, and you will share the roads with thousands of them, along with tractors and the occasional slow canal-side road. The best routes around here follow the dikes along the rivers, the Lek to the south, the Vecht to the north, where the road runs along the top of the dike with water on one side and green meadows and farms on the other. The weather changes quickly, with showers and strong winds, especially in autumn and spring.

Vleuten and De Meern have fuel, shops and cafés, and Utrecht offers everything. Have lunch by the canals in the city centre, where the old wharf cellars along the Oudegracht now house restaurants at water level, and try a slice of apple pie with whipped cream at any café.
t.dutch water defence lines@52.2,5.1:
The Dutch had a clever idea for defending their heartland: instead of building walls, they would drown the approaches. The Dutch Water Defence Lines, a World Heritage site, consist of a long belt of land around Amsterdam and Utrecht that could be flooded deliberately in wartime, with water deep enough to stop soldiers on foot and wagons, but too shallow for boats. Forts, dikes, sluices and pumping stations controlled the water. The New Dutch Waterline, built in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, ran south-east of Amsterdam through the area around Maarssen and the Loosdrecht lakes, and it was mobilised during the First and Second World Wars, though aircraft and modern artillery had made it largely obsolete by then.

Today the forts are hidden among trees, surrounded by moats, many of them restored and used as cafés, museums or event spaces. The fields that were meant to be flooded are green meadows, crossed by drainage ditches, with cows, willows and herons. Just east of here, the Loosdrecht lakes were created by peat digging centuries ago and now form a maze of water, reed beds and islands, popular with sailors and canoeists in summer.

The River Vecht, which flows north from Utrecht through Maarssen to Amsterdam, is one of the most charming rides in the country. In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, rich Amsterdam merchants built country houses along its banks, and the narrow road along the river passes manor houses, gardens, teahouses at the water's edge and old villages like Breukelen, which gave its name to Brooklyn in New York. The road is narrow and winding by Dutch standards and shared with many cyclists, so a calm pace is not only polite but necessary. The country is flat, but the wind can be strong, and rain showers come and go quickly.

Maarssen has fuel, shops and restaurants, as does Utrecht, a short way to the south. There are cafés at several of the old forts and along the Vecht, often with terraces by the water, perfect for a break. Try a portion of bitterballen, small crispy meat croquettes, or poffertjes, little pancakes with butter and powdered sugar, and if the weather is good, sit outside and watch the boats go by.
t.fort site and civil settlement of langen:
Elvis Presley spent his military service in Friedberg, a few kilometres from here, from 1958 to 1960, and lived in a rented house in the spa town of Bad Nauheim, where fans still leave messages on the wall outside and a square in the town bears his name. But nearly two thousand years earlier, other soldiers served in this region. The Roman frontier of the Upper Germanic-Raetian Limes, a World Heritage site, ran along the edge of the Taunus hills here, and at Langenhain, near Ober-Mörlen, the Romans built a fort with a civil settlement beside it, where traders, craftsmen and the families of soldiers lived. Today, the site is mostly fields and meadows, with information boards to help you imagine the walls, gates and buildings that once stood here.

The Wetterau, the broad plain to the east, has some of the most fertile soil in Germany, and the Romans were keen to keep it within their empire. They pushed the frontier forward to include it, creating a bulge in the line of the Limes around the plain, guarded by forts, towers, a ditch and a palisade. Further west, at Saalburg near Bad Homburg, a Roman fort has been rebuilt as it might have looked, with a museum, and it is well worth a visit to see what the frontier was like.

The Taunus is a favourite area for motorcyclists from the Frankfurt region, and the roads that climb into the hills from Bad Nauheim, Butzbach and Usingen are winding and fun, through dense forest and small villages. The Großer Feldberg, the highest point of the Taunus, is a popular meeting place for riders, with views over Frankfurt and the Rhine-Main plain, though it gets very busy at weekends and the police keep a close eye on speeds and noise. Some roads in the area have restrictions for motorcycles at weekends, so check the signs. The Wetterau itself is flatter, with fields and villages, and is good for relaxed riding.

Ober-Mörlen, about three kilometres away, has fuel and shops, and Bad Nauheim has more choice, with cafés and restaurants in its art nouveau spa district. Try the local apple wine, Ebbelwoi, with Handkäs mit Musik, a sour milk cheese marinated with onions, a Hessian classic.
t.fortlet eichkopf@50.4,8.6:
Deep in the forest on the eastern slopes of the Taunus, near Ober-Mörlen, the Romans built a small fortlet known today as Eichkopf, after the wooded hill on which it stands. It was one of the many minor installations along the Upper Germanic-Raetian Limes, the frontier that separated the Roman Empire from the free Germanic tribes, and it housed a small detachment of soldiers who patrolled the line and manned the nearby watchtowers. The outline of the fortlet is still visible as a low rampart and ditch among the trees, and nearby, the line of the frontier itself, with its bank and ditch, can be traced through the forest. It is part of the World Heritage site of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire.

Walking along the Limes in these woods is a peaceful experience. Beech and oak trees tower overhead, the forest floor is covered with leaves and moss, and the only sounds are birds, the wind and perhaps a woodpecker. In autumn, the colours are spectacular, and in spring, the forest is filled with the fresh green of new leaves. The Limes hiking trail follows the line of the frontier through the Taunus, with information boards explaining the sites, and it can be combined with short walks from the road.

The Taunus forest roads are a delight for riders: narrow, winding roads through dense woods, with changes in elevation and occasional views over the Wetterau plain to the east and the Rhine-Main area to the south. The roads from Ober-Mörlen and Butzbach towards Usingen, crossing the ridge, are particularly enjoyable. Watch out for wildlife, especially deer and wild boar, which can appear suddenly at dawn and dusk, and for wet leaves and moss on the road in autumn and after rain. At weekends, the area is popular with walkers, cyclists and other riders, so take care on blind bends.

Ober-Mörlen, about four kilometres away, has fuel and a few shops, and Butzbach, a little further north, has a pretty half-timbered old town with cafés and restaurants around its market square. Further south, near Darmstadt, the Messel Pit, a World Heritage site famous for its exceptionally preserved fossils, including early horses no bigger than a dog, makes an interesting destination for a longer ride.
t.watchtower wp 1 51@50.4,7.6:
The Upper Germanic Limes does not start with a bang. Near Bendorf, on the slopes where the Westerwald drops toward the Rhine at the Neuwied basin, it is a matter of reading the woods: a low bank here, a shallow ditch there, and the spot where a Roman watchtower once stood, numbered by archaeologists as WP 1/51. The towers were placed within sight of each other, timber at first and later stone, so that a signal could pass along the frontier faster than any rider. Standing here among the beech trees you are close to the northern end of a border that ran more than five hundred kilometres to the Danube.

Bendorf itself is a working town of some seventeen thousand people, spread along the Rhine with industry by the water and older villages tucked into the side valleys. Its suburb of Sayn is the reason many people stop: the ruined castle above the valley, the Sayn palace with its butterfly house, and the Sayner Hütte, a nineteenth century iron foundry hall whose cast iron frame was a landmark of early industrial building. Stromberg and Heimbach-Weis are the closest villages to the tower site, quiet and residential.

The roads up from the Rhine are what make the area fun. The Brexbach and Saynbach valleys cut into the Westerwald with tight, wooded climbs, damp patches under the trees and the odd gravel spill from a farm track, so take the first run steady. Higher up, the plateau opens into fields, small villages and long straights between bends, and on a clear day the views back over the Neuwied basin and across to the Eifel are wide and calm. Weekends bring a lot of bikers onto these valleys, and the local police know it, so expect controls in summer.

Fuel is easy in Bendorf and in Neuwied across the river, and there are bakeries and Turkish snack bars in town for a cheap lunch. The forest paths to the tower area are walkers' territory, so park at a village edge and go on foot. If you have time, the Roman fort at Niederbieber on the Neuwied side was one of the biggest on this stretch, and the modest finds and markers there give the tower sites around Bendorf their context. Late afternoon is the best hour, when the sun comes in low under the beech canopy and the river below turns to brass.
t.old jewish cemetery mainz@50.0,8.3:
Some of the gravestones on the sandy rise known in Mainz as the Judensand are close to a thousand years old. The oldest dated stone here goes back to the middle of the eleventh century, which makes this one of the oldest Jewish cemeteries in Europe. Together with sites in Speyer and Worms, Mainz formed the ShUM communities, centres of learning on the Rhine whose scholars shaped Ashkenazi Judaism for centuries, and in 2021 the three were listed together as a World Heritage Site. Mainz was Magenza in Hebrew, home to rabbis whose rulings were followed far beyond the Rhineland.

The cemetery is a quiet, walled place with weathered sandstone stelae in neat rows, some leaning, some restored, many inscribed in Hebrew. Access to the old part is restricted and normally arranged through tours or by appointment, so be ready to see it partly from the viewing area by the wall. Dress respectfully and remember that men are expected to cover their heads inside Jewish cemeteries.

Mainz itself rewards a pause off the bike. The red sandstone cathedral of St Martin dominates the old town, the Gutenberg Museum honours the man who brought movable type printing to Europe here in the fifteenth century, and the half timbered streets around the Kirschgarten are good for a coffee. The city began as the Roman legionary base of Mogontiacum, guarding the confluence of the Main and the Rhine, and Roman remains turn up all over town. In the evenings, a glass of Rheinhessen wine in a Weinstube with a plate of Handkäse is a very local way to end the day.

Riding in and out of Mainz is city riding: tram lines, cobbles in the old town, bridges with heavy commuter traffic and plenty of traffic lights. The roads become far more enjoyable once you cross the Rhine into the Rheingau and climb into the Taunus, where the Roman frontier towers that give the ride its name sit in the forest, or head south into the vineyard hills of Rheinhessen on quiet roads between wine villages. Morning and early evening are the times to avoid the city ring roads. Fuel stations are everywhere around the city, and Budenheim to the west is a calmer place to fill up than the centre.
t.sareung cluster@37.6,127.2:
A queen who outlived her husband by more than sixty years lies here. Sareung is the tomb of Queen Jeongsun, wife of King Danjong, the boy king of the Joseon dynasty who was deposed by his uncle in 1455 and later killed in exile. Jeongsun lived on in poverty outside the capital, and the story of her loyalty and grief became one of the most moving in Korean history. Her tomb, a grassy mound guarded by stone figures and approached along a path through pine forest, is one of the forty Royal Tombs of the Joseon Dynasty listed together as a World Heritage Site in 2009.

The Joseon tombs follow strict principles of geomancy, placed with mountains behind and water in front, and their layout, with a red spirit gate, a stone path, a T-shaped shrine and the burial mound on a terrace above, is the same throughout. The forests around the tombs, protected for centuries, are among the most natural woodland near Seoul. Sareung is also home to a nursery of traditional trees, and the setting is peaceful and green.

Namyangju, on the eastern edge of the Seoul metropolitan area, is a mix of city, river and mountain. The Bukhan river and the Han meet nearby at Dumulmeori, a famous spot for misty mornings and photographs, and the riverside roads are popular with cyclists. The mountains around offer good roads with curves and views.

Riding in South Korea has one important rule: motorcycles are not allowed on expressways, so you must use national and local roads. Around Seoul, these are often busy and slow, with many traffic lights. The roads along the Bukhan river toward Gapyeong and Chuncheon are more pleasant, with views of the river and the mountains, and are well known among Korean riders.

Namyangju keeps you supplied with fuel and food. Try the local food, including grilled pork, makgeolli, rice wine, and the dakgalbi of Chuncheon, spicy stir fried chicken, if you ride further east. The tombs are open to visitors with a small entry charge, and are quiet on weekdays.
t.royal tombs in songsan ri@36.5,127.1:
In 1971, workers digging drainage near a group of ancient burial mounds above the Geum river at Gongju broke into a brick tomb that had never been looted. Inside lay the remains and treasures of King Muryeong of Baekje, who died in 523, and his queen: gold crowns, ornaments, a stone tablet naming the king, and thousands of objects. It was one of the greatest archaeological finds in Korean history, and it is the centrepiece of the Royal Tombs at Songsan-ri, part of the Baekje Historic Areas World Heritage Site listed in 2015.

The tombs are closed to protect them, but a replica tomb and an exhibition hall explain the finds, and the Gongju National Museum, nearby, displays the treasures. Baekje was one of the Three Kingdoms of ancient Korea, with close ties to China and Japan, and Gongju, then called Ungjin, was its capital for some sixty years in the fifth and sixth centuries before it moved to Buyeo.

Gongsanseong, a fortress with stone walls running along a ridge above the Geum river, is the other main site in Gongju, with gates, pavilions and views over the town and the river. Walking the walls takes an hour or two and is lovely in the evening.

The riding around Gongju is pleasant, with national roads following the Geum valley and climbing into the hills. Magoksa, a Buddhist mountain temple, part of the Sansa World Heritage listing, lies in a valley northwest of the town, reached by a scenic road. Gyeryongsan National Park, to the east, has mountain roads and temples. Remember that motorcycles cannot use expressways in Korea, so plan routes on national roads.

Gongju has a fuel station or two and shops. The town is known for chestnuts, and chestnut dishes and sweets are sold everywhere. The Baekje Cultural Festival, held in autumn in Gongju and Buyeo, is a major event with parades and lanterns on the river.
t.gochang@35.0,126.9:
Ancient Korea built more dolmens than anywhere else on earth. These megalithic tombs, a huge capstone resting on smaller upright stones, were raised by Bronze Age communities some three thousand years ago, and the clusters at Gochang, Hwasun and Ganghwa were listed together as a World Heritage Site in 2000. The coordinates here lie in the Hwasun group, south of Gwangju, where hundreds of dolmens are scattered along a valley, some with capstones weighing many tonnes, and the quarry sites where the stones were cut can still be seen on the hillsides.

Walking the dolmen trail at Hwasun is a quiet pleasure: the stones sit in forest and fields, with the hills rising on either side, and you can imagine the effort needed to move such blocks without machines. Gochang, further northwest, has the densest cluster of dolmens of all, with a museum explaining how they were built.

The countryside of South Jeolla is green and agricultural, with rice paddies, persimmon orchards and wooded hills. Hwasun is known for its hot springs and for the Unjusa temple, with its unusual collection of stone pagodas and Buddhas scattered across a valley, the subject of many legends. Naju, to the west, was once the capital of the region and is famous for pears and for gomtang, a beef soup.

The riding in this region is relaxed, with quiet national and local roads winding through farmland and hills. Traffic is light outside the cities, and surfaces are good. Remember that Korean expressways are off limits to motorcycles. Summer is hot and humid, with monsoon rains in July, and autumn is the best season, with clear skies and colourful leaves.

Hwasun, twelve kilometres away, is where riders refuel and eat, and Gwangju, the region's big city, has everything. Jeolla food is famous across Korea for its abundance: a meal comes with a table full of side dishes, and the kimchi is renowned.
t.seonamsa temple@35.0,127.3:
An old stone bridge arches over a stream in the forest on the way up to Seonamsa, and the view through its curve to a pavilion beyond is one of the best known images of Korean temple architecture. The Seungseongyo bridge dates back to the Joseon period, and the temple behind it, on the slopes of Jogyesan mountain near Suncheon, has a history going back to the ninth century. Seonamsa is one of seven Korean Buddhist mountain monasteries listed in 2018 as Sansa, Buddhist Mountain Monasteries in Korea, chosen because they have remained centres of living religious practice for over a thousand years.

The temple is the head of the Taego order, which allows married monks, and its halls, gardens and old trees, including famous plum trees that blossom in early spring, give it a peaceful, unpolished charm. A path over the mountain links it with Songgwangsa, one of the three jewel temples of Korea, on the other side of Jogyesan, a walk of several hours.

Suncheon Bay, south of the city, is one of the most important coastal wetlands in Korea, with vast reed beds and tidal flats, home to cranes in winter and part of the Getbol, Korean Tidal Flats World Heritage Site. The reeds turn golden in autumn, and the sunset from the observatory over the bay is spectacular. The Suncheon Bay National Garden, created for an expo, is a huge park nearby.

The riding here is pleasant, with national roads along the coast and into the mountains, light traffic and good surfaces. The road to Seonamsa climbs through forest along a stream, and the coastal roads around Yeosu and Goheung offer views over islands and sea. Expressways are closed to motorcycles.

Suncheon, fifteen kilometres away, has fuel, banks and simple restaurants, and Beolgyo, on the coast, is known for its cockles, served in many ways in local restaurants. Suncheon's food is excellent, as everywhere in Jeolla.
t.pajusamreung cluster@37.7,126.8:
Close to the most heavily fortified border in the world, three royal tombs of the Joseon dynasty lie in a quiet pine forest in Paju, north of Seoul. Pajusamreung, the three tombs of Paju, include the resting places of Queen Jangsun and Queen Gonghye, both married to kings and both of whom died young, and of King Jinjong, honoured after his early death. Like all the Joseon royal tombs, they follow a precise layout of spirit gates, stone paths, shrines and grass mounds guarded by stone officials and animals, and they are part of the World Heritage listing of the Royal Tombs of the Joseon Dynasty.

The forest around the tombs is peaceful, with walking paths through pine and oak, and the site sees few foreign visitors. Gongneung, Sulleung and Yeongneung, the three tombs, are spread across gentle hills.

Paju lies on the Imjin river, which forms part of the border area with North Korea, and the Demilitarized Zone is close. Imjingak, a park near the border, has monuments to the Korean War, a bridge that prisoners crossed at the end of the war, and observation points looking north. Tours to the DMZ and the Joint Security Area at Panmunjom leave from Seoul and Paju, subject to security conditions. Heyri Art Village and the Paju Book City are modern cultural districts nearby.

Riding in Paju is mixed: busy roads and new towns near Seoul, quieter roads near the border, with military checkpoints and restricted areas. Do not stray into restricted zones, and follow signs carefully. National roads are the only option for motorcycles, as expressways are closed to them. The Freedom Road along the Han river is a motorway and off limits.

Goyang, ten kilometres away, and Munsan have fuel and services. Paju is known for its jangdan beans, grown on the fertile plains near the border, and celebrated with a festival in autumn; tofu dishes in local restaurants make the most of them.
t.limes section between watchtowers wp 1 2:
Two thousand years ago, the frontier of the Roman Empire in Germany began right here. The Upper Germanic-Raetian Limes, a line of watchtowers, forts, palisades and ditches stretching more than five hundred kilometres to the Danube, started on the right bank of the Rhine at Rheinbrohl, and the watchtowers numbered WP 1/1 and onwards marched away from the river into the wooded hills. This little section between Rheinbrohl and Bad Hönningen is the very beginning of the line, part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire World Heritage site.

Archaeologists use the WP numbers to map every known watchtower, and they are a reminder of how systematic the Roman frontier was. Towers stood within sight of each other, linked by a path and backed by forts with garrisons. At Rheinbrohl, a museum called the RömerWelt brings the frontier to life with reconstructions, hands-on exhibits and a recreated watchtower, which is far more evocative than the faint earthworks you might find in the forest.

The riding here is Rhine valley riding: the B42 runs along the right bank between Koblenz and Bonn, past vineyards, castles and riverside villages, with the river always beside you. It is scenic, but it can be busy, and the speed limits are low in the villages. The real fun is in the side roads that climb up into the Westerwald, the wooded hills to the east, where narrow, winding roads lead through forests and small villages. A ferry crosses the Rhine to Bad Breisig, which is a pleasant way to switch banks.

The Rhine is the main presence here, wide and fast-flowing, busy with barges and cruise ships. On the slopes above, vineyards produce Riesling and other wines, and the forests are mostly beech and oak. Schloss Arenfels, a castle above Bad Hönningen, adds a romantic touch to the scene, with its towers and battlements.

Bad Hönningen and Rheinbrohl are small towns with fuel, cafés and shops. Bad Breisig, across the river, is a spa town with thermal baths. Andernach, a little further south, has a famous cold-water geyser. If you are hungry, look for a riverside restaurant serving fish or a hearty Rhineland dish like Sauerbraten.
t.national park wadden sea niedersachsen@5:
Behind the dyke at Dornumersiel the land is flatter than a billiard table and nearly as green, and on the other side the sea comes and goes twice a day across a vast expanse of sand and mud. This is the Wadden Sea, the largest system of intertidal flats in the world, stretching along the coasts of the Netherlands, Germany and Denmark. The Lower Saxony section is a national park and part of a World Heritage site, and at low tide you can walk out across the seabed towards the East Frisian islands, ideally with a guide who knows the channels and the tides.

The landscape is shaped by the sea and by people's efforts to keep it out. Dykes run along the coast, protecting the low-lying marshland behind them, where cattle and sheep graze and windmills and wind turbines turn. Small harbours like Nessmersiel and Dornumersiel are home to fishing boats and ferries to the islands, such as Baltrum and Langeoog. The East Frisian villages, with their brick houses, churches and tea rooms, have a distinctive character, and the people here drink more tea per head than almost anywhere in the world, with rock sugar and cream that forms clouds in the cup.

Riding here is flat and windy, sometimes extremely windy. The roads are straight, narrow and well-surfaced, running along dykes and through villages, with little traffic outside the summer season. It is not a place for curves, but there is something meditative about riding under huge skies with the smell of salt in the air. Watch out for sheep on the dykes, farm vehicles and cyclists, who are numerous in summer.

The Wadden Sea is one of the most important bird habitats in the world, with millions of migrating birds stopping here to feed in spring and autumn. You can see oystercatchers, curlews, avocets and many other waders on the mudflats, and seals resting on sandbanks. The light here is often magical, with dramatic clouds and sunsets over the water.

Dornum, about eight and a half kilometres away, has fuel and basic services, and its moated castle is worth a look. Hage and Norden are larger towns with more options. In the harbours, look for a fish stand selling Krabbenbrötchen, a bread roll filled with North Sea shrimp, the classic coastal snack.
t.fort site and civil settlement of nieder:
On the heights above the right bank of the Rhine, opposite Koblenz, the suburb of Niederberg sits on top of a Roman fort. It is one of the forts of the Upper Germanic Limes, which ran through the hills here a few kilometres back from the river, and the label refers to the fort site and the civilian settlement that grew up around it, part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire World Heritage site. Not much is visible today, as the area is built over, but the location explains a great deal.

From up here, you understand why everyone wanted to control this spot. Just below lies the confluence of the Rhine and the Moselle, at the Deutsches Eck, the German Corner, with its huge equestrian statue of Emperor Wilhelm I. Above the Rhine, next to Niederberg, stands the fortress of Ehrenbreitstein, one of the largest in Europe, rebuilt by the Prussians in the nineteenth century after the French blew up its predecessor. A cable car crosses the Rhine from the old town of Koblenz to the fortress, offering fine views of the river and the city.

The riding around Koblenz is excellent. The Rhine valley south of here, through the Upper Middle Rhine Valley, is a World Heritage site of castles, vineyards and steep slopes, and the roads along both banks are scenic, if often busy. The Moselle valley to the south-west is even more winding, with tight loops, vineyards and wine villages. East, the Westerwald offers quiet country roads through forests and hills. Surfaces are generally good, but expect heavy traffic around Koblenz and on summer weekends along the rivers.

The Rhine here is broad and powerful, and the slopes above it are covered with forests and vineyards. In spring and autumn the light on the river can be beautiful, and the views from Ehrenbreitstein at sunset are spectacular. The fortress also hosts events and exhibitions, and its grounds are a pleasant place to wander.

Vallendar, about three kilometres away, has fuel and basic services. Koblenz itself, just below, is a city with everything you need, including a charming old town full of restaurants and wine bars. Order a glass of Riesling from the Moselle or the Rhine and sit outside in one of the squares near the old churches.
t.watchtowers wp 4 45 to 4 52 including th:
North of Frankfurt, the Wetterau opens out as a wide, fertile basin between the Taunus and the Vogelsberg, and the Roman frontier made a long bulge around it to bring this rich farmland inside the empire. This section of the Upper Germanic Limes, with watchtowers WP 4/45 to 4/52, runs through the woods and fields between Langgöns and Lich, at the northern tip of that bulge. The towers are long gone, but traces of the wall and ditch can still be found in the forest.

The landscape here is rolling and gentle. The Wetterau is one of the oldest farmed areas in Germany, known for its fertile loess soils, and the fields of wheat, sugar beet and rapeseed stretch to the horizon. To the north and west, the forests of the Hausberg and the Taunus rise, and to the east lies the volcanic landscape of the Vogelsberg, the largest volcanic area in Central Europe.

The riding is pleasant rather than spectacular. Country roads run between villages and through forests, with gentle curves and good surfaces. The roads into the Vogelsberg, to the east, are more interesting, with longer climbs, more curves and fewer cars. On weekends, the area around the Hoherodskopf, the highest point of the Vogelsberg, is popular with riders. To the west, the Taunus offers more hills and forests, with the Feldberg as its highest point.

Near Lich lies the ruined Cistercian monastery of Arnsburg, a lovely, peaceful place with Gothic arches open to the sky and a cemetery for soldiers of the Second World War. Lich itself is known for its brewery, whose beer is popular across Hesse, and its old town has half-timbered houses and a fine church. The nearby fort of Arnsburg was one of the Roman forts along this stretch of the Limes.

Langgöns, about five kilometres away, and Lich are both towns with fuel, shops and restaurants. Giessen, a university city, is a little further north. Look for a traditional Hessian inn serving Handkäs mit Musik, a tangy sour-milk cheese marinated with onions, and a glass of Ebbelwoi, the local apple wine.
t.watchtowers wp 1 21 to 1 22@50.5,7.4:
Above Leutesdorf, on the right bank of the Rhine between Neuwied and Bad Hönningen, the hills climb steeply from the river, covered with vineyards and forests, and the Roman frontier ran along their crest. Watchtowers WP 1/21 and 1/22 stood here in the early part of the Upper Germanic Limes, just a few kilometres from its starting point at Rheinbrohl, watching over the valley and the lands beyond. Today the tower sites are quiet spots in the woods, part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire World Heritage site.

Leutesdorf is a wine village with a long history. Its steep slopes produce Riesling and other wines, and the village has narrow streets, old houses and a riverside promenade. Across the river lies Andernach, one of the oldest towns in Germany, founded by the Romans as Antunnacum. Andernach is known for its cold-water geyser, the highest of its kind in the world, which shoots water up to sixty metres into the air. A boat trip takes you to the geyser on a peninsula in the Rhine, and a museum explains the geology behind it.

The riding is a mix of river valley and hills. The B42 along the right bank of the Rhine is scenic but busy, with frequent villages and low speed limits. The roads that climb up from Leutesdorf and Hammerstein into the Westerwald are much more interesting, with steep, twisting sections through vineyards and forests, and great views back over the river. On the other side, the Eifel offers volcanic landscapes, with crater lakes, such as the Laacher See, and quiet country roads.

The Neuwied Basin, where the Rhine valley widens briefly, was shaped by volcanic activity, and the area is rich in pumice and basalt. The last major eruption, around thirteen thousand years ago, created the Laacher See and covered the region in ash. The vineyards above Leutesdorf benefit from the warm microclimate of the valley, and the forests are home to deer, wild boar and many bird species.

Leutesdorf has a few restaurants and wine taverns, but for fuel, Andernach, about four kilometres away across the river, or Neuwied, are the better options. Sit on the riverside terrace with a glass of local Riesling and watch the barges go by.
t.watchtower wp 1 62@50.4,7.6:
Höhr-Grenzhausen smells faintly of kilns if you catch it on the right day. This small town on the western edge of the Westerwald, a few kilometres north-east of Koblenz, sits at the heart of the Kannenbäckerland, the jug-bakers' country, where potters have been turning the local grey clay into salt-glazed stoneware for centuries. The Roman frontier passed right through here too, and watchtower WP 1/62 was one of the posts on the Upper Germanic Limes as it ran across these hills, now part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire World Heritage site.

The clay is the real story. Deposits of fine white and grey clay lie just under the surface across the Westerwald, and from the sixteenth century onwards the potters of Höhr, Grenzhausen and neighbouring villages produced the blue-and-grey jugs, mugs and storage jars that were exported across Europe and beyond. You will recognise the style: grey body, cobalt-blue decoration, and that slightly pitted glassy surface that comes from throwing salt into the kiln at full heat. The Keramikmuseum Westerwald in town tells the story, and there are still working potteries where you can watch the wheels turn.

From a rider's point of view, the Westerwald is underrated. It is a rolling upland of forests, meadows and small villages, crossed by quiet roads with plenty of curves and few straight lines. The descents towards the Rhine valley, through steep wooded side valleys, are particularly good fun, with tight bends and quick changes of gradient. The A3 motorway passes right by Höhr-Grenzhausen, but you will want to leave it as soon as possible. Weather on the plateau can be noticeably cooler and wetter than in the Rhine valley below, and fog lingers on autumn mornings.

Back in Roman times, this was the edge of the known world for the garrison soldiers. Beyond the line of towers and the palisade lay the territory of Germanic tribes, and the watchtowers served as observation posts, signalling stations and checkpoints for trade. Today, little remains on the ground, but walking paths follow the line of the Limes through the woods, with information boards at key points.

Höhr-Grenzhausen, just over a kilometre away, has fuel, shops, cafés and a few restaurants. Koblenz, down in the valley, has everything else. Bring home a small salt-glazed mug if you have space in the panniers; it will survive the journey better than you think.
t.gyeongju historic areas@35.8,129.2:
For nearly a thousand years, until the tenth century, Gyeongju was the capital of the kingdom of Silla, and the whole city is a museum with traffic lights. Round the modern centre the old kingdom lies in plain sight: great grass-covered burial mounds in a park in the middle of town, the pond of Anapji where the court held feasts, the stone observatory of Cheomseongdae, one of the oldest of its kind in East Asia, and the forested hills of Namsan scattered with rock-carved Buddhas. UNESCO listed these areas together in 2000, and the pieces are spread around town rather than gathered in one compound.

The coordinates here are just east of the city, in the hill country where Gyeongju meets the sea. The mention of petroglyphs on the label is a reminder that people were carving rock long before Silla, and this part of Korea's south-east is rich in such carvings. Silla itself unified most of the peninsula in the seventh century, and its tombs have given up gold crowns and glassware that show how far its trade reached along the Silk Road.

On a bike, Gyeongju is a pleasant, mild-mannered city to ride. The streets are broad and the pace is slow, with low height limits on new buildings to protect the historic skyline, and the hills east of town have quiet, curving roads past Bomun Lake, where cherry trees bloom in early April and draw dense crowds. Further on, the road to Bulguksa temple and the Seokguram grotto, a separate World Heritage site, climbs through forest with tight bends. Coastal roads to Gampo and the East Sea give long views and fresh fish, and roads are generally smooth and well signed.

Gyeongju has all the fuel and food you could want, and the local speciality is the Gyeongju bread, a small sweet pastry filled with red bean paste, sold hot in paper bags. The best times are spring and autumn, when the weather is dry and the leaves turn; summer is hot and humid and the monsoon rains can be heavy. Many sites close on set days and charge small entrance fees, so check before you set off, and wear shoes you can walk in.
t.yaksu ri tomb@38.9,125.4:
Not every place on a list like this is somewhere an ordinary visitor can simply ride to, and Yaksu-ri is one of them. The tomb lies in the west of North Korea, near the coastal city of Nampo, and it is one of the painted tombs of Koguryo, an ancient kingdom that ruled much of Korea and Manchuria for several centuries. The group of tombs was listed by UNESCO in 2004, and visits are only possible on organised, escorted tours, which means that planning a motorbike trip here is not realistic.

The tomb itself is well known among historians for its murals. Painted on plastered stone walls in the early centuries of the first millennium, they show scenes of daily life in unusual detail: a procession of officials and soldiers, musicians, a household, a kitchen and stables, with figures in different costumes. The tomb belonged to a high-ranking person, though experts do not agree on who, and the paintings give a view of Koguryo society that is hard to find anywhere else. Some details also show influences from China and Central Asia, a reminder of how connected the kingdom was.

The landscape around is low hills and rice fields, and the Taedong river runs to the sea nearby. The West Sea Barrage at Nampo, a huge dam across the estuary, is a large piece of Cold War engineering, and the countryside on the way to Pyongyang, the capital, is a mix of farmland, cooperative villages and modest towns. Roads are wide and often empty of traffic, but their quality varies, and foreigners are accompanied by guides throughout.

Because I do not have reliable knowledge of fuel, food or road conditions for independent travellers, and since there are none in practice, I would rather say so than guess. If you are drawn to this subject, the better advice is to read about Koguryo, whose later tombs are also found in Chinese territory around Ji'an, where access is easier. For anyone planning travel, check your government's current advice, because the situation can change.
t.seolleung cluster@37.5,127.0:
You come up out of the Seolleung subway station into the glass towers of Gangnam, and a few minutes later you are standing in a pine grove with royal tombs. The Seolleung cluster holds the burial mounds of King Seongjong, who died in the fifteenth century, and his queen, together with the tomb of King Jungjong, a later ruler, at a short distance. The park, surrounded by office blocks and busy roads, has the stillness of a place that has been left alone for five hundred years, and it is one of the most surprising pieces of silence in the city.

The tombs belong to the Joseon dynasty, which ruled Korea from 1392 to 1910 and placed a great deal of importance on correct burial and ancestor rites. Each tomb follows the same pattern: a round grass mound, protected by stone sheep and tigers, with a stone lantern, scholar and military figures standing guard, and a T-shaped shrine with a red gate, where rites were performed. The 40 royal tombs of Joseon were listed by UNESCO in 2009, and many are inside Seoul or just outside it. Nearby, the Buddhist temple of Bongeunsa is another surprise among the high-rises.

The ride is a different matter. Central Seoul is a dense, fast and demanding city, with multi-lane roads, constant traffic, couriers on scooters weaving between cars and heavy speed enforcement with cameras. Riding in the city is not relaxing, and the best advice is to park near the park and walk. Early morning and Sunday are quieter. If you want proper riding, the roads east of Seoul along the Han river and into the hills of Gyeonggi province are much more enjoyable.

Gangnam has everything: fuel stations, convenience stores open all night, coffee shops by the thousand and Korean barbecue restaurants on every side street. The tomb park charges a small entrance fee and generally closes one day a week, so check the day before you go. Visit in autumn, when the maples and ginkgo turn and the mounds are ringed in gold.
t.jeongnimsa temple site@36.3,126.9:
Buyeo was the last capital of Baekje, one of the three ancient kingdoms of Korea, and it feels like the sort of town that remembers it. Baekje moved its court here in 538 and held it until it fell to an alliance of Silla and Tang China in 660, and the little river town on the Geum river has been quietly proud of that heritage ever since. The temple site of Jeongnimsa is at the heart of it, and what is left is a grassy rectangle with the foundations of the halls, a stone pagoda and a Buddha figure under a roof.

The five-storey stone pagoda is the main attraction, a tall, slender tower that is among the oldest and best preserved of its kind in Korea, with a graceful curve to its eaves. It also carries a strange inscription, carved by the Tang general who conquered the city, celebrating his victory, a record of conquest on a monument that was supposed to be sacred. The site was listed by UNESCO in 2015 as part of the Baekje Historic Areas, together with Gongju and Iksan.

For a rider, the Buyeo area is peaceful and pleasant. The Geum river runs slowly through flat farmland, with low hills, and roads along its banks are smooth and lightly trafficked, passing rice fields, greenhouses and small villages. It is easy riding and good for an unhurried afternoon, though in the main town the streets are narrow and a bit confusing. Summer is hot and humid, and the best seasons are spring, with fresh green fields, and autumn, when the hills turn gold and the sky is clear.

Buyeo is a town of thirty thousand people, so fuel and meals are easy to find. A pond called Gungnamji, near the town, was built in the seventh century by a Baekje king and is covered in lotus flowers in July, and the Nakhwaam rock above the river is linked to a legend of court ladies who threw themselves into the water during the fall of the city. The Baekje Incense Burner, one of the great treasures of Korean metalwork, was found nearby, and a small museum tells the story.
t.homam ri sasin@39.1,125.9:
The Four Guardians, the dragon of the east, the tiger of the west, the red bird of the south and the black tortoise entwined with a snake in the north, rule the walls of the Homam-ri tomb. Painted more than fifteen hundred years ago in the Koguryo kingdom, which dominated Korea and parts of Manchuria in those centuries, they are drawn in sweeping lines and bright mineral colours, and they twist across the stone as if in motion. The tomb is in the area around Pyongyang, in North Korea, and the whole group of Koguryo tombs was listed by UNESCO in 2004.

The Four Guardians had a job. In the cosmology the Koguryo shared with China, they protected the four directions of the universe and, in a tomb, the spirit of the dead person lying at the centre, so the paintings are less decoration than a map of the cosmos built around a grave. Ceilings in such tombs are often painted with stars and with the sun and moon, while the corridors are filled with processions and feasting scenes. This tomb, like Yaksu-ri, is a reminder of how sophisticated the kingdom's art was.

It would be misleading to describe a ride here, because it is not possible to explore North Korea on your own. Foreign visitors travel in organised groups with official guides, and independent motorcycling is not allowed. The roads around Pyongyang are wide, often with very little traffic, and the capital is a city of broad boulevards and monumental buildings, though what you see is carefully managed.

I do not have reliable information about fuel and food for travellers here, so I will leave that blank rather than invent it. If you want to see Koguryo art without these limits, look at the museum collections and publications, or at the tombs in the Chinese city of Ji'an, whose painted tomb chambers have been open to visitors for longer. In any case, check what your own government advises before you plan anything near this border.
t.olleung cluster@37.7,127.0:
Seoul's royal tombs are not all in the city centre, and the ones on this stretch lie in the green country just to the north-west, in a belt of forest, farmland and expanding suburbs that stretches towards the border. The cluster on our list is one of several groups of Joseon dynasty burial mounds, and the nearest sizeable town is Uijeongbu, nearly half a million people, with Goyang just beyond it. I cannot say exactly which of the tombs sits at these coordinates, but the pattern is consistent across the dynasty.

Joseon kings and queens were buried in carefully chosen places, according to the principles of geomancy, with a hill behind and water in front, and each tomb is a small landscape of its own. A round mound ringed by stone fences sits on a grass slope, with stone figures of civil officials, soldiers and animals set out along the approach, a T-shaped shrine for ceremonies and a red-painted spirit gate. The groves around them were protected for centuries, which is why many of the tombs lie in unexpectedly good woodland, with old pines and oaks. The 40 tombs were listed by UNESCO in 2009.

Riding here, the best of the landscape lies close to Bukhansan, the granite mountain park on Seoul's northern edge, where jagged peaks rise above the suburbs and hiking trails are busy on weekends. The roads are paved, busy and well marked, with some good winding sections on the edge of the hills, though traffic can be heavy, and speed cameras are common. On weekdays, mornings are calm, and in autumn the colour on the mountains is spectacular. Winters are cold and dry, and snow can make hill roads slippery.

Uijeongbu, about nine kilometres away, has plenty of fuel, restaurants and convenience stores, and it is famous for budae jjigae, a spicy stew made from sausages, noodles and kimchi that was born after the Korean War from American army rations. Entrance fees are small and the tomb parks usually close one day a week, so look it up before you go, and keep to the paths, because the grass mounds are sacred.
t.eisinga planetarium in franeker@53.2,5.5:
Eise Eisinga was a wool comber in the Frisian town of Franeker, not a professional astronomer, and in the 1770s he built the solar system on his living-room ceiling. The story goes that in 1774 a local pastor predicted that the planets would align and bring disaster, and the town panicked. Eisinga, who knew some mathematics, wanted to show the real movements, and over the next seven years he built a scale model of the planets, with a clockwork mechanism hidden in the attic that still moves them today. It is generally described as the oldest working planetarium in the world, and it was listed by UNESCO in 2023.

The house is a small canal-side building in Franeker, a quiet town in the north of the Netherlands. Franeker once had a university, founded in the sixteenth century and closed by Napoleon in the early nineteenth, and the town has a handsome town hall, a canal and a general air of having seen busier days. Friesland, with its own language, flag and a very strong sense of identity, is a flat country of pastures, black-and-white cows, windmills, and sky that fills most of the view.

On a bike, Friesland is all about wind and open roads. The routes along dikes are smooth, flat and fast, with the wind coming off the Wadden Sea, and it can push a bike around, so expect to lean into it. Speed limits are strictly enforced, and cameras are frequent, so keep to the posted limits. The famous Afsluitdijk, the thirty-two-kilometre dike that closes off the old Zuiderzee, is about thirty kilometres from here, and the harbour town of Harlingen is much closer. Cyclists are everywhere, and they have priority in many places.

Franeker is a town of around thirteen thousand, so you will find fuel, bakeries and cafes without difficulty. Try Frisian sugar bread, sweet and sticky, with coffee, and if you are here in winter, remember that this is the country of the Elfstedentocht, the legendary skating race that depends on very cold winters. Booking ahead is advisable for the planetarium, because it takes small groups, and it is closed on some days, particularly Mondays.
t.sint leonarduskerk@50.8,5.1:
The church of Saint Leonard rises over the little town of Zoutleeuw, in the fruit-growing country east of Leuven, and it is far grander than the size of the place suggests. In the Middle Ages the town, known in French as Léau, was a prosperous trading centre on a route between Brabant and Liège, and its burghers put their money into stone. Work on the church began in the thirteenth century and went on for generations, giving a late Gothic body with a tall tower, rich sculpture and a lofty, light interior with white walls and tall windows.

Inside, the church is a treasury. The most remarkable object is the sacrament tower, a slender stone structure about eighteen metres high that reaches almost to the vaulting, carved in the sixteenth century in a mixture of Gothic and Renaissance forms, with tiny figures and canopies. It is one of the masterpieces of its kind in Europe and is attributed to the sculptor Cornelis Floris. There is also a fine rood screen, a series of carved altars and a collection of paintings and church silver. The town's other buildings, including a Renaissance town hall and a beguinage, are also worth a look, though the place is small enough to cover on foot in an hour.

The countryside here is Hageland and Haspengouw, soft, rolling farmland with orchards of apple, pear and cherry, and the best time is April when the blossom is out, or September when the fruit is ripe. The roads are flat or gently undulating, narrow and often lined with trees, with surface quality that varies, and in Belgium you should watch for cobbles, mud left by tractors and cyclists. The roads between the villages are quiet, and short stretches of good tarmac make for relaxed riding. Rain is frequent, so be ready.

Zoutleeuw has a few thousand people, so you will find fuel, bakeries and cafes without any trouble, and larger places such as Tienen and Sint-Truiden are a short ride away. Try a Belgian waffle or a local beer in a cafe on the market square, or perhaps a slice of fruit tart in season. Check the church's opening hours before you go, because it is not always open outside the afternoon.
t.watchtowers wp 1 83 to 1 86@50.4,7.8:
The Limes was a long wall, in effect, that stretched for about 550 kilometres across Germany, from the Rhine near Koblenz to the Danube near Regensburg. It was built in stages from the first century AD, starting as a line of wooden watchtowers and a cleared strip through the forest, and then gaining a ditch, a palisade and, in places, a wall. The watchtowers were numbered by the German scholars who surveyed the line in the late nineteenth century, hence the codes such as WP 1/83, which mean watchpost number 83 in section 1. The Upper Germanic-Raetian Limes was listed by UNESCO in 2005.

Here, in the Westerwald hills north of the Lahn, the line passes through forest and farmland, and the watchtowers are small mounds or low stone foundations among the trees, with information boards, and in a few places, reconstructed towers. Nearby, the fortlet at Pfarrhofen and the other fortlets show how the frontier was held. It is a quiet and rather atmospheric place, where you can walk along the ridge and imagine a handful of soldiers watching for movements on the other side.

Bad Ems, a few kilometres away, is a nineteenth-century spa town in a narrow valley of the Lahn, where the Russian tsars, Kaiser Wilhelm I and Napoleon III took the waters. It also lent its name to the Ems Dispatch of 1870, the telegram that Bismarck edited to provoke a war with France. The elegant colonnades and the bathing halls give a different kind of history to the Roman mounds above the town.

The Westerwald is good riding country, with its forested ridges, small valleys and quiet roads, and the roads here follow the contours with tight, shaded bends and surfaces of mixed quality. The Lahn valley road is pretty, with castles above the river and the cycle path alongside. Spring and autumn are best, and in winter the hills can be icy. Traffic is light on the minor roads, but watch for farm vehicles and walkers, especially at weekends.

Bad Ems has fuel, cafes and restaurants, with all the services of a small spa town, and Koblenz is about twenty kilometres to the west. Carry a map or offline route, since signal can fade in the valleys, and use the marked Limes trail if you want to find the next tower.
t.watchtower wp 1 65@50.4,7.7:
Höhr-Grenzhausen is the capital of the Kannenbäckerland, the jug-bakers' land, a corner of the Westerwald where the clay is so good that people have been making pots from it for five hundred years. The grey stoneware, fired at high temperature and decorated in cobalt blue, was exported across Europe in the form of jugs, tankards and bottles, and the workshops and kilns still fill the town. The German Ceramics Museum in Höhr-Grenzhausen is one of the best of its kind, with objects from medieval jugs to modern art.

The watchtower on our list, WP 1/65, belongs to the Upper Germanic-Raetian Limes, the Roman frontier that crossed the Westerwald on its way from the Rhine, and it is one of a series of towers recorded by early surveyors. The Limes begins at the Rhine at Rheinbrohl, not far from here, where a small information centre and a reconstructed section of palisade and tower help you picture the line. I cannot tell you exactly what survives at these coordinates, but the forest around is typical, with traces of the ditch and mounds visible to a trained eye.

The ride is attractive. The roads climb from the Rhine valley at Koblenz into the Westerwald, with long, forested ridges, open meadows and small villages, and then drop back to the river, where the Rhine gorge, with its castles, vineyards and the Loreley rock, is a short distance away. The bends are generally smooth, and the surface is good on the main routes and rougher on the forest tracks. Traffic in the Rhine valley can be heavy, particularly on summer weekends, so start early and take the quieter side roads.

Höhr-Grenzhausen has fuel and a good choice of cafes, and the nearby town of Montabaur, with its hilltop castle, is a pleasant detour. Buy a piece of stoneware as a souvenir, but pack it carefully, since a saddlebag is a rough place for a jug. In autumn the Westerwald forests glow with colour, and the air smells of woodsmoke and wet leaves.
t.watchtowers wp 3 20 to 3 22@50.2,8.3:
The Taunus is the low, wooded range north of Frankfurt, and the Romans chose it as the place to draw their line. The Limes crossed the ridge at a height that gave good views over both sides, and watchtowers placed close together made it possible to send signals by fire and smoke from tower to tower. The numbers, such as WP 3/20, are from the survey carried out by German archaeologists at the end of the nineteenth century, and they refer to the third section of the line. The Upper Germanic-Raetian Limes was listed by UNESCO in 2005.

Here, near Idstein, the towers are low mounds and stone foundations in forest, with the Ferbach fortlet nearby, and the place is quiet and shady, with beech trees and a carpet of leaves. The fort of Zugmantel, a few kilometres away, was an important frontier post, and the Saalburg, near Bad Homburg, has a fort that was reconstructed in the early twentieth century and is now a museum, which gives a clear idea of what the buildings looked like.

Idstein itself is worth a look. The town has a well-preserved old centre with timber-framed houses, some of them carved and painted, a tower from the Middle Ages called the Witches' Tower, and a church with a painted interior, built by the counts of Nassau. The town was once a seat of the counts, and the castle courtyard has a fine view.

The Taunus is pleasant riding, with winding roads through beech and oak woods, small climbs and descents, and little villages on the way. The roads between Wiesbaden and Limburg are smooth and fast in places, and the quiet forest roads around Idstein offer more intimate bends. The Feldberg, the highest point of the range, is a popular goal, and it is busy on sunny weekends. Autumn brings red and gold, and winter can be icy at height. Idstein, three kilometres away, has fuel stations and cafes, and a Saturday market, and it is a good place for a break.
t.byeongsan seowon@36.5,128.6:
Byeongsan Seowon sits above a bend of the Nakdong river, a few kilometres from the village of Hahoe and about fifteen kilometres from Andong, in the rolling, rural interior of North Gyeongsang province. The river curves around a cliff face called Buyongdae, and the academy looks across the water to the opposite cliff in a way that is almost a painting. Andong, a city of about a hundred and thirty thousand people, is the nearest place of any size.

A seowon was a private Confucian academy, a school and shrine for the study of the classics, founded in the Joseon period by scholars who wanted to keep away from the politics of the capital. Byeongsan was founded to honour Ryu Seong-ryong, the prime minister during the Japanese invasions of the 1590s, whose memoir of the war, the Jingbirok, is considered a national treasure. The buildings are plain, low and handsome, made of dark wood with tiled roofs, set on terraces down the hill, and the finest is the pavilion called Manhyudae, a long open hall overlooking the river, where scholars sat to discuss poetry and philosophy. UNESCO included Byeongsan and eight other academies in its World Heritage list in 2019. Visit quietly, and take off your shoes when you enter any building.

The riding in South Korea's interior is better than its reputation. Roads are well surfaced, signposts are clear, speed cameras are everywhere, and traffic outside the cities is light, so a day among rice terraces, orchards and small mountains is easy. The roads along the Nakdong wind between hills and rice fields, with pretty villages of thatched and tiled roofs. Summers are hot and wet, with a monsoon season in July, and winters are cold and dry. The best months are late April to June and September to October, when the apple orchards blossom or the persimmons ripen.

Andong is the place for fuel and food. The local speciality is jjimdak, chicken braised with noodles, potatoes and soy, and the city is also known for salted mackerel and a famous distilled spirit, Andong soju. Hahoe village, nearby, is itself a World Heritage site, with a centuries-old clan village of tiled houses and a mask dance tradition. Yeongju and Mungyeong, further afield, have temples and bigger markets. Look for a small restaurant serving a set meal, with rice, soup and many little side dishes, and expect it to be generous.
t.archeological site in wanggung ri@36.0,1:
The Honam plain in south-western Korea is a wide, flat land of rice fields, and its northern edge near Iksan is the oldest rice country on the peninsula, where the kingdom of Baekje once had a second capital. Wanggung-ri is the site of a royal palace, about ten kilometres from the middle of Iksan, in fields gently rising to low hills. UNESCO recognised it in 2015 as one of the historic areas of Baekje, the old kingdom that ruled the south-west from the first to the seventh century.

Baekje was a sophisticated state, with a lively trade with China and Japan, and its craftsmen and monks introduced Buddhism and writing to Japan. In the early seventh century, King Mu is said to have built a palace here, and the site, excavated since the 1960s, shows the foundations of workshops, a garden with a pond, a water supply system and what may be the earliest known royal toilets in the region. A five-storey stone pagoda stands in the middle of the fields, in a plain, elegant style that was imitated in Japan. A few kilometres away, the Mireuksa temple site has the remains of the largest stone pagoda in Korea, partly rebuilt. The Mireuksa story involves King Mu's marriage to a princess of the rival Silla kingdom, which is told in legend and is certainly not proven.

For a rider the pleasure is the pace. The roads through the plain are flat and straight, with long sight-lines over rice paddies and the odd greenhouse, and the surface is excellent, while speed cameras are frequent and well signed. Further east, the roads climb into the Jeonbuk mountains with bends and forest views, and Maisan, a pair of rock peaks resembling horse ears, is a day away. Summers are humid, with a rainy season in July, and autumn, with golden rice and red maple leaves, is the finest season.

Iksan, a city of nearly three hundred thousand people, has all the fuel and food you want, and Wanju and Yeonmu are smaller towns. Jeonju, about twenty-five kilometres east, is the capital of Korean cuisine, famous for bibimbap, a bowl of rice mixed with vegetables, egg and chilli paste, and has a large old quarter of tiled houses. Take water, a hat and sunscreen to the site, since there is little shade.
t.rietveld schroderhuis@52.1,5.1:
On a quiet residential street in Utrecht, a few minutes from the centre by bicycle, stands a small box-shaped house made of white and grey planes, with black frames and touches of red, yellow and blue, which looks as though it had been made from a Mondrian painting. This is the Rietveld Schroder House, built in 1924 and inscribed by UNESCO in 2000 as a masterpiece of the De Stijl movement and of modern architecture. The old centre of Utrecht, with its cathedral tower and its canals, is under two kilometres away.

The house was designed by Gerrit Rietveld, a cabinet-maker turned architect, for Truus Schroder-Schrader, a widow with three children who wanted a house without fixed rooms. The result was extraordinary. The upper floor is one large open space that can be divided by sliding panels, like a stage set, with windows that open at the corner so that walls seem to disappear. Furniture, including Rietveld's famous red and blue chair, is built into the design. Truus lived in the house until her death in 1985, and visitors can see it as she kept it. Tours are small, guided and need to be booked ahead, and photography inside may be restricted.

Cycling is the Dutch way of getting around, and a motorcyclist in Utrecht needs patience. The city has narrow canal streets, one-way systems, trams and a swarm of cyclists with right of way, and parking is limited. The better riding is outside, on the dykes and country roads along the Kromme Rijn, the Vecht with its string of castles and country houses, and through the wooded ridge of the Utrechtse Heuvelrug to the east. The land is flat, the roads are good and speed limits are strict, with plenty of cameras. Wind is constant, rain can arrive at any time, and in winter the dykes can be icy.

Utrecht has nearly three hundred thousand people, all the fuel and food you could want, and countless cafes on the canal-side wharves, where the cellars were once used to store goods. Try a stroopwafel, a caramel waffle, with coffee, or a plate of herring in season. The best months are May, June and September, and a weekday avoids crowds at the house.
t.utrecht groot zandveld@52.1,5.1:
West of Utrecht, where the old city fades into meadows and a newly built suburb called Leidsche Rijn, a flat green belt of polder and ditches runs between the villages of Vleuten, Veldhuizen and De Meern. The low land here was part of a defence system that worked by water, the Dutch Waterline, and the Groot Zandveld label refers to this country. I cannot say what stands exactly on the spot, so I will describe the setting and what it meant.

The Dutch worked out centuries ago that the best defence of the western provinces was to open sluices and flood the fields to a depth of about thirty centimetres, too shallow for boats and too deep for soldiers and guns. The New Dutch Waterline, built in the nineteenth century, ran from the Zuiderzee to the Rhine, with a chain of forts, dykes and sluices that could be closed to flood the land in front of Utrecht and Amsterdam. Many of the forts survive, with earth ramparts, moats and brick casemates, and some are now museums or nature reserves. The line was already out of date by the First World War, but it was last used in 1940, and the system is inscribed with the Defence Line of Amsterdam on the UNESCO list.

Near Vleuten lies Castle De Haar, a magnificent neo-Gothic palace rebuilt in the 1890s by the architect Pierre Cuypers, who also designed the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam, for the Baron van Zuylen, whose wife was a Rothschild. It stands in the village of Haarzuilens, with moats, turrets and a large park, and it is a fairy-tale building. Slot Zuylen, on the Vecht, is a smaller and older castle that is also open to visitors.

The riding here is gentle and flat, on dyke roads and narrow lanes along ditches, with farms, cows and cyclists. Speed limits are low, there are many speed cameras, and many roads are used by cyclists, who have priority. The landscape is wide and open, with long skies, strong winds and sudden showers. Early morning mist over the polder in spring and autumn is lovely, while winter days can be raw and foggy.

Vleuten, with seven thousand people, has fuel, supermarkets and cafes, and Utrecht is only a few minutes away, with every kind of service. Order a coffee with a piece of apple pie, and watch the cyclists go by.
t.kottenforst sud villiper bach@50.7,7.1:
South of Bonn, between the Rhine and the Eifel foothills, the Kottenforst is a big forest that most people drive around and few really enter. For centuries it was a hunting forest of the Electors of Cologne, who ran straight rides through the trees for their parties, and some of those long avenues survive as forest tracks. Oak and beech dominate, with ponds and damp hollows where the Villiper Bach, a small stream, begins its journey toward the Rhine. In spring the floor is carpeted with wood anemones, and in autumn the leaf litter smells sharp and sweet.

Roman soldiers knew this country too. The Rhine formed the frontier of the empire here, with the legionary base of Bonna at Bonn and a line of watchtowers and posts along the river and across the hills behind it, and the numbered towers named on the maps for this area refer to that chain. The stones are mostly gone, but the logic of the landscape is clear: high ground with a view over the river plain, close enough to send a signal.

The nearest town is Wachtberg, with about twenty thousand people, and Meckenheim and Königswinter are within easy range. Wachtberg has an unusual history as the home of many foreign embassies and offices in the years when Bonn was the capital of West Germany, and the villages around still have an international air. Fuel is easy to find in all three towns, and bakeries and cafés abound.

For riding, the Kottenforst offers calm, shaded roads through the trees, with smooth tarmac and gentle bends, ideal for an early morning or a hot day. The edges of the forest open into fields and orchards, and to the east you can see the Siebengebirge, the seven hills crowned by the Drachenfels. Weekends bring cyclists, walkers and horse riders, so slow down on the forest roads. Spring and autumn are lovely, and winter fog can make the roads damp and slippery.
t.fort site and civil settlement of butzba:
Butzbach lies in the Wetterau, a fertile, rolling plain north of Frankfurt, with the wooded Taunus hills rising to the south. In Roman times, the Limes, the frontier of the Empire, ran through this country, and a fort stood on the site of today's town, with a civil settlement, or vicus, growing beside it to serve the soldiers. The Upper Germanic-Raetian Limes, a stretch of palisade, ditch and wall that ran for hundreds of kilometres, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and Butzbach is one of the places along its line.

Not far to the south, the Saalburg, a reconstructed fort in the Taunus, shows how these places looked, with gates, towers and barracks rebuilt, and it makes an excellent companion visit. In the Wölferheimer Wald, a signal tower marks another piece of the frontier system, one of many watchtowers that were placed in sight of each other, so that a fire or a flag could pass a warning along the line. You can feel the logic of the landscape on a clear day.

The modern town of Butzbach, with about twenty-five thousand people, has a handsome market square lined with half-timbered houses, a castle and plenty of places to eat. Fuel stations are easy to find, and there is no shortage of cafés and bakeries. The Hessian specialities are Handkäse mit Musik, a sour-milk cheese served with onions and vinegar, and Frankfurter green sauce, with eggs and potatoes, and apple wine is the traditional drink.

For riders, the Wetterau offers wide, gentle roads through farmland, with long views and light traffic, while the Taunus to the south has more twisting roads through beech woods, climbing to the old forts and the high ridge. The A5 motorway runs close by, so weekends can bring busy traffic. Spring blossom and the golden fields of late summer are lovely, and in autumn the beech woods glow. Check the weather, as the Taunus can be foggy and wet when the plain is dry.
t.watchtowers wp 5 11 to 5 12@50.1,9.0:
Between Hanau and the river Main, the plain is flat, fertile and dense with small towns, and it hardly looks like a frontier. Yet around the year 100 the Romans ran their Upper Germanic Limes down this way to meet the Main near Großkrotzenburg, with a palisade, ditch and a line of wooden watchtowers set at intervals of a few hundred metres. The towers on the maps are labelled by section and number, and WP 5/11 and 5/12 are two of them, neighbours in a long chain that once stretched across Germany for hundreds of kilometres.

Nothing tall stands here now. What you will find is a field edge, a row of trees, or the odd information board, but if you look at the ground you realise why the position was chosen: it is high enough to see across the open plain, with a clear sightline to the next tower. A fire or a flag could carry a warning along the line in minutes. This stretch of the frontier is included in the UNESCO listing for the Upper Germanic-Raetian Limes.

Erlensee, Rodenbach and Großkrotzenburg are all within about five kilometres, and each has fuel, a bakery and a place to eat. Hanau itself, a little farther, was the birthplace of the Brothers Grimm in the 1780s and has a monument to them in the market square. Großkrotzenburg has the remains of its Roman fort beside the Main, which is the obvious place to see the stones the towers once reported to.

Riding here is easy and unhurried. Flat, straight farm roads link the villages, with orchards, asparagus and strawberry fields in season, and a relaxed pace with a lot of cyclists. The Main bank has pleasant traffic-free stretches in the evening. There is nothing technical, but it is a satisfying link between the busy Frankfurt area and the hills of the Spessart and Vogelsberg to the east and north. Spring blossom and late summer harvest light are best, and winter fog can hang over the fields for days.
t.neuss reckberg wachtturm@51.2,6.8:
Neuss has been a garrison town for two thousand years, and it still carries the Roman name in a shortened form: Novaesium, the legionary fortress that stood on the Rhine near the mouth of the Erft, was one of the oldest Roman military sites in Germany, founded in the days of Augustus. The Rhine was the frontier here, the Lower Germanic Limes, with no wall but a river, fortresses and watchtowers like the one at Reckberg, and the whole line was added to the UNESCO list in 2021.

Reckberg lies on the left bank, on the edge of the Düsseldorf conurbation, among fields, allotments and suburban streets. A watchtower here would have watched the river traffic and the far bank, where the tribes of the Germanic lands lived. The site is a modest one, so go with the right expectations: an archaeological spot in a city landscape, where a bench and a sign tell the story. The pleasure lies in knowing what the flat plain once defended.

Düsseldorf, five kilometres to the east across the Rhine, is a big city, with all the fuel and food you could want, and its old town, the Altstadt, is famous as the longest bar in the world, serving Altbier, a dark, bitter beer, in small glasses. Neuss, with its Quirinus Minster and a good Roman museum at Hafen, is a comfortable place to stop for a coffee. The Rhine promenade in Düsseldorf is excellent for a late afternoon walk.

The riding is mostly urban or flat farmland, so expect traffic, roundabouts and the odd cobbled square. Early on a Sunday morning, the Rhine meadows are calm, with cyclists and herons. Further upriver, toward Cologne, and downriver toward Krefeld and the Lower Rhine, roads follow the old dikes, with wide views and strong headwinds in spring. Fog is common in late autumn, when the river valley fills with mist and the lights of the barges slide silently by.
The Kottenforst is a big, flat-topped wooded ridge south-west of Bonn, an island of oak and hornbeam in a landscape of fields and commuter towns. It was a hunting forest of the Electors of Cologne, and the straight avenues that cut through it, still named Allee, were laid out in the eighteenth century so that a hunting party could ride after game, or follow falcons, in a precise geometric pattern. Elector Clemens August, who built the Augustusburg palace at Brühl and the little hunting lodge of Falkenlust beside it, loved heron hunting with falcons, and the avenues were part of that grand and slightly absurd game.

The Wattendorfer Allee is one of those straight lines. Riding or walking here, you notice first how quiet it is. The woods are tall and cool, with beech and oak overhead, pale green in spring and rusty in November, and a smell of leaf mould and damp earth. Deer are common at dusk, and woodpeckers drum in the dead limbs. The forest also carries a good share of horses, hikers and cyclists, so a motorcycle should be used on the public roads only and the forest tracks left to people on feet and hooves.

For the rider, the pleasure is on the approach rather than the avenue itself. The roads that cross the Kottenforst and drop towards Wachtberg and the Rhine are gently winding, often tree-lined, and not very fast, with a surface that suffers from tree roots and winter frosts. From the western edge you can sometimes look east across the valley to the Siebengebirge, the cluster of rounded volcanic hills above Königswinter, with the Drachenfels as the best-known summit. On sunny weekends the tourist traffic from Bonn is thick, so a weekday morning is far better.

Wachtberg, three or four kilometres away, is a large municipality of twenty thousand people with fuel, bakeries and a few places for lunch, and Meckenheim and Königswinter are both within reach if you need more choice. This is a place for a calm hour between more demanding roads, to listen to the trees and look at the shapes cut by an eighteenth-century aristocrat who preferred geometry to nature.
t.key planning decision@53.3,7.2:
Where the Ems river meets the sea near Emden, the land runs out of ideas. East Frisia is flat and wide, laced with dykes, drainage ditches and wind turbines, and the horizon is a ruler line drawn under a very large sky. The label here is an administrative one, a planning decision, so it points to no single monument. What it describes is the landscape around the Dollart bay and the Wadden Sea shore west of Emden, where the sea has repeatedly eaten into the land and been pushed back by people with spades and later with machines.

Emden is the real anchor. It is a port city of fifty thousand people at the mouth of the Ems, shaped by shipping and by the Volkswagen plant that has dominated the working life of the region for decades. Much of the old centre was destroyed in the Second World War, so the town can feel more practical than pretty, but the harbour is lively, the old sailing ships tie up in the Ratsdelft, and the fish sandwiches along the waterfront are an honest local pleasure. East Frisians are also famous for drinking more tea than almost anyone, taken with a lump of rock sugar and a spoonful of cream, so a pot of tea is not a pleasant extra but a local reflex.

On the bike, it is all about wind. A westerly off the North Sea can lean a loaded motorcycle sideways on exposed stretches, and the dyke roads are straight, with no overtaking room and quick changes of direction when a village appears. Traffic is light, speed cameras are common, and the surface is generally smooth but marked by the soft ground. Put your helmet visor down against the insects in summer and wear an extra layer even in June.

Fuel is easy in Emden itself, about ten kilometres away, and in Bunde, which is a small town on the way to the Dutch border. The best time for a ride is late summer or early autumn, when the light on the water is low and clear and the geese begin to arrive from the north. Winter brings fog and a hard, bright cold that suits those who like the empty edge of Germany.
Kottenforst is the name of a forest, but on the ride it is a long, patient place to be. This is the southern end of that great woodland ridge above Bonn, and the Wattendorfer Allee is one of the straight, wide avenues driven through it in the eighteenth century for the Electors of Cologne. The avenues radiate from older hunting points, and they still run dead straight for kilometres, so that from the right spot you can look down a green corridor that ends in a pinprick of light.

What interests me here is the nature rather than the history. The Kottenforst is one of the larger wooded areas left in the Rhineland, and the trees are mostly old oak and hornbeam, with beech where the soil is drier. Small ponds and wet patches in the clay support amphibians, and the area is known for its bats and woodpeckers.
