The air is damp even on dry days, and the smell, especially after rain, is deep and earthy. Spring brings wild garlic and bluebells in places, and autumn brings mushroom pickers, who are not always happy to see a motorcycle.

Riding in the forest and around its edges is a slow business. The through roads are narrow, shaded and occasionally greasy with leaves, and the tracks are meant for walkers and horse riders, so stay on tarmac. On the western side the land drops towards the Swist valley and the orchards of the Rhineland, and on the eastern side it falls to the Rhine and a view of the Siebengebirge. Nothing here is fast, but the loops through Wachtberg and the villages around it are relaxed and well worth an unhurried hour.

Wachtberg, less than four kilometres away, is a sprawling municipality with several villages, with fuel, bakeries, and a few decent places to eat. Königswinter, farther on, is the tourist town at the foot of the Drachenfels, and Meckenheim is the quieter market town to the south-west, where the apple orchards begin. Weekday mornings and cool, bright October days give the best light through the trees.
t.fortlet rheinbohl@50.5,7.3:
Rheinbrohl is where Germany's longest Roman frontier begins. The Upper Germanic Limes, a line of watchtowers, palisades and forts, starts at the Rhine here and runs east and south for some five hundred kilometres across Germany. At the Rheinbohl fortlet you can see the lines of a small Roman post, a few dozen soldiers who watched the river approach and the crossing over to the left bank. It is a modest place in terms of stonework, but the idea is wonderfully clear: an empire decided that this is where it ended, and put a post on the end of it.

The landscape is the Middle Rhine in its broad, northern form, where the valley is wide, the hills are low and the river is full of barges. Bad Hönningen, Rheinbrohl and Bad Breisig face each other across the water, and there are car ferries at several points. The vineyards start a little upstream, and the Westerwald rises behind the town in a long wooded wall. Spring is gentle, summer is hot and busy with cyclists, and autumn brings mist on the water and wine festivals in the villages.

The riding is a real treat if you pick it well. The federal road along the right bank is busy and uneventful, but the hills behind are full of quiet, curving roads that climb through woodland and drop through small villages. The corners are tight enough to be fun, the views open suddenly when the trees clear, and the surface is generally good, if worn by lorries in places. Watch for the railway line along the river and for speed cameras in the small towns, which are numerous and unforgiving.

Practicalities are easy. Bad Hönningen, a mile or two away, has fuel, a bakery, and cafes with views of the Rhine, and Bad Breisig and Neuwied offer more choice. The Römerwelt museum in Rheinbrohl explains the frontier, and the small town is pleasant for a stroll along the riverbank. Come in the late afternoon, when the river turns copper, and stay for a glass of local Riesling in one of the wine bars. It is a quiet beginning to a frontier that is, in the end, a very long line.
t.watchtower wp 4 39@50.5,8.7:
The Wetterau is one of the richest farming plains in Germany, a broad, fertile basin north of Frankfurt where loess soil lies deep over old river gravel, and wheat and sugar beet grow in enormous fields. At its edge the Taunus hills rise to the south and west, and the Roman Limes ran along their northern slope, taking in the whole plain as a deliberately protected frontier region. Watchtower 4/39 stands in this open country near Butzbach, and the number marks one of the many posts that kept watch over fields that were, even then, valuable enough to defend.

The tower itself, like most on the line, has been reconstructed or marked rather than preserved, and what the visitor finds is a good viewpoint on a gentle swell of ground. The wide horizon is its real attraction: the fields roll off in all directions, wind turbines turn slowly on the ridges, and in summer the larks sing so loudly overhead that you stop to listen. Butzbach, a few kilometres away, is a pleasant old Hessian town with a half-timbered market square, a handful of good cafés and a long history that includes a Roman fort and a medieval trading post.

For a rider the Wetterau is a gentle ride rather than a mountain road. Straight stretches between villages give way to a few lazy bends where the road follows a stream, and the traffic is mostly local, though the A5 motorway carries heavy lorry flows nearby and the main roads can be noisy. The surface is generally good, but beware of mud on the road at harvest time, and of low sun that makes the junction signs hard to read. To the south, the road climbs into the Taunus and becomes a different, twisty country.

Butzbach has all the usual services, including petrol, bakeries and supermarkets, and Langgöns and Rockenberg offer smaller stops. Spring, when the rape is flowering yellow, and early autumn, when the stubble is gold, are the best times. In midsummer the heat on the open plain can be heavy, so take plenty of water.
t.limessection between watchtowers wp 1 93:
Bad Ems sits in a narrow, wooded bend of the Lahn river, where the valley is so steep that the town seems poured into the gap. It has been a spa since the Middle Ages, and by the nineteenth century it was one of the most fashionable in Europe. Kings, tsars and composers came to take the thermal waters, and the town is filled with grand hotels, a colonnaded Kurhaus and a Russian Orthodox church built for the Tsarist visitors. Dostoevsky came to take the cure in the 1870s, and in 1870 an incident in the park gave the town a place in history books.

That year, King Wilhelm of Prussia met the French ambassador on the promenade, and the diplomatic exchange that followed was edited by Bismarck into a telegram known as the Ems Dispatch. The sharpened version inflamed French public opinion and pushed France into the war with Prussia that Bismarck wanted. A small memorial in the park recalls the moment. It is a remarkable thing that a few lines of editing in a spa town could do so much harm, and the town carries it lightly.

The Limes belongs to a much older story. The Roman frontier crossed the Lahn near here on its way from the Rhine into the Taunus, and the numbered watchtowers mark the line that ran through the woods on the heights above the valley. A funicular, the Kurwaldbahn, climbs from town to the forested ridge, and walkers can follow the frontier line from the top.

The riding in the Lahn valley is excellent. The river road is a pleasure at moderate speed, twisting under cliffs and between vineyards and old iron-ore workings, and the roads that climb onto the Taunus and Westerwald ridges are full of tight bends and long views. The valley is narrow, so traffic is slow behind lorries and the occasional tour bus. Fuel is available in Bad Ems itself, and Nassau and Lahnstein are close. Autumn, when mist hangs in the gorge and the beech turns amber, makes the best ride, and a coffee in the Kurpark afterwards is a civilised end to it.
t.fortlet wingertsberg@50.4,8.9:
Wingertsberg is a low hill on the western edge of the Vogelsberg, near the small town of Hungen in Hesse, and the Roman fortlet that stood here was one of a series of small outposts along the Wetterau Limes. A fortlet held perhaps a few dozen men, enough to watch the line and signal to the main forts. Little survives above ground, so the interest lies mostly in knowing that the frontier ran here, across fields that are now ploughed in neat rows and crossed by farm tracks and cycle paths.

The landscape is an easy one. Hungen sits in the Horloff valley, in gently rolling farmland of wheat and sugar beet, with beech woods on the higher ground and an old castle, now a cultural centre, at the heart of the town. Behind it to the east, the Vogelsberg rises, a huge extinct volcanic massif of basalt that is one of the largest in Central Europe. The slopes are green and rounded, with forests and cattle pastures, and the villages are low and quiet, built of dark volcanic stone and half-timbering. In spring the meadows fill with yellow and the streams run clear.

For a rider the Vogelsberg is a pleasant surprise. It lacks the famous passes of the Alps, but it has a network of narrow, quiet roads that wind in long loops over the hills, with gentle gradients, good views and very little traffic. On warm weekends it is popular with motorcyclists from the Rhine-Main region, and the villages often have a Gasthof that is used to leathers at the door. The surface varies, with the occasional rough patch on the minor roads, and winter frost can last well into spring on the higher ground.

Hungen has fuel, supermarkets and several bakeries, with Berstadt and Wohnbach offering quieter stops. Come on a weekday in May or September, when the roads are empty and the light is soft over the plain, and treat the fortlet as a reason to slow down and look around rather than a destination in its own right.
t.watchtowers wp 1 27 to 1 29@50.5,7.4:
The Rhine at Neuwied is wide and brown and always busy with barges, and the flat basin around it was shaped by a catastrophe. About thirteen thousand years ago the Laacher See volcano, a little to the west, erupted with tremendous force and blanketed the area in pumice and ash, and the same tephra layer can still be found in sediments across much of Europe. Today the basin is orchards, vegetable fields and quarries for pumice and tuff, a quiet and fertile ground that gives no hint of its violent origin.

Neuwied itself is a town with an unusual history. Count Friedrich III of Wied founded it in 1653 after the Thirty Years' War had emptied the district, and he offered freedom of worship to anyone who would come. Lutherans, Reformed Christians, Mennonites, Moravians and Jews settled here, and the town grew rich on clockmaking and craft. Friedrich Wilhelm Raiffeisen, the founder of the cooperative banking movement, lived for a time in the district, and his name is on banks across Germany. Roman forts dot the area as well, since the frontier started a short distance north, and a big fort once stood at Niederbieber.

The numbered towers on this label belong to the Upper Germanic Limes, which has its western end at the Rhine near here. The riding is straightforward. Roads through the basin run flat among villages, with the busy Rhine road close by and quieter lanes through fruit plantations. Heading east, the land rises quickly into the Westerwald, and the bends begin. Heading west across the river, Andernach has a fine medieval town wall and a remarkable cold-water geyser, reached by boat from the Rhine bank, which is said to be the tallest of its kind in the world.

Neuwied has all the usual services, including petrol and a long riverside promenade, and Andernach on the opposite bank is a pleasant place for lunch. Spring is blossom time in the orchards, and early autumn brings the grape harvest on the slopes nearby. Avoid the hour of the commuter rush, and cross the river by the bridge or one of the car ferries for a change of scene.
t.limessection between watchtowers wp 1 60:
Höhr-Grenzhausen is a town that makes things out of mud. The Westerwald plateau here sits on one of Europe's finest deposits of stoneware clay, and for centuries potters have dug it, thrown it and fired it in salt-glaze kilns to make grey-and-blue jugs, tankards and storage jars. The area is called the Kannenbäckerland, the land of the jug bakers, and its pots were shipped down the Rhine and across the world. The Westerwald Ceramics Museum in Höhr-Grenzhausen tells the story, and several workshops in town still sell hand-made pieces. Take a mug home and you will be surprised how heavy it is.

The Roman frontier passed through this country as well, on its way from the Rhine over the Westerwald uplands. The numbers 1/60 describe a section of the Upper Germanic Limes where the line ran along a wooded ridge, with watchtowers placed on every rise. The woods have grown up since, and the traces of the frontier are mostly faint banks in the forest floor, though the signed trail is a pleasant way to see the land. A signal tower, one of several reconstructed to show how messages were relayed along the line, gives some idea of the view the soldiers had.

The plateau is gently hilly country of beech and spruce woods, small fields and sudden clay pits, and the riding is relaxed rather than dramatic. Roads climb and drop in easy curves and pass through villages whose houses are often slate-roofed and half-timbered. Near Koblenz, where the Rhine and Moselle meet, the plateau edge falls away into the valley, and the roads there are tighter and more fun. The weather on the Westerwald can be grey and damp, so be ready for wet tarmac, and for fog in the cold season.

Höhr-Grenzhausen has fuel, supermarkets and cafés, and Nauort and Weitersburg are quieter neighbours. Koblenz, a short ride south, has everything. Spring, with the beech leaves fresh, and autumn, with warm light on the clay-coloured fields, suit this part of Germany best.
t.kalkar bornsches feld@51.7,6.3:
Kalkar sits on a low terrace a few kilometres from the Rhine, close to the Dutch border, and everything about the landscape here is flat, wide and bright. The label points to the Bornsches Feld, a field on the edge of town that belongs to the Roman Lower Germanic Limes, the frontier that followed the Rhine itself rather than a wall or a palisade. UNESCO added the whole line to its list in 2021. Here, as elsewhere along the lower river, the Roman forts and camps stood on the river bank, the water served as the barrier, and what remains today is mostly in the ground and in the museums of Xanten, a little way up the Rhine.

Kalkar itself is a handsome surprise. It was a Hanseatic town in the late Middle Ages, and the market square is still lined with gabled brick houses and a stepped town hall. Inside the church of St Nicholas stands a collection of carved altars made by a school of woodcarvers who worked here in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, and the scale and detail of the figures is staggering for a place of this size. There is also a famous oddity just outside town: a nuclear fast breeder reactor that was built and never switched on, now converted into an amusement park, with a hotel and rides in the cooling tower.

The riding is plain and relaxed. Lower Rhine roads run straight between fields of potatoes, maize and sugar beet, with pollarded willows beside the ditches and poplars on the horizon. Wind can be strong, and the surface is mostly good, but corners are few, and the best moments come from the light across the flat land. The Reichswald forest, to the west, is a larger area of woods and offers tree-lined roads with a little more shade and some gentle undulation. Cyclists are everywhere, especially at weekends, so keep speed sensible and watch at junctions.

Kalkar has several petrol stations on its main roads, plus bakeries and cafés on the market square, and Rees and Uedem are close enough for a change of scene. Spring is the best season, when the polder is green and the cherry trees are in flower, and autumn brings geese from the Arctic, which graze the fields in their thousands. Midsummer is warm and bright, and winter can be raw, grey and extremely windy.
t.watchtowers wp 5 9 to 5 10@50.1,9.0:
The label gives only a pair of watchtower numbers, and the place itself is a swathe of flat country between Hanau and the Kinzig, where the suburbs of Erlensee, Rodenbach and Langenselbold have grown together into a continuous belt of houses, orchards and sports fields. In the second century the Roman frontier ran along this side of the Main plain before it turned south to the river, and the small towers, spaced at easy shouting distance, were the first line of warning. Nothing much remains above ground, and the nearby fort at Rückingen is known mostly from excavation. This is a stop for imagination rather than sightseeing.

Hanau, a few kilometres away, is better known as the birthplace of the Brothers Grimm, Jacob in 1785 and Wilhelm a year later, whose collection of folk tales was assembled in Hesse. The town is also a centre of the German goldsmith trade, and the Wilhelmsbad park, a late eighteenth-century spa garden with a carousel and a ruined castle folly, is a charming relic of the age when German princes built fake ruins for their guests. The Grimm statue on the old market square is a handy meeting point, and the castle at Philippsruhe on the Main is a pleasant walk.

The riding here is uneventful, and it would be dishonest to dress it up. The roads between the towns are built for commuters and are often busy, with traffic lights and roundabouts and the occasional cyclist on a long shared path. It makes more sense as a gateway than a destination. Head east and the land rises into the Spessart or north into the Vogelsberg, where the roads turn quiet and twisty. The Kinzig valley offers gentle corners and pleasant villages with timber-framed houses.

Fuel and food are no problem whatsoever. Erlensee, Rodenbach and Langenselbold each have several petrol stations, supermarkets and bakeries, and Hanau has all the rest. Weekday mornings are slow with commuters, so mid-morning is the best time to pass through, and late afternoon on Fridays is best avoided altogether. Take your break in the Wilhelmsbad park, which is quiet and green and gives a reason to remember that a Roman frontier was here.
t.national park wadden sea niedersachsen@5:
Here the Wadden Sea comes right up against the dyke. This is the coast of the Wurster Nordseeküste, between the Weser and Elbe estuaries, a country of low sea walls, drained farmland and wide skies, and the mudflats outside the dyke are part of the Lower Saxony Wadden Sea National Park. Together with the Dutch and Danish parts of the Wadden Sea, the area is a UNESCO World Heritage site, valued above all for the sheer scale of the tidal flats and the millions of birds that pass through on migration. When the tide goes out, it goes a very long way.

The nature here is the thing. At low water the flats are alive with worms, mussels and shrimp, and flocks of oystercatchers, curlews, knots and godwits probe the mud in long, nervous lines. Barnacle geese and brent geese arrive in autumn from the Arctic, and in some years the sky is dark with them. Seals sun themselves on distant sandbanks, though from the dyke they look like grey logs. The smell is salt, mud and seaweed, with an edge of diesel from the fishing cutters. Wadden walks with a licensed guide are popular, and it is vital not to wander out alone, because the tide returns fast and the channels fill from behind.

Riding along the coast is simple and rewarding in its own way. Narrow roads run behind the dyke, fields of wheat and cabbage lie on one side and the grass slope of the sea wall on the other, and a gentle climb over the crest gives a view of the sea or the mud, depending on the hour. Wind is a constant factor, often sideways, and the weather can change from sunshine to rain in minutes. Expect little in the way of bends, and a number of speed cameras in the villages.

The nearest sizeable town is Cuxhaven, about twenty kilometres away, with plenty of fuel, restaurants and a long beach at Duhnen where the wadden trips to Neuwerk island begin. Nordholz is closer and has the usual supplies. The fishing villages along the coast serve fresh shrimp rolls, and a plate of Nordseekrabben with bread is very hard to beat. Late summer and early autumn bring the best light and the best birds.
t.wolsong belt@35.8,129.2:
Gyeongju was the capital of the Silla kingdom for the better part of a thousand years, and the Wolseong belt is the heart of it. Wolseong means Crescent Moon Fortress, a low curved rise that once held the royal palace. Today you will see grassy embankments, the outline of old foundations, and a landscape more of absence than of monuments, which is exactly why so many Koreans come to stroll it, particularly at dusk and in the first week of April when the cherry blossoms are out.

Nearby, a few steps away, stand the elegant little Cheomseongdae, a stone tower from the seventh century that is usually described as an astronomical observatory, though scholars still argue about what it really did. The forest of Gyerim lies close, where the legend tells of the golden box found in the branches and the child inside it who founded the Kim clan. Gyeongju is often called the museum without walls, and that description is fair: the huge grassy burial mounds of Silla kings rise in the middle of town like green whales.

Getting here is easy, as Gyeongju is a city of 155,000 people, with fuel stations and restaurants in every direction. Pohang and the East Sea are about twenty-five kilometres away, and the mountain roads toward Haeinsa, the temple that houses the thirteenth-century Tripitaka Koreana woodblocks, take you through a Korean landscape of steep forested ridges, terraced fields and sudden, narrow valleys. Roads in Korea are generally excellent but are fiercely watched by speed cameras, which are announced by signs but not forgiving; keep an eye on your speed.

In the town centre the traffic is busy but not heavy, and parking near the monuments is simple enough. Try the local speciality hwangnam-ppang, a small round pastry with sweet red bean paste, which is sold in boxes at nearly every shop near the tombs. A bowl of ssambap, rice wrapped in leaves, makes a good lunch.

Best time to visit is spring or autumn, when the air is clear and the maples redden; in summer, the heat and humidity make walking miserable, and typhoon rain can arrive in late summer. Winter is cold but clear and quiet.
t.yungneung cluster@37.2,127.0:
Yungneung belongs to a tradition that most visitors to Korea never see: the royal tombs of the Joseon dynasty, forty of them scattered across the country and listed by UNESCO in 2009. This cluster lies south of Seoul near Hwaseong, a short way from Suwon, and it holds the tomb of Crown Prince Sado and, nearby, that of his son, King Jeongjo. Sado is the tragic figure of the dynasty. In 1762 his father, King Yeongjo, had him sealed inside a rice chest, where he died after eight days, after years of tension at court.

Jeongjo spent much of his reign trying to honour his father. He moved the tomb to this hill, built the great fortress of Hwaseong at Suwon in the 1790s, and made annual pilgrimages here with a long procession, which is re-enacted in some years. Standing in the quiet pine forest, with the mound of grass guarded by stone officials and horses, you get a real sense of that long mourning. Joseon tombs always sit on slopes facing south, with a hill behind and water in front, following geomantic principles, and the layout here is a good example.

The setting is quite suburban: Suwon has well over a million people, Osan is not far, and the roads around are fast, busy and lined with apartment blocks. So the riding is not the draw; it is a short, practical hop from the capital, easily done in an afternoon. Get here early or late in the day to avoid heavy traffic, and note that Korean speed cameras are frequent and strict. Fuel is everywhere and cheap by European standards.

In Suwon, you can eat well. The city is famous for its marinated beef ribs, galbi, and for fried chicken that arrives on a huge platter. Walk a stretch of the Hwaseong Fortress wall in the evening, when it is lit up, and the old and the modern seem comfortable together. Spring has cherry blossom and autumn has gold ginkgo and red maples, which are the best seasons. The Jongmyo ride takes you north into Seoul to the royal ancestral shrine, another listed place with a very different, ceremonial mood.
t.royal tombs of the joseon dynasty@37.2,1:
In the mountains of Gangwon Province, the town of Yeongwol sits where two rivers meet among steep forested ridges, and at the edge of it, in a stand of pines, lies Jangneung, the tomb of Danjong. Danjong became king as a boy of eleven in 1452. His uncle Sejo seized the throne a few years later, and the young king was exiled to Yeongwol, a remote and isolated place chosen for that reason, and died there in 1457, still a teenager. The tomb is a simple grassy mound that is part of the UNESCO group of Joseon royal burials, and it lies far from the other royal tombs, which cluster around Seoul.

Koreans feel the sadness of the story strongly. Danjong's loyal officials, remembered as the six martyred ministers, were killed for trying to restore him, and later generations came to honour him as a symbol of loyalty. The layout of the tomb follows the usual pattern, with stone figures lining the approach, a pavilion for the ritual, and a path that climbs gently up through the trees. It is a quiet and solemn place, with the sort of silence that feels deliberate.

Getting here is a pleasure on a bike. The mountain roads into Yeongwol wind through valleys with cliffs, small farms, and rivers cutting deep bends, and the traffic outside the holiday season is light. The famous Hanbando-shaped river bend at Seonam village, a short way outside, is a good place for a stop. Autumn brings flaming maples and golden larch, spring brings azaleas, and winter is clear but very cold, with ice on the shaded corners, so check conditions carefully. Heavy rains in July and August can cause landslides in the narrow valleys.

Yeongwol is a town of about twenty-five thousand people, large enough for fuel, restaurants and simple lodging, and Pyeongchang, about twenty kilometres north, has more if you need it. Mountain-style food is the speciality: buckwheat noodles, wild vegetable rice, and grilled trout from the cold rivers. The ride toward Andong and Dosan Seowon, the great Confucian academy, continues south through the Taebaek mountains into the heartland of traditional Korean culture.
t.yeongneung cluster@37.3,127.6:
The Yeongneung cluster lies in the countryside of Yeoju, a town on the Namhan River east of Seoul, and it is the resting place of King Sejong the Great, who reigned from 1418 to 1450 and is remembered above all for the creation of the Korean alphabet, hangul, announced in the 1440s. Koreans hold the king in deep affection, and a statue of him sits in the middle of Seoul. His tomb here is a joint one, shared with his queen, and it sits in a beautiful pine-covered setting with stone officials, horses and lanterns lined along the approach. The nearby tomb of King Hyojong, known as Nyeongneung, is part of the same area.

Yeoju is a quiet and rather pretty river town, and its main road follows the Namhan, which is broad and slow here. The area is known for rice, for ceramics, and for a large outlet centre on the edge of the town, which brings a surprising amount of weekend traffic. Not far away, the temple of Silleuksa sits on a bluff above the river, with a slender brick pagoda and lovely views over the water.

Riding in this part of Gyeonggi Province is not about mountains but about valleys, river roads and open farmland. The roads are good and well signed, and from the cluster you can follow the river for a gentle, scenic run. Weekend traffic is heavy near the outlets and on routes back toward Seoul, so a weekday or an early start makes a difference. Spring brings cherry blossom, autumn brings rice fields turned gold, and winter is crisp, though icy patches appear in the shade.

Yeoju has about thirty-seven thousand people, with fuel stations, restaurants and plenty of places to stop. Icheon, about fifteen kilometres to the west, is more famous for its pottery and its rice, and serves a famous steamed rice dish in earthenware pots. If you are riding on toward the other cluster, the lanes between the two give a good look at ordinary Korean rural life, with greenhouses, small orchards, village shrines and a great deal of hand-tended land.
t.key planning decision@53.4,5.7:
The coordinates here fall out on the tidal flats of the Wadden Sea, in the narrow channel between the Frisian mainland and the island of Ameland, and the label refers to the Dutch national policy that protects the area. It is hard to point at a spot, because there is no spot: the sea retreats twice a day, leaving miles of glistening mud, and then returns, often faster than you expect. The Wadden Sea is a UNESCO site shared by the Netherlands, Germany and Denmark, and it is the largest unbroken system of intertidal sand and mud flats in the world.

Its importance lies in what lives there. The mud is thick with worms, shellfish and tiny crustaceans, which feed vast numbers of migrating birds, including knots, oystercatchers and spoonbills. Common and grey seals rest on the sandbanks, and the whole system acts as a nursery for North Sea fish. You can walk on the flats with a guide, a tradition called wadlopen, from villages like Pieterburen, but this is a practice to be done only with an experienced guide, since the tide and fog can trap the careless.

For a rider, the interesting parts are the roads along the dykes. The Frisian coast is flat, open and breezy, with long straight sections along the sea wall, sheep on the grassy banks, and a sky that seems far bigger than elsewhere in Europe. Wind is the main character: a headwind from the north-west can make the day hard work, while a tailwind is a joy. Weather changes quickly, so keep rain gear handy. Spring and early autumn bring migrating birds, and summer evenings are long and golden.

The ferry from Holwerd runs to Ameland, where Nes and Hollum have a small supply of shops, fuel and restaurants, but on the mainland the larger towns of Dokkum and Leeuwarden offer more choice. Franeker, home of the Eisinga Planetarium, is the other direction on this ride. Built in a living room in the eighteenth century by a wool comber, Eise Eisinga, it is the world's oldest working planetarium, with a ceiling that models the planets. A cup of strong coffee with a slice of Frisian sugar bread makes a fine afterwards.
t.berg en dal aqueduct kerstendal@51.8,5.9:
Berg en Dal sits on the side of the Nijmegen ridge, a rare bump of ground in a country built mostly of rivers and polders. The ridge is a push moraine, a pile of gravel and sand shoved up by ice during the last glaciation, and it rises above the Waal and the German border forest of the Reichswald. In Dutch terms it is mountainous, with beech woods, steep lanes and villas set among trees, and the road through Kerstendal winds along the foot of the slope with real if modest bends.

This is also Roman country. Nijmegen was a legionary fortress and then a town, Ulpia Noviomagus, and it is often called the oldest city in the Netherlands. A town of that size needed fresh water, and the springs on the wooded ridge were an obvious source. The aqueduct that the label refers to is part of that Roman water supply, which carried water down from the hills to the settlement, and it is a reminder that these engineers thought about plumbing as seriously as roads and walls.

Close by you will find some surprising places. A museum of African art stands in the woods at Berg en Dal, and a biblical open-air museum, the Heilig Land Stichting, recreates scenes from the lands of the Bible. During the Second World War this area was at the edge of the fighting of Operation Market Garden in 1944, and the bridge at Nijmegen over the Waal, taken in a daring assault, is still remembered with reverence.

The riding is gentle but enjoyable, a rolling run of woodland lanes, with cyclists and walkers as the real owners. Weekends in the nice season are crowded with Dutch and German day-trippers, and speed limits are enforced, so go quietly and enjoy the trees. Autumn is the best time, with beech leaves turning copper, while winter can be icy in shady dips. The Reichswald ride continues into Germany over the border, where the forest road is wider and faster.

Fuel and food are easy: Berg en Dal and the nearby villages have small shops and cafes, while Nijmegen, a few kilometres away, has everything. Try a pancake at one of the forest cafes, the Dutch way of ending a ride.
t.the great spa towns of europe@50.5,5.9:
Spa is the little town in the Belgian Ardennes that gave its name to every spa in the world, and the story goes back a long way. The mineral springs here were known to the Romans, and Pliny is often cited as mentioning them, and from the sixteenth century they drew the nobility of Europe. In 1717 Peter the Great of Russia came to take the waters, and the Pouhon Pierre-le-Grand, a handsome pavilion over the main spring, is named after him. The town built a grand casino, a thermal baths building and a promenade, and a century later it became known as the Café of Europe, a place where kings, writers and intriguers rubbed shoulders.

UNESCO included Spa in 2021 in the Great Spa Towns of Europe, a group of eleven towns in seven countries that developed around mineral water and the culture of taking cures. Today the town still has a courtly, faded charm, with iron-and-glass galleries, bandstands and wooded paths up the hills. The water, which is low in minerals, is bottled and sold across the world under the Spa label, and you can drink from several fountains in the town for free, though it has a distinct taste of iron.

Riders know Spa for another reason. A few kilometres to the east lies the Spa-Francorchamps motor racing circuit, one of the most celebrated in the world, with the famous Eau Rouge and Raidillon sequence of corners. The Belgian Grand Prix has been held there for decades, and the circuit hosts motorcycle events too. The public roads in the surrounding Ardennes are not racetracks, however, and they are patrolled by police and speed cameras, so enjoy the scenery and keep to the limits.

The countryside here is excellent riding territory. Rolling forested hills, valleys with small rivers, and the high moorland of the Hautes Fagnes, the High Fens, to the east, which is the highest part of Belgium. The roads have long, flowing bends and decent surfaces, and the air is cool and damp, with morning mist in the valleys. Summer is the busiest period, especially on race weekends, when the area fills with motorsport fans. Autumn is quieter and the woods turn gold. Winter can bring snow and ice to the higher roads.

Spa has fuel stations, a good range of cafes and bakeries, and hotels of every kind. Try a Liège waffle, a plate of Ardennes ham or a local beer, and remember that the town sits among the wettest parts of Belgium, so pack for rain.
t.watchtowers wp 1 37 to 1 38@50.5,7.5:
Two numbered watchtower sites on the Roman frontier sit here in the Westerwald countryside above the Rhine, near the villages of Melsbach and Rengsdorf. The paired label is archaeologists' shorthand, because the Upper Germanic Limes was a chain of towers placed within sight of one another, a few hundred metres apart. These two were part of the line that ran from the Rhine near Rheinbrohl across the hills of Rhineland-Palatinate and on towards the Taunus, and the whole frontier is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, listed in 2005 as part of the larger Roman Limes complex.

Today you are in rolling, mixed farmland and beech woods, between the Neuwied basin on the Rhine and the higher ground of the Westerwald. The road here is the kind of ordinary secondary road the German interior does well, with smooth tarmac, gentle bends and a lot of woodland shade. You will meet commuters heading to Neuwied in the morning and evening, and cyclists on warm weekends, but outside those hours it is peaceful. The Wied valley, a little to the east, makes a good detour with tighter curves and pleasant river scenery.

For services, Neuwied about six kilometres away is the answer: a town of nearly seventy thousand people on the Rhine, with fuel, food and everything else. Rengsdorf and Melsbach are smaller but handy for a coffee. Neuwied has a strange history of its own, having been laid out by the Counts of Wied in the eighteenth century with a policy of religious tolerance that attracted Moravian Brethren, among other groups. Friedrich Wilhelm Raiffeisen, founder of the rural cooperative bank movement, also lived and worked in the area.

If you stand at the site and look along the ridge, you can imagine a soldier doing the same thing, watching the barbarian side for smoke. It is a small and humble place, which is entirely the point. Ride on with a bit more respect for how long this land has been fought over and farmed.
t.kottenforst nord durrenbruch 1@50.7,7.0:
A forest closer to a city than most people realise, the Kottenforst spreads over a low ridge between Bonn and the Eifel foothills, and the Dürrenbruch is one of the quiet corners of its northern half. The old prince-electors of Cologne used it as a hunting ground, cutting long straight rides through the trees that radiate like the spokes of a wheel, which is why the forest feels strangely geometrical when you look at a map. Today it is a Bonn-area refuge of beech, oak and hornbeam, cut by cycle paths and walking trails.

Be honest about the riding: this is not a motorcyclist's forest. Many of the interior tracks are closed to motor traffic, so the pleasure is in the approach, on the minor roads that ring the woodland from Alfter and Bornheim. Those roads are narrow, tree-lined and quite pretty in autumn, but they are also commuter routes for the Bonn suburbs, so the early mornings and late afternoons can be busy. A Sunday morning is calmer, but the forest is a favourite with local walkers, so go gently and stay on the public asphalt.

The label points to a stretch of the Roman landscape too. The Limes section here belongs to the Lower German frontier along the Rhine, and the region carries traces of Roman engineering, including the Eifel aqueduct, which carried water from the hills toward Cologne across this ridge. Little of it is visible without a guide, and what you notice most is the quiet.

Fuel is easy. Alfter has more than twenty thousand people, Bornheim has nearly fifty thousand, and Bonn itself is under ten kilometres away with every kind of food you might want. The forest is damp and fragrant after rain, with the smell of leaf-mould and wet bark that makes you want to take your helmet off and listen. If you do, you will probably hear woodpeckers, and in early spring the whole place rings with them.
t.watchtower wp 2 1 including fortlet bad:
Bad Ems has been a spa town since the Romans noticed the springs, and today it is a handsome, slightly faded place squeezed into the narrow Lahn valley between wooded hills. The town and its surroundings sit on the line of the Upper Germanic Limes, which the Roman Empire pushed through here to protect the valley and its minerals. A fortlet and a watchtower were built on the heights above the river, and the remains give the numbered label its meaning. Walk a short way up and you can see why the soldiers picked the spot: the slopes drop sharply to the water, and the view along the valley is long.

The Lahn here is lovely riding country. The road along the river bends with the water and gives views of old railway viaducts, steep woods and the occasional castle on a crag. Up on the ridges the lanes are tighter and steeper, with hairpins that make a bike feel properly alive. Traffic is moderate on the main valley road, heavier on summer weekends when cyclists and tourists fill the riverside, so early starts help. The Rhine is only a few kilometres to the west, and the contrast between its busy shipping and the Lahn's quiet bends is striking.

Bad Ems is large enough, with nearly ten thousand people, to have fuel, restaurants and cafes without difficulty. It has an unexpected piece of diplomatic history, because in 1870 a telegram from the King of Prussia, edited by Bismarck and known as the Ems Dispatch, helped push France into the war with Prussia. The spa buildings still carry the elegance of the nineteenth century, when European royalty came to take the waters, and Tsar Alexander II and Kaiser Wilhelm I were among the visitors. Russian Orthodox church architecture still stands in the town as a reminder.

If you are riding up to the tower site, go slowly on the narrow forest lanes and watch for walkers, because the Limes trail is popular. Late afternoon, with sunlight raking through the beeches, is the best time.
t.fort site and civil settlement of bad em:
Rome built in stone here, and then the town grew on top of it. Bad Ems stands where the Lahn winds through a tight gorge, and the fort and the civil settlement beside it formed a small frontier community, with soldiers, traders and families living in the shadow of the Limes. The Roman fort is now buried beneath the modern town, so the site is more an idea than a sight, but the Limes trail in the woods above makes the story easy to follow, and the town museum helps with the details.

You arrive here by one of the best small river roads in the Rhineland. The Lahn valley road is a ribbon of gentle curves, with the water on one side and steep, forested slopes on the other. It is not fast, and it should not be, since the road is shared with cyclists and day trippers, but the rhythm is easy and the scenery changes every few minutes. If you want more, climb out of the valley on one of the side roads toward the Westerwald or the Taunus, where tighter bends and hairpins reward patience. Weekday mornings and shoulder seasons are best.

This is a very easy place to stop. With almost ten thousand residents, Bad Ems has fuel, bakeries and restaurants, and the long promenade along the river is a pleasant place to sit. The spa heritage is strong: the warm springs were used by the Romans and later by a stream of European aristocrats, and the Kurhaus and colonnades still carry that grand nineteenth-century manner. Tsar Alexander II took the cure here, and the Russian church built for his visits remains. In 1870 the telegram that became known as the Ems Dispatch was drafted here, and historians argue over how much it triggered the Franco-Prussian War.

Fachbach, across the river, is small but pleasant for a short stop. There is not much else to say except that a Roman soldier posted here in winter would have hated the cold and loved the baths.
t.watchtowers wp 1 35 and 1 35a@50.5,7.5:
Pumice is the clue to this corner of the Rhineland. About thirteen thousand years ago the Laacher See volcano blew itself apart not far upstream, and the ash and pumice it threw out settled across the Neuwied basin, where it was dug, pressed into building blocks and carted off for centuries. Up on the hills above the basin, near Melsbach and Rengsdorf, the Romans chose the high ground for a pair of small watchtowers, one of which carries an extra letter in its number because archaeologists found a second structure next to it. They were part of the Upper Germanic Limes, which begins at the Rhine only a few kilometres away.

Riding here has the quiet character of the western Westerwald. The lanes run between meadows and patches of oak and beech, rising and falling with the folds of the land. There are no dramatic gradients, but the tarmac is generally good and the corners come at a pleasant, unhurried rate. Rengsdorf is a small resort-like village with a calm air, while the Wied valley a short ride east gets tighter and more wooded and makes a good loop in the afternoon. Expect farm traffic, the odd school bus, and on dry weekends a scattering of other bikes.

Fuel is a matter of planning. Melsbach and Rengsdorf are villages of two to three thousand people, so you may find a small station, but Neuwied, about five kilometres off, is the reliable answer with a proper range of services. If you want to understand the Roman side of the story, the tower at Rheinbrohl on the Rhine, where the frontier begins, is the place that explains it best, and it is a short run downhill.

I like this section because it shows how modest the Limes really was. No dramatic walls, just a line of timber and stone lookouts and a ditch, gradually swallowed by farmland and forest. Pull over where the lane widens, shut the engine off for a moment, and listen to the wind in the beeches. That, more than any museum, tells you what a sentry heard.
t.kottenforst nord am wei en stein 2@50.7,:
Bornheim is asparagus country, and if you ride past the Kottenforst in late spring you will see why. The sandy soil on the Rhine terraces just south of Cologne suits the white spears perfectly, and from roughly April to the end of June the farm stands along the roads sell them by the kilo, along with strawberries that follow soon afterwards. This is the Vorgebirge, a low ridge between the Rhine plain and the Eifel foothills, long used for market gardening and orchards, and the Weißer Stein stop sits in the woodland at its edge.

The forest itself is a patch of oak and beech with broad rides cut through it, a legacy of the prince-electors who hunted here from the eighteenth century. The straight avenues radiate from old hunting lodges, and from the air they look like a pattern drawn with a ruler. On the ground you notice mainly the quiet and the smell of damp leaves. The tracks inside are meant for walkers, riders on horses and cyclists, so keep the motorbike on the public roads around the edge, where the lanes are narrow, lined with trees and occasionally rutted by farm machinery.

Alfter and Bornheim are both substantial towns, with twenty-two thousand and nearly forty-nine thousand people respectively, so fuel and food are minutes away. Bonn lies a short run to the east and gives you plenty more, including the Beethoven house in the old town and the Rhine promenade, which is a good place for a long, slow lunch. Bonn was the capital of West Germany for forty years, and you can still feel the faint, solid, civil-service seriousness in its streets.

The best time to come is in the shoulder seasons. In spring the fruit blossom and the asparagus sellers give the route a festive air, and in autumn the leaves turn bronze and the light is soft and low. Summer afternoons can be hot, and the road surface has patches of tar-melt in the worst of it. Pick a morning, eat something local, and let the Rhineland's gentle, slightly smug prosperity wash over you.
t.watchtower wp 1 93@50.3,7.7:
Dausenau is the village that leans, or at least its church tower does. The tower of St Kastor, in the Lahn valley just a couple of kilometres from this watchtower site, tilts noticeably, giving the half-timbered lanes below it a slightly drunken air that tourists enjoy. The tower stands beside a gate of the old town wall, and the village is a pretty, slightly sleepy place where the Lahn bends through steep wooded slopes. The Roman tower number on the label belongs to the Limes that ran up and over the hills above the valley, and the site lies on the heights rather than in the village itself.

Getting here is half the fun. The Lahn valley road between Nassau and Bad Ems is a ribbon of smooth bends hugging the river, with the railway squeezed in beside it and vine-like woodland climbing the slopes. Climb out of the valley by the side roads and you meet steeper, more twisty tarmac with a couple of hairpins, where the trees close in and the surface gets patchy with leaf litter in autumn. Take it gently on wet days and watch for cyclists on the Lahn cycle path, which draws plenty of traffic on summer weekends.

Bad Ems is only a short way down the river, with almost ten thousand people and every service you might need, from fuel to a good cafe. Dausenau itself has a couple of village eateries and a bakery, but do not count on late opening hours. The Roman frontier here is quiet and unmarked in the main, and the walk up through the beeches to the tower site is more satisfying than the site itself, since the woods have a deep stillness and good birdsong in spring.

If you want one image to carry away, make it the crooked church tower catching the last light at the end of the day, with the river dark below and the hills fading into blue. It is an old, human sort of place, and the Romans were only the first of many to pass through.
t.kottenforst sud oben der krayermaar@50.7:
The southern Kottenforst is the Bonn locals' own backyard, and on a fine Sunday it feels like it. Tracks and rides cross the woodland in all directions, and the people on them are walkers, joggers, riders and families on bicycles rather than motorbikes. The name on the label, with its mention of a pond-like hollow called Maar, hints at the wet, clay-lined depressions that dot this plateau and hold water after rain. Underneath lie old Roman remains too, including part of the Eifel aqueduct that carried water toward Cologne, though you will see it only if you know where to look.

The roads around the woods are the ones to ride. Lanes out of Alfter, Röttgen and Ippendorf thread between fields and tree lines with a few tight bends, and the surface is generally decent, though it suffers in the freeze-thaw months. To the east you catch glimpses of the Siebengebirge, the volcanic hills across the Rhine, with the Drachenfels as the best known. That gives the route a lovely backdrop on clear days. The one drawback is commuter traffic, which makes the early morning and late afternoon slow.

Fuel is easy, since the stop lies about five kilometres from both Alfter and the centre of Bonn. The city has more than three hundred thousand people and a certain faded grandeur from its time as the capital of West Germany, between 1949 and the move to Berlin. It is also the birthplace of Beethoven and, rather less loftily, of the gummy bear, since the Haribo company was founded in Bonn in 1920. You can follow either legacy, but the sweet shop is faster than the museum.

Come here for a quiet loop and a bit of rest rather than for thrills. The forest has good shade in summer and a lovely carpet of wild garlic in spring, and the smell, if you stop and let it reach you, is surprisingly strong and green. The ponds hold frogs and dragonflies, and the whole place feels more rural than a stone's throw from a federal city has any right to be.
t.bergpark wilhelmshohe@51.3,9.4:
There is a giant on the hill above Kassel, and he has been there since the early eighteenth century. The Hercules statue, a copper figure on top of an octagonal structure and a huge stepped pyramid, crowns the Bergpark Wilhelmshöhe, which the Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel began laying out around 1700 as a statement of his power. Below it, a long cascade of steps and basins sends water tumbling down the hillside, and on certain afternoons from May to early October the water features run for the public in a spectacle that takes well over an hour to reach the bottom. UNESCO listed the park in 2013, and it remains one of the largest hillside parks in Europe.

The place is, frankly, a walker's, but the ride up is part of the day. Kassel sits in a basin ringed by the Habichtswald hills, and the approach roads climb through beech woods in a mix of gradual curves and sharper bends. Weekend traffic to the park can be thick, and parking fills early on water-game days, so arrive in the morning if you can. On a clear day the view from the foot of the Hercules reaches across the city and out to the Hessian hills beyond.

Kassel is a big city, nearly two hundred thousand people, so fuel and food are no problem. Baunatal, next door, is home to a large Volkswagen plant. The Brothers Grimm lived and worked in Kassel for years and collected many of their tales from local storytellers, and the city hosts the Documenta art exhibition every five years. In the early nineteenth century Napoleon's brother Jérôme ruled the Kingdom of Westphalia from here, and the palace was renamed Napoleonshöhe for a time.

For the riding proper, head west and south into the Kellerwald, a wooded upland with a national park and beech forests that are also part of a UNESCO listing. The roads there are quieter and more twisting, a better reward than the city traffic. Pick a spring day when the beech leaves are fresh and the park smells of wet stone.
t.watchtower wp 3 19 to 3 21@50.2,8.3:
The Taunus does not shout. It is a rounded, forested upland north of Wiesbaden and Frankfurt, and the Roman frontier crossed it on its way from the Rhine to the Main. These numbered watchtowers near Idstein belong to the Upper Germanic frontier, which in this part of Hesse ran through woods and clearings along the high ground. Archaeologists have recorded the tower positions along the line, and the asterisks in the label are their way of marking sites that are uncertain or only partly known. In practice you find woodland, a trail and the faint trace of an old bank.

The riding is smooth and relaxed. Roads around Idstein and Niedernhausen roll through farmland and beech wood, with long, open bends and a good surface, and if you drift south toward the Rheingau the hillsides begin to fall steeply toward the Rhine. Weekend traffic is heavy near the motorway corridor, but a few kilometres to either side the lanes empty out. Mist in the valleys on autumn mornings is especially nice, and the beech woods turn gold in October.

Idstein is a town of nearly twenty-three thousand people and is the obvious place for fuel and food. Its old centre is full of timbered houses, many of them elaborately carved, and a medieval tower, the Hexenturm, rises above the roofs as a reminder of the dark side of local history. Niedernhausen, a few kilometres away, is larger than it looks and has all the usual services too. A decent bakery and a bench in the old square are enough for a proper break.

Do not expect a visitor centre at the Limes site itself. The reward is the atmosphere, and the knowledge that a Roman sentry once looked out over this same quiet, wooded horizon. Go on a weekday morning for the best chance of solitude, and keep a layer in the pannier, because the Taunus can be cooler and wetter than the Rhine valley below.
t.limessection north of arzbach@50.4,7.7:
North of Arzbach the land lifts out of the Lahn valley and into the Westerwald, and the Roman frontier did the same. The Limes here is a section rather than a single tower, a line where a ditch, bank and a string of watchtowers once ran across the ridge. It is a faint thing now, a low earthwork under trees, but you can follow it on foot if you know where to look, and the local Limes trail marks the way. The nearest villages, Arzbach and Kadenbach, are small and quiet, with only a couple of thousand people between them.

On a motorcycle the area is a gentle tangle of lanes and wooded hills. The roads rise out of the valleys in a series of shallow switchbacks, and on the ridge they flatten into long, easy bends between fields. The surface is generally good, with only the odd patch of gravel, and on a weekday the traffic is light. Spring and autumn are the best times, when the woods are fresh or coloured and the air is clear enough to show the line of hills rolling away toward the Taunus.

Services are in Bad Ems, about five kilometres away, a spa town of nearly ten thousand people with fuel, restaurants and a long riverside promenade. The Lahn valley below has the most dramatic scenery in the area, with steep wooded slopes, old railway viaducts and the occasional castle, and it makes a pleasant contrast to the plateau. If you have time, ride down to the river for lunch and climb back up again by a different road, and you will come away with a feel for how the landscape fits together.

What I like about sections like this is that they tell you something simple. A frontier is not a wall around a country, it is a line drawn across a hillside and patrolled by bored men, and it only becomes monumental when we look back. Take a quiet minute among the trees, and let the thought settle.
t.colonies of benevolence@53.0,6.4:
In 1818 a former army officer named Johannes van den Bosch had a plan to cure poverty with heathland and a spade. His Maatschappij van Weldadigheid, the Society of Benevolence, bought up wasteland here on the border of Drenthe and Friesland and settled poor families from the cities on small farms, with a strict regime of work and discipline. Frederiksoord and Wilhelminaoord were the first colonies, and Veenhuizen, a little further east, later became a penal colony. UNESCO listed the Colonies of Benevolence in 2021, a rare case of a World Heritage Site that began as a social experiment.

The countryside is the point. You ride through a ruler-straight landscape of long avenues, regimented rows of trees, little white-trimmed farmhouses and fields cut out of old heath. It looks tidy, and slightly unreal, because every road was laid out with intent. This is Dutch riding, which means low speed limits, cycle lanes along nearly every road and traffic cameras that are not shy, so enjoy it as a calm morning ramble rather than a sporting run. The nearby Drents-Friese Wold, a national park of heath, pine and sand drifts, makes an excellent contrast and a good place for a walk.

Practicalities are simple. Haulerwijk and Norg are villages with a couple of thousand people each, and Oosterwolde, about nine kilometres off, is the larger town where fuel and a proper lunch are easy to find. In the colonies themselves you will find museums and small cafes, and in good weather the terraces fill with cyclists. The prison museum at Veenhuizen is surprisingly absorbing, and the old cell blocks give an honest picture of how the experiment drifted from charity into confinement.

Spring and early autumn suit the area best. The heather blooms purple in late summer, and low mist in the cold months gives the straight lanes a ghostly look. The wind can be sharp across the open fields, so a windproof layer is wise. Come with a slow mind, and the place rewards you with the odd, quiet feeling that someone once believed this empty ground could be made perfect.
t.watchtowers wp 1 36@50.5,7.5:
Julius Caesar put a bridge across the Rhine somewhere near here in 55 BC, a feat of carpentry that his own account says took ten days. Scholars still argue about the exact spot, but the Neuwied basin is one of the favourite candidates, and that gives the surrounding hills an extra layer of legend. A century and a half later the Romans came back for good and built the Limes along the heights above the river, with a chain of timber towers watching the Germanic side. The asterisk on this tower's number marks it as a conjectural position rather than a confirmed one.

What you find now is a quiet piece of upland near Melsbach, with fields, hedges and mixed woodland spread over a gentle plateau. The Rhine is close, and the road down into the basin drops through the trees in a few well-made curves before opening onto a broad, busy floodplain with barges drifting past. The traffic around Neuwied is heavier than up on the plateau, so the best riding is on the ridge lanes, where cars are few and the corners are easy to read. Mornings are clear and calm, while afternoons in summer bring haze from the river.

Neuwied itself, a town of nearly sixty-seven thousand people, is five kilometres away and has everything a rider needs. Fuel is easy there, and the Rhine promenade makes a handy place to sit with a coffee and watch the shipping. The town was laid out in a planned grid in the seventeen hundreds by the local counts, and its tolerant policy drew craftsmen of several faiths. Another Roman remnant, the big fort at Niederbieber, once stood on the Wied just inland, and its soldiers could have seen the same hills.

You will not find a visitor centre at the tower site, and that is part of the charm. Park where it is safe, walk the last stretch, and stand a moment under the trees. The Roman soldier who stood here was probably cold, probably bored, and certainly looking north.
t.watchtowers wp 4 59 to 4 71 including th:
The Wetterau is a broad, fertile basin north of Frankfurt, one of the best farming landscapes in Hesse, and the Romans fenced it with a frontier that ran in a wide arc through the grain fields. This group of watchtowers, with its numbers running from 4/59 to 4/71, lies near Hungen and Lich on the eastern side, where the plain begins to rise toward the Vogelsberg. Close by stands the Eichkopf fortlet, and a few kilometres to the north the ruins of the big fort at Arnsburg lie beside the remains of a Cistercian abbey, a double dose of history under tall trees.

The roads are straightforward and enjoyable. Between the villages the Wetterau lanes run across open farmland in long curves, with big skies and the odd wind turbine. Further east the Vogelsberg rises, a vast extinct volcano and the largest basalt massif in central Europe, and its roads are gently winding and quiet, with forests and meadows and the occasional viewpoint. It is not a place for excitement, but the pace suits a relaxed day, and in late summer the cornfields glow and the hay smells sweet.

Lich is the town to know, with nearly fourteen thousand people and a good range of shops and cafes. It is also home to a well-known brewery, whose beer you will see on tap across the region. Hungen, a smaller town with just under five thousand people, has a castle, a few restaurants and a petrol station or two, so fuel is rarely a problem here. The abbey ruins at Arnsburg, in a wooded valley by the river Wetter, are a lovely quiet spot for a picnic, and they are free to wander.

Like the Limes elsewhere, the tower sites here are modest, a few earthworks, a stone marker or two, and a sign explaining what you cannot see. That is no reason to skip them, because they make the surrounding landscape feel inhabited. When you ride on, you may find yourself noticing the lines of hedges and the old field edges, wondering which of them follow a Roman instruction.
t.bonn@50.7,7.1:
Bonn is a university city that spent forty years pretending to be a capital, and it carried it off with a modest air. After the war it became the seat of the West German government, and the former federal quarter along the Rhine still has the clean, low-key look of ministries designed not to impress. Before that, Bonn had been a seat of the Cologne prince-electors, whose baroque palace now houses the university, and it was also the birthplace of Beethoven, whose small house in the old town is one of the most visited composer museums anywhere.

A good time to be here is early April, when the cherry trees on the Heerstrasse and the lanes of the Altstadt burst into pink. The blossom is a local ritual, and photographers appear in force. For the rest of the year the town has a calm university rhythm, with students on bicycles, cafes on the market square and an easy riverside promenade along the Rhine. Take the little ferry across to Beuel if you want a view back to the town and the Siebengebirge, the line of old volcanic hills on the far bank, topped by the ruin on the Drachenfels.

For riders, Bonn is a staging post rather than a destination in itself. The city has over three hundred thousand people, so fuel, parking and food are never a problem, although the traffic is slow at rush hour and the one-way systems can confuse. The good riding begins out of town, either south along the Rhine toward Bad Honnef and the Siebengebirge, or west into the Eifel foothills where the roads tighten and climb. The Ahr valley, once a famous wine stretch and badly hit by floods in 2021, lies roughly an hour away and is recovering.

If you want one quiet hour, walk through the botanic garden behind the palace at Poppelsdorf. It is shaded, green and rarely crowded, and it gives you a little of the old electoral Bonn without a ticket queue. Then head out and ride.
t.watchtowers wp 1 24 to 1 26@50.5,7.4:
The Wied is a small river with a big job, because it marks the point where the Romans' Rhine frontier turned inland. A short ride from the water, between Melsbach and Neuwied, stands a cluster of watchtowers numbered 1/24 to 1/26, with a small fortlet called Lochmühle nearby. The towers belong to the Upper Germanic Limes, which was listed as part of the Roman Frontiers World Heritage Site in 2005, and these sit near its southern start by the Rhine.

Riding here means threading between the Rhine and the Westerwald. Down in the basin the roads are flat and busy, connecting Neuwied to the neighbouring villages through light industry and orchards, but a few turns later you are in woodland and rolling pasture where the traffic thins. The Wied valley lanes are the best of it, with sheltered curves along the stream, old mills and the occasional wooden footbridge. It is not a big-hills kind of ride, but it has a pleasant continuity, and early in the day, when the mist burns off the fields, the light is lovely.

Neuwied is under four kilometres away and big enough that fuel is no worry and food is plentiful. The Rhine promenade is a good place for a break, and the zoo on the edge of town is popular with families. A short way inland sat the large Roman fort at Niederbieber, home to a unit of the frontier army, and finds from it are kept in local museums.

Think of this stretch as a quiet hinge, the place where the Limes begins. Soldiers here lived between two worlds, the busy river and the silent forest, and that duality lingers in the landscape. In spring the orchard blossom adds a soft white edge to the lanes, and in autumn the vines on the Rhine slopes turn the hillsides to rust. Pull over when you see a gap in the trees, let the engine tick, and look north.
t.archipelago of san lorenzo@28.6,-112.8:
Out in the middle of the Gulf of California, in the channel that narrows between Baja California and the Sonoran coast, there is a scattering of rock islands that nobody lives on. San Lorenzo and San Pedro Mártir are two of them, protected as part of the Islands and Protected Areas of the Gulf of California. The Midriff Islands are famous among naturalists because the tides here move enormous volumes of water through narrow gaps, which churns up nutrients and feeds one of the richest marine systems on Earth. Whales, dolphins, sea lions, and clouds of seabirds all come for the harvest.

San Pedro Mártir is the dramatic one, a steep volcanic cone whitened by guano, thick with blue-footed and brown boobies, pelicans and cormorants, with giant cardon cacti on its slopes. San Lorenzo is a longer, lower ridge of rock, desert in its heart, and home to a sea-lion colony and specially adapted lizards and rodents. You cannot ride to either of them, of course. The point on the map is a spot in open water, and visits are by licensed boat from the peninsula, with strict rules on landing and distance from wildlife.

So the riding part belongs to the shore. The usual departure is Bahía de los Ángeles, on the Baja side, reached by Highway 12 from the transpeninsular road, a good paved ride of about an hour through boojum trees, cardón forests, rocky hills and then a sudden drop to a blue bay with islands lying offshore. The road is straight in places, with a few gentle bends and dips, and wind can be a nuisance, especially in winter and spring when northerlies come down the gulf. Heat in midsummer is intense, so the cooler months, from October to April, are the sensible time. Whale sharks gather in the bay in warmer months, and fin whales are seen in spring.

Services are modest. Bahía de los Ángeles is a small fishing and sport village with a couple of stations or fuel sellers whose supply can run short, so take fuel at the main highway junction and carry extra. There are family restaurants serving fresh fish tacos and shrimp, small hotels, and campsites on the beach. Bring water, sun protection and cash in pesos, since cards are patchy, and book any boat trip ahead through a licensed operator.
t.kottenforst nord domhecken 4@50.7,7.0:
West of the Rhine, between Bonn and the low hills of the Vorgebirge, a broad belt of oak and beech woodland covers a plateau called the Kottenforst. For centuries it was a hunting preserve of the Electors of Cologne, who lived in Bonn, and the forest still carries the marks of that history. Long straight rides, called Schneisen, cut through the trees in star patterns, laid out so that riders and hounds could drive deer toward the hunters, and some of these old alleys are now cycle paths and walking tracks. The southern and northern parts of the woodland are now a nature park, shared with the Ville, part of the Rhineland's wider belt of forests.

The Domhecken area lies on the northern part, close to Alfter, a municipality of about twenty-two thousand people. The woods here are a mix of old oak with younger beech and hornbeam, with small streams, ponds and clearings, and in spring the ground is a carpet of wood anemones and bluebells. Deer and wild boar live here, along with woodpeckers, nuthatches, buzzards and the occasional red kite. Local people walk dogs, ride horses and jog, so the forest feels like a shared park rather than wilderness.

For motorcyclists, the point to understand is that German forest tracks are generally closed to motor vehicles, and signs prohibit them on most paths, so the interest here is in the surrounding public roads. The Landesstraßen that cross the Kottenforst are well surfaced, with gentle bends through tunnels of trees, particularly lovely in autumn when the leaves turn, and they are lightly policed with speed cameras. The Vorgebirge, a ridge to the north, has fruit orchards and farm shops with apples, strawberries and asparagus in season. Mist often fills the woods in the early morning, and ice can linger in shaded patches in winter.

Alfter, three kilometres away, has fuel stations, bakeries and supermarkets, and Bonn is a short ride, with its Beethoven house, the Rhine promenade and many cafés. For something local, try a Rheinischer Sauerbraten with dumplings and red cabbage, or a Kölsch beer, the light local brew. Parking at forest car parks is usually free but sometimes limited, and mobile signals are good. Keep to the signed paths on foot, and give horses plenty of room if you meet them on a road.
The southern end of the Kottenforst lies where the plateau west of Bonn begins to tilt toward the Eifel, and the ground, which is flat and wooded to the north, starts to roll in low hills around Wachtberg and Meckenheim. Anyone who has walked the Kottenforst on a Sunday knows the Professorenweg, a long forest track whose name is thought to come from the university professors of Bonn who took their daily constitutional along it, thinking aloud with a colleague. I cannot vouch for the details, but the habit of walking and arguing in these woods is easy to believe, especially on a misty autumn morning when the beeches are bronze.

This part of the woods is older and more mixed than the northern edge, with big beeches, oaks, some conifer plantations, and boggy hollows where alder and willow grow. The ground holds water, there are small ponds, and frogs and newts breed in spring. Roe deer step out at dusk, and the sound of a woodpecker echoes through the trunks. The air, after rain, smells of leaf mould and wet bark in a way that suddenly makes a day at the office seem remote.

A motorcyclist should treat the forest tracks as off limits, since German law keeps motor vehicles off most unpaved forest paths and fines can be sharp. The public roads around are a different story. From Wachtberg, the lanes drop and climb through orchards and small villages, with views toward the Siebengebirge and the Drachenfels across the Rhine on a clear day. To the south the Ahr valley opens, with its vineyards, red wine and winding road along the river, though parts of the valley are still marked by the catastrophic floods of 2021, and some sections have been rebuilt. Rain and leaf-fall make autumn mornings slippery, and the roads can ice up at dawn in winter.

Wachtberg, three kilometres away, is a municipality of twenty thousand people, with fuel and bakeries, and Bonn and Bad Godesberg are within easy reach for anything more. Bad Godesberg has a hilltop ruined castle and the old diplomatic quarter from the days when Bonn was the capital of West Germany. Local pubs serve Rhineland dishes such as Himmel un Ääd, black pudding with apple and potato, and the beer is Kölsch. Parking at forest car parks is generally free, and the paths are well signed for walkers.
t.fort site and civil settlement of heddes:
The Roman frontier in Germany, the Limes, begins at the Rhine near Rheinbrohl, and a few kilometres upstream the town of Neuwied sits on the river, its district of Heddesdorf lying on the site of a Roman auxiliary fort. The fort was one of a chain of garrison posts in the Neuwied basin, a wide, fertile bowl of the Rhine valley with a mild climate, and the soldiers who lived here controlled the river crossing and the road toward the frontier. A civil settlement, a vicus, grew beside the fort, with traders, craftsmen and families. Nothing stands today above ground, because the fort lies under houses and streets, and what survives is documented in the finds in the local museum, in markers and in the street plan.

The Limes as a whole, from the Rhine to the Danube, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site under the name Upper German-Raetian Limes, and this point is a piece of that long chain. Neuwied has other claims. It was founded in the seventeenth century by a count who welcomed religious refugees, including the Moravian Brethren, who built a neat quarter with a grid of streets that still shows. Friedrich Wilhelm Raiffeisen, the founder of the cooperative banking movement, lived in Heddesdorf and died there in 1888, and a museum recalls his work.

Riding in the area is relaxed. The Rhine valley road, the B42, runs alongside the river with views of ships, castles and vineyards, though traffic can be heavy, and small lanes climb into the Westerwald, with its wooded hills, ponds and half-timbered villages. Roads are generally well maintained, with moderate bends, and fog often lies on the Rhine in autumn mornings. In summer, the Rhine flood plain can be hot and thundery. Spring, with blossom in the orchards, is pleasant.

Neuwied is a city of about sixty-seven thousand people, so fuel, workshops, restaurants and hotels are all easy to find. The Rhine promenade, with its flood defences, is a good place for a walk, and the town has a zoo and a palace, Schloss Monrepos, in the nearby woods. Try a plate of Rhenish roast beef with dumplings, or a fresh river fish. Parking in the centre is paid, and signage for low-emission zones should be checked when entering larger cities. Keep an eye out for Rhine barges at the quayside.
t.limessection between wp 4 36 and 4 37@50:
Between the hills of the Taunus and the soft farmland of the Wetterau, the Roman frontier ran in a long, mostly straight line for most of the second and third centuries. This is Hesse, and the numbering that gives the place its odd label, watchtowers 4/36 and 4/37, refers to the standard system archaeologists use to count the Limes watchposts section by section. The point lies near Butzbach, a town of twenty-five thousand people where the frontier crossed the Wetterau and the local fort once held a cavalry unit. The section in question consists of the earth traces, a low bank and a ditch, that the Romans built in front of their wooden palisade, with towers spaced at regular intervals behind.

What you actually see is subtle. The Limes here has been worn down by farming and by time, and in many places it is a slight rise in a field or a line of trees that has grown on the old bank. In a few places signs or reconstructed towers explain the system. It helps to think of the frontier as a surveillance line rather than a defensive wall, for watchers on towers, a ditch to slow cattle thieves and a palisade to channel traffic toward gates where tax could be collected. The whole of it is part of the UNESCO Upper German-Raetian Limes.

The countryside is among the gentlest in Hesse, with fields of wheat and sugar beet, orchards, small streams and low hills, and the wind sweeps across the open Wetterau. Roads are well surfaced, with mild curves and some country lanes that run straight for a kilometre or two. The Taunus to the south offers more demanding bends, forest and view points, notably around the Feldberg. In summer, harvest machinery appears on the lanes, and in winter fog hangs on the plain. Spring and autumn are lovely.

Butzbach, about two kilometres away, has a market square lined with half-timbered houses, a museum with Roman objects and plenty of shops and cafés, with fuel on the roads around the town. Frankfurt is about forty kilometres to the south, and Giessen a similar distance north. Try a pork schnitzel with Frankfurt green sauce, and in the autumn the cider called Äppelwoi, if you are not riding. Observe the signs on field tracks, as farm lanes are often closed to motor traffic, and take care when passing tractors.
t.watchtower wp 4 81@50.4,8.9:
A Roman watchtower on the Limes was, in essence, a lookout with a roof. The stone ones were about five metres square and perhaps ten metres high, with a ground floor for storage, an upper room for a handful of soldiers, and a wooden gallery with a window or a balcony from which a lamp, a horn or a flag could be used to signal. Where the tower stood, a small patch of ground was cleared, with a ditch around it, and the garrison lived in the tower itself or in a nearby hut. Number 4/81 stands in Hesse, in the Wetterau, between Echzell and the village of Hungen, in a landscape of farmland and low volcanic hills.

The Wetterau is a fertile basin with a loess soil that the Romans valued, and their frontier crossed it on a long, almost straight line from the Taunus toward the Main, drawing the border between the empire and the lands of the Chatti. The big forts, such as the one at Echzell, supported the towers with cavalry, and the supply roads connected them, but out here at the tower you were alone with the wind, and the chance of seeing smoke on the next hill. Reconstructed towers at a few places in Hesse show what this looked like, but here you must imagine it.

Riding around Echzell is easy and slightly sleepy. The country roads cross open fields and orchards, with a few climbs towards the Vogelsberg, an extinct volcano, whose slopes offer more engaging curves. Surfaces are good, and the villages are of half-timbered houses with farm yards. A tractor or a combine can be a long way ahead of you, so patience is useful. Summer afternoons can be hot, and thunderstorms roll over the hills in the evening.

Echzell, three kilometres away, has about six thousand people, with a bakery, shops, a few inns and a petrol station, and the town of Nidda is a bit further. Fill your tank in the larger places before heading into the quiet lanes. The Limes line is part of the UNESCO Upper German-Raetian Limes, and an information board or marker may stand beside the footpath. Please do not climb on any remains, and stay on the public ways, since farmland is private.
t.limessection between wp 4 81 and 4 82@50:
Between two neighbouring watchtowers the Romans left a short piece of frontier that today looks like almost nothing, and that is part of its charm. The line between Wachtposten 4/81 and 4/82 runs through the fields of the Wetterau east of Frankfurt, close to Echzell, where the earth wall and ditch of the Limes can still be traced as a long, low swelling in the farmland, sometimes crowned by a hedge or a row of trees that have grown on it. Beneath the field, archaeologists have found postholes of the palisade, which stood about three metres high and was made of split oak trunks.
