The point of a stretch like this is the surveying. The Romans laid out the Limes in the Wetterau almost dead straight, over rolling ground, sighting from tower to tower with poles and fires, and over long sections the line departs from the straight by only a few metres. The accuracy suggests that they cut it deliberately, as a clear marker, rather than following the lay of the land. It was less a barrier to armies than a customs line and a way to control movement. The frontier lasted until about the middle of the third century, when pressure from the Alemanni led the Romans to withdraw behind the Rhine and Danube.

In practical terms, the countryside is open, with big skies, and the roads here are straight and quiet, with the occasional gentle bend at a hedge or a farmstead. Wind sweeps the plain, so in cold weather a windproof layer is welcome, and in late summer the harvest dust hangs in the air. In spring, rapeseed paints whole fields in yellow, and in autumn the land turns brown and fog settles in the early hours.

Echzell, two or three kilometres away, has fuel and everyday shops, and the museum in the village displays finds from the Roman fort. The nearest larger centre is Hungen, with more services, and Friedberg and Büdingen are within a short ride, with medieval centres worth a walk. Local food is simple, with Handkäse mit Musik, a sour milk cheese with onions, and Apfelwein. Please stay on public tracks, since field edges are private, and take your rubbish with you.
t.watchtowers wp 4 40 to 4 44 including th:
The Taunus ridge rises north of Frankfurt like a long, forested wall, and the Romans did not try to cross it. Their frontier line swung around its northern slopes, through the Wetterau, and then down toward the Main, and this section lies near Langgöns, close to the valley of the Lahn and a short ride from Giessen. The five towers of the stretch numbered 4/40 to 4/44 followed the ridge lines in a sequence that let each one see the next, and a signal tower on the Johannisberg, a modest hill, linked them. Of all these only footings and mounds remain, but the surveying logic is easy to read once you stand on high ground and look toward the next rise.

Roman soldiers who served here came from many provinces. Auxiliary units drawn from places as distant as Spain, Syria and Thrace were posted along the Limes, and their gravestones, found in local museums, give names and ranks in Latin. The line was abandoned in the middle of the third century, and the local people took the stone for their own buildings, so that a medieval church wall may contain a block from a Roman tower. The Upper German-Raetian Limes is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

The country here is a mix of orchards, small woods and low hills, among them the foothills of the Taunus and the Vogelsberg, and the roads between the villages are well surfaced, with moderate curves, short climbs and patches of woodland shade. Lanes sometimes narrow to a single track, and farm vehicles appear without warning. In spring the blossom is thick on the apple trees, and in autumn the woods are mellow. Winter mornings can bring black ice on shaded stretches, and in summer thunderstorms break suddenly in the afternoons.

Langgöns, three kilometres away, has about twelve thousand people, fuel stations, shops and several bakeries and restaurants, and the university town of Giessen, a short ride to the north, offers more. Try a plate of local Hessian dishes, such as grüne Soße, a green herb sauce eaten with potatoes and eggs, or a cup of coffee and a slice of Zwetschgenkuchen, plum cake, in season. Many of the paths to the tower sites are forest tracks closed to motor vehicles, so leave the bike at a car park and walk, and carry a map, since mobile signals are patchy under the trees.
t.east wall area 1a to 1c@54.5,9.7:
When the Vikings built their trading town of Hedeby at the head of the Schlei, a long narrow inlet of the Baltic, they chose a spot with a short portage to the North Sea rivers, making it one of the great crossroads of Northern Europe. To protect the isthmus between the two seas, the Danes built a long earthwork called the Danevirke, begun in the eighth century and strengthened for centuries after, with a rampart, a ditch and in places a brick wall added in the twelfth century by King Valdemar. Hedeby and the Danevirke are together a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The East Wall, the Ostwall, is the eastern arm of the system, running through the countryside near Kosel above the Schlei.

On the ground, the Danevirke looks like a long, grassy bank in a field, with a ditch beside it and trees growing on the top. It is easier to understand at the Danevirke Museum, near Dannewerk, which explains how the barrier was built, rebuilt and fought over, from the Viking age until the war of 1864, when the Danes withdrew from it in the face of Prussian and Austrian forces. The frontier it protected moved back and forth over centuries between Danish and German control, and this region of Schleswig has an unusually mixed identity, with Danish minority schools and Low German dialects.

The countryside is gentle farmland, with knobbly fields, hedgerows called Knicks, lakes and the long waters of the Schlei, and roads run in easy curves between villages. The flat horizons and big skies are typical of Schleswig-Holstein. Rider-friendly surfaces and moderate traffic make it a relaxed place, though wind off the Baltic can be strong. Summer is the busiest time on the Baltic coast, and spring and autumn are quieter. Mist hangs over the meadows in the morning.

Kosel, three kilometres away, is a village of about thirteen hundred people, and Eckernförde, six kilometres off, is a lively Baltic port with fuel, shops, a smokehouse tradition and a harbour full of boats. The city of Schleswig, with its fishing village Holm and its castle, Gottorf, is a short ride to the north-west. Try a smoked herring roll or a Kieler Sprotte, a smoked sprat, and a plate of Holstein pork with red cabbage. The Hedeby museum, a short drive away, has reconstructed Viking houses beside the water and is worth a visit on a dry day.
t.watchtower wp 1 84@50.4,7.8:
Bad Ems is a small spa town in the winding valley of the Lahn, where the river cuts a deep trench through the hills of the Taunus and Westerwald. Its warm springs were known to the Romans, and it gained fame in the nineteenth century, when the Russian tsar, the Prussian king and the whole of European society came to take the cure. In July 1870 King Wilhelm of Prussia was walking on the promenade when the French ambassador approached him, and the telegram that described the encounter, edited by Bismarck for the press, helped push France into the war that led to German unification. The Ems Dispatch, as it is called, is one of the famous editorial acts in diplomatic history.

Up in the hills above Arzbach, a little way from the spa, the Roman frontier crossed the high ground, and the watchtower marked 1/84 stood on a ridge with a view down toward the Lahn. The tower is gone, though the site may be marked, and the Limes line here is part of the UNESCO Upper German-Raetian Limes. It is a landscape of oak and beech woods, open meadows, and small streams that run down toward the Lahn.

The riding is a pleasure, with twisty roads linking small villages, climbing out of the valley and dropping again, with a surface that is mostly sound. The Lahn valley road from Koblenz toward Bad Ems and Nassau runs beside the river through gorge scenery, with castles on the heights and a railway on the opposite bank. It is a popular run for motorcyclists on weekends, so expect company, and the local police pay attention to speed. In winter the hills see snow and ice, and fog fills the valley. Spring and autumn are especially beautiful.

Arzbach, a village of under two thousand people a kilometre away, is small, and the nearest bigger town with fuel is Bad Ems, about five kilometres off, with a casino, a pump room and a spa park, and Koblenz, a larger city at the meeting of the Rhine and Moselle, is a short ride on. Try a plate of Westerwald specialities, such as potato dumplings with sauerkraut, or a coffee on the Lahn promenade. Forest tracks near the tower site are generally closed to motor vehicles, so walk the last stretch, and wear shoes with good grip on the wet leaves.
t.watchtowers wp 1 32 to 1 34@50.5,7.5:
Just north of Neuwied, the Westerwald begins to climb out of the Rhine valley, and the Roman frontier ran up through the woods from its starting point on the river, rising and falling over the low ridges. The Limes here is the Upper German section in its earliest stretch, where watchtowers 1/32 to 1/34 stood close together on the hillside above the Wied, a small river that runs through a pretty, wooded valley to join the Rhine. Melsbach, a village of two thousand people next to the point, lies in this valley, and the surrounding hills are a mix of beech forest, meadow and the fields of the Neuwied basin.

The three towers stood close together on the hillside, near enough that soldiers could pass messages by shouting or by signal. What remains is a series of low mounds in the forest, and the line of the old palisade ditch. The Rhine end of the Limes has an information centre in Rheinbrohl, with a reconstructed tower and a Limes museum, which makes an excellent starting point to understand the frontier, and it lies only a short distance downriver. The whole is part of the UNESCO site.

The riding is attractive and quiet. The Wied valley and the lanes of the Westerwald offer smooth roads with plenty of bends, steady climbs and descents, and frequent views over the hills and the Rhine plain. Forest roads in the area are narrow, with a thick cover of leaves in autumn, so grip can be poor. Rain is common, with fog on the heights in winter. Early morning rides give the best light and the least traffic, and the Rhine in the distance catches a silver haze.

Melsbach has a few shops and an inn, and the nearest large town is Neuwied, five kilometres away, with fuel stations, supermarkets and restaurants. Try a plate of Westerwald dishes, with potatoes and smoked sausage,, and a local beer if you are not riding. Neuwied also has a Rhine-side promenade and a zoo, which is fun for a break. Walk the last stretch to the tower sites, because most forest tracks are closed to motorised traffic.
t.watchtower wp 1 88@50.4,7.8:
In the hills above the Lahn, in the Westerwald near Arzbach, the Roman frontier made a long, curving loop through a country of oak and beech forest, and watchtower 1/88 was one of the posts on its line. This district was thick with towers, and several neighbouring numbers lie within a few kilometres. The Romans placed them wherever the ground gave a good view, usually on a rise or a ridge, so that from one you could see the smoke or lamp of the next.

The experience of the site is about the woods themselves. The Westerwald is a rainy plateau, with soils that are heavy and wet, and its forests of beech, oak and spruce are dark and quiet, with moss on the stones and bracken on the slopes. In clearings you find small ponds and peat bogs, and the call of woodpeckers and buzzards. The tower mound itself is a low heap, possibly with a marker or an information board, and it is easy to miss in leaf. The Limes is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site that stretches from the Rhine to the Danube.

For riders, the lanes around Arzbach are narrow, twisty and well surfaced, with a few steep climbs, and the area is a staple of the local motorcycle scene. Cattle graze in the open land, and fallen branches and mud after storms are common. In February the roads can be icy, and in July the shade of the woods is welcome. It makes a good short loop combined with the Lahn valley road, with its castles and railway, and the elegant spa town of Bad Ems is the usual stop.

Arzbach is two and a half kilometres away, and Bad Ems, four kilometres off, is the nearest town of any size, with fuel stations, cafés and a spa park along the river. Koblenz is the bigger city, with its Deutsches Eck, the corner where the Moselle meets the Rhine. Take a coffee in Bad Ems or a plate of Westerwald dumplings, and be ready for cool, wet weather even in summer. Forest tracks close to the tower are generally closed to motor vehicles, and a short walk from a car park is the way to reach them.
t.fort site of hungen inheiden@50.5,8.9:
Hungen lies in the eastern Wetterau, on the edge of the Vogelsberg, the great extinct volcano of central Hesse, and the village of Inheiden is a short distance from it, in a fold of rolling farmland. The Roman fort at Inheiden was one of the smaller auxiliary forts on the Wetterau Limes, a modest rectangular enclosure with a ditch and a wall of earth and timber, later rebuilt in stone, and it held a unit of a few hundred soldiers. A fort of this size had a headquarters building in the middle, barracks, a granary, a bath building outside the wall and a small settlement of traders and families beside it.

Today the fort has vanished beneath the fields, and only a farm track and the modern road suggest its position. Finds from excavations, such as pottery, coins and bits of armour, are kept in local and regional museums, and the fort belongs to the UNESCO Upper German-Raetian Limes. What the place offers is perspective. You stand in a field of wheat or sugar beet, with the wind moving through the crop, and know that two thousand years ago there was a base here, with horses, smoke and Latin commands, and that this peaceful ground was a frontier.

Riding in the area is pleasant and unhurried. The roads are well surfaced and often empty, rolling over low hills with long views to the Vogelsberg and the Taunus, with curves that are gentle rather than demanding. The Horloff valley has small lakes, which attract birdwatchers, and nearby the village of Hungen has a castle and a half-timbered centre. In summer, grain harvest brings dust and combines, and in autumn fog can lie in the hollows. Mid-spring, with the rapeseed in flower, is the best.

Hungen, under two kilometres away, has about four and a half thousand people, with a petrol station, bakeries and a few inns, and Echzell, eight kilometres off, is the nearest larger place on the data. Giessen and Friedberg, both in a half hour, have more services. A Hessian apple wine, Äppelwoi, and a local sausage, Ahle Wurst, are typical, though riders should keep to a cup of coffee. Field paths are private or restricted, so view the site from the public road or from marked paths, and take care when passing farm vehicles.
t.town hall and roland on the marketplace:
In 1404 the merchants of Bremen put up two statements of independence in their market square, a Gothic town hall and a stone statue of a knight, Roland, standing five and a half metres tall with a sword in his hand and a shield at his feet. The town hall was later given a Renaissance front in the Weser style, rich with arcades and sculptures, in the early seventeenth century, and the great hall inside has a ceiling hung with model ships. Roland, who looks out over the square towards the cathedral, symbolised the city's freedom from the archbishop, and a local saying holds that as long as Roland stands, Bremen will remain free. Both were inscribed by UNESCO in 2004.

Bremen was a member of the Hanseatic League and is still officially the Free Hanseatic City of Bremen, a city-state of its own, together with Bremerhaven. On the north side of the square the cathedral, with its two towers, is a landmark, and beside the town hall stands a small bronze statue of the Bremen Town Musicians, a donkey, dog, cat and rooster stacked on each other's backs from the Grimm fairy tale. Locals say you should hold the donkey's front hooves and make a wish. Nearby, the narrow alley of Böttcherstraße is a brick-built curiosity of the 1920s, with a glockenspiel of porcelain bells, and the old quarter of Schnoor, a maze of tiny houses, is full of craft shops.

Riding in the centre is not the plan. The market square is a pedestrian zone, and the surrounding streets have trams, cobbles, restricted zones and a low-emission area, so park outside and walk. Beyond the city, the flat country of Lower Saxony and the Weser valley offers quiet roads. The wind from the North Sea is a constant, and rain showers can come at any time of year, so a waterproof layer is a good idea. The best time to visit is spring through early autumn, though the Christmas market in December is also a draw.

Bremen has half a million people and every service you could ask for, including plenty of fuel stations on the ring roads, workshops and a very wide choice of places to eat. Try a bowl of Knipp, a local sausage with oats, or Kohl und Pinkel in winter, and a coffee, since Bremen has a long history as a coffee-roasting port. The city is known for beer, and Beck's is brewed here. Look for parking garages near the old town, and be aware of rules on emission zones for vehicles from other countries.
t.kottenforst nord domhecken 2@50.7,7.0:
The Kottenforst sits on a terrace between the Rhine plain and the hills of the Vorgebirge, and its northern edge comes right up against the settlements of Alfter, Bornheim and Bonn. The ground here is clay and loess, wet in winter and hard in summer, and it has made good soil for farming around the woods. The Domhecken area lies on the edge, and I cannot tell you the story behind the name of this particular spot. The pattern, though, of woodland surrounded by old hedgerows and farm tracks, is typical of the Rhineland.

What gives the place its interest is the edge. You come out of a stand of beech into open fields of cabbage, strawberries and asparagus, while the lignite country of the Rhenish coalfield lies not far to the west, a sharp reminder that this is also industrial country. The Vorgebirge, just north, is the fruit-and-vegetable garden of Cologne and Bonn, and its farm shops sell apples, plums and pumpkins in autumn. Hawks and buzzards hunt the field margins, and in spring the hedgerows are white with blackthorn.

The ride is gentle and varied. The lanes between Alfter and Bornheim and Roisdorf are narrow and smooth, with village crossings, speed bumps and cyclists, and they link to quieter roads through the woods. The Rhine is a short distance east, with its flood plain and ferry crossings, and the Siebengebirge on the far side adds a dramatic skyline. Weekends in fine weather bring walkers, dog owners and families, so ride with consideration. Early autumn mornings are lovely, with mist lying between the beech trunks, and winter fog can be thick.

Alfter, three kilometres from here, has fuel stations, supermarkets and bakeries, and Bonn is a short ride north-east. Try a Rhenish Reibekuchen, a potato pancake with apple sauce, at one of the farm stalls or markets. Forest tracks near the Domhecken are closed to motor vehicles, and parking is usually found at designated forest car parks. Mobile signals are good, and the paths are well signed for those who wish to walk.
t.watchtower wp 4 37@50.5,8.7:
Two names appear for this spot, and both belong to the same stretch of frontier that crosses the Wetterau near Butzbach. A watchtower numbered 4/37 stood here in the second century, one in a chain of tall lookouts built just behind the Limes palisade, with a view along the line to the neighbouring towers and out across the forest to the north, the land of the Chatti. Little remains today, a low platform of earth and some fallen stones, perhaps with a marker, but towers like this were the eyes of the Roman army, and their quiet watching was the daily business of the frontier.

The setting is a different place from the open fields to the east. This is the foot of the Taunus, where the ground rises in low, wooded ridges and the villages sit in shallow valleys. The woods are mixed oak and beech, with small streams, and in spring the floor is carpeted in wild garlic, whose smell drifts into the lanes. Roe deer step out at dusk, and the sound of a cuckoo is common in May. Butzbach itself is a medieval town that grew up beside the line.

I would call the riding here modest but nice. The roads between Butzbach and the villages on the edge of the Taunus are smooth and quiet, with gentle bends and short climbs through forest, while the Taunus proper, to the south, has livelier routes with hairpins and views, including the climb to the Feldberg, which is popular with motorcyclists on dry weekends and watched by the police. Wet leaves in autumn and ice in winter are the main hazards, and fog can fill the valleys in October. The best time is May to June, when the woods are fresh.

Butzbach is two kilometres away, with a good range of shops, fuel stations and restaurants, and its position on the main road makes it easy to reach. The local bakeries sell pretzels and plum cake, and in the Wetterau a Sunday lunch usually means roast pork. Forest tracks are closed to motorised traffic, so leave the bike in a village and walk the last distance, with a map in your pocket.
t.daeseong dong tumuli@35.2,128.9:
The tumuli of Daeseong-dong lie on a low hill above the Gimhae plain, close to the Nakdong river delta in the south-east of Korea. They are the royal cemetery of Geumgwan Gaya, one of the small kingdoms of the Gaya confederacy, which flourished alongside the better-known Three Kingdoms of the Korean peninsula, and for centuries after it was swallowed up by its neighbour Silla in 532, it was largely forgotten. Archaeology has changed that. Excavations show a wealthy society, strong on iron, which was exported to Japan and to the Chinese colonies to the north, and the burials contain armour, horse gear, pottery and iron ingots that served almost as currency. UNESCO listed the Gaya Tumuli in 2023.

The legend is even better than the facts. According to the old chronicles, six golden eggs descended from heaven in a box, and from the first came King Suro, who founded the kingdom. His queen, Heo Hwang-ok, is said to have sailed from a distant land called Ayuta, which many Koreans identify with India, and a large share of the country's Kim family trace their line to the pair. Visitors from India occasionally arrive to see her tomb, and a friendly bond exists between the two places.

Riding here is gentle and flat, a contrast with Korea's mountains. The city of Gimhae is a sprawl of industry, apartment blocks and rice paddies, with wide boulevards and heavy traffic, and the airport for Busan lies close by. The best weather comes in late spring and autumn, while summer is humid and the monsoon rains arrive in July. Winter can be cold but is often dry and sunny. Roads are good and well signed, and speed cameras are common, so watch the limits.

Fuel is simple. Gimhae is a city of more than three hundred thousand with stations on every main road, and expressways run to Busan and Changwon. Look for a bowl of dwaeji gukbap, the pork and rice soup that Busan made famous, in a small restaurant near the old market.

The tumuli themselves are low, grassy mounds on a ridge with a view of the plain, quiet in the morning, with a museum nearby that tells the story of the Gaya in some detail.
t.yangdong cluster donggangseowon confucia:
Yangdong is a village that still lives like the old Korea of the Joseon dynasty. It lies in a valley north of Gyeongju, in a bowl of low wooded hills, and it is home to some of the finest surviving traditional houses in the country, hundreds of tiled-roof and thatched homes spread over the slopes. Two great clans have dominated it for centuries, the Wolseong Son and the Yeogang Yi, and their families built the large tile-roofed mansions on the high ground with the thatched houses of the tenants below. The neat layout follows the principles of feng shui: the main houses face south with a hill behind and a stream in front. UNESCO listed Yangdong along with Hahoe in 2010 as the Historic Villages of Korea.

The Confucian academies, the seowon, were private schools where scholars studied and honoured sages. Donggangseowon, near the same part of Gyeongju, honours a Neo-Confucian scholar of the Joseon period, and the pavilions and quiet courtyards are a good example of the style. Together with the village, they show how the learned clans passed their time and their power in the countryside.

The riding is pleasant and quiet. Roads around Gyeongju are wide and well surfaced, and when you leave the city towards the villages they narrow into lanes between rice fields and orchards. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with blossoms, then colourful foliage, and a clear light. Summer is hot and humid, and winter can be very cold. The Seokguram grotto, on the ride list, sits high on Mount Toham, east of Gyeongju, and its approach road climbs through pine forest with a few tight bends.

Fuel is on the main roads, and the city of Pohang, an industrial port to the north-east, has more stations and a large steel works, which gives a very different feel to the region. Yeonil is a smaller town in between. The village has a few simple restaurants and tea houses, and you may find rice cooked in an earthenware pot with local vegetables.

The village is lived in, so keep quiet, do not look into private courtyards, and park outside the lane.
t.tumuli park belt@35.8,129.2:
Gyeongju's tumuli look like a row of green breasts rising out of a lawn, and that is exactly what makes the Daereungwon park so memorable. The mounds are the royal tombs of the Silla kingdom, which ruled the south-east of the Korean peninsula for nearly a thousand years, and eventually unified the peninsula in the seventh century. The kings and queens were buried in chambers of wood and stone, sealed under a mountain of river stones and then covered with earth, and in some of them excavators found treasures: gold crowns with branching antler-like uprights, belts, earrings and glass vessels from as far away as the Mediterranean.

One of the mounds, Cheonmachong, the Heavenly Horse Tomb, has been opened so that you can walk inside a reconstruction of the burial chamber. The horse painted on a birch-bark saddle flap, a galloping white horse with its tail streaming, was found inside and has become an emblem of the city. The tombs are scattered in the middle of town, and the Cheomseongdae observatory, a bottle-shaped stone tower from the seventh century, is a short walk away. Gyeongju is often called a museum without walls, because ancient things are everywhere, even beside the cafes and bakeries.

Riding in Gyeongju is a delight if you choose your time. The city is flat and the streets are wide, and the roads around the park have lots of bicycles, tour buses and scooters. In April the cherry blossoms along the Bomun Lake road and the streets around the tombs are famous, and the crowds can be thick, so I would come on a weekday morning. Summer is steamy and winter can be bitterly cold, but a clear autumn day, with persimmons ripening, is hard to beat.

Fuel is available in Gyeongju, a city of over a hundred and fifty thousand, with stations on the ring roads, and Yeonil to the east adds a few more. Local specialities include Gyeongju bread, a small pastry filled with sweet red bean paste, and ssambap, a meal of rice with a spread of side dishes wrapped in leaves.

Walk the park at dusk, when the mounds are floodlit and the town goes quiet, and you will feel the age of the place.
t.sansa@36.5,127.8:
Songnisan is a mountain with a long reputation, and the temple Beopjusa sits on its lower flank, in the middle of the country in North Chungcheong province, among pines, rock outcrops and clear streams. Tradition says the monk Uisin founded it in the middle of the sixth century, after returning from India with scriptures carried on a mule, and the name means Temple of the Dharma Abode. It was destroyed in the Japanese invasions of the sixteenth century and rebuilt, and its great wooden hall, Palsangjeon, is the only five-storey wooden pagoda still standing in Korea, a tall tiered structure that rises over the courtyard.

Beopjusa is one of seven Buddhist mountain monasteries, the Sansa, inscribed by UNESCO in 2018. They are not only places of worship but also places that have kept alive a tradition of study and meditation, in the mountains, where monks live in a way that has changed slowly. The Sansa temples are loosely arranged, in a pattern that follows the contours of the land, and the sense of a quiet retreat is part of the design.

The riding is a pleasure. The roads around Songnisan National Park wind through forested valleys, with views of rocky peaks, and the road from Boeun climbs in a series of bends to the temple car park. The best times are late spring, with fresh leaves and azaleas, and late October, when the maple and oak turn red and gold, and the crowds in the park can be thick. Winter brings snow and ice, so check conditions. Summer is warm and wet, with sudden storms.

Fuel is easy at Boeun and Goesan, where the stations are on the main roads, and the city of Cheongju, with more than six hundred thousand people, is the large centre nearby. Near the temple entrance there are restaurants serving mountain vegetables, pajeon pancakes and makgeolli, the milky rice wine.

The ride list goes next to Dosan-seowon, the Confucian academy at Andong, a good day's ride south-east through quiet country. The contrast between a Buddhist mountain monastery and a Confucian school, so close in space and so different in spirit, is one of Korea's treasures.
t.anak tomb no 2@38.5,125.5:
Goguryeo painted its dead. In the fourth and fifth centuries, the rulers and nobles of this northern kingdom, which at its height held much of Manchuria and the northern half of the Korean peninsula, were buried in stone chambers beneath earthen mounds, and the walls were covered in murals that show hunting parties, processions, kitchens, stables and the gods of the four directions. Anak Tomb No. 2 lies near the town of Anak in South Hwanghae province in North Korea, in the same cluster as its better-known sibling Tomb No. 3, whose inscription gives a date equivalent to AD 357 and whose procession scenes are famous. The complex of Koguryo tombs was inscribed by UNESCO in 2004.

I have to be straight about the access. North Korea is not a country where a foreign rider can wander at will on his own motorcycle; visits are only possible on organised tours, with guides, fixed itineraries and restrictions on photography, and for most of the last few years even those have been suspended or very limited. So this stop is one to read about rather than to plan for, and I would check the current rules of your own government before thinking further.

What I can tell you is the landscape and the historical background. Hwanghae is rolling farmland, with low hills, terraced rice fields and villages of tiled houses, in the western part of the country, south of Pyongyang and not far from the sea. Anak town, a place of about twenty thousand people, is a local centre, and the larger town of Chaeryong lies to the south. Winters here are cold and dry, with snow and bitter winds from Siberia, and summers are hot and wet with a monsoon peak in July and August.

The murals themselves fascinate historians because they preserve a world otherwise lost. Costumes, musical instruments, and architecture appear in lively scenes, and the mythical creatures, the azure dragon, the white tiger, the vermilion bird and the black tortoise-snake, guard the corners of the heavens. They influenced the art of neighbouring Korean kingdoms and of Japan, and some scholars see echoes in the later Takamatsuzuka paintings in Nara.

Few places on this list are as far from a simple ride-in stop, but the paintings deserve to be known.
t.baekje historic areas@36.5,127.1:
Gongju is where the kingdom of Baekje retreated when it was almost destroyed. In 475 the armies of Goguryeo, the northern rival, swept south and took the capital at Hanseong, near modern Seoul, killing the king, and the survivors moved the court to Ungjin, as Gongju was then called, a defensible site on the Geum river with a fortress on the hill above. For about sixty years it served as the capital, until the court moved further south to Sabi, now Buyeo, in 538. The UNESCO listing of Baekje Historic Areas, in 2015, covers Gongju, Buyeo and Iksan.

The great find came by accident. In 1971, workmen digging a drainage channel at the tomb cluster of Songsan-ri uncovered an intact brick-lined tomb, the burial of King Muryeong, who died in 523, and his queen. It had never been robbed, and inside were gold ornaments, jade, bronze mirrors and a stone guardian beast with iron horn, along with inscribed tablets giving the date. It is among the most important archaeological finds in Korean history, and the objects are now displayed in the national museum in Gongju. The tomb itself is closed to protect it, but a replica allows you to see the form.

The fortress of Gongsanseong still crowns the ridge above the river, with its stone and earth walls running for a couple of kilometres, and you can walk the ramparts for views over the town and the slow, wide Geum. The national museum in town holds the finds from the royal tombs and is worth an hour on a rainy day.

For riders, the roads around Gongju are good and the countryside gentle, with rice fields, chestnut groves and low wooded hills. Chestnuts are Gongju's pride, and in autumn roadside stalls sell them roasted or boiled, along with sweet chestnut pastries. Spring brings cherry blossom, early summer brings the humid heat, and October is the best month, with clear air and golden fields. The roads are well signed, with speed cameras along the main routes.

Fuel is easy in Gongju, a city of over seventy thousand, and in Sejong, the new administrative capital to the north-east. The tidal flats of Getbol, on the ride list, lie to the west on the Yellow Sea coast, a vast expanse of mud that comes alive with shorebirds, crabs and clam diggers at low tide.
t.rock paintings of the sierra de san fran:
Far down the Baja California peninsula, in the mountains above the Pacific coast, are some of the finest rock paintings in the Americas. The Sierra de San Francisco is a rugged range of volcanic mesas and deep canyons, and in the shelters and overhangs along the canyon walls the Cochimí people and their ancestors painted enormous figures: humans, deer, rabbits, birds, snakes and whales, in red, black, white and yellow. Many of the human figures are life-size or bigger, with arms raised, some pierced by arrows, and the older panels are thought to be a few hundred to several thousand years old. UNESCO listed the site in 1993.

The paintings are remote and protected, and visiting them is an expedition rather than a stop. The village of San Francisco de la Sierra is the base, and visitors need to arrange permission and a local guide through the authorities in San Ignacio, and then go by mule or on foot into the canyons, with a camp overnight. You cannot simply turn up on a motorcycle and walk in, and this is a good thing, since the paintings are fragile. Plan the trip a long way ahead.

The riding in the area is a classic. Highway 1 runs the length of Baja California, and the stretch between Guerrero Negro and Santa Rosalía crosses the Vizcaíno desert, a huge protected landscape of cardon cactus, boojum trees and sand, then climbs over the volcanic mesas to the green oasis of San Ignacio, with its date palms and an old Jesuit mission built in the 1700s. The road is straight and long, with strong crosswinds, little traffic, and few services. Summer is blisteringly hot, and the best season is from November to April, when the air is clear and the temperatures mild.

Fuel is a real concern. Pumps are widely spaced, and some run out of one grade, so fill up at each opportunity, especially at Guerrero Negro, Vizcaíno and San Ignacio, and carry a spare can if you can. Bring plenty of water.

In winter, grey whales come to the nearby lagoons of Ojo de Liebre and San Ignacio to calve. It is a ride that combines two of the great wonders of the peninsula.
t.wesel fluren flurener feld 2@51.7,6.6:
Where the Lippe meets the Rhine, the Romans came and went. Wesel stands at that confluence, and the long straight valley of the Lippe was one of their invasion routes into Germania in the years around the birth of Christ, when the generals of Augustus pushed east of the Rhine and built camps along the river. The fields called Flürener Feld lie just outside the town, on flat arable land, and they are part of the Lower German Limes, the Roman frontier along the Rhine which UNESCO inscribed in 2021. What the listing preserves is below the soil: ditches, post holes and the faint outlines of military camps, visible mostly as crop marks from the air. On the ground you see a field, a hedge and the sky.

Wesel itself has had a rough history. It was a Hanseatic town and a Prussian fortress, with a great citadel whose gate, the Berliner Tor, still stands, and it was almost totally destroyed in the last weeks of the Second World War, when Allied bombing and the crossing of the Rhine in March 1945 left little standing. The Cathedral of St Willibrord, a Gothic church, was rebuilt, and the Rhine bridge, a long, modern steel span, has been replaced more than once. The town has a quiet, rebuilt feel with a pleasant river front.

This is a place for an easy day on a bike. The Lower Rhine is flat and open, with poplars, willow-lined ditches, pastures with black and white cows and long, straight roads crossing a huge sky. There are no bends to speak of, but the light on a clear morning, with mist lifting off the river, is beautiful, and the wind can be strong from the west. Winter brings flocks of Arctic geese, a sight and sound that many riders do not expect. The roads are well surfaced but narrow, and bicycles share them heavily, especially at weekends.

Wesel has fuel and supermarkets, being a town of over sixty thousand, and Hamminkeln just to the north has more. The riverside cafes serve simple German fare, and in spring asparagus appears on every menu.

Take the ride list south to Monheim, where the Roman fort of Haus Bürgel lies on the bank of the Rhine, and the story of the frontier carries on.
t.wesel fluren flurener feld 3@51.7,6.6:
Hamminkeln gives this stretch of the Lower Rhine its odd claim to a place in military history. On the morning of 24 March 1945, as part of the Allied operation to cross the Rhine, thousands of British and American airborne troops landed around Hamminkeln and Wesel by parachute and glider, in daylight, into a countryside of farms and woods, and the fighting was fierce. Many gliders were shot down, and the losses were heavy. The area has quiet memorials, and it is worth knowing that the fields you ride through carry that history as well as the older, Roman one.

The Roman story is subtle. The Lower German Limes was a frontier of forts, watchtowers, roads and harbours stretching from near Bonn to the North Sea, and its remains are largely buried in the Rhine's floodplain. Flürener Feld 3 is one of a group of sites near Wesel where traces of Roman military activity lie under the plough, and it fits into the larger picture of a river frontier that was held for four centuries before the empire's armies withdrew in the fifth century.

For a rider, the interest lies in the landscape in between, and the best of it is the Bislicher Insel nature reserve, a floodplain where the Rhine, left to roam, has made oxbow lakes, reedbeds and meadows. Herds of Konik horses graze there, and in winter the area fills with white-fronted and bean geese that fly in from Siberia, so that the sky is loud at dawn and dusk. Roads along the dike are quiet, with views across the water, though some are closed to motor traffic, so respect the signs.

The land is flat and the weather is changeable, with rain that can arrive in a moment from the west. Spring is bright, with blossom in the orchards, and the late summer harvest fills the roads with tractors. Autumn mists suit the geese.

Wesel, with more than sixty thousand inhabitants, and Hamminkeln, with nearly thirty thousand, both have fuel and bakeries. Pick up a snack at a Bäckerei, since the area is mostly farmland. Bunnik-Vechten, on the ride list, lies across the Dutch border near Utrecht, where another Roman fort stood on the Rhine, and the trip crosses the Rhine delta into the Netherlands.
t.uedem hochwald hochwald 1@51.7,6.4:
Hochwald is a ridge of woods, which is a surprising thing to find in the flat country of the Lower Rhine. The ground here was pushed up by the glaciers of the Ice Age, which shoved sand and gravel into long, low ridges known as push moraines, and the woods that cover the ridge near Uedem have been left in peace for generations. Beech and oak form a canopy over the old lanes, and in autumn the leaf litter is deep and the air smells of mushrooms. For a rider used to the endless flatness of the Niederrhein, even a modest hill feels like an event.

The Roman connection is a quiet one. The Lower German Limes ran along the Rhine to the west, and the high ground near Uedem and Xanten was of strategic interest, since a ridge gives a view, and sites of this kind often turn up traces of camps and watchposts under the forest floor. Nothing is on show, and you should not expect signs or ruins, but there is a pleasure in knowing that sentries once stood where you are riding.

The towns nearby are curious. Kalkar, a short way north, has a beautifully preserved market square, a gothic church full of carved wooden altars made by medieval workshops, and, outside the town, the shell of a nuclear power station that was finished in the 1980s but never switched on, and has been turned into an amusement park, with a swing carousel in the cooling tower. Uedem is a small place, and its airbase nearby hosts a NATO control centre, which brings the odd military vehicle on the road.

The riding is relaxed. Narrow roads wind through the woods and fields, with some gentle bends and long straights, and the surface is generally good. Cyclists and farm vehicles are common, and the roads around the forest can be damp and slick with leaves in the autumn. Spring is lovely when the woods fill with bluebells and wild garlic, and summer is warm with plenty of shade.

Fuel is easy at Kalkar, a town of about fourteen thousand, and at Uedem, with some eight thousand, and both have shops and cafes. The ride list heads west across the Dutch border to Tiel, in the river country of the Betuwe.
t.wesel fluren flurener feld 4@51.7,6.6:
Here the Rhine bends through some of the emptiest farmland in western Germany. The fields at Flüren, north of Wesel, are flat enough to see a church tower from ten kilometres away, and the land runs in long, straight lines of willows, poplars and drainage ditches towards the Dutch border. This is the Niederrhein, a region where people have lived with floods for as long as they have farmed, and where the cycling routes are signposted better than the main roads.

Underneath the fields, the Romans left their traces. The Flürener Feld sites are listed as part of the Lower German Limes, the frontier on the Rhine, and what they are thought to preserve are the faint outlines of camps and installations that archaeologists have found through aerial photographs and geophysical survey. These are sites for the imagination. A rider can park at a field edge and look at a patch of wheat, and the knowledge that an army camped on it two thousand years ago is the whole attraction. The ride list, which links these fields with Monheim-Haus Bürgel, tells a story of a frontier that was dotted with forts at regular intervals along the river.

The weather rules the Lower Rhine. Winds off the North Sea cross the open fields without hindrance, and on a stormy day they can push a loaded bike off line, so keep a firm grip on the bars on the bridge crossings and the exposed dike roads. In winter, fog settles on the flat land and can last all day, and in late autumn the geese arrive in their thousands, crossing the sky in skeins. Spring is the best time, with cherry and apple blossom in the orchards and the first asparagus, which is a local passion.

Wesel has everything a rider might need, including supermarkets, stations and plenty of places for coffee. For quiet roads, the lanes along the Lippe and the dikes of the Rhine are best, avoiding the main highways which carry heavy lorries.

Pack rain gear, and be ready for a very big sky.
t.gongsanseong fortress@36.5,127.1:
Gongju was once called Ungjin, and for sixty-odd years in the fifth and sixth centuries it was the capital of the kingdom of Baekje, when the court fled south after Goguryeo armies destroyed its first capital near modern Seoul. The fortress of Gongsanseong stands on a ridge above the Geum river, with the town spread out below, and its walls, over two kilometres long, follow the contours of the hill. Much of the stone you walk along dates to a rebuilding in the Joseon period, but the site itself is Baekje, and so is the feeling of a defendable high ground with a wide river as its moat.

The fortress has one famous refugee from a later era. In 1624, King Injo fled here from a rebellion in Seoul and stayed for a few days, and he is said to have rewarded a tree for sheltering him. You can walk the full circuit in an hour or so, with views over the river and the town, and the pavilion of Gongbukru stands near the north gate. Archaeologists have found the royal palace area on the ridge, but the real treasures came from a tomb nearby: the burial of King Muryeong, which was found intact in 1971 with its gold ornaments, and is the best-preserved royal tomb of the kingdom. The Baekje sites here and at Buyeo and Iksan were listed as World Heritage in 2015.

For motorcycling, South Korea is a country of mountains and cameras, and the roads around Gongju are no exception. The Geum river valley is gentle, and the nearby Gyeryongsan National Park offers forest roads, temples and granite peaks. Speed cameras are everywhere, announced with big signs, and they are enforced, so keep to the limits. Rural roads have a good surface and clear signs in Korean and English. Autumn is the highlight, when the maples and ginkgoes turn gold and red, and the countryside is full of drying persimmons and harvested rice fields.

Gongju has about seventy thousand people, so it has plenty of fuel stations, restaurants and places to stay. The town is known for its chestnuts, which turn up in cakes, bread and rice dishes, and a bowl of chestnut makgeolli, the milky rice wine, goes down well after a day in the saddle. Winter can be cold and icy, and summer is humid, with a monsoon in July, so spring and autumn are best.
t.kaesong namdae@38.0,126.6:
Few capitals in Korea's history have left so little room for an ordinary traveller. Kaesong, the Goryeo capital from the early tenth century to the late fourteenth, stands in the south of North Korea, a few kilometres from the demilitarised zone and the village of Panmunjom, and its Namdae Gate, the great southern gate of the old city, is the best-known monument of the place. The gate was first raised in 1394, just after the Goryeo dynasty fell, and it has been repaired many times, most recently after wartime damage. It stands in the middle of a traffic circle, with its heavy tiled roof and a bell nearby.

I should be honest about the riding: there is none for visitors. Independent travel in North Korea is not possible, and any foreigner who sees Kaesong does so on a controlled tour, in a bus, with guides. So this is a stop for the armchair, the history reader and the map. What can be said is that the surrounding country is hilly and wooded, with ridges around Mount Songak to the north, and that the town sits in a bowl of low mountains in the same landscape as the border area to the south. The old industrial park that once employed North Korean workers for South Korean firms was closed in 2016.

Goryeo, which gave Korea its name in the West, was a medieval Buddhist state famous for its celadon pottery, its printing with movable metal type, and its resistance to Mongol invasions. Kaesong was a rich merchant town, and it was also the home of Korea's early ginseng trade, which still defines the town's reputation. In 1392 the general Yi Seong-gye, who founded the Joseon dynasty, seized power, and on the stone bridge of Seonjukgyo in Kaesong the loyalist scholar Jeong Mong-ju was killed, leaving a stain on the stone that guides say never fades. The historic monuments of Kaesong were added to the World Heritage list in 2013.

For food, Kaesong has a name for an elaborate spread of small dishes, often served in brass bowls, and for sweet cakes and pickles. The main roads in the area are wide and often empty of traffic, and the countryside is a patchwork of terraced fields and pine hills. If these facts are all you want, they are enough, and I would encourage you to see the equivalent Goryeo sites on the southern side of the border, such as the museums in Seoul.
t.mausoleum of king wang kon@38.0,126.5:
Wang Kon, the founder of Goryeo, was a merchant's son from the coast who became a warlord and then a king, and he took the throne in 918 after the collapse of the earlier Silla order. The kingdom he built gave the modern word Korea its name. When he died in 943, he was buried on the hillside west of his capital at Kaesong, and the tomb has been rebuilt more than once. The present mausoleum, called Hyonjongnung, with its stone figures and a mound looking over the hills, was extensively restored in the 1990s, a fact that guides sometimes mention and sometimes do not.

I have to say plainly that riding here is not possible for independent travellers. This part of North Korea is controlled, and foreigners reach Kaesong only on a guided tour, so all that this entry can offer is the shape of the land and the story behind it. The city sits among low mountains with Mount Songak above, in the same bowl that held the capital of a medieval kingdom, and the royal tombs are scattered across the valleys to the west, in a landscape of pine, terraced fields and stone walls. Autumn there is crisp and clear, and winter is dry and cold.

Goryeo was a Buddhist kingdom. Its kings sponsored vast printing projects, including the Tripitaka carved on wooden blocks that survives in the south at Haeinsa, a response to the Mongol invasions that devastated the country in the thirteenth century. Its potters invented a unique celadon with inlaid designs, a famous glaze that European collectors prized when it reached them. The rulers took their legitimacy from the memory of Wang Kon, and so the mausoleum was treated with the highest reverence for centuries, and officials were sent to make offerings there.

Kaesong has a reputation for its cuisine and its ginseng, and visitors are often served an elaborate meal of many small dishes in brass bowls. The town's streets are lined with old tiled houses, and traffic is light. Anyone who wants to place this tomb in the context of the wider Goryeo story could visit the National Museum of Korea in Seoul, which shows celadons and Buddhist art of the period. The road network south of the demilitarised zone leads to dozens of other tombs and temples.
t.beopjusa temple@36.5,127.8:
Look up from the car park at Beopjusa and you see an enormous bronze Buddha, thirty-three metres tall, standing in the open air against a backdrop of granite peaks. He is a modern figure, finished at the turn of the millennium, but the temple he guards is very old: tradition says the monk Uisin founded it in 553, bringing Indian scriptures back to Korea in a donkey's pack. Its main attraction, Palsangjeon, is a five-storey wooden pagoda with eight panels depicting scenes from the Buddha's life, rebuilt in the 1960s on an older design, and one of the few such wooden pagodas in Korea.

The mountains behind are the Songnisan range, a national park of bare granite ridges, oak and pine woods, with Mount Munjangdae at just over a thousand metres. The name Songni means leaving the profane world. A famous old pine near the entrance, called the Minister Pine, takes its name from a story that King Sejo, travelling to the temple in the fifteenth century, found a branch lowered to let his carriage pass, and gave it an official rank in thanks. It is a good story and a charming tree.

The rest of the region is satisfying riding country. The roads that lead into the Songni range from the lowlands wind up through forest and over passes, and the one known as Malti Pass is a favourite with Korean riders, with a long string of tight bends and views across the valleys. The surface is well kept, though it can be damp in the shade, and cameras watch the straights, so keep to the limits. At weekends, tourist buses and families fill the temple road, so a weekday morning is calmer. In autumn the whole valley turns red and yellow, and it is also the most crowded period.

Beopjusa is thirty kilometres from the nearest big town, and the village outside the gate has noodle restaurants and a few places for tea, but the nearest dependable fuel is in Boeun, a small town down the valley famous for its jujubes, the dried red dates sold in every shop. Take some home or try them as a hot drink. The ride goes on to Buseoksa, another mountain temple, on a route through hill country and farming valleys.
t.berg en dal de holdeurn south@51.8,5.9:
The Netherlands is famous for having no hills, which makes the ridge at Berg en Dal a small, comic exception. East of Nijmegen, the land rises in a line of wooded heights, shaped by the Ice Age, when a great glacier pushed up a mound of sand and gravel, and the highest point barely reaches a hundred metres. It looks modest on paper, but after the flat polders it feels like an alpine foothill, with beech and pine woods, steep little lanes, villas among the trees and views across the Waal valley into Germany. The name Berg en Dal means hill and valley, and the Dutch mean it.

The hills also hold Roman history. The Romans built a chain of forts and watchtowers along the Rhine, the frontier of the empire that is called the Lower German Limes, and Nijmegen was one of its most important sites. Parts of the frontier were put on the World Heritage list in 2021. Holdeurn, the woodland and hamlet to the south, lies in the same ridge-and-forest country, and the ride from here goes to Moers-Asberg, on the other side of the border in Germany, where the Roman fort of Asciburgium once stood on the Rhine.

The area has another, more recent story. In September 1944, Allied airborne troops landed on these heights as part of Operation Market Garden, and the fighting around Groesbeek and Nijmegen was fierce. A Canadian war cemetery lies on the ridge nearby, with rows of white stones among the trees, and the Liberation Museum nearby tells the story. In Berg en Dal, the Afrika Museum is also worth a visit, with its large collection of African art in a park.

For riding, this is a quiet, tidy corner. Lanes run through the woods with gentle climbs and bends, speed limits are low and enforcement is firm, and cyclists have priority, in great numbers, especially at weekends. The best light comes in autumn, when the beech leaves turn copper and the woods smell of damp earth. Spring brings bluebells and blossom. Winter can be wet and grey, with an icy wind from the east.

The nearest bigger town is Nijmegen, a lively old university city a few kilometres west, with plenty of fuel stations, cafes and hotels. In the village, you will find a few good places for coffee and apple pie, a Dutch classic. Be careful on the narrow roads, and give cyclists plenty of room.
t.nijmegen kops plateau kopse hof south@51:
Every July, a river of walkers pours through Nijmegen. The Four Days Marches, which have been held since 1909, attract tens of thousands of people who walk thirty, forty or fifty kilometres a day for four days, and the whole city welcomes them with flowers and music. The marchers cross the great bridge over the Waal, which is one of the widest rivers in the country, and the Kops Plateau, a rise on the edge of the old town, is part of the same landscape. In the second half of the twentieth century it was a place of sandpits and playing fields, but an older story lies beneath it.

The plateau is where the Romans first set up camp in Nijmegen. Before the permanent legionary fortress at the Hunerberg, an earlier military camp stood here, around the end of the first century BC, when Roman armies pushed to the Rhine, and archaeologists have found the ditches and post holes of the first soldiers. Nijmegen is often described as the oldest city in the Netherlands, and the claim rests on this long Roman presence. The ride goes from here to Kalkar and the Kalkarberg in Germany, along the old frontier of the Rhine, past fields, orchards and quiet villages.

The riding here is flat and gentle, and the pleasure comes from the river. The Waal flows wide and brown, with barges passing, and the dike roads are lined with willows and farmhouses, with views over the water meadows. The new bridge, called De Oversteek, a white arch, crosses the river west of the city, and the old bridge, the site of a famous crossing by American paratroopers in September 1944, lies at the centre. Winds can be strong and bring rain from the west, and in winter the floodplains are often under water.

Nijmegen is a large student town, so there are fuel stations, bike shops and cafes on every corner, and bars and music fill the old centre in the evenings. Traffic in the city is thick at rush hour, with buses, bicycles and cars, and speed cameras are common, so the Dutch limits are best respected. The nearby suburb of Hengstdal is quiet, and the woods to the south and east offer a little more adventure on the small lanes that climb the ridge.
t.nijmegen hunerberg@51.8,5.9:
Julius Civilis was a Batavian noble who had served in the Roman army, and in the year 69 he turned against it. The Batavians, a Germanic people who lived on the Rhine delta, rose in revolt during the civil war that followed Nero's death, and for a year they threatened Roman power on the northern frontier. Nijmegen, then a Batavian town, was burned, and when the rebellion was crushed, the Romans built a new, massive legionary fortress on the Hunerberg, a rise on the edge of the town, to keep control. The Tenth Legion, called Gemina, was stationed there for more than thirty years, and the settlement that grew beside it became a Roman town with a grid of streets, baths and a market.

Little of it is visible now, as the fortress lies under the suburb that bears the hill's name, but a short walk reveals traces: sections of Roman town wall elsewhere in the old centre, and finds in the museum at the Valkhof, the hilltop park by the river where Charlemagne is said to have had a palace. The museum has helmets, tombstones, jewellery and pottery from the soldiers and townspeople, giving the place a human face. The frontier here is part of the World Heritage property of the Lower German Limes.

The ride from here follows the line of the Rhine frontier east to Kalkar in Germany, over the flat farmland between the rivers. It is easy, quiet riding, on back roads past orchards, asparagus fields and little brick villages, with wide views and a lot of sky. Be careful on the roads at harvest time, when mud from tractors can be slippery, and in the early morning, when mist hangs over the fields. The strong winds of the lowlands can push a bike around, so keep a firm grip on exposed stretches.

For a stop, the old centre of Nijmegen has a good range of cafes, where you can order a plate of fries with mayonnaise or a coffee with apple pie. It is a lively university city, with a pedestrian-friendly centre, so park outside and walk in. Fuel is easy to find on the ring roads, and bike shops and workshops are plentiful. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with long, soft light, while summer can be warm and wet in turn, and winter is damp and often grey.
t.waterton glacier international peace par:
In 1932, the people of Alberta and Montana decided that two parks that shared a border might as well share a name. Waterton Lakes National Park in Canada and Glacier National Park in the United States became the world's first International Peace Park, a gesture of friendship that grew from a suggestion by Rotary clubs. UNESCO later recognised it as a World Heritage Site, and the two parks are managed together for wildlife, even though visitors cross a border to get from one to the other.

The landscape is spectacular. The Rocky Mountains meet the prairie here without any foothills in between, so the mountains seem to rise straight out of the grass. On the Canadian side, Waterton Lake is a deep, narrow glacial lake surrounded by steep peaks, with the red-roofed Prince of Wales Hotel on a bluff above the water, a landmark since the late 1920s. Wind is a constant, and gusts of over a hundred kilometres an hour are not unusual. Grizzly and black bears, elk, bighorn sheep and mountain goats live here, and it is common to see wildlife from the road.

The riding on the Canadian side includes the Akamina Parkway, a short, winding road to Cameron Lake, and the Red Rock Parkway, with its views of coloured stone. For many riders, the real prize is across the border in Montana, where the Going-to-the-Sun Road crosses the Continental Divide at Logan Pass, at about 2,026 metres. This is one of the great mountain roads of North America, narrow, with steep drops, though vehicle size limits apply, and it opens fully only in late June or July, depending on snow.

The border crossing at Chief Mountain is open only in summer, so check hours before you plan the route, and carry your passport. The town of Waterton Park, a short distance from here, has fuel, groceries, restaurants and places to stay, though everything fills up in July and August. Bring bear spray if you plan to walk, and a warm layer, since the weather changes quickly.
t.hannover@52.4,9.7:
Hannover does not seek attention, which is part of its character. The capital of Lower Saxony, with about half a million people, is a flat, green, practical city on the Leine river, famous for its trade fairs, and for speaking what Germans consider the purest standard German. Large parts of the centre were destroyed in the Second World War, and the rebuilding is mostly plain, but there are fine things inside it: the Herrenhausen Gardens, a baroque garden of clipped hedges and fountains, the Maschsee, a big lake laid out in the 1930s where locals sail and jog, and the new town hall, a copper-domed building from 1913 with a lift that rises inside the dome.

Hannover also has deep historical links. The philosopher Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz lived and worked here for decades as librarian and adviser to the dukes. And the dukes became kings of Great Britain in 1714, when the Elector of Hanover took the British throne as George I, so for more than a century, the same family ruled both places.

This stop, on the western edge near Seelze, is a return point more than a destination. The Leine and the Mittelland Canal run through the area, with industrial buildings, harbour cranes, allotments and low houses. It is the place where a day of countryside ends and the city begins, and where traffic starts to slow.

Practical matters are straightforward. Fuel is available at stations on the main roads, and the supermarkets and bakeries open early. Rush hour, between about seven and nine in the morning and four and six in the evening, is heavy, and the motorways around the city, especially the A2, can be jammed, so plan to arrive outside those times. Parking for a motorcycle in the city centre is easy to find, and the tram network is efficient if you want to leave the bike. For a quiet evening, the Maschsee shore is a good place to walk.
t.kottenforst nord durrenbruch 2@50.7,7.0:
Southwest of Bonn, an old forest runs for miles across a low plateau, a place of oak and hornbeam, beech and quiet paths. The Kottenforst is one of the few big woods in the Rhineland, and the area known as Durrenbruch, on the northern side, is typical: flat, damp, shady, with wide forest roads, ditches, small ponds and a thick floor of leaf litter. Its name means dry marsh, a typically contradictory piece of German, and the ground really does flip between puddle and dust depending on the season.

The forest was a hunting ground of the Electors of Cologne, who ruled the region from Bonn and rode out here in the eighteenth century with their courts, and straight alleys cut through the trees radiate from old hunting lodges. Later it was used for timber, and today it belongs to the regional forestry service and to the people of Bonn, who run, cycle and walk here in great numbers. Wild boar, deer, woodpeckers and owls live in the woods, and in spring, bluebells and wood anemones carpet the ground.

Do not expect to ride through the woods themselves. Forest tracks here are closed to motor vehicles, and the paths are meant for walkers and cyclists, so keep to the public roads around the edge. These are quiet, tree-lined and pleasant, running through villages like Alfter, a town of about twenty-two thousand people just to the north. The riding is gentle, with long, easy bends and gentle gradients, and the hazards are mostly cyclists, joggers and dogs.

Fuel and food are easy in Alfter and in Bonn, which is a few minutes away and has everything. Bonn was the capital of West Germany until 1990 and is the birthplace of Beethoven, and it is also home to the headquarters of Haribo, the gummy bear company, founded here in 1920. The best seasons are spring, when the forest is fresh, and autumn, with warm colours and a smell of damp leaves. Winter mornings can be foggy. A walk among the trees is a quiet complement to a day on the road.
t.kottenforst nord domhecken 3@50.7,7.0:
The Domhecken, the cathedral hedges, takes its name from the way the old hedgerows and tall trees here once met overhead like the roof of a church. The area in the northern Kottenforst, a short distance from the town of Alfter, is part of the great forest south-west of Bonn, and it carries the traces of old land use: hedge banks, ditches, boundary stones and long, straight forest roads laid out for hunting parties.

The Kottenforst stands on a terrace of ancient Rhine gravels and clay, left by the river when it flowed at a higher level, and the poor, wet soil has kept it from being turned into farmland. As a result, it is one of the largest continuous woods in the Rhineland, covering around four thousand hectares. Oak and hornbeam dominate, in a pattern shaped by centuries of coppicing, and the result is a woodland of crooked, many-stemmed trees that look quite unlike the straight spruce plantations of the hills.

In the eighteenth century, the Electors of Cologne, who had their court in Bonn, used the forest for hunting, and they built a lodge at Herzogsfreude and cut straight avenues through the trees. The sport was hawking and boar hunting, and the surviving paths still radiate from these old meeting points. Beyond the forest, the Roman aqueduct that carried water from the Eifel to Cologne passed nearby, and fragments of the channel can still be traced along the hills.

Motorised access to the woods is restricted, so a rider's role here is limited to the public roads that skirt the forest. These are quiet, wooded lanes with gentle bends and little traffic outside the commuting hours, connecting small villages. Watch for cyclists, walkers and horse riders, particularly at weekends, and for wild animals at dawn and dusk. In autumn, wet leaves on the road can be slippery.

Alfter and Bonn have fuel, bakeries and restaurants, so there is no need to carry any extra. Spring is the best season, when the forest is fresh, and the woodpeckers are loud. Winter can be dark, wet and cold, though a frosty morning among the bare trees has its own charm.
t.kellerwald@51.1,9.0:
Beech trees cover the hills of the Kellerwald in north Hesse, and they are old ones. This is one of the places where UNESCO recognised the ancient beech forests of Germany, listed in 2011, because here the trees have been left largely alone, and the forest has the feel of what Central Europe looked like before farming took over. The trunks are smooth and grey, the canopy is high and the floor in spring is covered with a sheet of white wood anemones. In autumn, the leaves turn copper and gold, and the forest is full of light.

The Kellerwald-Edersee National Park, created in 2004, covers the best parts, a rolling country of steep slopes and narrow valleys above the Eder reservoir. Wildcats, black storks, woodpeckers and bats live in the woods, and the park is also home to herds of red deer that are heard roaring in autumn. A network of marked trails leads through the trees, and a treetop walkway gives a view of the forest from above.

The Edersee, the lake at the northern edge of the park, was created by a dam finished in 1914, one of the biggest in Germany at the time. In May 1943, British bombers breached the dam in the Dambusters raid, and flooding killed many people in the valley below. When water levels fall in dry years, the ruins of villages that were flooded when the dam was built can re-emerge from the lake, which makes for an eerie sight.

The roads of the Kellerwald are a pleasure for riders. They wind through forest and over hills, with easy bends, and there is little traffic during the week. Surfaces are generally good, though leaves, damp patches and forestry vehicles can complicate things. In summer, weekends around the lake are busy. Frankenau, a small town about five kilometres away with a few thousand inhabitants, has fuel, a baker and a few inns, and Bad Wildungen, a larger spa town, has more. Autumn is the best season for colour, and spring for flowers. Bring a layer, because the forest can be cool and damp.
t.watchtowers wp 1 30@50.5,7.5:
Rheinbrohl, on the Rhine, is where the Upper Germanic Limes begins, and from there it climbs the hills of the Westerwald and heads east and south for roughly 550 kilometres to the Danube. Watchtowers were numbered along the way, and WP 1/30 is one of the early ones, in the first section after the Rhine, in wooded country a couple of kilometres from the village of Melsbach. The Romans built the frontier in the second century, with timber towers first and stone later, and it marked the edge of their empire for around a century and a half.

Today, you are more likely to find a grassy mound or a low bank than anything grand. Reconstructed towers and a replica palisade give a sense of how it looked, while on the ground, the line shows up as a ridge among trees. UNESCO listed the Upper Germanic-Raetian Limes in 2005, as part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire, and the fact that you can still follow it for such a distance, through forest and field, is striking.

The country here is soft and green, with rolling hills, beech and oak woods, and small valleys, and the Wied river runs close by on its way down to the Rhine at Neuwied. Villages are quiet and tidy, with half-timbered farmhouses, and fields of rape and grain. In spring, the meadows are full of flowers, and in autumn, the woods are warm with colour. Mist hangs in the valleys on cool mornings.

The Westerwald is good for easy riding. The roads follow the contours, with long bends and gentle gradients, and traffic is light outside weekends. There are many small turns onto farm tracks, so watch for mud and gravel. Fuel is available in Neuwied and in larger villages, with a few bakeries and inns along the way. About two thousand people live in Melsbach, so do not count on much there. Dress for a change in weather, since showers come off the hills quickly, and leave time for a walk along the line of the old frontier, with a flask of coffee.
t.limessection between watchtowers wp 1 88:
Few people expect to find a Roman frontier running through a spa town, but the Limes did cross the Lahn near Bad Ems, and the stretch around the Lahn valley is one of the most scenic parts of its whole length. At this point, watchtower WP 1/88 a stands in the hills above Dausenau, a village of a few hundred houses on the river, a couple of kilometres from the spot. The frontier ran along the heights and dropped to the water, and the Romans controlled the river crossing from both sides.

Dausenau itself is delightful, with half-timbered houses, a medieval town wall with towers, and a church whose tower leans at an alarming angle, a result of soft ground and ageing timber. Bad Ems, a short ride downstream, was a fashionable spa in the nineteenth century, a favourite of Russian tsars and German kings. It is also the place where in 1870 a telegram known as the Ems Dispatch was edited by Bismarck in a way that helped to push France and Prussia into war. The grand spa buildings and the long promenade by the river give the town a faded elegance.

The Lahn valley is a wooded, winding river canyon, with steep slopes, vineyards in places, and ruined castles on the heights. The Limes is part of the UNESCO listing of 2005, and you can follow marked trails that lead to the towers and earthworks. The hills are covered in oak and beech, and in the evening, the light turns warm.

The roads along the Lahn and over the hills are fun for riders, with plenty of bends and good views, though they can be crowded with cyclists, walkers and caravans in summer. Surfaces are good, and there are several small bridges and narrow village streets, so slow down. Fuel is available at Bad Ems, with a few supermarkets, bakeries and restaurants, and rooms are easier to find midweek. Spring and autumn are the most pleasant times, and early on a clear morning, the air in the valley is wonderful.
The Professorenweg, the Professors' Way, was a path where Bonn's university teachers walked in the afternoons, and the name still suggests thoughtful strolling. It runs along the high ground of the southern Kottenforst, in the hills of Wachtberg, above the Rhine valley, and the area has been a favourite for walkers since the days when Bonn was a quiet university town on the river rather than a capital.

The southern part of the Kottenforst is hillier than the northern part, with views opening between the trees across the plain to the Siebengebirge, the seven hills on the other side of the Rhine, with the ruin of Drachenfels castle on its summit. Legend says a dragon lived there, killed by Siegfried of the Nibelungen, who bathed in its blood. On a clear day, the line of hills looks like a painted backdrop, and in autumn, with the leaves turned, the view is wonderful.

Wachtberg is a scatter of villages on a ridge, with orchards, meadows and the occasional vineyard on the slopes, a fruit-growing region with a prosperous, tidy character. The area was home to many embassies and government staff when Bonn was the capital of West Germany, and some of the large villas date from that period. Farther south, the Ahr valley, a famous red wine region, is a short ride away.

Motor vehicles are not allowed on the forest paths, so riders stay on the public roads that wind around the edge of the forest and across the ridge. These are good, quiet roads with easy curves and some fine views, and the main hazards are cyclists and walkers on sunny weekends, and farm vehicles in harvest time. Fuel is available in Wachtberg and Bonn, which has all services, and the nearby Rhine promenade at Bad Godesberg is a pleasant place for a coffee. Spring, with blossom on the orchards, and autumn, with colour in the beeches, are the best seasons. Winter fog can reduce visibility on the ridge.
t.kovirke area 8@54.5,9.6:
Kovirke is the name of one of the oldest sections of the Danevirke, the great earthwork that guarded the southern border of Denmark for the better part of a thousand years. From the early eighth century, the Danes built ramparts, ditches and later brick walls across the narrow neck of land between the Baltic and the North Sea, and the system grew in stages. Neighbouring sections have names of their own, the Crooked Wall among them, and the Kovirke is among the earliest. The line runs through fields and woodland, a long bank that you can see best in the low light of morning or evening.

Not far away lies Hedeby, or Haithabu in German, the great Viking trading town on the shore of the Schlei inlet. For about three centuries, from the ninth century, it was one of the largest trading centres in northern Europe, with ships from Scandinavia, the Baltic, the Rhine and beyond bringing furs, amber, silver and slaves, and it was destroyed in the eleventh century. UNESCO listed Hedeby and the Danevirke in 2018. A museum has a reconstructed set of Viking houses, and the finds, including a preserved longship, are remarkable.

The landscape of Schleswig is flat and open, with the long finger of the Schlei winding between reedy shores, and the sky is huge. Fields of rape, barley and maize stretch to the horizon, and the air smells of salt and cut grass in summer. The area has been the site of border disputes between Denmark and Germany, and the two cultures still overlap, with Danish minority schools and churches in the area.

Riding here is easy, with quiet roads, long straights, and some pleasing curves along the water. Wind is the main challenge, as there is almost nothing to stop it. Fahrdorf, a village about three kilometres away, has a baker and a few services, and the town of Schleswig, a short ride beyond, has fuel, supermarkets and restaurants. Smoked herring is a local favourite. Late spring and early autumn are the best times, and winter is cold and grey.
In the Kottenforst, a Maar is not a volcano's crater, as it would be in the nearby Eifel, but a small pond or wet hollow in the forest floor, and the Pfaffenmaar, the priests' pond, is a good example. The word has been used locally for centuries for any round, water-filled depression, and these hollows give the forest a dotted pattern of reeds, alders and dark water. The reason is the heavy clay under the thin soil, which holds rainwater and keeps parts of the woods boggy for much of the year.

The result is a forest with a wetland character, and it supports a lot of life. Amphibians breed in the ponds, with newts, frogs and toads in spring, dragonflies hover over the water in summer, and the damp ground suits alder and willow. Woodpeckers hammer in the oaks, and at dusk, you may see a roe deer at the edge of a clearing. The forest smells of wet leaves and moss, even on a dry day.

Underneath the woods runs the line of the Roman aqueduct that brought spring water from the Eifel to Cologne, a channel about ninety-five kilometres long, mostly buried, built in the first century. Along its route, paths and information boards mark where it can be seen, and in a few places along the Villerucken ridge, you can still see parts of the structure. It is one of the longest aqueducts of the Roman world, and its presence here, in a quiet forest, comes as a surprise.

Motorcycles cannot use the woodland tracks, so the riding is on the public roads that border the forest, which are quiet and tree-lined. Watch for cyclists, walkers and dogs, especially at weekends, and for wet leaves in autumn. Alfter and the nearby city of Bonn offer fuel, food and rooms, and the Rhine promenade is a pleasant place for a rest.
