Spring, when the forest is fresh, and the frogs are loud, is lovely, and winter has its own bare-branched charm. Boots help if you want to explore on foot.
t.eckernforde bay@54.5,9.8:
Eckernförde Bay is a long, narrow arm of the Baltic that cuts into the coast of Schleswig-Holstein between the Danish Wohld and the Schwansen peninsula, and the little port of the same name sits at its head. The water is shallow, the beaches are wide and sandy, and the whole place has the relaxed air of a north German seaside town, with a promenade, a harbour full of boats and a smell of smoked fish. The altitude here is a modest eight metres, and the horizon is all sea and sky.

The town is known for its smoked sprats, the Kieler Sprotten's nearest rival, which are sold hot from small smokehouses near the harbour. The bay was also a naval base for many years, and the German navy still has a presence nearby, a reminder that this quiet coastline has long had strategic importance. Behind the town, the land is a mix of low hills, farmland and woods, with small villages and the traces of Viking-age and medieval history never very far away. Windeby, a few kilometres inland, is famous for the Iron Age bog body found nearby in the 1950s.

The riding along the bay and across Schwansen is gentle, not a challenge. Roads run between fields of rapeseed and wheat, often lined with trees, with long straights and occasional bends, and the surface is usually good. In summer the coast road can be busy with holidaymakers, and the wind off the Baltic can be strong, so be ready for gusts on exposed stretches. Early mornings and evenings are the best times, when the light over the water is soft and the beach is almost empty.

Swimming is the draw here. The Baltic is not warm, and the water takes time to heat up, but on a calm summer afternoon it is clear and calm, with a shallow slope and sandy bottom, and a dip after a long ride is a good reward. Eckernförde, with over twenty thousand people, has petrol stations, cafés and restaurants in plenty, and a fish roll by the harbour is a classic lunch.

The ride combines the bay with the Schlei, the long inlet to the north, where small villages and coffee stops invite a slow pace.
t.buchholz@53.3,9.9:
Buchholz in der Nordheide is not a place that anyone writes songs about, but it is a useful one. It sits on the southern edge of the Hamburg metropolitan area, where the suburbs give way to heath and pine forest, and it is the town where the Lüneburg Heath begins for anyone coming out of the city. With about thirty-seven thousand people it has everything: fuel, supermarkets, cafés and a station, and it is a sensible place to begin or end a ride from Hamburg.

The name Nordheide refers to the northern part of the heath, a landscape of sandy soil, heather and juniper that was created by centuries of grazing and wood-cutting. Without grazing, the heath turns into forest, so the local sheep, the grey horned Heidschnucken, have become a conservation tool as well as a symbol. In late summer, usually in August and September, the heather flowers purple and the country around Buchholz becomes a landscape of pink and violet.

The riding south and west of town is relaxed. Roads wind between pine woods and farmland, past thatched farmhouses and small ponds, and the surface is good. Corners are gentle, traffic is moderate, and there are several small villages such as Jesteburg and Bendestorf that offer cafés and a pleasant stop. On this ride the heath is a first act, before the long run to the North Sea dikes, where the land flattens out and the wind picks up.

Early mornings in autumn, when mist lies over the heath and the first light catches the heather, are particularly lovely. Midday in summer can be busy with day-trippers from Hamburg, and weekends fill the cafés. Take small roads where you can, and watch for horse riders and cyclists, which are everywhere in this region.

Buchholz itself is a pleasant but unremarkable town, with a pedestrian centre, a few restaurants and an easy-going feel, and it works best as a gateway. Fill up, grab a coffee, and then head for the lanes.
t.watchtower wp 1 31@50.5,7.5:
The Roman frontier in Germany was not a wall in the way that Hadrian's was in Britain. It was a line of wooden towers, small forts and a ditch and palisade, running for hundreds of kilometres from the Rhine near Neuwied to the Danube, and the stretch here, near Melsbach, is where it began. The Upper Germanic-Raetian Limes, as it is formally called, is a World Heritage Site, and the numbered watchtowers, of which this is one, were the eyes of the frontier.

The towers stood in sight of one another, so a signal could pass along the line, and soldiers manned them in small groups. Little remains of most of them today beyond a low mound, a foundation or a reconstruction, and that is part of their charm. You stand in a quiet woodland clearing in the Westerwald, with oak and beech all around, and you try to imagine a signal fire and a lookout in a cold wind.

The countryside here is rolling, wooded and green. Roads leave the Rhine valley and climb into the Westerwald, with long, easy bends, small villages and farmland, and the surface is generally good. There is not much traffic away from the main roads, and the lanes are pleasant to ride, although fallen leaves in autumn and farm mud in spring can make bends slippery. It is a modest ride rather than a dramatic one, but it has a gentle rhythm.

Neuwied, about four kilometres away, has over sixty-six thousand people and every kind of service, including fuel and food. Melsbach and Rengsdorf are smaller villages with a shop or two and a bakery. A Westerwald speciality is the Kannenbäckerland pottery from further east, though you will find the usual German bakery cakes and sausages more easily.

The ride links this tower with the little fort at Neuss-Reckberg on the Lower Germanic frontier along the Rhine, a nice pairing of the two parts of the Roman line. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with clear air and good light, and a walk in the woods before you leave is a good way to stretch.
t.kovirke area 6@54.5,9.6:
The Danevirke is the longest ancient earthwork in northern Europe, a system of ramparts, ditches and walls that crossed the narrow neck of Jutland at the base of the peninsula. Over several centuries, from the early Middle Ages into the twelfth, the Danes built and rebuilt it, closing the land route between the Baltic and the North Sea. Kovirke is one of its branches, and the section here, near Fahrdorf, preserves a piece of the bank that you can still see rising in the grass and the trees.

Tree-ring dating of timber found in the system points to a first major phase in the 730s, and later kings extended and strengthened it, culminating in a brick wall built in the twelfth century. It was a political statement as much as a defence, a way of saying that this was the border of the Danish realm. The Danevirke and the nearby Viking trading town of Hedeby were inscribed together on the World Heritage list in 2018, and they make a pair, the trade centre and the border.

The countryside here is quiet, low and open. Roads run between fields, through small villages and along the shore of the Schlei, with gentle curves and good surface, and the wind blowing over the flat land is the main thing to notice. It is not a thrill ride but a thoughtful one, best in the evening when the light slants across the earthworks and shows them clearly. Traffic is light except on the main road near Schleswig.

Fahrdorf is small, with about two and a half thousand people, and has basic services, but for fuel and a larger choice of restaurants you should head toward Schleswig, a short ride away, or to Kappeln on the Schlei, which has a good range of smoked-fish stalls. The Schlei herring is a speciality of the area.

Wear sturdy shoes for the walk, because the paths can be muddy, and bring something to read the information boards, since the earthworks look like low hills until someone points them out.
t.east wall area 2d@54.5,9.8:
For anyone who likes to see how a frontier was really made, the East Wall of the Danevirke is a good place to stand. It is a long rampart running north-south across the base of the Jutland peninsula, a bank of earth and clay, with traces of timber and later brick, and in the section by Windeby you can see it as a low ridge across the fields. The Danes built and rebuilt it over several centuries, and it was one of the largest construction projects of the early medieval north.

The Danevirke guarded the narrow strip of land between the marshes of the Eider and the Schlei inlet, the only dry route between the Baltic and the North Sea. Whoever held it controlled the way into Denmark, and the king who owned it could tax the trade passing through the nearby port of Hedeby. The whole system, including the ramparts and Hedeby itself, is a World Heritage Site, listed in 2018, and the East Wall is one of its major parts.

Windeby, a small village two kilometres away, is better known for another find. In 1952 a body was found preserved in a peat bog near here, a young person who had died in the Iron Age, and for decades the so-called Windeby Girl was one of the best-known bog bodies in Europe, though later research changed ideas about the sex and cause of death. The find is a reminder of how deep the layers of history run in this quiet country.

The roads in the area are gentle and enjoyable. They cross low farmland, with hedgerows, red-brick villages and occasional glimpses of the Baltic, and the surface is good. There are no real hills, so the wind is the main feature, and in spring and early summer the rapeseed fields turn the whole land yellow. Eckernförde, a few kilometres east, has fuel, cafés and fish stalls, and it is the best place to stop.

Take a walk along the earthwork and read the information panels, which explain the building phases. An evening visit, when the sun is low, shows the contours better than a midday one.
t.kottenforst nord domhecken 1@50.7,7.0:
The Kottenforst is a large forest on the hills west of Bonn, a remnant of the woodland that once covered the Rhine plain, and its northern part, near Alfter, is a quiet, old-fashioned place of oak and beech. For centuries it was a hunting forest of the Electors of Cologne, who ruled from Bonn, and the straight rides that cut through it, laid out for hunting parties, are still visible as long avenues between the trees. A hunting lodge of the eighteenth-century elector Clemens August stands in the forest to the south.

The name Domhecken contains the word for hedges, and it points to an old kind of boundary. In the Rhineland, hedges were once planted and woven into dense barriers to mark property or to keep game in or out. Whatever the exact origin of the name, the forest has long been a managed landscape, and you can feel that in its straight rides and old banks. The ground is damp in places, and in spring the floor is carpeted with wood anemones and bluebells, while in autumn the beech leaves turn the whole forest copper.

The roads around the Kottenforst are gentle. They run between villages and fields, with long avenues of old trees and easy bends, and the surface is generally good. Traffic builds up close to Bonn at rush hour, but at other times the lanes are quiet. The forest itself is crossed by many tracks, but most are closed to motor vehicles, so leave the bike at the edge and walk. Cyclists and dog walkers are common at weekends.

Alfter, with nearly twenty-two thousand people, is the nearest town, and Bornheim and Bonn are close behind, so fuel, food and beds are no problem. Bonn, the former capital of West Germany, is a pleasant, easy-going city with the Rhine and the Siebengebirge hills on its doorstep. The area is also known for its fruit orchards and for Rhenish dishes such as sauerbraten and Himmel un Ähd, a plate of black pudding, apples and mashed potato.

The ride from here links the forest to Xanten, far downriver, where the Romans built a great city on the Lower Rhine. Choose a morning in spring or a clear day in autumn, when the forest light is at its best.
t.st michael s lutheran church@52.2,9.9:
St Michael's in Hildesheim is a church that was built to a vision. Bishop Bernward, a teacher and craftsman as well as a churchman, began it around the year 1010 and died in 1022, and the church was consecrated in 1033. He designed it with a double apse, with a choir at each end, and with two transepts and six towers, a symmetrical plan that is one of the best examples of Ottonian architecture. The layout reflects a view of the world in which the church was a model of heaven.

Inside, the pale columns and round arches have a calm severity, and above the nave a painted wooden ceiling, made around 1200 and showing the Tree of Jesse, the family tree of Christ, is one of the great medieval works of art in Germany. The ceiling was protected during the Second World War, while the building itself, bombed in March 1945 along with the rest of the old town, was rebuilt in the following decades. The church has been Lutheran since the sixteenth century, and the cathedral, with its famous bronze doors made for Bernward, is part of the same World Heritage listing. The ride goes on from here to the Carolingian Westwork at Corvey.

Against the apse of the cathedral grows a wild rose said to be a thousand years old, which was badly damaged in the bombing and sprouted again from its roots in the rubble, and the town has made it a symbol. Hildesheim itself is a lively place of about a hundred thousand people, with a reconstructed market square that gives some idea of how the medieval town looked.

For a rider, Hildesheim sits in a green, rolling landscape between the Harz and the Leine valley. Roads run through farmland, woods and small villages, with a good surface and gentle curves, and the Harz foothills, to the south-east, offer more winding stretches. The city centre is busy, with cobbles and one-way streets, so park outside the old town. Fuel and food are easy to find, and the local cuisine includes hearty north German dishes.

Choose a bright morning, when the church interior is lit by the windows, and take time to look up.
t.twin column tomb@38.9,125.4:
Before anything else, an honest note: independent travel in North Korea is not possible, and visitors can only go on organised tours with official guides, so a ride here is a matter of reading about a place rather than taking a route. With that said, the Twin-Column Tomb sits near Yonggang, a town of about thirteen thousand on the plain near the coast, not far from the larger city of Nampo, and it belongs to the Koguryo kingdom, one of the Three Kingdoms of ancient Korea.

Koguryo was a powerful state that ruled much of the Korean peninsula and Manchuria from the first century BC until 668 AD, famous for its horsemen, fortresses and painted tombs. UNESCO listed a group of these tombs in 2004, including some near Pyongyang and others on the Nampo plain. The tomb here gets its name from two octagonal stone pillars that support the entrance of the main chamber, a distinctive architectural feature. Inside, the walls were once decorated with murals of daily life, guardians and the four mythical beasts of the cardinal directions, though the condition of the paintings varies and access to tombs is often restricted to protect them.

The landscape around is flat farmland on the edge of the Taedong river's estuary, with rice fields, orchards and low hills, and the roads are typically quiet, with few private vehicles. Official visits tend to follow set itineraries, and spontaneous stops are rarely allowed. Facilities for fuel, food and lodging, where available to visitors, are arranged by guides, and the best that can be said from a distance is that Nampo is a significant port with a large barrage across the river mouth.

The murals are of real interest to art historians, because they preserve the look of the clothes, houses, banquets and hunting scenes of a kingdom that left few written records. The style influenced Korean and Japanese art, and the paintings in Takamatsuzuka in Japan show similarities.

If you have a chance to see one of these tombs, expect a low mound, a small stone entrance and a dim interior, kept cool and protected. If not, books and museum displays in Seoul and elsewhere offer replicas.
t.historic monuments and sites in kaesong@:
Kaesong was the capital of the Koryo dynasty from 918 until 1392, and the name Korea comes from the name of that kingdom. A prosperous trading city, it was a centre of Buddhism, celadon pottery and printing, and the court at its height was among the most refined in East Asia. When the Joseon dynasty took over in 1392, the capital moved to Seoul, but Kaesong remained known for its merchants, who were pioneers in ginseng trading and banking, and its cuisine, which many Koreans still regard as among the most elegant in the country.

I should be plain that this is another place that cannot be reached by an independent rider. Kaesong lies in North Korea, just north of the demilitarised zone, and foreigners may only visit it on organised tours, with official guides and fixed itineraries. What I can offer is some context. The city's historic monuments and sites were listed by UNESCO in 2013, and include the remains of the palace, the walls and gates, the Koryo Museum, once a Confucian academy, the Sonjuk Bridge, and royal tombs on the hills around the city. The bridge is famous for a dark story: the loyal scholar Jeong Mong-ju was killed here in 1392 by men sent by the future Joseon king, and a brownish stain on the stone is said to be his blood, and bamboo is said to have grown at the spot.

The setting is a basin surrounded by hills, with Songak mountain behind the old palace, and a landscape of terraced fields, pines and small villages. The old quarter has traditional tile-roofed houses, courtyards and narrow lanes, and the city is known for ginseng and for its table d'hôte dishes. The city has more than three hundred thousand people, so as a place it is large, though what visitors see is arranged by their hosts.

Because I cannot describe the road, I will leave the riding out. If you ever travel here by official arrangement, the best months are spring and autumn, when the hills are green or gold, and winter is bitterly cold.

For readers with an interest in Korean history, Kaesong is a place that rewards reading before travelling, and the museums in Seoul hold many Koryo treasures.
t.manwoldae kaesong chomsongdae@38.0,126.5:
On the slope of Songak mountain, a terrace of stone foundations and steps marks where the Koryo kings had their palace, known as Manwoldae, the moon-full terrace. The name suggests the beauty of the setting rather than the architecture, and the complex was largely destroyed by Red Turban invaders in 1361, so what survives is the platform and the stone staircases that climbed it. A few hundred metres away stands the Chomsongdae, a stone platform with stone supports that is traditionally described as an astronomical observatory, built in the Koryo period and used to watch the sky, though like many such claims, its exact use is a matter of scholarly discussion.

A frank word about access: Kaesong is in North Korea, a short way north of the border, and foreign visitors can only go as part of an organised tour. That means no independent riding, no choosing your own stops, and no way to plan fuel or food for yourself, so what follows is a picture of the place rather than a route. The monuments are part of the UNESCO-listed historic sites of Kaesong, together with the old city walls and the Sonjuk Bridge.

The terrain is soft and green. Pines grow on the slopes, apricot and persimmon trees stand in the villages, and the stone of the old palace is warm brown where the grass has been cut back. In spring, azaleas and cherry blossom appear on the hillside, and in autumn the forest on Songak is golden and red. The sky tends to be clear and dry in autumn, which is the best season.

Koryo was one of the great periods of Korean culture. Its potters made celadon, a pale green glaze admired across Asia, and its printers produced the Tripitaka Koreana, a massive set of Buddhist scriptures carved onto more than eighty thousand wooden blocks, stored today at Haeinsa in the south. Metal movable type was used in Korea in the thirteenth century, long before Gutenberg, and Kaesong's scholars were part of that world.

The city has a long culinary tradition too, with elaborate multi-dish meals and sweet rice cakes, and it was a ginseng centre. Enthusiasts of history may find more to read than to see, since much of what the Koryo built was lost in war.
t.ryonggang great tomb@38.9,125.4:
Close to the Taedong river, on a plain that gently slopes down to the Yellow Sea, a low grassy mound hides a chamber that has survived for about fifteen hundred years. The Ryonggang Great Tomb, or Yonggang Taemyo, belongs to the Koguryo kingdom, and it is the largest of a group of tombs at Yonggang, near Nampo, that UNESCO listed in 2004 among the Complex of Koguryo Tombs. Its stone chambers are reached by a passage, and inside are painted walls, with the sort of scenes that make these tombs special: guardians, spirits, scenes from life, and the four great beasts of the cardinal directions, the Blue Dragon, White Tiger, Red Bird and the Black Tortoise.

I have to be clear that this is another place where a traveller cannot simply turn up on a bike. The tomb is in North Korea, where visits happen only through official tours with guides, so this is a story from a distance. What can be said about the area is that it is flat and agricultural, with rice fields, villages, orchards and, to the west, the port of Nampo, an important harbour whose giant sea barrage across the Taedong estuary was built in the 1980s.

The Koguryo people were horse-riding warriors who ruled a large kingdom, rivalling China, and were skilled builders of mountain fortresses. In the seventh century they resisted the invasions of the Sui and Tang empires, but eventually fell in 668 to a coalition of Tang and Silla. Their tombs, painted with delicate lines and bright mineral colours, are the best evidence of how they lived, dressed and imagined the afterlife. Researchers have noted that some paintings show Chinese influences, and others look distinctly local.

The mound itself, typical of the tombs of the period, is square at the base and rounded above, and was originally sealed to protect the dead. Entry is controlled to preserve the paintings from humidity and mould, and replicas are on display in museums.

If you are interested in the Koguryo, there is a good deal to see across the border in China, at Jian, where another set of tombs and the great stele of King Gwanggaeto stand.
t.uedem hochwald hochwald 12@51.7,6.4:
Between Uedem and Kalkar, the Hochwald is a block of forest on a low ridge in the flat country of the Lower Rhine, a few kilometres from the Dutch border. It looks like a quiet, orderly German woodland, with rows of pine and beech, forest tracks and the smell of resin, but the ridge has a hard history. In February and March 1945, during the Allied offensive to clear the area between the Maas and the Rhine, known as Operation Veritable, the Hochwald was part of a German defensive line, and some of the fiercest fighting of the campaign took place among its trees, with tanks bogged in mud and infantry digging in under shell fire.

Traces of the war still occasionally appear, and the local villages hold small museums and memorials. Uedem, a town of about eight and a half thousand, has a Dutch-looking centre rebuilt after the war, with a church and a market square, and Kalkar, a little larger, is a handsome small town with a brick Gothic church whose interior is famous for its carved wooden altars from the late Middle Ages, among the best in northern Europe. Kalkar's market square, with its old town hall, is a pleasant place for a coffee.

For riders, the Lower Rhine is easy and flat. The roads cross wide agricultural land, fields of grain, potatoes and asparagus, with long straight stretches, tree-lined lanes, and farmhouses with brick barns. There are few bends, but the roads are quiet, the surface is good, and the cycle paths are excellent. The area is one of Germany's great cycling districts, so expect plenty of cyclists, especially at weekends, and take care at junctions. Wind from the west is common and can be strong on open sections. In the forest the tracks may be restricted, so keep to public roads.

Fuel, supermarkets and cafés are easily found in Uedem, Kalkar and the larger town of Goch to the north-west. Asparagus season in late April and May is a local celebration, with the white spears served with ham and potatoes at every restaurant.

Spring and early autumn are the best months, with mild days and clear light. In winter fog and drizzle can settle in.
t.bridge with the twelve holes@52.1,5.2:
Utrecht is built on its water, and the first thing you notice is that the canals sit well below street level, with wharf cellars and walkways at the water's edge. The label here describes a bridge with twelve holes, but I do not know which crossing the name refers to and I will not guess, so I will tell you about the setting instead. The coordinates lie on the south-eastern edge of the city, near De Uithof, the big university and hospital campus, where the old city gives way to polders and the green belt along the Kromme Rijn.

The landscape is ruled by water management. The Dutch spent centuries pumping, draining and diking this low country, and Utrecht was a key point on the old Roman frontier along the Rhine and later on the New Dutch Waterline, a defensive system of fortresses and areas that could be flooded to keep out invaders. Old forts such as Rijnauwen stand not far away, and some of them are open to visitors.

For a rider, the Netherlands is a lesson in patience. Speed limits are low, speed cameras are everywhere, and the cycle network is so dense that bicycles have the right of way in countless places. Cyclists on dedicated paths cross roads at roundabouts and junctions, and you must give way carefully. Roads can be narrow and winding on the dikes, with a long drop on one side, and wind can be strong. Parking for motorbikes is free in many places but regulated in the centre of Utrecht. The city centre is largely pedestrianised, and canals are protected, so use the car parks on the edge.

Utrecht has over two hundred and ninety thousand people, and fuel, shops, cafés and bike repair are all easy. De Uithof, a small district within the city, has campus cafés and little else. The Dom Tower, rising 112 metres, is the tallest church tower in the country, and the climb to the top offers views across the flat landscape on a clear day.

The Rietveld Schröder House, a landmark of modernist design, stands on the east side of the city and is open by guided tour. In spring, the fields bloom with tulips farther west, and autumn brings mist on the meadows.
t.sluice@52.1,5.1:
Utrecht's canals once lay at the heart of a busy inland port, and the sluices and locks that controlled the water are quiet reminders of that system. At these coordinates, a short distance south-east of the centre, a sluice marks a point where the city's waterways, fed by the Kromme Rijn and the Vecht, were managed to keep the level steady and allow boats to pass. I do not know which particular sluice the label refers to, so I will not describe a specific structure, only the kind of thing it is.

Locks and sluices in the Netherlands are small works of civil engineering, with heavy wooden gates, iron paddles and a keeper's house, often built in brick with a date stone. Barges still pass through them, along with pleasure boats and canoes, and in summer the waterside terraces around Utrecht fill with people. The canal network is part of the character of the city, and walking along the Oudegracht, with its wharf cellars now converted into cafés and shops, is the best way to see it.

The ride here is gentle and short. From the city's southern edge, minor roads follow the water through meadows, past farms with thatched roofs and rows of pollarded willows, and the horizon is wide and flat. These are narrow roads, shared with cyclists, who rule the lanes, so slow down and give them space. The Dutch road rules are strict, with fines for speeding and for riding without a helmet in some categories, so check the limits, which are generally 30 or 50 in towns and 60 or 80 outside. Parking for bikes is plentiful at the edges of the city, and the centre is a pedestrian haven.

Utrecht has all the fuel, shops, restaurants and hotels you could need, and De Uithof, nearby, has student cafés and little else. Local specialities include stroopwafels, thin waffles with a caramel filling, and a plate of bitterballen, deep-fried meat croquettes, with a glass of beer.

The best time to visit is late spring or early autumn, when the light is soft, the terraces are open and the crowds are manageable. Winter can be grey and damp, but a hot chocolate by the canal has its charm, and if the water freezes, skaters appear.
t.uedem hochwald hochwald 7 1@51.7,6.4:
South of the village of Uedem the forest is called the Hochwald, and the number on the label is a forestry compartment, so I will describe the woodland and the country around it instead of a single spot. The Lower Rhine here is a flat, green landscape of fields, hedgerows and patches of pine and beech, with long views and a big sky. The coordinates lie between Uedem and Xanten, with Xanten the larger of the two at about twenty-one thousand people, so fuel and supplies are best found there.

Xanten is worth the detour for its Roman past. The Romans built a large settlement, Colonia Ulpia Traiana, on the Rhine here in the early second century, and today an archaeological park, one of the largest in Europe, has reconstructed buildings, including a section of the city wall, a temple and a large amphitheatre, set in the open fields where the real city stood. In the medieval town, the cathedral of St Victor, a Gothic church, rises above the old streets, and the town is linked in legend with Siegfried, the hero of the Nibelungenlied, who is said to have been born here.

The riding is flat, quiet and straightforward. The roads cross the plain in long straight sections, interrupted by gentle bends around farms and woods, and the surface is generally excellent. Cyclists are everywhere, and so are agricultural vehicles in spring and autumn, so the pace is relaxed. Wind can be a challenge on open sections, and fog gathers in the low fields on autumn mornings. In the forest, many tracks are closed to motor vehicles, and signs should be respected.

Uedem has fuel and basic shops, but Xanten offers a wider choice of restaurants, supermarkets and hotels. In late spring, white asparagus appears on every menu, and local bakeries sell sweet cakes and fresh bread. The nearby Rhine, with its wide river meadows and ferry crossings, is a pleasant place for a break, and birdwatchers come in winter to see geese and swans gathering on the floodplain.

Spring and early autumn are lovely, with mild air and soft light, while midsummer weekends bring cyclists in large numbers, and winter brings damp, grey weather.
t.catavina@29.7,-114.7:
Cataviña is a landscape from another planet, and it happens to have a road through it. The pin sits in the middle of Baja California's central desert, where enormous granite boulders lie scattered across the hills as though a giant had been juggling them, and the plants are among the strangest on earth. Cirio trees, known in English as boojum, rise like upside-down carrots up to ten metres tall, with a few spiny branches at the top, and the cardón cactus, the world's tallest, stands in forests of its own. The whole area is protected as the Valle de los Cirios reserve.

Highway 1, the Transpeninsular, runs through here, and it was finished only in 1973. Before that, the peninsula was a land of ranches, missions and boat connections, and the Jesuits and Dominicans who built small missions here in the eighteenth century had to supply them by sea. Nearby caves hold rock paintings made by the Cochimí people, who lived here for centuries, in red and black pigment, showing human figures and animals. The little settlement of Cataviña has a few motels, a restaurant and an air of being at the end of everything.

The ride is a delight. The road runs south in a series of gentle, rolling bends through the boulders, with no guardrails, a narrow shoulder and long views of empty land. The surface is generally good, but potholes and rough edges appear, and cattle sometimes stand on the asphalt. Wind and heat dominate. Summer afternoons can exceed forty degrees, and winter nights drop close to freezing. Spring, when wildflowers cover the ground after rain, is the best season.

Fuel is the major practical issue. The supply in Cataviña has been unreliable over the years, so do not count on it, and instead fill the tank at El Rosario to the north or Guerrero Negro to the south, carrying a spare can if you can. Cash in pesos is wise, as cards are not always accepted. Water, sunscreen and a hat are essential. If you stop for the night, the stars here are exceptional, with no light pollution to spoil them.
t.guerrero negro@28.0,-114.1:
Guerrero Negro is a town built on salt and whales, in that order. It sits on the Pacific side of Baja California, at the border between the northern and southern states, and the pin lies just beyond the edge of town, where the road crosses the 28th parallel and a monument shaped like a giant steel eagle marks the line. Clocks change here too, with Baja California Sur an hour ahead. Beyond the town, the lagoon of Ojo de Liebre stretches out in a flat, glittering sheet.

The salt works are the world's largest, with evaporation ponds covering hundreds of square kilometres, and the white piles of salt gleam in the sun like snow. The name of the town, Black Warrior, comes from an American whaling ship that was wrecked on the sandbars at the entrance of the lagoon in 1858. A century and a half later, the lagoon is a whale sanctuary, part of the El Vizcaíno biosphere reserve listed by UNESCO. Every winter, from about January to April, grey whales travel here from the Arctic to give birth, and boat trips take visitors close enough to touch the barnacled backs of curious mothers and calves.

The riding that leads here is long and open. Highway 1 crosses a flat, scrubby desert, with the road laid out in straight lines, wide skies and the occasional gust of crosswind. The surface is generally good, though trucks coming the other way throw up grit, and the distances between settlements are great. The ride from Cataviña takes several hours, and a stop in the middle, at a roadside restaurant, is welcome. In the evening, the light on the salt flats is extraordinary.

Fuel is available in Guerrero Negro, a town of thirteen thousand, and it is the place to fill up before the long run south. Restaurants serve fresh seafood, particularly clams, scallops and fish tacos, and a few simple motels offer rooms. Whale-watching tours should be booked in advance during the season. Keep cash in pesos, and carry water for the road. If you arrive at dusk, the cold air smells of salt and the sky fills with stars.
t.mulege@26.9,-112.0:
Mulegé is a green surprise in a very brown country. The town sits where a small river reaches the Gulf of California, and a belt of date palms follows the valley inland, so that after hours on dry, spiny desert road you drop through a gap in the hills and find yourself among palms, orchards and the scent of water. The pin lies on the edge of town, close to the river mouth. The old mission church, founded by the Jesuits in the early eighteenth century, stands on a rise above the river and looks out across the palms.

The town has an odd history. For decades, the territorial prison on the hill above the river was famous for having no locked gates, and the inmates were allowed to leave during the day to work in the town, returning at night to sleep. The system is said to have worked because there was nowhere to go in the desert, and the building is now a small museum. Dates, oranges and figs grow along the river, and the town's pace is slow and friendly, with a plaza, a few shops and some small restaurants.

South of Mulegé, Highway 1 runs along the shore of Bahía Concepción, one of the loveliest stretches of road in Baja. The bay is a long, sheltered arm of the gulf, with turquoise water, white beaches and rocky headlands, and the road dips and climbs along it in short bends with views at every turn. It is a ride to take slowly. The surface can be rough, and in places the shoulder is narrow, but traffic is light. In the hot months, the water is warm enough to swim in all day.

Fuel is available in Mulegé, which is a town of under four thousand but has a station, and there are more in Santa Rosalía to the north and Loreto to the south. Food is simple and good, with tacos, fresh fish and clams from the bay, and a few hotels have shaded gardens. Keep cash, since cards are not accepted everywhere. If you plan to camp on the beaches south of town, bring water and be ready for strong sun, as there is little shade.
t.durbuy@50.4,5.5:
Durbuy bills itself as the smallest city in the world, a claim based on a charter granted in 1331, and while the title is more marketing than fact, the little town on the Ourthe river in the Belgian Ardennes is a delight. Its old centre, packed into a bend of the river beneath a limestone cliff, is a tangle of cobbled lanes, stone houses and small squares, with a castle above that has belonged to the same noble family for centuries.

The place has a certain polish. The streets are lined with restaurants, chocolate shops and boutiques, and a topiary park nearby shows box hedges clipped into shapes of birds and animals. Weekends and school holidays bring crowds from Belgium and the Netherlands, so the place can feel like a stage set, but mornings and weekdays are calm, and the cobbles, the church tower and the sound of the river are charming.

The Ardennes are a land of forests, valleys and slow rivers, with limestone caves, including the great caverns at Hotton and Han-sur-Lesse. The region also has a darker memory. In the winter of 1944 and 1945, the Battle of the Bulge was fought across these hills, and towns such as La Roche-en-Ardenne, a short ride south, and Bastogne, further on, carry memorials and museums. Cold, snow and fog shaped that battle, and on a grey November day it is not hard to imagine.

Riding here is a pleasure, with the roads following the Ourthe and its side valleys, climbing through beech and oak forest and dropping into small stone villages. Surfaces are generally good, though cobbles in the old towns are slippery in the wet, and Belgian roads can have patches of rough concrete and potholes. The weather is wet and changeable, with rain possible at any time, so pack waterproofs. Weekend traffic is heavy in summer, with cyclists and canoeists on the river.

Durbuy has petrol stations on the edge of town and plenty of places to eat. The Ardennes are known for their ham, smoked and cured, and for local beers and cheeses. A plate of ham, bread and cheese, with a cold beer, is a classic lunch. Parking in the old town is limited, so use the signed car parks and walk in.
t.hamelin@52.1,9.4:
In Hamelin, the rats are on the pavement. A trail of little brass rats leads through the old town to the Rattenfängerhaus, the house of the Pied Piper, and the town has built its identity around the legend. According to the story, in 1284 a stranger in colourful clothes came to Hameln, as the Germans spell it, and offered to rid the town of its rats. He led them into the Weser with his pipe, the citizens refused to pay him, and he returned and led away their children. The earliest records speak of a loss of a hundred and thirty children, and historians still argue over what actually happened.

Hameln is a handsome town of nearly sixty thousand people on the Weser, with half-timbered houses and fine examples of the Weser Renaissance style, a regional style of carved stone gables and ornate bay windows from around 1600. The Hochzeitshaus, the old wedding house, is a good example, and in summer actors perform the legend on Sundays in front of it. There are plenty of cafes and restaurants, and bakers sell little pastries in the shape of rats.

The ride to Hameln from the north and west follows the Weser valley, with gentle curves, fields, hills and woodland, and a string of small towns. The roads are mostly smooth and well kept, with long views from the ridges. In summer, the river is busy with cyclists, and in autumn mist lies on the water in the morning.

The town has fuel stations on the edge, and bike dealers, supermarkets and hotels. Come early if you want to see the old town without the crowds, and walk down the Osterstraße, the main pedestrian street, to the Pied Piper's house. The story was collected by the Brothers Grimm, and the Fairy Tale Route, which links towns associated with them and their tales, passes through here. It is a quiet and charming finish to a long ride.
t.husum@54.5,9.1:
Theodor Storm called Husum the grey town by the sea, and he meant it kindly. The poet and novelist, who was born in the town in 1817, wrote about the dykes, the fog and the wide, grey skies of the North Frisian coast, and the phrase has stuck. His house is a museum, and his novella The Rider on the White Horse, about a dyke-builder fighting the sea, is the great story of this coast.

The town, with about twenty-one thousand people, has a pretty harbour with old warehouses and fishing cutters that still land North Sea shrimp, and a market square with a fountain and a tall church. In March, the park around the castle is carpeted with purple crocuses, a spectacle that draws visitors. Fuel and food are easy here, with petrol stations, supermarkets and a number of fish restaurants along the quay. Try the Krabbenbrötchen, a bread roll with fresh shrimp, which is the quintessential Husum lunch.

The riding out here is flat and open, with long, straight roads across marshland, often on top of a dyke, with sheep grazing on the grass. It is not twisty, but the landscape is huge, with an enormous sky and a horizon that curves. Wind is the main factor. It can be strong, particularly from the west, and a crosswind on an exposed stretch can be tiring. Keep your speed steady and your grip relaxed.

In summer the days are long and bright, but the weather is changeable, and a sudden shower can sweep in from the sea. Autumn brings migrating birds, and in the winter the geese arrive in large flocks. The Wadden Sea, the tidal flats of the North Sea, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and a short ride from the town will take you to the dyke, where you can watch the tide come in.
t.st peter ording beach edge@54.3,8.6:
The beach at St. Peter-Ording is so wide that the sea is sometimes a long walk away. The sand stretches for about twelve kilometres along the west coast of the Eiderstedt peninsula, up to two kilometres wide at low tide, and is one of the broadest in Germany. The restaurants on the beach stand on tall wooden stilts, like something from a fairy tale, because the tide and storm surges can cover the sand.

The place is a spa and seaside resort, with about four thousand people in the village and many more in summer. Kitesurfers, windsurfers and sand yachts use the wide beach, and the wind is a constant. The village has fuel, food and hotels, though for a larger choice of services the town of Tönning, about twenty kilometres away, is the nearest with more than five thousand people. In some places cars are allowed to drive on the beach for a fee, but check the rules on site before taking a motorcycle onto the sand, since it can be soft and the tide moves fast.

The ride here crosses the Eiderstedt peninsula, a low, flat land of dykes, sheep and wide skies, with thatched farmhouses on their artificial mounds called Warften. The road is straight and exposed, and the wind makes it a physical ride, with crosswinds that push the bike across the lane. Spring and autumn are quieter, and the light is excellent. In summer the beach is crowded, and the road in is slow at weekends.

The tidal flats are part of the Wadden Sea National Park, an important area for birds, and in spring and autumn huge flocks of waders gather on the mud. A walk on the sand at sunset, with the light low and the sea a thin silver line, is the best way to finish the ride. Bring a windproof jacket, since the breeze can be chilly even in July.
t.steinau an der strasse@50.3,9.5:
The Brothers Grimm spent part of their childhood here, and the town has not forgotten it. Jacob and Wilhelm lived in Steinau from 1791 to 1796, when their father was the district magistrate, and they played in the courtyard of the Amtshaus, a handsome half-timbered building that is now a museum. The Fairy Tale Route runs through the town, and the old market square has a fountain and a plaque dedicated to them.

Steinau lies on the old Via Regia, the royal road that linked Frankfurt with Leipzig and eastern Europe, and that explains the strange name, Steinau an der Straße, Steinau on the road. The long main street, lined with half-timbered houses, was a staging post for travellers and merchants, and the castle of the counts of Hanau, a squat fortress with a moat and round towers, still stands at its end. A puppet theatre, the Marionettentheater, performs versions of the fairy tales in a small hall, and has done so for decades.

With over eleven thousand people, Steinau has the fuel, food and services you need, and nearby Schlüchtern is bigger still. The Kinzig valley runs through the town, a quiet, green and gently winding valley between the Spessart hills and the Vogelsberg, and the roads here are wonderful for easy touring, with smooth surfaces, long bends and little traffic. Villages are small and neat, with half-timbered houses and a church tower.

Spring is the best time here, when the orchards blossom, and in autumn the woods turn red and gold. Summer weekends are busy with families visiting the museum, so a weekday visit gives the best experience. A bakery or a small guesthouse on the main street is a good place to stop, and you may hear a story or two from the locals. If you stay long enough, the evening light on the old walls is lovely.
t.hann munden three rivers@51.4,9.7:
Hannoversch Münden is where two rivers lose their names. The Werra and the Fulda meet here, and from this point on the water is called the Weser, which flows north for more than four hundred kilometres to the North Sea. The town sits at the meeting point, with water on three sides, and has so many half-timbered houses, more than seven hundred, that it feels like a stage set, with carved beams, painted gables and a cobbled main street.

The old town has a Renaissance castle, built by the Guelph dukes, and a town hall with a lovely carved facade. The doctor and travelling quack Johann Andreas Eisenbarth, who became a legend in German folk songs, died here in 1727, and every summer, plays and processions recall him. The old stone bridge over the Werra still carries traffic, and the riverbanks have a long path for walking and cycling.

With about twenty-five thousand people, Münden is large enough to have fuel, supermarkets and a good choice of cafes, and it sits at the edge of the Weser uplands, a hilly, wooded region with roads that wind along the river and over the ridges. The ride along the Weser or the Fulda is a pleasure, with long bends, trees on both banks, and hardly any traffic on the minor roads.

The label calls this a swim stop, and in summer the rivers are popular for swimming, canoeing and sunbathing. The water is generally clean, but currents can be strong, and the banks steep, so take care. The best time is a warm summer afternoon, when the light on the half-timbered houses is golden. Mist rises from the rivers in the early morning, and the old town has a hush that disappears by ten o'clock. If you have time, walk up through the lanes to the church of St Blasius and look back across the roofs: the whole triangle of land between the rivers is laid out beneath you, and you can see how the town grew up around the water.
t.weserstein photo@51.4,9.7:
There is an old verse on the stone: where the Werra and the Fulda kiss, they lose their names, and from the kiss the Weser flows, German to the sea. The Weserstein stands on the tip of the land where the two rivers meet, in a small park on the edge of the old town of Hann. Münden, and it has been put up for a long time, so the stone has the patina of weather and moss.

It is a small stop, not a sight on the scale of a cathedral, but a good place for a photograph and a pause. A path leads through the park, with benches and trees, and on a calm day the two rivers can be seen flowing side by side, a different colour for a short stretch, before they merge. Standing there, you can hear the weir and the traffic on the old bridge a few steps away, which is a reminder that this is a living town and not a monument.

Above the town, the Tillyschanze, an observation tower built in the early twentieth century on a hill, commemorates the time that the imperial general Tilly captured Münden in 1626 during the Thirty Years War. From the top there is a view across the old town, the rivers and the forested hills. A road climbs to it through the woods, with a few tight bends, and the ride is short and enjoyable.

The Weser Cycle Path runs along the river, and in summer there are many cyclists. The riverside car park fills up at weekends, so try to arrive early. Fuel and food are in the town centre, which is a few minutes away on foot. Morning light on the water is lovely, and the old town is quiet before the day trippers arrive. Come in spring, when the trees along the river are in fresh leaf and the water is high, or in autumn, when the mist hangs over the confluence.
t.gottingen@51.5,9.9:
Göttingen is a university town that has never been shy about it. The Georg-August University was founded in 1737 and became one of the leading centres of science in Europe, and the roll of people who studied or taught here includes the mathematician Carl Friedrich Gauss, the physicists Max Planck and Werner Heisenberg, the Brothers Grimm, and a long list of Nobel laureates. The student population gives the city a lively, young feel, with bicycles everywhere.

The centre is a pleasant maze of half-timbered houses, narrow lanes and cafes, anchored by the old town hall and its market square, where a small fountain topped with a statue of the Goose Girl, the Gänseliesel, stands. By tradition, newly graduated doctors must kiss her, which has made her, it is said, the most kissed girl in the world. The city has over a hundred and twenty thousand people and every service a rider could need, with fuel, bike shops, supermarkets and a huge choice of restaurants at low prices, aimed at students.

For a meal, you can find German classics, such as schnitzel and sausage with potato salad, as well as Turkish, Italian and Asian places, and plenty of bakeries and cafes. The city is a good stop for lunch, but parking in the centre is limited, so leave the bike at a car park on the edge, and walk in. The old ramparts, now a tree-lined walk, make a nice stroll.

The countryside around Göttingen is gentle, with green hills, beech woods and farmland, and the roads leading out are well surfaced, with long bends and light traffic. In summer, the beech woods on the hills east of town are shady and cool. Spring and autumn are lovely, and the winter can bring ice to the lanes. Come on a weekday morning for easier parking and quieter roads.
t.einbeck return road@51.8,9.9:
Einbeck is where bock beer began. In the Middle Ages the town was one of the great brewing centres of the Hanseatic League, and its strong, dark beer was exported across northern Europe. When Bavarian brewers copied it, the name Einbecker was heard as ein Bock, a billy goat, and so a beer style got its name. The town still has a brewery, and the goat appears on the labels.

The old town is a delight, with a huge number of half-timbered houses, carved with figures and inscriptions, and a market square lined with fine buildings. Much of the town burned down in 1540, and was rebuilt with a regard for style that gives it a unity unusual in Germany. With about twenty-eight thousand people, Einbeck has every practical convenience, from fuel stations to supermarkets, and a large selection of restaurants and cafes, where you can try the local beer.

For riders, there is a bonus. The PS.Speicher, a museum in an old grain store near the centre, houses a large collection of cars and motorcycles, with exhibits that range from early machines to postwar classics. It is a fine place to spend an hour or two out of the rain, and the displays are well presented. There is a cafe on site.

The roads around Einbeck are quiet and winding, running through the hills of the Weser uplands and the Leine valley, with beech woods and farmland and a succession of small, tidy villages. Kreiensen, a few kilometres away, is a railway junction with a long history. The summer is warm, the autumn colours are good, and in winter ice can lie on the shady roads. A glass of Einbecker Bock and a hearty plate of local sausage, after a day on the bike, is the way to end the evening.
t.wunstorf@52.4,9.4:
Wunstorf has an airbase and a lake, and neither is what you expect from the name. The town, with about forty-two thousand people, lies on the Leine west of Hanover, and the nearby military airfield is home to the German Air Force's transport aircraft. The lake is the Steinhuder Meer, a short ride to the north, the largest lake in north-west Germany and so shallow that you can nearly wade across it. It is a popular place for sailing, with the little town of Steinhude on its southern shore selling smoked eel to visitors.

Wunstorf began around a convent founded in the ninth century, and the old collegiate church still stands, a plain stone building. The town is a practical stop, with fuel stations, supermarkets and bakeries, and the roads converge here from Hanover, Nienburg and the Weser. It is a good place to fill the tank at the start of a ride, with a quick coffee before you set off.

The country around the Steinhuder Meer is flat, with moors, meadows and reeds, and the roads run straight and quiet, with wide skies and wind as the main hazard. A nature park surrounds the lake, with trails and birdwatching points, and in spring and autumn the migrating birds are a draw. The ride is gentle, and it makes a good warm-up for the hills to the south and west.

Weather in the plain can be changeable, with a cold wind off the lake in spring and autumn. Summer is warm and pleasant, but weekends bring a lot of traffic from Hanover, so go early. A smoked eel sandwich at the lake, a bag of fresh strawberries from a farm stall and a quiet hour on the shore are the pleasures of a day here. Steinhude is also known for the little sailing boats called Auswanderer, flat-bottomed and low in the water, a reminder that the lake is shallow enough that hardly anyone can drown in it.
t.externsteine rock sight@51.9,8.9:
The Externsteine are a row of sandstone towers that rise from the Teutoburg Forest like fingers, some nearly forty metres high, weathered into strange shapes and standing apart from the surrounding hills. They are among the most famous natural monuments in Germany, and a place where history, legend and politics have mingled for centuries.

On the largest rock, a relief carved in about 1115 shows the Descent from the Cross, one of the greatest medieval stone carvings in northern Europe, with a sculpted Christ and mourners, and a path and stairs lead to a chapel carved into the rock. Many people believe that the rocks were a pagan holy place before that, though the evidence is thin. In the twentieth century, the Nazis made use of the site in their invented version of German prehistory, and the rocks are still sometimes visited by groups with questionable beliefs, which is why the guides take care to tell the history straight.

The nearest town is Horn-Bad Meinberg, with about seven thousand people in the Horn area, and the larger city of Detmold is a short ride away. The roads through the Teutoburg Forest are among the best in this part of Germany, with smooth surfaces, long bends and climbs through beech and spruce woods, past little villages and ponds. At weekends, they are busy with riders, so watch for fast groups and take your time.

Fuel and food are in Horn and Detmold, and a small cafe near the rocks sells coffee and cake. The site is easy to reach from the road. Early morning is a good time to visit, when the mist hangs between the rocks and the crowd has not yet arrived. In spring and autumn, the beech forest is at its best, and in winter the rocks can be icy.
t.detmold ridge road@51.9,8.9:
Detmold has a giant looking over its shoulder. On a hill in the Teutoburg Forest above the city stands the Hermannsdenkmal, a copper statue of the Germanic chieftain Arminius, who defeated three Roman legions in the year 9 AD, raised on a stone base and holding a sword to the sky. It was completed in 1875 after decades of work, in the first flush of German national feeling, and at about fifty metres is among the tallest statues in the country. The exact site of the battle is still debated, and most scholars think it took place farther north, at Kalkriese.

The city itself, with about seventy-four thousand people, was the seat of the princes of Lippe and still has a palace in the Weser Renaissance style, with fine gables and a courtyard. Johannes Brahms worked here as a court musician in the late 1850s, teaching the princess and conducting the choir, and the city is proud of the connection. The open-air museum, the largest of its kind in Germany, has hundreds of old farmhouses, mills and workshops moved from all over Westphalia and set in a wooded landscape, and it makes a fascinating afternoon.

For riders, the Teutoburg Forest ridge road, the Hermannsweg road and the lanes that climb through the beech woods are a delight, with smooth surfaces and tight, flowing bends. The ridge is steep on the eastern side, and the views from the viewpoints are excellent. Fuel, bike shops, hotels and restaurants are all available in Detmold, and the old town has a pedestrian zone with cafes.

The weather is mild but changeable, with rain at any time of year. In summer, the forest is cool and shady, while in autumn the beech leaves turn a deep copper. Come on a weekday, since weekends are busy with day trippers. A visit to the monument, followed by a climb up its stairs for the view, makes a fine break.
t.cochem@50.1,7.2:
Cochem has a castle that is younger than it looks. The Reichsburg, perched on a hill above the town, was built in the eleventh century, destroyed by French troops in 1689, and left a ruin for nearly two hundred years, until a Berlin businessman bought it and rebuilt it in neo-Gothic style in the 1870s. The result is a storybook castle, with turrets and pointed roofs, and a view over the Moselle that is among the finest in the valley.

The town lies in a bend of the river, with narrow lanes, half-timbered houses and a market square, and it is one of the most visited places on the Moselle. It has about five thousand people, with fuel, food and hotels, and a wine culture that dominates the place. The steep vineyards that climb the slate slopes produce Riesling, with a crisp, mineral flavour, and the wine taverns in the old town pour it by the glass. A mustard mill in the town offers tastings, and a chairlift climbs to a viewpoint over the valley.

The Moselle Wine Route, the Moselweinstraße, follows the river for more than two hundred kilometres between Trier and Koblenz, and the stretch around Cochem is among the best. The road is narrow and winding, with long bends beside the water, small villages with church towers, and vineyards so steep that harvesters work on ropes. Traffic can be heavy in the high season, with tourist coaches and cyclists, so ride in the early morning or late evening.

Nearby, a railway tunnel, the Kaiser Wilhelm Tunnel, was built in the nineteenth century to cut across a loop in the river, and at over four kilometres is among the longest in Germany. Autumn is the harvest season, with colour in the vines and new wine in every cellar, and the valley is at its best. Mist often fills the valley in the early morning, and the afternoon light on the slate is warm.
t.stadthagen@52.3,9.2:
Stadthagen is the capital of a country that no longer exists. For centuries, the town was the seat of the counts and princes of Schaumburg, a small state between Hanover and the Weser, and the Renaissance castle, built in the sixteenth century, still stands at the edge of the old town, with carved gables. The mausoleum of the princes, in the grounds of the St Martini church, is decorated with a bronze sculpture of the Resurrection by the Dutch sculptor Adriaen de Vries, one of the masterpieces of its period in Germany.

The town has about twenty-three thousand people, and is a practical stop, with fuel, supermarkets, bakeries and cafes. The market square has a Renaissance town hall and many half-timbered houses, and coal mines operated here until the 1960s, a part of the town's past that is recalled in a small museum. The ridge of the Deister, a wooded range of hills, rises to the south, and Bückeburg, with its palace, lies a short ride to the west.

The roads around Stadthagen are flat to gently rolling, with farmland and woods, small villages and a calm atmosphere. This is the northern edge of the German uplands, and the roads head south toward the Deister and the Weser hills, climbing in gentle bends through beech woods. The surface is mostly good, though some of the minor roads are patched, and traffic is light.

The weather is mild, but changeable, with rain showers at any time of year, so carry a waterproof. Summer is warm and pleasant, and the autumn colours in the Deister are lovely. A coffee at one of the cafes on the market square, with a slice of local cake, is a good way to spend a break, and the town is quiet in the evening. If you walk out to the Deister edge, you will find old mining relics half hidden in the beech woods, and the contrast between the tidy town and the overgrown pits is oddly moving.
t.stade old town@53.6,9.5:
Stade has a harbour that looks like a painting. The old Hanseatic port, with a basin surrounded by tall, narrow gabled houses, a wooden crane and old warehouses, is the heart of the town, and the long, still water reflects the buildings so well that photographers return again and again. The town lies on the Schwinge, a small tributary of the Elbe, about forty kilometres west of Hamburg, in a flat landscape of marshes, orchards and dykes.

For about seventy years from the 1640s, Stade was part of Sweden, and the Swedish period left traces in the architecture and the street plan. The Schwedenspeicher, a large brick warehouse on the harbour, is now a museum of the town's history, including the Swedish period and the Bronze Age finds of the region. With about forty-five thousand people, Stade has all the services, with fuel stations, supermarkets and many cafes and restaurants, and a cobbled old town that is a pleasure to walk.

East of the town begins the Altes Land, the largest fruit-growing area in northern Germany, a strip of orchards along the Elbe with timber-framed farmhouses decorated with brick patterns and carved gates. In spring, the apple and cherry blossom turns the whole area white and pink, and the roads through it are among the most beautiful in the north, though they are narrow and busy with cyclists. In autumn, the farm stalls sell apples, plums and cider.

The riding here is flat and relaxed, with the wind as the main challenge. The roads along the dyke give views over the river, with big ships gliding past on their way to Hamburg. The best times are the blossom season, in late April and early May, and early autumn, when the light is soft. In summer, weekends can be busy, so aim for a weekday, and finish with fish and a glass of beer on the harbour.
t.stade@53.6,9.5:
Stade is a Hanseatic town that most riders cross without noticing, which is a shame, because it is one of the better-looking small cities in the north German lowlands. It sits on the Schwinge, a sluggish little river that reaches the Elbe a few kilometres away, and the old harbour basin in the middle of town still has a wooden crane and a row of gabled brick and timber houses leaning over the water. Sweden held the town for most of the later seventeenth century, and it was a serious military post in those years, which is why the fortifications and the ring of moats around the centre are so well preserved.

For a rider it is, first of all, a practical place. With more than forty thousand people it has fuel, supermarkets and bakeries without any fuss, and the ring road lets you fill up and be gone in ten minutes. If you have the time, though, leave the bike near the harbour and walk. The cobbles in the old streets are rough and wet in the morning, and you do not want to be riding on them with cold tyres. A coffee beside the water is a good way to start a ride that is going to spend the day on flat, straight and often windy roads.

The land around here is the point. To the east lies the Altes Land, a drained Elbe marshland that is one enormous orchard, with apple and cherry trees planted on dykes between narrow ditches. In late April and early May the blossom is so thick that the whole strip along the river smells sweet, and the traffic of day-trippers from Hamburg is thick as well, so go on a weekday if you can. The farmhouses there are the famous half-timbered kind, with decorated brick infill and carved gate beams, and they set the tone for the timber frame theme that runs through the ride.

Westerly wind is the main hazard on this coast. With nothing to break it between the North Sea and the Elbe dyke, a gusty day makes a heavy bike twitchy on the exposed stretches, and the best riding conditions are early on a calm morning in late spring or in September, when the light turns golden and low over the fields. Hamburg is under an hour east if you need to give up, and the bigger fuel stations on the edge of Stade stay open late.
t.wilseder berg heath roads@53.2,9.9:
There is a certain humour in calling a hill of 169 metres a mountain, and the people of the Lüneburg Heath enjoy it. The Wilseder Berg is the highest point in the whole of north-western Germany's lowlands, a rounded dune-like summit of sand and heather that the last ice age left behind, and the view from the top, across a rolling sea of heath, juniper and distant forest, is wide enough that you stop thinking about the height. The hamlet of Wilsede at its foot is closed to cars, which is how it kept its thatched barns and its little museum of heath life. You can ride to the edge of the reserve, park, and walk in.

What matters for a rider is the web of small roads around the reserve, which connect Egestorf, Bispingen and Schneverdingen. They are quiet, mostly smooth and almost entirely free of hairpins, and the pleasure is in the rhythm: a gentle rise over a heath ridge, a swing through a sandy pine plantation, a village green with an old oak and then open sky again. Do not expect a technical challenge. Do expect cyclists, horse riders and the occasional carriage, and a strong sense of being in a landscape that does not hurry. Sand can blow onto the tarmac at corners and after rain the dark leaf litter under the pines is slippery.

The heath is protected, and it has been for a long time, as one of Germany's first nature reserves, set up in the early 1920s when the old way of grazing was beginning to die out and the open ground was being planted with forest. Heidschnucken sheep still graze it, and they are the reason it looks the way it does. In the Totengrund, a hollow near the hill, the old pastureland is especially fine, and in late summer it glows purple when the heather is in flower. Early in the morning in September, when mist lies in the hollows, it is quieter than the weekend peak. The nearest fuel is in Bispingen or Schneverdingen, the larger of the two, and there are plenty of small cafés and farm shops in between where you can buy heather honey and heath sheep sausage.
t.soltau@53.0,9.8:
Soltau is a working town on the western edge of the Lüneburg Heath, a place of around twenty thousand people on the little Böhme river, and a stop here is for fuel, a sandwich and a look at your map. I say that with affection. The riding you came here for is out on the heath and the Aller valley, and Soltau gives you the services to do it without worry. There are several filling stations on the through roads, supermarkets with decent bakery counters, and a pedestrian centre where you can sit outside and drink coffee on a sunny day without anybody asking you for anything.

It is also a town with an odd mix of roles. Its best-known attraction is an amusement park, the Heide Park, which pulls families in from Hamburg and Hanover every summer, and the signs for it appear on every road for miles. Outside the park season, and outside holidays, the traffic is mild. The town is in flat country at about sixty metres above sea level, and the land around it is a patchwork of pine plantation, farmland and the remains of heath, with the occasional dune. The soil is thin and sandy, and that is why heather and Scots pine have always done well here.

For a rider the approach from the south or east is much like the rest of the region: long straights through forest, gentle bends over streams and a lot of cyclists. Be careful with the animals. Roe deer cross these forest roads at dawn and dusk, and a bike does not survive a collision with one. In the autumn there is also the matter of mud and wet leaves where tractors have used the lanes, so slow down when the surface looks dark. The best seasons are late spring, when the birch and beech leaves are fresh, and September, when the light is low and the heath is still in colour.

If you need more than fuel, the smaller villages around Soltau, Neuenkirchen and Wietzendorf among them, have inns serving the usual heath dishes, such as lamb, asparagus in season, and plain cakes.
t.schwansen villages@54.6,9.9:
Schwansen is the little peninsula that sticks out into the Baltic between the Schlei inlet and Eckernförde Bay, and it is one of the quieter corners of Schleswig-Holstein. The land is low, rolling and green, at only a few tens of metres above the sea, and the villages of Damp, Waabs and Rieseby are separated by fields, small woods and hedgerows. It was once part of the old Danish duchy of Schleswig, and the mix of Danish and German history shows in the names and the architecture.

The characteristic feature of the landscape is the Knick, a hedge-topped earth bank that divides the fields, planted by farmers centuries ago to shelter crops and mark boundaries. The lanes that run between them are narrow and gently winding, giving a sense of riding in a green tunnel, and in May the rapeseed fields flare yellow against a blue sky. The manor houses of the peninsula, large brick houses with parks, recall the days of the Danish and German nobility who owned the land, and some are open to visitors.

The sea is never far away. On the northern shore the Schlei, a long, narrow fjord-like inlet, winds inland toward the town of Schleswig, and on the southern side the open Baltic shows through the trees. Damp is a seaside resort with a long beach and a small harbour, busy in summer and almost empty in autumn. Waabs has a pleasant beach and a quiet shore, and the cliffs of the coast are low but bring a sea breeze.

The riding is easy and relaxed, with very little traffic and a surface that is mostly good, though patched on the minor lanes. The gradients are gentle, and the pleasure lies in the rhythm of the bends and in the smell of the sea and cut grass. Wind can be strong, and rain showers sweep in quickly, so carry a waterproof.

Fuel is not guaranteed in the small villages; Kappeln, nine kilometres away, is the nearest town of any size and has stations and shops. Cafes in the villages serve coffee and cake, and a stop at a farm shop for local produce is a good idea. Late spring and early autumn are the best seasons.
t.kappeln schlei@54.7,9.9:
Kappeln is a small Baltic port on the Schlei, the long narrow inlet that cuts forty kilometres into Schleswig-Holstein, and its harbour has the busy, salty feel of a working fishing town. Wooden boats line the quays, nets hang to dry, and gulls wheel above the fish stalls. The town sits at the point where the Schlei narrows, so a bridge crosses it, and from the quay you can watch it lift to let tall-masted sailing ships through.

What makes Kappeln unusual is the herring fence, the Heringszaun, a trap of stakes and nets set across the water at the edge of town. It is said to be the last working one in Europe, and it catches herring as they swim in during spring, a method that has been used on the Schlei for centuries. Smoked herring and fresh fish are sold in the town, and a plate of Matjes with potatoes and sour cream is a local classic. A windmill named Amanda, a Dutch-style mill on the quay, stands over the harbour and is a favourite subject for photographers.

The region is called Angeln, the homeland of the Angles, the tribe that crossed to Britain in the fifth century and gave England its name, and the countryside has a flat, hedged, pastoral look that echoes a very old past. The surrounding villages have thatched cottages and farm shops, and the roads run through fields to the sea.

For riders, Kappeln is a coffee-and-fish stop: the roads in and out are straightforward, with moderate traffic and a good surface, and the pleasure is in the harbour itself. With nearly ten thousand people the town has fuel stations, supermarkets and plenty of cafes, and it is easy to park by the water. In summer the quays are busy with visitors, and a table with a view of the boats is hard to find on weekends.

The best time is spring, when the herring run and the light is clear, or in early autumn, when crowds have thinned. Wind off the water can be cold, so carry a layer even on a sunny day.
t.rinteln@52.2,9.1:
Rinteln lies on the Weser, in the hills of Lower Saxony where the river cuts through a gap in the wooded ridges, and it has the look of a town that was prosperous in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries and was then left in peace. Half-timbered houses with carved beams line the old market square, and the town hall and the Nikolai church stand among them. The architecture belongs to what is known as the Weser Renaissance, a decorative style with gables, bay windows and carved ornament that spread along the river in that period.

For about two hundred years, from 1621 until 1810, Rinteln had a university, one of the small German universities of the early modern period, and the scholarly tradition left its mark on the town. Today the old streets are pleasant to wander, with cafes and shops, and a weekly market fills the square. The Weser itself flows broad and green past the town, with a riverside path and a ferry in places, and the hills of the Weser Uplands rise on either side.

For a rider Rinteln is a convenient fuel gate. With nearly twenty-eight thousand people it has several stations and supermarkets, and it sits on the main route between Hannover and the hills. After a fill-up the best roads lie to the south and east, in the quiet lanes of the Extertal and the Lippe hills, with wooded slopes, curving valleys and light traffic. To the north the long wooded ridge of the Wesergebirge rises, with roads that climb through beech wood.

The Weser valley is also a landscape of legend. Not far downriver stands Hameln, where the Pied Piper is said to have led the children away in the thirteenth century, and the whole region is dotted with castles and half-timbered villages. The roads are well surfaced and mostly gentle, and weekends see many motorcyclists, so there is a friendly, busy atmosphere at cafes.

Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with clear air and good light. In summer the valley can be hot, and in winter fog collects along the river. Whatever the season, Rinteln makes a comfortable, easy halt.
t.extertal hill roads@52.1,9.1:
South of Rinteln the land rises into the Lippe hills, and the Exter valley runs up through them in a quiet, winding way. The area has a name among riders for its relaxed and flowing roads, and it is easy to see why: the lanes follow the folds of the land, climbing gently through beech and oak woods, dropping to small streams and passing through villages of half-timbered houses with red tiled roofs. It is a landscape on a human scale, with no big peaks or dramatic views, just mile after mile of green.

The region belonged for centuries to the small principality of Lippe, one of the many tiny states that made up the German map until the nineteenth century, and the old courts and castles of the area still show their traces. The little towns are not grand, but they have a tidy, well-kept look, with market squares and Protestant churches. Farmland fills the valley floors, with cattle, maize and cereals, and on the hills the forest is managed for timber.

The roads here are good, with smooth surfaces, flowing bends and moderate gradients, and the speed limits on the minor roads are generally sensible. On weekends the area attracts many riders, and the cafes and inns on the routes fill up, so a weekday ride gives the quietest conditions. Police checks and radar are not unknown in the villages, so keep to the limits. The shade of the forest keeps the air cool in summer, and in the early morning mist lies in the valleys.

Rinteln, about ten kilometres away, is the nearest big town and has fuel and food; Aerzen and Dörentrup are alternatives, both of respectable size. The villages along the way have small shops and a few inns, but opening hours can be limited, particularly on Sundays and in the afternoon, so plan ahead for lunch.

Late spring, when the beeches are bright and fresh, and early autumn, when the leaves turn bronze, are the best times for the ride. In winter the roads may be icy in the shaded valleys, and snow can close the higher lanes for short periods.
t.barntrup ridge@52.0,9.1:
Barntrup is a small town in the Lippe uplands, and the ridge above it gives one of the pleasanter views in this part of Germany. The land here is a series of long, wooded ridges separated by wide, farmed valleys, and the road along the top gives views over the patchwork of fields, with villages scattered between. It is a landscape of modest scale, but with a calm beauty that grows on you the longer you ride.

The town has an old centre of half-timbered houses and a castle with water-filled moat, and the surrounding area has a tradition of furniture making, with workshops and factories scattered through the villages. Blomberg, five kilometres away, is one of the best-preserved small towns in the region, with a ring of old walls, a castle and streets of carved wooden houses.
