Bad Pyrmont, a spa town a little further south, has a handsome palace, formal gardens and a long history of taking the waters.

The riding is smooth and relaxed. The roads follow the ridges and valleys, with long, easy bends, moderate climbs and a surface that is mostly in good condition. Traffic is light except on the main road through Barntrup, where trucks and local commuters mix. The forest sections are shaded and cool in summer, and the open stretches give wide views. Autumn is spectacular, with the beech woods turning copper and gold.

Barntrup, with nearly ten thousand people, is a practical stop with fuel, shops and cafes. The main street has bakeries, and a pause for coffee and cake is easy. Larger towns nearby, such as Blomberg and Bad Pyrmont, have every service, so the area is well provided for.

The region also has a layer of history in the Teutoburg Forest, a short distance to the west, where a Germanic leader named Arminius is said to have defeated three Roman legions in the year 9, a battle that shaped the history of Europe. A huge monument to him stands on a hill near Detmold, and its copper figure is visible from far away. A visit makes a fine detour if time allows.
t.friedrichstadt@54.4,9.1:
Friedrichstadt feels as though a piece of Holland has been dropped on the flat marshes of North Frisia. The town was founded in 1621 by Duke Friedrich III of Holstein-Gottorf, who invited Dutch Remonstrants, a persecuted Protestant group, to settle on the banks of the Treene, and they brought their architecture with them: canals lined with stepped-gable brick houses, bridges, trees and little quays. The result is a miniature Amsterdam, complete with canal boats, and it is a delight to walk.

The duke hoped to make the town a rich trading post, and it did not quite work out that way, but the place became known for something else, religious tolerance. Remonstrants, Lutherans, Mennonites, Catholics and Jews all lived here side by side at a time when Europe was tearing itself apart, and the town still has a number of churches and a Jewish cemetery that tell of that mix. A handful of them stand within a few minutes' walk of each other.

For a rider the town is a delight after the flat roads of the marsh. The old centre is compact, with a small market square and cafes along the water, and a stop here with a coffee and a piece of cake is easy. Parking on the edge of the old town is straightforward. The surrounding country is classic marshland, with dikes, drainage ditches, grazing sheep and a huge sky, and the roads run straight for kilometres, with the wind from the North Sea often strong.

The town is small, about two and a half thousand people, so for fuel the safe choices are Tönning, the nearest larger town, or Husum a little further north. Along the way there are small farm cafes, and local specialities include fresh fish, shrimp and a hearty plate of North Frisian dishes. The weather changes fast, with cloud, wind and bright sun in the same hour, so layers are useful.

Late spring, when the meadows are bright and the lambs are out, and early autumn, when the light is warm and the geese are flying, are the best times to visit.
t.husum harbour@54.5,9.1:
Husum calls itself the grey town by the sea, a phrase taken from the poem by the writer Theodor Storm, who was born here in 1817 and who made the town and its misty coast famous in his novellas. The grey is more affectionate than gloomy: the sky over the North Sea can be a pale silver, and the old harbour in the centre, with its brick warehouses and shrimp cutters bobbing at the quay, looks its best under a soft, cloudy light.

The harbour is the heart of the town. Small fishing boats set out for North Sea shrimp, and in the cafes and stalls along the quay you can buy them freshly cooked, eaten out of a paper bag with a roll. The harbour basin leads off the main square, which has a large market and is lined with gabled houses. A castle stands at one end of the town, set in a park that fills each spring with a vast number of crocuses, a purple carpet that is one of the sights of the north.

The North Sea coast here is a unique landscape. At low tide the sea retreats and the Wadden Sea, a vast area of mudflats, appears, home to seals, huge flocks of waders and a rich marine life, protected as a national park and a World Heritage site. The dikes that hold back the sea are high green banks where sheep graze, and a walk on top of one gives a wide view across the flat marsh. The tide comes and goes with surprising speed, and the sound of the wind and the calls of birds fill the air.

The roads leading in are flat and straight, with a strong wind from the sea often blowing across them, so ride with attention and a firm grip. With around twenty-one thousand people Husum has fuel, supermarkets and good places to eat, and parking near the harbour is easy outside peak season. Summer weekends are busy with day trippers.

The best time is spring, for the crocuses and the clear light, or early autumn, when the sea has a moody beauty. Bring a windproof layer, because the breeze off the water is cool even in July.
t.kiel canal towpath view@54.3,9.8:
The Kiel Canal is the most heavily used artificial waterway in the world, a claim that surprises most people who have never stood beside it. It cuts ninety-eight kilometres across the base of the Danish peninsula from the North Sea at Brunsbüttel to the Baltic at Kiel, saving ships a long detour around Denmark, and it was opened in 1895 under the German emperor. The spot on the towpath near Schacht-Audorf, close to Rendsburg, is a fine place to watch it work.

The scene is hypnotic. A huge container ship or tanker glides past at walking pace, its hull towering above the bank, so close that you can read the name on the bow and wave to the crew. The ships seem to move across the fields, because the canal sits low in the landscape, and a freighter appears above the hedges as though it were sailing through the meadows. Cars cross the canal on high bridges, and the old low-level ferries, which are free to use, ply back and forth in places.

The canal has an unusual place in the landscape of Schleswig-Holstein. The countryside on either side is farmland, rolling and green, with cattle, rapeseed and hedges, and the contrast between the quiet fields and the vast industrial vessels is striking. Rendsburg itself is known for an iron railway bridge with a suspended ferry hanging beneath it, one of the few of its kind in the world, a piece of engineering from the early twentieth century that still carries passengers.

The roads along the canal are flat, straight and fast, with a good surface and light traffic outside commuting hours. The wind can blow strongly across the open land, so hold the bars firmly. Riding here is not about corners but about the pleasure of an easy road, a wide sky and the occasional ship. A picnic on the bank is a good idea.

Büdelsdorf, about seven kilometres away, has about ten thousand people and the fuel and shops you need, and Rendsburg is next door with more. Spring and early autumn have the clearest light, and a still morning is best for photographs of the ships.
t.rehburg hills@52.5,9.2:
Rehburg-Loccum lies on the north edge of the Rehburg hills, a modest ridge of wooded sandstone that rises from the flat plain west of Hannover, and for riders from the city it is the nearest thing to a mountain. The hills are not high by any measure, but they are covered in beech and oak, and the roads that cross them climb and twist in a way the plain never does, with a sense of enclosure and a welcome shade in summer.

The town takes its second name from Loccum, a Cistercian monastery founded in the twelfth century that remains one of the best-preserved medieval abbeys in northern Germany. After the Reformation it became a Protestant institution and is still a centre of the Lutheran church, with a seminary for pastors. The brick church, its plain Romanesque and early Gothic lines, and the cloister with its stone vaults are open to visitors, and the quiet of the place is striking. The monks' old fishponds and farms still shape the landscape around it.

Rehburg itself is a small spa, with a spring and a park, and it has a gentle, old-fashioned air. The hills above are criss-crossed by walking paths, and the views from the ridge reach over the plain toward the Steinhuder Meer, the large shallow lake a short distance to the east. On clear days the water gleams between the trees.

The roads are a mix of smooth and patched, with moderate bends, and the traffic is local, with some weekend riders from Hannover. The climbs are short and the descents open, so the ride feels like a pleasant exercise rather than a challenge. Wet leaves in autumn can be slippery on the shaded bends, and in winter ice may linger in the hollows.

The town has nearly eleven thousand people, so fuel, shops and cafes are easily found. Cafes near the monastery serve coffee and cake, and the grounds are a pleasant place to rest. Spring, when the beech leaves emerge a vivid green, and autumn, when they turn copper, are the best times for the ride.
t.mardorf lake road@52.5,9.3:
The Steinhuder Meer is the biggest lake in Lower Saxony, and it is shockingly shallow: for most of its area it is no more than a couple of metres deep, so that on a hot day you can wade a long way out and still stand. Mardorf, on the north shore, is the beach side, with a long strip of sand, a promenade and a swimming area, and the water warms up quickly in summer, so it is a pleasant place to cool off after a day in the saddle.

The lake is a favourite playground for sailors from Hannover, and its flat water and steady breeze suit small dinghies and windsurfers. The shallowness also makes it a sanctuary for birds. Reedbeds around the shore hold herons, grebes and many ducks, and the moorland to the north, the Meerbruch nature reserve, is a protected area of bog and wet woodland. The famous local food is smoked eel, taken from the lake and served in the fish restaurants of Mardorf and Steinhude, a tradition that goes back centuries.

On an island in the middle stands the Wilhelmstein, a small fortress built in the eighteenth century by Count Wilhelm of Schaumburg-Lippe, one of the more inventive minds of his age. He built it on an artificial island as a military school and a stronghold for his tiny state, and it was one of the earliest places to train officers in a scientific manner. Small boats run to it from the shore in summer, and a visit is a fine excursion.

The lakeside road is flat and gentle, with long views of water through the trees and a surface that is generally good, though busy on warm weekends when Hannover empties onto the shore. Parking at Mardorf fills early. Cyclists and walkers share the paths and lanes, so ride calmly. Fuel is not abundant right on the shore; Rehburg-Loccum, eight kilometres away, and Hagenburg are better bets for stations and shops.

The water is cool in June and warm by August. A morning swim and a plate of smoked eel make a good midday break, and the sunset over the lake from the western shore is memorable.
t.wilsede heath core@53.2,9.9:
Few places in northern Germany are as carefully protected from people like us as Wilsede. The village sits in the middle of the Lüneburg Heath nature reserve, one of the oldest in the country, and it is closed to motor traffic. Bikes included. The sandy lanes leading in are for walkers, cyclists and horse-drawn carriages, and the car parks on the edge, at places like Undeloh and Niederhaverbeck, are where you leave the machine. Take it as a gift rather than a punishment. A short walk in boots, after hours on the saddle, is exactly the right pace for this landscape.

The heath itself is not wild nature in the strict sense. It was made by centuries of grazing, when farmers let sheep strip the woods and keep the ground bare and acidic. What grows back is heather, juniper and birch scrub, and the hardy grey-horned Heidschnucken sheep still keep it that way. In late August and September the whole thing flushes purple and the air smells honeyed and dry, and that is when the reserve gets crowded. The Wilseder Berg, at 169 metres the highest point in the northern lowlands of Lower Saxony, is a gentle hill that gives a view over this carpet. Go on a weekday morning in early autumn, when the mist is still hanging in the hollows, and the effect is closer to a painting than a landscape.

On the way in, the approach roads through the reserve's edge are what you will remember. They are narrow, mostly smooth, and follow the lie of the land through birch and pine, with sudden openings into heather. Speed limits are low and enforced with a certain friendly stubbornness, and there are horses and cyclists, so ride as if you were a guest. Which you are.

Services are not in the heart of the heath. Bispingen, about ten kilometres off, is the nearest town of any size, and Egestorf and Handeloh have smaller shops and cafés. The village inns around the reserve serve heath lamb and buckwheat pancakes, and the baked buckwheat cake is a local classic worth sitting down for. Bring a jacket, because the open sand and the wind will remind you that you are in the north.
t.eider barrage viewpoint@54.3,8.8:
The Eider barrage is a piece of engineering that most people drive across without noticing, which is a pity. It closes the mouth of the Eider river near Tönning, on the west coast of Schleswig-Holstein, with a line of huge steel gates that stay open for the tide and slam shut when a storm surge threatens. It was built in the years after the great North Sea flood of 1962, finished in the early 1970s, and it shortened the dike line along the coast by a considerable margin while keeping the Eider's estuary alive for ships and wildlife.

You can ride across it, and you should stop at either end. The road runs along the structure with wide water on both sides, wind shoving you gently around, and gulls hanging in the gale like kites. On the seaward side the Wadden Sea opens out, a landscape that changes by the hour: at low tide it is mud, sandbars and seals, at high tide it is grey water to the horizon. The whole area belongs to the Wadden Sea national park and is a UNESCO site, which explains the birdwatchers with long lenses you will see on the dike.

The riding in this region is very particular. Roads are flat, straight and exposed, with long views of dike lines, sheep and wind turbines turning in the same direction. Crosswinds are the one real hazard, and a gust on the barrage or an open stretch of road can nudge a light bike sideways. The weather is changeable, and rain can come in horizontally, so a waterproof layer should live in the pannier. Summer evenings, when the light goes long and yellow and the tourists have gone, are the best.

Practicalities are simple. The nearest proper town is Tönning, a few kilometres off, with fuel, a harbour with a pretty old timber crane, and plenty of fish sandwiches. Garding and Wesselburen are smaller but have supermarkets and cafés. Out on the barrage there is not much beyond a car park and a tiny visitor building, so bring a drink and layers, and take your time. A cold wind straight off the North Sea is part of the deal.
t.busum harbour@54.1,8.9:
Büsum is where Dithmarschen meets the North Sea, a small resort and fishing port that spent a few centuries as an island before the sea gave up and the land joined it to the mainland in the sixteenth century. These days it is a cheerful and slightly salty place, full of day-trippers and holidaymakers, with a harbour that still has a working fleet of shrimp cutters. The little grey shrimp, known locally as Krabben, are the thing to eat here: sold from stalls on the quay in paper cones or stuffed into a bread roll, with the smell of diesel and seaweed thrown in free.

The harbour is the heart of it. Red and blue cutters lie against the quay, nets hang drying, and the gulls watch everything with professional interest. When the tide goes out the area around the harbour shows its true nature as a stretch of Wadden Sea mud, and a walk to the dike will show you the long, flat coastline that never quite decides whether it is land or water. Seals and many wading birds use these flats, and on the right day you may see a seal trip from the harbour heading out.

Getting here is half the point. The roads from Heide and Meldorf run dead straight across the flat farmland, between ditches and dikes, with wind turbines for company. It is easy riding, but on a bad day with a strong westerly it is also tiring riding, with the front wheel nudged constantly. Summer weekends bring queues and crowded parking, so plan for midweek or an early start. The cobbled bits and sandy edges near the harbour need a little care.

For services the town is small, with fewer than five thousand residents, but it has what a visitor needs: places to eat, shops and parking. If you need a proper fuel station, remember the nearest bigger town is Meldorf, fourteen kilometres away, and it is wise to tank up there before the coastal detour. A late afternoon here, with the tide coming in and a hot fish roll in your hand, is a good way to end a day of dike riding.
t.schleswig old town@54.5,9.6:
Schleswig lies at the head of the Schlei, a long, narrow inlet of the Baltic that reaches inland like a fjord and gives the town the feel of a harbour that forgot the sea. The old part is a gentle, slightly sprawling affair: a cathedral with a tall brick spire visible from the water, a baroque castle called Gottorf on an island across the way, and, down by the water, a remarkable fishermen's settlement called Holm, a little village of small houses grouped around a churchyard and a tiny chapel.

Of everything here, Holm is the one to walk. The houses are low and tidy, painted in gentle colours, with cats on the doorsteps and nets still stored in sheds. It has been fishermen's territory for centuries, and you can feel that the place had a rhythm of its own long before cars. The cathedral, with its altar carved by Hans Brüggemann in the sixteenth century, is a short walk off and worth a look if it is open.

The region has deeper layers. A few kilometres away lie the remains of Haithabu, or Hedeby, a Viking trading town that was one of the biggest in northern Europe a thousand years ago and now has a museum and reconstructed houses. It is on the UNESCO list, and visiting it explains why the Schlei has been a crossing place for so long. Schleswig was long a border town between Danes and Germans, and the history of that tug of war runs through the region's language and culture, including a place for Danish minority schools.

For riders, the town is a good stopping point. It has about twenty-four thousand people, so fuel, supermarkets and food are no problem, and the waterfront has places to sit with a coffee and a fish roll. The approach roads in from Kiel, Eckernförde or Flensburg are quiet agricultural lanes, flat to gently rolling, lined with hedgerows known as Knicks. Cobbles in the old town are rough and the streets narrow, so park on the outskirts. Morning is calm and the water is flat, and that is the best time to see it.
t.porta westfalica view road@52.2,8.9:
Here the Weser river does something that rivers in the north German plain rarely do: it cuts through a hill range. The Wiehengebirge arrives from the west and the Wesergebirge from the east, and between them the river has carved a gap about a kilometre wide, the Porta Westfalica, the Westphalian Gate. Behind it the land opens out into the great flat plain toward Hanover and the sea. For centuries this was a natural doorway, and the people who held it controlled the route.

Two hills mark the gate. On the western one stands a huge monument to Kaiser Wilhelm the First, built in the 1890s in a heavy classical style with the emperor on a pedestal under a canopy, looking over the valley with a fairly confident air. Nobody has ever called it subtle. According to local legend, the hill was also a place where the Saxon leader Widukind once held out against Charlemagne, which is why the whole area has a faintly mythic reputation among Germans. You do not have to care about any of that to enjoy the view, which on a clear day stretches across the river, the towns of Minden and Porta Westfalica, and the plain spreading out beyond.

The riding along the ridge roads is pleasant rather than dramatic. The roads climb in a series of curves through beech woods, then come out at points with long views. Surfaces are generally good, and there are some tight bends where the hill slopes steeply. Expect cyclists and weekend walkers in fine weather, and take care on damp days when leaves lie on the road. Early morning in autumn, with mist in the valley, gives the best light for photographs.

Services are simple here. Porta Westfalica itself has more than thirty-six thousand inhabitants, so fuel, supermarkets and cafés are at hand within a couple of kilometres, and Minden, about five kilometres off, has a handsome old centre with a long history as a river town. Bad Oeynhausen is a spa town a little further. Park the bike at the base, and walk up if you want the full view.
t.springe@52.2,9.6:
Springe is the small, practical town at the foot of the Deister, the long wooded ridge that rises southwest of Hanover and gives the city its nearest bit of real hill country. It is not a place most people plan a day around, and that is fine. It is where the plain ends and the hills begin, and the first sign of that is a sudden change in the road, from straight and flat to curving and shaded.

The town does have one thing of real interest, the Saupark. It is a huge enclosed hunting forest on the edge of town, created in the seventeenth century by the dukes of Hanover and known as one of the oldest of its type in Germany. Wild boar, red deer and even bison have lived there, and part of it is now a wildlife park you can walk through. There is something quietly impressive in the idea that rulers once ordered a whole forest to be fenced so that they could chase animals inside it in comfort.

As a fuel stop, Springe is useful and uncomplicated. It has almost thirty thousand people, a number of petrol stations along the main roads, supermarkets and a modest old centre with a few half-timbered houses and bakeries. If you are coming from Hanover, this is the last easy place for fuel before the hills, and the road south from here toward Bad Münder and the Süntel region is where the riding begins to get better. Riders heading for the Weser valley use it the same way.

A few small practical things. Traffic can be heavy at commuting times because Springe is within easy reach of Hanover, so aim to be through before eight in the morning or after nine. Weekends in good weather bring walkers to the Deister car parks, and cyclists on the quieter lanes. Take a minute to look at the ridge when you leave: its wooded line runs straight along the horizon and tells you where the land has been squeezed upward by something older and bigger than anything the dukes ever built.
t.bad munder ridge road@52.2,9.5:
Between the Deister and the Weser lies a small cluster of low, forested ridges, and the road above Bad Münder runs along the edge of one of them. The land here is part of the Weser Uplands, a modest country of beech woods, limestone outcrops and small spa towns, and the name Süntel belongs to the ridge just beyond. It is not high, but it is steep enough on its flanks to make for lively riding.

Bad Münder itself is a spa town with salt springs, which is a reminder that this whole belt of land sits on old salt deposits. The brine bubbled up for centuries and was used for salt boiling and later for treatments, and the town carries its bath title with a certain faded dignity. The streets have a small, quiet market square and a scattering of timbered houses, with a rather lovely old church. It is a decent place to stop for coffee, and it has a few fuel stations.

The history of the neighbouring ridge is darker. In the year 782, during Charlemagne's long campaign to subdue the Saxons, a Frankish force was ambushed and destroyed on the slopes of the Süntel, and the king's reaction at Verden shortly afterwards, where thousands of Saxons were reportedly killed, is among the more infamous moments of the period. It is a faraway story, but it changes how a quiet beech wood feels when you ride through it.

On the bike, the ridge road is the kind of thing you remember in the evening. It climbs from town in a loose series of bends, through forest with dappled light, then runs along the top with glimpses of the valley on one side and the next ridge on the other. Surfaces are variable, generally good but patched, and there are tight, blind corners where fallen leaves and damp make a difference. Traffic is light apart from sunny weekends. In autumn the forest turns a coppery colour that makes the whole climb worth it, and in summer it is the cooler option. Hameln, with its Pied Piper, lies ten minutes to the west.
t.hameln old town river@52.1,9.4:
Everyone knows the story, and in Hameln you cannot get away from it. In 1284, according to the legend, a stranger in a coloured coat came to town to rid it of rats with his pipe, was cheated of his fee, and led the children away instead. The tale is probably built on some real event, maybe an emigration or a catastrophe, but nobody knows which. The town has embraced it with enthusiasm: rats in the shop windows, rat-shaped bread, a summer play staged in the street and a mechanical glockenspiel show at the Hochzeitshaus that draws a crowd every day.

Beyond the legend, Hameln is a handsome river town with some of the best Weser Renaissance architecture in Germany, a style from around 1600 marked by elaborate gables, carved bay windows and rich ornament. The Rattenfängerhaus, the house of the Rat-catcher, has a famous facade. Streets around the centre are pedestrianised, and a stroll takes you from the market to the Weser embankment, where the river flows broad and calm and excursion boats tie up in summer.

For a stop, this is simple. The river is the point: sit on the bank or on a terrace with a drink and watch barges and rowing boats. Locals sometimes call this part of the Weser a riviera when the sun is out, with some irony, but on a warm day people do lie on the grass. I would not recommend swimming in the main channel, which has traffic and a current, so treat the water view as just that.

With nearly sixty thousand people, Hameln has every service: fuel, supermarkets, restaurants and cafés in profusion. Parking a motorcycle near the centre is possible, though the cobbles in the old streets are uneven and slippery after rain, and in summer the tour groups can make the lanes feel tight. Arriving from the hills, the road drops into the valley and the town appears quite suddenly, with the spire of the Marktkirche above the roofs. Go early or late for peace, and eat something that does not look like a rat.
t.rinteln weser overlook@52.2,9.1:
Rinteln is a Weser town that sits in a narrow bend of the river, with the ridge of the Weser Hills on one side and low farmland on the other. The overlook is up on that ridge, where the road leaves the town and climbs through trees to a spot with a good view of the valley. From it you can see the river wind through the meadows, the town's church spires and red roofs in the bend, and the next line of hills in blue haze behind.

The town below has an old and slightly surprising history. For nearly two centuries, from the early seventeenth century until the early nineteenth, Rinteln had its own university, a rare thing for a place so small. It was founded by a local count and closed under Napoleon's reorganisation of the region. The market square still has fine half-timbered houses from the Weser Renaissance period, and a big Gothic church, and the streets around have an unspoilt, compact feel that comes from having been mostly bypassed by industry.

The riding up here is easy and engaging, rather than testing. The road climbs through beech wood in a handful of bends, and the surface is mostly smooth. In the valley, the road runs along the river through villages with their farms and orchards. Cyclists use the Weser cycle path heavily, so expect them on summer weekends, and give them room. Morning light on the water is lovely, and evening gives the valley a golden glow that photographs well from the overlook. In late autumn mist collects in the river bend and the ridge stands above it like an island.

For services, Rinteln is the obvious answer, with about twenty-eight thousand people, fuel stations, supermarkets and a good range of cafés and restaurants in the centre. The overlook itself has little more than a parking area and perhaps a bench, so bring your own water if the day is hot. A short walk in the beech wood will do you good before you head back down to the river road and onward. The Weser Hills are a landscape that does not shout, and rewards riders who slow down.
t.porta westfalica ridge@52.2,8.9:
The ridge above the Porta Westfalica is where the Wiehengebirge, a long thin line of hills running east to west, comes to an abrupt end at the Weser river. Seen on a map, the range looks like a ruled line suddenly cut by a knife. In fact it is a belt of Jurassic limestone and sandstone, tilted and eroded over millions of years, and the river found its way through at the weakest point. That geology is the reason the road along the crest is so quietly satisfying: it follows a sharp edge, with steep wooded slopes falling away to the north and gentler land to the south.

The ridge also carries a heavier history. Late in the Second World War, the hills near Hausberge and Barkhausen were used to build underground production halls in old mine workings, using forced labour from a satellite camp of the Neuengamme concentration camp. The tunnels are still there, and a small memorial in the area records what happened. It is an uncomfortable fact to find in such a calm woodland, and it deserves a minute of quiet before you ride on.

Today the road is a pleasant, winding country route. It rises through beech and oak in a series of gentle bends, passes a television tower and a couple of old inns, and comes out at clearings with views across the plain toward Minden, whose cathedral and flat roofs lie to the north. The Mittelland Canal, one of Germany's great waterways, crosses the Weser near Minden in an aqueduct, a surprisingly good thing to watch from above if a barge is passing. The surface is mostly smooth, although tree roots lift the verge in places, and some corners are blind. On warm weekends there are plenty of walkers and cyclists, so the best time is a weekday morning.

Services are down in the valley rather than on the ridge. Porta Westfalica has fuel stations and supermarkets, and nearby Minden has a bigger choice, with a handsome old river town centre and a long record as a Prussian fortress and Weser port. Bad Oeynhausen, about nine kilometres away, is a spa town with a large park. Fill up before climbing, and bring water.
t.rinteln coffee road@52.2,9.1:
Some stops exist to fill the gap between one good road and the next, and the coffee road in Rinteln is one of those. It runs along the edge of the town where the Weser valley is flat and the lanes are lined with orchards, plain houses and the occasional old half-timbered farm. Nothing here is dramatic, which is exactly the point. After the bends of the hills, it is a pleasant way to slow the pulse.

Rinteln is a good place to find coffee, because it is a town people actually live in rather than a tourist set. The market square has half a dozen bakeries and cafés with tables outside in fair weather, and the Saturday market brings farmers from the surrounding Schaumburg area with vegetables, eggs and sausage. The regional taste leans to the plain and hearty: rye bread, ham, and in autumn plum cake, which Germans take seriously, sold in huge trays by the slice. The pastries are very good, and the prices are low compared with a big city.

The riding in and out is simple. The roads from the hills drop gently into the valley, and a few kilometres of straight, quiet road run along the river. Sheep and horses graze on the meadows by the water, and in spring the verges are full of dandelions and cow parsley. Expect cyclists on the river path and farm vehicles at harvest time. The surface is generally fine, with a few patches near the old bridges.

You will not struggle for services. Rinteln has fuel, supermarkets and restaurants, and the market square is within a short walk of any parking place. Look up at the buildings around the square, where carved beams show the old trading wealth of the town. The Nikolaikirche, a large Gothic church, stands close by and is worth a brief visit if it is open. Take your time with the coffee and enjoy the pause, because the next stretch of road into the Weser Hills is a great deal more serious.
t.einbeck@51.8,9.9:
If you drink bock beer, you owe Einbeck a toast. In the Middle Ages this small Hanseatic town became rich on exporting its strong, dark beer, which was carried by wagon all the way to Munich, where brewers later copied it. In the Bavarian accent the name Einbeck turned into Oanbock and then simply Bock, which is how a town in Lower Saxony ended up giving its name to one of the great beer styles. The town still brews, and the smell of malt sometimes drifts through the streets.

The old centre is one of the best preserved half-timbered towns in the north. A great fire in the sixteenth century destroyed most of the earlier buildings, and the rebuilt streets show off carved beams, painted panels and the sort of sturdy gables that only a rich burgher class could pay for. The market square is lined with fine houses, with a tall church tower above, and you can spend a pleasant hour just walking around and reading the inscriptions on the old timbers.

For a rider, Einbeck is a practical gate between the Leine valley and the hills of the Solling and Harz edge. It has almost twenty-eight thousand people, with fuel stations on the ring roads, supermarkets and no shortage of places to eat. Parking a bike near the centre is easy, but the old streets have cobbles that are slick when wet, so walk the last bit. If you want to eat something local, look for dishes with beer in the sauce, or sausage and potatoes with a glass of the local brew, within sensible limits for a person who still has to ride.

The roads around Einbeck are mostly quiet and agricultural, running over low hills with long views of fields and woods, then climbing gently into forest toward Dassel and the Solling. Traffic is light apart from commuters near the town. Weather comes from the west and can change quickly, so it is worth watching the sky. Late summer, when the grain is gold and the light low, makes this country look its best.
t.dassel forest road@51.8,9.7:
Dassel is a small town on the western edge of the Solling, the broad wooded upland that fills the space between the Leine and the Weser. Its name is not much known outside the region, but one of its sons altered the map of Christian Europe. Rainald von Dassel, born into a local noble family, became archbishop of Cologne in the twelfth century and, in 1164, brought the relics of the Three Kings from Milan to Cologne, which is why Cologne's enormous cathedral exists in the form it does. Pilgrims came in their thousands, and the money paid for the cathedral. A statue of Rainald stands in the town, and the town is proud of the link.

The forest road itself is the real attraction. It leaves Dassel and climbs into the Solling through spruce and beech, a country of long, smooth, rolling hills with few villages. The surface is generally good, and the bends are wide and gentle, so you can ride at an even rhythm and look at the trees. In the morning the mist often sits in the low parts of the forest, and the sun comes through the trunks in slanting columns. It is a quiet, almost meditative bit of riding, with deer sometimes standing at the edge of the road at dawn or dusk.

Be a little careful in autumn, when leaves and wet needles make the surface slick on shaded corners, and in winter, when the higher stretches can hold ice well after the valley has thawed. Forestry trucks use some of these roads, particularly where timber is being removed after storms and beetle damage, and they leave mud on the tarmac.

Dassel has just over eleven thousand people in its municipal area, enough for a petrol station, supermarkets and a few bakeries and cafés, though not much more, so Einbeck, to the east, is the more sensible place for a full meal and fuel. Fill the tank before you commit to the Solling roads, because the forest has few services and villages are small. A bottle of water and a light jacket are the only extras you need.
t.uslar solling@51.7,9.6:
Uslar is where the Solling begins to feel like real country. The town sits at the western foot of that big, rounded upland, on the little Ahle stream not far from the Weser, and it has the unhurried look of a place that serves the farms and forests around it. The old centre has a handful of timbered houses, a church and a modest square, and that is about the extent of its showing off. Behind it, the forest rises in dark folds.

The Solling is an old, worn-down plateau of red sandstone, which gives the soil a rusty colour in ploughed fields and quarry cuts, and the sandstone has been quarried for centuries. Weser Renaissance buildings along the river use it for window frames and steps, and you will notice the warm red tone in villages as you ride through. The plateau is mostly beech and spruce, with wide clearings, and it forms part of a nature park that takes in both the Solling and the Vogler. Moorland and small streams run in the high part, and this is a place where black storks are said to nest and where red deer make their autumn noise.

The road up from Uslar is a proper climb by northern German standards, though not anything an Alpine rider would notice. It winds through woods in long, easy bends, with a steady gradient and good visibility, and the sun flickers through the branches. The surface is mostly sound. Because the plateau is high enough to catch weather, mist can drop in quickly and the temperature falls, so a spare layer is sensible even in late spring. In autumn the beeches go gold and copper, and the whole slope seems lit from within.

Uslar has about sixteen thousand people in its municipality, so fuel stations, supermarkets and a few bakeries and inns are available, and it is the sensible last place to stock up before the forest. Inside the Solling the villages are small and the services thin. Bodenfelde, down in the Weser valley, is the other nearby option. If you want to eat, local game dishes and sausage appear on inn menus in autumn, and the portions are generous enough to need a rest afterward.
t.bodenfelde river@51.6,9.6:
Bodenfelde is a small town on the Weser at the southern tip of Lower Saxony, where the river is still young, having been born a little way south at Hann. Münden from the meeting of the Werra and the Fulda. From here it flows north through the Weser Uplands, between the Solling on the west bank and the wooded slopes on the east, and the valley is one of the quieter and prettier river landscapes in the region.

The river is the reason to stop. A path along the bank gives you a view of the water, which is broad, olive-green and slow, and on a warm day you may see canoes drifting past and families sitting on the grass. Swimming in the Weser is something locals do in places where the current is gentle and the bank is easy, but it is a working river and has barges and unpredictable currents, so ask before you do it, and do not leave your boots on the bank unattended. Most riders will be content with a sit and a look.

The riding along the valley is easy and soothing. The road follows the river, passes through farm villages with big timbered houses and orchards, and rises now and then over a low spur on gentle bends. Surfaces are good, the traffic is thin outside weekends, and there is rarely a reason to hurry. A short way upstream lies Bad Karlshafen, a tiny planned town laid out in the early eighteenth century for Huguenot refugees, with white baroque houses around a harbour basin. It is an unlikely thing to find on the edge of Hesse, and worth a detour of a few kilometres.

Services in Bodenfelde itself are modest, a bakery or two, a shop and perhaps an inn, so do not count on a long list. The nearest larger town is Uslar, about six kilometres away, and it has a proper fuel station and supermarkets. Take water and a snack, and use the river stop as a pause, not a destination. Early morning, with mist lifting off the Weser and the sound of birds, is the time that suits it best.
t.westensee shore@54.3,9.9:
The Westensee lies a short way west of Kiel, a long, branched lake set in rolling country of fields, woods and low glacial hills. It is the biggest lake in the area, and around it lies a nature park that is roughly shaped like a lung between the city, the Kiel Canal and the Eider lowlands. The shore is a mixture of reed beds, small beaches, boat jetties and wooded banks, and the sense of calm after the city traffic comes quickly.

The area is dotted with country houses, the old manor estates that shaped the land of Schleswig-Holstein for centuries. Emkendorf, nearby, was a famous centre of cultural life in the late eighteenth century, when the owners welcomed poets, philosophers and politicians to a kind of salon in the country, and the place became a meeting point for the German Enlightenment and early Romanticism. The estate buildings and park still stand. It is a fitting backdrop for a lake whose shores are mostly peaceful and unbuilt.

For a ride this is a gentle beginning rather than a thrilling one. The lanes around the lake are narrow, with hedges called Knicks, low earth banks planted with hazel and hawthorn that divide the fields and that are a signature of Schleswig-Holstein. They give a feeling of riding in a green corridor, and they hold hedgehogs, hares and songbirds. The surfaces are mostly good, but farm traffic leaves mud at harvest and manure in spring, and the occasional tractor will take over the whole road. Expect cyclists on sunny afternoons, and watch out for walkers at the lake accesses.

Practically, the lake is a rural area with village shops and a few cafés, but not much in the way of fuel. Kiel, to the east, has everything, and Rendsburg to the north has plenty. Flintbek, on the rim of the nature park, is the nearest sizeable town. Fill up before leaving the city, take water, and enjoy the quiet. Early on a still morning, when mist hangs on the lake and the first cyclists are just setting off, it is easy to forget that a big port city is fifteen minutes away.
t.bredenbek forest road@54.3,9.9:
Between Kiel and Rendsburg the land has a gentle rumple, and the woods near Bredenbek are among its better parts. The forest is mixed, beech and oak with patches of spruce, and it sits in the middle of an agricultural area where large fields are divided by Knicks and farm tracks. Here the roads are narrow, quiet and well shaded, a world away from the roar of the nearby motorway.

What shapes the area more than anything is the Kiel Canal, the busiest artificial waterway in the world by ship traffic, a few kilometres to the north. Dug in the 1890s to give the German navy a quick route between the Baltic and the North Sea, it cuts straight through the base of the peninsula, and the sight of a huge container ship gliding past between fields is one of the oddest in Germany. The canal is crossed by a string of ferries, which are free to use and run all day, and taking one is a small pleasure in itself. If one comes, park, enjoy the scenery and let the ship go by first.

The forest road is more subtle than the canal. It runs in curves over gentle slopes through the trees, with a lot of light flicker and some stretches where roots have lifted the tarmac. In summer the shade is welcome, and in autumn the leaves come down thick on the corners, so watch for slippery patches. Hares and deer cross the road at dawn and dusk, and buzzards sit on fence posts. The surface is generally good, with the odd muddy patch near field entrances.

Bredenbek is a tiny village and does not offer much in the way of shops, though a farm stall or small café may be open in the season. For fuel and food, Osterrönfeld, on the canal about eleven kilometres away, is the closest sizeable place, and Rendsburg, a little beyond, has a full range. Bring water and a snack, and keep a little extra time in the schedule for the canal ferries and the occasional tractor. It is an easy, friendly stretch of riding, best on a bright, cool morning.
t.geltinger birk coast edge@54.8,9.9:
The Geltinger Birk is the north-eastern tip of Angeln, a low, windy peninsula that pushes out into the Baltic where the Flensburg Fjord opens to the sea. It is one of the largest nature reserves on the Baltic coast of Schleswig-Holstein, a landscape of dunes, salt meadows, lagoons and old alder woodland, with large areas given over to semi-wild grazing. Hardy cattle and small horses roam the meadows, and their grazing keeps the land open and rich in flowers and insects. On a clear day, you can see across the water to the Danish island of Als.

The Birk is a bird place first. In spring and autumn huge flocks of migrating geese, ducks and waders pass through, resting in the shallow waters, and in winter the area holds many species that come from the far north. Birdwatchers set up scopes along the paths, and a quiet visitor can see white-tailed eagles, cranes and a wide variety of ducks. The sound of the wind in the reeds and the cry of gulls is constant. The air smells of salt, seaweed and cut grass.

The reserve itself is for walkers, so you leave the bike at the edge and go in on foot. Paths lead through the grazing land to the beach and the dune, and it is a flat, easy walk of an hour or two. Do bring a windproof jacket, as the wind blows hard from the sea, even in summer. The roads to the area are quiet and flat, with open views over fields and sky, and large windmills turn slowly in the distance. Farm vehicles are the main hazard, and gusts can push a light bike sideways.

There is little in the way of services at the coast edge. The villages of Gelting and Steinberg have small shops and a few places to eat, but for a full range of services the nearest larger town is Kappeln, on the Schlei, about twelve kilometres away, with fuel stations, supermarkets and a pretty harbour with a lifting bridge. Plan fuel before you head out to the coast, and take some water. Late afternoon, when the low sun brings out the colour in the meadows, is a lovely time to be here.
t.sankt peter ording beach air@54.3,8.6:
Sankt Peter-Ording has one of the widest beaches in Europe, a vast plain of pale sand that stretches for some twelve kilometres along the western edge of the Eiderstedt peninsula and runs out so far at low tide that the sea is a thin line on the horizon. On the dunes stand the famous stilt houses, wooden restaurants and beach huts on tall legs, built that way because the North Sea sometimes comes right up to the dune foot at high water and storm tides. They look like something from a child's drawing, and they are a charming place for a coffee.

The air is the real attraction. The wind off the North Sea carries a salty, iodine-rich tang, and the town has been a sea-air spa for well over a century, with a tradition of treatments for chest complaints and allergies. Even if you are not looking for a cure, a long walk on the sand with the wind in your face clears the head after a day of riding. Kite-surfers, sand-yachters and horse riders share the beach, and in strong wind the sky is full of bright wings.

The way there is a flat, straight ride over the Eiderstedt marshland, which is a landscape of sheep, dikes and old farmhouses built on mounds, with big skies and long views. The wind is the main factor, and a crosswind on the exposed road can be tiring. Summer weekends bring heavy traffic, and the road into the resort can crawl, so go early or on a weekday. Be aware that access to the beach and the car parks usually carries a visitor fee, and that driving on the sand itself is allowed only in certain designated areas, not for motorbikes in general, so check the signs.

Water here is the Wadden Sea, a tidal zone with shifting sandbanks and strong currents, so swimming should be done in the supervised areas, and you should keep an eye on the tide. The nearest sizeable town is Tönning, some twenty kilometres away, but Sankt Peter-Ording itself has shops, restaurants and fuel in the village, and Garding is a small town on the way. A hot fish soup and a bench in the lee of a dune make a fine end to an exposed ride.
t.eider barrage photo@54.3,8.8:
For photographers, the Eider barrage is a study in lines. The great steel gates, the concrete piers and the long road across the structure make strong geometric shapes against a sky that is usually enormous, and the water on both sides changes colour with the weather and tide. It is a very graphic subject, and it rewards a bit of planning. Morning and evening light bring out the texture of the metal, and a low sun from the west turns the water silver and the sky pink.

The side of the structure to work from depends on what you want. From the seaward side you look across the mudflats and sandbars of the estuary toward the horizon, and at low tide there are shining patterns in the mud, with seals sometimes hauled out on the banks and wading birds probing the edge of the water. From the landward side you see the calm basin, the gates and the line of the dike, with sheep grazing on the green slopes. At high tide the whole place looks very different, with the water lapping near the top of the banks and the gulls riding the wind.

Wind is your main opponent here. A steady westerly makes the use of a tripod difficult, and the sand and spray can get into equipment, so keep a cloth handy and stay away from the edge in a strong blow. The weather moves fast, and a dramatic cloud bank can arrive from the west in the middle of a sunny afternoon. If you are lucky you will get a rainbow over the water. Overcast days, which are common, give a dull light, so bring patience for waiting.

The area is part of the Wadden Sea national park, and you should keep to the paths and avoid disturbing the birds, especially in the breeding season in spring and early summer. Parking near the barrage is limited, so be careful not to block the access road. There are no facilities at the site itself beyond a small car park, and the nearest services are in Tönning, about nine kilometres away, with fuel stations, supermarkets and cafés. Garding and Wesselburen have smaller shops. Dress warmly, even in summer, because the wind makes the temperature feel several degrees lower than the thermometer says.
t.eckernforde@54.5,9.8:
Eckernförde sits on a bay that curves into the Baltic like a cupped hand, and its old harbour is where a day in the northern lowlands comes to rest. The town is known above all for smoked fish, and in particular for the Kieler Sprotten, small, golden-brown sprats that are named after Kiel but are traditionally made here, in smokehouses along the water. They are eaten whole, by hand, with a bit of bread, and they taste of oak smoke and salt. If you eat one thing in Eckernförde, make it that. A fish roll with fried herring or plaice is the safer alternative, and plenty of harbour kiosks sell them.

The town has also had a short, unlikely moment of military glory. In April 1849, during the first war between Denmark and the German states over Schleswig-Holstein, the Danish warship Christian the Eighth and a frigate entered the bay and were shelled from shore batteries until the larger ship caught fire and blew up. It remains one of the few successful artillery duels between land and sea in that era, and the town marks it with a monument. Today a naval base occupies part of the shoreline, and grey warships and submarines come and go.

The old town is a compact one, with narrow lanes, half-timbered houses and a Gothic church, and a promenade that runs along the water to a long pier and a beach. In summer the beach fills with families, and the water is shallow and warm, but even in cooler weather the walk along the front is pleasant. The old pier and the sailing boats are a favourite subject for painters and photographers, and the sea light here is clear and bright.

The ride in from Kiel or Schleswig is mostly on quiet country roads across the Schwansen and Dänischer Wohld peninsulas, a gently rolling farmland of Knicks, brick villages and wide views. Surfaces are generally good, and the corners are open. For services the town has about twenty-three thousand people, so fuel stations, supermarkets and bakeries are all easy to find, and there is no shortage of places to sit down and eat. Parking is easiest at the edge of the old town, with a short walk to the harbour. A lunch of sprats, a pot of coffee and a bench by the water is hard to beat.
t.schwansen backroads@54.6,9.9:
Schwansen is a blunt thumb of land between the Schlei and the Bay of Eckernförde, and it is one of the most underrated corners of Schleswig-Holstein. The countryside is gently rolling farmland, divided into fields by Knicks, those hedge-topped earth banks that give the Baltic coast its distinctive patchwork, and dotted with old estates, thatched barns and brick villages. The sea is always near, on one side or the other, and glimpses of water through gaps in the hedge give the roads a pleasing sense of mystery.

The area has a distinctly Danish feel, which is no accident. This was border country for centuries, and for much of the Middle Ages it belonged to the Danish crown, with Danish place names and Danish habits that lingered long after the political border moved. The languages of the area were Low German, Danish and Frisian, and you still see double-language signs in places farther north. The villages of Schwansen have names like Rieseby and Waabs, and the big landowners built manor houses with long drives and avenue trees, some of which are still in private hands.

The backroads are the best way to see it. They run in gentle undulations, over small bridges and through patches of beech wood, with low stone walls, lines of poplar and old oaks, and every few kilometres a church tower. The surface is generally good, though some roads are narrow and patched, and farm vehicles take up the whole width at harvest. On a clear day the road sometimes opens to a view of the Baltic with sails on the water. Wind is a factor, and the weather changes quickly, so be ready for a sudden shower.

Services are modest. Damp, on the coast, is a holiday resort that grew up in the 1970s and has shops, cafés and a long beach, and villages like Waabs and Rieseby have a shop or a bakery. For fuel and a bigger choice, Kappeln, on the Schlei, about nine kilometres away, is the nearest town with fuel stations and supermarkets, and Eckernförde to the south has more. Plan the tank accordingly. Spring, when the rape fields are bright yellow, and early autumn, with stubble gold and the sky enormous, are the best times for this quiet, reflective ride.
t.schleswig@54.5,9.6:
Schleswig is a town you eat in with history around your ears. The quickest way to understand it is to walk to the harbour on the Schlei, where fish smokehouses and small restaurants sit beside a basin of yachts and the old cathedral spire rises over the roofs behind. Smoked herring, Schlei eel and fried plaice are all on offer, with potatoes and a pot of tea or coffee, and a table by the water on a warm day is hard to beat. Prices are fair, portions generous, and nobody hurries you.

A few kilometres south lies the Danewerk, the great line of earthen ramparts that the Danes built across the narrow neck of the Jutland peninsula, beginning as early as the fifth century and extended over the next six hundred years. It was a defensive wall against the Germans and Franks, and its remains, grassy banks several metres high, can still be walked. At one end stood the Viking trading town of Haithabu, which lay on the Schlei and was among the largest settlements in northern Europe about a thousand years ago. Both are listed as a World Heritage site, and the museum at Haithabu has reconstructed longhouses and a remarkable collection of finds.

In the town itself, on an island in the Schlei, stands Gottorf Castle, a huge, pale baroque pile that was the seat of the dukes of Schleswig-Holstein-Gottorf. It now houses two state museums, one of art and one of archaeology, and the archaeology museum has one of the most extraordinary collections in Germany, including a large wooden ship from the fourth century found in a Danish bog, and the bodies of Iron Age people preserved in peat. It is a strange and sobering place to spend an hour.

The ride in and out is simple, with quiet farmland roads in every direction and a long, open approach along the Schlei from the east. Schleswig has about twenty-four thousand people, so fuel stations, supermarkets and bakeries are all easy, and parking near the harbour is straightforward, if the cobbles around the old town are rough. Weekends in summer fill the harbour with visitors, so arrive before noon. After a meal, you can go on along the Schlei toward Kappeln or turn west toward the North Sea coast.
t.daun@50.2,6.8:
Daun is the capital of the Vulkaneifel, and the name is accurate: this is a country of dead volcanoes, and the evidence is all around the town. Instead of cones, the Eifel has maars, round lakes that fill the craters left when rising magma met groundwater and blew itself apart. Three of them lie within a few kilometres of Daun, the Gemündener, Weinfelder and Schalkenmehrener Maar, deep and dark and ringed with woods, and the sight of such perfectly round water in the middle of ordinary hills is oddly moving. The Weinfelder Maar has a small chapel on its shore that makes a very good photograph.

The town sits on the little Lieser river at around four hundred metres, among hills topped with beech and spruce, and it is a place of practical size and pleasant character, with a mix of old and new buildings and a handful of castles and ruins nearby. A volcano museum explains the geology, and there are a good many walking routes through the maar landscape. Fuel stations, supermarkets and bakeries are all present, since Daun has nearly nine thousand people, and the main street has several places to eat. Local menus favour plain Eifel food, such as potato dishes, sausages and game in autumn.

The roads around Daun are the reason many riders come to the Eifel. They climb and fall through forest and open moor, with a mix of long, flowing bends and tighter curves where the road crosses a valley, and the surface is generally good, though the dampness of the region can leave moss and leaves in shaded sections. The Nürburgring is within an hour's ride, and the area draws large numbers of bikes on summer weekends, which means police checks and noise restrictions in some villages. Be considerate of residents, and respect the speed limits, which are enforced on many stretches.

Weather in the Eifel is changeable, with low cloud, fog and sudden rain a possibility in any month, and the air is cooler than in the Rhine valley. Pack a waterproof layer. Spring brings broom, with great sheets of yellow on the hillsides in May, and autumn brings colour and mist, with the maars steaming on cold mornings. A weekday ride in September or early October, when the crowds have thinned, is the best time to see this country.
t.manderscheid@50.1,6.8:
Manderscheid has two castles facing each other across a gorge, and the story of how they came to be there is a classic of medieval feuding. The Oberburg and the Niederburg stand on opposite ridges above the loops of the Lieser river, a hundred metres or so apart, and they were built by rival branches of the same family, who spent several centuries arguing about who owned what. Both are now ruins, atmospheric in the true sense, with broken towers and arches overlooking a deep wooded valley, and a short footpath leads between them. Of the two, the Niederburg is the more complete.

The Lieser is the real star of the landscape. It winds through the valley in a series of tight loops, almost closing back on itself, and the gorge it has cut is steep and thickly wooded, with outcrops of dark rock above the water. On a clear morning the river is the colour of tea, and the hillside is full of birdsong. In the town above, a small spa tradition survives, and the main street has several cafés and a Kneipp pool in the woods, a place where you wade through cold water to get the circulation going.

The road down into the valley and up the other side is one of the better short pieces of riding in the Eifel. Tight bends, blind corners and a fair gradient make for a lively few minutes, and the surface is generally good, though shaded sections hold damp and leaves collect in autumn. Traffic is light on weekdays, and heavy on summer weekends, when riders and walkers fill the lay-bys. Use the pull-offs to look at the castles, and keep your eyes on the road in between.

Manderscheid is a small town of around a thousand people, so services are limited to a couple of shops, a bakery and a few inns and cafés. For proper fuel stations and supermarkets, the nearest is Daun, about twelve kilometres away, and Wittlich, to the south, is larger still. Fill up before you come. A pot of coffee on a terrace with a view of the castle ruins is the right way to spend half an hour, and if you have time, take the footpath down to the river and back, which is a short but steep walk. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with fresh green or gold.
t.zeven country roads@53.3,9.3:
Zeven lies in the middle of the Geest, the sandy ridge of country that runs through the heart of Lower Saxony between the marshes of the coast and the lowlands of the south. The land is gently rolling, with pine woods, heath remnants, big farms and wet meadows in the valleys, and the villages are built around old churches and clusters of oaks. It is not a landscape that shouts, and it makes for easy riding, with long, quiet roads that curve between fields and woods and rarely see much traffic.

The town has an old and surprising history. A Benedictine convent was founded here around the end of the tenth century, and for several hundred years it was an important religious house, with a church that still stands in the town centre. After the Reformation it became a Protestant foundation, and the convent buildings remain a landmark, with a quiet, cloistered feel that contrasts with the busy market. The surrounding region was also the site of one of the more curious episodes of the Napoleonic wars, the Convention of Klosterzeven in 1757, in which the Hanoverian army surrendered to the French and which was repudiated within months. It shows how important this small town once was.

The roads in the countryside around Zeven are among the more relaxed in the region. They wind through villages with brick farmhouses, through patches of birch and pine, and across small streams, with gentle bends and a smooth surface for the most part. In summer the air smells of cut hay and resin, and in autumn the mist lies in the valley bottoms. Be wary of tractors and farm trailers, especially at harvest time, and of deer at dawn and dusk. Wind on the open stretches can be strong, but the woods give shelter.

Zeven has about twelve thousand people, so fuel stations, supermarkets and bakeries are in good supply, and the market square has several cafés and a Saturday market. Parking is simple. There are no great sights to hurry toward, and that is part of the charm: the point is the rhythm of the road, the long views across the fields, and the way the afternoon light turns the farms gold. A weekday in spring, when the hedges are in blossom and the fields are green, is a pleasure.
t.ottersberg wumme roads@53.1,9.1:
The Wümme is one of the quieter rivers of northern Germany, a dark, slow stream that winds through meadows and moorland east of Bremen, and the roads that follow it near Ottersberg are made of long, soft curves. The land is flat and wet, with reeds, alders and pollard willows along the banks, and on still mornings the mist hangs low over the water and the cattle stand in it to the knees. It is the sort of landscape painters came to find in the late nineteenth century, and many of them stayed.

The most famous colony was at Worpswede, a little way to the north, but a smaller and gentler one grew up at Fischerhude, a village within Ottersberg's municipality, where the Wümme splits into channels and the thatched farmhouses sit among tall trees. The painter Otto Modersohn lived and worked there, and the village is still full of artists' studios, galleries and craft shops, with an old water mill and a number of lovely half-timbered houses. A walk along the river there gives you exactly the view the painters saw: still water, reflected trees and a low sky.

The riding is easy and gentle. The roads are narrow and often straight, with occasional sharp corners where the road crosses a bridge or bends round a farm, and the surface is generally good, though patched in places. Traffic is light on weekdays, but fine weekends bring cyclists and tourists, particularly around Fischerhude, and parking there is limited. Keep an eye out for farm machinery and for deer on the verges. The weather comes off the North Sea, so a sudden shower is always possible, and the light after rain is superb.

Ottersberg has about twelve thousand people in its municipality, so fuel stations, supermarkets and bakeries are on hand, and there are a few cafés in the village centre. For a photograph, the best spots are along the river near Fischerhude and on the meadow roads, particularly in the early morning or late evening, when the low sun picks out the trees and the water. Bring a layer, since the damp air of the moors can chill you quickly. A stop at a café for coffee and a slice of apple cake completes the picture.
t.rotenburg return road@53.1,9.4:
Rotenburg on the Wümme is the town you eat in on the way home. It is a calm, prosperous place of about twenty-two thousand people, set on a stretch of the Wümme where the river is wide enough for rowing boats, with a market square, a handful of old half-timbered houses and a surprising number of good bakeries. It lacks the tourist crowds of the better-known towns, and that is exactly what makes it a good place to sit down with a plate and a pot of coffee.

The local food is solid and unpretentious. In winter the regional dish is kale with Pinkel, a smoked, spiced sausage, served with boiled potatoes and mustard, and often followed by a schnapps. It is eaten after the first frost, according to local tradition, and there are even kale tours with a good deal of drinking. In summer, you will find asparagus, strawberries and fresh fish on menus, and every baker sells cakes in great variety. The roll with a slice of ham or cheese and a coffee is cheap and filling.

The road home from Rotenburg runs across the flat plain toward Hamburg and Bremen, past peat moors, birch scrub and big sheds for poultry and pigs. The landscape is open and sometimes bleak in winter, with big skies and a few lines of poplars, but in spring and summer it is green and soft. The roads are straight and fast, so the wind is the main hazard, and a sudden crosswind from a passing lorry can be felt. Surfaces are mostly good. In late afternoon the sun goes low and golden behind you, and the shadows of the poplars stretch across the road.

Practical matters are easy. Fuel stations are on the edges of town, supermarkets are in the centre, and parking is simple near the market. If you have time, a short walk along the Wümme to the old mill is a quiet reward, and the park nearby has benches and ducks. The town is a convenient place to rest before the last stretch of the day, and the drive back is easier on a full stomach. Dress for evening, since the air cools quickly once the sun drops.
t.coppenbrugge ith road@52.1,9.5:
The Ith is the sort of ridge that makes a rider look twice at the map. It is a long, narrow limestone wall about twenty kilometres from end to end, rising steeply from the farmland to a crest of nearly four hundred and fifty metres, and it runs northwest to southeast like a great fold in the earth. The slopes are covered with old beech forest, and along the crest are cliffs and rock outcrops that attract climbers, with caves and potholes in the limestone below. The villages at its foot, Coppenbrügge among them, look up to it with a faint air of respect.

Coppenbrügge itself is a small town with an old history, once the seat of the counts of Spiegelberg, whose castle ruins stand on a hill above the centre. The family died out in the sixteenth century, and the lands passed to Brunswick, but the ruin and the market square speak of the time when this was a small capital in its own right. The surroundings are peaceful, and a few rock formations and caves in the woods have names and legends attached to them.

The road along the Ith is a pleasure for riders who like quiet. It climbs from the valley in a succession of curves through beech wood, with the light flickering through the trees, and then follows the crest or runs just below it with glimpses of the plain on one side. The tarmac is generally good, but some stretches are narrow, with tight corners and little warning, and leaf litter and moss collect in the shade. On weekends, walkers and cyclists use the road, particularly near the car parks that serve the rock climbing areas. It is quieter on weekdays, and the best time of year is early autumn, when the beech leaves turn.

The forests on the Ith hold wildlife, including deer, wild boar and, in the crags, peregrine falcons. The limestone supports a rich plant life, with orchids in the clearings in late spring. Services are in Coppenbrügge, which has about eight thousand people, with fuel stations, a supermarket and a few places to eat, and Springe lies a short way north with more. Fill up before the climb, and carry a drink. The ridge is a place for slowing down.
t.eschershausen hils road@51.9,9.6:
Eschershausen is a small town at the foot of the Hils, and its main claim to fame is a writer. Wilhelm Raabe, one of the great German novelists of the nineteenth century, was born here in 1831, and his books about small-town life, with their humour and melancholy, are still read, particularly the Chronicle of Sparrow Alley and The Hunger Pastor. A modest museum in the town honours him, and the place has a quiet pride in its son. You do not need to have read a word of his work to enjoy the town, but the connection adds some weight to the plain streets.

The Hils itself is a broad, forested ridge of Lower Saxony hill country, running between the Leine and the Weser, and the road over it from Eschershausen is a long, steady climb through beech and spruce forest. The highest point is just under five hundred metres, which is not alpine, but the ridge is exposed to the weather and the temperature on top is noticeably cooler than in the valley. The forest is dense and quiet, with few buildings, and you pass long stretches without a house in sight.

The road is a good one, with a smooth surface for the most part and long, flowing bends that suit a relaxed rhythm. At the top, the road flattens and runs along the ridge for a few kilometres, with glimpses through the trees of the countryside below. Traffic is light, apart from timber lorries and the odd cyclist. In autumn, leaves and wet needles lie on the corners and demand care, and in winter, ice can linger in the shaded sections long after the lowlands have thawed. Mist is common on the ridge, and visibility can drop quickly.

Services in the forest are nonexistent, so the best approach is to fill the tank and stock up beforehand. Stadtoldendorf, about five kilometres away, has about six thousand people, with fuel stations and supermarkets, and Holzminden, farther west on the Weser, is larger. The area is also full of small monuments to the past, including the ruined monastery at Amelungsborn, founded in the twelfth century, and fine old half-timbered villages. Early on a weekday in October, with mist in the valleys and colour in the trees, this is a quietly splendid road.
t.alfeld@52.0,9.8:
Alfeld has a secret that surprises many visitors: a factory building that changed the history of architecture. On the edge of the town stands the Fagus Works, a shoe-last factory designed by a young Walter Gropius in 1911, with great sheets of glass wrapped around the corners of the brick structure, so that the building seems to float. It was one of the first buildings to use a curtain wall of glass, and it is a forerunner of the Bauhaus style that Gropius would found in the 1919. The works still produce shoe lasts and are a World Heritage site, with a visitor centre and guided tours that explain how the place worked.

The town itself is a quiet, handsome one on the Leine river, with a marketplace framed by half-timbered houses and a remarkable town hall from the sixteenth century, with elaborate carved decoration and a stepped gable. The old streets are quiet, the squares have fountains and benches, and a number of the timber houses have long inscriptions along the beams. It was one of the first towns in the region to adopt the Reformation, and its churches carry that history.

As a food stop, Alfeld is easy. It has about nineteen thousand people, so fuel stations, supermarkets and bakeries are close at hand, and there are several cafés and restaurants around the market, with tables outside in good weather. Local fare is plain Lower Saxon, with sausage, potatoes, cabbage and cake. Parking a motorbike near the market is simple, though the cobbles are rough and slippery when wet. The roads leading into town are quiet and pleasant, running along the Leine valley between wooded hills, with long views over meadows and fields.

Riders passing through often use the town as a base for the surrounding hills, since the Sieben Berge, a ridge of wooded hills to the west, offer curving roads through beech forest, and the Hils rises to the south. The weather here is changeable, with sudden showers possible, and a waterproof layer is wise. If you are interested in architecture, allow at least an hour for the Fagus Works, since a rider rarely gets a chance to stand in front of a building that altered modern design. A coffee and a slice of plum cake in the market, after the tour, makes a gentle afternoon.
t.elze@52.1,9.7:
Elze is a modest town on the Leine, between Hannover and Hildesheim, and it exists in a rider's day for one good reason, which is that it has petrol stations. That is not meant as an insult. A small, level-headed Lower Saxon town of nearly ten thousand people, set in the broad river valley with farmland on one side and wooded hills on the other, Elze does what a fuel gate should do, quickly and without drama. Pumps sit along the main roads, a supermarket and a few bakeries are in the centre, and you can be on your way again in ten minutes.

The surroundings are more interesting than the town. The Leine valley here is a broad, flat trough of fertile land, bordered to the west by the long wooded ridge of the Sieben Berge, a line of hills that gives the area its horizon, and to the east by the low plateau around Hildesheim. In the fields you see sugar beet, wheat and rape, with the occasional church spire or farm cluster. The river itself is slow and tree-lined, and a footpath follows it for a long way. A short walk along the bank clears the head and gives a view of ducks and herons.

The roads that leave Elze toward the hills are a pleasant relief after the straight roads of the valley. They climb through beech woods in gentle bends, with the surface mostly smooth and the traffic light. In autumn the leaves lie thick on the corners, and in winter frost lingers in shaded sections. Weather comes from the west and can change fast, so keep a layer handy. The region is not famous for dramatic scenery, but it is a quietly attractive stretch of countryside, with small villages, old churches and half-timbered farms.

If you need more than fuel, Alfeld and Gronau, a few kilometres away, offer more choice, and Hildesheim, about twenty kilometres to the northeast, has a famous old centre and a cathedral with a thousand-year-old bronze door. But if all you want is a full tank and a coffee, Elze is the place. Do the checks on tyres and chain while the pump runs, and take the chance to stow the jacket liner. The morning light on the river is a decent consolation prize for such a practical stop.
t.finkenwerder ferry feel@53.5,9.9:
Some rides begin in a car park, and some begin on a boat. The ferry across the Elbe from the Landungsbrücken to Finkenwerder is one of the better openings to a day on the road, because for the price of a public transport ticket you get a half-hour cruise through the biggest port in Germany. The passenger ferries run out past the great cranes, the dry docks and the container terminals, with huge ships sliding by at what feels like arm's length, and the smell of diesel, salt and wet rope. If you are starting from the other side, the feeling is the same in reverse.

Finkenwerder itself is an odd place, a former fishing island in the Elbe, a half-rural enclave inside Hamburg, with a village of thatched houses and old fishermen's cottages beside a modern aircraft factory. The Airbus plant here assembles and paints a good number of the company's planes, and when a new aircraft is ready you can see it on the apron beside the river, a huge white shape among the apple trees. The contrast is an unlikely one, and it is part of the island's charm. The writer Gorch Fock, born here as Johann Kinau in 1880, wrote tales of the sea, and the German navy named its sail training ship after his pen name.

The island has a long tradition of fishing, and the Finkenwerder fishermen's old plaice, caught in the Elbe, is still a local dish. Orchards on the edge of the island belong to the Altes Land, the great fruit-growing region on the south bank of the river, and in spring the blossom comes right to the doorsteps. A short stretch of dike on the western side gives a long view down the river, with ships heading for the sea.

For riders, the start from here is gentle. The roads leave the island over a causeway and head south and west through orchards, along dikes, across flat farmland with sky on every side. The landscape is soft and flat, so the riding is easy and quiet, and in the early morning the light on the river is pearl. Fuel stations and shops are in the town, and the ferry is simple to use, though motorbikes need to check the vehicle ferry timetables. Wind off the river can be sharp, so a layer is wise.
t.jork orchard roads@53.5,9.7:
The roads of the Altes Land are organised by water, and in Jork you can see how. The little river Este runs through the village and out toward the Elbe, and parallel dike roads follow it on both banks, with farms strung along them like beads on a thread.
