The orchards lie behind the farms in long, narrow strips, and a network of drainage ditches runs between them, each one marked by a footbridge to a field. It is the ordered result of eight centuries of drainage by Dutch settlers, and the pattern has barely changed.

The main route through it all is known as the Obstmarschenweg, the Fruit Marsh Road, which runs for more than twenty kilometres along the dike and passes the finest of the old farmhouses. Their ornate gates, carved with sayings and dates, stand at the roadside like the entrances to small kingdoms. Riding the dike road is slow work, with a low speed limit, a rough surface in places and cyclists everywhere in good weather, but that is the point. You do not hurry through an orchard.

The seasons here are so distinct that you would almost think of different places. In late April and May the trees come into bloom, pink and white, and the air is thick with the scent of blossom and the hum of bees. In July the cherries ripen, and farm stalls sell them by the kilo. In September and October the apples are picked, and the roads are full of tractors and trailers heaped with fruit. In winter, when the trees are bare, the landscape is stark and flat, with frost on the ditches and mist over the dike.

Roadside stalls sell fruit, juice, jam and cider, and farm cafés serve apple cake and coffee on summer afternoons. Be prepared for honesty boxes, and carry coins. The Altes Land is a tourist destination in the blossom weeks, with coaches and cars crowding the dike, so go on a weekday and early, if you can. Jork has about twelve thousand people in its municipality, and fuel stations and supermarkets are on the edge of the village. Wedel and Hamburg are a short ride away. Bring a bag for fruit, since it is hard to resist.
t.stade old town food@53.6,9.5:
Stade's old town is built around a harbour, and the harbour is built around a tidal creek, the Schwinge, which loops into the centre and ends in a basin lined with merchants' houses. Brick gables, a wooden treadwheel crane on the quay and cobbles polished smooth by centuries of cartwheels make the Hansehafen look like something from a Dutch painting. In the Middle Ages Stade was one of the main ports on the Elbe, a rival of Hamburg, and its prosperity shows in the old buildings. The place went quiet when the river silted up, and the quiet saved it.

Another chapter shaped the town in the seventeenth century. After the Thirty Years' War, Stade came under Swedish rule, and for about seventy years it was the Swedish capital of the German territories, with a garrison and an administration. The Swedes left their mark in the street layout and in the Schwedenspeicher, a large brick warehouse by the harbour that now serves as a museum. It is a reminder that this quiet Lower Saxon town was once a piece of a northern empire.

As a food stop it is a very good one. The old town has a good range of cafés, bakeries and restaurants, many of them with tables on the quayside in summer, and the food leans toward fish, with plaice, herring and eel on offer along with simple dishes of potatoes and sausage. The Altes Land is next door, so apples and cakes are excellent, and apple cake with cream is the town's unofficial dessert. Prices are reasonable, service is relaxed and no one minds if you linger over a coffee.

With about forty-five thousand people, Stade has fuel stations on the outskirts and supermarkets in the town, and parking a bike near the old centre is usually easy, though the cobbles are rough and slippery when wet. The ride in from Jork or Hamburg is flat and easy, with orchards, dikes and the occasional view of the Elbe. A weekday visit means quieter streets. If you have an hour, walk around the old moat ramparts, which are now a green ring of park. The light on the water in late afternoon is lovely.
t.pocheon lake and forest@37.3,127.3:
Nothing about Icheon announces itself as a starting line for a motorcycle ride, and that is why it makes a good one. The city, with nearly two hundred thousand people, sits in the central part of Gyeonggi province, south-east of Seoul, in a basin of rice fields, pear and peach orchards and low hills. The fuel gate here is the practical end of the suburbs, and from here the roads drift north toward the mountain country around Pocheon, a long way off, near the border with North Korea.

Icheon has two proud local products: rice, and pottery. The rice, grown in the fertile plain with clean water, was once served to Korean kings and is still sold with the city's name on the bag. The ceramics have an even longer history. Potters have worked here for centuries, and the village of Sagimakgol, with its rows of kilns and shops, is still the centre of a lively tradition, making celadon, white porcelain and rough, honest tableware. A half hour wandering the village is time well spent.

Gwangju, to the north-west, is where the great fortress of Namhansanseong stands on its mountain, a UNESCO World Heritage site that served as a refuge for kings, most famously in the winter of 1636, when King Injo withdrew here during a Qing invasion and held out for weeks before surrendering. The fortress walls run along the ridge for kilometres, and the story of the siege is told in several Korean films. It makes a good stop on the way in or out.

A practical note: motorcycles are not allowed on Korean expressways, so the routes here follow national roads and local roads, which are busy and full of traffic lights but are usually well surfaced. Delivery scooters dart in and out, and drivers can be unpredictable. Fuel stations are everywhere, and many are self-service. Convenience stores sell hot drinks, snacks and instant noodles which you can cook on the spot, a very Korean pit stop. Early mornings are the best time to ride out of the city, and in autumn the colours begin to show in the hills by mid-October.
t.pocheon lake and forest high point@37.0,:
Flat country again: this pin falls on the plain south of Seonghwan, around Pyeongtaek and Asan, about sixty kilometres south of Seoul and not far from the Yellow Sea, and it is called a high point only because the ride needed one. The land here is a broad, low basin of rice, orchards and greenhouses, with small hills like islands, and the highest thing in view is usually an apartment block or a motorway viaduct.

The district is nonetheless rich in memory. Asan is the home of Hyeonchungsa, the shrine to Admiral Yi Sun-sin, the naval commander who defeated the Japanese fleets during the invasions of the 1590s and who grew up in the area, and the shrine, set in a quiet grove of pines with a pond and a small museum, is one of the most revered sites in the country. Close by, Onyang has the oldest hot springs in Korea, used by kings and commoners for centuries, and the public baths are cheap and steamy. Osan, to the north, was the scene of the first clash between American and North Korean troops, in July 1950.

Seonghwan itself is known for pears, large, crisp and sweet, and in autumn, stalls beside the road sell them by the box, wrapped in paper. A little to the south, in Cheonan, the walnut cake, a small warm pastry filled with sweet red bean paste, is sold in the station and along the main street, and it makes a fine, sticky snack for a break. Many riders buy a bag and eat it at the next stop.

For riding, the plains offer little, and the point is to get through them. Roads are straight, with traffic lights and speed cameras that are strictly obeyed, and heavy lorries serve the factories and ports. Motorcycles are not allowed on Korean expressways, so riders use the national roads and local roads, which run parallel and are usually in good condition. Fuel is easy, with stations at every junction, and towns like Asan and Osan have plenty of choice. Convenience stores offer hot drinks and instant noodles. In late spring, the paddies are flooded, and the evening sky reflects in them, and in October the fields turn gold.
t.pocheon lake and forest scenic road@37.2:
Korea's west coast is a country of mud. The tide here rises and falls by up to nine metres, one of the greatest ranges in the world, and at low water the sea retreats for kilometres, leaving mudflats that gleam like silver and fill with wading birds. This stop falls on the coast south-west of Ansan, near the island of Daebudo and the long sea wall that joins it to the mainland, and the whole landscape is about water, sky and light.

The sea wall at Sihwa, nearly twelve kilometres long, was built in the 1990s to enclose a bay for farmland and later became a lake, and it carries a road across the water. At its midpoint, a tidal power station, the largest in the world by capacity, uses the flow through the sea gates to generate electricity, and a viewing platform and visitor centre allow a closer look. Riding the causeway is a strange experience, with the open water on both sides and the sky wide above, and the wind can be fierce.

Daebudo, at the end, is a low island with vineyards, beaches and small fishing villages. It is popular with weekend visitors from Seoul, who come for the grilled shellfish, served on charcoal braziers at seaside restaurants, and for the hand-cut noodles in clam broth, a warm, salty bowl that is perfect after a cold day. Sunset on the mudflats, when the sky turns orange and the wet sand reflects it, is one of the best sights on this coast. Wear windproof clothing, because the breeze off the water is cold in all but the summer months.

Hwaseong and Ansan, the nearest big cities, are twenty-five to thirty kilometres away, and each has several hundred thousand people and every kind of shop. On the island and the sea wall, services are limited to restaurants, a few cafes and one or two fuel stations, so fill up on the mainland. The roads near the coast are flat and well maintained, but weekend traffic to Daebudo can queue for kilometres. Weekday mornings are quiet. Fog can drift in from the sea in spring, and in winter the wind is bitter. Beware of the tides if you walk on the flats, because the water returns fast.
t.namyangju river@37.6,127.2:
Namyangju lies where the Han river's two great branches come together, the North Han running down from the mountains of Gangwon and the South Han from the east, and the point where they meet, a few kilometres east of the city at Dumulmeori on the Yangpyeong bank, is one of the loveliest spots near Seoul. The name means two waters, and the broad, calm river, framed by hills, is a favourite subject for photographers at dawn, when mist rises from the surface. Paldang, where the river is dammed, has become the favourite gathering place for riders and cyclists from the capital.

The city has several things worth knowing. It is the birthplace of Jeong Yak-yong, known as Dasan, the great scholar of the late Joseon dynasty who wrote on government, science and farming, and his home and memorial are open to the public, with a small museum and a garden by the river. Namyangju also has the royal tombs of Gwangneung, the resting place of King Sejo, set in a forest that is one of the best-preserved in the country, and those of Hongneung and Yureung, where the last two emperors of Korea are buried.

With ninety thousand inhabitants, Namyangju has plenty of fuel and food, and the stations along the riverside road are open late. The roads along the river are among the pleasantest around Seoul, with views of the water and wooded slopes, and a good number of cafes and restaurants overlooking the river, serving coffee, noodles and grilled fish. Weekends bring many riders, cyclists and day-trippers, so the roads are busy, and it is better to come early. On a weekday morning, the river is quiet and the light soft.

Remember that motorcycles are not allowed on Korean expressways, so the routes from Seoul follow the riverside national road and its neighbours, which carry plenty of traffic and have speed cameras every few kilometres. These are marked by signs, and drivers slow down, only to accelerate again after them. Autumn brings red and gold to the hillsides, and winter freezes the river edges and covers the reeds in frost. In summer, humidity is high, and sudden downpours in the monsoon season can make the road slippery. Plan your stops for coffee along the way, and enjoy the water.
t.gapyeong lake road@37.8,127.5:
Gapyeong is a river town in the mountains east of Seoul, where the Bukhan river is dammed to form Cheongpyeong lake, and the roads along the shore are among the best loved in the region. The town, at the gate of the high country, has about fifty-five thousand people, and its streets are full of cafes, pensions and shops catering to weekenders from the capital. The air is cooler than in the city, and the hills around the lake are covered in pine and oak.

The district has a surprising number of visitor attractions. Nami Island, a small tree-lined islet in the river reached by ferry or zip wire, was the setting of the television drama Winter Sonata, and draws crowds from across Asia. The Garden of Morning Calm, a landscaped park in the hills, is beautiful in all seasons, with lantern festivals in winter. In October, Gapyeong hosts a jazz festival on a river island, and thousands of people camp along the banks.

Gapyeong also has a serious history. In April 1951, in the Korean War, Canadian, Australian, New Zealand and British soldiers held back a major Chinese attack in the valley, in what is known as the Battle of Gapyeong, and several memorials commemorate it. Walking among them is a quiet and moving experience. Local products include pine nuts, which grow on the mountain slopes and are sold in shops and used in porridge, tea and cooking.

For riders, the lake road is a fine, winding ride, with views of the water and the hills, and it offers plenty of places to stop. The roads are generally well surfaced, though busy at weekends, and it is best to ride on weekdays or early in the morning. Fuel and food are easy in the town. Chuncheon, twenty kilometres further, is famous for dakgalbi, spicy stir-fried chicken, and is a popular destination. Fog hangs on the lake on cool mornings, and in autumn the mountains turn red and gold. In winter, take care on shaded corners where ice may linger, and remember that motorcycles are not allowed on the expressways, so you must use the lake road and its parallel routes.
t.cheongpyeong food@37.7,127.4:
Cheongpyeong lake is a long, narrow reservoir created in the early 1940s when a dam was built across the Bukhan river, and its waters now fill several arms of the valley, with the road following the shore. The dam was built to produce electricity for the growing city of Seoul, and it remains a source of power and drinking water. The shoreline, with its steep wooded slopes and small coves, is far more attractive than the story of its origin would suggest.

Riverside restaurants are the main attraction for a food stop. Along the water, family-run places serve maeuntang, a spicy freshwater fish stew with vegetables and chilli, and grilled river fish with rice and side dishes, brought to the table in a series of small plates that seem to multiply as the meal goes on. Pajeon, a savoury pancake with spring onions, comes with the local rice wine, though riders must say no to the latter. Lunch is generally served between eleven and three, and many places close in the afternoon.

The area is also a place of weekend retreat for the people of Seoul, who come to walk, fish and enjoy the clean air. Pensions and campsites are scattered along the shore, and there are paths for hiking in the hills above. The lake is calm in the morning, and mist often hangs on the surface, with fishermen in small boats waiting for the day to warm. In autumn, the reflection of the red maples on the water draws photographers.

Gapyeong, thirteen kilometres away, and Hwado, a little farther, have more than fifty thousand and a hundred thousand people respectively, and both have fuel stations, supermarkets and rooms. Small shops near the lake may sell snacks and drinks, but fuel is not reliable, so fill up beforehand. The road is winding and well maintained, though traffic can be heavy on summer and autumn weekends. Be careful on the sharp bends and in tunnels, where the light changes suddenly. Motorcycles are not allowed on Korean expressways, so this lakeside road is the usual route, and a good one. In winter, ice and snow can close or slow sections, and the air is cold and dry.
t.danyang river and passes@37.4,126.9:
Anyang sits on the southern edge of Seoul, in the narrow valley between Gwanaksan and Surisan, and it is the kind of city that exists mostly as a place people pass through. The fuel gate here marks the start of a long journey toward the east of the country, and the name of the ride suggests a far-off destination, Danyang, a river town in the mountains of North Chungcheong province, but this is the suburban end, and the first task is simply to escape the sprawl.

Anyang's name means peaceful, a rather hopeful label for a city of over six hundred thousand people. It has some surprises. The Anyang Art Park, in the hills at the edge of town, is a sculpture park and gallery with works by artists from many countries scattered through the woods along a stream, and the city has held a public art festival there. Gwanaksan, the rocky mountain to the north, is a popular hiking area for locals, and a temple on its slopes, Yeonjuam, hangs on a cliff ledge in a way that surprises first-time visitors.

The practical facts are plain. Anyang has fuel stations on every main road, many of them open round the clock, and the supply of food is endless, from Korean barbecue to street snacks. Convenience stores sell hot drinks and ready meals, and the delivery scooter, ridden at speed in every direction, is part of the traffic. Motorcycles are not allowed on the expressways, so heading east means using the national roads, which are slow near the city and speed up as the suburbs thin.

The best time to leave is early. Traffic builds from seven in the morning and stays heavy until after nine, and on weekends, the roads to the east fill with cars heading for the mountains. If you start before six, you will be well out of the city before the crowds appear. The air in the early light is cool and clear, and in autumn the hills around the city glow with colour. Check your tyres and gear before leaving, and enjoy the quiet streets while they last.
t.danyang river and passes high point@37.4:
You might expect a high point near Incheon and Ansan to be a hill. In practice it is a gentle crest of the flat land near the Yellow Sea, between the great port city of Incheon and the industrial suburbs of Ansan, and the highest things around are the apartment blocks and the low, wooded ridges of Surisan. This is the heart of the Seoul metropolitan area, with more than twenty million people within an hour, and the landscape bears the marks of it.

Incheon has a great deal of history for such a modern place. It was opened as a treaty port in 1883, and its Chinatown, with its red gates and noodle houses, dates from that era. In September 1950, General MacArthur's forces landed at Incheon in a daring amphibious operation that turned the course of the Korean War, with the extraordinary tides making the landing as risky as it was successful. A memorial park on the hill above the harbour tells the story.

Not far away, on the coast near Sorae, the old salt pans of the tidal flats have been preserved as an ecological park. For decades, workers raked salt from shallow evaporation ponds, and the wooden warehouses and windmills of the last works stand beside the water, with reeds and wading birds taking over the flats. The park is a quiet place, and a reminder of how recently this region was a landscape of salt and fishing. Bucheon, to the north, is known for its film and comic festivals.

Riding here is about getting through, and the main requirement is patience. Roads are busy, with traffic lights, buses and delivery scooters, and the surface is generally good. Fuel is plentiful, and so is food. Remember that motorcycles are not allowed on expressways, so you must use the national roads, which are a maze of junctions in this area. A navigation app is a great help. In late afternoon, the low sun turns the haze orange, and the evening sky over the Yellow Sea is often spectacular. Fog can also roll in from the sea on spring mornings, so use your lights.
Goyang lies north-west of Seoul, between the Han river and the hills, and is the gateway to the country that leads to the border. The point marked here falls near Haengju, on the bank of the Han, where a fortress on a hilltop commemorates one of the great victories of the Imjin war. In 1593, a Korean force of about two thousand soldiers and civilians under General Gwon Yul, with the help of local women who carried stones in their skirts, repelled a far larger Japanese army, an event remembered as one of the three great victories of the war.

From the fortress, the river runs wide and slow, with reeds on the banks and the long lines of bridges visible in the distance. The embankment road along the Han is a favourite for cyclists, and the sunsets from the hill are good. Goyang, with over a million people, is a city of apartment towers, shopping malls and flower parks, and it has a large lake park that holds a big flower festival every spring.

To the north, Paju is home to Heyri Art Village, a collection of galleries, studios and cafes built in a distinctive modern style, and Paju Book City, a publishing district with bookshops and libraries. Both are worth a stop, and the buildings are an unusual example of planned creativity. Beyond them lies the Imjin river, and the border zone, where military checkpoints, barbed wire and watchtowers are part of the landscape. Foreign visitors should carry passports and expect to be checked.

Fuel stations are plentiful in Goyang, and a few more can be found in Munsan, to the north. Motorcycles are not allowed on the expressways, but the local roads, including the riverside road, give good access. They are fairly flat and often busy, with frequent traffic lights and speed cameras. For a quieter ride, early morning is best, when mist rises from the river and the light is soft. In winter, the river edges freeze, and large flocks of migrating birds gather on the water, a striking sight against the grey sky. The air is cold and dry then, and the sun sets early.
t.danyang river and passes photo pull off@:
The border is close here, and the landscape knows it. This pull-off sits near Munsan, about eight kilometres from the Imjin river, in the north of Paju, where the land is a mix of rice fields, army camps and fenced-off riverbanks, and signs in several languages warn visitors about restricted areas. The Demilitarised Zone lies a short distance to the north, a strip of land four kilometres wide that has been empty of civilians since 1953, and which, strangely, has become a refuge for wildlife.

At Imjingak, a park on the south bank, a number of monuments and memorials stand together. The Bridge of Freedom, a rail bridge over the Imjin, carried thousands of prisoners of war back to the south in 1953, and the colourful ribbons and messages tied to the fence tell of families separated by the division of the country. A steam locomotive, riddled with bullet holes, stands nearby as a relic of the war. Nearby, the Odusan Unification Observatory looks across the river toward North Korea, and on clear days the fields and villages on the far side are visible through binoculars.

The wildlife is a surprise. Because the zone has been undisturbed for decades, it provides habitat for rare birds, and in winter, white-naped and red-crowned cranes arrive from Siberia and feed in the paddies. Watching them rise from the fields at dawn, with a mist on the river and distant guard posts in silhouette, is an unforgettable sight. Early morning is also the best time for photography, before tourists and tour buses arrive.

Rules matter in this area. Photography is restricted near military sites, and some roads require permits or pass checks, so follow signs and instructions from soldiers. Munsan has forty-three thousand people and offers fuel stations, restaurants and shops. Motorcycles are not allowed on the expressways, though the local roads are fine. In winter, the cold is severe, with temperatures well below freezing, so dress warmly, and in summer, the monsoon rains can be heavy. If you plan to visit Panmunjom or the tunnels, book in advance, since access is controlled.
t.danyang river and passes@37.5,127.4:
East of Seoul, the road to Yangpyeong passes through Gwangju, a hilly city that has little to do with its namesake in the south, and the lunch stop here, between Yangpyeong, Gwangju and Hanam, sits in a belt of valleys, orchards and weekend restaurants. The Gyeongan stream runs through, shallow and clear over stones, and the slopes on both sides are covered in pine and oak. It is a countryside that Seoulites treat as their back garden, so it fills up on Saturdays and empties on Mondays.

Gwangju has a long link with ceramics. From the fifteenth century, the royal kilns of the Joseon dynasty were centred on the Bunwon area, and for about four centuries they produced the fine white porcelain used at court, with its pure surface and restrained decoration. The work was done by skilled potters supervised by officials, and the kilns were chosen because of the clay, the water and the forest for firewood. Today, a museum and kiln site near the Han river tells the story, and the white porcelain of that time is regarded as one of the glories of Korean art.

Food in the hills here is mountain food. Restaurants near the roads serve dotori-muk, a cool, soft jelly made from acorn starch, dressed with soy sauce and sesame, and bibimbap with wild greens, along with simple dishes of grilled duck and tofu stew. Meals come with a dozen small side dishes, replenished on request, and the portions are generous. Prices are fair, and the food is usually excellent. Sit on the floor, as is traditional, and take your time.

For riding, the roads in this area are mostly gentle, with long bends and good surfaces, running through valleys and over low passes. Traffic is heavy at weekends, particularly near popular restaurants and parks, and parking can be a scramble. Fuel is plentiful in Yangpyeong, Gwangju and Hanam, which each have between eighty and a hundred and thirty-five thousand people. Remember that motorcycles are not allowed on Korean expressways, so local roads are your main option, and a navigation app set to avoid them is useful. In autumn, the ridges glow red and yellow, and in the early morning, mist hangs in the valleys until the sun clears it.
t.blankenese view@53.6,9.8:
Blankenese hangs on a steep hillside above the Elbe, and for a city as flat as Hamburg it comes as a surprise. This was once a fishing village, separate from the city until the 1930s, and the old part still has the look of a place that grew up by itself, with narrow, winding lanes, tiny houses clinging to the slope and a network of stairways, said to number in the dozens and to contain thousands of steps, linking them. Captains and pilots lived here, and their houses have views over the river that were once a working necessity and are now a luxury.

The Elbe is wide at this point, almost a mile of grey-green water, and the commercial heart of the port is just upriver. Container ships, bulk carriers and cruise liners pass close inshore, and from the beach at the foot of the hill you can sit on the sand and watch them slide by, with the great engines throbbing and the flags of the world fluttering. Further downstream at Wedel, a ship-greeting station called Willkomm-Höft plays the national anthem of each passing foreign ship, a tradition that dates to the 1950s.

For a rider arriving to finish the day, the approach is by way of the Elbchaussee, a long, tree-lined road above the river, lined with old merchant villas, and then down into the village by narrow, steep lanes. The final streets are cobbled, tight and usually busy with walkers, so go slowly, and park near the station. In spring, the fruit orchards of the Altes Land across the water bloom white and pink, and in autumn the light on the river is soft and golden.

Fuel is available in Hamburg's western suburbs and on the main roads, and the village has cafés, fish restaurants and bakeries. The evening is the best time, when the lights of the ships glow on the river and the hillside lamps flicker on.
t.signal de botrange@50.5,6.1:
Belgium's highest point is a gentle bump in a moor, and the country is rather proud of it. Signal de Botrange stands at 694 metres in the Hautes Fagnes, a high plateau of peat bog in the east of Wallonia near the German border, and it is so modest that a short stone staircase was built on top to give it a little extra height. Climb the steps and you reach a round 700 metres, which is, technically speaking, as high as anyone in the kingdom can stand, and the view across the heather and the fir trees is an unexpectedly open one.

The Hautes Fagnes, known in German as the Hohes Venn, is a nature reserve of raised bogs, heath and spruce, and it has a bleak beauty. Wooden boardwalks cross the wettest parts, so that walkers can keep to the paths and the fragile plants and mosses beneath. The weather here is famous for being foul, with fog, rain and wind far more common than sunshine, and temperatures several degrees below those of the lowlands. In winter, cross-country skiers use the plateau, and there is a small cafe and a visitor centre by the car park, where waffles are served to people with cold hands.

For a rider, this is a lovely part of the Ardennes, a landscape of forest, moor and small valleys, with roads that wind between villages and cross the plateau in long, flowing bends. The surface is usually good, the traffic is moderate, and in summer the heather turns the moor purple. Fog can come down quickly, so keep your visor clean and your speed sensible, and watch for patches of damp on the shaded stretches. The famous Spa-Francorchamps circuit lies a short distance to the west, and on race weekends the roads are crowded with motorcycles and cars.

Malmédy, about ten kilometres to the south, is the nearest town and has fuel, restaurants and a famous carnival, the Cwarmê, that takes place in the weeks before Lent. The old town is a pleasant place for a coffee, with cobbled streets and a church, and the nearby Eupen and Monschau, across the German border, make good extensions to the ride. The area has a mixed culture, with French, German and a local Walloon dialect spoken in different villages.

Go on a clear day if you can, and carry a layer even if the valley is warm, because the plateau makes its own weather.
t.boppard@50.2,7.6:
Boppard sits on the biggest bend in the Middle Rhine, where the river swings so sharply that it looks like a lake from the hills above. It is a handsome town of about sixteen thousand people with a long riverside promenade, a Roman past, and a backdrop of steep vineyards, and it is one of the better places along the Rhine Gorge to stop, because it has proper size, proper shops and enough character to hold your attention. The Middle Rhine from Bingen to Koblenz is a UNESCO World Heritage site, and Boppard is one of its more substantial towns.

The Romans built a fort here, called Bodobrica, and parts of its walls still stand in the old town, among medieval churches and half-timbered houses. The Rhine was an important trade route for centuries, and Boppard had its own toll station, which gave the town both wealth and conflict with the archbishop of Trier. The slope above the bend, known as the Bopparder Hamm, is one of the largest continuous vineyards in the region, and its Riesling is well regarded. A chairlift climbs to a viewpoint known as the Vierseenblick, where the river appears as four separate lakes from above, a trick of the bends.

The ride along the river is the main attraction. The B9 runs close to the water, with views of castles, ferries and cargo ships on the other side, and the railway line right beside it, carrying frequent freight and passenger trains. It is a busy road, with traffic and some noise, but the scenery is hard to beat. For a quieter option, climb into the hills on the side roads that lead to viewpoints and small villages, where the corners are tighter and the air smells of woodland. The roads in the Hunsrück plateau are smooth and curvy, with little traffic.

Boppard has fuel, supermarkets and many cafes and restaurants, so it is an easy stop. Riesling is the wine to order, and a plate of Flammkuchen or a slice of something sweet can follow. Watch your speed on the river road, as cameras are common in the villages.

Early morning is quiet on the water, and in autumn, the mist rises off the river and the vineyard leaves turn red and gold.
t.st goar@50.2,7.7:
St. Goar is a narrow riverside town built beneath a large castle, and the castle is what you came for. Burg Rheinfels rises on the hill above, a huge ruin with tunnels and cellars that is the largest fortress ruin on the Middle Rhine. It was built in the thirteenth century by the Counts of Katzenelnbogen to collect tolls from passing ships, and it grew into a vast complex that withstood a siege by French troops in the seventeenth century, only to be blown up by the French in 1797 after they took the area. Walking through the underground passages with a torch is a bit like exploring a stone beehive.

Opposite, on the east bank, stand Burg Katz and Burg Maus in the neighbouring town of St. Goarshausen, whose names, Cat and Mouse, are the result of an old joke about the Katzenelnbogen counts. The two towns are linked by a car ferry, which crosses the Rhine at regular intervals and lets riders switch banks without a long detour. It is a small pleasure, riding onto a ferry with the whole Rhine Gorge around you, and the crossing takes only a few minutes.

The town takes its name from Goar, a hermit of the sixth century who settled here and gave shelter to travellers, and who later became a saint. The Rhine at this point runs narrow and deep, with strong currents, and passing ships needed local pilots. The river's nearby bend and the cliffs gave rise to the legend of the Loreley, just a short ride away. On the road, the B9 follows the west bank, with the railway line close by, and the corners are gentle and the views are wide. The ride up to Burg Rheinfels is a short, steep climb, with a few hairpins and a car park near the entrance. Take it slowly, because it is narrow and shared with walkers. The back roads into the Hunsrück hills are quiet and twisty, a good alternative if the river road is crowded.

With just over three thousand people, St. Goar has fuel and a handful of shops, but Boppard, about twelve kilometres north, has more choice. Restaurants along the riverfront serve Riesling and local dishes, and the terraces are pleasant on summer evenings, with ship traffic sliding past.

Come in spring or autumn to avoid the crowds, and enjoy the mist rising off the water.
t.loreley@50.1,7.7:
The Loreley is a rock, and not a very tall one, but it has a story that made it more famous than most mountains. It is a steep slab of slate on the east bank of the Rhine, rising well over a hundred metres above the water, at a point where the river narrows and deepens and the current turns treacherous. Boatmen once lost ships here, and the rock's echo and the swirling water gave rise to a legend: a beautiful maiden sits on the summit combing her golden hair and singing, and sailors who look up at her forget the rocks below and are wrecked.

The legend is not ancient. It was shaped by the Romantic poets of the early nineteenth century, and above all by Heinrich Heine, whose 1824 poem, set to music by Friedrich Silcher, became one of the best-known German songs. Today a statue of the Loreley sits on a spit of land at the harbour in St. Goarshausen, looking out across the water, and the rock is the centrepiece of a visitor centre on the plateau above. A road leads up to it from the town, and the view from the top, over the Rhine Gorge and the villages along it, is one of the finest in the whole valley.

For riders, the way up is a pleasure. The road climbs from the river through forest in a series of tight bends, and the surface is generally good. Up on the plateau, the landscape is open and gentle, with wide skies and a mix of woodland and fields. From here you can follow side roads along the ridge, where the traffic is light, and the views to both sides of the gorge appear and vanish between the trees. The river road below is busy but beautiful, with the railway alongside and castles on every spur.

The nearest services are in St. Goar and St. Goarshausen, which have a few shops, and Boppard, about fourteen kilometres away, has more choice. A café and restaurant at the visitor centre serves coffee and cake, and in summer the plateau hosts open air events in an outdoor theatre set into the hillside.

The best time to come is late afternoon, when the sun lights the cliff and the river turns gold. If you can, stay for sunset.
t.bacharach@50.1,7.8:
Bacharach is so small and so well preserved that it feels more like a model than a town. About two thousand people live inside a medieval wall with tall watchtowers, in half-timbered houses that lean toward each other over cobbled lanes. Above the roofs, the ruin of the Wernerkapelle, a Gothic chapel never completed, stands against the sky, and higher still, Burg Stahleck sits on its spur and now serves as a youth hostel with one of the best views in the valley. Legend ties the name to Bacchus, the god of wine, and the town's wine trade was already famous in the Middle Ages.

The wine is Riesling, grown on steep slate slopes, and it was so prized in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries that Bacharach became one of the main wine trading centres on the Rhine. Today the vineyards still cling to the slopes behind the town, and a few family estates welcome visitors for tastings. Timber-framed taverns in the lanes serve the local wine with simple food, and the courtyard of an old inn is a pleasant place on a summer evening. A few kilometres downstream, the Pfalzgrafenstein, a small toll castle shaped like a ship, sits on an island in the river near Kaub, and it is one of the strangest and most photogenic buildings on the Rhine.

The riding along this stretch of the Rhine is classic. The B9 runs through a narrow gorge with the river on one side and vineyards on the other, passing castle after castle on the heights, with curves that are gentle and a surface that is generally good. It is not a fast road, but it is a beautiful one. The railway runs beside it and can be loud, since freight trains pass through at all hours, so do not expect a quiet night in a room facing the tracks. For a quieter ride, side roads climb to the plateau, where the villages are tiny and the traffic is light.

Fuel is a question here. Bacharach is small, and Oberwesel, a few kilometres downstream, has a bit more, while Bingen am Rhein, about fourteen kilometres away, has everything. It is wise to top up there. In town, a wine tavern or a café on the old market square serves a good lunch, and the place is easy to explore on foot.

Visit in spring or autumn, when the crowds are smaller. The vineyards are at their best in October, with the leaves red and gold.
t.beilstein@50.1,7.2:
Beilstein has fewer than two hundred residents and looks like it has been waiting several centuries for visitors. The village clings to a steep bank of the Moselle, with narrow stepped lanes, half-timbered houses, a tiny market square and the ruins of Burg Metternich above it, and the whole thing is so compact you can walk it in twenty minutes without trying. Locals sometimes call it the Sleeping Beauty of the Moselle, and it does feel as though it escaped modernisation by being too awkward to reach.

The castle ruin, once the seat of a local lordship, was burned by French troops in the late seventeenth century and never rebuilt. The village below has a Baroque Carmelite monastery church, home to a famous black Madonna that draws pilgrims, and a medieval tower where the town's old fortifications survive. The steep slate vineyards around it produce excellent Riesling, much of it grown on slopes so steep that the work must still be done by hand, with winegrowers using ropes and small monorails. A glass of it at a table in the square is hard to beat.

The ride along the Moselle is calm and bendy. The road follows the river as it winds in great loops between steep vineyard slopes, passing villages with half-timbered houses and church spires. The surface is generally good, the corners are gentle and traffic is moderate, though weekends and the harvest season bring more cars, tractors and cyclists. Be alert for tourist traffic and narrow village streets, especially in Beilstein itself, where bikes are better parked at the edge of the village than ridden through the lanes.

Fuel is not available in the village. Cochem, about seven kilometres upstream, is the nearest sizeable town, with petrol stations, supermarkets and the large Reichsburg castle looking down from its hill. It is worth a stop on its own. In Beilstein, a handful of wine taverns and cafés offer light meals, often with local sausage, bread and cheese, and a glass or two of wine for those not riding on.

The best time is September and early October, when the vineyards turn gold and the grape harvest brings activity to the valley. The light is warm and mist drifts over the river in the morning.
t.schalkenmehren maar@50.2,6.9:
Three round lakes lie in a row beside the village of Schalkenmehren, and none of them is really a lake. They are maars, craters blasted out of the Eifel when rising magma hit groundwater and the whole thing detonated. The explosions threw out a ring of ash and broken rock, the hole filled with rain, and what remains is a perfect circle of still water in a bowl of grass and trees. The Eifel has dozens of them, and the Dauner Maare, just next to the town of Daun, are the best-known cluster: the Schalkenmehrener, Weinfelder and Gemündener Maar, each only a short walk from the next.

The Weinfelder Maar, also called the Totenmaar, has a small chapel on its shore and a reputation for sadness that comes from old plague stories. The Schalkenmehrener is the sociable one, with a camp site, a bathing beach and a few cafés. You can walk the shoreline in an hour. The last volcanic activity in the Eifel was only about eleven thousand years ago, which in the history of the planet is yesterday afternoon.

This is hill country rather than mountain country. The roads around Daun climb out of the valleys onto high plateaus of fields and conifers, then dip again into narrow wooded valleys, so a ride here is a pattern of long gentle sweeps with the odd hairpin where a stream has cut deep. The surface is mostly good, though patches of broken tarmac appear after hard winters, and the Eifel is well known among German riders, so on fine weekends there is a lot of company. The Nürburgring is within an hour, and you will sometimes hear it before you see anyone from it. The weather here can be wet and cool even in July, and fog on the heights is common in autumn.

Daun, four kilometres away, has about eight and a half thousand people, with fuel stations, a supermarket and a good selection of cafés. It is the sensible place to resupply. In the village itself you will find simple inns serving Eifel food: heavy, filling dishes of potatoes, sausage and sauerkraut, and a lot of pork, accompanied by a regional beer. The mineral water from nearby Gerolstein is excellent and sold everywhere.

The maars look their best in still, early light, when a skin of mist lies across them.
t.ksar ghilane@33.0,9.6:
Ksar Ghilane is where southern Tunisia stops pretending to be a country and becomes the Sahara. It lies on the edge of the Grand Erg Oriental, the great sea of sand dunes that rolls across the border toward Algeria and Libya, and the oasis is a small patch of date palms around a warm spring that bubbles up in the sand. The spring water is hot enough to be a pleasure on a cool evening, and travellers have swum there for generations, climbing out to watch the stars come out over the dunes.

Nearby stands a ruined Roman fort, the ksar that gives the place its name, built to guard the southern frontier of the empire against desert raiders. Its walls of stone and sandstone sit on a low hill above the oasis, and it is a reminder that people have crossed this country for thousands of years. Later nomads and traders also used the area, and it still has a frontier feel.

The approach is part of the adventure. The way from Douz or from the Tataouine side crosses stony plains and sandy tracks, and surfaces vary from tarmac to rough piste, with soft sand in patches. Motorcyclists should not underestimate the risk: sand sections can catch a heavy bike, and heat, wind and distance leave little room for error. Check current road and track conditions locally before setting out, and carry plenty of water, spare fuel and a means of communication. The best months are October to April; summer is dangerously hot. Dawn and late afternoon give the best light, and the dunes turn gold and pink.

Facilities exist but are basic, with camps and small guesthouses, simple meals of couscous, lamb or flatbread cooked in the sand, and sweet tea. Fuel availability can be unreliable, so fill the tank at the last big town and bring a spare can if you can. Mobile signal is patchy. Do not wander far into the dunes without a guide and a good idea of where you are.

The silence at night is the thing that stays with you: no engines, no lights, only wind, and a sky so crowded with stars it seems unreal.
t.lake mcdonald lodge@48.6,-113.9:
The lodge is the old hotel on the lake, built in 1913 and 1914 as a Swiss-chalet-meets-hunting-lodge confection of cedar logs, with antlers on the walls and a big stone fireplace in the lobby. Great Northern Railway took it over in the 1930s as part of its drive to bring wealthy easterners west by train. The hotel faces Lake McDonald, the largest lake in Glacier National Park, about ten miles long and more than 450 feet deep, ringed by forested ridges. Its shoreline is paved with small stones in red, green and purple, polished by the water, and so clear that it looks like a mosaic.

The road here is the western end of Going-to-the-Sun Road, one of the great engineering projects of American motoring, opened in 1933 after more than a decade of work, much of it by hand on cliffs. On the lake shore it is easy: a calm, tree-lined road with gentle curves and cool air. This is where you regain your bearings before the climb. The speed limit is low, and rightly so, as deer and tourists are plentiful. The road is generally open all the way to Logan Pass only from late June or early July until mid-October, and recent summers have sometimes needed vehicle reservations, so check the park's current rules before you set out. Vehicles longer than about twenty feet are banned on the high part, which cuts out most big motorhomes.

The lodge is a good place for coffee on the veranda, and a meal in the dining room, though it can be busy in summer. On a still morning the lake is a flat sheet with the peaks upside down in it, and you can walk to the shore in a minute. Boat tours leave from the dock. In the evening the sun slides behind the western ridges, and the whole valley goes blue and cool.

Fuel is the sort of thing you must plan for. West Glacier and Apgar, at the park entrance about eighteen kilometres west, have small shops and some petrol, and Columbia Falls, about thirty-five kilometres away, has proper stations, supermarkets and motels. Bear spray is sold locally, and bears are a real presence, so keep food locked away.
t.the loop@48.7,-113.8:
The Loop is the one proper hairpin on the western side of Going-to-the-Sun Road, and it is the place where the road, which has been climbing steadily up the valley, finally gets tired of going straight and turns back on itself in a big, left-handed sweep. It is a pull-out and trailhead as well, so you can stop and look at the road from the outside. A trail leads from here up to Granite Park Chalet, a stone mountain hut, and a lot of walkers set out from the parking lot.

For a rider the corner is the signature of the climb. Below it the road follows the valley wall with a series of long, smooth bends, with the McDonald Creek valley opening below and the big peaks beginning to show. Above it, the road rises toward Logan Pass in a high, slanting traverse cut into the cliff, with walls on one side and a long drop on the other, no shoulder to speak of, and low stone parapets which are sturdy but not tall. It is a ride that demands attention and gentle hands, and the narrow lanes make it a good idea to hug the right side. The oncoming traffic often includes a motorhome or a red tour bus, one of the old fleet of open-top White Buses that carry visitors. Early morning or evening is far better for riding than midday.

The landscape here changes in character as you climb. Cedar and hemlock give way to subalpine fir, and the glacier-carved valley shows its U shape clearly, with waterfalls dropping from the hanging valleys on the far wall. Late snow lingers in gullies until July, and the road crews often have to blast through drifts in spring. The weather can switch quickly, and afternoon showers are common, so bring rain gear.

Columbia Falls is the nearest sizeable town, a good half hour from the lodge, and West Glacier has a few more basics. The parking area is small and fills early, so arrive in the morning if you can. The corner sits right in grizzly and black bear country, so carry spray if you plan to walk, and stay within sight of other people.
t.logan pass@48.7,-113.7:
Logan Pass sits at 2,026 metres on the Continental Divide, and it is the top of the road. After the cliffs and the long traverse from the west, the road flattens into a little saddle ringed by peaks, with a visitor centre, a parking lot that fills before most people have finished breakfast, and a boardwalk heading off across a meadow of alpine flowers. It is the highest point reached by any paved road in the park, and it feels like it. Snow sits in the hollows well into July.

The ride up from either side is the point of the whole route. From the west you come up the long traverse above the Loop, with the valley dropping away; from the east you climb from St Mary through a mix of tight bends and bare slopes. Both sides ask for care, with narrow lanes, low walls, and big drops, and both are at their best early or late in the day. The road is generally open between roughly late June and mid-October, depending on snow, and there can be timed-entry or reservation systems in some summers. Vehicles of more than about twenty feet long or eight feet wide are banned on the upper part, which is a blessing for anyone on two wheels.

The wildlife is the other attraction. Mountain goats wander near the visitor centre and the trail to Hidden Lake Overlook, a mile and a half or so of boardwalk and path, and bighorn sheep and marmots are often around. Pikas squeak among the rocks. Grizzlies sometimes appear on the slopes above. Keep a good distance from goats, which can be assertive about salt, and never approach a bear. The pass is named for William Logan, the park's first superintendent, and the surrounding peaks include Clements Mountain and Reynolds Mountain.

Weather is as variable as the scenery: you can arrive in sun and find horizontal sleet within the hour, and wind on the divide can be strong. Pack layers and gloves in all seasons. Fill up at Columbia Falls or West Glacier on the west side, or at St Mary on the east, and bring food and water with you, since only limited seasonal supplies are available.
t.st mary lake@48.7,-113.5:
St Mary Lake is the east side of the story. Where the west is damp and thick with cedar, the east is drier, more open and far windier, because the mountains of Glacier fall away abruptly onto the plains of Blackfeet country. The lake lies in a long glacial trough about nine miles long, a deep blue, with a tiny island, Wild Goose Island, sitting like a ship in the middle. It is one of the most photographed spots in the park, and with good reason: the island, the peaks behind and the sky above make an almost absurdly tidy composition.

The road runs along the north shore in a long, quiet descent, past turnouts and trailheads, and the character is different from the west. The curves are gentler, the walls less vertical, and the views open and sweeping, but the wind is a serious matter. Gusts funnel down the valley and can hit a motorcycle sideways, particularly at the east end. It is not unusual for the lake to be a mess of whitecaps while the sky is blue. In shoulder season the temperature drops, and an afternoon thunderstorm can drift over in minutes. Riding it at evening, with the light low and soft, can be lovely.

The land to the east of the park is the Blackfeet Reservation, and the mountains here have long been sacred to the Blackfeet, who call the range the Backbone of the World. The Great Northern Railway, which opened the park to tourism, ran trains to nearby stations, and the old Sun Point chalets were part of that story. The village of St Mary at the east entrance has a small collection of shops, restaurants and motels, and is a convenient base.

Fuel is available at St Mary, which is the dependable source on this side of the park, with a small supermarket and several places to eat. Out on the road the only facilities are seasonal, mostly toilets and a few shops. If you are crossing west, remember to fill up before you start, because the next fuel is on the far side of the pass. The road over Logan Pass is closed to larger vehicles and often to everyone in winter, so check conditions. Bear spray is wise, and so is a windproof layer.
t.wilseder berg heath@53.2,9.9:
The highest point of the Lüneburg Heath is 169 metres above sea level, which sounds like nothing until you stand on top of it and look out over a sea of purple. Wilseder Berg is a gentle swell in a landscape that otherwise rolls like a calm ocean, and from the summit you can see miles of heather, birch, and juniper stretching to the horizon, with the occasional church spire or farm roof. In late summer, when the heather blooms, from about mid-August to September, the whole heath turns a deep, vivid pink, and it is the kind of sight that makes Germans of all ages take out their cameras.

The heath is not natural in the way a mountain is. It is the result of centuries of human use: farmers cut the forest, grazed their sheep on the thin sandy soil, and cut the heather for fuel and bedding. The sheep that do the work, the Heidschnucken, with their curled horns and shaggy grey coats, are still grazed here to keep the landscape open. The nature reserve, one of the oldest in Germany, protects the heath, and the traditional villages in it, such as Wilsede, have thatched farmhouses and are largely closed to cars.

That is the practical point for a rider: you cannot ride up. Wilsede is a car-free village, and the way in is on foot, by bicycle, or by horse-drawn carriage, from car parks at places such as Undeloh or Döhle. Leave the bike there, put on some walking shoes, and allow an hour or two for the walk. The rest of the heath roads, on the other hand, are lovely: narrow, quiet, and lined with birch and pine, with gentle bends and a surface that is generally good. Traffic is heavy on sunny weekends in August, when the coaches arrive.

Fuel is available in Bispingen, about ten kilometres away, and Egestorf is a smaller village nearby. There are cafes and inns in Undeloh and Wilsede, serving buckwheat pancakes, sweet or savoury, and heath lamb. In winter the heath is quiet, brown, and often frosty. Mornings in September, when mist lies over the heather, are very good. Carry a rain layer, because the weather over flat country can change fast, and the wind has nothing to stop it.
t.soltau lunch window@53.0,9.8:
Soltau is a practical northern German town, and it makes no apologies for that. It sits on the edge of the Lüneburg Heath, on the Böhme river, and it has a pedestrian centre of brick buildings, a modest market, and a reputation as a place where families come for a day out, since a large amusement park and a thermal bath complex are nearby. For a rider on the roads of the heath, it is the best place for a lunch and a refuel.

The town grew around the salt trade, as many in the region did, and its name is thought to be related to salt, though its history is mostly that of a market town in an agricultural region. The surrounding countryside is heath, pine forest, and farmland, and the sandy soils support asparagus, potatoes, and sheep. Heidschnucken, the heath sheep, are a speciality, and the meat is dark and strong, often served with beans and potatoes.

The roads around Soltau are quiet and straight, with the sort of gentle bends that suit an easy afternoon. The minor roads through the heath are a classic route, with birch and pine alleys, open views, and a surface that is generally good. Speed cameras are common in towns, and the limits are strictly enforced, so keep an eye on the signs. In late summer, the heather draws crowds, and weekends are busier, with cyclists, cars, and horse-drawn carriages. Midweek mornings are quieter.

Soltau has everything you could need. Fuel stations are on the edges of town, supermarkets and bakeries are plentiful, and there are cafes and restaurants on the main streets. Neuenkirchen, about ten kilometres away, is a smaller place with fewer services. It is worth stopping for a proper German bakery stop, with fresh bread rolls, cake, and strong coffee. In winter, the weather can be cold and damp, with fog and frost, and the roads can be icy early in the morning. The best season is late summer and early autumn, when the heath is in bloom and the light is soft.
t.hameln old town@52.1,9.4:
Hameln, known to English speakers as Hamelin, owes its fame to a piper. According to the legend, recorded in the town's chronicles, in 1284 a stranger in a coloured coat promised to rid the town of rats, led them into the Weser with his pipe, and when the townspeople refused to pay, he led away their children as well. The story has been told by the Brothers Grimm and by Robert Browning, and the town has embraced it wholeheartedly: rat-shaped souvenirs, a pied piper show in summer, and bronze rats on the pavements.

Behind the legend lies a handsome town. Hameln sits on the Weser river, and its old centre is a showcase of Weser Renaissance architecture, with richly carved half-timbered houses, stepped gables, and decorative stonework. The Hochzeitshaus, or wedding house, and the Rattenfängerhaus, the Rat-Catcher's House, are two of the finest. The streets are pedestrianised, with the rat motif repeated on every corner, and the whole centre is easy to explore on foot after you park the bike.

The riding around Hameln is gentle and pleasant. The Weser Uplands, with their wooded hills, castles, and half-timbered villages, begin here, and the B83 follows the river upstream toward Bodenwerder and Holzminden. The roads are smooth, with long easy curves, and the scenery is soft rather than dramatic. Traffic in town can be busy, and the one-way systems are confusing, so use the car parks on the edge and walk in. In summer, weekend visitors fill the pedestrian streets, and midweek mornings are quieter.

Fuel and food are no trouble in a town of nearly sixty thousand people. There are stations on the main roads, supermarkets, and a wide choice of cafes and restaurants, from traditional inns serving pork and potato dishes to ice cream parlours on the squares. Aerzen, a smaller town about nine kilometres away, is quieter. In summer, the Piper play is staged on Sundays in front of the Hochzeitshaus, and it makes a good break. Winters are cold and damp, and the river can flood after heavy rain, but the old town looks lovely under frost.
t.ruhler schweiz@51.9,9.5:
The name Rühler Schweiz is a small joke, in the way many German hill regions have been called Switzerland by proud locals who wanted to say something flattering about steep ground and green woods. It is not Switzerland, and it makes no claim to altitude, but it is a pleasant, wooded patch of the Weser Uplands, close to the river near Bodenwerder, where the land rises into forested ridges and narrow valleys, and the road finds a rhythm of gentle bends and sudden views.

The Weser is the thing that gives the area its character. The river flows north between the Solling hills to the east and the Lipper Bergland to the west, and the villages along it have long depended on it for trade, transport, and fishing. Timber rafts floated down the river for centuries, and the half-timbered houses along the banks show the wealth that came from it. Much of the countryside is beech and oak forest, which turns gold and copper in October and offers a lovely light in the low sun.

For a rider, these are the roads you remember for the quiet. The surface is generally good, with some patches, and the bends are mostly open, with the odd tight corner where a road drops to a stream. Traffic is light, apart from tractors and the occasional tourist coach. The gradients are modest, but in wet weather the leaves and mud can make the surface slippery, and in autumn, fallen leaves are a hazard. Morning mist often hangs over the river and the fields.

Bodenwerder, about three kilometres away, is the nearest sizeable place, with fuel, a bakery or two, and several cafes. It is the town of Baron Münchhausen, the teller of impossible tales, who was born here in 1720. Kirchbrak, a smaller village, has limited services. Holzminden, farther upstream, is a larger town. The best seasons are spring, when the beech leaves are fresh green, and autumn, when the colours are rich. In winter, snow can fall on the hills, and the roads are not always cleared quickly.
t.koterberg viewpoint@51.9,9.3:
The Köterberg is the highest hill for miles around, a broad, bald dome rising to just under five hundred metres on the border between Lower Saxony and North Rhine-Westphalia, and from the top the view over the Weser Uplands is wide and green. Forest, farmland, and small villages fold into one another toward the horizon, and on a clear day you can see for fifty kilometres or more. A television tower and a small cafe mark the summit, and in the evening the sunset is lovely.

The hill is popular with glider pilots and paragliders, who use the winds that rise against its slopes, and on a fine day colourful canopies drift above the meadows. In winter, a short ski lift runs on the northern slope when snow is deep enough. The hill is also part of the area known as Lipperland, a region with its own dialect, its own history of small principalities, and a long tradition of farming, linen, and brick-making. The villages around it, such as Polle, with its castle ruins above the Weser, are worth a detour.

The ride up is the pleasure. From the villages below, the road climbs in a series of curves through meadows and woodland, with a good surface and a moderate gradient, and the top opens suddenly into a broad, grassy summit. The bends are tight enough to be fun, and the traffic is light on most days. At weekends in fine weather, the car park fills, and the road is busier. Beware of loose gravel at the edges, and of wet leaves and mud after rain, and watch for cyclists on the climb.

Schieder-Schwalenberg, about nine kilometres away, has stations, shops, and cafes, and Polle is smaller. The summit cafe offers coffee and cake, with the view as a free extra. Bring a jacket, because the wind at the top is stronger than in the valleys, and the temperature can fall quickly. Late afternoon is the best time for photographs, when the light is warm and the haze softens the horizon.
t.jork orchards@53.5,9.7:
The Altes Land is a strip of fruit orchards along the south bank of the Elbe, just west of Hamburg, and Jork is its heart. It is the largest continuous fruit-growing area in northern Europe, and in late April and May the blossom is so thick that the whole landscape seems to be wrapped in white and pink. In autumn, the trees are heavy with apples, and roadside stalls sell them by the sack. The scent of blossom in spring, or of fallen fruit in autumn, is as strong as the fog off the river.

The land itself is a work of human ingenuity. In the twelfth century, Dutch settlers were invited by the Archbishop of Bremen to drain and cultivate the marshes, and they built a network of dykes, ditches, and canals that still shapes the countryside. The farmhouses, built in half-timbered style with decorative brickwork and elaborate gates, are some of the finest in northern Germany, and the long, narrow farm plots run from the river dyke to the back of the marsh. Boats once carried the fruit to Hamburg, and the old Este river is still lined with beautiful houses.

The riding is gentle and charming rather than exciting. The roads follow the dykes and ditches, with long straights, low bridges, and sudden right-angled bends, and the surface is mostly smooth, though patches and bumps exist. Traffic can be heavy in blossom season, when Hamburg residents flood out for the day, so early starts and weekdays are better. The narrow roads and unexpected turns demand attention, and cyclists are everywhere. In summer, the farm shops sell cherries and plums, and there are cafes in converted barns.

Jork is a proper town of twelve thousand people, with fuel, shops, and restaurants, and Hamburg is about thirty kilometres away. Guderhandviertel, a smaller village nearby, is quieter. Try a slice of apple cake and a glass of local cider, and take a few minutes to look at the farmhouses. Spring blossom is the main event, usually in the first half of May, and the September and October harvest is the second. Winter is quiet, and the Elbe fog can be heavy, but the villages are still pleasant.
t.fagus factory alfeld sight@52.0,9.8:
The Fagus Factory is a shoe-last factory that changed the course of architecture, and it sits unassumingly beside the railway line in Alfeld, a small town on the Leine river. The buildings were designed by the young Walter Gropius, with Adolf Meyer, and built between 1911 and 1913 for Carl Benscheidt, a manufacturer who wanted a modern, light-filled factory. What they produced, with glass walls that wrap around the corners of the brick structure with no supporting pillar in the way, was one of the first buildings in the world to look genuinely modern, a forerunner of the Bauhaus that Gropius would found in 1919.

The factory is still working, which makes it special. Shoe lasts, the wooden or plastic forms on which shoes are made, are still produced in some of the buildings, and the company runs a visitor centre and guided tours that explain the design and the history. UNESCO added the complex to the World Heritage list in 2011. It is a good stop for anyone who appreciates design, and even a short walk around the outside, with its clean lines and large windows, is rewarding.

Alfeld itself is a pleasant surprise. The old centre has half-timbered houses and a Renaissance town hall from the sixteenth century, and the town is a quiet and friendly one. The river Leine runs through the valley, with hills on either side, and the surrounding area is a mix of farmland and woodland. It is a pleasant place for a break, with cafes on the market square and a couple of bakeries nearby.

For a rider, Alfeld is a useful stop with fuel, supermarkets, and food, and the roads around it, through the Leine valley and into the Hils, are quiet and pleasant, with gentle bends and a good surface. Delligsen, a smaller town about five kilometres away, has fewer services. Parking at the factory is straightforward, though visits to the interior depend on tour times, so check ahead. Mornings are the best time for photographs, when the glass catches the light, and the best season is spring or autumn, when the weather is mild and the roads are quiet.
t.duingen hils road@52.0,9.7:
The Hils is a modest range of wooded hills in southern Lower Saxony, and it offers some of the best quiet riding in the region. The roads run along ridges and through beech forest, with gentle, flowing bends, a decent surface, and views that open suddenly over the farmland of the Leine valley. It is a landscape that never quite makes a fuss, and for that reason it is a pleasure to ride, with almost no traffic on a weekday and the smell of damp leaves in the shade.

Duingen, a small town at the foot of the Hils, is known for its pottery. The clay found here has been used since the Middle Ages, and by the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries the town was producing stoneware that was sold across northern Europe. Potters still work in the area, and a small museum tells the story of the trade. Old clay pits and kilns appear in the landscape, now overgrown, a quiet reminder of what the town was built on.

The forest is the main attraction. Beech and oak dominate, with a scattering of spruce, and in autumn the colours are spectacular, with a carpet of golden leaves beneath the trees. Roe deer are common, and red kites circle overhead, a bird that Lower Saxony is proud of. The roads here can be wet and slippery under the leaf cover, and mud from forestry work can appear on the surface, so ride carefully, particularly in the hollows where the sun never reaches.

Duingen has a few shops and cafes, but if you need fuel, Alfeld, about eight kilometres away, is the better bet, with stations, supermarkets, and restaurants. Brüggen, a smaller village nearby, has basic services only. A bakery stop in Duingen is a good way to start or end the day. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, and in winter, ice can linger on the shaded roads. Wear a warm layer, because the hills catch the wind, and carry a map or a charged phone, since signs in the forest are not always clear.
t.bodenwerder weser@52.0,9.5:
Bodenwerder is the home town of a man who was never quite able to tell the truth, and the town has made him a hero. Baron Münchhausen, Hieronymus Carl Friedrich von Münchhausen, was born here in 1720 and lived in the family manor beside the Weser, and as an old man he entertained dinner guests with fantastical tales of riding on a cannonball, pulling himself out of a swamp by his own hair, and flying to the moon. A writer collected the stories, and the baron became a literary legend. The old manor is now the town hall and holds a museum, and a fountain shows him on his cannonball.

The town itself sits on a bend of the Weser, with a bridge, a promenade, and a row of old half-timbered houses along the water. It is a quiet, friendly place, with a river that has served as a highway for centuries. Barges and pleasure boats pass, and cyclists follow the Weser cycle path along the bank. The hills of the Weser Uplands rise on both sides, covered with beech forest, and the river valley is wide and green.

The riding along the Weser is gentle and pleasant. The B83 follows the river, with long, flowing curves, easy gradients, and good views, and the minor roads climb into the forested hills on either side. Traffic is moderate, with tourist coaches and tractors, but the pace is relaxed. Look for gravel at junctions and for slow farm machinery around harvest time. In autumn, mist lies on the river in the morning, and the hills glow with colour. In winter, the road can ice over in shaded places.

Bodenwerder has fuel, a supermarket, bakeries, and a few cafes and restaurants, and it is a sensible place to rest and refuel before the next section. Hehlen, a smaller village about three kilometres away, has fewer services. A stop on the riverfront, with a coffee and a view of the water, is a nice way to break the day. Be prepared for the occasional flood: the Weser rises in wet weather, and the promenade is sometimes under water. The best seasons are spring and autumn, and the town is quietest in the early morning.
t.steinhude@52.5,9.4:
The Steinhuder Meer is the largest lake in Lower Saxony, and it is a curious one. It is about thirty square kilometres in area but very shallow, no more than three metres or so in most places, and that gives it a warm, brownish water and a character more like a vast pond than an alpine lake. The shore is low and reedy, with sandy beaches in some places, woods and meadows behind, and the whole place feels relaxed, a favourite for Hanoverians who want to sail, swim, or eat fish in the sun.

In the middle of the lake lies a small artificial island, Wilhelmstein, a fortress built in the 1760s by Count Wilhelm of Schaumburg-Lippe. The count was a military innovator, and he established a military school on the island, where Gerhard von Scharnhorst, later a leading Prussian army reformer, studied. The fortress can be reached by boat, and its circular walls and small buildings are a charming and slightly absurd place to visit. The village of Steinhude, on the southern shore, has a harbour and a lakeside promenade, with half-timbered houses and fishing nets drying.

The speciality is smoked eel, caught in the lake and smoked in small smokehouses in the village. It is rich, oily, and delicious on dark bread, and a few stands and cafes sell it along the waterfront. Whitefish and pike-perch are also on the menu, and the cake in the cafes is substantial. The lake is also a bird reserve, with a large wetland on the western side that attracts migrating ducks, geese, and waders.

For a rider, it is a place for a gentle stop: parking near the harbour, an hour or two on the shore, and an ice cream or a fish roll in the sun. The roads around it are flat and quiet, with long straights and gentle bends, and the surface is generally good. Fuel is available in Wunstorf, about seven kilometres away, and in Hagenburg, a smaller place nearby. Weekends in summer are crowded, with day-trippers from Hanover, so go early or on a weekday. Swimming is possible from the beaches, and the water is shallow and warm, though it can be murky.
t.rehburg forest road@52.5,9.2:
The Rehburg hills are a gentle ridge of wooded sandstone that rises above the flat country west of Hanover, and the roads through them are among the quietest and most enjoyable in the region. They are not high, only a few hundred feet above the plain, but they feel like a different country, with beech and oak forest, steep little valleys, and the smell of leaf mould and pine. The roads wind through the trees in gentle, flowing bends, and the light, filtered through the canopy, flickers across the surface.

The area has a long history of healing and prayer. Bad Rehburg, a small spa town on the edge of the hills, was a fashionable resort in the nineteenth century, famous for its mineral springs and its peaceful parks. A few kilometres away stands Loccum Abbey, a Cistercian monastery founded in the twelfth century, with a fine Romanesque and Gothic church of brick and stone. It has been a Lutheran institution since the Reformation, and it remains a working religious community, with a seminary and an academy. Its cloisters and church can be visited, and the atmosphere is quiet and calm.

Riding here requires respect for the conditions. The roads are narrow, with sudden bends, and leaves, mud, and gravel can appear on the surface, particularly after rain or forestry work. Deer and wild boar cross at dusk and dawn, so keep your speed sensible after the light fades. Traffic is light, mostly local, with a few weekend visitors and cyclists. The best season is autumn, when the beech leaves turn gold and the forest is full of colour, though spring has a freshness of its own.

Rehburg-Loccum, about half a kilometre away, has fuel, a supermarket, bakeries, and cafes, so it is the natural place for supplies. Wölpinghausen, a smaller village about six kilometres away, has limited services. Take a break at a cafe in Rehburg, perhaps with a slice of cake and a coffee, and enjoy the quiet. The Steinhuder Meer is only a short ride to the east, and makes a pleasant addition to the day. In winter, frost lingers on the shaded roads, and snow is possible.
t.winsen aller@52.7,9.9:
The Aller is a slow, brown, unhurried river that crosses the flat country between the Lüneburg Heath and Hanover, and Winsen is one of the small towns that has grown up on its banks. The surroundings are the sandy lowlands of Lower Saxony, with pine plantations, maize fields, and the long, level horizon that makes the sky feel enormous. It is not a place of drama, and it does not pretend to be, but there is something satisfying about a town where the river is the best part of the afternoon.

The Aller has shaped life here for centuries. It once carried goods between the heath and the Weser, and its meadows flood in wet seasons, which is why the settlements stand on slightly higher ground. The river banks are lined with willows and alder, and in summer there are quiet spots where a rider can sit in the shade with a drink and watch the current. Herons and kingfishers are common, and cyclists on the Aller cycle path pass at regular intervals.

For a motorcyclist, Winsen is a calm, easy stop. The roads in the area are flat, with long straights and gentle bends, and the surface is generally good, with a few patches. It is a landscape that suits a relaxed ride, with farm shops selling asparagus in spring and potatoes in autumn. Traffic is light, apart from tractors and the odd lorry, and speed limits in villages are strictly observed. After rain, the river road can have puddles and mud, and in autumn, mist hangs on the water in the early morning.

The town has fuel, a supermarket, bakeries, and a few cafes, and Wietze, about six kilometres away, is a smaller neighbour with its own services. Swimming in the river is possible in some places in summer, though the water is brown and the current can be stronger than it looks, so look for signed spots and take advice. A picnic by the water is a pleasant alternative. Late spring and early autumn are the best times, with mild air and soft light, and in winter the river can freeze at the edges.
t.wietze@52.7,9.8:
Wietze is a village with a surprising secret: it was once one of the most important oil fields in Europe. Oil was found seeping from the ground here in the nineteenth century, and by 1859 drilling had begun, among the earliest in the world. In the early twentieth century the field was one of the largest in Germany, with derricks crowding the heath, and for decades the oil that came from Wietze helped to fuel a growing industrial nation. By the middle of the century the wells were running dry, and the derricks were gone, but the village remembers.

The German Oil Museum, set on the old oil field, tells the story, with preserved derricks, pumps, and machinery, and a historic drilling rig that can be climbed. Wooden derricks stand in the trees, and the ground around still holds the shape of old pits. For anyone with a fondness for engines and old machines, it is a fascinating place, and even a quick look from the road is worth the detour. The site also shows the human side of the boom: the cramped lodgings, the long hours, and the dangers of the work.
