The riding around Wietze is gentle and quiet. The Aller flows beside the village, and the flat roads follow the river through meadows and pine woods, with long straights and easy bends. The surface is generally good, and traffic is light. Sandy side roads can be loose, especially after dry spells, and in autumn, leaves and mud can make the surface slippery. It is the sort of country in which an hour goes by without a car, and the main event is the smell of pine resin and warm sand.

For a coffee return, Wietze has a bakery, a couple of cafes, and a supermarket, and the fuel station on the main road is convenient. Winsen, about six kilometres away, is the larger neighbour with more choice. The museum has seasonal opening hours, so check before you go, and bring a rain layer, because the weather is changeable. The best seasons are spring and autumn, and a late-afternoon stop in the warm light is a pleasant end to a day on the flat roads of the Aller valley.
t.namhansanseong ridge loop@37.1,127.1:
Osan is the dormitory belt south of Seoul, a city of around a hundred and sixty thousand people in Gyeonggi Province, and for a rider heading into the mountains it is where you fill the tank and take a breath. Here, the gentle plain begins to rise toward the hills, and to the north, an hour or so up the road, lies Namhansanseong, the mountain fortress that the Joseon kings used as a refuge. The city is mostly apartment blocks and factories, with a United States air base nearby, and a lively street life of noodle shops, barbecue restaurants and convenience stores.

Namhansanseong has a story worth knowing before you go. In the winter of 1636, when the Manchu Qing army invaded Korea, King Injo fled to the fortress with his court and was besieged there for about forty-five days, in bitter cold and short of food, until he surrendered and bowed to the Qing emperor. The memory is a painful part of Korean history, and the fortress, whose walls climb the ridges for miles around the mountaintop, is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site, with a wooded park inside and a path along the ramparts.

For riders, a few things about Korea are worth knowing. Motorcycles are not allowed on expressways, so you will use national routes and local roads, which are often busy and full of traffic lights and speed cameras. Cameras are frequent and the fines are real, so respect the signs. Petrol stations are plentiful and almost always staffed, and the attendant will fill the tank for you. Convenience stores sell coffee, snacks and rice triangles at any hour. The roads in the hills are well surfaced and wind through forest in tight bends, with wet leaves and gravel in autumn.

Osan, four kilometres away, has everything you need, from fuel and food to a place to park. The climate is hot and humid in summer, with a monsoon in July, and the best seasons are April to May and late September to October, when the air is clear and the leaves are turning. Winter can bring ice on the hill roads, so check the weather. Start early, because the traffic builds quickly, and the evening rush hour on the main roads is brutal.
The coordinates fall on the western side of the peninsula, on the flat, rice-growing plain around Dangjin, in South Chungcheong Province, and the high point of this loop is more a matter of perspective than height. The land here is low, and most of the horizon is formed by the soft, rounded hills that rise from the paddy fields, with the broad estuary of Asan Bay and its tidal flats lying just beyond. The sea on this coast has some of the largest tides in the world, and at low water the mud flats stretch for miles, shining under the sky, with wading birds feeding at the edge.

It is old country. The fortress town of Haemi, not far to the south, was built in the fifteenth century to guard the coast against raiders, and its stone walls still enclose a grassy interior with a few restored buildings. In the nineteenth century it became a place of sorrow, when hundreds of Korean Catholics were executed here during the persecution of 1866, and it is now a pilgrimage site, visited by the Pope in 2014. The sombre mood of the place is balanced by the softness of the countryside, the rice fields and low hills that surround it.

Dangjin itself is a working town of about thirty thousand, close to a major steelworks and power station, and the plain has the usual Korean mixture of tidy farms, greenhouses and factories. Riding here is easy and flat, along national roads through the paddy country, with speed cameras at every few kilometres. The scenery is gentle, and the pleasure is in the light, particularly in late afternoon, when the sun slants across the flooded fields in spring and the golden rice in autumn. In summer the heat and humidity are heavy, and thunderstorms build in the afternoon.

Fuel and food are easy: Dangjin, Seosan and a string of smaller towns along the roads have stations and restaurants, and the region is known for its seafood, including the crab stews and shellfish of the west coast. Expressways are closed to motorcycles, so plan to use the national highways. The best time is spring or autumn, when the air is clear and the fields are green or gold.
t.daegwallyeong high road@37.7,128.8:
Daegwallyeong is the pass over the Taebaek range between the plateau of Pyeongchang and the sea at Gangneung, and the name means the great mountain pass. It stands at about eight hundred and thirty metres, high enough that the air is noticeably cooler and clearer than on the coast, and it is a place that Koreans associate with wide skies, grazing sheep and, in winter, heavy snow. The famous highland sheep ranch and the rows of white wind turbines on the ridges are visible from the road, and the whole landscape feels more like Europe's uplands than Asia's.

Seoul to the east coast used to be a long day's journey, and the old road over Daegwallyeong, with its many hairpins, was the main route. The expressway has since taken most of the traffic, running through long tunnels, but the old road has been kept, and for a rider it is the better one. It climbs from Gangneung through forest in a long run of tight bends, and over the top it opens out onto the grassy highland, with long views down the slopes to the sea on a clear day. It is a famous road among Korean motorcyclists, and on weekends, many gather at the pass, so expect the car park to be full of bikes and the road to be lively.

The asphalt is in decent shape, but as a mountain road it has its hazards: fog is common, particularly in the morning and in spring, ice lingers on the bends in winter, and it can snow here when it is raining on the coast. Speed cameras and police checks are common on the more popular routes. The nearby area was a centre of the 2018 Winter Olympics, held at Pyeongchang and Gangneung, and there are still sports venues in the hills, along with ski resorts and hot-spring hotels.

Gangneung, thirteen kilometres below, has fuel, restaurants and shops, and the coffee for which the city is known. At the pass itself, there are cafes, a sheep farm, a handful of stalls selling grilled corn and potatoes, and views. The highland is famous for its cabbage and potato crops, and for beef and lamb, and the cool air makes a warm bowl of noodles taste even better. The best times are late spring and early autumn, when the grasses are green or golden, and the sky is clear.
t.gangneung coast@37.8,128.9:
Gangneung is the capital of Korea's east coast, and it has a reputation for coffee that is nearly as strong as its reputation for beaches. The city sits where the Taebaek mountains meet the East Sea, with a long, bright shore of fine pale sand, and the water here is clear and cold, with surf in summer that draws swimmers and surfers. From July to August the beaches are crowded, with umbrellas and families, and in the other months they are wide and quiet, with the odd surfer in a wetsuit and the sound of waves.

The coastline has several distinct personalities. Gyeongpo, the main beach, lies beside a lake and a pine grove, and it has been a retreat for officials and poets since the Joseon dynasty. Anmok Beach has a street of cafes with views across the sand, where baristas make coffee by the cup with a pride unusual in a seaside town. Further north, Jeongdongjin is the place Koreans go to see the sunrise, with a railway station that stands right on the beach and a hotel built in the shape of a ship on the cliff above.

Gangneung is a city with a lot of history. Ojukheon, a house in a bamboo grove, is the birthplace of the Confucian scholar Yi I, known by his pen name Yulgok, and of his mother, the painter and calligrapher Shin Saimdang, who is on the fifty-thousand-won banknote. The town also has a famous speciality, soft tofu, cooked in a village where the tradition of making it with seawater goes back centuries. The city's food is dominated by seafood, with raw fish, squid and the sweet, tender crab of the East Sea.

Riding the coast road, Route 7 and the quieter roads beside the sea, is a joy. The road is flat or gently rolling, with long views, and the traffic is heavy only at holiday weekends. Speed cameras are frequent, so keep to the limits. Fuel is no problem in the city, which has a population of nearly two hundred thousand, and there are petrol stations along the coast. Watch for sand on the road near the beaches and for wet patches from sea fog. The best months are May, June and September, when the water is warm enough and the crowds are thin.
t.odaesan return roads@37.7,128.6:
Odaesan is a mountain range rather than a single peak, five high summits ringed round a green bowl in the Taebaek mountains, and the name means five terraces. The highest, Birobong, reaches about fifteen hundred and sixty metres, and the whole massif is protected as a national park, with dense forest of oak, hornbeam, maple and, lower down, Korean fir. The air is clean and cool, the streams run clear and the sound of water is never far away.

For more than a thousand years the mountain has been a centre of Korean Buddhism. Woljeongsa, a temple at the foot of the range, was founded in the seventh century by the monk Jajang, who brought relics from China, and its nine-storey octagonal stone pagoda is one of the finest in the country. Up the valley, Sangwonsa holds a bronze bell cast in the early eighth century, the oldest surviving bell in Korea. The walk from the temple gate along the river is lined by a long avenue of old fir trees, so tall and straight that the light comes down in shafts, and in autumn it is one of the places Koreans go to find the colour.

The roads back down toward Gangneung and the coast are some of the finest in the region. They drop through the forest in long, flowing bends, following river gorges and crossing ridges, with good surfaces and little traffic outside the weekend and the autumn weeks. The corners are not extreme, but they are constant, and the road moves from deep shade to open sunlight and back again. Be alert for wet leaves and fog, which gathers in the valleys in the mornings, and for the slow farm vehicles and buses on narrower stretches. In winter, ice and snow can close the higher sections.

The temple areas have small restaurants serving mountain vegetables, buckwheat noodles and the rice-and-herb dishes of Buddhist cooking, and the tea is excellent. Weekends in the second half of October are packed, so go on a weekday if you can, and bring warm clothes, because the mountain is much cooler than the coast.
t.susan ri tomb@38.9,125.4:
Susan-ri is a burial mound near the west coast of North Korea, a few kilometres from the Taedong River estuary and the barrage that closes it off. Under the earth lies a stone chamber painted with murals from the Goguryeo kingdom, which ruled the northern Korean peninsula and much of Manchuria from the first centuries BC until 668 AD. The tomb belongs to the Complex of Koguryo Tombs, which UNESCO listed in 2004. The wall paintings show figures, animals and the four guardian creatures of the cardinal directions, and they are among the oldest and most vivid pictures in the region.

An honest note first. This is not a place where an independent motorcyclist can ride in. Foreign visitors to North Korea travel in organised groups with official guides, on set routes, and independent motorcycle touring is simply not on offer. What can be said here is about the land and the history, which are worth knowing about even from a distance.

The country around is a flat, intensively farmed plain along the Taedong and the Yellow Sea coast, with low hills rising behind. Rice fields, orchards and small villages sit between big roads that carry little traffic. Nampo, the nearest large city, is the main port for Pyongyang and lies on the river mouth, with the West Sea Barrage, an eight-kilometre dam, closing the estuary. Yonggang, a smaller town nearby, is the local centre.

Goguryeo is a point of pride in Korea and a point of dispute with China, which also lists tombs of the kingdom within its borders. The kingdom had a capital at Pyongyang from the fifth century and built walled mountain cities that were easy to defend. Its tombs were mounded with earth and covered in grass, and the chambers inside were sealed with stone doors and painted by court artists. They survived looters and centuries of damp, and the paintings have been a difficult conservation task.

For anyone curious, the best way to see them is through scholarship, museum exhibits in South Korea and Japan, and the careful photographs published by the UNESCO team. The landscape is gentle, the climate has hot, wet summers and cold, dry winters, and spring and autumn are the pleasant seasons.
t.seoul@37.6,127.0:
Seoul is a capital that sits in a bowl of granite mountains, and that is why it feels so layered. Bukhansan rises behind the old palaces to the north, Namsan stands in the middle with its tower, and the Han River slides through the south. The city has been the Korean capital since 1394, when the Joseon dynasty chose it, and the royal palace of Gyeongbokgung was built soon after. A fortress wall still climbs some of the ridges, and walking even a short section gives a fine view over the roofs. Insadong, with its tea houses and craft shops, and the hanok streets of Bukchon preserve the old style of wooden courtyard houses among the modern towers.

Riding in Seoul is not for the faint-hearted. Traffic is dense, lanes are fast, and delivery riders thread through everything at high speed. The city has a ring of expressways and a web of bridges across the Han, and parking is scarce and often expensive. If you must ride in, plan your route with care and consider leaving the bike outside the centre and taking the metro, which is clean, cheap and extremely efficient. The rewards of a ride out of the city are close: within an hour you can be in Bukhansan National Park, or on quiet mountain roads east of the capital with long views and few cars.

Food is the reason many people come. Barbecue restaurants fill the evenings with smoke and talk, street vendors sell tteokbokki, a chewy rice-cake dish in red sauce, and the markets at Gwangjang serve fresh bindaetteok, a mung bean pancake fried to order. Coffee shops are everywhere and open late. The Cheonggyecheon stream, restored from under a highway in 2005, makes a pleasant walk through the middle of the city.

Fuel is easy to find, although petrol stations in the centre are fewer than on the outskirts. Spring brings cherry blossom, autumn brings crisp air and clear sky, and both are the best times to visit. Winter is bitterly cold with dry winds, and summer is humid, with heavy monsoon rain through July.
t.naseong city wall@36.3,126.9:
Buyeo was once called Sabi, and for more than a century in the sixth and seventh centuries it was the capital of Baekje, one of the three kingdoms of ancient Korea. Baekje was a seafaring, artistic state that traded with China, sent scholars and craftsmen to Japan, and shaped Japanese Buddhist art. The kingdom fell in 660 when a joint army of Silla and Tang China overran the capital. Naseong, the outer city wall, is what remains of Sabi's defences: a long earthen rampart that once enclosed the town, running along the hills to the north and east and meeting the Geum River, which formed a natural moat on the other side. You can walk sections of it under old pines, and the grassy mounds are quiet and unassuming.

The legend of Nakhwaam, the Rock of the Falling Flowers, is told along the river nearby. According to the story, three thousand court ladies threw themselves from the cliff above the water rather than be captured. Historians doubt the number, but the cliff is real and so is the sadness of the tale. The Geum is a wide, slow river, and the view from the rock is pleasant, with a ferry across the water.

The riding here is gentle. Flat farmland, paddy fields and low hills make up the landscape of Chungcheong, with country roads between villages and the occasional old stone bridge. The surface is generally good, speed cameras are frequent, and the terrain suits a relaxed day. Buyeo is a small town, about thirty thousand people, with fuel and decent restaurants, and Nonsan, a bit further, is bigger. Buyeo is known for its lotus ponds, especially the restored Gungnamji, a pond with a pavilion that glows pink and white in July and August.

The museum in town holds the Baekje incense burner, a gilded bronze piece of great delicacy found in a ditch near the temple site at Neungsan-ri, and it is regarded as a masterpiece of the period. It is worth an hour's visit. Come in spring or early autumn, when the air is clear and the heat has not yet built up.
t.kangso three tombs@39.0,125.4:
The three tombs at Kangso stand in a quiet part of the countryside near the west coast of North Korea, not far from the Taedong River. They date from the Goguryeo kingdom, probably from the late fifth or early sixth century, and each is a grass-covered mound over a stone chamber. The Great Tomb is the best known, painted inside with a vivid picture of the Four Guardians: the Azure Dragon of the east, the White Tiger of the west, the Red Phoenix of the south and the Black Tortoise entwined with a snake of the north. The painted ceiling shows clouds, flying figures and mythical creatures. The group belongs to the Complex of Koguryo Tombs, which UNESCO listed in 2004.

As with other North Korean sites, an honest word is needed. Independent travel is not possible, and foreign visitors go on tightly organised tours with a guide and a driver. The tombs cannot be reached on a self-planned motorcycle trip, so what follows is context for those who want to understand the place.

Kangso lies in the district of Nampo, and the land is flat and watery, with rice paddies stretching toward the Yellow Sea. The Taedong flows to the sea near here, closed off by the long barrage that stands between river and ocean. Yonggang is the nearest small town, and Nampo, about twenty-five kilometres off, is the large port city. The weather has four distinct seasons, with a cold and dry winter, humid summer and a lovely autumn.

The Four Guardians have a history far beyond Korea. They come from Chinese cosmology and appear in tombs, temples and palaces across East Asia, and the Goguryeo painters gave them an elegance and energy that is unmistakable. Some experts see Daoist influence, others a distinctive Goguryeo spirit, and their vigour is often compared with later Korean art. The paintings have faded in some tombs and required major conservation, and those at Kangso are among the best preserved.

For those who cannot visit, replicas of these murals can be seen in museums in South Korea, and the research on them is well published. They are a reminder that the border between two states runs through a shared culture, much older than the line itself.
t.cologne@50.9,7.0:
Cologne's cathedral is the first thing you notice and the last thing you forget. The twin spires climb a hundred and fifty-seven metres above the Rhine, and the building took more than six hundred years, from 1248 to 1880, to finish, a scale of ambition that still feels slightly absurd. It survived the bombing of the Second World War, which flattened much of the surrounding city, and the sight of the black Gothic stone rising out of postwar rubble in old photographs is one of the great images of the period. Climb the tower if your knees allow; the view is the best in the city.

The city is much older than the cathedral. The Romans founded a colony here in the first century and named it after the emperor's wife Agrippina, and the word Colonia is the origin of the name Cologne. The Römisch-Germanisches Museum next to the cathedral shows a huge Roman mosaic where it was found. Cologne is also a city of beer and carnival. Kölsch, a pale, light beer served in tall thin glasses, is the only thing you should order in the brewery pubs of the old town, and the arrival of a new glass is automatic until you place your coaster on top.

The riding starts, like most big-city starts, with a bit of patience. The Rhine splits the city, and the bridges, such as the Hohenzollern railway bridge with its thousands of padlocks, can be congested at rush hour. Low-emission zones, one-way streets and tram lines are the order of the day. Once you are out of the urban area, the Kottenforst and the Eifel to the south give the best escape, with forest roads, gentle hills and quiet villages, and the Siebengebirge on the far side of the Rhine has some lovely twisty roads.

Fuel and food are no problem in a city of nearly a million people, with stations on every main road and bakeries at every corner. Weekdays are best for the way out, since the weekend brings visitors and local cyclists in numbers. The smell of the city is a mix of river, brewery and traffic. On a clear morning the light behind the cathedral is a good moment for a photograph before you roll away.
t.archaeological border complex of hedeby:
Hedeby, or Haithabu in German, was a Viking town on the shore of the Haddebyer Noor, a small branch of the Schlei, and for about three centuries it was one of the most important trading places in northern Europe. It was founded in the early 800s and grew into a market town where Frisian, Saxon, Slavic, Danish and Swedish merchants met, trading furs, amber, iron, glass and slaves. At its height it may have had a thousand or more inhabitants, and a semicircular rampart, open to the water, protected the whole settlement. In 1066 it was sacked and burned by a Slavic force, and the surviving population moved across the water to Schleswig.

Excavations in the twentieth century revealed that the waterlogged ground had preserved wood, leather, textiles and even a warship, found in the harbour. The museum at the site, a low building with a grass roof, shows the finds, including the remains of a longship, and a short walk away stand reconstructed Viking houses with thatched roofs and smoky interiors, which are lovely on a quiet weekday. UNESCO added Hedeby, together with the Danevirke, to the World Heritage List in 2018, as an outstanding example of a trading town linking Scandinavia to the continent.

The riding around the site is easy and rural. A narrow road leads down from the main road toward the Noor through fields and low trees, and there is parking near the museum. On summer weekends the place can be busy with families and school parties, and in the early morning or late afternoon it is very quiet. The Schlei, with its reed-fringed shores and sailing boats, is a few minutes away, and the villages round about have small bakeries and cafes.

Fuel and food are best found in Schleswig, only a few kilometres to the north-east, where stations, supermarkets and restaurants are plentiful. Groß Rheide and Dannewerk are small and have limited facilities. Bring a warm layer, since the wind comes across the water without anything to stop it, and the smell of wet reeds and woodsmoke from the reconstructed houses hangs in the air. Standing by the water, it is not hard to imagine a longship slipping in from the fjord with a cargo of furs.
t.whale sanctuary of el vizcaino@27.8,-114:
The Vizcaíno desert crosses the Baja California peninsula at its waist, a wide, flat plain of salt, scrub and cardon cactus that runs from the Pacific to the Gulf, and in it lies a sanctuary for the grey whale. El Vizcaíno Biosphere Reserve, one of the largest in Latin America, takes in two huge coastal lagoons where the whales come every winter to mate and give birth. UNESCO listed the sanctuary in 1993.

The town of Guerrero Negro, about twenty-seven kilometres away, grew up around the salt works. The giant evaporation ponds on the lagoon shore make the world's biggest salt-producing operation, and from the road the ponds look like pale mirrors. The town takes its name from the whaling ship Black Warrior, wrecked here in the 1850s. Ospreys build huge nests on poles and platforms around town, and a huge steel eagle monument marks the border between Baja California and Baja California Sur on Highway 1.

The ride down the peninsula is long, straight and hypnotic, with desert, shimmering heat and glimpses of the sea. The road is narrow and has little shoulder, trucks and campers share it, and crosswinds blow dust. Night riding is unwise because cattle, burros and potholes appear without warning. Winter, from December to April, is the best season for both whales and comfortable temperatures, while summer heat in the desert can reach forty degrees.

Fuel is available in Guerrero Negro, which has several stations, and it is wise to fill up whenever you can, since the next ones can be a long way off. The town has simple motels and restaurants serving fish tacos and clams. Whale-watching trips to the lagoon run in season from Guerrero Negro, with local guides. Carry water, a hat and cash, and remember that the sanctuary has rules to protect the animals.
t.laguna san ignacio@27.0,-113.2:
San Ignacio lagoon lies on the Pacific coast of Baja California Sur, about seventy kilometres by dirt road from the town of San Ignacio, and it is famous for a rare event: the grey whales that come here every winter to give birth sometimes approach small boats and let people touch them. The behaviour began in the 1970s and is still a mystery, but whales and calves come alongside, roll and look up, which has moved many a hardened traveller to tears.

The town of San Ignacio is a surprise in the desert. A spring-fed river runs through it, and a lush palm oasis of date palms, citrus and figs surrounds a quiet plaza, with a church at its head. The mission, founded by Jesuits in 1728, was completed by Dominicans in 1786 in thick lava stone, with a facade of carved saints. The Sierra de San Francisco, to the north, holds rock paintings, huge red and black figures of humans and animals on cliff walls, painted by an unknown people many centuries ago, and reached with guides on mule trails.

The road to the lagoon is rough, a graded track through salt flats and low scrub that can wash out after rain, and the final stretch is soft. It is not for heavily loaded road bikes. Many visitors go by vehicle with a tour company, camping at simple camps run by local families under a cooperative. Whale season runs from about January to March, with the best encounters often in February. Wind from the sea is cold, and the sun is strong.

Services are minimal. San Ignacio has fuel, small hotels and restaurants serving shrimp tacos and date sweets, and these are the last reliable supplies before the lagoon. Carry water, food and a spare tyre kit, and let someone know your plan. Respect park rules and the guidance of local guides, since the whales set the terms. It is one of the great wild-animal encounters, and worth the dust.
t.laguna ojo de liebre@27.8,-114.2:
Ojo de Liebre, which means hare's eye, is a huge shallow lagoon on the Pacific side of Baja California, and every winter it receives the largest gathering of grey whales on earth. The animals travel about ten thousand kilometres from the Bering and Chukchi seas, one of the longest migrations of any mammal, to give birth in warm, sheltered water. Calves are born between January and March, and in the lagoon, mothers teach them to swim and surface.

The lagoon was once called Scammon's Lagoon after the whaling captain Charles Scammon, who found it in 1857 and slaughtered hundreds of whales over the following years, nearly wiping out the species. Protection came in the twentieth century, and the population recovered, and today grey whales are a conservation success story. Local families, many of whom came as salt workers, now run boats and camps from a landing near the shore, taking small groups out on the water.

A trip out in a small panga is quietly astonishing. Whales surface beside you, blow clouds of mist, spy-hop, lifting their heads straight up to look around, and sometimes pass under the boat. Dolphins, pelicans and ospreys add to the show. The wind off the sea is chilly, so dress warm and windproof, and bring a hat and sun protection. Rules limit boats' distance and time, and the guides know when to stay back.

The dirt road from Highway 1 to the lagoon is about twenty kilometres, graded but washboarded, and sandy in places, so go slowly on a road bike or leave it and join a tour. Guerrero Negro has fuel, motels and restaurants, and is the base for most visitors. Season runs from December to April. Book a boat in advance during holiday weekends, bring cash, and plan to be on the water in the morning when the sea is calm.
t.maastricht@50.9,5.7:
Maastricht sits in the thin tail of the Netherlands that squeezes between Belgium and Germany, and you feel the border pressure the moment you leave town. Within a quarter of an hour on a bike you can be in Wallonia, and Aachen is not much further east. The Maas, which the French call the Meuse, runs straight through the middle, and the name of the city is simply the Latin for crossing the river. Romans put a bridge here, and the Sint Servaasbrug, still carrying traffic in its medieval form, is often called the oldest bridge in the country.

The old centre is a tangle of squares and churches that survived better than most Dutch towns. The Vrijthof is dominated by the Romanesque basilica of Saint Servatius, and a few steps away a former Dominican church has been turned into a bookshop, which is the kind of thing this city does well. The Treaty of Maastricht, the one that created the euro, was signed here in 1992, though the locals are prouder of their vlaai, the fruit pies of Limburg, which you should buy before you even think about a proper lunch.

As a place to start a ride it is easy and a little dull in the best sense: the roads out are flat, tidy, and fast to leave. The interesting riding begins to the south and east, where the land folds up into the Heuvelland, the only real hills in the country. Lanes climb and drop between orchards, half-timbered farms and little brick villages, and the surface is generally good, though tractors and cyclists in numbers are normal, especially on a dry weekend. Speed limits are enforced with cameras all over the Netherlands and you should assume that any long straight has one.

Under the Sint Pietersberg south of the centre runs a maze of old marl quarries, tunnelled for centuries, so the city is in a sense hollow beneath its hill. That limestone is also why you find so much pale stone in the older walls.

Fuel is no issue at all in a city of this size, and the ring roads have stations on every side. Parking a motorcycle in the centre is simplest at the edges of the pedestrian zone, and the riverside cafes along the Maas are the natural place to sit down for a coffee before you point the front wheel toward the border.
t.utrecht@52.1,5.1:
Utrecht is the middle of the Netherlands in a very literal way, and it feels it: trains from everywhere come through the station, and everything else is arranged around a canal that sits lower than the street. The Oudegracht has wharves and cellars cut into its banks, once warehouses for goods unloaded straight from boats, now cafes with tables at water level. Above it all stands the Dom Tower, a little over a hundred metres of Gothic stone, which you will see from the ring road long before you arrive.

The city began as a Roman fort on the Rhine and became the seat of a bishop, and for centuries it was the religious capital of the Low Countries. In 1579 the northern provinces signed the Union of Utrecht here, the first step toward the Dutch Republic. A more modern sort of fame belongs to Gerrit Rietveld, whose Schröder House, all crisp planes and primary colours, still looks like next year rather than the 1920s. Dick Bruna, who drew Miffy, was born in the city, and the rabbit is on the pavements and in the museum.

For a rider, Utrecht is a launch pad rather than a destination. The ring and the motorways are busy, and you want to be out of the built-up belt quickly. Heading east, the ground rises a little into the Utrechtse Heuvelrug, a wooded ridge of sand and gravel left by ice, where small roads wind through pine and heath and past country houses. To the north-west the river Vecht meanders on a narrow dike road lined with eighteenth-century estates, slow and pretty, with a speed limit that deserves respect. This is also where the old Dutch water defences run: forts and flooded fields built to protect Amsterdam, a theme you will meet again on the road toward the Pampus fort.

Weather is the usual Dutch mix, so a layer in the top box is sensible even on a warm day, and wind across the polders can be stronger than the trees suggest. Fuel is simple, with stations all around the edge of town and along every main road out. The best hour to roll out is early on a weekend, before the cycle lanes and the market stalls fill the city and the traffic lights start to bunch up.
t.groningen@53.2,6.6:
Look at Groningen from the Martinitoren and you understand the whole north of the Netherlands in one view: the city is a dense knot of brick and canal, and beyond it the land goes flat and open all the way to the Wadden Sea. The tower, a bit over ninety metres of church spire, has been the landmark for centuries. The Grote Markt below it is a big square that fills with students, since the university dates from 1614 and a large part of the population is under thirty. That makes the evenings livelier than you would expect from the quiet reputation of the province.

The country around is a landscape that was built by hand. Farmers heaped up mounds called wierden, the local word for the terpen of Friesland, so that their houses stayed dry when the sea came in, and nearly every village sits on one with a small Romanesque church of brick on top. Many of those churches are locked, but a key is often held in the village and the interiors, with painted vaults and old organs, are worth the question. Out in the east the Dollard bay marks where a storm flood tore a hole in the coast in the Middle Ages. Beneath the fields lies the big gas deposit that made the region rich and later made it shake, and in some villages the cracked walls tell that story better than any museum.

Riding here is about distance, light and wind. The roads run dead straight along drainage channels, and with the sky so wide the weather is visible for an hour before it reaches you. A westerly can make a fast stretch hard work and a head-on crosswind a real nuisance, so keep the shoulders loose. Dike roads are narrow and the speed limits are low, and cameras are common. In the evening the light goes long and gold across the fields, and cattle stand knee-deep in a low mist on cool nights.

The city has all the fuel you could need, and the ring road has stations on every side. After a day in the open it is a pleasure to come back to somewhere with warm brown cafes along the canals, where a plate of something local and a dark beer are easy to find.
t.hannover@52.2,9.9:
The dot lies south of Hannover in the valley of the Leine, near Sarstedt and Giesen, where the plain of the Hildesheimer Börde begins. This is one of the most fertile regions of Germany, with deep black loess soil that grows wheat, sugar beet and vegetables, and the horizon is a long line of fields, wind turbines and church spires. It is not a place for bends, but for easy kilometres, and it is where the ride, having visited the Kyffhäuser mountains in Thuringia, finds its way home.

The Kyffhäuser, far to the south-east, is a small range with a large legend. A huge monument, finished in 1896, stands on the ridge in honour of Kaiser Wilhelm I, and below it, a cave is said to hold the sleeping Emperor Frederick Barbarossa, who will wake when the ravens stop circling the mountain and restore the empire. The road up to the monument has tight hairpins through beech forest, a short and lively contrast to the plains.

Nearer to the dot, there are historical sights worth a few minutes. The neo-Gothic Marienburg castle, a short distance to the south-west near Nordstemmen, was built in the 1860s by King George V of Hanover as a gift to his wife, and it looks like something from a fairy tale, with towers and turrets on a wooded hill. Hildesheim, to the south-east, has a thousand-year-old rose bush on its cathedral wall and a restored old town.

Riding in the Börde is quiet and open. The roads are straight, with long views, and crosswinds can be strong. In harvest season, sugar beet trucks and combine harvesters share the lanes, and mud on the road is common, so be careful on corners. Sarstedt and Giesen are ordinary small towns with limited charm, but they have what you need.

Fuel and food are easy. Sarstedt has several stations and supermarkets, and bakeries open early, selling the sort of dark bread and sweet pastries that Lower Saxony does well. Hannover is only twenty minutes up the road. The best time is in late spring, when the fields are green and the rape is yellow, or at harvest, when the air is full of straw and dust.
t.hamburg north west edge@53.6,9.8:
Rellingen and Halstenbek lie on the north-western rim of Hamburg, in the Pinneberg district, and for anyone heading toward the North Sea they are the last of the city before the land opens out. This is tree-nursery country: Halstenbek and its neighbours form one of the largest centres for growing trees and shrubs in Europe, and in summer the fields are filled with orderly rows of young oaks, beeches, rhododendrons and roses, which gives the district a clean and scented feel.

Rellingen has a curious claim to fame. Its church, built in the 1750s, is a Baroque Protestant church of unusual elegance, with a bright interior and a high tower, and it is considered one of the most beautiful in Schleswig-Holstein. A short ride away is Pinneberg, a town with a small castle and an old centre, and further south, Wedel offers a view of the Elbe and its ship greeting station, where passing ships are welcomed with their national flag.

The ride's real subject, though, lies a hundred kilometres to the north-west: the dikes of the North Sea coast and the great flat sands of St. Peter-Ording, a seaside resort on the Eiderstedt peninsula whose beach is several kilometres wide at low tide. The road runs across marsh and farmland, with sheep on the dikes, tall skies and the smell of salt. The riding is easy and open, with long straights and plenty of wind, and the beauty is in the light and space.

Getting out of Hamburg is the challenge. The suburbs are dense, traffic is heavy at rush hour and the main roads are full of lights and cameras. The best plan is to leave early, before the commuters, when the roads are empty and the mist lies on the fields. Speed limits are low in the towns, and the Autobahn A23 carries a lot of heavy traffic.

Fuel is easy here, with stations on every main road and supermarkets in each village. Bakeries open early, and a rundstück, a crusty roll with ham, is a good start to the day. Be sure to fill up before leaving the built-up area, because the marshes have fewer stations. North German weather is changeable, so carry a rain jacket. A bright, windy morning in May or September is an excellent time to head west.
t.hanau@50.1,8.9:
Hanau sits where the Kinzig flows into the Main, east of Frankfurt, and it is the starting point of the German Fairy Tale Route because it is the birthplace of the Brothers Grimm. Jacob was born here in 1785 and Wilhelm a year later, and a large bronze monument of the two seated figures stands in front of the town hall on the market square. Hanau has about eighty-nine thousand people and was heavily damaged in the Second World War, so it is not a pretty old town, but it has a pleasant riverside and a long tradition of goldsmithing and jewellery.

The fairy tale route runs about six hundred kilometres to Bremen, following the places in the lives and stories of the Grimms, and the stretch to Kassel takes in some of the finest country in Hesse. A short way along is Steinau an der Straße, where the brothers spent part of their childhood in a half-timbered house, and the old town has a castle with a puppet theatre. Gelnhausen, further on, has the ruins of the great imperial palace of Barbarossa, built in the twelfth century on an island in the Kinzig, and a charming half-timbered centre.

Beyond that, the road climbs into the Vogelsberg, an ancient volcano field of rounded hills, woods and meadows that is among the largest basalt areas in Europe. The roads here are gentle, with long sweeping bends and little traffic, and the villages are neat and quiet. Fulda, with its baroque cathedral and abbey, is a handsome city, and the road continues north toward Kassel, where the Brothers Grimm worked for decades and where a museum holds their manuscripts and household copies of the tales. The Bergpark Wilhelmshöhe, with a giant statue of Hercules above a cascade of waterfalls, is a world heritage site and an astonishing sight.

Getting out of Hanau is simple enough, though the roads around Frankfurt are busy and the autobahn is the fastest option. Once in the countryside, the riding is relaxed, with decent tarmac and well-signed routes.

Fuel and food are easy, and cafes are everywhere. Look out for Handkäse mit Musik, a local cheese dish with onions and vinegar, if you are feeling brave, and a glass of apple wine in the Frankfurt style. The best time for the route is late spring or early autumn, when the forests are green or gold and the roads are quiet.
t.hannover south edge@52.3,9.8:
Pattensen is a small town on the southern fringe of Hannover, in the Calenberger Land, where the flat plain of the city meets the first gentle swells of the hill country that runs south toward the Weser. Its old centre has half-timbered houses and a medieval church, and the streets have a sleepy, slightly farm-like atmosphere even though the suburbs of the city are barely a few kilometres away. For a rider wanting to head south, this is the right place to start, because the main roads out of the city are behind you and the quiet roads begin almost at once.

The ride is named for Hann. Münden, a town about a hundred kilometres to the south, where the Werra and the Fulda come together to form the Weser. A stone at the point where they meet says that the two rivers lose their names and become one, and the old town, with more than seven hundred half-timbered houses, is among the best preserved in Germany. The town has a legend about Doctor Eisenbarth, an itinerant surgeon of the early eighteenth century who is said to have performed daring operations, and a costumed play recalls him in summer. Three rivers, in fact, include the Weser, and the confluence makes the valley wide, green and calm.

On the way you ride through a succession of low wooded ridges and river valleys. Between Hannover and Münden lie the Leinebergland, the Solling forest and the Reinhardswald, a large woodland of old oaks that is said to have inspired some of the Grimm fairy tales. The roads are generally smooth and winding, with lots of gentle bends in beech forest, and traffic is light outside weekends. Surface can be patchy in the forest, particularly after winter, and leaf litter makes autumn mornings slippery.

Fuel is easy at Pattensen and in the suburbs, and the small towns along the way have stations and bakeries, but the forests have few services, so fill up when you can. A good lunch stop is one of the village inns serving schnitzel or the regional Braunschweiger sausage.

Weather in Lower Saxony changes, and a clear morning can turn damp by afternoon. The light on the hills in late May, when the beeches are freshly green, is lovely, and so is October, when the forest turns copper.
t.hannover south east@52.3,9.8:
The Hannover fair grounds, one of the biggest exhibition centres in the world, lie just to the north of Laatzen, and for a few days each year the whole region fills with trade visitors. The dot sits on the southern edge of the city, at the gate of the Laatzen suburb, among a mix of warehouses, shopping centres and tidy residential streets. It is not a place that anyone visits for itself, but it is the right doorstep for a ride east to the Harz, because the autobahn and the quiet back roads both start here.

The Harz is the high point of northern Germany, a rounded range of granite and slate whose highest summit, the Brocken, reaches 1,141 metres and is often wrapped in cloud. It is famous for witches. Goethe set the Walpurgis Night scene of Faust on the Brocken, and every year on the night of 30 April, locals dress as witches and dance on the hills. A narrow-gauge steam railway still puffs to the summit from Wernigerode, and the sight of the little locomotive with its plume of white steam against dark spruce is one of the region's best photographs.

The overnight stop is Quedlinburg, a town of about twenty-four thousand people at the northern edge of the Harz, which has more than a thousand half-timbered houses and is on the UNESCO list. Henry I, the first king of the Germans, is said to have been elected here in 919, and the castle hill carries a Romanesque church of great beauty and a treasury that survived the centuries. The town has a particular atmosphere in the evening, when the day visitors depart and the lamps come on along the cobbled lanes.

The riding in the eastern Harz is excellent. Roads climb in broad bends through spruce forest and cross high moorland, with wide views over the plain, and the Selke valley has a particularly lovely winding road. Rübeland has caves open to visitors, and Thale has a rock plateau, the Hexentanzplatz, reached by cable car. Weather can be wet and misty, and the upper roads may have snow into spring.

Fuel is easy in Laatzen and on the autobahn, and in the Harz towns of Halberstadt and Wernigerode. Bring a warm layer for the summit.
t.hannover@52.4,9.6:
Seelze sits on the western edge of Hannover, where the Leine river and the Mittelland Canal run almost side by side across a flat plain, and its principal claim on the map is as a railway town. A huge marshalling yard has long dominated its southern flank, and the freight trains that rumble in and out give the place a faintly industrial rhythm. The countryside beyond is quiet, with fields, poplars and farm tracks, and a long, low line of woodland on the horizon.

That line is the Deister, a wooded ridge about fifteen kilometres to the south-west, which was once a centre of coal mining and is now a favourite of local walkers and mountain bikers. A little farther north, the Steinhuder Meer, the largest lake in Lower Saxony, is a shallow, reed-fringed expanse, popular with sailors and with flocks of migrating birds. Wunstorf, a small town nearby, has a Romanesque abbey church and an air base that occasionally brings giant transport planes low over the roads.

The ride that ends here has visited two great gaps in the hills. The Porta Westfalica is where the Weser breaks through the Wiehengebirge and the Wesergebirge, and a huge monument to Kaiser Wilhelm I, completed in 1896, stands on one side of the gap, with a view over the valley and the plain beyond. The Solling is a quiet upland forest further south, a landscape of beech and spruce with narrow roads and almost no traffic.

The riding in the Seelze district is flat and plain, and the main hazards are farm vehicles, cyclists and wind. In summer, the evening light on the fields is excellent, and the mist rises from the Leine in the early morning. Speed cameras guard some of the larger roads, and road works are common in the area.

Fuel is easy in Seelze and Letter, with stations on the main roads and supermarkets in the centre. Cafes and bakeries are found in most of the villages. Hannover's city centre is only a few kilometres away, so a last coffee in the old town, around the Marktkirche, is an option.
t.hannover@52.4,9.9:
On the eastern side of Hannover, the city stretches into leafy suburbs, and the dot lies near the Mittelland Canal, among tidy housing estates and patches of woodland. Hannover is a big, sensible city, rebuilt after heavy bombing in the Second World War, and it has an unexpectedly green heart in the Eilenriede, a city forest of old oaks and beeches, one of the largest urban forests in Europe, where people ride, jog and walk dogs between the lakes and meadows.

The ride from here goes east to the Elm and the Lappwald, two low, wooded ridges near the old border, where half-timbered villages sit among fields and beech woods. Königslutter, nearby, has a magnificent Romanesque cathedral, the Kaiserdom, whose stone carvings include lions and strange creatures, and the town is a good place for an unhurried look. The Harz edge and the Oker valley are the high point of the day: the Oker flows through a narrow gorge of granite and spruce, with a winding road, and a waterfall at Romkerhalle, a popular stop.

The roads of the Elm are quiet, narrow and gently winding, through woods of beech and oak, with farm lanes branching off. The Oker valley road is a classic, with sharp bends and rock walls, though it is busy at weekends, with bikers and cyclists sharing the tarmac. Surfaces vary, and in autumn, wet leaves make corners slippery, so a gentle approach pays off.

Fuel and food are easy on this side of the city. Lehrte and Laatzen, the nearest large towns, have supermarkets, stations and cafes. In the Harz foothills, Bad Harzburg and Goslar are both good for coffee. Goslar, with its imperial palace and half-timbered streets, is a World Heritage site, and an easy and rewarding place to stop.

In summer, the afternoon sun is warm and the evening long. If your trip finishes at dusk, the light on the city's spires and the Eilenriede's canopy makes for a quiet, satisfying arrival.
t.hannover@52.5,9.8:
North of Hannover, near Langenhagen and Isernhagen, the city turns into a district of villas, horse paddocks and big gardens, and the sky fills with the sound of aircraft. Hannover Airport lies in Langenhagen, and the approach and departure paths pass low over the roads. The suburban landscape is flat, tidy and a little anonymous, but after a long day among hills and forests, it is exactly what is needed for a gentle landing.

The ride that finishes here has explored two different ranges. The Ith and Hils are narrow limestone ridges, running north-west to south-east between the Leine and Weser, with beech forests, cliffs and viewpoints, and a number of steep, winding roads that rise in tight bends. The Ith has a long ridge-top track where climbers practise on the limestone crags, and the road beneath it is an enjoyable run through villages. The Leinebergland is a gentle rolling country of woods, valleys and farms, with roads that rise and fall continuously.

The other half of the route lies to the north, in the Harburger Berge and the Lüneburg Heath, an area of sandy hills, pine woods and open heather that glows purple in late August and September. The Harburg hills, just south of Hamburg, are a gentle forested ridge, and the Lüneburg Heath is among the best-known landscapes in northern Germany, with flocks of heather sheep, called Heidschnucken, grazing the moors.

At the edge of Hannover, riding is straightforward but busy. The roads around the airport are wide and fast, there are speed cameras, and traffic is heavy at rush hour. The city's inner streets have tram tracks, and cobbles in the old town can be slippery when wet. A little patience goes a long way.

Fuel and food are very easy, with a wide choice of stations, supermarkets and restaurants in Langenhagen and Isernhagen. Many bakeries open early, and cafes are open late. Hannover is known for its lack of fuss, and a plain meal of Schnitzel or fish, with a glass of the local Herrenhäuser beer, is the right way to end a ride.
t.naarden fortress@52.3,5.2:
Seen from the air, Naarden is a star. The little town in the Gooi, thirty minutes east of Amsterdam, is wrapped in a perfectly geometric twelve-pointed fortress, with ramparts, moats and bastions arranged in a double ring that was one of the most advanced designs in seventeenth-century Europe. It was built to defend the approach to Amsterdam and later became part of the Dutch Water Line, the system of flooding fields that protected the heart of the country. Inside the walls, the houses sit in neat little streets, and the old town is quiet and well preserved.

The history here includes a dark moment. In 1572, during the Eighty Years' War, Spanish troops entered Naarden after the town surrendered, and the people were massacred, a story still told in the town. The philosopher and educator Jan Amos Comenius, a Czech refugee who spent his last years in Amsterdam, is buried in Naarden, and a small mausoleum commemorates him. The Grote Kerk is the setting each spring for a traditional performance of Bach's St Matthew Passion, which attracts a devoted audience.

For the rider, Naarden is a pleasant place for a halt rather than a place to ride. The streets within the walls are narrow and cobbled, and parking in the middle is limited, so leave the bike outside the ramparts and walk in. The ramparts themselves make a nice stroll, with water and grass on both sides, and the walls are lovely in autumn. Roads in the surrounding Gooi are flat, quick and busy with commuters, cyclists and trams, so you need to take care at junctions and roundabouts. Speed cameras are common, and fines are heavy. On the way east, the roads climb gently toward the Veluwe woodland, and the landscape changes into heath and forest.

Bussum, just over two kilometres away, is a town of thirty thousand and has fuel, supermarkets and a good choice of cafes. Within the old walls there are small restaurants and bakeries around the market square. Weekdays are quiet, and weekends bring tourists.
t.hannover west escape@52.4,9.5:
The Deister is a long, wooded ridge that rises abruptly from the flat country west of Hannover, and this starting point lies at its northern foot, in the farmland between Groß Munzel and Großgoltern. Barsinghausen, a town of fourteen thousand about seven kilometres away, is the gateway to the hills. Coal was mined in the Deister until 1957, and traces of that industry survive in the old shafts and railway embankments that you find in the forest.

The area is a good place to begin a ride because the roads quickly shake off the suburban feel. Within ten minutes you can be on winding lanes through beech woods, past fields of wheat and sugar beet, and on the way to the Weser hills beyond. The Extertal and Lippe uplands lie to the south-west, a region of low hills, deep valleys and half-timbered villages, where the roads are quiet and the corners are gentle.

North German weather is something to be reckoned with. The wind sweeps across the plain with little to stop it, and showers can arrive suddenly, so pack a waterproof even on a sunny morning. The best months are May and June and again in September, when the light is clear and the woods are fresh or golden. Traffic is moderate on weekdays, but fills up on sunny weekends, particularly near the larger villages and viewpoints.

Fuel is no problem here, with several stations in Barsinghausen and around the ring road of Hannover, and the usual run of bakeries and cafés in town. Start with a full tank and a good breakfast, and you will not need to stop for a while. Hannover itself, a short ride east, is a city with a long British connection, since its ruling family took the British throne in 1714, and the Herrenhausen gardens, laid out for the electors, are worth a morning if you have one to spare. For now, though, the Deister is waiting.
t.hannover@52.4,9.5:
Coming back into Hannover from the west, the city rises out of flat farmland a little too modestly, with the green mass of the Deister ridge behind you and the tower of a power station somewhere ahead. Hannover does not shout. It is a city of half a million people that was flattened by bombing in the Second World War and rebuilt with more sense than glamour, and the best of it is tucked into corners you have to know about. The Maschsee, a big artificial lake dug by hand in the 1930s as a work programme, is the place the locals walk, run and sail on summer evenings.

Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, the philosopher and mathematician who co-invented calculus, spent the last forty years of his life here in service to the ruling family, and the Hannover trade fair, the world's largest industrial show, has filled the city's hotels every spring since the late 1940s. For tourists there is a red line painted on the pavement that leads walkers through the old town, a very Hannover solution to the problem of how to show someone around.

The ride home is the opposite of dramatic, and that is its charm. The last hour from the hills runs along rural roads through the Calenberg country, past fields of sugar beet and wheat, and the little villages of Groß Munzel and Großgoltern, with their brick farms and half-timbered barns. The wind, if there is one, comes from the west and carries a smell of cut grass and diesel. Egestorf, five kilometres away, has the nearest bigger shops, and Barsinghausen has more.

Fuel is plentiful across the whole district, with stations every few kilometres on the roads towards the ring, so you can relax about range here. If you have a spare hour, park near the New Town Hall and take the lift up the dome for a view across the city, which flattens out into plain on every side. Then find a table outside somewhere on the Leine, order a beer, and let the engine tick as it cools.
t.hannover south east edge@52.3,9.8:
Laatzen is where Hannover's southern edge turns into the exhibition halls, a town of forty thousand, with the great fair grounds a few minutes away. The Expo of the year 2000 was held on this side of the city, and the vast halls and the odd, slightly futuristic pavilions that survive give the district a strange, half-empty feel on a quiet morning. It is a spot to meet and set off, not a place to linger.

South of here the Leine plain stretches towards Hildesheim, an agricultural landscape of sugar beet, wheat and wide skies, with the Harz mountains a faint blue line in the distance on a clear day. The villages, Pattensen and Sarstedt among them, are brick-built and low, with the odd church tower rising above the roofs. Pattensen has a small old centre with timber-framed houses and is a good place for a bakery stop.

The route from here heads to the Oker valley and the hills around Clausthal, which is the most interesting part. That means going from flat farmland to forested Harz mountains in a couple of hours, through Goslar and the Oker gorge, where the road follows the river between granite cliffs. The Harz has real hairpins, steep forested slopes and, in winter, snow, so plan the season accordingly. Spring and early autumn are best.

Traffic on the plain can be heavy, especially when trade fairs are on, and roundabouts and traffic lights come thick and fast. The bypass roads help, but there is no way to avoid the stop-and-start entirely. Fill up here, because the cities on the plain have plenty of fuel and the mountains have far fewer stations, and eat something before you leave, since you will be a while. Hannover is cheap and easy to leave, and the contrast with the hills is what makes the day. Just make sure you know which road you want before you join the motorway.
t.rendsburg high bridge@54.3,9.7:
The Rendsburg high bridge is the sort of structure that makes people stop and take photographs, even if they do not care about engineering. Completed in 1913, it carries a railway line over the Kiel Canal on a long iron girder, 42 metres above the water so that the tallest ships can pass underneath. The railway does not simply cross the canal, however; it loops down and around the town on an enormous spiral so the trains can lose height gently, and the result is a steel ribbon that circles over the roofs.

Hanging from the bridge is the other attraction, a transporter ferry, a platform suspended from rails that glides across the canal carrying cars and pedestrians. There are very few of these left in the world, and this one is still running and costs next to nothing to use. Riding onto it is a small adventure, and the view of ships passing close overhead is worth the short wait.

The Kiel Canal, which opened in 1895 as the Kaiser Wilhelm Canal, links the North Sea with the Baltic, saving ships a long trip around Denmark, and it is one of the busiest artificial waterways in the world. Watching a huge container ship slide silently past a quiet town street is one of those odd, memorable northern German sights. The roads that run beside the canal are straight, flat and quiet, with a service road on each bank and long views through the trees.

The point lies at ten metres above the sea, close to the centre of Rendsburg, a town of twenty-eight thousand with fuel stations, supermarkets and plenty of places to eat. Büdelsdorf, next door, is big as well. The wind blows constantly over the open country, and you will feel it on the bridge approaches. Allow time for the ferry, since it only carries a few vehicles at a time, and bring a camera. The best light comes in the late afternoon, when the ironwork turns a deep red-brown and the ships glow.
t.loccum abbey sight@52.5,9.2:
The old Cistercian abbey of Loccum stands among the fields and forests of western Lower Saxony, about four kilometres from the town of Rehburg-Loccum, and it has been here since 1163. That alone makes it an unusual place, since it survived the Reformation and became Protestant without being dissolved, and it is still a Lutheran monastic community, where trainee pastors study and monks live much as they did centuries ago. The long brick church, with its plain, high-vaulted interior, is a fine example of the austere Cistercian style.

The Cistercians chose their sites with care, favouring quiet valleys with clean water and good soil, and Loccum is a textbook case: a green, well-watered hollow, with ponds and meadows around the cloister buildings. The monks cleared forest, drained marshes and improved the land, and over the centuries the abbey grew rich and powerful. The abbot still has a special status in the Lutheran church, a curious relic of that past.

Riding here from Hannover brings you through a flat, green landscape, with the Rehburg hills rising gently to the south and the great shallow lake of Steinhuder Meer lying to the east, the largest lake in Lower Saxony. The roads are quiet and straight, with the occasional bend through woodland, and cyclists are common. Sandy soils and pine woods mix with fields of maize and wheat, and the villages are small and prosperous.

Rehburg-Loccum has just under eleven thousand people and has fuel, shops and a few places to eat, while Leese and Wölpinghausen are smaller. The abbey grounds are open to visitors, though church services and events can limit access, so check before you come. Walk through the cloister if you can, and listen to the silence. It is a rare quiet spot for a rider, and a good place to turn the engine off for ten minutes and think about nothing at all.
t.neustadt am rubenberge@52.5,9.5:
Neustadt am Rübenberge is a town that spreads wide across the flat country northwest of Hannover, one of the larger municipalities in Lower Saxony by area, with some forty-six thousand people living in the centre and dozens of villages around it. The Leine river slides past the old town, which has a castle called Landestrost from the sixteenth century, and the broad, low plain around it is where the Hanoverian farmers grew their wealth.

This is a food stop, in the plainest sense of the phrase. The town centre has bakeries, cafés and restaurants, and you should be able to find a decent plate of schnitzel or a currywurst, a German classic, without any trouble. If you want something more local, look for asparagus in spring and for smoked fish in the shops. Do not expect the town to be pretty, because it was rebuilt in a practical way, but it is friendly, and the market square is a comfortable place to sit.

Nearby, the great moorland and shallow lake of Steinhuder Meer, north-west of here, are worth a detour. The lake is only a couple of metres deep, and it is popular with sailors, who can wade out into the water if they run aground. The old moors around it are protected and full of birds, and the villages on the shore, such as Mardorf, serve smoked eel, a local speciality.

Fuel is easy, since Neustadt has stations along the main roads, and the larger town of Wunstorf lies nine kilometres south for backup. The roads out of town are flat and straight, running through farmland, with the occasional wind-bent tree and a dusting of farm mud. Take it easy through the villages, where the speed limits are enforced, and watch for tractors. It is a modest, practical stop, and it does what it says on the label.
t.hamburg@53.6,9.8:
Pinneberg, Halstenbek and Rellingen lie just north-west of Hamburg, and between them they make up one of the largest tree-growing regions in Europe. For miles on end the fields are filled with rows of young trees, shrubs, roses and rhododendrons, grown for gardens and parks all over the continent. In May, when the rhododendrons bloom, the whole district turns into an unlikely riot of colour, and the roads between the nurseries are some of the most pleasant on the edge of the city.

Rellingen has a church that is a famous example of north German Baroque, built in the middle of the eighteenth century for a Protestant congregation, with a centralised design and a bright, airy interior. The town itself is a quiet, tidy suburb. Pinneberg, the district capital, has a pleasant old centre, with a moated residence called the Drostei, now a cultural centre, and a handful of cafés on the main street.

This is where the ride finishes, back at the edge of the city after a long day on the coast, and it feels like a gentle landing. The roads here are flat, with slow bends and few surprises, and the traffic picks up on the approach to Hamburg, so stay alert. After the open dikes and big skies of the North Sea, the neat hedges and garden fences of the suburbs feel almost cosy. The wind drops, the air gets warmer, and you can finally take your gloves off.

Fuel is plentiful, with stations at every roundabout and big supermarkets in Pinneberg and Halstenbek, a town of sixteen thousand. If you want a good place to rest, the nurseries sometimes have cafés, where you can have a coffee among the plants. Check the opening times, since they change with the season. Hamburg is a short hop away, and the first sight of the harbour cranes on the horizon tells you the day is nearly done.
t.haithabu sight@54.5,9.6:
Haithabu, known in Danish as Hedeby, was the greatest Viking trading town in northern Europe, and its site lies on the shore of the Haddeby Noor, an inlet of the Schlei, only three kilometres from the town of Schleswig. From the eighth century to the eleventh, ships from Scandinavia, the Baltic, the Frisian coast and even the Islamic world met here, because the town sat at the narrowest point of the Jutland peninsula, where goods could be hauled overland between the North Sea and the Baltic, avoiding the stormy journey around Denmark.

Everything was burned and abandoned after a raid in 1066, and the town never came back. That is lucky for archaeologists, because the site was left alone, and the wet ground kept wood, leather and textiles in excellent condition. Excavations have found workshops, jewellery, coins from distant lands and the wrecks of ships, including a long warship. A museum on the site shows finds and has reconstructed houses on the original plots, a good way to understand how cramped and busy the town must have been. Haithabu and the great earthwork of the Danevirke were inscribed together as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2018.

For a rider it is a quiet, flat place, with the road running through meadows and reed beds beside the water, and a slight smell of mud and fish in warm weather. The best time to come is in the morning, before the school groups and coaches. Walk along the shore and the old rampart, which still curves around the site in a half-circle, and you can almost feel the size of the town.

Fahrdorf, a few kilometres away, has some shops and a bakery, but for fuel and a proper lunch go to Schleswig, a town of twenty-four thousand, where there are stations and a fine harbour. The ground is only eight metres above sea level, so there are no hills, only long views over the water. Bring a jacket, since the wind can be sharp even in summer. The Viking festival days are a lively time to visit, but check the dates.
t.hannover west edge@52.4,9.7:
Hannover's western edge is mostly rail yards, canal bank and green fringe, and it tells the city's industrial story more honestly than the old town does. The Mittelland Canal, the long artificial waterway that links the Rhine and the Elbe, passes near Seelze, and barges move quietly along it all day, a calm, almost hypnotic sight. The Leine river is close too, with its wide floodplain, and the city's factories once clustered along both.

Hannover has long made things. The tyre company Continental was founded here in 1871, and the biscuit maker Bahlsen, famous for its Leibniz biscuits, has been in the city since the nineteenth century. This part of the city has little of the polished charm of the centre, but it has a gritty authenticity, and it is where many locals live and work. Ronnenberg and Seelze are practical towns, with shops, stations, and the ordinary bustle of commuter life.

For a rider, the beauty is in leaving. In half an hour the suburban ring thins, and you reach farmland and the long, wooded ridge of the Deister, whose slopes the road climbs and descends in a series of gentle bends. The Weserbergland beyond, with its half-timbered villages and quiet valleys, is the real destination, and the route is a sweep through it, along minor roads that follow rivers and cross wooded hills. The Weser itself is wide and slow, a typical north German river.

Traffic is the issue on the edge of the city, with its junctions, traffic lights and slow commuters, so start early on a weekday or on a quiet Sunday. Fuel is not a concern, with plenty of stations and a supermarket on every corner, and Seelze, with some thirty-three thousand people, has all you need. Fill up here, because the hills have fewer pumps. A bakery coffee and a quick check of the tyre pressure, and you are away to the south-west.
t.hannover south west@52.2,9.6:
Springe sits at the southern foot of the Deister, a ridge of beech forest that runs across the landscape between Hannover and the Weser hills. It is a town of nearly thirty thousand, with an old centre of half-timbered houses, and it has its own claim to fame: the Saupark, a large walled forest that was once a royal hunting ground for the Hanoverian rulers, still home to wild boar and deer. The wall can be followed for miles, and gives a sense of how seriously the nobility took their hunting.

This starting gate is on the edge of town, with the ridge rising behind it, and the roads that leave here are some of the best in the region. They climb gently through the forest and out onto quiet farmland on the far side, with valleys, small villages and wide views. Wennigsen and Bad Münder, both with their own spa histories and half-timbered cores, are close by. The hills around here are not high, but they are well wooded, and the roads wind in ways that make the day feel longer.

Weather matters more than you might think. The Deister catches the rain, and low cloud can hang over the ridge for days in autumn and winter, while the summer brings the occasional thunderstorm. Spring and early summer are lovely, with fresh green beech leaves and clear air, and the autumn colour is gold and rust. The forest roads can be damp and covered in leaves, so take it easy on the corners.

Fuel is no problem in Springe, with stations on the main roads and several supermarkets, and the larger town of Bad Münder am Deister has more. This is a good place to start the day with a coffee and a fresh roll, because the next stop may be a long way off. The ride goes on to the Weser, and then through the Solling, a vast forested upland, so make sure everything is ready before you go. A short walk around the town centre is a pleasant way to warm up.
t.hoxter old town view@51.8,9.4:
Höxter sits on the west bank of the Weser, one of the old river towns of the Weserbergland, and its centre is a close-packed cluster of half-timbered houses and a church tower. This is the view you want: the roofs, the river and the forested hills beyond. The town has thirty thousand people if you count its surrounding villages, and a long history that began when the Franks built a river crossing here.

The great monument is just outside the town, at Corvey. This Carolingian abbey, founded in the ninth century, has a massive westwork, a fortress-like entrance hall, that survives almost unchanged, and it was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2014. Corvey was one of the great centres of learning in medieval Germany, and later its library became one of the richest in the country. The poet Hoffmann von Fallersleben, who wrote the words of the German national anthem, worked as librarian here and is buried in the abbey grounds.

The roads around Höxter are a pleasure. The Weser valley is broad and green, and the road follows the river, with low hills and forests rising on both sides. Further on, the Solling opens into a huge area of beech and spruce forest, with quiet roads that wind through the trees and over low passes. The bends are gentle and flowing, with very little traffic, and in the early morning there is often mist on the river. Autumn and late spring are the best seasons.

Fuel is easy in Höxter, which has several stations and supermarkets, and Boffzen and Fürstenberg are smaller villages along the river. Fürstenberg is known for its porcelain, made there since the eighteenth century. Park near the old town, walk to the river and find a bench, and you have the best view in the area. A bakery coffee and a slice of cake is the right reward for the miles, and there are plenty of places to buy them. The light in late afternoon on the old roofs is lovely.
t.hannover@52.2,9.6:
The ride ends where it began, at the foot of the Deister near Springe, with the long wooded ridge behind you and the plain of Hannover stretching away in front. After a day in the forests of the Solling and the quiet valleys of the Weser, the return is a gentle comedown, with roads that grow straighter and busier as the city gets closer. The ridge itself is a good landmark, a long dark line against the sky that tells you home is near.

Bad Münder am Deister, a spa town of nearly nineteen thousand, lies just to the south, and it has been known for its salt springs for centuries. The old centre has timber houses and a spa park, and it is a pleasant place to finish the day with a coffee. Further south along the Weser, a ride of less than an hour, lies Hamelin, the town of the Pied Piper. According to the legend, a stranger in colourful clothes led the rats and later the children of the town away with his music, a story that has been told since the Middle Ages and still draws visitors to Hamelin.

The road home runs through gentle farmland, with wide fields of wheat and sugar beet, and the last light of the day catching the church towers. The Deister's beech forest, which covers the ridge, turns golden in autumn, and the roads that climb through it are quiet and winding. Watch for deer at dusk, because they cross the road without warning, and for cyclists on the way back in.

Springe has plenty of fuel and food, and Wennigsen, a larger village six kilometres away, offers more of the same. It is a good place to stop, check your bike, and take a long look at the evening sky. The weather over the Deister can change quickly, so if clouds are building, put your waterproofs on before you set off for the last leg. It's an easy, comfortable finish, and the right kind of ending to a long day.
t.rendsburg canal view@54.3,9.7:
The Kiel Canal is the busiest artificial waterway in the world, measured by the number of ships, and in Rendsburg you can see why. The town sits right on its bank, and ships glide silently through the middle of the landscape, appearing over the fields like something out of a dream. Opened in 1895 as the Kaiser Wilhelm Canal, it cuts across the neck of the Jutland peninsula, linking the North Sea and the Baltic and saving vessels a long and stormy voyage around Denmark.

Free ferries still cross the canal at several places, a cheerful survival in a country that likes to charge for things, and the bank roads give you a quiet, straight run beside the water. You can stop on a bank and watch a tanker or a container ship go by, so close that you can see the crew. The sheer size of the vessels in a landscape of cornfields never quite loses its strangeness.

Rendsburg is a town of twenty-eight thousand, on the old frontier between Holstein and Schleswig, which was marked by the Eider river. The medieval centre is small, and the real attractions are the old arsenal and the garrison buildings. Next door, in Büdelsdorf, the Carlshütte ironworks, founded in the 1820s, has been turned into an art venue that hosts a big sculpture show every summer, an unexpected treat in a small town.

Fuel and food are no problem here, and there are plenty of bakeries, cafés and supermarkets. The point sits just ten metres above sea level, and the wind blows freely across the water, so be ready for gusts. If the day is fine, find a bench on the canal bank, with a coffee, and let the ships go by. The air smells of diesel and cut grass, and the horn blasts echo across the fields. It is a calm, surprisingly absorbing place to spend half an hour.
t.hannover@52.3,9.5:
The last hour of a long ride is often the quietest, and the approach to Hannover from the west has a calm of its own. The point lies in the Calenberg country, near the villages of Großgoltern and Groß Munzel, with the dark ridge of the Deister to the south and the flat plain of the Leine stretching away to the north. Egestorf, five kilometres away, has the nearest shops and fuel, and Barsinghausen is just beyond.

If you are coming home from the Teutoburg Forest and the Externsteine, you have had a long day. The Externsteine, a group of tall sandstone pillars in the forest near Horn-Bad Meinberg, have been a place of pilgrimage and speculation for centuries.
