A medieval relief carved into the rock shows the descent from the cross, and nobody quite knows what earlier peoples may have done there. They make a striking contrast with the plain and orderly fields around Hannover, which seem tame by comparison.

The country here is soft and ordinary and all the more restful for it. The roads run straight across fields of sugar beet and wheat, interrupted by small brick villages with square church towers, and the Deister's beech forest lifts the horizon to the south. In late afternoon the light slants across the stubble, and the long shadows of the hedgerows stripe the road. A sudden shower can sweep across the plain in minutes, so keep an eye on the sky to the west.

For a final stop, Egestorf has a bakery and a couple of cafés, and Barsinghausen, with its fourteen thousand people, has everything. The local coal mining ended in the 1950s, and the old pithead buildings are now part of a museum, which tells the story of the Deister's underground past. If you have half an hour, walk into the forest and look at the old mining paths. Then switch the engine on, and the last stretch into the city is a gentle glide.
t.schleswig harbour sight@54.5,9.6:
Schleswig lies at the head of the Schlei, a narrow, winding arm of the Baltic that reaches forty kilometres inland and looks more like a river than a fjord. The harbour is small and cheerful, with sailing boats, a few pleasure steamers and a promenade where people stroll and eat fish rolls. Across the water you can see the roofs of the old town, and above them the slim spire of the cathedral, whose tower rises to well over a hundred metres and dominates the skyline for miles.

The cathedral holds a treasure, the Bordesholm Altar, a huge carved oak altarpiece made in the early sixteenth century by the sculptor Hans Brüggemann. Not far away, on a spit of land by the water, is Holm, an old fishermen's village of tiny, brightly painted cottages and narrow lanes, with its own small church and graveyard. It is the sort of place where the clocks seem to run slowly. Further out, Gottorf Castle, once the seat of the dukes of Schleswig-Holstein-Gottorf, now holds major museums.

The roads along the Schlei are some of the finest in the region for a relaxed ride. They wind through villages, past reed beds and small harbours, with the water glinting through the trees, and the traffic is light outside the summer. The country is flat but never dull, with big skies and plenty of birds, including herons, swans and the occasional sea eagle. Wind is the main factor, since the water funnels the breeze, and the weather can change in minutes.

Schleswig is a town of twenty-four thousand, with fuel stations, supermarkets, bakeries and a number of good restaurants, many of them specialising in fish. Smoked herring and Schlei fish are local favourites. Neuberend and Fahrdorf, smaller villages nearby, have a few cafés. If you have time, walk along the harbour and look at the boats, then choose a table with a view. The water, the light and the birds will do the rest.
t.friedrichstadt canal@54.4,9.1:
Friedrichstadt looks, at first glance, like a piece of Holland that has wandered north and settled down in Schleswig-Holstein, and the resemblance is no accident. Duke Frederick III of Holstein-Gottorf founded the town in 1621 as a haven for Dutch Remonstrants, a Protestant sect that was being persecuted at home, and he hoped they would bring trade and skills to his marshy corner of the country. They brought canals, gabled brick houses and a tidy grid of streets, and the town is still laid out that way today.

What made Friedrichstadt unusual was its tolerance. Lutherans, Mennonites, Catholics and Jews all settled here, each with their own church or synagogue, and the town prided itself on religious freedom at a time when most of Europe was tearing itself apart over the issue. Walking the canals, with their little humped bridges, you can still feel something of that spirit. The market square is lined with stepped gables, and the canals are crossed by small wooden bridges, with boat trips available in summer.

The surrounding countryside is flat, open marsh, with the Eider and Treene rivers meeting nearby, and the roads run straight over dikes and across drained fields, with sheep grazing and wide skies overhead. The wind is a constant, and on a stormy day it can blow hard, so lean into it. Further west the Eiderstedt peninsula pushes out into the North Sea, with its church towers and thatched farms, and it is one of the most distinctive landscapes in Germany.

Friedrichstadt is small, with about two and a half thousand people, so fuel may not be convenient, and the nearest larger town is Tönning, eleven kilometres away, where you will find stations and supermarkets. There are cafés around the market square, and a bakery or two, so lunch is easy enough. Park near the canal, and walk a circuit of the old streets. If the sun is out, the brick glows red against the blue water, and the town looks almost like a painting.
t.hannover east edge@52.4,9.9:
On the eastern flank of Hannover the city dwindles into a landscape of canals, cement plants and wide, sugar-beet fields, and the point sits right in the midst of it. This is not postcard Germany but working Germany, which has its own appeal. The Mittelland Canal, the big east-west waterway that links the Rhine and the Elbe, runs close by, and barges of a thousand tonnes slide along it as calmly as swans. Misburg, just to the north, was a cement town for a century and still carries traces of that heavy industry, with chalk pits turned into lakes.

Lehrte, a town of forty-four thousand some eight kilometres away, owes its existence to the railway. Lines meeting there in the mid-nineteenth century made it a junction, and the town grew around the crossing of tracks. It is a handy provider of petrol stations, supermarkets and fast food, with a station that still shunts goods trains through its yards. The suburb of Laatzen, near the trade-fair grounds, is the other practical neighbour.

For a motorcyclist the early miles are about escaping. The roads leave the city along straight, flat arteries, with traffic lights and roundabouts and a thread of commuters, and the trick is to get off the main routes quickly onto the lanes between the villages. Within a few kilometres you are on narrow tarmac threading between fields and small woods, past brick farms and the odd wind turbine. The soil is rich loess, dark and fertile, the same soil that made the farmers of the Börde region wealthy, and in summer the grain stands tall and gold.

Weather here is a matter of wind. There is little to stop the westerlies, and on a blustery day the straights are hard work, so give yourself margin. Early on a spring morning, when the air is crisp and the sun low, this is a pleasant start. The way east leads on toward Helmstedt and the edge of the old frontier, so check your fuel and your tyres, and enjoy the open road.
t.hannover south east escape@52.3,9.8:
The southeastern edge of Hannover is where the city dissolves into the villages of the Calenberg land, and the first miles of this ride are a gentle introduction to it. Laatzen, a town of forty thousand, lies three kilometres away, while Pattensen and Hemmingen sit a little further out, each with its own old village heart and a ring of newer houses. The Leine river meanders through the meadows between them, and its floodplain, wide, green and often shrouded in morning mist, gives the district a quiet, watery character that surprises people who only know the city.

Pattensen has the most to see. Its centre keeps a collection of half-timbered houses around an old church, and the little streets are pleasant for a short wander. A hill south of Hannover called the Kronsberg, which was built up for the Expo of the year 2000, carries a row of wind turbines and a model neighbourhood, and from its top you can see the whole plain and, on a clear day, the faint line of the Harz in the south.

Riding here is easy, and the trick is to keep to the small roads. Lanes between the villages are well surfaced, with gentle bends around fields of sugar beet and wheat, small copses and the occasional avenue of old lime trees. The land is almost flat, so there are no climbs and few surprises, but the soil is some of the best in Germany, and the farms look prosperous. Weekend cyclists are common, and the lanes along the Leine are shared with walkers and dog owners.

The first of the proper hills comes after an hour or so, as the road approaches the Deister and the Weser uplands, and it is a good idea to start with a full tank. Hemmingen and Pattensen have stations and bakeries, and Laatzen has everything. A coffee and a roll at a village bakery, and you are away. Check the forecast, because the plain offers no shelter from a sudden squall, and the sky can turn quickly.
t.kappeln bridge@54.7,9.9:
Kappeln guards the middle of the Schlei, and its bridge is the town's pulse. The Schlei is a long, narrow inlet of the Baltic that winds forty kilometres inland to Schleswig, and the bridge at Kappeln is where the road crosses it. It is a double-leaf bascule bridge, which opens at set times to let sailing boats pass, and when it lifts, traffic stops and everyone gets out to watch. Waiting for it is part of the local rhythm, and you will not be hurried.

Just below the bridge stands the herring fence, a V-shaped trap of stakes and nets driven into the shallow water, one of the last of its kind in Europe. The Schlei herring fishery goes back centuries, and the catch is still smoked and sold in town. Kappeln is a pretty place, with a harbour lined with old merchant houses, boats rocking at their moorings and a smell of tar and smoke. It has nearly ten thousand people, with fuel, supermarkets and places to eat.

The countryside around is called Angeln, a gently rolling peninsula between the Schlei and the Flensburg Fjord, from which the Angles are said to have set out for Britain in the early Middle Ages. It is a quiet area of low hills, hedgerows, thatched farms and red-brick churches, and the roads are made for relaxed riding, with soft curves and long views over fields. Nearby, the village of Arnis, on the opposite bank, has about three hundred inhabitants and claims to be the smallest town in Germany, a fun detour.

At eight metres above sea level, you are never far from the water, and the wind coming up the Schlei can be sharp. Come on a weekday morning to avoid the weekend crowds and the bridge queues, and have a smoked fish roll while you wait. Süderbrarup, ten kilometres away, and Gelting are smaller places with the basics. In late summer, when the light is warm and the water is still, there are few better places to be.
t.worpswede artists village@53.2,8.9:
Worpswede began as a rebellion. In 1889 a handful of young painters, tired of the academies and their studio light, moved to a village in the Teufelsmoor, the Devil's Moor, north of Bremen, to paint what they saw: black peat canals, birch trees, huge skies, and people who cut turf for a living. Fritz Mackensen, Otto Modersohn, Fritz Overbeck, Heinrich Vogeler and, a few years later, the painter Paula Modersohn-Becker made the village a household name among art lovers, and the colony they founded grew into something like a small, permanent festival of the arts.

Today Worpswede is a village of around nine thousand people, with galleries, craft shops, studios and museums spread along a single winding main street. Vogeler's house, the Barkenhoff, with its white gables and garden, is open as a museum, and some of the buildings are experimental creations from the early twentieth century, with strange rooflines and expressionist brickwork. The village sits on a low hill, the Weyerberg, which at fifty-odd metres counts as a mountain in this flat land, and from its top you can see the moor stretching away in every direction.

The moor is the real subject. Reed-fringed canals, flat meadows and tall pale sky make a landscape of quiet drama, especially in early morning when mist rises off the water and the cranes call. The roads around Worpswede are narrow and straight, running along drainage ditches, with sudden bends where they cross a canal. Surfaces can be patchy, because peat soil sinks, so keep an eye out for dips and ripples. On weekends the village is thick with day-trippers and cyclists, and you will do better on a weekday.

Fuel is available in Worpswede and in Lilienthal, nearly nine kilometres away, which is a bigger town with supermarkets. The cafés along the main street do a good coffee and a slab of cake, and some serve a local speciality, a sweet bread with raisins. Give yourself an hour for the galleries, because the paintings are the best explanation of why the place looks the way it does.
t.marienburg castle view@52.2,9.8:
The castle of Marienburg looks as if a Hollywood studio had been told to build the perfect German fairy-tale palace, and in a sense it was an act of devotion: King George V of Hanover, who was blind, had it built in the 1850s and 1860s as a birthday present for his wife, Queen Marie, on a forested hill above the Leine valley. The architect, Conrad Wilhelm Hase, packed it with towers, turrets, pointed windows and steep roofs in the neo-Gothic style, and the result is a skyline of such romantic excess that visitors often assume it is medieval.

The irony is that the royal family hardly enjoyed it. In 1866 Prussia annexed the Kingdom of Hanover, and George and Marie went into exile in Austria, so the castle spent much of its life as a symbol of a vanished kingdom. It stayed in the hands of the House of Hanover for generations, and for years the question of who owns what has caused a sharp family quarrel and a lot of legal paperwork.

The view from the road is the thing. You see the castle from the valley, across fields and meadows, with its towers rising above the trees, and the best photographs are taken in the soft light of early morning or in the low light of evening. The roads here, around Nordstemmen and Elze, are gentle and well surfaced, with long curves through farmland and a pleasant roll over low ridges. The nearby hills are part of the Leine uplands, where the river flows north towards Hannover.

Nordstemmen, a town of thirteen thousand, is the closest place for fuel and food, only two kilometres off, and Elze is a little further. Bakeries and cafés are plentiful. If you decide to go up to the castle, be prepared to walk the last stretch, and to share the path with coach parties in summer. Visiting hours are limited in winter, so check before you go. The photograph from the valley, though, is free, and available whenever the sun is out.
t.finkenwerder@53.5,9.9:
Finkenwerder is an island that is not quite an island, a long, low spit of land in the Elbe that belongs to Hamburg and feels like a village. For centuries its people were fishermen, who sailed out into the North Sea in their sturdy boats and returned to a row of brick houses with thatched roofs, and the old quarter still has a sleepy, nautical atmosphere. The writer Johann Kinau, who published under the name Gorch Fock and wrote tales of the sea, was born here, and the famous German sail-training ship was named after him.

The island has another claim to fame, which sits uncomfortably beside the thatch: it is the site of a large Airbus factory, where aircraft are assembled, painted and flown out from a runway on the edge of the Elbe. Huge jets come and go over the village, and the contrast between old fishing cottages and airliners is one of the odd sights of Hamburg. You can see the planes from a viewing spot, and enthusiasts gather at the fence.

The ferry from Finkenwerder to the city centre is part of the public transport system, a pleasant half-hour crossing along the harbour, with views of the container terminals, the shipyards and the old fishing quarter. Nearby, the apple orchards of the Altes Land begin, and the island is known for an old apple variety, the Finkenwerder Herbstprinz, which is still sold at local stalls in autumn.

For a rider, the end of the ride here is pleasantly slow. The roads on the island are quiet and low, with speed limits that are enforced, and there is much to look at. Ottensen and Altona lie across the river, with fuel and plenty of cafés, though you will need to take the tunnel or the bridge to reach them, so fill up before the last stretch. A fish roll on the quay, with the wind in your hair and the planes overhead, makes a decent end to a long day.
t.hamburg@53.4,9.9:
Hamburg's high ground is not very high. The highest point in the whole city, a wooded hill called the Hasselbrack, reaches only about 116 metres, and it lies in the Harburg Hills, just a few kilometres from this point on the southern edge of the city. Still, in a country as flat as north Germany, those hills are a real change of scene, and the road that runs through them is one of the best for riders on the south bank of the Elbe.

The point sits near Neu Wulmstorf, a town of twenty thousand on the border between Hamburg and Lower Saxony, and not far from the Fischbeker Heide, a nature reserve of sandy hills, heather and juniper that blooms purple in August and September. The heath is the remnant of a landscape created by centuries of grazing, and the sheep that graze it now keep it open. Paths wind through it, and on a clear evening the light on the heather is extraordinary.

The roads around here are small and winding, running between hedgerows, over gentle rises and through patches of pine and birch. After the open flatlands of the Elbe, the bends come as a pleasure, and the soft, sandy smell of the heath is quite different from the damp air of the marshes. Traffic is light outside commuting hours, though the main roads towards Hamburg are busy at rush hour.

Seevetal and Harburg both lie within ten kilometres, with plenty of fuel and food. Neu Wulmstorf itself has supermarkets, bakeries and a few cafés, and the surrounding villages are quiet and neat. If the weather is good, stop for a walk on the heath, and take your helmet off for a few minutes. The silence and the open sky make a good end to a ride, and the city is only a short run away.
t.kovirke area 7@54.5,9.6:
South of Schleswig, in the narrow neck of land where the Jutland peninsula pinches itself between the Baltic and the North Sea marshes, lies one of the longest ancient monuments in Europe. This is the Danevirke, a system of earth ramparts, ditches and walls that runs for about thirty kilometres across the country, and the label here, Kovirke Area 7, refers to one of its sections, the Kovirke, whose name is usually translated as the Cow Work. Today the walls are grassy banks in fields, easy to miss if you are riding fast, but they once barred the way into Denmark.

The geography explains everything. The land between the Schlei, an arm of the Baltic reaching deep inland, and the marshy valleys of the Treene and the Eider on the west is only a few kilometres wide, and any army marching north along the old Army Road, or any herd of cattle driven south on the Ox Road, had to come through the gap. A wall there could shut the gate. The Danes knew it, and so did their enemies, and over many centuries the line was extended and rebuilt.

Today the area is a quiet agricultural landscape of fields, hedges and the odd farm. The roads that cross the line are small and gentle, running through villages such as Dannewerk and Fahrdorf, and the traffic is light. In 2018 the Danevirke was inscribed by UNESCO, together with the Viking town of Hedeby, as a World Heritage Site, so it is increasingly visited, and there are information boards and walking paths.

Schleswig is only five kilometres away, a town of twenty-four thousand, with fuel, supermarkets and plenty of cafés. Fahrdorf and Dannewerk are small but have a bakery or a pub. Walk along the rampart, which is easy underfoot, and think about the men who dug it with spades and baskets. It is a quiet, grassy place, and it rewards slow looking more than speed.
t.connection wall area 8@54.5,9.5:
Here the Danevirke stops being a faint line in the grass and becomes something you can touch, and the label calls it a connection wall. Archaeologists use that term for the short sections that tie the main rampart to its neighbours, the walls that stitched the whole system into one barrier from the Schlei to the western marshes. Area 8 lies in the heart of the system, a short walk from the village of Dannewerk, whose name simply means Danes' Work.

The most striking part of the Danevirke is a wall of brick, built in the twelfth century under King Valdemar the Great. It is one of the earliest large brick structures in Scandinavia, and the technique, newly imported from the south, was a statement of power, as bricks were rare and costly in a country of earth and wood. The wall stretches for several kilometres, a long red line against the green, and its weathered face is still impressive, with the patterns of the old brickwork visible in places.

The ride to get here is flat and easy, through farmland with big skies, and the roads become smaller and quieter as you approach the village. The surfaces are generally good, and traffic is light. The nearby motorway is audible in places, a reminder that the old route north is still the main one. Schuby, with about two and a half thousand people, is the closest place with a few shops, and Schleswig has all the fuel and food you might need.

Dannewerk has a museum devoted to the Danevirke, with finds from the excavations and a good explanation of the construction phases. The staff are helpful, and a visit makes the whole landscape come alive. Check the opening times in advance, since small museums keep limited hours. Come on a dry day, bring a jacket for the wind, and allow time to walk along the wall. The light in late afternoon, when the sun slants across the brick, is especially fine.
t.arched wall@54.5,9.5:
The Danevirke is a monument you walk along more than you look at, and the Arched Wall is a good place to see why. The rampart here bends in a long gentle curve across the fields, a green bank with a ditch beside it, and from the top you can follow its shape to the horizon. The line has the odd, deliberate look of something designed by people who understood the ground: it skirts a wet hollow here, climbs a low rise there, and always keeps the high side on the Danish side.

History crowded round this place more than once, but the most recent chapter was in February 1864. The Second Schleswig War was only weeks old, and the Danish army was dug in along the Danevirke, expecting a Prussian and Austrian assault. A hard frost made the marshes passable and threatened to let the enemy go around the flank, so on the night of the fifth to the sixth, the Danes quietly abandoned the line and marched north. It was a sensible decision and a national humiliation. Within two months the Prussians stormed the Danish positions at Dybbøl, and the duchies of Schleswig and Holstein were lost to Denmark for more than half a century.

The riding is mild and the countryside is simple, with the roads running between fields of grain and rape and crossing the line at gentle angles. Dannewerk, with a thousand inhabitants, lies a couple of kilometres off, and Schuby is a little further. Tractors are the main obstruction, and cyclists the main company. In summer the verges are bright with poppies and cornflowers, and the sound of skylarks drifts down from the sky.

The nearest town of any size is Schleswig, four kilometres away, with fuel, supermarkets and cafés. Park at one of the signposted points and walk along the bank, which is open to the public. Be careful where the ground drops into the ditch, and avoid trampling crops. The wall is a quiet, rather moving thing, and the best way to take it in is slowly, with the wind in your face and an open sky.
t.connection wall area 9 north wall area 4:
Nobody can say for certain who first dug the northern end of the Danevirke, but the best evidence points to a king named Godfred. The Frankish chroniclers record that in the year 808 this Danish ruler, a rival of Charlemagne, ordered a great wall built across the neck of the peninsula to protect his kingdom from Frankish attack. Tree-ring dating of timbers from the early rampart has found wood felled in the 730s, so the story is older and more complicated than a single king, but Godfred's name is tied to the Danevirke, and he is also linked to the founding of the trading town of Hedeby nearby.

This section combines two parts of the system, a connection wall and the North Wall, and the North Wall is the oldest and the most northerly of the barriers. In its first form it was a timber palisade behind a ditch, with earth heaped up behind it and a gate for the main road. Over the centuries it was lengthened and strengthened, and later kings added new walls and ditches, so that what you see today is a layer cake of building phases.

The place is at its best in the quiet of early morning, when mist lies on the fields and the bank looks like a long green wave. There are marked paths and a few information boards, though much is left to the imagination. Roads around Dannewerk are narrow and little used, and you can usually park at the roadside near the footpath.

Dannewerk is a village of a thousand people and has little for the traveller beyond a pub or a bakery, while Schuby offers a few shops. For fuel and a proper lunch go on to Schleswig, about four kilometres off. The ground is dry and sandy, a gift to walkers, though it can be boggy after heavy rain. Wear sturdy shoes, bring some water, and give yourself half an hour to follow the rampart through the trees. It is the nearest thing to meeting a Viking king in person.
t.hedeby@54.5,9.6:
Hedeby is the name the Danes used for a town that the Germans call Haithabu, and for roughly three centuries it was one of the great ports of the Viking world. It lay at the head of an inlet, the Haddeby Noor, on the narrow neck of the peninsula where goods could be carried overland from the North Sea to the Baltic, and its streets are said to have held perhaps a thousand people at its height, a huge number for the time. Traders arrived from Norway, Sweden, the Frankish lands, the Slavic coast and even the distant Islamic world, to sell furs, amber, iron, slaves, glass and silver.

An Arab-Jewish merchant from Spain, Ibrahim ibn Yaqub, visited in the tenth century and left a famous account, in which he described it as a large town with little food and a lot of noise, where the people sing in a way that sounds like the barking of dogs. It is a rare outside view of Viking life and it is not flattering, but it is vivid. The town was attacked and burned several times, and after its final destruction in 1066 the surviving inhabitants moved across the water to the new town of Schleswig.

The semicircular rampart that once enclosed Hedeby is still visible on the land side, a great horseshoe of earth in the meadow, and a reconstructed settlement of Viking houses stands near the water. Excavations began in the early twentieth century and continue still, with the dig turning up combs, coins, boots and, in the harbour, the wreck of a long warship. The museum shows the best of the finds and has a reconstructed ship.

The road in is quiet and flat, through meadows and past reed beds, and the water beside it is calm and often full of birds. Fahrdorf is the closest village, and Schleswig, three kilometres away, has everything else. Bring a layer against the wind off the water, and give the museum an hour. The grass and the sky and the sound of the reeds are the same as they were when the ships came in.
t.kovirke area 1@54.5,9.5:
Kropp is the town that this stretch of the Danevirke leans on. It is a modest place of about six thousand people, set just off the motorway that runs from Hamburg to Denmark, and in practical terms it is the closest place with proper services. The wall itself lies a few kilometres to the north, in fields and hedges near the villages of Dannewerk and Groß Rheide, and at this point it runs westward towards the marshy valley of the Treene, where the old defence simply ended in wet ground that no army could cross.

The idea of the Danevirke is that it closes a gap, and that gap is not a straight line. It is a corridor of firm sandy ground, a spine of low hills called the Geest, bordered on both sides by bog and water. Travellers and drovers from the south had always followed it, so the wall blocked the one dry road. The Ox Road, the old drovers' route from Jutland down to Hamburg, followed the same ridge, and herds of cattle once walked it by the thousand. In some places you can still follow the old trackway in the field edges.

The land is open and farmed, a patchwork of grain, maize and grassland, divided by hedgerows called Knicks, the typical banked hedges of Schleswig-Holstein. The roads that cross it are small and quiet, with long straights, the odd bend, and a series of low rises that give you a view over the plain. Wind is often the main issue. A west wind comes straight off the North Sea with nothing to stop it, so a strong headwind is a real possibility.

Kropp has fuel stations, a supermarket and a bakery, and Groß Rheide, a small village, has hardly anything. Fill up in Kropp before the last stretch, and carry something to drink. If you want a break, the quiet lanes around the wall are good for a leg-stretch and a view across the countryside. The skies here are wide, and in late afternoon the colours of the fields are rich.
t.kovirke area 3 to 5@54.5,9.5:
An earthwork is a good place to watch birds, and the grassy banks of the Danevirke are better for wildlife than the intensive fields on either side. Here the ramparts have been left as pasture and rough grassland for centuries, so they have become a long, narrow nature reserve, a green corridor through the farmland. In summer the banks are alive with butterflies, grasshoppers and bees, and in the evening bats flicker along the hedgerows. Skylarks and yellowhammers sing from the fence posts, and kestrels hover over the open ground.

This section, labelled Kovirke Areas 3 to 5, runs through the country near Dannewerk and Kropp, in the middle of the system. The wall is lower here than in some places, worn down by ploughs and weather, but the ditch is still easy to see, and the line runs straight across a gentle slope. It is a place to get off the bike, walk for ten minutes, and listen. The sound of the wind in the grass is quite different from the noise of an engine.

The ride is gentle, along tidy country roads between fields of maize and wheat, past farms with red-brick barns and the occasional thatched roof. The surfaces are good, the junctions are sparse, and the traffic is mostly local farmers and cyclists. Come early in the day for the best light and the most birdsong, and avoid harvest time, when slow combine harvesters can hold you up for miles. After rain, tractors leave mud on the road, so watch for slippery patches at the field entrances.

Dannewerk is two kilometres away and is the village that gave the whole monument its name, with a little museum, a church and a few farms. Kropp, a town of six thousand, is the sensible place for fuel and food, and Schuby is another option. Bring a rain jacket, because the weather on the plain changes quickly. A small flask of coffee makes the walk along the bank a pleasure. It is an easy place to spend an hour.
t.crooked wall areas 3 to 4@54.5,9.4:
Hollingstedt is a village of only a thousand people, but a thousand years ago it was a harbour that connected two seas. Ships came up the Treene, a slow, winding river that runs from the North Sea marshes, as far as Hollingstedt, and from there goods were carried by wagon the last few kilometres across the neck of the peninsula to Hedeby on the Baltic side. It was the western half of a transport system that let Viking traders avoid the dangerous voyage around the tip of Denmark, and the Danevirke was built to guard the land bridge between them.

Archaeologists have found traces of the old river port, including wooden structures and boat parts, and the Treene valley still has a damp, secret quality. The river meanders through meadows, alder carrs and reed beds, with herons standing in the shallows. The Crooked Wall, a section of the Danevirke named for its bend, runs through the country east of here, one of the more irregular pieces of the whole system. It follows the edge of a wet valley and the contours of the land with a looseness that suggests it was dug in a hurry.

The riding here is lovely in a modest way. Roads run through flat farmland and along the river, with big skies and long views, and the villages are small and neat. Groß Rheide and Silberstedt, both a few kilometres off, are the nearest neighbours. Surfaces are generally good, but farm traffic leaves mud and straw, and in autumn the leaf litter can be slippery. The wind from the west is a steady companion.

For fuel and a proper meal, the nearest sizeable place is Kropp, about ten kilometres away, and Schleswig is not much further. Hollingstedt has a small inn and a bakery at best. It is a place to stop for ten minutes at the river and let your mind wander back to the long ships and the rolling wagons. In May the meadows are yellow with buttercups, and the water is full of the sound of frogs.
t.connection wall area 3@54.5,9.6:
Where the Danevirke meets the water, it has to do something clever, and here at Fahrdorf you can see the point. The wall that is labelled Connection Wall Area 3 ties the western ramparts to the fortified town of Hedeby, running down toward the shore of the Schlei, an inlet that reaches far inland. At the water's edge the ground is soft and wet, and the builders used it as part of the defence, so the bank peters out in reeds and mud.

The village of Fahrdorf, with about two and a half thousand people, sits on a narrow causeway between two arms of the Schlei, and has been a crossing point for centuries. A bridge once connected it to Schleswig by way of a long wooden causeway, and the old route can still be traced. Today the village is a pleasant, rather sleepy place, with a harbour for small boats and a view across the water to Schleswig's cathedral spire.

The landscape is a fine mixture of water and field. The Schlei is not a river but an arm of the Baltic, brackish and slightly salty, and it supports an odd blend of fish and birds. In winter, swans and geese gather on the water, and in spring the reed beds fill with warblers. The road follows the shore for some distance, giving good views, and the corners are soft and slow. The tarmac is generally good, but the wind can be sharp on the exposed stretches.

Schleswig, three kilometres away, has everything you need in the way of fuel, shops and places to eat, and Fahrdorf itself has a small supermarket and a bakery. Dannewerk is a few minutes inland. Walk a short way along the bank, and the connection between wall and water becomes clear. If you can, come in the evening, when the light turns the Schlei to silver, and the reeds are full of the last birdsong of the day. It is a gentle place, where history lies quietly in the grass.
t.kovirke area 2@54.5,9.5:
The village of Dannewerk gave its name to the great monument that surrounds it, and it is a small place with a big story. About a thousand people live here, in a scatter of farms and houses along the road, and a museum on the edge of the village does what a museum should: it explains why the grass banks in the fields matter. Inside you find a model of the whole system, tools and weapons from the excavations, and a clear account of the many phases of building, from the timber palisade of the eighth century to the brick wall of the twelfth.

This section, Kovirke Area 2, lies a couple of kilometres south of the village, in farmland, and the best way to appreciate it is to see it after the museum. The Kovirke is generally understood as a later addition, built to strengthen the defences in the Viking Age, and it forms an extra line south of the older walls. In 2018 UNESCO recognised the whole complex, along with Hedeby, as a World Heritage Site, and visitor numbers have grown, although the place is still very quiet.

The ride into Dannewerk is easy, with small roads through farmland and low hills, many of them lined with hedges and the occasional avenue of oaks. Traffic is mostly local, and the surfaces are good. The land is open and the wind constant, so lean into it. Spring brings fields of yellow rape, summer brings tall corn, and autumn brings misty mornings and a smell of plough.

Groß Rheide and Kropp lie nearby, and Kropp, with about six thousand people, is the nearest place with fuel stations and supermarkets. Dannewerk itself has a pub or a bakery at best. Take a coat, because the museum is small but the walk afterwards is worth doing, and the weather can turn. Stand on the rampart for a minute and look south across the fields. That is the view the sentries had, and the horizon has barely changed.
t.crooked wall areas 1 to 2 main wall area:
For Danes, the Danevirke is more than an archaeological site, because over the centuries it grew into a symbol. In the nineteenth century, when national feeling was rising across Europe, the Danes saw the old wall as the guardian of their southern border and of their identity, and the name was given to songs, newspapers and political societies. The idea that the true frontier lay at the Eider river, not at the present border, drove a bitter struggle between Danish and German nationalists, a conflict that ended in war and in the loss of the duchies in 1864.

The sections labelled Crooked Wall Areas 1 to 2 and the Main Wall form the heart of the system. The Main Wall, with its ditch and bank, is the part that most people picture when they think of the Danevirke, and it has the strong, simple lines of something built to a plan. It was raised in the tenth century, according to tree-ring dates, probably under King Harald Bluetooth, and was heightened and faced over the following centuries. After the First World War, plebiscites in 1920 finally drew a new frontier, further north, which still runs between Germany and Denmark today.

The ride here runs across the flat farmland near Groß Rheide, among fields of grain and maize, and the roads are small and quiet, with the odd gentle bend and a little tractor traffic. The surfaces are good, and the villages are tidy and well kept. The land is open to the wind, and the sky seems very big. On a clear day, you can see the church towers of several villages at once.

Kropp, six kilometres away, has the fuel and the shops, and Dannewerk and Schuby have little more than a bakery and a pub. Bring something to drink, and a jacket against the wind. Walk a short way along the bank and stand on top. You can feel the weight of the history, and the plain good sense of the people who chose the spot. It is a very peaceful place for such a contested one.
t.east sea coastal@37.4,126.8:
The label says East Sea, but the pin is on the opposite side of the peninsula, in Incheon, on the Yellow Sea, so it is best to begin by being honest about that. Incheon is South Korea's third-largest city, with some two and a half million people, a port and an airport that is the country's main gateway, and it sits on a coast with some of the biggest tides in the world, up to nine metres between high and low. At low water the sea retreats for kilometres, leaving a grey, gleaming plain of mud where people walk out to dig for clams.

The city has a layered past. It opened to foreign trade in 1883, and the district around the old port, with its steep streets of colonial-era buildings, became Korea's first Chinatown, where jajangmyeon, the black-bean noodle dish now eaten across the country, is said to have originated. In 1950, General MacArthur's landing at Incheon turned the course of the Korean War, and a memorial in Jayu Park recalls it. Today the area around Songdo is a showpiece of new towers and tidy parks, and the Incheon Bridge, over twenty kilometres long, sweeps across the bay toward the airport.

The ride from here goes east to the opposite coast, across the Taebaek mountains to the East Sea, a day of about three hours of driving each way if you go by the expressway. The best approach is to take the Yeongdong Expressway east, leave early to beat the traffic, and then follow the coastal road south or north with the ocean on your side. The coast road is open, with curves along the headlands, pine forests, white sand and clear water, and in summer it is crowded, while in spring and autumn it is calm.

Fuel is everywhere in Incheon, and on the expressways every rest area has a station, with good food, from noodle soups to fried chicken. Korea drives on the right, tolls are paid with a card, and speed cameras are common. The main hazards are heavy traffic around the capital region on weekends and fog in the mountains in the early morning. Go early.
t.namyangju@37.6,127.2:
Namyangju lies east of Seoul, where two rivers, the Bukhan and the South Han, join to form the Han, and the meeting place is one of the most pleasant landscapes in the capital region. A quiet bend of water, reeds, boats and low hills with Mount Cheonma standing behind, it has been a place for poets and philosophers for centuries. The town, with ninety thousand people, is a base for riders heading up the Bukhan valley, and its lanes are lined with cafes with river views that are popular on weekends.

The town is the birthplace of Jeong Yak-yong, known as Dasan, a scholar of the late Joseon dynasty who wrote hundreds of books on administration, science and ethics, much of it while in exile for eighteen years. His house and memorial hall, on the riverbank, are a pleasant place to walk, and the paths follow the river among willow trees and lotus ponds. Dasan wrote that a government should serve the people, a radical idea in his time, and Koreans still hold him in high esteem.

The riding here is the reason people come. The river road, along the Bukhan, is a pleasant, winding route with gentle curves and wide views, and the road from here toward Gapyeong rises into forested hills with a few more serious bends. At weekends, the roads are crowded with riders, cyclists and cars, and the cafes along the river fill up. A weekday or an early start is the answer. In autumn, the maples colour the hillsides, and in winter, the river sometimes steams in the cold, with snow on the hills.

Namyangju has stations on every main road, and plenty of places to eat, from noodle shops to grilled duck, a regional favourite. The surface is generally excellent, and the signage is clear, though speed cameras are frequent and enforced. Watch the lights where the roads cross the railway, and take care at the dusk when cyclists share the river path. A cup of coffee at a riverside cafe is the right way to begin or end a ride.
t.pocheon lake@37.3,127.3:
Icheon is a quiet, rice-growing city in Gyeonggi Province, to the south-east of Seoul, and a good place to learn how Korea has treated clay for a thousand years. The city is known for its ceramics, and its kilns have produced celadon and white porcelain since the Goryeo and Joseon eras. UNESCO named it a Creative City of Crafts and Folk Art in 2010, and the ceramic village of Sagimakgol, with its working kilns, shops and a museum, is a pleasure to walk through. Local potters will often let you try the wheel, and the pieces they make are used on tables across the country.

The other pride of Icheon is its rice. Grown on the broad fertile plain of the region, the grain was once reserved for the king, and it is still sold as a premium product, with the flavour of fresh nuts. The surrounding land is a patchwork of paddies, orchards and low hills, and the hot springs in the area make it a popular place for a weekend soak. In autumn, the rice fields turn golden and the fruit trees are heavy with pears and persimmons.

The ride this stop belongs to goes north, toward the lake and forests of Pocheon, a longer journey through the capital region. The roads from Icheon run through farmland and small towns, with plenty of traffic lights and a mix of rural and suburban scenery, before the expressway links bring you to the hills. It is not a technical ride, but it has a calm rhythm, and the countryside has a gentle beauty, particularly in the morning when mist lies on the paddies. Watch for tractors, farm trucks and elderly farmers on slow motorbikes.

Fuel is simple to find in Icheon, with stations on every main road and in town, and the restaurants serve local rice with a variety of side dishes, a meal that suits a rider. Korea drives on the right, and tolls on expressways are paid by card or at the gates. Spring and autumn are the most pleasant seasons, and the roads are quieter on weekdays. Look out for the ceramic shops by the road, where a single bowl makes a lasting souvenir.
t.danyang river@37.4,126.9:
Anyang sits just south of Seoul, an industrial and residential city of more than six hundred thousand people, and the pin lands within its limits. It does not look like a place for a story, but it has a few. The name means something like peaceful and safe, and was given in the tenth century after a Buddhist temple, Anyangsa, that once stood here. Today the city has a long stream, the Anyangcheon, with a green path along its banks, and, on the hillside near Mount Samseong, the Anyang Art Park, where sculptures and installations by artists from around the world are scattered through the woods.

The label is for a trip to the Danyang River and its mountain passes, far in the south-east, and the city is a handy starting point for it. Danyang, in North Chungcheong, is where the Namhan River curves between steep limestone cliffs and the high ridges of Sobaeksan, and the roads between are among the nicest in central Korea. Passes such as Jungnyeong take you up through forest in long, clear bends, with tunnels and bridges that give wide views over the valleys, and the traffic is usually light on weekdays.

The first stage of the ride is the escape from the capital, a stretch of expressway that can be crowded at weekends. Leaving at dawn pays off. Once beyond the satellite cities, the land opens, and the roads wind through farmland and forested hills, with small towns and apple orchards. In autumn the maples colour the slopes, and the air is clear. Winter can bring ice and snow to the high passes, so check conditions before going.

Anyang is a place with stations on every road, and shops and convenience stores that sell hot drinks and snacks all night. The expressway rest areas serve noodles, rice dishes and good coffee. Korea drives on the right, and cameras are everywhere, with limits clearly marked, so keep your speed in check. If you have a spare half hour before you leave, walk along the stream or visit the art park, and you will start the day with a quieter mind.
t.bozeman@45.7,-111.0:
Bozeman lies in the Gallatin Valley, a broad, flat bowl of farmland at about 4,800 feet, ringed by mountains on every side. The Bridger Range stands to the northeast, the Gallatin Range to the south and the Tobacco Roots to the west, and snow stays on the high summits well into summer. The town started in the 1860s as a supply point for miners and settlers, named after John Bozeman, who blazed a trail from Wyoming to the Montana gold fields through the hunting grounds of the Sioux, a route that led to war.

Today it is a lively college town with some forty-odd thousand residents, centered on Montana State University. Main Street is lined with restaurants, breweries, outdoor shops and cafes, and the energy is that of a place that is growing fast. The Museum of the Rockies is well known for its dinosaur collection, including a remarkable set of Tyrannosaurus rex skeletons found in eastern Montana, and the paleontologist Jack Horner, who advised on the Jurassic Park films, worked there for decades.

For riders, Bozeman is a gateway. To the south, Highway 191 follows the Gallatin River through a canyon of cliffs and pine toward Big Sky and Yellowstone, with long bends and the river running beside you. The scenery is fine and the traffic can be heavy in summer, with trucks and rafting buses. Bridger Canyon Road to the north gives a quieter option through ranchland and aspens, and Hyalite Canyon, south of town, has a reservoir and waterfalls at the end of a narrow road. Bozeman Pass to the east, on the old route of the Northern Pacific Railway, is the quick way to Livingston.

Weather deserves respect. Summer days are warm and dry, with cool nights, and afternoon thunderstorms can build over the ranges. Snow can fall in any month at higher altitude, and the high passes see closures in winter. Wind funnels through the valley, especially in spring and fall.

Services are excellent. Fuel is available at stations all over town and in nearby Belgrade, and the city has motorcycle shops, grocery stores and plenty of breakfast spots. If you are heading toward the park, fill up before the canyon, since stations are sparse along the Gallatin.
t.rudesheim@50.0,7.9:
Rüdesheim lives on one lane and a very good view. The lane is the Drosselgasse, a few metres wide and a couple of hundred long, packed with wine taverns, music and tourists, and often described as the merriest street in Germany. The view is the Rhine, which here turns from a broad lowland river into the Rhine Gorge, a narrow, castle-lined channel of steep slate slopes that is UNESCO-listed. On the hill above the town, the Niederwald Monument, a huge bronze Germania unveiled in 1883 to mark German unification, stands over the vines, and you can reach it by cable car over the vineyards.

The wine is Riesling, grown on steep terraces of slate and quartzite, and the local specialty is Rüdesheimer Kaffee: hot coffee, a generous measure of Asbach brandy, sugar and whipped cream, usually served in a glass mug with some theatre. It is sweeter and stronger than it looks, so one is enough before riding. The town is full of cafés and wine bars, and the Brömserburg, a medieval castle by the river, holds a wine museum. Opposite lies Bingen, with the Mouse Tower on its island, and the legend of Bishop Hatto, who was supposedly eaten by mice for his greed.

For the rider, this is the finish of the Rhine Romantic Route, which follows the river through its most famous section. The roads on both banks are busy but scenic, with castles every few kilometres, and the wine villages offer lunch and a view. Surfaces are generally good, with a mix of town streets, riverside stretches and bends up into the vineyards. Summer weekends bring heavy traffic, tour coaches and cyclists, and the narrow streets of the old town can be slow going, so arrive early if you want a parking space.

Rüdesheim has about ten thousand people and plenty of fuel, though the stations are on the edge of town and busy in season. The boats that cross to Bingen and run up the gorge are a good way of seeing the Loreley rock from the water. In October the harvest brings a different atmosphere, with the vineyards busy and young wine in every cellar. Winter is quiet, with fog on the river, and some of the taverns shut, though the Christmas market has its devotees.
t.nurburgring@50.3,6.9:
Few roads in the world have a nickname as earned as the Nordschleife, which Jackie Stewart christened the Green Hell. It winds for about twenty-one kilometres through the forested hills of the Hohe Eifel, with well over a hundred corners, big climbs, blind crests and a drop of nearly three hundred metres between its lowest and highest points. It was built in the 1920s as a work-creation project for a depressed region, and above it, on a basalt cone, stand the ruins of Nürburg castle, a twelfth-century fortress that gave the circuit its name. The tower is still there, and from it you can look out over the whole area.

Most days of the year, the track is closed for testing or racing, but on many evenings and weekends it opens to the public in sessions called Touristenfahrten, when anyone with a road-legal vehicle can pay per lap and take it on. Motorcycles are allowed, but the track has no run-off in many places, the surface changes grip suddenly and accidents are frequent, so respect it. If you do not fancy it, the grandstands are free to sit in, and there is a noisy, friendly crowd at the car park, with bikes of every kind. Check the calendar before you arrive, because it changes and closures are common.

The country around is the volcanic Eifel, a high, rolling, forested plateau with small farm villages, and fog can sit over it for days. The nearest villages, Adenau and Kelberg, are small, with fuel stations, bakeries and guesthouses used to motorcyclists, and Daun, eighteen kilometres off, is the nearest larger town. The Hohe Acht, at 747 metres the highest point of the Eifel, rises just to the west of the circuit, with a lookout tower that gives a long view.

From here the Eifel Volcano Route runs south to Gerolstein, through country dotted with maars, round crater lakes formed by gas explosions thousands of years ago. The roads are smooth and flowing, with long curves through forest and over open ridges, and the traffic is usually light outside event weekends. The weather is cool and wet, even in summer, and the mornings are often foggy. Be careful on wet tarmac and in the autumn leaf fall, and watch for speed cameras and police near the track, where noise limits are enforced.
t.gerolstein@50.2,6.7:
Gerolstein is best known for water, and the water is the story of the place. The town lies in a bowl of the Kyll valley, and under it flows mineral water from the volcanic ground, rich in carbonic acid and minerals, which is bottled and sold across Europe under the town's name. You can see the factory at the edge of town and taste the water at the public springs, where it comes out fizzy, cool and slightly metallic. About seven and a half thousand people live here, so fuel, shops and restaurants are plentiful.

The surroundings are geologically odd. Cliffs of grey dolomite, a limestone-like rock formed in a warm Devonian sea about four hundred million years ago, rise abruptly above the town, with names such as the Munterley and the Hustley, and the paths up to them give fine views. The Buchenloch cave, in the same cliff, was lived in by Stone Age hunters, and bones of mammoths and cave bears have been found. Nearby, the Eifel's volcanoes left behind craters and cinder cones, and the area is part of a UNESCO Global Geopark.

A few kilometres to the east, at Pelm, the Kasselburg castle ruin stands on a rock with a wolf and bird of prey park on its slopes. The flying displays in the afternoon are a favourite with families. In town, the Erlöserkirche, a Protestant church of the nineteenth century, has a plain brick tower. Local food in the Eifel is hearty and unfussy, with potato dishes, smoked ham and sausages and plenty of apple cake, and the Kyll valley has good trout.

The Eifel Volcano Route ends here, after a long ride through craters, forest and moorland, and for the final stretch the roads follow the river through shaded valleys with gentle bends. The surface is generally good, the traffic modest, and the landscape rolling, though the weather can be cold and foggy. Autumn is spectacular, with beech and oak turning red and gold, and the maar lakes lying like dark mirrors. Winter can bring ice and snow to the plateau, so the high roads can be tricky. Gerolstein itself is a pleasant spot to finish, with a bench by the river and a bottle of the local water.
t.west glacier@48.5,-114.0:
West Glacier is a small collection of lodges, cafes and gift shops at the western entrance of Glacier National Park, a few hundred yards from the gate and the railway, and it is the starting point for Going-to-the-Sun Road. The Great Northern Railway built much of the tourism here, advertising Glacier as America's Switzerland in the early twentieth century, and constructing grand lodges in the mountains. Trains still pass through the village on the line from Chicago to Seattle, and the sound of a long freight is part of the soundtrack.

The park is a wild landscape of jagged peaks, deep U-shaped valleys, high lakes and the remnants of glaciers, which have shrunk dramatically in the past century. Its mountains are made of ancient sedimentary rock, in layers of red, green and grey, thrust up and carved by ice. Lake McDonald, the largest lake in the park, lies just beyond the entrance, ten miles long and over four hundred feet deep, and its shoreline is covered with smooth, multi-coloured pebbles that shine under the clear water.

Going-to-the-Sun Road, which was completed in 1932, is a masterpiece of mountain engineering, fifty miles long, clinging to cliffs and crossing the Continental Divide at Logan Pass, at about sixty-six hundred feet. The road is narrow, with tight bends, steep drops and a low stone wall, and no guard rails in places. Vehicles over a certain size are prohibited on the narrowest section, and in busy years the park has used timed-entry reservations, so check the park website before you go. The upper road is usually clear of snow from late June or July until October, but weather can bring early closures.

There is a gas station and a few shops in West Glacier, but the larger town of Columbia Falls, about twenty kilometres away, has more choices, and it is wise to start with a full tank, since fuel is not sold in the park. Grizzly and black bears live in the park, so carry bear spray if you plan to hike, and keep your distance from wildlife. Early morning is quiet and pleasant, with mist on the lake, while afternoons are crowded. Dress in layers, since the temperature at the pass can be freezing in summer.
t.st mary@48.7,-113.4:
St. Mary is a little village on the eastern edge of Glacier National Park, and here the mountains meet the prairie with a bump. To the west rise the peaks, steep and dark, with the long finger of St. Mary Lake at their foot, while to the east the land opens out into rolling grassland as far as the horizon. The village is a cluster of cafes, motels, a store and a visitor centre, and it is the eastern gateway to Going-to-the-Sun Road.

The land to the east belongs to the Blackfeet Nation, whose reservation shares a long boundary with the park. The Blackfeet called the mountains the Backbone of the World, and the high peaks are sacred to them, as they have been for generations. Many of the names of features in the park come from their language, and the tribe operates businesses and cultural centres in the area. The nearby town of Browning has a museum devoted to Blackfeet history and art, and a rodeo and festival each July.

Wind is the defining feature of this side of the Rockies. The mountains hold back moisture, but west winds roar across the divide and sweep down onto the plains with remarkable force, so on a motorcycle you should expect gusts that can be extremely strong, particularly at the lakeshore. The road from Logan Pass descends in a series of long bends, with a famous viewpoint over the lake and little Wild Goose Island, a tiny speck of land that seems to float on the water. The descent is thrilling, but demands attention, with rock walls on one side and a drop on the other.

You can find basic services in St. Mary, including cafes, gift shops and a petrol station, but it is a small place, so fill up in the morning, since the next big supplies are at Browning, about thirty-seven kilometres south-east, and in Cardston across the Canadian border to the north. Summer is the busy season, and many businesses close from October to May, so check ahead. Pack a warm layer and a windproof jacket. Early evening is a lovely time here, when the low sun lights the peaks and the crowds thin.
t.elze return road@52.1,9.7:
Elze is the sort of small town you only really know if you have been passed through it on the way home. It sits on the Leine river south of Hannover, in the gentle, folded country that Lower Saxony people call the Leinebergland, where a river valley, a railway and a main road all squeeze past one another between low wooded ridges. With about nine and a half thousand inhabitants, it has what a rider needs after a long day: fuel, a supermarket, a bakery and the kind of cafe where the coffee comes with a small biscuit and no commentary.

The country around it is quietly interesting. East and west of the valley, long ridges of limestone and sandstone with names like Külf, Sieben Berge and Hils rise a couple of hundred metres above the farmland, covered in beech woods that turn copper in October. The roads that wander over them are the point of a ride in this region: mostly tidy, mostly empty, with long, flowing bends rather than hairpins. Down in the valley, the Leine meanders through meadows, and the villages have red-roofed farmhouses and half-timbered barns. In nearby Alfeld, the Fagus factory, designed by Walter Gropius in the years before the First World War, is a UNESCO site and a landmark of modern architecture, with glass corners that were revolutionary in their time.

As a return road, the stretch toward Hannover is more practical than romantic. Traffic builds in the afternoon, with commuters and trucks, and the final run through the suburbs is a slog, so it is worth timing your trip to avoid the rush hour. On the way, farm roads offer calmer alternatives, with views across a flat, wide landscape of sugar beet, wheat and rapeseed. In spring, the yellow fields are dazzling; in late summer, harvest dust and tractors slow everything down.

Elze itself is a good place to take stock. A short stop for a coffee and a pastry, a check of tyre pressure and a look at the map, and you are ready for the final stretch. If you are low on fuel, fill up here rather than gambling on the smaller villages ahead. The light in the evening, low and golden across the fields, gives the last miles a sort of quiet reward, and you may find you are in no hurry to arrive.
t.hannover north east edge@52.4,9.9:
Hannover is not a city that people brag about, and that suits a motorcyclist, because it means the escape routes are uncrowded. The north-eastern edge, where the suburbs of Isernhagen and Burgdorf give way to farmland and pine woods, is where a ride in this part of Lower Saxony begins. The land is flat and sandy, shaped by ice-age meltwater, and it seems to hold its breath before the moors and heaths of the Lüneburg country begin. On the way out you pass the city's famous green space, the Eilenriede, one of the biggest city forests in Europe.

This is a good place to start because the first twenty minutes go quickly. Busy suburban roads lead to quiet lanes between fields of rye, potatoes and maize, with avenues of old oaks and the odd half-timbered farmhouse with a thatched or red-tile roof. In April, May and June, around Burgwedel and the villages to the north, asparagus season is celebrated, and roadside stalls sell the white spears by the kilo. The pace is easy, the corners are gentle, and the surface is generally good. It is a place to warm up your riding rather than test it.

Early in the morning is best, when mist hangs over the fields and the traffic is still asleep. On weekdays, commuters flood the main roads, and the autobahn is no place for a relaxed start. If you are leaving on a Sunday, you will find the villages quiet, with church bells and the smell of mown grass. Weather can change quickly in northern Germany, with a stiff wind off the plain and sudden showers, so a waterproof layer is sensible.

For practical needs, the edge of a large city is helpful. Fuel stations, supermarkets and bakeries line the main roads in Isernhagen and Burgdorf, and you can top up and buy a coffee before you go. The nearest bigger centres are Burgdorf, a town of around thirty thousand, and the city of Hannover itself, behind you. Once you pass the last roundabout and head north-east, the road opens, the sky widens, and you can relax into the ride. It is a modest start with plenty of promise.
t.schwansen fields@54.6,9.9:
Schwansen is a low, rolling peninsula in the north of Schleswig-Holstein, tucked between the Baltic inlet of Eckernförde Bay to the south and the long, narrow fjord of the Schlei to the north. The land was shaped by the ice sheets, which left behind a patchwork of gentle hills, hollows and fertile soil, and it is farmed with a care that shows. In May, vast fields of rapeseed turn the whole landscape a startling yellow under a pale northern sky, with the sea glinting on one side. In summer, wheat, barley and maize take over.

The ride across Schwansen is the kind that has no highlight and is all the better for it. Roads wander along field edges, through avenues of beech and oak, and past old manor houses, the estates that have dominated the region for centuries, many with long brick drives and white-painted farmhouses. Villages such as Damp and Waabs lie a few kilometres from the coast, with churches of brick and fieldstone, and small lanes lead to the beach. Surfaces are generally good, with low traffic and long, easy bends, and the wind off the Baltic is a constant companion, often fresh enough to make a jacket welcome.

The area has seen its share of history. This is border country, long contested between Denmark and the German states, and the war of 1864, in which Prussia and Austria took Schleswig and Holstein from Denmark, was fought nearby. Danish heritage is still visible in place names, dialect and a sizeable Danish minority, and the Schlei, a former Viking trade route, leads to the old town of Haithabu, a major trading centre of the Viking age.

For services, the villages are small, so plan your stops. Kappeln, about nine kilometres from here, on the Schlei, has fuel, shops, cafes and its famous herring fence, a traditional fish trap that is the last of its kind in Germany, and Eckernförde on the other side of the peninsula is bigger and busier. In the coastal villages, a fish roll with smoked herring or a slice of cake in a farm cafe is simple and satisfying. Come in May for yellow fields, or on a calm September evening, when the light is gold.
The road begins in a village that exists because of a railway. West Glacier and the neighbouring Apgar area sit at the southern foot of Lake McDonald, where the Great Northern Railway once dropped passengers to a string of park hotels, and the park's west entrance is still here. In the 1910s the railway company promoted the new national park as a kind of American Switzerland, building chalets across the mountains, and that image of alpine adventure still hangs over the place.

Before you ride, a few facts worth knowing. The Going-to-the-Sun Road is about fifty miles long, and it took more than a decade to build, opening in 1933. It crosses the Continental Divide at Logan Pass, but only for part of the year, because the snow on the top is deep enough that crews spend weeks each spring ploughing it. The full road typically opens around late June or early July and closes again in the autumn, depending on the weather, so check the park's current status. There is also a vehicle entry fee, and in recent years the park has experimented with timed reservations for the busiest months, so look at the current rules before you go.

Fuel is not available along the road. Fill up here or in Columbia Falls, about twenty kilometres to the west, which has several stations and supermarkets, and Whitefish is a short way beyond. The village has a handful of shops, a visitor centre and places to eat, so use it to pick up food and warm layers, because the temperature on the pass can be twenty degrees lower than down here.

The first miles are gentle. The road runs along the shore of Lake McDonald under tall cedars and hemlocks, with the water showing through the trunks, and the surface is smooth and fairly flat. It is a good place to settle into the ride before the serious climbing starts. The lake is the largest in the park, ten miles long, and its colours are remarkable on a calm day, with pebbles of red and green argillite glowing under the clear water.

Aim to start early, because the middle of the day brings heavy traffic and long lines of cars, and the pass itself fills up by mid-morning. Be patient with the speeds, keep an eye out for cyclists on the shoulder, and remember that the park's rules limit the size of vehicles on certain sections.
Lake McDonald Lodge is a big log building with a deep porch, and it looks as though it belongs in a Swiss mountain story that someone transplanted to Montana. It went up in 1913 and 1914 as a hotel built by a local entrepreneur, and the Great Northern Railway later took it over and promoted the area for tourists. The architecture is Swiss chalet in style, with massive timbers, stone fireplaces and animal heads on the walls, and the interior is lovely and a little smoky, with a comfortable, slightly faded feel.

The lake in front of it is the real star. Lake McDonald is about ten miles long and more than four hundred feet deep, carved by a glacier that once filled the whole valley, and the water is so clear that you can see the coloured stones on the bottom from the shore. The mountains rise steeply on the far side, still wearing snow in early summer, and in the morning, when the surface is flat, they are reflected perfectly. It is easily among the most photographed views in Montana.

For the rider, this is a mellow stretch of the road. The road runs close to the water through dense forest of cedar, hemlock and larch, with shafts of light coming through the trees and a damp, resinous smell in the air. The corners are easy, the surface generally good, and the speed limit low. Because the road here is relatively sheltered, it can be cool and shady even on a hot day, and a dry road in the morning can be damp from the spray of waterfalls in the afternoon.

The lodge has a restaurant and a gift shop in season, and it is a good place to stop for a coffee or a lunch. Boat tours leave from the dock, and some of the older wooden launches have been in service for decades.

Wildlife is plentiful. Bears, both black and grizzly, live in the park, and you should carry bear spray if you plan to walk on the trails. Elk and deer graze in the meadows near the lake, and bald eagles hunt over the water. If you stop for photographs, keep your distance and never feed the animals, and the park's rangers will thank you.
Here the road stops following the valley and starts climbing the wall of it. The Loop is a single tight hairpin, a looping bend where the highway turns back on itself to gain height on the west face of the Garden Wall. It is the first of the dramatic engineering features of the route, and after the gentle lake shore, it sets the tone for what follows: the road is cut into the cliff, with a stone wall on the outside and a deep drop beyond.

The engineers who designed it, working in the 1920s, faced an unusual constraint. The park service insisted that the road should fit into the landscape and not scar it, so the builders used local stone for the parapets and arranged the alignment to follow the contours of the mountain. Hand labour and dynamite carved the ledge, and the work was dangerous. The result is a road that looks as though it grew out of the rock, and it has become a National Historic Landmark.

For a motorcyclist, the Loop is a good test of your low-speed control. The hairpin is tight, the surface can be damp or gritty, and traffic from both directions may be slow and uncertain, with drivers looking up at the view and not at the road. Take it gently, stay well within your lane, and keep your eyes up through the turn. There is no guardrail to speak of, only the low stone wall, so a mistake would matter.

Beyond the Loop, the road climbs steadily along the face of the Garden Wall, a long, jagged ridge of the Continental Divide, with waterfalls dropping from the snowfields above. In early summer you can hear them over the engine, and in places the spray crosses the road. A few pullouts offer views back down the valley to Lake McDonald, a long ribbon of blue at the bottom of the trees.

Be prepared for the weather. The west side of the divide is wetter than the east, and clouds can come in quickly, dropping the temperature and the visibility. Wear a warm layer, even in July. There are no services here, so make sure you have fuel and water. And if the pullouts are full, as they often are by late morning, just keep going: the best views are the ones you catch in motion.
Logan Pass is the summit of the road, at 6,646 feet, and the only point where it crosses the Continental Divide. From here, water flows west toward the Pacific and east toward the Atlantic, and at Triple Divide Peak, a little to the south-east, a single raindrop can even end up in Hudson Bay. The pass sits in a high, rocky bowl under the sharp edge of the Garden Wall, and when you arrive, you feel as though you have reached the roof of the park.

The visitor centre here is the busiest spot in Glacier National Park, and its car park is usually full by mid-morning in summer, so arrive early or late if you can. Motorcycles can sometimes squeeze into small gaps, but the area is crowded and the surface can be slippery with gravel. Snow often lingers into July, and even in August the nights are cold and the wind can be fierce. A warm layer and gloves are essential, because the temperature at the top can be freezing even when it is warm in the valleys.

The high meadows around the pass are among the most beautiful in the park. In July and August they are carpeted with wildflowers, glacier lilies, beargrass and paintbrush, and mountain goats and bighorn sheep wander through them with remarkable calm. Hoary marmots whistle from the rocks. A boardwalk trail leads from the visitor centre up to Hidden Lake Overlook, a walk of about a mile and a half each way, with a view down to a blue lake cupped in the rock. Keep a safe distance from the animals, and check for bear warnings before you walk.

The road itself is a feat of engineering. When it opened in 1933, it was the first road to cross the park, and it required years of blasting and the building of tunnels, bridges and retaining walls. Each spring a crew of plough drivers works for weeks to clear drifts that can be eighty feet deep in places, and the work often runs into June. When you ride it, you are enjoying their labour.

There are no services on the road itself beyond the visitor centre's basic facilities, so carry fuel and water. Weather changes fast at this height, and snow or hail in summer is not unusual. If the sky turns dark, do not hang about: get over the pass and down the other side, where the wind and cloud are often less severe.
East of the divide, the whole landscape changes character. The road drops from the high pass and runs beside St. Mary Lake, a long, narrow expanse of deep blue water surrounded by steep peaks, and the air feels drier and windier. Forest is thinner and the mountains are more rugged. This is the rain shadow side of the park, where the clouds have dropped most of their moisture on the west, and the grasslands of the Great Plains lie just beyond.

The lake is among the park's best known and most photographed sights. It is about nine miles long, a deep trench scoured by a glacier, and its water is a vivid blue that changes with the light. A small, rocky island, Wild Goose Island, sits in the water and appears on countless postcards. Peaks rise steeply on both sides, and in early summer they are streaked with snow and waterfalls. The best views come from the road itself, where small pullouts give a view along the length of the lake.

This section is a joy to ride, but it demands attention. The road hugs the shore with a series of gentle curves, and the wind funnelling down the valley from the plains can be strong, pushing you sideways. Gusts are common in the afternoon. The surface is generally good, but expect patches of repair and the odd rock that has tumbled onto the pavement. Traffic is usually lighter than on the west side, though the pullouts and trailheads fill up in summer.

Wildlife is a regular presence. Black bears feed on berries in the slopes above the road, and bighorn sheep sometimes pick their way along the cliffs. Watch for animals crossing at dusk and dawn, and for drivers stopping suddenly to look.

The park has a few small stores and eating places on this side, but fuel is limited, so make sure the tank is full before you leave the east entrance area. The long evening light is a gift: in late June the sun does not set until nearly ten, and the peaks glow gold and pink above the water. If you can plan for an early start, you will have the lake almost to yourself.
St. Mary is where the mountains end and the prairies begin, and the change is dramatic. Behind you, the peaks of Glacier National Park rise in a wall of rock and snow, and in front, the land opens into rolling grassland that stretches east for hundreds of miles. The little settlement at the park's eastern entrance is a handful of motels, a store and a few places to eat, but it sits in one of the most spectacular positions in Montana.

The land to the east belongs to the Blackfeet Nation, whose reservation borders the park and whose people have lived in the shadow of these mountains for centuries. To them, the peaks are sacred, and the area is known in their language as the Backbone of the World. The town of Browning, about thirty-seven kilometres away, is the tribal headquarters, and has the Museum of the Plains Indian and a good selection of shops and services. The reservation is a place of vast skies and big-hearted hospitality, and the Blackfeet name appears on many places in the park.

For a rider, St. Mary is a crossroads. US Highway 89 runs north to the Canadian border and south toward Browning and the Rocky Mountain Front, a lovely open road with long views of the peaks, though strong winds are the rule. The wind here is famous, and it can blow steadily at forty or fifty miles an hour, so be ready for crosswinds, especially on the prairie sections. Another road leads to Many Glacier, a deep valley with lakes and a historic hotel, a worthwhile excursion for a long day.

Fuel is available in the St. Mary area, but supplies can be limited and prices are higher than in the towns, so top up when you can. Browning, Cut Bank and Babb are other places to refuel, and distances are long, so do not push your luck. Check opening times for restaurants and stores, which can be short outside summer.

The best time to ride is on a still morning in July or September. Summer afternoons bring thunderstorms and heavy winds, and a sudden drop in temperature, while the autumn light is crisp and golden. Prairie dogs and ground squirrels scatter ahead of you, and hawks wheel on the updrafts. Whichever way you head, the mountains look their best in the rear-view mirror at the end of the day.
